units.la: Non estis nescii, Amplissimi Viri, Domini sapientissimi, inde ab annis viginti septem de societate (vt vocant) Iesu celebrem exstitisse in Gymnasio Romano Robertum Bellarminum Politianum, qui grandeis controuersiarum tomos aduersus hęreticos, vt ait, huius temporis perscripserit. Quibus scriptis eo plus lucis, dignitatis, auctoritatisq; & celebritatis videtur accessisse, quòd iam de sententia Roman. Pōtificis in collegium Cardinalium Romæ adscitus est, & R. E. Cardinalis siue Presbyter, siue Diaconus, nihil nostra refert) titulo S. Mariæ in via inscriptus appellatusq;
units.tr: You are not unaware, most distinguished sirs, most wise gentlemen, that for twenty-seven years Robert Bellarmine of Montepulciano, a famous figure in the Roman college of the so-called Society of Jesus, has been writing, as he puts it, large volumes of controversies against the heretics of this age. These writings seem to have gained all the more light, dignity, authority and renown because, by decision of the Roman Pontiff, he has been admitted into the college of Cardinals at Rome and named and styled Cardinal of the title of St Mary in Via (whether he is a priest or a deacon makes no difference to us).

units.la: Etsi autem scripti ab illo controuersiarum tomi, tres principio dati, ex scriptorum fere omnium, quos gens Pontificia nouit, symbola consarcinati atque compacti sunt; tum ipsius qui auctor dicitur, tum aliorum συνεπιζόντων opera, studio atque industria; tamen non destitit ille ex eo tempore idem opus novare alternis ferme biennijs, aut ad summum triennijs; & locupletare suis accessionib. Harum duo fuerunt genera: nam aliæ accessiones factæ sunt interpolatis locis hic illic quâ-plurimis, aliæ adiectis atque impactis[?] in corpus illud controuersiarum opusculis varijs, quæ ab illo per occasionem temporibus diuersis perscripta sunt: prout huius libri exemplo singuli videre possunt.
units.tr: Although the volumes of controversies written by him, three of which were first issued, were patched together and compiled from the materials of nearly all the writers the Papist people know, both by his own work and by the labours and zeal of others working alongside him [συνεπιζόντων], nevertheless from that time on he has not ceased to renew this same work, roughly every two years, or at most every three, and to enlarge it with additions. These were of two kinds: some additions consisted of passages interpolated here and there in very many places, while others consisted of various short treatises, written at different times on particular occasions, which were inserted into that body of controversies, as each reader can see from the example of this book.

units.la: Atque hoc quidem consilio nec vsq; adeò visus est existimationi suç[?] consulere, nec commoditati legentium, quos multiplex eiusdem rei editio sumptibus grauioribus & frequentioribus onerauit: sed duo tamen apud multos & ad miraculum vsque (vt ita dicamus) est assequutus vnum, quòd diligentia istius collectæ & cinni laboriosissimi ex Pontificiorum omnium sententijs comportati pellexit multos, vt libros ipsius de doctrina Christiana & controuersis locis eius consulerent: Alterum, qp nouatio eiusdem operis multorum animos inflammauit, vt idem scriptum legerent relegerentque sæpius, & ipsum noui alicuius fructus noua accessione ingenuit, prout res nouæ, aut etiam nouatæ sitientibus ingerij calcaria solent addere, vt idem argumenta[?] & [illegible, ~1 letter] editentur sæpius & recolat diligentius.
units.tr: With this plan he seems not to have consulted his own reputation so very much, nor the convenience of his readers, whom so many editions of the same work have burdened with heavier and more frequent expense. Yet among many he has achieved two things, almost to a marvel, if we may put it so. The first is that the diligence of that collection, and the most laborious assembling of the opinions of all the Papists, has drawn many to consult his books on Christian doctrine and on the disputed topics. The second is that the renewal of the same work has inflamed the minds of many, so that they read and re-read the same writing more often, and are kept at it by the new fruit of each new addition. Just as novelties, or things renewed, are wont to spur thirsty minds, so these same arguments are published more often and studied more diligently.

units.la: Quapropter etiam editione vltima, quæ In Golstadio prodijt superiore anno, pro eo quod tres solum ante hac fuerunt tomi, quatuor dati sunt ab eodem auctore, & primus, quem propter accessiones varias oportuit spissescere[?] in duos tomos differtus est: adeo materia in manibus illius fermentata est, forte etiam in posterum fermetaretur grauius, nisi onus galeri illius Cardinalitij hominem aliis distractu oppresserit. Legitur itaq; Bellarminus à multis studiose, & opus ipsius semel, iterum, tertio, quarto, quinto manibus auctoris subactum interpolatum q; teritur à plurimis, qui aliquid remaius, vt maius mole, præstitum ab ipso arbitrantur: & ita legitur vt his persuadeat, illos ad quærendum & cognoscendum amplius excitet, non paucis vero sit desidiæ suæ & ψυχῆς θανατισμοῦ[?] in causa religionis nostræ velamentum. Quàm multos enim Deus bone, in Germania audiui, & in hoc Belgio, quàm multos in Gallia, qui hos puluillos suis cubitis miseri confutos putant, vt à veritate scripturæ, à religione, à pietate aberrent speciosi-us! Ignoscat illis pius miserationum pater, eosque afficiat vera pietatis atque fidei conscientia, vt eiurato studio falsi, quo ardent voluntarie, immigrent in castra Domini, & Spiritu eius duce, Scriptuaque indice, ad veram abnegationem fui & fidem in Deum adducantur. Sunt tamen profecto, sunt multi qui Bellarmino dicenti & scribenti credunt, qui folia Sibyllæ altera esse putant, qui testimonia & rationes inuictas ab ipso produci existimat; qui denique de scriptis eius haud secus gloriantur quàm si veritas esset divina ipsa, & hic murus aheneus pro veritate staret in oculis omnium.
units.tr: For this reason, too, in the latest edition, which came out at Ingolstadt last year, where there had previously been only three volumes, the same author has given four, and the first, which had to be thickened by various additions, has been spread over two volumes. So much has the matter fermented in his hands, and perhaps it would have fermented more vigorously in future, had not the burden of that Cardinal's hat weighed the man down and distracted him with other concerns. Bellarmine is therefore read eagerly by many, and his work, handled by the author once, twice, a third, fourth and fifth time, interpolated, is worn thin by very many who think something greater has been achieved by him, as if by sheer bulk. It is read in such a way that it persuades these readers and stirs them to seek and learn more; but for not a few it is a veil for their own sloth and for the killing of the soul [ψυχῆς θανατισμοῦ] in the cause of our religion. For how many, good God, have I heard of in Germany and in this Belgium, how many in France, who think these pillows, propped up miserably on their elbows, a more specious way of straying from the truth of Scripture, from religion and from piety! May the merciful Father of all compassion pardon them, and may the awareness of true piety and faith move them, so that, renouncing the study of falsehood with which they burn of their own will, they may pass over into the camp of the Lord and, led by his Spirit and guided by Scripture, be brought to true self-denial and to faith in God. Yet there truly are many who believe Bellarmine when he speaks and writes, who think his pages are the leaves of the Sibyl, who suppose that unanswerable testimonies and arguments are produced by him, and who boast of his writings no less than if they were divine truth itself, as if this brazen wall stood for the truth in the sight of all.

units.la: Mihi verò, cui & divina veritas & salus communis cordi est, prout ad hoc studium Deo opt. max. auctore in Christo sum excitatus iam diu, multiplicia hæc mala, quæ hoc argumento orbem Christianum tenet diu multumque cogitanti, nulla commodior ad obsi-stendum via hactenus fuit oblata, quàm si eadem illa scripta, quæ tanti animadverto fieri atque prædicari ordine eodem quem præformauit ipse in scriptis suis perseques examinarem [illegible, ~4 letters] (vt loquuntur) singula, & subnotarem paucis quæ à veritate divina, à rebus ipsis, à salute videtur abludere. Nam etsi viris doctis quàplurimis hac memoria nostra autvisum est certo consilio partes solū aliquas destringere, aut datū est per voluntatem Dei disceptare de una, altera, aut tertia, si forte, controuersia; id tamen diuturna experientia cùm à me ipso, tū à bonis consimiliter fuit obseruarum, istam operam partiaciam [?] ab aduersariis, licet iniuria, dedespici,& viros illos quamuis magnos tradu-ci temere,tanquam si aut in ea solum re versa-ti essent aut ad alias ineptiores essent, & se im-pares oneri huic esse facto suo plane fateretur. Quod genus criminationis re & veritate sal-sum opiniones tamen imperiti vulgi & eorum qui dissentiunt occupat incessitq; facilime. Hæc cogitatio, ut alias taceam, multis iamdiu instantibus eo me adduxit, ut ad disputationes Bellarmini examinandas & pro veritate Dei in Scripturis comprehensa confutandas ve-niens,ijsdem cancellis quos manus ipsius po-suit labyrinthum errorum, quos conscuit co-pia maxima, Ariadneo, et potius diuino sacræ Scripturæ filo ductus percurrerem, facerem-que testatum bonis, quæ ab ipso dicuntur be-ne,nos religione maxima & Christiana sim-plicitate optime acquiescere; quæ secus ea nos sine iracundia, peruicacia, aut contumelia (q[?] Christianis pectoribus indignum) refellere. Atq; huius studij & laboris mei partes aliquot in lucem publicam his paucis annis prodierunt, ut ædificationi publicæ pro modulo meo, quæ[?] Christus mihi admetitur, Christiana veritate & simplicitate consulerem, sperans & confi-dens in Domino, ut tum hoc facto meo mul-tæ Christianæ animæ falso dispungedo, & ve-se[?] agnoscendo amplectendoq;[?] reddantur ap-tio tiores; tum ij qui dissentiunt, fi veritati non possunt adh c assentiri, saltem lenitatem & æquitatem animi adhibere erga eos discant hoc exemplo meo, qui in causa fidei veritatisq; diuinæ non possunt adeo sermonibus ipsorum subscribere, nisi contra fidem suam & scripturis haustàm & contra conscientiam, quod impium, venire velint. Hoc enim sanctè dico, testis Dominus, & religiosè profiteor, neq; me, neq; bonos quà plurimos in eadem naui versantes, capere ex contentionibus voluptatem, in hac arena causa gloriæ vllius dimicare, aut laureolam ex hoc miftaceo (quod aiunt) quærere: profanum, inhumanum, impium ausum futurũ effet, nos autem iustitiæ, sanctimoniæ, humanitati, pietati inseruimus, fecundum Deum ad ædificationem vtilem: sed necessitatem nobis diuinitus esse impositam, vt proveritate ipsius iustè & religiosè stantes, calcatis ordij & furoribus mundi, seruiamus fratribus nostris coram hoc Sole in charitate ad ædificationem vtilem & salutarem omnium. Hoc officium vtut vetat mundus, tamen quia Deus iubet præftanius vltro, & dum spiritum hunc ducimus, præstituri fumus in Domino quam maxima fide diligentiaq; possumus. Ille, ille doctor mentis, dutor animi, auctor operis certò benedicturus est. Hoc itaq; animo atq; in hunc modum de controuersijs quinque antehac diximus, quas Bellarminus tomo suo 1. & parte secundi contexuit. De Scriptura sacra & traditionibus prima controuersia diximus; secunda de Deo & persona beneficioq; Christi: tertia, de capite Ecclesiæ quod aspectabile volunt esse, id est, Rom. Pontifice: quarta de ecclesia atq; Concilijs: quinta denique de membris Ecclesiæ militantis, & in hac peregrinatione agentis [?]ἐνδημοῦντες[?] à Domino, vt Paulus 2. Cor. 5. loquitur. Restabat vt Bellarminus de statu Ecclesiæ membrorumq; ipsius diceret, quę ex hac vita in alteram immigrarunt. Nam etsi ex hac vita migrantij quoq; homines qui in tartara iusto Dei iudicio detrudütur (sic enim malos ταρταρῶσαι [?] dicitur Deus 2 Pet. 2.) tamen recte Bellarminus abstinuit ab ea quæstione de impiorum statu quos morti æternæ addixit Deus; quia instituit de controuersijs fidei disputationes suas. Non poterat aut ratio mortis æternæ & tormentorum infernalium proprie & per se ad rationem fidei pertinere hanc si quis minutatim volet excutere (vt olim fecerunt fanatici medacib. suis reuelationib. visionibusq;) non veritati seruit, sed vanitati & curiositati damnosæ, quâ vera pietas refugit di-ligentissime- Recte itaque Bellarminus de iis tantum mouit controuersiam qui ex hac vita in alteram immigrarunt. Sed illud non omnino recte quòd classes illorum facit duas si. nec vllo Dei aut scripturæ sacræ testimonio : vnam eorum, qui adhuc hærent in itinere ad vitam: alteram eorum qui vita illa beata in cœlis perfruuntur. Nâ iter esse defunctis advita putât q̃ Purgatorium dicitur : hoc cũ emesi sunt, tũ demũ vitam illa censentur viuere. De priore illa classe agitur in sexta hac controuersia, ad posteriorem septima pertinet. Ac de statu quidem animarum quę solutę a suo corpore in locum alterum migrauerũt, nõ fuit tempore Apostolorum aut seculo proximo controuersia. Nam duo tantum status fuerunt habiti, ac pro inde loca duo sui statui attributa ; beatorum statui, beatorum locus; & damnatorum statui locus damnatorũ, qui vulgo inferorũ nomine designatur. Etsi hoc inferorum nomen longè est angustius quam proprie sit vox Græcorum ᾅδης, vt recte Græci auctores obseruarūt. Est enim ᾅδης communiter omnis animarum locus invisibilis ex quo ab hoc corpore abscesserunt, siue gloriæ in cœlis, siue in diuerso statu quilibet alius. In eo verò discrepauerunt iam olim sententiæ, quod alij duob. solum locis animas post hanc vitam capi statuerunt, quorum alterum Christus vocauit παράδεισον, paradisum, alterum ᾅδης inferum oppositè; alij Trib. alij plurib. put error semper novus ex ore[?] gignitur, & multiplicatur maximé. Nam vno absurdo posito sequuntur multa, quod vulgo dici solet. Duo loca veritas ipsa defun-ctis tribuit, prout homines sese bene aut malé in vita gesserunt: locum vitæ bonis & benedi-ctis Dei, malis locum mortis. Atq; hic quidem locus quem mortis dicimus, non fuit vulgo propter varios pœnarum gradus in locadiver-sa distributus, quia communis est omni-um carcer, quamuis tormentis differen-tibus. Quapropter nec locum vitæ propter varios gradus gloriæ illius aut illius status animarum dividi in diversa quasi cochlea oportebat. Nam status communis vitæ stationē communem habet, quamuis gradib. inter se differentib. Aliud est domus sive statio, aliud status, aliud deniq; gradus in statu differēs. Abutuntur quidē multi verbis Christi dicētis Ioan. 14.2. in domo Patris mei mansiones multæ sunt: sed nihil aliud sibi Christus his verbis voluit, quam domū Patris multorum capacem esse. Alioquin si variæ mansiones intelligerentur à Christo ut gens Pontificia tradit de variis locis, pugnaret illud cum celeberrima illa & decantatissima veterum, & Pōtificiorum doctrina, qui Apostolis & martyrib. affirmant beatorum sedem esse statim à morte attributam, nec Purgatorium illos transuenisse: nam Chri-stus eo loco diserte Apostolos ipsos, si quem[?] quam alloquitur. His autem duob.locis postea per errorem veterum suae quaedam appendices accreuerunt. Nam primum hominib.pijs qui ad beatam quidem vitam sunt designati, sed nondum(vt putabatur)perdu&ti,sinus Abrahae attributus est, decuius interpretatione inter veteres aliqua semper fuit controuersia, tam-quam vestibulum & procoction exspectatium consummationem beatae vitae: deinde veroa-lius praeterea locus excogitatus est pro iis pur-gandis,qui hic nondum fuerant purgati a pec-catis suis ,quem locum dixerunt Purgatorium.
units.tr: For my part, to whom both divine truth and the common salvation are dear, and who have long been roused to this work by Christ, under God the best and greatest, while I have long and often considered the many evils that this subject has brought upon the Christian world, I have found no more convenient way to resist them than to examine, one by one and in the same order that he himself laid out in his writings, those works which I see being so greatly admired and proclaimed, and to note briefly what seems to depart from divine truth, from the facts themselves, and from salvation. For although many learned men in our time have thought it best, by deliberate plan, to attack only some parts, or, as God has allowed, to dispute about one, another, or perhaps a third controversy, long experience has shown me, and others like me, that this partial work is despised by our adversaries, though unjustly, and that those men, however great, are rashly accused as if they had dealt with only that one matter, or were less capable in other matters, and as if they confessed by their own action that they were unequal to this burden. This kind of charge is false in fact, yet it very easily takes hold of the opinions of the unlearned crowd and of those who dissent. This thought, to pass over others, has for a long time pressed upon me and led me, coming to examine the disputations of Bellarmine and to refute them by the truth of God contained in the Scriptures, to run through the labyrinth of errors, which he has set up within the very barriers of his own hand and which a very great multitude has followed, guided not by an Ariadne's thread but rather by the divine thread of Holy Scripture. I have also made it clear to good men that whatever is rightly said by him, we rest in very great reverence and Christian simplicity; and that whatever is otherwise, we refute without anger, obstinacy, or insult, which is unworthy of Christian hearts. And some parts of this study and labour of mine have come out into the public light in these few years, so that, as far as my small ability allows, which Christ has measured out to me, I might serve public edification with Christian truth and simplicity, hoping and trusting in the Lord that by this work of mine many Christian souls may be made more ready both to reject what is false and to recognise and embrace what is true; and that those who dissent, if they cannot yet assent to the truth, may at least learn from my example to show gentleness and fairness of mind toward those who, in the cause of faith and of divine truth, cannot so subscribe to their statements, unless they wish to act impiously, against their faith drawn from the Scriptures and against their conscience. For I say this solemnly, the Lord is my witness, and I declare in the fear of God that neither I nor the many good men who are in the same ship take pleasure in contention, nor do we fight in this arena for the glory of any man, nor seek a little laurel from this muddy (as they say) mess; that would be a profane, inhuman, and impious undertaking. Rather, we have devoted ourselves to justice, holiness, humanity, and piety, and, according to God, to useful edification; but we are bound by a necessity laid upon us by God, that standing rightly and reverently in his truth, and trampling underfoot the tumults and rages of the world, we should serve our brothers, before this sun, in charity, for the useful and saving edification of all. Though the world forbids this duty, yet because God commands it of his own accord, and while we are led by this spirit, we shall in the Lord perform it with the greatest faith and diligence we can. He, that Teacher of the mind, Guide of the soul, Author of the work, will surely bless it. With this purpose, then, and in this manner, we have already spoken of the five controversies, which Bellarmine has woven together in his first volume and in the second part. In the first controversy we spoke of Holy Scripture and the traditions; in the second, of God and of the person and benefits of Christ; in the third, of the head of the Church, which they wish to be visible, that is, the Roman Pontiff; in the fourth, of the Church and of the Councils; and finally, in the fifth, of the members of the militant Church, who while living in this pilgrimage are "absent from the Lord" [ἐνδημοῦντες], as Paul speaks in 2 Cor. 5. It remained for Bellarmine to speak of the state of the Church and of its members who have passed from this life into the other. For although men who depart from this life are also cast down into the underworld by the just judgment of God (for thus God is said to "cast down to Tartarus" [ταρταρῶσαι] the wicked, 2 Pet. 2.), Bellarmine rightly abstained from that question concerning the state of the ungodly, whom God has doomed to eternal death, because he had undertaken disputations about the controversies of faith. The account of eternal death and of infernal torments, if one wishes to examine it in minute detail (as the fanatics once did with their lying revelations and visions), belongs properly and in itself not to the account of faith; it serves not truth but vanity and harmful curiosity, from which true piety most diligently shrinks. Therefore Bellarmine rightly raised controversy only about those who have passed from this life into the other. But it is not altogether right that he makes two classes of them, one of those who still linger on the way to life, the other of those who enjoy that blessed life in heaven, and this without any testimony of God or of Holy Scripture. For he thinks that the dead are on a journey to life, which is called Purgatory; only when they have completed this do they then count as living that life. The former class is the subject of this sixth controversy; the latter belongs to the seventh. Now concerning the state of souls which, released from their bodies, have migrated to another place, there was no controversy in the time of the Apostles or in the next age. For only two states were recognised, and accordingly two places were assigned to those two states: to the state of the blessed, the place of the blessed; and to the state of the damned, the place of the damned, which is commonly designated by the name of the underworld. Yet this name of the underworld is far narrower than the proper meaning of the Greek word ᾅδης [hades], as the Greek authors rightly observed. For ᾅδης is commonly every invisible place of souls from which they have departed from this body, whether of glory in heaven or of some other different state. But the opinions have long differed on this point: some have held that souls after this life are received in only two places, one of which Christ called παράδεισος [paradise], Paradise, and the other, in contrast, ᾅδης, the underworld; others have held three, others more. Error always breeds anew from the mouth, and multiplies most of all. For once one absurdity is granted, many follow, as is commonly said. Truth itself assigns two places to the dead, according as men have behaved well or ill in life: to the good and blessed of God, the place of life; to the wicked, the place of death. Now this place which we call the place of death was not divided into different places according to the various degrees of punishment, since it is a common prison for all, though with differing torments. Likewise, the place of life ought not to be divided into diverse parts, as if it were a snail's shell, according to the various degrees of that glory or of that state of souls. For a common state has a common dwelling, though its degrees differ among themselves. A house or station is one thing, a state another, and finally a degree differing within a state is another. Many indeed abuse the words of Christ, who says in John 14.2: "In my Father's house there are many mansions"; but Christ meant by these words nothing else than that the house of the Father is capacious for many. Otherwise, if many mansions were understood by Christ as the Papists teach, as various places, that would conflict with that most famous and most celebrated doctrine of the ancients and of the Papists, who affirm that the seat of the blessed was assigned immediately after death to the Apostles and martyrs, and that they did not pass through Purgatory; for in that passage Christ explicitly addresses the Apostles themselves. But afterwards, through the error of the ancients, certain additions grew onto these two places. For first, to pious men who were indeed destined for the blessed life, but not yet (as was supposed) brought to it, the bosom of Abraham was assigned; concerning its interpretation there has always been some controversy among the ancients, as an antechamber and a waiting place for the completion of the blessed life. Then, next, another place was devised for the purging of those who had not yet been purged of their sins in this life, which place they called Purgatory.

units.la: Rursum vero quia videbant purgari in mun-do reos duobus modis, priuatione boni, & sensu mali inuadentis prementisque, Purga-torium illud duobus item distinxerunt mo-dis. Nam alij poenam damni in priuatione & mora boni positam statuerunt solum, qua solam proprie agnouerunt olim Graeci: alii poenam sensus quasi expurgantibus tormen-tis temporalibus addiderunt, quam Latini iamdiu profesi sunt,&contentiosissime pro-pugnarunt. Deniq; somnia somnijs, & com-menta commetis accesserunt, animos super-stitione implentia, & exhaurientia domos.
units.tr: Again, since they saw that the guilty were purged in this world in two ways, by the privation of good and by the sense of evil attacking and pressing upon them, they likewise divided that Purgatory in two. Some held that the punishment consists only of the loss and delay of good, the only punishment the Greeks formerly acknowledged as proper. Others added a punishment of sense, as if temporal torments were cleansing them, and the Latins long ago professed this and defended it most contentiously. Finally, dreams were added to dreams and fictions to fictions, filling minds with superstition and draining households.

units.la: Hunc vero locum Purgatorij non Scri-ptura ptura statuit,sed pepcrit coiectura hominum. quorum mentes superstitio credula occupa-verat, post animis superstitio audaciam indi-dit,ut de rebus ignotis pronunciarent,pedem inferentes in ea quæ non viderant, ut ait Pau-lus Col.2 18.temereq inflati carnis suæ intel-ligentia. De aliis locis insuper nihil dicam, quia hoc rei caput est, quod Bellarmino vsum est propugnare: nos vero non juvat litem ex lite nectere, qui veritatem in pace & sanctimonia colimus, vestigia Domini nostri persequetes. Quid enim nobis profuerit unguis, quod ai-unt, in ulcere? Cū itaq; hic de Purgatorio locus tanti apud illos videatur esse, ut multi non du-bitaverint immaneis quosdam centones ad probationem argumenti huius perscribere, & quiduis ad firmamentum causæ(si ullum esse potest) advocare; quorum exemplo & ductu Bel-larminus in idem scamma descedere coactus est, ut Rom. Ecclesiæ in hoc quoq; argumento subsidia sua contribuat: non potui quin ordi-ne illius servato sextam hanc controversi-am saltem aliquo modo destrigerem, & pau-cis quam modestissime per nos fieri potuit dogma istud lucrosum docentib. sed revera omnibus damnosum confutare. Cū autem duas huius tractationis partes Bellarminus nobis præformauerit: unam,ꝗ fit Purgatorii. priore libro; alteram, quæ circumstantiæ Pur-gatorij, secundo: ad utrumque ordine respon-dimus: sed ad posteriorem breuissimè, quia priore confutata inanis posterior quæstio esse-&ta est. Non enim placuit in reb. nugacib. ope-rosos esse. Huic vero labori sexto adtexuimus alterum argumetum, quod disputator adiecit in postrema editione suæ controuersiæ; de Pō-tifice. Nam cum ante annos aliquot homo quidam Gallus arrepta occasione ex eo quod Sixtus V. Regem Nauarrenum & Principem Condensem excommunicare fuerat ausus, quem illi publicè mendacij nomine reprehē-derunt, scriptum Italico sermone edidisset cuius inscriptio fuit Auiso Piacenole, &c. in quo Pontificem vehementer confodit prolatis etiam ex auctorib. Italis Dante, Petrarcha, & Bocatio testimonijs, visum est disputatori nostro scriptum illud confutare publicè, & in postrema editione suis illis controuersijs fidei interiungere. Ac mihi quidem videtur consilium illud Bellarmini à pietate, charitate & prudentia politica abesse plurimùm. Nō enim pietatis est priuatas causas huius temporis & iam intermortuas controuersijs de fide publica nostra coniungere: non est officium charitatis, neq; politicum cineres illos incendij publici commouere. Nisi quis forte hac Iesuitarum conditionem esse putauerit, vt malo fato bo-norū nati, inprimis autem Galliæ, curent ex-stincta incendia, & tyrannidi Hispanę ministrent studiosissime. Sic ad piscatione turban-tur aquę sic ad commoditatem populationū miscentur incendia: quas artes ab Hispano regio hæc vestra vidit exercitas, & vestra ciuitas ingemuit συμπάθως[?]. Sed quia factū(quod aiunt) infectum esse non potest & alea à Bellarmino iacta est, quam suis illis tomis causam hac particularem indidit, quauis emortuam, ne in posteritatem moreretur (nempe interest Iesuiticę pietatis, vt semper in Christiano orbe exstent carbones & malleoli ad incendia publica paratissimi) hic mihi sextus labor ex confutatione appendicis illius adductus est; quā magnus ille disputator suis controversiarum tomis inferciuit: ex utroq; argumento pios lectores sperutilitatem[?], ex posteriore etiam voluptatem aliquam percepturos. Hunc vero sextum laborem meum V. A. nomini visum est inscribere, quia ita iubet ordo publicus florentissimæ regionis vestræ, postulant vestra in causam publicam merita, & me hoc decet facere, quia iam amplius decennium colonus sum patriæ huius vestrę; cui dum superest vita per Dei gratiam depędere statui hoc colonarium pro iure vestro & officio meo: prout jāaliis
units.tr: But Scripture did not establish this place of Purgatory; the conjecture of men did. Credulous superstition had first occupied their minds, and afterwards superstition gave them the audacity to pronounce on unknown things, "entering into those things which they have not seen," as Paul says (Col. 2:18), "vainly puffed up by the understanding of their flesh." I will say nothing further about other passages, because this is the main point which Bellarmine has undertaken to defend. But we do not find it helpful to tie lawsuit to lawsuit, we who cultivate the truth in peace and holiness, following the footsteps of our Lord. For what would it profit us, as they say, to have a nail in an ulcer? Since this place about Purgatory seems to be of such importance to them that many have not hesitated to write out huge patchworks to prove this point, and to summon whatever they could to the support of their cause (if any support can be had), and since, following their example and lead, Bellarmine has been forced to come down to the same bench, so as to contribute the supports of the Roman Church in this argument too, I could not but, keeping his order, at least in some measure dispose of this sixth controversy, and refute, as briefly and as modestly as we could, that doctrine which is profitable to its teachers but in truth harmful to everyone. Since Bellarmine has laid out for us two parts of this treatment, one on what Purgatory is, in the first book, and the other on the circumstances of Purgatory, in the second, I have replied to both in order; but to the latter very briefly, since once the former was refuted the latter question was shown to be empty. For it did not please me to be laborious over trifling matters. To this sixth labour I have added another argument, which the disputant added in the latest edition of his controversy, concerning the Pope. For some years ago a certain Frenchman, seizing the occasion that Sixtus V had dared to excommunicate the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé, whom they publicly rebuked as liars, published a writing in Italian entitled Avviso Piacevole, etc., in which he savagely stabbed the Pope, bringing forward also testimonies from the Italian authors Dante, Petrarch and Boccaccio. It seemed good to our disputant to refute that writing publicly and to join it, in the latest edition, to his controversies on the faith. And to me indeed that plan of Bellarmine seems far removed from piety, charity and political prudence. For it is not a matter of piety to join the private quarrels of an earlier age, now long dead, to our public controversies about the faith; it is not a duty of charity, nor good policy, to stir up the ashes of a public conflagration. Unless perhaps someone thinks this is the character of the Jesuits, that by an evil fate for good men, especially in France, they take care to rekindle fires that have been put out, and most zealously serve the tyranny of Spain. Thus waters are troubled for fishing, and fires are kindled for the convenience of plunder. Your city has seen these arts practised by the Spanish king, and your city has groaned with sympathy [συμπάθως]. But since what is done (as they say) cannot be undone, and the die has been cast by Bellarmine, who in those volumes added this particular cause, though it was already dead, so that it might not die out for posterity (for it is in the interest of Jesuit piety that there always be embers and firebrands in the Christian world, ready for public fires), this sixth labour of mine has been prompted by the refutation of that appendix which that great disputant stuffed into his volumes of controversies. From each argument I hope the pious readers will gain some usefulness, and from the latter also some pleasure. I have judged it fitting to inscribe this sixth labour to your name, V.A., because the public order of your most flourishing region so requires, your merits towards the public cause demand it, and I ought to do so, because I have now been a colonist of this your fatherland for more than ten years. While life remains to me, by the grace of God, I have resolved to pay this tribute of a colonist as a due to you and a duty to myself, just as I have already done for other

units.la: aliis civitatibus communi ordine laudatissimo, qui inter ipsas observatur, hic honos est à me habitus. V A itaque submisse rogo, hunc qualemcunq; factum laboris mei à me accipiatis æquo & fauente animo, ut pensum officii mei testimonium publicum honoris vestri & symbolum animi mei erga V.A. pro-pensissimi, si quid ego causa publica aut pri-vata vestra præstare potero, quod V.A. reipu. & Ecclesiæ bono, honori, existimationi, orna-mento commodaturum esse unquam videbitur.
units.tr: cities, in the common and most praiseworthy order which is observed among them. So I humbly ask V.A. to accept this product of my labour, however small, with a fair and favourable mind, as a public testimony that I have discharged my duty, and as a token of my very devoted feeling towards V.A. If I can do anything for you in public or private affairs which will be seen to be of benefit, honour, esteem or ornament to the commonwealth and the Church, I will be glad to do it.

units.la: Amplissimi viri, Domini prudentissimi, Deum oro & patrem Domini nostri Iesu Christi gratiosè V.A. protegat ab omni malo, confirmet in omni bono, consiliaq; conatus & actiones vestras dirigat ad gloriam suam & communem patriæ, Ecclesiæ reliquæ publ. vestræ utilitatem salutemq; vestram. Lugduni Batavorum Kal. Septembr. MDCXI[?].
units.tr: Most distinguished men, prudent lords, I pray that God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ will graciously protect V.A. from every evil, confirm you in every good, and direct your counsels and actions to his glory, to the common good of the fatherland and the Church, to the benefit of your public affairs, and to your own salvation. Leiden, 1 September 1611.

units.la: FRANCISCI IUNII ANIMADUERSIONES AD ROBERTI BELLARMINI POLITIANI LI-bellum recens controversiæ 3.appo-situm, qui inscribitur Appendix ad libros de summo Pontifice, &c.
units.tr: FRANCIS JUNIUS'S REMARKS ON THE RECENT LIBEL OF ROBERT BELLARMINE OF POLITIANO, PLACED AFTER THE THIRD CONTROVERSY, WHICH IS ENTITLED AN APPENDIX TO THE BOOKS ON THE SUPREME PONTIFF, ETC.

units.la: IN CAP. I. ART. I.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER I, ARTICLE I.

units.la: ID TEMPVS aduenisse nunc cernimus:] non tamen nunc primum: nam quàm multas, obsecro, fabulas scriptores multi è gurgustiis Pontificum excitati prodiderunt! quàm ineptas, insulsas, improbas, indecentes, impias? Certè ut myriadas taceam, Jacobus de Voragine, Lipomannus, Surius, alij id tempus facto suo jamdiu testatur esse, quum fabulis offerciuerunt[?] mundum, & earum obiectu dolosè pias mentes auocant à lectione Scripturæ sacræ: pro thesauro carbones, quod aiunt.
units.tr: That time has now come, as we see: but it is not the first time. For how many fables, I beg you, have many writers, raised up from the Pontiffs' hovels, put forth! How silly, insipid, wicked, indecent and impious they are! Certainly, to pass over myriads, Jacobus de Voragine, Lipomannus, Surius and others long ago bore witness to that time by their own work, when they stuffed the world with fables and by putting them before pious minds, craftily draw them away from reading holy Scripture: carbon for treasure, as they say.

units.la: 2 Ibid. nunc tandem (Caluiniani, verbi Dei & sap.] si unus fecit, ut ais, Bellarmine, cur plureis nominas? si ignotus & incertus auctor, cur Caluinianos obruis coniectura tua? Christiani sumus per Dei gratiam, neque de Caluini aut alterius cuiusquam nomine, nisi aduersario impetu & sycophantico[?] notati sumus. Quoties hæc falsa conuicia legimus. toties insusurrantem audimus Christum, beati eritis, quum vos conuiciis affecerint. &c. Matth.5.11. quid tum, si fabulosae? nam & fabulis sua sunt {ἐπιμυθία[?]}, & fabulae multae non sunt perpetuae fabulae, sed interspersam veritatem habent. Quod si impurae sunt quaedam, quam purum se ostendit Pontificum natio! qui fabulis impuris operam dari malunt quam purae Scripturae Dei (nam hanc seuerissime vetant in vulgo, illas circumferri & volitare in vulgo sinunt) & qui eas solum expungi & tolli curant quibus se perstringi sentiunt, neglecta Dei, & naturae ratione, & honestatis publicae. Omne ius & fas ludificari licet, modo ne stringatur [illegible, ~8 letters] pater, aut aliqua radatur ipsius squamula. Quod Caluinianis tribuit, vt vocat, fabulae.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. now at last (Calvinists, of the Word of God and wisdom) If, as you say, Bellarmine, one man wrote it, why do you name several? If the author is unknown and uncertain, why do you batter the Calvinists with your conjecture? We are Christians by the grace of God, and we have been marked not by the name of Calvin or of anyone else, except by hostile attack and sycophantic slander. As often as we read these false insults, we hear Christ murmuring to us: blessed are you when they shall revile you, etc. Matthew 5.11. What then, if the fables are shameful? For fables also have their own morals, and many fables are not entirely fables, but have truth scattered through them. But if some are impure, how pure the Papist nation shows itself to be! They prefer that impure fables be put to work rather than the pure Scripture of God (for they most strictly forbid this among the common people, while they allow those fables to be passed around and flutter among the common people), and they take care that only those things be cut out and removed by which they feel themselves touched, neglecting the reason of God and of nature and of public decency. All law and right may be mocked, provided that the Father is not struck, or any little scale of his shaved off. This is what they attribute to the Calvinists, as they call it, fable.

units.la: non ergo cautere, gladio, reste, incendio: quod hactenus factitatum. Maiores vestri, Bellarmine, morbum animi esse putauerunt, tu cerebri: bene est, quod nouus Hippocrates mitiorem medicinam adhibendam putat, pronunciatque. Certe mali sunt medici, quos nondum violentae istius taedet chirurgiae, quam Papatus occupauit tamdiu.
units.tr: Therefore not cautery, sword, halter, or fire: which has been practised until now. Your ancestors, Bellarmine, thought the disease was of the spirit; you think it is of the brain. It is good that the new Hippocrates thinks and pronounces that a milder medicine should be applied. Surely they are bad physicians who are not yet weary of that violent surgery which Papacy has held for so long.

units.la: 5 canes latrant, & mordent, non loquuntur: vtri illud faciant mundus videt, iudicabit Deus. de Romano Pontifice & Antichristo diximus controuersia 3. Eiusdem generis sunt sequentia: quae non sufficit dici, non possunt probari.
units.tr: 5 dogs bark and bite, they do not speak: which of the two they do, the world sees; God will judge. We have spoken of the Roman Pontiff and Antichrist in controversy 3. Of the same kind are the following: what it is enough to say, cannot be proved.

units.la: 6 Ibid. in ipsum Christi vicarium Sixtum V. euomat:]iste Francifcanus fuit: ergo Francisci Aliia-tis, non Christi vicarius, ac potius simia Francisci.
units.tr: 6 Ibid. vomits against Sixtus V, the very vicar of Christ: This man was a Franciscan; therefore a Franciscan of Francis, not a vicar of Christ, but rather an ape of Francis.

units.la: 7 Ibid. ad quos Iudices aduersarius provocauit, falsum:non appellauit Iudices ille, sed produxit testes, quos ad iltos sermones produxit iam olim vis illa veritatis. Nam si vestri non sunt, Bellarmine, at testes sunt tamen: sinautem vestri sunt, liceat nobis cum Tullio dicere in orat. pro Quintio: opinor tuum testimonium, quod in alienare lene esset, id in tua, quoniam contra te est, gravissimum debet esse. Profecto Pius V. Pontifex, quum Petrarcham vestrum castraret, iis quae non rescidit, aliquod perhibuit testimonium: quae rescidit, celebriora effecit quum nouacula Pontificia sua eraderet illa ex Petrarchae operibus.
units.tr: 7 Ibid. to whom the adversary appealed as judges, False: he did not appeal to judges, but brought forward witnesses, whom that power of truth long ago brought forward to these discourses. For if they are not yours, Bellarmine, they are nonetheless witnesses; but if they are yours, let us say with Cicero in his speech for Quinctius: I think your testimony, which would be slight against another, must be most weighty against you, since it is against you. Indeed, Pope Pius V, when he castrated your Petrarch, bore some testimony to those things he did not cut out; those he did cut out he made more famous, when with his papal razor he scraped away those passages from Petrarch's works.

units.la: 8 Ibid. imperitia & temeritatis coarguam: in arena ipsa videbitur.
units.tr: 8 Ibid. I will convict him of ignorance and rashness: It will be seen in the arena itself.

units.la: In Cap. II.
units.tr: In Chapter II.

units.la: I Art.I. inscriptionem famosi libelli paulisper infi-ciamus.]quid, famosi? criminatio falsa. Demonstrat ipsa inscriptio, atque praefatio libri. Sic enim ad verbum inscribitur, & tradit praefatio in ipso limine operis: Responsio facta ad excommunicationem Sixti V. contra Serenissimum Regem Navarrae, & contra Excellentiam Principis Condensis: quae excommunicatio affixa est Romae ultimo Octobris 1585. Sequuntur praefationis verba: Henricus gratia Dei Rex Navarrae, Princeps Bearni, primus Par & Princeps Franciae, opponit sese declarationi Sixti V. qui se Papam Romanum dicit, asserendo illam falsi plenam esse, & tanquam de re illegitima pronocat ad Curiam Parium Franciae, quorum in numero primum honorem obtinet: & quantum spectat ad peccatum haeresEos, quod falso in praedicta declaratione ipsi imponitur, dicit & asserit Dominum Papam (salua reuerentia sanctitatis toties insusurrantem audimus Christum, beati eri-tis, quum vos conuiciis affecerint. &c. Matth. 5. 11.
units.tr: I Art. I. Let us for a little while deny the title of the defamatory libel. What, defamatory? It is a false accusation. The title itself and the preface of the book demonstrate this. For it is inscribed word for word thus, and the preface gives it at the very threshold of the work: Response made to the excommunication of Sixtus V against the most serene King of Navarre, and against the Excellency of the Prince of Condé: which excommunication was posted at Rome on the last day of October 1585. The words of the preface follow: Henry, by the grace of God King of Navarre, Prince of Béarn, first peer and prince of France, sets himself against the declaration of Sixtus V, who calls himself Roman Pope, asserting that it is full of falsehood, and as something illegitimate he appeals to the Court of the Peers of France, of whom he holds the first rank; and as far as concerns the sin of heresy, which is falsely imposed on him in the said declaration, he says and asserts that the Lord Pope (saving the reverence due to his holiness) ... we hear Christ murmuring again and again: blessed are you when they shall revile you, etc. Matthew 5.11.

units.la: 3 Ibid. narrationibus partim fabulosis, partim im-puris] quid tum, si fabulosæ? nam & fabulis sua sunt ἐπμωδία[?], & fabulæ multæ non sunt perpetuæ fabulæ, sed interspersam veritatem habent. Quod si impuræ sunt quædam, quàm purum se ostendit Pontificum natio! qui fabulis impuris operam dari malunt quàm purè Scripturæ Dei (nam hanc seuerissimè vetant in vulgo, illas circumferri & volitare in vulgo sinunt) & qui eas solùm expungi & tolli curant quibus se perstringi sentiunt, neglecta Dei, & naturæ ratione, & honestatis publicæ. Omne ius & fas ludificari licet, modò ne stringatur τετράπλευρος[?] pater, aut aliqua radatur ipsius squamu-la. Quod Caluinianis tribuit, vt vocat, fabulæ.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. with narratives partly fabulous, partly impure What, if they are fabulous? For fables also have their own morals, and many fables are not entirely fables, but have truth scattered through them. But if some are impure, how pure the Papist nation shows itself to be! They prefer that impure fables be put to work rather than the pure Scripture of God (for they most strictly forbid this among the common people, while they allow those fables to be passed around and flutter among the common people), and they take care that only those things be cut out and removed by which they feel themselves touched, neglecting the reason of God and of nature and of public decency. All law and right may be mocked, provided that the [illegible] Father is not struck, or any little scale of his shaved off. This is what they attribute to the Calvinists, as they call it, fable.

units.la: 4 Art.3. helleboro curandi esse videantur.] non ergo cautere, gladio, sefte, incendio: quod hactenus factitatum. Maiores vestri, Bellarmine, morbum animi esse putauerunt, tu cerebri: bene est, quòd nouus Hippocrates mitiorem medicinam adhi-bendam putat, pronunciatque. Certè mali sunt medici, quos nondum violentæ istius tædet chirur-giæ, quam Papatus occupauit tamdiu.
units.tr: 4 Art. 3. they seem to need to be cured with hellebore. Therefore not cautery, sword, halter, or fire: which has been practised until now. Your ancestors, Bellarmine, thought the disease was of the spirit; you think it is of the brain. It is good that the new Hippocrates thinks and pronounces that a milder medicine should be applied. Surely they are bad physicians who are not yet weary of that violent surgery which Papacy has held for so long.

units.la: 5 Art. 4. canina eloquentia inuehatur.] canes la-trant, & mordent, non loquuntur: vtri illud faciant mundus videt, iudicabit Deus. de Romano Pontifice & Antichristo diximus controuersia 3. Eius-dem generis sunt sequentia: quæ non sufficit dici, non possunt probari.
units.tr: 5 Art. 4. he rails with dog-like eloquence. Dogs bark and bite, they do not speak: which of the two they do, the world sees; God will judge. We have spoken of the Roman Pontiff and Antichrist in controversy 3. Of the same kind are the following: what it is enough to say, cannot be proved.

units.la: 6 Ibid. in ipsum Christi vicarium Sixtum V. euomat:] iste Franciscanus fuit: ergo Francisci Alisia-tis, non Christi vicarius, ac potiùs simia Francisci.
units.tr: 6 Ibid. vomits against Sixtus V, the very vicar of Christ: This man was a Franciscan; therefore a Franciscan of Francis, not a vicar of Christ, but rather an ape of Francis.

units.la: 7 Ibid. ad quos Judices aduersarius pronocauit,] falsum: non appellauit Iudices ille, sed produxit testes, quos ad istos[?] sermones produxit iam olim vis illa veritatis. Nam si vestri non sunt, Bellarmine, at testes sunt tamen: sinautem vestri sunt, liceat nobis cum Tullio dicere in orat. pro Quintio: opinor, tuum testimonium, quod in alienare leue esset, id in tua, quoniam contra te est, grauissimum debet esse. Profecto Pius V. Pontifex, quum Petrarcham vestrum castraret, iis quae non rescidit, aliquod perhibuit testimonium: quae rescidit, celebriora effecit quum nouacula Pontificia sua eraderet illa ex Petrarchae operibus.
units.tr: 7 Ibid. to whom the adversary appealed as judges, False: he did not appeal to judges, but brought forward witnesses, whom that power of truth long ago brought forward to these discourses. For if they are not yours, Bellarmine, they are nonetheless witnesses; but if they are yours, let us say with Cicero in his speech for Quinctius: I think your testimony, which would be slight against another, must be most weighty against you, since it is against you. Indeed, Pope Pius V, when he castrated your Petrarch, bore some testimony to those things he did not cut out; those he did cut out he made more famous, when with his papal razor he scraped away those passages from Petrarch's works.

units.la: 8 Ibid. imperitiae & temeritatis coarguam: in are-na ipsa videbitur.
units.tr: 8 Ibid. I will convict him of ignorance and rashness: It will be seen in the arena itself.

units.la: In Cap. II.
units.tr: On Chapter II.

units.la: I Art.I. inscriptionem famosi libelli paulisper inspi-ciamus.] quid, famosi? criminatio falsa. Demonstrat ipsa inscriptio, atque praefatio libri. Sic enim ad verbum inscribitur, & tradit praefatio in ipso limine operis: Responsio facta ad excommunicationem Sixti V. contra Serenissimum Regem Nauarrae, & contra Excellentiam Principis Condensis: quae excommunicatio affixa est Romae vltimo Octobris 1585. Sequuntur praefationis verba: Henricus gratia Dei Rex Nauarrae, Princeps Bearni, primus Par & Princeps Franciae, opponit sese declarationi Sixti V. qui se Pa-pam Romanum dicit, afferendo illam falsi plenam esse, & tanquam de re illegitima prouocat ad Curiam Pa-rium Franciae, quorum in numero primum honorem ob-tinet: & quantum spectat ad peccatum haeresis, quod falso inpraedicta declaratione ipsi imponitur, dicit & asserit Dominum Papam (salua reuerentia sanctitatis sua)mentiri[?] falsò,&c. Consule Iurisconsultos, Bel-larmine, & famosi libelli qui dicantur, vide:cogi-ta, quod fit ius publicum Regum & Principum, et iam de iure vestro canonico : expende, quod fit ius regni Galliae, & curiae illius Parium, quae iam tot sectas in Gallia perdurauit: quae sint personae, Rex Nauarrae & Princeps Condensis, quae conditio honoris, sensus, dictorum, factorum, quae ratio illorum, respice:tum animum mihi aduerte ad ius Christi, & Ecclesiae ab eiusmodi processu, dum sapuit, abstinentis: obserua denique antegressum factum audaciamque Pontificis, qui nulla vocatione & auctoritate à Deo & Christo (cuius vices mentitur) instructus, Regem illum & Principem haereseos falsò accusatum, nec haereticum, nec relapsum, in sua ipsius causa, inuocatum, inauditum, nec confessum, nec euictum facto, iure, aut vlla praesumptione iuris, temere atque ἀκρίτως[?] sine vl-la iusta legitimáque Concilij aut alia quauis cognitione audet proscribere. Ad haec profecto si bene attenderis, comperies Sixtum illum V. seditiosum & sanguinarium Francisfcanum auctorem fuisse famosi libelli, quem falsò vestiuit excommunicationis nomine, tanquam si per illud tem-pus exclamauisset quod pueri solent, νέα χελιδών[?]. Regem vero Nauarrae & Principem Condensem ex iure gentium ad iustam defensionem sui attendisse, & indignissimam illam famosi libelli à Sixto V. conscripti iniuriam depulisse per ἀντιτροπο-ίαν[?] & retortionem iniuriae: quem modum iura publica hominibus priuatis indulgent, Proceribus ratio ipsa imperat, dum alia omnis via assequendi iuris praecluditur. Famosi libelli auctor fuit Sixtus. Rex vero & Princeps depulsores. Quodnam ius illud, Bellarmine, vestrum, quo famosi libelli purgatur auctor, & damnantur depulsores? hoc non hominum est ius, sed luparum Romae praebentium ubera alumnis suis, & incurrentium in bonos perfidiosissimè.
units.tr: Article 1. Let us look a little at the title of this infamous libel.] What, infamous? It is a false accusation. The title itself and the preface of the book show this. The title reads word for word: Response made to the excommunication of Sixtus V against the most serene King of Navarre and against the Excellency of the Prince of Condé, which excommunication was posted at Rome on the last day of October 1585. The preface continues: Henry, by the grace of God King of Navarre, Prince of Béarn, first peer and prince of France, opposes himself to the declaration of Sixtus V, who calls himself the Roman Pope, asserting that it is full of falsehood, and as a matter of no legal standing he appeals to the Court of Peers of France, of which he holds the first place. And as far as concerns the sin of heresy, which is falsely imputed to him in the aforesaid declaration, he says and asserts that the Lord Pope, saving the reverence due to his holiness, lies falsely, etc. Consult the jurists, Bellarmine, and see what are called infamous libels. Consider what the public law of kings and princes is, and then your own canon law. Weigh what the law of the kingdom of France is, and of that court of peers which has endured in France through so many sects. Look at who the persons are, the King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé, and at their rank, their sense, their words and deeds, and their reasons. Then turn your mind to the law of Christ and of the Church, which, while it was wise, abstained from such a procedure. Finally, observe the prior deed and the audacity of the Pontiff, who, instructed by no calling or authority from God or Christ (whose place he falsely claims), dares rashly and without judgement (ἀκρίτως), without any just and lawful council or any other inquiry, to proscribe that King and Prince, falsely accused of heresy, neither a heretic nor a relapsed one, in his own cause, not summoned, not heard, not confessed, not convicted by any deed, by law, or by any presumption of law. If you attend carefully to these things, you will find that Sixtus V, that seditious and bloodthirsty Franciscan, was the author of the infamous libel, which he falsely clothed with the name of excommunication, as if at that time he had shouted what boys are wont to shout: "a new swallow" (νέα χελιδών). The King of Navarre and the Prince of Condé, on the other hand, had regard, by the law of nations, to their just self-defence, and by retaliation (ἀντιτροπονία) and the retorting of the injury, they repelled the most unworthy injury of the infamous libel written by Sixtus V. This is the means which public law allows to private persons, and which reason itself commands to nobles when every other way of obtaining their right is closed off. Sixtus was the author of the infamous libel; the King and the Prince were the repellers of it. What law is this of yours, Bellarmine, by which the author of an infamous libel is cleared and those who repel it are condemned? This is not the law of men, but the law of the she-wolves of Rome, who offer their teats to their foster-children and perfidiously attack good men.

units.la: 2 Ibid. iucunda narrationis, & tanquam placida confabulationis] Grammaticum me inuitum facies, mi homo, & sermone tuo. Aniso[?] illud vestrum non est narratio, aut confabulatio, sed monitum: quod barbaries vestrorum Iureconsultorum auisamentum vocat. In caeteris disputatorem sino [illegible, ~8 letters], quia rebus, non verbis, argumentorum telis, non equisonum phaleris pugnari convenit. Christus famosos libellos nunquam scripsit: & faciat vicarius?
units.tr: 2. A pleasant narrative, and as it were a peaceful conversation.] Against my will you make me a grammarian, my good man, and against your own speech. That piece of yours is not a narrative or a conversation but an admonition, which the barbarism of your jurists calls an auisamentum. In other matters I leave the disputant [illegible], since it is fitting to fight with things, not words, with the weapons of argument, not with the trappings of a horse-dealer. Christ never wrote infamous libels: will his vicar do so?

units.la: 3 Artic. 2. & exultant in rebus pessimis.] haec omnia de nobis dicuntur falsò. Utrumque iniquum est, tum intorta ab auctore criminis in probos & innocentes criminatio, tum imputatio in omnes maledica, si quis forte aliquid fecerit consilio suo, non autem publico. Sed haec iuris Romani sunt, & Bellarminei scilicet.
units.tr: 3. Article 2. And they exult in the worst things.] All these things are said of us falsely. Both are unjust: the accusation, turned by the author of the charge against upright and innocent men, and the imputation of slander against all, if anyone by chance does something on his own counsel and not in public. But these are matters of Roman law, and of Bellarmine's law, to be sure.

units.la: 4 Artic. 3. nullius haeresis maculis, nulla schismaticorum colluvione sedetur.] haec homo Italus arrogat Italiae falso. Nam de urbe supercilium ortum est, ut loquitur Hieronymus c. legimus, distin. 93. de supercilio schismata: quæ quàm multa Romæ extiterint, historiae testantur, testis Ammianus de Damaso & Ursicino agens, & scandalum gentibus oblatum describens studiosissimè, ut Christianos pude-ret. De urbe est Novatus & alij: de urbe est apostasia per secundam bestiam procurata, Apoc. 13. de Italia sunt Socini, Gribaldi, Alciati, Gentiles, Blan-dratae, Stancari, & similes multi errorum hærefeúmque artifices. Atheorum denique legiones atque examina, quæ ex illo abyssi puteo non cessant
units.tr: 4. Article 3. It is not calmed by the stains of any heresy, nor by the filthy mass of schismatics.] This Italian man claims for Italy things that are false. For the haughtiness has arisen from the city, as Jerome says in the chapter Legimus, distinction 93, on haughtiness and schisms. How many schisms have arisen at Rome the histories bear witness, as does Ammianus, who, in treating of Damasus and Ursinus, describes most carefully the scandal offered to the Gentiles, so that Christians should blush. Novatus and others came from the city; from the city came the apostasy brought about by the second beast, Rev. 13. From Italy came the Socinians, Gribaldi, Alciati, the Gentiles, Blandrata, Stancari and many similar artisans of errors and heresies. Finally, the legions and swarms of atheists, which never cease to come up from that pit of the abyss...

units.la: Ibid. Latinas literas ignorabas] hæc Rhetor crepet, non dicat Theologus.res ipsa loquitur so-cus.
units.tr: Ibid. You were ignorant of Latin letters.] Let the rhetorician rattle on about this; the theologian should not say it. The matter itself speaks well enough.

units.la: Art. 4. Romana fides Apostolico ore laudata in Italia populis incorrupta, & inuiolata permaneat.] dat disputator verba: quæ res ipsa euincit falsi. Neque hoc dicit eo loco Paulus, neque vsquam veritas. Quòd si etiam de Roma diceretur ista (non dicuntur autem) tamen de Italia tota non esset bona & necessaria consequentia.
units.tr: Article 4. Let the Roman faith, praised by the apostolic mouth, remain uncorrupted and inviolate among the peoples of Italy.] The disputant deceives with words, which the thing itself proves to be false. Paul does not say this in that place, nor does the truth say it anywhere. And even if these things were said of Rome (but they are not said), it would not be a good and necessary consequence for all of Italy.

units.la: Artic. 5. latius præsides religione diuina, quàm dominatione terrena.] totam hanc propositionem confutauimus. 3. lib. 1. & 2. & 4. confutauimus. de locis Prosperi & Leonis ibidem diximus lib. 2, cap. 14. & 16. & alibi.
units.tr: Article 5. Presidents more widely by divine religion than by earthly dominion.] We have refuted this whole proposition: we refuted it in books 1, 2 and 4 (the third book), and we discussed the passages of Prosper and Leo in book 2, chapters 14 and 16, and elsewhere.

units.la: Ibid. atque ab ipso communi Patre omnium Christianorum] Negamus Romanam Ecclesiam esse Ecclesiarum matrem, & Rom. Papam esse communem omnium Christianorum Patrem. illud Ecclesiæ catholicæ, hoc Dei solius est attributum proprium, vt controuersia 3. & 4. probauimus. neganus ista verè de populis quibusdam Septemtrionalibus, aut de Italia prædicari.
units.tr: Ibid. and from the common Father of all Christians himself.] We deny that the Roman Church is the mother of the churches, and that the Roman Pope is the common Father of all Christians. The former is an attribute of the catholic Church, the latter the proper attribute of God alone, as we proved in controversies 3 and 4. We deny that these things can truly be said of certain northern peoples, or of Italy.

units.la: Art. 6. lethale venenum vulgi auribus instillaret.] hic quoque dantur verba φιλοφρονως nos in contrarium iisdem verbis, & iustius, possemus vti. Sed velitari in hac tractatione non est nostrum. Quòd sequentibus spondet de vigilantia Pastorum, falliturnam sermo Dei non est vinctus, 2. Tim. 2. 9. nec potest obstrui.
units.tr: Article 6. Would instil a deadly poison into the ears of the crowd.] Here too words are given in a friendly manner (φιλοφρόνως); we could use the same words against them, and more justly. But to skirmish in this treatment is not our business. What he promises in what follows about the vigilance of the ministers is false, for the word of God is not bound, 2 Tim. 2:9, nor can it be obstructed.

units.la: Ibid. quas ne fando quidem vnquam audiuerit. en hominis prudentiam: qui non vult perpeti ut libellus ille Auifo piacenole, in aures populi Italici, manusve peruenat, & tamen in aures omnium gentium sermone Latino diffundit, quod vix Italia ipsa vernaculo sermone suo esse cognouisset. Hoc vero imprudentiae Bellarminae, sed prouidentiae diuinae factum. Sic hostibus veritatis suae illudit Deus.
units.tr: Ibid. Things which he would never have heard even by rumour. Behold the prudence of the man: he does not want that little pamphlet Avviso piacevole to reach the ears or hands of the Italian people, and yet he spreads it in Latin into the ears of all nations, which Italy itself could hardly have known in its own vernacular. But this was done not by Bellarmine's imprudence but by divine providence. Thus God mocks the enemies of his truth.

units.la: 11 Art.7. ne quo modo corrumpantur sensus eorum, & excidant a simplicitate quae est in Christo.] Exemplum dispar, & finis falsus. Nam Rabsaces in Deum inuehebat, hic in Rom. papam: vix pilus in medio est scilicet. Tu ille verbo agebat, quod volare solet irreuocabile, vt ait Satyricus, hic scripto petebat Italiam, quod scriptu quia permanet, dum exsulare Bellarminus ex Italia voluit, diffudit in gentiu omnium conscientiam scripto Latino suo. Ne ego quidem sciuissem de illo scripto, nisi me Bellarminus facto prudente suo monuisset: hanc ego illi refero gratiam.
units.tr: 11. Article 7. Lest in any way their senses be corrupted and fall from the simplicity that is in Christ.] The example is unlike and the purpose false. For Rabshakeh railed against God, while this man attacks the Roman pope: there is scarcely a hair's breadth between them, to be sure. The one attacked by word, which, as the satirist says, flies irrecoverably; this man attacks Italy in writing, which, because it remains, while Bellarmine wished to be exiled from Italy, has spread into the conscience of all nations through his Latin writing. I would not even have known of that writing, had not Bellarmine, by his prudent act, warned me of it: I give him thanks for this.

units.la: 12 Art.8. Gallusne fuerit, an Gallum simulauerit,] certe Gallum fuisse confirmat typographus praefa-tione sua: & fuisse audio ex certis testibus: sed quid hoc ad causam? aut etiam ad nos?
units.tr: 12. Article 8. Whether he was a Frenchman, or pretended to be one,] Certainly the printer confirms in his preface that he was a Frenchman, and I hear this from certain witnesses. But what does this have to do with the case, or even with us?

units.la: 13 Ibid. Aurigam, vel nautam, quam virum nobili loco natum decebant.] & quis ita loquitur, obsecro, vt Bellarminus hic facit, nisi ὁ ἀπὸ τῶν ἑξήκοντα[?] ἐρχ-μένος, ut Athenienses dixerunt? Non facis paria, Bel-larmine, in hoc officiorum genere; sed vincis.
units.tr: 13. A charioteer or a sailor, which a man born in a noble place would have been unbecoming.] And who, I beg you, speaks thus, as Bellarmine does here, except one "who comes from the sixty" (ὁ ἀπὸ τῶν ἑξήκοντα ἐρχόμενος), as the Athenians said? You do not make equal the duties of this kind of office, Bellarmine; but you surpass them.

units.la: 14 Art.9. cur latet in tenebris, qui tam ferociter sum-mo Christianorum Praesuli m.] cur rogas? quia glo-riam fugit a suis, a vobis persequutionem; contra vero publico se seruat & seruit. Demonstrat Ty-pographus, dicens: estote autem certi, auctorem (cuius nomen taceo, quòd eum abesse nouerim ab omni vana gloria longissimè) esse natione Gallum, &c. Sequentia, quà de Pontifice, quà de auctore libelli enunciatur, negamus omnia.
units.tr: 14. Article 9. Why does he lie hidden in the shadows, who so fiercely [attacks] the highest prelate of Christians.] Why do you ask? Because he flees glory from his own people, and from you persecution; on the contrary, he keeps and serves himself in public. The printer shows this, saying: Be assured, however, that the author (whose name I pass over, because I know that he is far removed from all vain glory) is by nation a Frenchman, etc. We deny all the following statements, both those made about the Pontiff and those made about the author of the libel.

units.la: Ibid. qui male agit, odit lucem. ] contrà verò qui ipse prodit in lucem, non agit male: hoc fecit illius libelli auctor. Agit enim Christus de opere, non de nomine personæ. Itaque disputator argumentatur malè ex diuerso. sed hoc probat Iesuitarum Logica.
units.tr: Ibid. He who does evil hates the light. On the contrary, he who himself comes forward into the light does not do evil. This is what the author of that little book has done. For Christ is speaking of the deed, not of the name of the person. So the disputant argues badly from the opposite case. But this is what the Jesuits' logic proves. ## ON CHAPTER III.

units.la: IN CAPVT III.
Art. 1. in Christi vicarium impie debacchatur. ] negamus & hunc debacchari, & illum Christi vicarium esse. Eadem ratio sequentium.
units.tr: Art. 1. He rages impiously against Christ's vicar. We deny both that this man rages and that that man is Christ's vicar. The same reasoning applies to what follows.

units.la: Ibid. Pontificem Romanum Antichristum esse affirmat. ] de hoc argumento est controu. 3. liber totus tertius.
units.tr: Ibid. He affirms that the Roman Pontiff is Antichrist. The whole of the third book of the third controversy deals with this argument.

units.la: Ibid. par pari sine dubio referet, & stulto secundum eius stultitiam respondebit. ] par negatur esse falsum enunciatum vero: stultum negatur eum esse, qui sapientiam diuinam audit, & de plano homine peccati ex ea iudicat. Sequens itaque affirmatio, quà nos, quà illum spectat, omnino falsa est.
units.tr: Ibid. Like will answer like without doubt, and will answer the fool according to his folly. It is denied that a like answer is a true statement. Nor is the man a fool who hears divine wisdom and judges from it a man plainly given to sin. The following assertion, therefore, whether it is taken as applying to us or to him, is wholly false.

units.la: Art. 2. Antichristus enim in nomine suo veniet, ] Danielis locos proprie ad Antichristum non pertinere, nec illum Christi Ioan. 5. pertinere singulariter, ostendimus lib. 3. cap. 2. controuersiæ 3.
units.tr: Art. 2. For Antichrist will come in his own name, we have shown in book 3, chapter 2, of controversy 3 that the passages of Daniel do not properly pertain to Antichrist, nor does the passage in John 5 pertain to him in particular.

units.la: Ibid. nonne & in litteris seruum seruorum Dei se palàm appellat? ] non sequitur, si ita sese appellat, ergo eum ita esse & facere vt appellat sese: nam & perduelles transfugæ se falsò vocant quàm fidelissimos, vt magis incautos circumueniant mentitæ illius fidelitatis specie. Sic etiam rebellionis auctor & apostasiæ, populo inspectante, omnia offert vero suo domino, & religione iurisiurandi ad mantelum perfidiæ suæ abutitur, fallens populum, & excutiens indignè dominum. Sic idem pro summi sui honoris titulo se vicarium prædicat domini sui, quem ex facto ut perditū simulata fidei & officiorum specie: sic dominum suum publicè & priuatim colit, & cultum procurat illius in speciem, donec commoditatem adeptus fuerit subruendi illum funditus & sibi vindicandi omnia vt domino, inque rem suam vertendi: Infirma itaque est Bellarmini argumentatio à sermone, significque, & demonstratione alicuius operis adstruens officij sui veritatem. Hæc quidem argumentatio in rebus, promissionibus, operibusque diuinis est necessaria planè: in rebus verò, sermonibus, & factis hominum, quamuis Pontificum, est tantummodò contingens, non vllo modo necessaria: ergo inconsequens.
units.tr: Ibid. Does he not even openly call himself the servant of the servants of God in his letters? It does not follow that, because he calls himself so, he therefore is and does what he calls himself. For even deserters and traitors falsely call themselves most faithful, so that they may more easily take in the unwary by the appearance of that feigned loyalty. Thus too the author of rebellion and apostasy, with the people looking on, offers everything to his true lord, and abuses the sanctity of his oath as a cloak for his treachery, deceiving the people and shamefully casting off his lord. So the same man, for the title of his highest honour, proclaims himself the vicar of his lord, whom he has in fact treated as lost, under the pretence of faith and duty. Thus he worships his lord publicly and privately, and promotes worship of him in appearance, until he has gained the opportunity of overthrowing him utterly, claiming everything for himself and turning it to his own advantage. Bellarmine's argument, which infers the truth of his office from his speech, his signs, and the demonstration of some work, is therefore weak. This kind of argument is plainly necessary in the case of God's affairs, promises and works. But in the words and deeds of men, even of Popes, it is only contingent and in no way necessary. Therefore it is inconsequent.

units.la: 6 Ibid. Qui vero seruum, sacerdotem, vicarium, cultorem Christi & verbis & factis se profitetur, certè non eleuatur supra omnem D.] non sequitur ex particulari, non ex suppositione falsa. Nam professio aut vera est, aut falsa, vniuersè aut ex parte solùm. Non est autem vera Pontificis Rom. professio, nec sibi vniuersè constans, neque perpetua. Nam qui verbis ita se profitetur, idem se patitur vocari Dominum Deum nostrum Papam: sic enim habetur in glossa sub finem extrauag. cum inter nonnullos, qui factis nonnullis ita profitetur, idem factis innumeris euertit illam professionem suam, vt in controuersiam 3. [?] sæpe ostedimus, quod id quod Dei solius est assumit sibi, præter, supra, contra diuina
units.tr: 6 Ibid. But whoever professes himself in word and deed to be a servant, a priest, a vicar, a worshipper of Christ, certainly is not raised above every [...] It does not follow from a particular case, and not from a false supposition. For a profession is either true or false, either wholly or only in part. But the profession of the Roman Pontiff is not true, nor is it consistent throughout or perpetual. For he who professes himself thus in words also allows himself to be called "Our Lord God the Pope"; for so it is stated in the gloss at the end of the extravagant cum inter nonnullos. And he who professes himself thus in certain deeds overturns that same profession by countless deeds, as we have often shown in controversy 3, that he assumes to himself what belongs to God alone, beyond, above and against divine

units.la: iura faciendo arbitratu suo;idque eo nomine, quòd homo spiritualis est, si homo; & Spiritum Christi in Ecclesia habet, ut caput Ecclesiæ, ad plenitudinem potestatis. ô tempora! ô mores! De Petro, de Pontifice, quà se vicarium Christi & successorem Petri prædicat, sexcenties dictum. Falsa igitur conclusio.
units.tr: laws, doing as he pleases. And he does this on the ground that he is a spiritual man, if he is a man, and that he has the Spirit of Christ in the Church as head of the Church, to the fullness of power. O the times! O the manners! Concerning Peter, and concerning the Pontiff insofar as he proclaims himself the vicar of Christ and successor of Peter, it has been said six hundred times. The conclusion is therefore false.

units.la: 7 Art.3. iidem ipsi ⁊Antichristum non esse doceant?] negatur.
units.tr: 7 Art. 3. Do the same men teach that he is not Antichrist? Denied.

units.la: 8 Ibid. & non eum potius qui se supra omne numen eleuaret? ] de loco Danielis diximus nota 4. Pauli locus non aduersatur, sed statuit sententiam nostram. Nam etsi verbo & lignis se Deo & sanctis submittit Pontifex, re tamen & veritate contra quàm profitetur facit; quum & multa statuit quæ nemo potest instituere nisi solus Deus, & sanctos indigetat, ut asseritur controuersiæ 7.lib.1.cap 8. & seq. facit Pontifex sanctos, ut Senatus Rom. olim faciebat Deos, quod Tertullianus in Apolog. obiicit. Eleuat se profecto supra numen, qui ea facit quæ ad solam auctoritatem numinis pertinent: eleuat se supra sanctos, cuius auctoritate fit ut habeantur & colantur sancti. Cohęrentia sunt hæc omnia, nec pugnant inter se.
units.tr: 8 Ibid. And is it not rather he who raises himself above every divinity? We have spoken of the passage of Daniel at note 4. The passage of Paul does not oppose us, but confirms our view. For although the Pontiff submits himself to God and the saints in word and by signs, in fact and truth he acts contrary to what he professes. He establishes many things which no one can establish except God alone, and he invokes the saints, as is asserted in controversy 7, book 1, chapter 8 and following. The Pontiff makes saints as the Roman Senate once made gods, which Tertullian objects to in his Apology. He certainly raises himself above God who does those things which pertain to the sole authority of the Deity. He raises himself above the saints, by whose authority it comes about that they are held and worshipped as saints. All these things cohere and do not contradict one another.

units.la: 9 Art. 4. in sola Italia atque Hispania paucos quosdam inuenire potuit, qui sedem Apostolicam, ut æquum erat, venerarentur? ] hæc sunt quæ dicit auctor illius moniti ad verbum: & cio vede apertamente ognuno, eccetto alcuni pochi vestri, o misera Italia, & ofchiana Spagna, liquali potendo viuere amano meglio di perire, & potendo vedere, amano meglio di rimanerfi ciechi: tanto potere ha sopra di loro le delicie di questo ciecho & maluagio mondo. Latinè sic ferme verbum de verbo expresseris: atque hoc videt aperte vnusquisque, exceptis nonnullis paucis vestris, ô misera Italia, & ô serua Hispania, qui vbi possent viuere, malunt perire; & vbi possent videre, malunt permanere cæci: tantum supra eos possunt delicia huius cæci & improbi mundi.
units.tr: 9 Art. 4. Could he find only a few in Italy and Spain alone who would revere the Apostolic See, as was right? These are the words of the author of that admonition, rendered word for word: And I see that everyone plainly sees this, except a few of your people, O wretched Italy, and O enslaved Spain, who, though they could live, prefer to die; and though they could see, prefer to remain blind: so great is the power over them of the delights of this blind and wicked world. In Latin one could render it roughly word for word thus: And this everyone sees plainly, except a few of your people, O wretched Italy, and O enslaved Spain, who, where they could live, prefer to perish; and where they could see, prefer to remain blind: so much do the delights of this blind and wicked world prevail over them.

units.la: Ostendit his verbis auctor ille, quisquis est, quemadmodum in natura, sic etiam in rebus spiritualibus & in hoc ipso argumento esse duplicem videndi modum; vnum confusum, alterum distinctum: confuso visionis modo, id est (vt Scholastici loquuntur) aliquali, videre omnes gentes communiter Papam Antichristum esse; distincto verò hoc & singulari videndi modo non omneis videre, & eos maximè qui videre fugiunt voluntarie. Quod vident homines confuse, id ita vi lucis & rei veritate aperta vident, vt sua infirmitate aut voluntate confuse videant, quia aut non possunt magis, aut etiam nolunt: quod verò distinctè videt, id vi lucis internæ & externæ, & lumine supernaturali vident; vi quidem lucis, omnes; lumine verò supernaturali, electi solùm. Quid autem hic Bellarminus? indistinctè negat quæ ille auctor optimè distinxerat: & quia miser mundus, & in eo gentes quamplurimæ distinctè non vident id quod obscurè & confusè plerique vident, id eas omnino videre negat. Negationem probat multis exemplis multorum. sed quid probari attinet? Nam auctor ille omnes id videre dicit communiter, siue confuse videant, siue distinctè, & verum est: hic omnes videre distinctè negat, & hoc quoque verum. Non pugnant autem, si qua subcontraria (vt vocantur male) de re eadem dicta sunt diuerso respectu. Frustra igitur omnes probationes istæ, quia nihil faciunt ad causam. Etsi multæ sunt in eis quæ controuerti possent, atque haud scio an reuinci falsi. Sed non est nostrum extra oleas vagari: non lubet insanire. Quod autem dicebat ante, In Anglia vero, nonne Catholicorum pro Rom. fide pugnantium pleni sunt carceres? haec & sequentia dicuntur falsò: quod omnibus lippis & to-soribus notum. Nam ex seditiosis Bellarminus facit Catholicos, ex manipulo vno aut altero coniuratorum legiones bonorum quàm plurimas. Vigilans somniat. De aliis fabulis sequentibus otiosi viderint: nos ad rem ipsam praestat descendere.
units.tr: In these words that author, whoever he is, shows that in nature, and likewise in spiritual things and in this very question, there is a twofold manner of seeing: one confused, the other distinct. With the confused manner of seeing, that is (as the Schoolmen say) in a certain sense, all peoples commonly see that the Pope is Antichrist. With the distinct and particular manner of seeing, not everyone sees this, and especially those who voluntarily refuse to see. What men see confusedly they see by the force of light and the truth made plain, yet they see it confusedly because of their weakness or their will, since either they cannot see more clearly or they do not wish to. What they see distinctly they see by the force of inward and outward light and by supernatural light: by the force of light, all men; by supernatural light, the elect only. But what does Bellarmine do here? He denies without distinction what that author had distinguished very well. And because the wretched world, and within it very many nations, do not see distinctly what most men see obscurely and confusedly, he denies that they see it at all. He proves the denial with many examples of many people. But what is the point of proving it? For that author says that all see this commonly, whether they see it confusedly or distinctly, and that is true. Here Bellarmine denies that all see it distinctly, and that too is true.
