Nor do these statements conflict, if things said of the same matter in a subcontrary way (as they are badly called) are said with different respects. So all those proofs are useless, because they have nothing to do with the case. Although many of them could be disputed, and I am not sure they could not be shown to be false. But it is not our business to wander beyond the bounds; we have no wish to rave. As for what he said before, In England, are not the prisons full of Catholics fighting for the Roman faith? these and the following statements are false, as is known to everyone who has eyes or can see. For Bellarmine makes Catholics out of seditious men, and out of one or two handfuls of conspirators, very many legions of good men. He dreams while awake. The idle may look into the other fables that follow; it is better for us to get down to the matter itself.

units.la: In Caput IV.
units.tr: On Chapter IV.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. adesse iam annum à Lutheri praedicatione septuagesimum, ] fallitur disputator in hac sua propositione. Nam adesse quidem annum septuagesimum auctor ille dicit, sed à Lutheri praedicatione septuagesimum non dicit. glossema disputatoris est. Quomodo ergo septuagesimus? inquies. nimirum per allusionem ad illos septuaginta annos, quos Ieremias praedixerat, vt habetur 2. Chron. 36.21. Ie-rem. 25.11. & 29.10. & Dan. 9.2. &c. Ac ille quidem septuagesimus, quo ludaei auctoritate Cyri reuersi sunt, typus fuit proprius atque destinatus illius plenitudinis temporum, de qua dicit Apostolus 2. Cor. 6.2. ecce nunc praestitutum illud tempus acceptum, ecce nunc dies salutis, & cui propterea illud Esaiae tribuitur, exite e medio eorum, & separamini, &c. ibidem 2. Cor. 6.17. Sed tamen quemadmodum illa typicè de exitu dicuntur ex Babylonia, anagogicè vero de liberatione nostri in tempore Euangelij per Christum, ita etiam per quamdam singularem ἐφαρμογὴν [?], id est, applicationem & accommodationem iustam, de quauis liberatione spirituali ex spirituali tyrannide: enunciantur ista per allusionem quamdam & modum paroemiæ, ad quem auctor ille videtur respexisse. Nam tenebræ illæ spirituales & tyrannis Pontificia captiuitate figurantur, annus promulgatæ liberationis atque exercitæ, anno illo septuagesimo, quo Iudæos Cyrus remisit in regionem suam: ac proinde hic annus conuenienter septuagesimus appellatur. Sed excurrit Bellarminus contrà in suam illam circumscriptionem & interpretationem imaginariam de anno septuagesimo à Lutheri prædicatione: & quum auctorem illum vt phreneticum exagitat, ipse sibi Suffenus est, & de suis commentitiis interpretationibus suauiter φλυαφεῖ. Negamus omnia: Romæ eandem fidem esse quæ semper fuit: Christi religionem in Germania Lutheri opera in perditissimam hæresin mutatam esse, & quæ sequuntur, φλυαφωδεῖς λῆρες.[?]
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. that the seventieth year since Luther's preaching is now at hand, ] The disputant is mistaken in this proposition. For that author does say that the seventieth year is at hand, but he does not say that it is the seventieth since Luther's preaching. The words "since Luther's preaching" are the disputant's own gloss. How then is it the seventieth? You will say: plainly by an allusion to those seventy years which Jeremiah foretold, as is found in 2 Chron. 36.21, Jer. 25.11, 29.10, and Dan. 9.2, etc. That seventieth year, in which the Jews returned by the decree of Cyrus, was a proper and designated type of that fullness of time of which the Apostle speaks in 2 Cor. 6.2, behold, now is the accepted time, behold, now is the day of salvation, and to which, for that reason, the saying of Isaiah is applied, come out from among them, and be separate, etc., in the same passage, 2 Cor. 6.17. Yet just as those words are said typically of the exodus from Babylon, but anagogically of our deliverance in the time of the Gospel through Christ, so too, by a certain peculiar application [ἐφαρμογήν], that is, a fitting and appropriate accommodation, they are said of any spiritual deliverance from spiritual tyranny, by a kind of allusion and in the manner of a proverb, to which that author seems to have had regard. For those spiritual darkness and Papal tyranny are prefigured by the captivity, and the year of liberation proclaimed and carried out is prefigured by that seventieth year in which Cyrus sent the Jews back to their country; and so this year is fittingly called the seventieth. But Bellarmine rushes against that circumscription and his own imaginary interpretation of the seventieth year from Luther's preaching, and while he harries that author as a madman, he is himself a Suffenus, and sweetly babbles [φλυαφεῖ] about his own invented interpretations. We deny all of it: that at Rome the faith is the same as it always was; that the religion of Christ in Germany was changed by Luther's work into the most destructive heresy; and what follows is babbling nonsense [φλυαφωδεῖς λῆρες].

units.la: IN CAP. V.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER V.

units.la: 1 Art.1. neque quid sit fides aut hæresis, unquam di-dicisse. Audaces affirmationes, quas alij sycophantias dixerint. Atqui, mi homo, nemo nouit quid sit fides, nisi qui habet: nemo nouit quid sit hæresis, nisi qui caret hæresi illa quæ agitur: si enim tenetur ea, non nouit eam, si aliquo modo nouit, fit αὐτοκατάκριτος.[?] Fidem habet auctor ille profitetur-que, cur negas? hæresin tibi, non sibi inesse ait: si suam nemo nouit, cur magis tibi quàm illi fidem haberi iubes? iudicabit Dominus Deus veritatis per verbum veritatis suæ, iudicabunt pij ex eodem verbo. Sequentes sales suo loco relinquimus: nihil ad nos: qui eis tamen falsò adspergi auctorem nouimus.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. nor ever to have learned what faith or heresy is. Bold assertions, which others would call slanders. But, my good man, no one knows what faith is except the one who has it; no one knows what heresy is except the one who is free of that heresy under discussion. For if he holds it, he does not know it; if he knows it in any way, he becomes self-condemned [αὐτοκατάκριτος]. That author professes faith and says so; why do you deny it? He says that heresy is in you, not in himself. If no one knows his own heresy, why do you order that faith be given to you rather than to him? The Lord God of truth will judge by the word of his truth, and the godly will judge by the same word. We leave the following witticisms in their place: they have nothing to do with us, though we know that the author is falsely splattered with them.

units.la: 2 Ibid. iudicium ipsi suum Ecclesiae iudicio praeserunt.] puta si vera Ecclesia est, & ex canone veritatis divinitus ipsi tradito, qui est Scriptura sacra, iudicium facit. hoc enim iudicium Dei est & Christi, qui est supra omnia, huic ergo iudicio qui suum praeserunt contumaciter, vere dicuntur haeretici: ut controversia 4. expositum.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. they set their own judgment above the judgment of the Church.] Suppose the Church is true and makes its judgment from the rule of truth given by God, which is holy Scripture. For this judgment is the judgment of God and of Christ, who is over all things. Therefore those who obstinately set their own judgment above this judgment are rightly called heretics, as was explained in controversy 4.

units.la: 3 Ibid. quos Euangelium & symbolum integre colere, ample&i, ac sequi non ignoratis?] Integre colere dicuntur ij qui & verba tenent & substantiam vel sensum ipsorum. verba tenent integre aeque Anabaptistae ac Pontificij, substantiam vero & sensum integrum nec hi nec illi tenent: falsa igitur est argumentatio: nam sensum apud Pontificios non retineri integrum hae ipsae docent controversiae, & animadversiones nostrae cum huius controversiis comparatae.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. whom you know do not keep the Gospel and the creed whole, nor follow them?] Those are said to keep something whole who hold both the words and the substance or sense of them. The Anabaptists keep the words whole just as the Papists do, but neither these nor those keep the substance and sense whole. The argument is therefore false. For that the sense is not kept whole among the Papists is taught by these very controversies, and by our animadversions when they are compared with the controversies of this man.

units.la: 4 Ibid. quasi is Apostolicum symbolum depravarit adiectione vocis, Romanam, ad voces (Catholicam & Apostolica) auctor illius libelli loquitur de Symbolo Apostolico secundum substantiam & sensum ipsius. nam etsi Nicaeno & Constantinopolitano symbolo duae voces adiectae sunt, una & Apostolica, tamen quia veritatis eiusdem sunt [illegible, ~3 letters] [?], eas nemo in dubium vocat. Sed quia iam Pontifices in suis formulis non hoc desiderant, sed verum etiam volunt vocem, Romanam, adiici tanquam [illegible, ~6 letters] [?] & ad discretionem essentialem Ecclesiae pertinentem, quod est salsissimum, prutera hoc additamentum a Pontificibus finibus suas extendentibus adiectum auctor libelli optimo iure exagitat. Non est autem vox ista, Romanam, adiecta ad verbum Symbolo Apostolico, ne in Concilio quidem Tridentino, vbi Symbolum Nicænum cū adiectione Constantinopolitanę Synodi expressum est: sed reipsa tamē & praxi ordinaria istud additamētū à Christianis exigitur, tāquā omnino necessariū.Sic in Concilio Treuiresi anni 1549.cap.de fide orthodoxa,&c. ponūtur hæc verba:Nihil proinde aliud credendū, tenendū, aut docendū est, nisi quod sanƈta Rom. tenet & docet Ecclesia, omnium consentientium Ecclesiarum mater & magistra: eum vero qui à fide catholica & Rom. Ecclesiæ recedit, necesse est à veritate & capite deficere.Et in Pontificali Rom. vbi traditur ordo ad reconciliandum apostatam schismaticum vel hæreticum, qui abiurat, solius Ecclesiæ Rom. mentionem facit.Ego, inquit, talis cognoscens veram, catholicam, & Apostolicam fidem, anathematizo hic publicè omnem hæresin, præcipuè illam de qua hactenus exstiti infamatus, quæ adstruere conatur hoc vel illud : consentio autem sanƈtæ Romanæ Ecclesiæ & Apostolicæ sedi, & ore & corde profiteor me credere sic vel sic, & eamdem fidem tenere, quam sanƈta Rom. Ecclesia auƈtoritate Euangelica & Apostolica tenendam tradit. Imò in forma iuramenti quod præstat electus Episcopus, nec Deo iam nec Christo dat fidem, sed Romanæ Ecclesiæ solis, his verbis: Ego N. electus Ecclesiæ M. ab hac hora in antea fidelis & obediens ero beato Petro sanƈtaque Rom. Ecclesiæ, & Domino nostro Domino N. Papæ N. suisque successoribus, &c. Quousque tandem, ô Domine Iesu Christe, feres impietatem istam & tyrannidem tenebrarum horrendam?Non debet autem cuiquam videri mirum, si homo Gallus id affirmauerit quod ante annos tredecim in tota Gallia personaūerat. Nam post infamem illam Parisiensem lanienam formulę iuramenti singulis in locis præscriptę sunt,& ab infirmis hominibus exactæ quàm atrocissimè, quibus in fidem & verba solius Ecclesiæ Rom.iurare cogebantur.Exstant formulæ in Actis passim,& in historiis: ex quibus formulis confirmatur plane auctoris illius dictum, articulum Symboli Apostolici de Ecclesia ex eo additamento censeri apud Pontificios oportere. Vera igitur est auctoris illius querimonia, quum ait: Niuno (difano giudicio) si mera Heretico chi crede all'Vangelo[?],&c. quæ ad verbum ita reddimus: Nemo sani iudicij putabit eum hæreticum qui credit Euangelio, nec vllum fidei articulum negat, non adiungendo ei, non detrahendo punctum vnicum, & qui amplestitur toto corde Christum verum hominem & Deum pro suo redemptore & seruatore vnico, & qui in summa credit omnes articulos Symboli Apostolici: inter quos fit mentio huius, nimirum sanctæ illius Ecclesiæ catholicæ & Apostolicæ, sine adiectione alia: cum neque verbo Dei, neque doctrina Euangelica, neque Apostolorum, cui soli credit & hæret, imperatum sit vt adiungatur hæc vox, Romanam, ac potius blasphemia, quatu, ô Papa, tibi facis ex vna particulari vniuersalem vnam, & ex vno corporis membro, caput, cum maxima in totum corpus & caput simul iniuria, quod caput est vnicum, nimirum solus Iesus Christus Dominus noster. Fuit certè homini Gallo certa occasio & maxima necessitas παρακλησιν[?] illud exprobrandi, quum vici & compita nuper in tota Gallia isto additamento crepuissent. Bellarminus itaque in sequentibus frustra est. Nam hoc Symbolo vel additamento ad Symbolum, velut solenni formula, suos in Gallia recognoscebant iudicio publico qui volunt audire catholici. sola vox ista, Romana, vox salutaris fuit, quum in harpyiarum catholicarum manus deuentum esset.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. as if he had corrupted the Apostles' Creed by adding the word Roman to the words (Catholic and Apostolic) The author of that libel speaks of the Apostles' Creed according to its substance and sense. For although two words were added to the Nicene and Constantinopolitan creeds, one of them "apostolic," yet since they belong to the same truth [illegible], nobody calls them into doubt. But since now the Pontiffs do not want this in their formulas, but actually wish the word Roman to be added, as [illegible] and as something belonging to the essential distinction of the Church, which is most absurd, the author of the libel rightly and most justly attacks this addition made by Pontiffs who extend their boundaries. Now, this word Roman was not added to the wording of the Apostles' Creed even at the Council of Trent, where the Nicene Creed is expressed together with the addition of the Constantinopolitan Synod. Yet in actual practice this addition is demanded by Christians as wholly necessary. Thus in the Council of Trier of 1549, in the chapter on the orthodox faith, etc., these words are laid down: Therefore nothing else is to be believed, held, or taught than what the holy Roman Church, the mother and teacher of all the consenting churches, holds and teaches; and whoever departs from the Catholic faith and the Roman Church must necessarily fall away from the truth and from the head. And in the Roman Pontifical, where the order for reconciling an apostate, schismatic, or heretic who abjures is set out, he makes mention only of the Roman Church. I, he says, knowing myself to be such, acknowledge the true, Catholic, and Apostolic faith, and here publicly anathematize every heresy, especially that of which I have hitherto been infamously known, which attempts to maintain this or that; and I consent to the holy Roman Church and the Apostolic See, and with mouth and heart I profess that I believe thus or thus, and hold the same faith which the holy Roman Church delivers to be held on the authority of the Gospel and the Apostles. Indeed, in the form of oath which an elected bishop takes, he gives his faith neither to God nor to Christ, but to the Roman Church alone, in these words: I, N., elected to the Church of M., from this hour onward will be faithful and obedient to blessed Peter, and to the holy Roman Church, and to our lord N., Pope N., and his successors, etc. How long, O Lord Jesus Christ, wilt thou bear this impiety and the dreadful tyranny of darkness? Nor should anyone think it strange if a Frenchman has affirmed what, thirteen years ago, was openly proclaimed throughout all of France. For after that infamous Parisian slaughter, formulas of oath were prescribed in each place and exacted most savagely from weak men, who were forced to swear to the faith and words of the Roman Church alone. These formulas survive everywhere in the Acts and in histories, and from them the saying of that author is clearly confirmed: that among the Papists the article of the Apostles' Creed concerning the Church ought to be counted as having this addition. The author's complaint is therefore true, when he says: No one of sound judgment would consider him a heretic who believes the Gospel (the one who is no heretic believes the Gospel), etc., which we render word for word thus: No one of sound judgment will think him a heretic who believes the Gospel, and denies no article of faith, adding nothing to it and taking away not a single point; who embraces with his whole heart Christ, true man and God, as his only Redeemer and Saviour, and who in sum believes all the articles of the Apostles' Creed; among which is mention of that holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, without any other addition, since neither the Word of God, nor evangelical doctrine, nor that of the Apostles, to whom alone he gives credit and adheres, has commanded that this word Roman be joined to it; but rather it is blasphemy, what do you make of yourself, O Pope, out of one particular church a universal one, and out of one member of the body a head, with the greatest injury to the whole body and to the head at once, since the head is one, namely our Lord Jesus Christ alone. The Frenchman certainly had a sure occasion and the greatest necessity for hurling this exhortation [παράκλησιν] at them, since recently in all of France the streets and crossroads had rung with this addition. Bellarmine, then, labours in vain in what follows. For by this Creed, or by this addition to the Creed, as by a solemn formula, those in France who wished to hear Catholics acknowledged their own, by public judgment. This word Roman alone was a word of salvation, when things had come into the hands of the Catholic harpies.

units.la: 5 Art.2. eam catholicam, Apostolicam, Romanam appellare, ] hoc illud est quod auctor libelli dicit: quid ergo est quod de vocibus tam exiliter & captiosè disputatur, quum de re constat? Rationes verò sequentes, quæ ad confirmationem adferuntur, nihil hanc causam adiuuant, quia de Ecclesia Rom. secundum illud tempus quo Patres illi scribebant enunciantur: vt suis locis ostendimus. Nam de locis qui adducuntur Cypriani, Ambrosij, Nazianzeni, Hieronymi, & Augustini diximus controu. 3. lib. 2. cap. 15. & 16. & lib. 4. cap. 3. & 4. & alibi sæpe. Futilis est, quæ ignorationem elenchi fallit, argumentatio.
units.tr: 5 Art.2. that they call it catholic, apostolic, Roman, ] This is exactly what the author of the booklet says. Why then is so much fuss made, in such a petty and captious way, over words, when the matter itself is agreed? The reasons that follow, which are brought forward to confirm the point, do nothing to help this cause, because they speak of the Roman Church as it was in the period when those Fathers were writing, as I have shown in their proper places. For the passages cited from Cyprian, Ambrose, Gregory Nazianzen, Jerome and Augustine, I have already dealt with them in Controversy 3, book 2, chapters 15 and 16, and book 4, chapters 3 and 4, and often elsewhere. The argument is futile: it deceives by ignoring the point at issue.

units.la: IN CAPVT VI.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER VI.

units.la: 1 Art.1. Romanum Pontificem per ea testimonia designari, ] de hoc argumento actum est controuersiæ 3. lib. 3.
units.tr: 1 Art.1. that the Roman Pontiff is designated by those testimonies, ] This question was treated in Controversy 3, book 3.

units.la: 2 Art.2. Sed Paralogismum tibi condono, ] & ego, Bellarmine, condono tibi paralepsin siue ἀπωσιωπήν[?], qua verba illius auctoris cætera retices, vt paralogismum conficias. Frontem tuam primùm liceat retegere, vt condonem tibi paralepsin pari modo, quo tu paralogismum auctori illi condonasti. Italieis ergo illis verbis quæ adtulisti, & hæc sequentia adferri oportuit: Deh considera bene queste parole, & poi riuolge gli occhi a i fatti di cotesto scelerato, a cui i Re, & i sommi imperadori son costretti di basciare (a grande onta loro) il puzzolente piede, & cio facendo gli rendono (come esser deono) la douuta vbidienza, come a Dio in terra. hæc verba omnino addi oportuit, quia ad substantiam argumentationis pertinent. Age, inquit, considera bene hæc verba, postea vero bus exactæ quàm atrocissimè, quibus in fidem & verba solius Ecclesiæ Rom. iurare cogebantur. Ex-stant formulę in Actis passim, & in historiis: ex quibus formulis confirmatur plane auctoris illius dic-tum, articulum Symboli Apostolici de Ecclesia ex eo additamento censeri apud Pontificios oportere.
units.tr: 2 Art.2. But I forgive you the paralogism, ] And I, Bellarmine, forgive you the paralepsis, or aposiopesis [ἀπωσιώπησις], by which you leave out the rest of that author's words in order to construct your paralogism. Let me first be allowed to unmask your own face, so that I may forgive you the paralepsis in the same way that you forgave that author his paralogism. Therefore, along with the Italian words you cited, the following sentence ought to have been quoted as well: Ah, consider well those words, and then turn your eyes to the deeds of this villain, before whom kings and the highest emperors are forced to kiss (to their great shame) his stinking foot, and in doing so they render him (as they ought) due obedience, as to God on earth. These words should certainly have been added, because they belong to the very substance of the argument. "Come," he says, "consider these words well; but afterwards..." …oaths exacted most atrociously, by which men were compelled to swear to the faith and the words of the Church of Rome alone. Formulas of this kind are found everywhere in the Acts and in the histories, and from these formulas it is plainly confirmed that what that author said is true: that under Papal rule the article of the Apostles' Creed concerning the Church must be understood in light of that addition.

units.la: Vera igitur est auctoris illius querimonia, quum ait: Niuno (di fano giudicio) stimera Heretico chi crede all'Angelo[?], &c. quæ ad verbum ita reddimus: Nemo sani iudicij putabit eum hæreticum qui credit Euangelio, nec ullum fidei articulum negat, non adiungendo ei, non detrahendo punctum unicum, & qui amplectitur toto corde (Christum verum hominem & Deum pro suo redemptore & seruatore unico, & qui in summa credit omnes articulos Symboli Apostolici: inter quos sit mentio huius, nimirum sanctæ illius Ecclesiæ catholicæ & Apostolicæ, sine adiectione alia: cum neque verbo Dei, neque doctrina Euangelica, neque Apostolorum, cui soli credit & hæret, imperatum sit ut adiungatur hæc vox, Romanam, ac potius blasphemia, qua tu, ô Papa, tibi facis ex una particulari uniuersalem unam, & ex uno corporis membro, caput, cum maxima in totum corpus & caput simul iniuria, quod caput est unicum, nimirum solus Iesus Christus Dominus noster. Fuit certè homini Gallo certa occasio & maxima necessitas παράχαραγ-μα illud exprobrandi, quum vici & compita nuper in tota Gallia isto additamento crepuissent. Bel-larminus itaque in sequentibus frustra est. Nam hoc Symbolo vel additamento ad Symbolum, velut solenni formula, suos in Gallia recognosce-bant iudicio publico qui volunt audire catholici. Sola vox ista, Romana, vox salutaris fuit, quum in harpyiarum catholicarum manus deuentum ef-set.
units.tr: The complaint of that author is therefore true, when he says: No one of sound judgement will take him for a heretic who believes the Gospel (?), etc. which we render word for word: No one of sound judgement will think him a heretic who believes the Gospel and denies no article of faith, neither adding to it nor taking away a single point, and who embraces with his whole heart Christ, true man and God, as his one redeemer and saviour, and who in sum believes all the articles of the Apostles' Creed, among which there is mention of that holy catholic and apostolic Church, without any further addition. For neither the Word of God, nor the Gospel teaching, nor the Apostles, in whom alone he believes and to whom he adheres, has commanded that this word be added, Roman. Rather, it is blasphemy, by which you, O Pope, make of one particular church a universal one, and of one member of the body the head, to the greatest injury of the whole body and of the head as well, since the head is one, namely Jesus Christ our Lord alone. Certainly a Frenchman had a sure occasion and the greatest necessity to reproach that [παράχαραγμα] counterfeit, since in recent times the streets and crossroads of all France had resounded with this addition. Bellarmine, therefore, labours in vain in what follows. For by this creed, or addition to the creed, as by a solemn formula, those in France who wish to be heard as Catholics acknowledged themselves in public judgement. That one word, Roman, was the only saving word, when things had come into the hands of the Catholic harpies.

units.la: eam catholicam, Apostolicam, Romanam appellare, ] hoc illud est quod auctor libelli dicit: quid ergo est quod de vocibus tam exiliter & captiosè disputatur, quum de re constat? Rationes vero sequentes, quae ad confirmationem adferuntur, nihil hanc causam adiuuant, quia de Ecclesia Rom. secundum illud tempus quo Patres illi scribebant enunciantur: vt suis locis ostendimus. Nam de locis qui adducuntur Cypriani, Ambrosij, Nazianzeni, Hieronymi, & Augustini diximus controu. 3. lib. 2. cap. 15. & 16. & lib. 4. cap. 3. & 4. & alibi saepe. Futilis est, quae ignoratione elenchi fallit, argumentatio.
units.tr: that they call it catholic, apostolic, Roman, ] This is exactly what the author of the booklet says. Why then is so much fuss made, in such a petty and captious way, over words, when the matter itself is agreed? The reasons that follow, which are brought forward to confirm the point, do nothing to help this cause, because they speak of the Roman Church as it was in the period when those Fathers were writing, as I have shown in their proper places. For the passages cited from Cyprian, Ambrose, Gregory Nazianzen, Jerome and Augustine, I have already dealt with them in Controversy 3, book 2, chapters 15 and 16, and book 4, chapters 3 and 4, and often elsewhere. The argument is futile: it deceives by ignoring the point at issue.

Therefore, along with the Italian words you cited, the following sentence ought to have been quoted as well: Ah, consider well those words, and then turn your eyes to the deeds of this villain, before whom kings and the highest emperors are forced to kiss (to their great shame) his stinking foot, and in doing so they render him (as they ought) due obedience, as to God on earth. Age, inquit, considera bene hac verba, postea vero refer oculos ad facta istius scelerati, cui Reges & Imperatores summi coguntur osculari magno pudore suo fatidos pedes: atque hoc faciendo reddunt ei (vt ipsi quidem aiunt) debitam obedientiam, tamquam Deo in terra. hæc profecto paralogismum ita soluunt, vt paralepsin disputatoris in lucem proferant. Nam Irenæi verborum hunc sensum attulit: Qui seruus est re & professione, & tamen vult adorari quasi Deus, is Antichristus est: Pontifex re & professione seruus est, non etiam seruum seruorum seipsum nominat, & tamen vult adorari quasi Deus: Ponti-sex ergo Rom. Antichristus est. Assumptionis u-num membrum disputator ponit, alterum reticet commodo suo, vt superior esse causâ videatur. Pro-bat hoc assumptionis membrum à solenni usu o-sculandorum pedum: qui honor apud Christianos supra quàm humanus est, divinus igitur, & à Pon-tifice exigitur, vult ergo honore divino affici ut Deus.
units.tr: But I forgive you the paralogism, ] And I, Bellarmine, forgive you the paralepsis, or aposiopesis [ἀποσιώπησιν], by which you leave out the rest of that author's words so that you can construct your paralogism. Let me first strip off your brazenness, so that I may forgive you the paralepsis in the same way that you forgave that author his paralogism. So the Italian words you cited ought to have been accompanied by the following: Well then, consider these words carefully, and afterwards turn your eyes to the deeds of this wretch, whom kings and the highest emperors are forced to kiss (to their great shame) his stinking foot; and in doing so they give him (as they themselves say) the obedience due to him, as to God on earth. These words absolutely had to be added, because they belong to the substance of the argument. Come, he says, consider these words well, and then turn your eyes to the deeds of this wretch, whom kings and the highest emperors are compelled to kiss, to their great shame, his stinking feet; and by doing so they render him (as they themselves say) the obedience due, as to God on earth. These words, certainly, resolve the paralogism in such a way that they bring the disputant's paralepsis into the light. For he has produced the sense of Irenaeus's words thus: whoever is a slave in deed and profession, and yet wants to be adored as God, is Antichrist. The Pope is a slave in deed and profession; he does not even call himself the servant of servants; and yet he wants to be adored as God. Therefore the Roman Pontiff is Antichrist. The disputant sets down one member of the minor premise and omits the other to suit his own purpose, so that he may seem to be the superior in the case. He proves this member of the minor premise from the customary and solemn practice of kissing feet, an honour which among Christians is more than human, and therefore divine, and which is demanded from the Pope. Therefore he wants to be honoured with divine honour, as God.

units.la: 3 Ibid. Non igitur (ut tu fingis) Irenæus dicit, cum sit seruus, quasi Deus vult adorari. Eadem & fronte uteris, Bellarmine, & fide. Atqui gratum esse te erga auctorem illum anonymum oportebat, quòd Irenæi verba contraxisset, ne videretur longior. Sic habet Irenæus lib. 5. aduersus hæreses, cap.21.de An-tichristo dicens, quoniam exsistens apostata & latro quasi Deus vult adorari, & cum sit seruus, Regem se vult præconari. In crimen falsi incidis, & impingis alteri, Bellarmine, peccatum tuum. Irenæus ipse purgat auctorem illum, nobis tacentibus, te convincit falsi.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. Therefore it is not (as you pretend) that Irenaeus says, since he is a servant, he wants to be worshipped as God. You use the same brazenness, Bellarmine, and the same good faith. Yet you ought to have been grateful to that anonymous author for having abridged Irenaeus's words, so that they should not seem too long. Irenaeus says this in book 5 against heresies, chapter 21, speaking of Antichrist: since, being an apostate and a robber, he wants to be worshipped as God, and though he is a servant, he wants to be proclaimed king. You fall into the crime of forgery and lay your own fault upon another, Bellarmine. Irenaeus himself clears that author, while we say nothing; he convicts you of falsehood.

units.la: 4 Ibid. neque ipse se Regem appellat, neque ab aliis appellari cupit.] nomen fugit, rem vsurpauit iam-diu,quod diu, quod apostatæ & latrones solent. quomodo enim rex non sit, qui æquè temporalis, ac spiritualis gladij sibi dominium arrogat? c. vnam sanctam. extra. de maioritate & obedientia. quid est Regem esse, nisi hoc est? Sed ita [illegible, ~12 letters] quod est in prouerbio.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. He does not call himself king, nor does he wish to be called so by others.] He avoids the name but has long since seized the thing, as apostates and robbers are wont to do. For how is he not a king, who arrogates to himself lordship over the temporal and the spiritual sword alike? c. Unam sanctam, extra, de maioritate et obedientia. What is being a king, if not this? But so [illegible] which is the proverb.

units.la: 5 Ibid. non posse nisi per summam impudentiam Antichristi nomen ad Rom. Pontificem trahi. ] negamus sequi ex dispari: nam illud ex certis & euidentibus Scripturæ verbis adducitur, vbi de Antichristo agitur, vel aduersariorum ipsorum testimonio: sequentia vero quæcunque adferuntur, non sunt eiusmodi. Nam aut ex mera coniectura sunt absque vlla auctoritate Scripturæ, vt illud, Antichristum futuram genere Judæum, atque ex tribu Dan. aut ex locis ἀλληγορουμένοις[?], & falsa eorum interpretatione, vt quum dicit Hierosolymis regnaturum, & in templo quod Salomonis dicebatur fefurum, & tribus annis cum dimidio regnaturum: aut denique ex locis alienis, vt quum verba ἀντίοχος[?] de Antiocho Epiphane à Daniele dicta ad Antichristi causam traducuntur, idola omnia submoturum, &c. Non potest bona esse consequentia ex dictorum eiusmodi comparatione. Quæ Irenæus ex certo Dei verbo dixit, ea validam argumentationem præbent, non autem quæ ab humana coniectura, aut incerta interpretatione.
units.tr: 5 Ibid. It cannot be that the name of Antichrist is drawn to the Roman Pontiff except through the greatest impudence. ] We deny that this follows by parity of reasoning. For the one point is drawn from certain and evident words of Scripture, where Antichrist is treated, or from the testimony of the adversaries themselves; but whatever follows is not of that kind. For it is either mere conjecture, without any authority of Scripture, as in the claim that Antichrist will be a Jew by race and of the tribe of Dan; or else it comes from allegorical [ἀλληγορουμένοις] passages and their false interpretation, as when he says that he will reign at Jerusalem, and will sit in the temple which was called Solomon's, and will reign for three years and a half; or finally it comes from passages foreign to the subject, as when the words [ἀντίοχος] spoken by Daniel about Antiochus Epiphanes are transferred to the cause of Antichrist, that he will remove all idols, and so on. No good inference can be drawn from a comparison of sayings of this kind. What Irenaeus said from the certain Word of God provides a valid argument; but what comes from human conjecture or uncertain interpretation does not.

Nam Irenæi verborum hunc sensum attulit: Qui seruus est re & professione, & tamen ult adorari quasi Deus, is Antichristus est: Pontifex re & professione seruus est, non etiam seruorum seruum seipsum nominat, & tamen ult adorari quasi Deus: Pontifex ergo Rom. Antichristus est. Assumptionis unum membrum disputator ponit, alterum reticet commodo suo, ut superior esse causa videatur. Probat hoc assumptionis membrum à solenni usu osculandorum pedum: qui honor apud Christianos supra quàm humanus est, diuinus igitur, & à Pontifice exigitur, ult ergo honore diuino affici ut Deus.

Eadem quoque sequentium Hieronymi verborum ratio, vt alibi ostendimus. Aliud tunc Ecclesia Romana fuit, aliud nunc est: non sequitur in causa tam dispari.
units.tr: 6 The pagans speak of Rome, not of Christian Rome, ] We deny that this distinction is relevant, as we have shown in Controversy 3, book 2, chapter 2. For Rome is spoken of simply, as a city and a common place, not as limited by those distinctions. John assigns both times to one and the same Rome in Apoc. 17, and it is not Rome but the Church that he means. Nor is it this Church, but that Church which was then nearer to the times of the Apostles, clinging to the truth and simplicity of Christ. The disputant wishes to deceive through ignorance of the elenchus. The same reasoning applies to the following words of Jerome, as we show elsewhere. The Roman Church was one thing then and is another now. It does not follow in a case so unlike.

units.la: IN CAP. VII.
units.tr: In Chapter VII.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. Quamobrem & hoc inter mendacia numeretur.] non est iusta consequentia ex homonymia vel aequiuocatione sumpta: nam etiam Episcopi interdum in iure Canonico summi Pontifices dicuntur, & obseruauit glossa. Sed auctor libelli ad vsum praesentem respexit: & sensum Gregorii. Neque vero simpliciter dixit ille Pontificem summum, sed coniunctim (quod iste diuidit artificiose) chi ardisce di chiamarsi sommo Pontifice & vni-uersale, id est ad verbum, qui audet nominare sese summum Pontificem & vniuersalem. Bellarminus coniuncta diuidit, inconsequens igitur ex aequiuocatione & diuisione rerum coniunctarum argumentatio.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. Wherefore this too is to be counted among the lies.] The inference is not valid, since it is drawn from a homonym or an equivocation. For even bishops are sometimes called supreme Pontiffs in canon law, and the gloss has noted this. But the author of the pamphlet had regard to present usage, and to the sense of Gregory. Nor did Gregory simply call him "supreme Pontiff," but joined the words together (which the other man artificially divides): who dares to call himself supreme Pontiff and universal, that is, word for word, who dares to name himself supreme Pontiff and universal. Bellarmine divides what is joined, so the argument is inconsequential, resting on equivocation and the division of connected terms.

units.la: 2 Ibid. in eo sensu ab illo accipiebatur, quasi solus ipse esset Episcopus,] negatur, nec vllo ex loco antiquitatis, ne ex Gregorio quidem, haec probari potest interpretatio. Ioannes ille optime sciebat nec solum ieiunatorem se esse, nec solum esse posse Episcopum: nam si solus, quorum fuisset Archiepiscopus? scopus? sed Gregorius figuratè loquutus est, quum ita diceret lib. 4. epist. 38. & sequentibus ibidem explicauit (vt contr. 3. lib. 2. cap. 31. exposuimus) nam aliud est universalem dici communiter, vt dice-bantur Patriarchae, aliud universalem singulariter, de quo Gregorius & Ioannes disputabant.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. in that sense it was taken by him, as if he alone were bishop,] We deny it. This interpretation cannot be proved from any passage of antiquity, not even from Gregory. That John knew very well that he was not only a faster, and could not be the only bishop. For if he were the only one, whose archbishop would he have been? But Gregory spoke figuratively, as he did in book 4, letter 38, and explained it in the following letters (as we set out in Controversy 3, book 2, chapter 31). For it is one thing to be called universal in a general sense, as the patriarchs were called, and another to be called universal in the singular, which is what Gregory and John were disputing about.

units.la: 3 Ibid. appellatio illa in Romanum Pontificem optime quadret] negamus eo sensu quadrare, quo à Bellarmino ethero[?] Pontificiorum dicitur.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. that title fits the Roman Pontiff very well] We deny that it fits in the sense in which Bellarmine uses it for the Papists.

units.la: 4 Ibid. à Concilio Chalcedonensi S. Leoni tributum idem Gregorius refert] ob latum dicit Gregorius: sed fallitur æquiuocatione. Nam οἰκουμενικὸς[?] dicebatur siue universalis quisque Patriarcha respectu collegij Patriarchici, quod collegium ex ordine tum instituto collegium erat cōsilij oecumenici, id est, ad omnes Ecclesias in vniuerso terrarum orbe constitutas pertinentis: huius, inquam, collegij respectu Romanus, Constantinopolitanus, Alexandrinus, & Antiochenus oecumenicus dicebatur iadiu, quum ista Gregorius scriberet. Cum vero Ioannes ille Constantinopolitanus alio sensu acceperit, eumque sensum Gregorius sequutus ita affirmauerit, falsum est quod scribit Gregorius: neque ex actis Chalcedonensis Concilij, quæ exstant, neque ex canonibus, neque ex literis vllis probari potest.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. Gregory reports that the same title was given to St Leo by the Council of Chalcedon] Gregory says so, but he is misled by an equivocation. For οἰκουμενικός [oikoumenikos] was applied to each universal patriarch in relation to the patriarchal college, which was then, by the order established at that time, the college of the ecumenical council, that is, belonging to all the churches established throughout the whole world. In relation to this college, I say, the Roman, Constantinopolitan, Alexandrian and Antiochene patriarchs were already called ecumenical, when Gregory was writing these things. But since that John took it in another sense, and Gregory followed that sense and affirmed it, what Gregory writes is false. It cannot be proved either from the extant acts of the Council of Chalcedon, or from its canons, or from any letters.

units.la: 5 Ibid. non se Episcopum universalem, sed seruum seruorum appellat:] non appellat quidem vulgo, sed præstat semper & se præbet ipsum universalem Episcopum. præterea vocat per æquiualens, quum se vicarium Christi, caput & sponsum Ecclesiæ vocat, contra. 3. lib. 2. cap. vltimo: tum quæ hæc modestia est hominis, qui se quidem non ita vocat, sed, per suos vocari patitur & curat tanto supercilio?hoc Gregorius noluit pati.
units.tr: 5 Ibid. he does not call himself universal bishop, but servant of servants] He does not indeed call himself that in common usage, but he always carries out and presents himself as universal bishop. Moreover, he calls himself by an equivalent title, when he calls himself vicar of Christ, head and bridegroom of the Church, as against 3, book 2, last chapter. Then what modesty is this in a man who does not indeed call himself so, but allows himself to be called so by his own people, and takes care of it with such haughtiness? This is what Gregory refused to allow.

units.la: 6 Ibid. merito illi tribuuntur, qui toti Ecclesiae praepositus est:]haec negantur omnia, Papam toti Ecclesiae esse praepositum, & istud nomen illi merito tribui.
units.tr: 6 Ibid. rightly are they given the title who are set over the whole Church:] All of these things are denied: that the Pope is set over the whole Church, and that this name is rightly given to him.

units.la: 7 Ibid. hoc ipse Antichristus non esset, quod eius praecursor esset, falsa consequutio [illegible, ~12 letters] Nam Gregorius ita loquebatur secundum rationem sui temporis, & nascentis primum istius appellationis, quam Ioannes ille ieiunator dictus sibi arrogabat ex auctoritate Imp Mauricij, & Synodi cuiusdam habitae Constantinopoli. Statuit autem Gregorius, si quis incipit hoc nomen sibi arrogare, eum praecurrere Antichristo, & praenunciare id quod nasciturum est propediem, atque ex isto tumore, quo grauidatus est, exsiturūm. Qui proclamat, inquit, is Antichristo praecurrit: qui autem proclamatur & proclamationem sequitur, is Antichristus est. Proclamant administri & praecursores ipsi, non autem Antichristus: proclamat Bellarminus cum suis gregalibus eo sensu vniuersalem Episcopum, & proclamatur Rom. Pontifex: nonne haec conueniunt cum argumentatione Gregorij? Exponit scribens adConstantiam Augustam lib.4. epist.34. Sed in hac eius, inquit, superbia quid aliud, nisi propinqua iam Antichristi esse tempora designatur? & ad Eusebium Thessalonicensem lib. 7. epist.69. iam (ut videmus) mundi huius termino propinquante in praecursione sua apparuit humani generis inimicus. & similia multa. Ioannes igitur ille, qua proclamabat vniuersalem Episcopum, proclamabat Antichristum prae foribus exsistentem: qua se proclamabat, & nondum proclamabatur obsistentibus Ecclesiis, grauidum vterum suum lethali hoc malo ostendebat, sed cuius ori siue orificio(vt vocant Medici) Ecclesiae aliae Dei, ne pareret, obstruebant. Cauillatur ergo disputator hac defensione sua, cum naturalem ordinem rerum Gregorius indicauerit, & secundum eum loquutus sit. Ioannes, inquit, ille Constantinopolitanus nititur Antichristum: enitetur pollicitas: praecurrit ille, & praecurrent administri, quicunque Episcopum vniuersalem pronunciabunt. Sic postera Ecclesia Rom. Pontificem enixa est vniuersalem Episcopum, cui praeciae & administri operantur. In his Iesuitę sunt, vniuersalem Episcopum contentione maxima pronunciantes. Frustra igitur sequentia.
units.tr: 7 Ibid. this would not be Antichrist himself, because he would be his forerunner, False consequence [illegible, about 12 letters]. For Gregory spoke in this way according to the circumstances of his own time, and of the first emergence of that title, which the man called the faster claimed for himself by the authority of the Emperor Maurice and of a certain synod held at Constantinople. Gregory laid down that if anyone begins to claim this name for himself, he runs before Antichrist and announces what is soon to be born, and what will come forth from that swelling with which he is pregnant. "He who proclaims," he says, "runs before Antichrist; but he who is proclaimed and follows the proclamation is Antichrist." The ministers and forerunners themselves proclaim, not Antichrist. Bellarmine, with his fellow-herd, proclaims the universal bishop in that sense, and the Roman Pontiff is proclaimed. Do not these things agree with Gregory's argument? He explains it in writing to Constantina Augusta, book 4, letter 34: But what, he says, is indicated by this pride of his, except that the times of Antichrist are now near? And to Eusebius of Thessalonica, book 7, letter 69: Now, as we see, with the end of this world drawing near, the enemy of the human race has appeared in his forerunner. And there are many similar passages. So that John, in proclaiming a universal bishop, was proclaiming Antichrist standing at the gates. In so far as he proclaimed himself, and was not yet proclaimed because the Churches opposed him, he was showing his womb pregnant with this deadly evil. But the other Churches of God were stopping up the mouth or orifice of it (as the physicians call it), lest it give birth. The disputant therefore quibbles with this defence of his, although Gregory indicated the natural order of things and spoke according to it. "That John of Constantinople," he says, "strives after Antichrist; he will struggle to fulfil his promises; he runs before, and his ministers will run before, whoever shall pronounce a universal bishop." So the later Church of Rome gave birth to a universal bishop, for whom the forerunners and ministers labour. Among these are the Jesuits, who with the greatest effort proclaim a universal bishop. Therefore what follows is in vain.

units.la: In Cap. VIII.
units.tr: On Chapter VIII.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. & inimico animo quicquid stomachus fugge-rebat euomuisse.] Locus est Synodi Remensis ca. 28. prout Acta eius ante biennium edita sunt Francofurti ad Maenum. Calumniam autem esse quod Bellarminus refert, vt auctoritatem Synodi eleuet, duobus argumentis probabimus: primum quod ipsa Arnulfi Aurelianensis oratio, quae tota in actis legitur, adeo pia & docta & luculenta est, vt tum se ipsa probet satis, tum Synodus illa probauerit: deinde quod eadem acta & apologiam eorum Girbertus ipse edidit, qui postea Siluester II. dictus est, & cuius pietatem eruditionemque aduersus aliorum testimonia Onuphrius asserit in Platinam, atque Bellarminus eum sequutus auctorem, controu. 3. libro 4. cap. 12. Dignissima certe est lectu Arnulfi illius Aurelianensis oratio, indigna tam iniquis censoribus.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. and, with hostile spirit, vomited whatever his bile dictated.] This is from the Synod of Reims, chapter 28, as its Acts were published two years ago at Frankfurt am Main. That Bellarmine's report is a slander, meant to diminish the synod's authority, I will prove by two arguments. First, Arnulf of Orléans' own speech, which is read in full in the Acts, is so pious, learned and lucid that it both proves itself sufficiently and was approved by that synod. Second, Gerbert himself, who was later called Silvester II, published these same Acts together with their defence, and Onuphrius, in his work against Platina, asserts his piety and learning against the testimony of others. Bellarmine, following that author, also does so in Controversy 3, book 4, chapter 12. Arnulf's speech of Orléans is certainly well worth reading, and it is unworthy of such unfair critics.

units.la: 2 Ibid. vnine Episcopo Gallo, an Synodo Episcoporum omnium provincia eiusdem fidem habere oporteat. ] primùm ea non est sententia vnius Episcopi, quam tota Synodus approbauit: deinde verò exemplum quod Bellarminus adfert, non est de sententia vlla, sed tantùm de ratihabitione & comprobatione sententiæ, quam comprobationem omnes iudices in re forensi iustis cognitoribus atque iudicibus, omnes Episcopi & confessus Ecclesiastici debent συνεπιμαρτυρεῖν, nisi iusappellationis interuenerit. Hoc tam Rom. Episcopus debet sententiæ Episcoporum qui iustè & legitimè cognouerint de re aliqua, quàm alij Romano debét. Cognouerat Rom. Episcopus de quibusdam, & ex cognitione excommunicauerat eos: hoc alij comprobant, prout officium ipsorum fuit ex iure communi. Idem si fecissent alij, etiam Rom. Episcopus tenebatur comprobare. Longè dispar est horum exemplorum ratio:cùm in Arnulphi exemplo feratur iudicium, in hoc iudicium latum comprobetur. Nam illic res iudicari ex cognitione certa, hic res iudicata pro veritate haberi solet ex hypothesi vel suppositione cognitionis illius certæ.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. by one bishop of Gaul, or by a synod of all the bishops of a province, ought the same faith to be held.] First, this is not the opinion of one bishop, which the whole synod approved. Second, the example Bellarmine brings is not about any opinion at all, but only about the ratification and confirmation of a judgment. In a legal matter, all judges, all bishops and ecclesiastical assessors ought to co-witness [συνεπιμαρτυρεῖν] such confirmation for lawful investigators and judges who have rightly and legitimately examined some matter, unless an appeal has intervened. The Roman bishop owes this to the judgment of bishops who have rightly and lawfully examined some matter, just as others owe it to the Roman bishop. The Roman bishop had examined certain persons and had excommunicated them on the basis of that examination; others confirmed this, as was their duty under common law. If others had done the same, the Roman bishop too would have been bound to confirm it. The reasoning of these examples is far from alike: in Arnulf's example a judgment is delivered, while in the other a judgment already delivered is confirmed. For there the matter is judged from certain knowledge, whereas here a judged matter is usually held as true on the hypothesis or supposition of that certain knowledge.

units.la: In Cap. IX.
units.tr: On Chapter IX.

units.la: 1 Art.1. Pontificis auctoritatem mirifice prædicant atque defendit. ] vtrumque negamus. Nam etsi Antichristum diserte non vocat, tamen & opera quæ sunt Antichristi frequenter exprobrat, & variè exagitat auctoritatem illius.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. They extol and wonderfully defend the authority of the Pope.] We deny both parts. For although he does not expressly call him Antichrist, he nonetheless often reproaches him for the works of Antichrist, and variously assails his authority.

units.la: 2 Ibid. ita simul diligeret & timeret. ] exordium Bellarminus adfert: & quis nescit mulceri lectoré exordio? at postea quanto flumine inuehit in mala, & proterit auctoritatem illius? vt quum dicit: En quid quò trahere te habent hæ occupationes maledictæ, si tamen pergis ut capistri ita dare te totum illis, nihil tui tibi relinquens. Item, Quid tamen, si te philosophia huic totum repente devoveris? praedecessores tui non ita consueverunt: eris molestus quam pluribus, quasi qui a Patrum vestigiis subito deviaveris. &c. & paulo post: Agitentur causæ, sed sicut oportet. Nam is modus qui frequentatur, exsecrabilis plane, & qui non dico Ecclesiam, sed nec forum deceret. & quæ sequuntur, de consideratione libro I.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. so that he might at the same time love and fear him.] Bellarmine brings forward the opening. And who does not know that a reader is soothed by an opening? But afterwards with what a torrent he rushes against the evils and tramples on his authority, as when he says: Look what these accursed occupations want to drag you into, if you persist in giving yourself wholly to them like a halter, leaving nothing of yourself for yourself. Likewise: What, however, if philosophy has suddenly devoted you wholly to itself? Your predecessors did not so act. You will be a nuisance to very many, as one who has suddenly deviated from the footsteps of the Fathers. And a little later: Let causes be pleaded, but as is fitting. For that method which is commonly followed is plainly detestable, and would not befit the Church, let alone the courts. And what follows, from the book On Consideration, book 1.

units.la: 3 Ibid. nec modo ovium, sed & Pastorum tu unus omnium pastor.] sic Bernardus loquitur ex hypothesi receptæ jam in vulgo interpretationis, ut ampliùs Eugenium afficeret. Demonstrat ipse, quum postea subjicit, Ergo juxta canonas tuos alij in partem solicitudinis, tu in plenitudinem potestatis vocatus es. Sic loquitur ex usu communi receptoque, non ex suo proprie singulari sensu.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. not only of sheep, but you alone are the shepherd of all the shepherds.] Bernard speaks thus on the hypothesis of an interpretation already received among the common people, in order to press Eugenius more. He shows this himself when he goes on to add: Therefore, according to your canons, others were called to a share of the care, but you were called to the fullness of power. So he speaks according to common and received usage, not according to his own peculiar sense.

units.la: 4 Ibid. Orbe, inquit, exeundum ei qui forte volet explorare quæ non ad tuam summi Pontificis pertineant curam.] & hæc ex hypothesi recepti jam in Ecclesia usus, ut modò dicebamus. At Bernardus ibidem quàm grauiter! At quomodo non indecens tibi voluntate pro lege uti, & quia non est ad quem appelleris, potestatem exercere, negligere rationem? Tune major Domino tuo, qui ait, non veni facere voluntatem meam? quamquam non minus detesti quam elati animi est, veluti rationis expertem non pro ratione, sed pro libitu agere: nec judicio agi, sed appetitu. Quid tam bestiale? et si indignum cuiuis utenti ratione vivere ut pecus, quis in te reclore omnium tantam contumeliam naturæ, honoris injuriam ferat? &c. quæ sequuntur plu-rima.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. Let him, says he, go out of the world who perhaps wishes to examine matters which do not pertain to the care of you, the supreme Pontiff.] This too comes from the hypothesis of a usage already received in the Church, as we were just saying. But see how gravely Bernard elsewhere writes in the same place! But how is it not unbecoming for you to use your will as law, and, because there is no one to whom you may appeal, to exercise power and neglect reason? Are you greater than your Lord, who said, I did not come to do my own will? Yet it is no less a mark of a detestable and haughty spirit to act, like one devoid of reason, not by reason but by whim, and to be driven not by judgment but by appetite. What is so bestial? And if it is unworthy for anyone who uses reason to live like cattle, who, O you who rule over all, will bear such an insult to nature and such an injury to honour? And very many things follow.

units.la: 5 Ibid. vicarium Christi, Christum Domini, Deum Pharaonis. ] & haec ab eadem hypothesi profecta: quae non esse quidem Eugenium, sed debere esse pronunciat. sed a veritate Dei sunt illa quae Bernardus intonat: A te tamen mos iste, vel potius mors ista non coepit: in te utinam desinat. Sed reliqua prosequamur. Inter haec tu Pastor procedis deauratus, tam multa circumdatus varietate. Oues [?] quid capiunt? si auderem dicere, daemonum magis quam ouium pascua hac. Scilicet sic facilitabat [?] Petrus, sic Paulus ludebat, & quae sequuntur.
units.tr: 5 Ibid. vicar of Christ, Christ of the Lord, God of Pharaoh.] These too proceed from the same hypothesis, which declares that Eugenius is not indeed these things, but ought to be. But the things Bernard thunders are from the truth of God: Yet this custom, or rather this death, did not begin with you: may it end in you. But let us pursue the rest. Among these things, you, the Pastor, advance gilded, surrounded by so much variety. What do the sheep [?] get? If I dared to say it, these pastures are more those of demons than of sheep. Clearly Peter was thus making light of it, thus Paul was playing, and what follows.

units.la: 6 Ibid. haec quippe huius praerogativa sedis] non est, mirum, si ita ad Innocentium Bernardus scripsit: nam primum ita erat usus illius temporis, quamuis corruptissimus: praeterea id iam olim ex more antiquo obtinuerat (ut dicitur Concilij Nicaeni 1.can.6.) ut in causis publicis & communibus Ecclesiarum Pontifex Rom. appellaretur, tamquam Occidentalis Patriarcha, qui ordinem cognitionum & Conciliorum, bonumque Ecclesiarum pro sua conditione & ratione Ecclesiarum Christi procuraret communicatis cum fratrum consessu consiliis, non iure auctoritatis, sed ordinis ministerio: ut recte ipse quoque Bernardus in libro 1.de consideratione observavit. Conclusionis contumeliam tacendo refellimus. auctorem anonymum Bellarmine, [κείνεσι σφανοῖς?], quum ita proscindis voce.
units.tr: 6 Ibid. for this indeed is the prerogative of this see.] It is no wonder if Bernard wrote thus to Innocent. For first, this was the usage of that time, though very corrupt. Moreover, it had long before been established by ancient custom (as is said in the first Council of Nicaea, canon 6) that in public and common causes of the Churches the Roman Pontiff should be appealed to, as Patriarch of the West, who, with the counsels of the brethren's assembly shared, would look after the order of hearings and of councils and the welfare of the Churches of Christ, according to his position and the reason of the Churches, not by a right of authority but by a ministry of order. Bernard himself rightly observed this in his first book On Consideration. We refute the insult of the conclusion by keeping silent about it. I address the anonymous author Bellarmine [κείνεσι σφανοῖς?], since you tear him apart with such words.

units.la: In Cap. X.
units.tr: On Chapter X.

units.la: 1 Art.1. Ioannes Aventinus auctor sit parum probata fidei] hoc forte concedi posset, siquid de suo
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. John Aventinus is an author of little-proven faith] This might perhaps be conceded if he seemed to say something of his own.

units.la: Auentinus dicere videretur: sed cum illam orationem solum exscripserit, non video cur eius fides reprehendi possit, praesertim cum in principio singulorum librorum auctores laudet qui in manus ipsius peruenerunt. de odio Pontificum quod disputator obiicit, nihil est. Auentinus Germanus fuit, amans Imperij, & genti suæ[?] (vt fit)nonnihil tribuens: sed quis nescit quantis artibus quàm diutissime dignitati Imperij & Germanicæ libertati lint[?] inlidiati[?] Pontifices? id pleraeque omnes historiae ab annis ferme septingentis docent lucu-lentissime, & Auentinum ab ista indigna contumelia purgant.
units.tr: But since he has only copied out that speech, I do not see why his good faith can be called into question, especially since at the start of each book he names the authors whose works came into his hands. As for the hatred of the Popes which the disputant alleges, there is nothing in it. Aventinus was a German, a lover of the Empire, and (as is usual) somewhat partial to his own nation. But who does not know by what arts the Popes have for very many years, nearly seven hundred, been working against the dignity of the Empire and German liberty? Almost all the histories teach this most clearly, and they clear Aventinus of this unworthy charge.

units.la: Quid opus est porrò scribi historias, si nihil, nisi ab auctoribus qui iam exstent publicè, adferri potest? quorsum Romæ Vaticana Bibliotheca est, & aliæ alibi? quorsum vbique regnorum, ciuitatum, & municipiorum acta in tabulariis? Infirma sane solutio:hi tres, aut alij non dixerunt: ergo non ita est. quis sic argumentatur in rebus humanis sapiens?
units.tr: Why, then, should histories be written at all, if nothing may be cited except from authors who are already in print? Why is there a Vatican Library at Rome, and others elsewhere? Why are there records of kingdoms, cities and towns in archives everywhere? This is certainly a weak answer: "these three, or others, did not say it; therefore it is not so." Who among wise men in human affairs reasons like this?

units.la: 2 Ibid. nihil enim tale exstat apud alios historicos, acne ap. ] nihil sequitur ex auctoritate(vt loquuntur) negatiue. Nam alios sibi ad manum fuisse libros Auentinus docet exponitque à quibus habuerit, & apud quos inueniri possint.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. For nothing of the kind is found in other historians, not even in ap. ] Nothing follows negatively from authority, as they put it. For Aventinus tells us that he had other books at hand, and he sets out where he got his material and where those books can be found.

units.la: 3 Ibid. non quid irati homines tunc effutirent, sed vtri bonam causam tuerentur, ]
units.tr: 3 Ibid. not what angry men then blurted out, but which side defended the good cause,

units.la: tertium omittit artifex apprimè necessarium, puta substantiam rei atque veritatem. Nam & irati verum interdicunt & bona causa interdum agitur male & falsis adiumentis. Tria oportet concurrere, bonitatem causæ, veritatem dictorum, & (quoad eius fieri potest) vacuitatem à perturbatione.Sed priora illa duo, quorum alterum omittit disputator, sunt essentialia, tertium contingentis accessionis est:quæ accessio non minus, atque haud scio an magis de iis affirmari possit qui Pontificum defenderunt partes.
units.tr: The author leaves out a third thing that is absolutely necessary, namely the substance of the matter and the truth. For angry men also speak falsely, and a good cause is sometimes pursued badly and with false aids. Three things must come together: the goodness of the cause, the truth of what is said, and (so far as it can be managed) freedom from passion. But the first two, one of which the disputant leaves out, are essential; the third is an incidental addition. And this addition can be affirmed no less, and I am not sure whether it can be affirmed even more, of those who have defended the Popes' side.

units.la: 4 Ibid. Fridericos Imperatores sanctos fuisse, & iniuste à Pontificibus oppugnatos.] sapientes & magnanimos vocat auctor anonymus: sed fefellit Bellarminum adiectio similis ex Apoc. 13. 7. Sed esto, dixerit sanè: profecto de Friderico I. testes sunt multi grauissimi, inter quos Ottho Frisingensis,& Radeuicus. de Friderico II. quem tot calumniis obruerunt iniquè Pontificij, satis dixero, si Auentini verba lib 7. Annalium adduxero. Imperatorem Fridericum secundum, inquit, Cæsarem Augustum, haud dubiè secundum Carolum magnum potentissimum vtilissimumque reipub. Christianæ, atque sine controuersia sapientissimum Principem fuisse, Nicolaus Cusa Episcopus Brixinensis Flamen Rom. vir vndecunque doctissimus testis est, atque Ægidius Romanus, Bituricensis in Gallia Pontifex, philosophus atque Peripateticus insignis: qui in libris quos scripsit de institutione regia ad Francia Occidentalis Imperatores hosce ad illius exemplar properare cohortatur &c. quæ sequuntur.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. that the Emperors Frederick were holy men, and were unjustly attacked by the Popes.] The anonymous author calls them wise and magnanimous men, but Bellarmine has been misled by a similar addition drawn from Rev. 13.7. But granted, let him say so: certainly there are many very weighty witnesses about Frederick I, among them Otto of Freising and Radevicus. As for Frederick II, whom the Papists have unjustly overwhelmed with so many calumnies, I will say enough if I cite the words of Aventinus from book 7 of his Annals: "The Emperor Frederick II, Augustus Caesar, was beyond doubt, after Charlemagne, the most powerful and most useful prince for the Christian commonwealth, and without controversy a most wise prince," says Nicholas of Cusa, bishop of Brixen, a Roman flamen, a man learned in every field, as a witness; and Giles of Rome, archbishop of Bourges in Gaul, a philosopher and distinguished Peripatetic, who in his books on royal institution urges the rulers of Western France to hasten toward that model of his, and so on, as what follows says.

units.la: 5 Ibid. rem ipsam, vt erat, literis prodiderunt.] dicendum potiùs, vt erat perscripta in actis Pontificum,& ab auctoribus Pontificiarum partium: qui gratiam Pontificum productis ipsorum actis, &c suppressis aliis venabantur: nam & hos in omni tempore habuit Germania.Scilicet [illegible, ~20 letters] hæc demum est sapientia, lapis philosophicus.
units.tr: 5 Ibid. they handed down the matter itself, as it was, in writing.] It should rather be said: as it was written up in the records of the Popes, and by authors of the Papal party, who hunted for the Popes' favour by producing their records and suppressing others. For Germany has always had such men too. Certainly [illegible, about 20 letters]. This, at last, is the wisdom, the philosopher's stone.

units.la: 6 Art. 2. qui tamen satis aperte meliorem causam Pontifici tribuit.] consequentia falsa. Nam contrà melius aliquis dixerit, Deum ad poenitentiám & humilitatem eius, quamuis simulatam aut temporariam, respexisse, licet in causa mala. sic Deus olim Achabo fecerat 1.Reg. 21. nihil itaque VVimphelingius Gregorium I X. adiuvat.
units.tr: 6 Art. 2. who nonetheless quite plainly grants the better cause to the Pope.] A false inference. For one might rather say the opposite: God looked upon his penitence and humility, even if feigned or temporary, though his cause was bad. So God once did for Ahab, 1 Kings 21. Therefore Wimpheling does nothing to help Gregory IX.

units.la: 7 Ibid. unde eum percussit Pontifex anathemate, &c. haec omnia ex actis Pontificum, infensissimo-rum Friderici II. hostium, in primis verò Innocen-tij IV. qui in Concilio Lugdunensi quicquid tetri potuit comminisci aut ex adulatorum sermonibus comportare, non dubitauit in Fridericum II. euo-mere. Atqui id etiam videndum fuerat, ut expone-retur, quibus artibus, qua perfidia, quaque violen-tia vsi sunt Pontifices, ut Fridericum illum opprimerent, & quàm gravibus iniuriis exacerbauerint indesinenter animum illius. Extant Petri de vi-neis, quem legatum ad Concilium Lugdunense miserat, epistolæ: extant & Friderici aliquot nuper editæ, ex quibus haec melius cognosci possunt, & ex Auentini Annalibus, quos perscripsit diligentissimè.
units.tr: 7 Ibid. whereupon the Pope struck him with anathema, etc. All these things come from the records of the Popes, who were the most bitter enemies of Frederick II, and above all of Innocent IV, who at the Council of Lyons did not hesitate to pour out in full whatever foul charge he could invent or gather from the words of flatterers against Frederick II. Yet it ought also to have been examined, so that it might be explained by what arts, what treachery and what violence the Popes used to crush that Frederick, and how grievously they continually exasperated his spirit with injuries. There survive the letters of Pietro della Vigna, whom he had sent as envoy to the Council of Lyons; and there survive some letters of Frederick himself, published recently, from which these things can be better known, and from Aventinus's Annals, which he wrote out most diligently.

units.la: 8 Art.3. atque haec sunt videlicet pia illa opera, ob quæ sanctum Imperatorem & unctum Dei aduersarium appellauit,] Krantzius criminationes à Pontificibus obiectas Friderico refert, iniurias quas illi fecerunt, & causas defensionesque Friderici reticet: vtrumque à bono atque fideli historico bona fide referri oportuit, Sed Krantzius Pōtificum[?] fuit beneficiarius: quæ beneficia cursum impediunt ve-ritatis.nobis verò magis amica veritas. Tum historiam temporum eadem fide Bellarminus turbat, vt Fridericum oneret: nam quae hic narrantur pleraque ex Krantzio: si[?] forte, post Gregorij I X.obitum gesta sunt, quid ergo attinent ad brutum illud fulmen quod iaculatus est Gregorius ? Illum autem Imperatorem sanctum non vocat vsquam auctor anonymus: inepta verborum eius interpretatione inscitaque falleris, Bellarmine. hoc tantum est quod dicit, non fore vt cogitata Sixti V. succedant, prout successerunt tempore Ottonum, Henricorum, Ludouicorum & Federicorum sapientum magnanimorumque Impp. contra quos datum fuit Rom. Pontificibus, vt attollerent cornua felicitérque pugnarent, vt contra sanctos & vnctos à Domino, etiamque eos vincerent: respiciens nimirum ad verba Ioannis Apoc.13.7. En tibi Italica illius verba: Onde non ti dee parere strano, se i tuoi rei pensieri non ti possono riuscire come ti sei imaginata, & come ti riuscirono nel tempo degli Ottoni, degli Henrici, de Ludouici, & de Federici(pursaui[?] & magnanimi Imperadori) contra li quali ti su concesso d'alzar le corna, & di combattere felicemente, come contra i santi & vnti dal Signore, anzi di vincergli. sensus enim est, quemadmodum datum est ei pugnare & vincere contra sanctos & vnctos Domini,Apoc. 13.7. Si tamen peruicaciter ita vis accipi, profecto Nicolaus Cusanus & Aegidius Bitu-rix plus fidei obtinebunt apud bonos, quàm inimicorum omnium, vel Pontifi-cum calumniae.
units.tr: 8 Art. 3. and these, of course, are the pious works on account of which he called the Emperor holy and the anointed adversary of God,] Krantz reports the accusations which the Popes brought against Frederick, and the injuries they did him, but he passes over Frederick's causes and defences. Both should have been reported in good faith by a good and faithful historian. But Krantz was a beneficiary of the Popes, and such benefits hinder the course of truth; for us, truth is the better friend. Then Bellarmine disturbs the history of the times with the same lack of faith, in order to burden Frederick. For most of what is narrated here comes from Krantz. And if perhaps these things were done after the death of Gregory IX, what then do they have to do with that empty thunderbolt which Gregory hurled? The anonymous author nowhere calls that Emperor holy. You are mistaken, Bellarmine, through an inept and unskilled interpretation of his words. What he says is only that the designs of Sixtus V would not succeed as they succeeded in the time of the Ottos, Henrys, Ludwigs and Fredericks, wise and magnanimous emperors, against whom the Roman Pontiffs were granted the right to raise their horns and fight successfully, and even to conquer them, as if against the holy and anointed of the Lord. He is plainly looking at the words of John in Rev. 13.7. Here are his Italian words: "So it should not seem strange to you if your evil designs cannot succeed as you imagined, and as they succeeded in the time of the Ottos, the Henrys, the Ludwigs and the Fredericks (wise and magnanimous emperors), against whom you were permitted to raise your horns and fight successfully, as against the holy and anointed of the Lord, indeed to conquer them." For the sense is: just as it was given to him to make war on and conquer the saints and anointed of the Lord, Rev. 13.7. Yet if you insist on taking it so stubbornly, Nicholas of Cusa and Giles of Bourges will surely obtain more credit with good men than the calumnies of all the enemies of the Popes put together.

units.la: IN CAP. II.
units.tr: IN CAP. II.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. Ioachimum Calabrum testem adducit, Eius haec verba sunt: Fu in quel medesimo tempo, molto chiaro & famoso l'Abbate Gioachino di Calabria, il quale chiama egli anchora il Papa Antichristo, & ha illustrata l'Apocalysse di varie pitture & annotationi in vulgare Italiano. id est ferme ad verbum, fuit eo-dem tempore valde clarus & famosus Abbas Ioa-chinus Calaber, qui clamat ipse etiam Papam Antichristum, & illustravit Apocalypsin variis picturis & annotationibus vernaculo sermone Italico. Non dicit auctor ille anonymus, vocari Pontificem Rom. ab eo Antichristum disertis verbis, quod illa nunquam tulissent saecula, sed hoc tantum sibi voluit, ita eum depingere ac si Pontificem Rom. prout est in hoc tempore, clamaret Antichristum esse: quemadmodum etiam idem auctor de Aligherio Dante & aliis asserit. Non adferam quae Henricus Erfordiensis in Chronico cap. 93. de eo asserit, quia librum Euangelij aeterni quidam opus esse Abbatis Ioachimi negant. Omnino certe variis in locis Apocalypseos non disi-mulat Romam fore Babylonem illam spiritualem, nisus Augustini & Hieronymi auctoritate nominatim. Sic partis 2. textu II. in Apoc. 6.12. Babylonem illam alloquens, lege vigilanter, in-quit, in operibus Patrum, si Petri & Ioannis testimo-nio nescis: lege inquam in operibus Hieronymi & Augustini, & quid de te scriptum sit, aut quae tu sis, ex illorum tibi poterit aperiri sententiis. & partis 6. textu 13. dicit: non solum ex auctoritate huius libri & ex praesente loco traditum est nobis à Patribus, quod Roma fit in spiritu Babylon, verumetiam exfententia Petri, qui scribens aliquibus ex urbe Roma, salutat vos, inquit, Ecclesia quae est in Babylone. In eadem vero fore bestiam secundam, quae & Pseudo-propheta dicitur, locis aliquot profitetur: imo & textu 2.eiusdem partis pronunciat. Reges terrae esse Praelatos Ecclesiarum, quorum aliqui fornicantur cum Babylone. Pontifices certe in Praelatis Ecclesiarum censentur, si quisquam. Coniungantur quae dicit idem in parte 2.textu 11. Audiant ergo, velint nolint, audiant quod experturi sunt filij potentissima meretricis, antequam vadant, & non reuertantur, ad terram tenebrosam & opertam mortis caligine. Audiant, inquam, audiant falsi Christiani, quorum occasione agitur ut veri Christiani coronentur martyrio. Ipsi enim Reges, qui percussuri sunt fornicariam, ut emundent superficiem terrae, ipsi (ut ostenditur in sexta parte) pugnaturi sunt cum Agno, &c. Reges isti, inquit, Praelati sunt, & cum Agno pugnaturi: quid hic facturus Pontifex? nam Praelatorum est caput secundum ipsos. Ad haec & similia respicere Bellarminum oportuit, non auctoris anonymi illius torquere verba.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. He cites Joachim of Calabria as a witness. His words are these: There was at the same time a very clear and famous Abbot Joachim of Calabria, who also calls the Pope Antichrist, and has illustrated the Apocalypse with various pictures and annotations in the Italian vernacular. That is, almost word for word: There was at the same time a very famous Abbot Joachim of Calabria, who himself also proclaims the Pope Antichrist, and has illustrated the Apocalypse with various pictures and annotations in the Italian vernacular language. That anonymous author does not say in so many words that the Roman Pontiff is called Antichrist by him. Such a thing would never have been tolerated in those ages. He meant only this: that Joachim portrays him so, as if he were proclaiming that the Roman Pontiff, as he is at this time, is Antichrist. The same author makes the same claim about Dante Alighieri and others. I will not cite what Henry of Erfurt says about him in his Chronicle, chapter 93, since some deny that the book of the Eternal Gospel is a work of Abbot Joachim. Certainly, in various places of his commentary on the Apocalypse, he does not hide that Rome will be that spiritual Babylon, relying expressly on the authority of Augustine and Jerome. Thus in part 2, text 11, on Apocalypse 6.12, addressing that Babylon: Read carefully, he says, in the works of the Fathers, if you do not know it from the testimony of Peter and John: read, I say, in the works of Jerome and Augustine, and what has been written about you, and what you are, can be revealed to you from their opinions. And in part 6, text 13, he says: It has been handed down to us by the Fathers not only on the authority of this book and from the present passage that Rome becomes Babylon in spirit, but also from the saying of Peter, who, writing to some from the city of Rome, says: "The Church which is in Babylon salutes you." In several places he professes that the second beast, also called the False Prophet, will be in the same city. Indeed, in text 2 of the same part he pronounces: The kings of the earth are the prelates of the Churches, some of whom commit fornication with Babylon. Certainly the Popes are counted among the prelates of the Churches, if anyone is. Let what he says in part 2, text 11, be joined to this: Let them hear, then, whether they will or not, let them hear what the sons of the most powerful harlot are about to experience, before they go and do not return, to the dark land covered with the gloom of death. Let them hear, I say, let them hear, false Christians, on whose account it comes about that true Christians are crowned with martyrdom. For the very kings who are going to strike the harlot, so as to cleanse the surface of the earth, they themselves (as is shown in the sixth part) are going to fight with the Lamb, etc. These kings, he says, are prelates, and are going to fight with the Lamb. What will the Pontiff do here? For according to them he is the head of the prelates. Bellarmine ought to have looked at these and similar passages, not twisted the words of that anonymous author.

units.la: 2 Ibid. ut contra potius frequenter de illo summo cum honore scripserit. Scripsit quidem honorifice de Pontifice, ut Rom. Episcopo, respectu vocationis, tum verae illius qua Episcopus Rom. Ecclesiae fuit, tum istius praesumptae, qua πνευματικὸς[?] iam eo tempore credebatur: sed aliud est, quum agit de eo secundum vocationem illam in temporibus illis praecedentibus apertionem sigilli sexti, ut ipse loquitur: aliud quum agit de eodem subsequutis temporibus post apertionem illius, quum Solem, & Lunam in tenebras versum iri, & stellas de cae-lo casulo casuras pronunciat. Non pugnant,quæ diuersa ratione, & de diuerso tempore dicta sunt.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. that he has rather often written of that man with the highest honour. He did indeed write honourably of the Pope as Bishop of Rome, with regard to the calling, both the true one by which he was Bishop of the Roman Church and the supposed one by which he was already then believed to be [πνευματικὸς] spiritual. But it is one thing when he speaks of him according to that calling in those earlier times, before the opening of the sixth seal, as he himself puts it; it is another when he speaks of the same man in the times that follow its opening, when he declares that the sun and moon will be turned into darkness and the stars will fall from heaven. These statements are not inconsistent, since they were made for different reasons and about different times.

units.la: 3 Ibid. neque vsque ad consummationem mundi fidem eius vllo vnquam tempore perituram. ] & nosidem credimus profitemurque de vera Ecclesia Romana & proprie dicta, non autem de æquiuoca Papali. Distinguit ipse Ioachimus Abbas disertis verbis,quum ait partis 6. textu 5.ciuitas quæ dicta est Babylon,non tantum Romana ciuitas existimanda est aut ipsa (quod absit) secundum totum, sed vniuersa multitudo hominum impiorum & natorum secundum carnem,de quibus dicit Apostolus: sicut tunc qui secundum carnem natus fuerat, persequebatur eum qui secundum Spiritum, ita & nunc. communis videlicet ciuitas, sed in qua maior pars meliorem vincit, communis vterus in quo nascuntur Iacob & Esau, vt ibidem dicit textu 13. Itaque vt veram Ecclesiam docet permansuram Romæ, ita & falsam illam subituram docet iudicium Dei : vt textu 17.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. nor will his faith ever perish at any time until the end of the world. We too believe and profess this of the true Church of Rome, properly so called, and not of the equivocal Papal church. Abbot Joachim himself distinguishes this in express words when he says in part 6, text 5: The city which is called Babylon is not to be regarded as only the city of Rome, or, which God forbid, as the whole of it, but as the entire multitude of impious men and of those born according to the flesh, of whom the Apostle says: "As then he who was born according to the flesh persecuted him who was according to the Spirit, so also now." It is, namely, a common city, but one in which the greater part overcomes the better, a common womb in which Jacob and Esau are born, as he says in the same place, text 13. So, just as he teaches that the true Church will remain at Rome, so he teaches that the false one will undergo the judgment of God, as in text 17:

units.la: Verumtamen quia causa tantorum scelerum in vrbe fornicaria principaliter manet, ad iustum superni iudicis pertinet examen, vt magna illa meretrix quæ prouocat alios ad delictum, iudicetur prius, qui autem seducti sunt ab ea, referuntur ad luctum, &c. sic alibi.
