Et huic falsæ præfuturum caput pronunciat part. 4. textu 13. dicens: sic verisimile videtur, quod sicut bestia illa quæ ascendit de mari habitura est quemdam magnum Regem de sella sua, qui sit similis Neronis, & quasi Imperator totius orbis, ita bestia quæ ascendet de terra habitura sit quemdam magnum Prælatum, qui sit similis Simonis Magi, & quasi vniuersalis Pontifex in toto orbe terrarum, & ipse sit ille Antichristus de quo dicit Paulus, quod extollitur & aduersatur supra omne quod dicitur Deus,&c.
units.tr: Yet because the cause of so great crimes chiefly remains in the fornicating city, it belongs to the just examination of the supreme Judge that that great harlot, who provokes others to sin, be judged first; but those who have been seduced by her are referred to mourning, etc. So also elsewhere. And he pronounces that this false church will have a head, in part 4, text 13, saying: So it seems likely that, just as that beast which rises from the sea is going to remove from his seat a certain great king, like Nero, and as it were emperor of the whole world, so the beast which rises from the earth is going to have a certain great prelate, who is like Simon Magus, and as it were universal Pontiff in the whole world, and he himself is that Antichrist of whom Paul says that he exalts himself and sets himself against everything that is called God, etc.

units.la: 4 Ibid. Babylonis se filios contremiscant] recte: nam agit de Ecclesia impiorum quae est Romae, abs qua veram Ecclesiam distinxerat, ut proxime in nota 3.retulimus.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. let the sons of Babylon tremble] rightly so: for he is speaking of the church of the impious, which is at Rome, and from which he had distinguished the true Church, as we noted just above in note 3.

units.la: 5 Ibid. Romanum Pontificem intelligendum esse dicit, ] non affirmat Abbas, sed proponit hypothetice per disiunctionem: si Angelus iste (Christus est, &c. & paulo post: quod si Angelus iste Romanus Pontifex intelligendus est, &c. est autem omnino vera prior interpretatio. Præterea si daretur (quod tamen falsum est) ageret tantum de Pontifice uno aliquo illius aetatis, non de ordine Pontificum seculis istis futuro communiter. Est igitur solutio & falsa, & inconsequens.
units.tr: 5 Ibid. he says that the Roman Pontiff is to be understood] the Abbot does not affirm this, but puts it forward hypothetically by way of alternatives: if that angel (is Christ), etc., and a little later: but if that angel is to be understood as the Roman Pontiff, etc. The former interpretation is altogether true. Moreover, even if it were granted (which is in fact false), he would be speaking only of one particular Pontiff of that age, not of the order of Pontiffs to come in common throughout these ages. The solution is therefore both false and inconsequential.

units.la: 6 Ibid. cum adversarius locum nullum attulerit pro mendacio suo?] strictim videlicet attingebat auctor, Ioachimi Calabri sensum: cuius locos aliquot modò attulimus. Hæc igitur satis, ut à mendacio vindicetur. Sequentia omnia nihil ad nos.
units.tr: 6 Ibid. since the opponent has produced no passage in support of his lie?] The author was, of course, only touching briefly on the meaning of Joachim of Calabria, whose several passages we have just now cited. So much, then, is enough to clear him of lying. Everything that follows is of no concern to us.

units.la: In Cap. XII.
units.tr: On Chapter XII.

units.la: 1 Art. 2. si carmina amatoria, si fabulas, si somnia scripserunt, unde illis auctoritas tanta, ut contradici neque at?] si per omnia consistere horum auctoritatem dixisset ille & in omni argumento esse inluctabilem, ut est Scripturae sacrae auctoritas, verum disputator dicturus esset. Sed iniquè facit, qui rem enunciatam κατὰ[?] de hac particulari causa, ita accipit universe: nam etiam homo nequam potest verum pro testimonio dicere, & firmum eius testimoniem dicere, similiterque scriptor a-morum, imo & ridicularius testimonium ita per-
units.tr: 1 Art. 2. If they wrote love songs, fables, and dreams, whence do they have such authority that they cannot be contradicted?] If he had said that their authority holds good in every respect and is unshakeable in every matter, as the authority of Holy Scripture is, the disputant would be right to object. But he acts unfairly who takes a statement made [κατὰ] about this particular case as if it were made universally. For even a worthless man can tell the truth as a witness, and his testimony can be firm; and likewise a writer of love poems, or even a comic writer, may write in such a way that his testimony cannot be contradicted. He does not speak of testimony in general, but of the testimony of this particular matter.

units.la: κατὰ[?]: the Greek word is printed in small type and is doubtful; read as best possible. scribere ut ei nequeat contradici. Non enim de quouis testimonio universè dicit, sed de argumenti huius testimonio singulariter.
units.tr: [Editor's note: the Greek word κατὰ[?] is printed in small type and is doubtful; read as best possible.] ...write in such a way that he cannot be contradicted. For he does not speak of any testimony whatever in general, but of the testimony on this particular subject alone.

units.la: 2 Ibid. ut suo loco ostendam, ] negantur ista, de quibus in cap.14. videbitur, & capitibus seq.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. as I will show in its place.] These claims, which will be seen in chapter 14 and the following chapters, are denied.

units.la: 3 Ibid. cum donationem Constantini & lepram eius Baptismo curatam affirmat? ] neque fidem non habendam esse Danti affirmat auctor ille, neque illa à Constantino & Siluestro facta historicè referre Dantem, sed tantum ex hypothesi sermonis publici refert poëticè quæ ad argumentum suum pertinebant: præsertim, cùm iam fabula donationis illius in corpus iuris canonici relata esset, quam tamen ipsi Canonistæ conscientia quadam falsitatis Paleam inscripserunt, distinct. 96.c. Constantinus
units.tr: 3 Ibid. since he affirms Constantine's donation and his leprosy cured by baptism?] That author does not affirm that Dante should not be believed, nor does Dante relate historically that those things were done by Constantine and Silvester. He reports poetically, merely on the basis of the public talk, what pertained to his argument. This is especially so since the fable of that donation had already been carried into the body of canon law, where the canonists themselves, with a certain awareness of its falsity, entitled it the Palea, Dist. 96, c. Constantinus.

units.la: II. Sequutus est poëta, inquit auctor ille anonymus, communem opinionem, quòd Constantinus imp.[?] conuersus ad fidem temporali Ecclesiam donauerit: sed non inuenitur in vlla historia, &c. historici rerum veritatem exponunt, poëtæ etiam communes opiniones adferunt, atque eisdem superstruunt. Quapropter festiuè idem ipse Dantes poëtica licentia illudens narratione[?] isti & opinioni communi, cant. 20. de paradiso, fingit aquilam imperij dicentem de Constantino magno Imperatore:
units.tr: II. The poet followed, says that anonymous author, the common opinion that the Emperor Constantine, converted to the faith, gave the Church temporal possessions; but it is not found in any history, etc. Historians set out the truth of events; poets also bring forward common opinions and build upon them. Therefore Dante himself, playfully mocking that narrative and common opinion with poetic licence, in Paradiso canto 20, feigns the eagle of the empire speaking of the Emperor Constantine the Great:

units.la: L'altro, che seque con le leggi, & meco: Sotto buona intention, che se mal frutto, Per ceder al Pastor, si sece Greco: Hora conosce, comme'l mal dedutto Dal suo ben operar, non gli e nociuo, Auegna che sia'l mondo indi distrutto.
units.tr: The other, who follows with the laws and with me, under a good intention which bore bad fruit, made himself a Greek by yielding to the Shepherd. Now he sees how the evil drawn from his good work does him no harm, though the world has been destroyed by it.

units.la: id autem est ferme ad verbum, Alter (nimirum Constantinus) qui sequitur Davidem cum legibus mecum (verba sunt imperialis aquilae) Sub bona intentione, quæ facit malum fructum. Ad cedendum Pastori Siluestro Papæ,se fecit, Græcum,id est,migra-uit in Græciam, & statuit imperium Constantinopoli: Iam cognoscit quomodo malum deductum De sua bona operatione, nimirum luxus & depravatio Ecclesiæ ex bonorum, honorumque & potestatis copia,non est ipsi noxiu, Utut eueneritesse mundum ex eo destructum & euersum, puta illa quæ dicitur Constantini munificentia, quum Ecclesia occasione ista ruit in perditionem indignissimam. Non temere Landinus alicubi in Dantem, proprium esse poetarum adfirmat mentiri: quemadmodum & Tullius libro de legib. 1. eos inique affirmat facere, qui veritatem desiderant in operibus eiusmodi. Hoc auctor anonymus in Dante obseruauit: non eum reprehendit aut accusat falsi,quod poetam egerit.
units.tr: That is almost word for word: "The other" (namely Constantine), "who follows David with the laws with me" (these are the words of the imperial eagle), "under a good intention, which produces bad fruit. By yielding to the Shepherd," that is, to Pope Silvester, "he made himself a Greek," that is, he migrated into Greece and set up the empire at Constantinople. "Now he knows how the evil drawn from his good work," namely the luxury and corruption of the Church from the abundance of goods, honours and power, "does him no harm, though the world is destroyed and overturned by it," that is, by what is called Constantine's munificence, when the Church, on that occasion, fell into a most unworthy ruin. Landino, in more than one place on Dante, rightly affirms that it is the characteristic of poets to lie, and Cicero in the first book of the Laws says that those who look for truth in works of this kind act unjustly. The anonymous author has observed this in Dante; he does not reprehend or accuse him of falsehood for doing what a poet does.

units.la: 4 Ibid. Ait deinde Papæ domesticos fuisse.] sic loquutus est auctor συνεκδοχικῶς[?] caussa compendij: quam rationem in omni sermone translatitiam esse nouerunt omnes.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. He then says that they were the household of the Pope.] The author has spoken synecdochically [συνεκδοχικῶς] for the sake of brevity, a figure which everyone knows is common in every kind of discourse.

units.la: 5 Ibid. Dantes enim factione Gibellinus, non modo non domesticus, sed etiam hostis Pontificum fuit.] fuisse factione Gibellinum, falsum est. Contra enim testis est Landinus in vita illius, tam æquo animo fuisse Dantem, ut Guelphos in duas factiones diuisos, Alborum & Nigrorum, conciliare tentauerit prudentia & auctoritate summa, quumque frustra tentari à se animaduerteret, officio Prioris (qui tum summus in repub. Florentina magistratus fuit) sese abdicasse. Idem etiam Vellutellus adfirmat luculentius. Et quamuis postea iniurias pergraueis pro optimis illis officiis accepisset, quibus exsul etiam apud aduersarios viuere coactus est, tamen nulla vnquam perturbatione ab illa equitate animi abduci se passus est, vt iidem auctores docent, & ipse in omnibus scriptis suis testatur constantissime. Apud Gibellinos vixit, quum a Guelphis Florentia exclusus esset auctore Comite Ga-briellio, qui tum summam potestatem in repub. obtinebat, & Dynastes erat: sed nunquam eius a-nimus fuit immutatus, quin omnium conciliatio-ni & paci publicae studuerit. Hostem Pontificum fuisse quis credat hominem erga omneis amantissimum atque officiosissimum? Contra vero Landi-nus, Vellutellus, & Sansouinus uno ore testantur, quum Bonifacius Pontifex reconciliandis inter se Florentinis operam adhiberet Caroli Valesij, & de rebus Florentinorum inter se digladiantium Ca-rolus in urbe cognosceret, fuisse Dantem per illud tempus Romae, paulo ante oratorem missum ad Pontificem, vt gratias ageret de concordia & pace ciuium, cuius pacis auctor fuerat Bonifacius. quis hostem gratias acturum oratorem mittat? nisi quis forte ex Poli-tio Marrucinorum oriundus hoc imprudens factum Florentinae genti tribuerit.
units.tr: 5 Ibid. For Dante, a Ghibelline in party, was not only not of the household, but was even an enemy of the Pontiffs.] That he was a Ghibelline in party is false. On the contrary, Landino bears witness in his life of him that Dante was so even-minded that, when the Guelphs were divided into two factions, the Whites and the Blacks, he tried with great prudence and authority to reconcile them; and when he perceived that his attempt was in vain, he withdrew from the office of Prior (who was then the highest magistrate in the Florentine republic). Vellutello also affirms the same, more clearly. And although afterwards he received grievous injuries in return for those excellent services, and was forced to live in exile even among his opponents, yet he never allowed himself to be drawn away from that equanimity by any disturbance, as the same authors teach, and as he himself testifies most constantly in all his writings. He lived among the Ghibellines when he had been excluded from Florence by the Guelphs, through the agency of Count Gabriellino, who then held the chief power in the republic and was a lord; but his mind was never so changed that he did not strive for the reconciliation of all and for public peace. Who could believe that a man so loving and so dutiful towards everyone was an enemy of the Pontiffs? On the contrary, Landino, Vellutello and Sansovino testify with one voice that when Pope Boniface was working to reconcile the Florentines among themselves, and Charles of Valois was taking cognisance of the affairs of the Florentines who were fighting among themselves in the city, Dante was at Rome at that time, having been sent shortly before as envoy to the Pope, to give thanks for the concord and peace of the citizens, whose author Boniface had been. Who would send as envoy to give thanks a man who was an enemy? Unless perhaps someone, a native of Pollutium in the land of the Marrucini, were to attribute this blunder to the Florentine people.

units.la: 6 Ibid. antiquior & doctior S. Bernardus fuit.] at Christus antiquissimus est & doctissimus omnium, antiquiores & doctiores Apostoli, &c. qui summi istius Pontificis dignitatem nesciuerunt, & fuissent euersuri, si vel emergentem ex suis tenebris a-nimaduertissent felice illo seculo, cui infelices tenebrae postea successerunt.
units.tr: 6 Ibid. St Bernard was older and more learned.] But Christ is the oldest and most learned of all, and the Apostles are older and more learned, who did not know the dignity of this supreme Pontiff, and would have overthrown it had they noticed it even emerging from its darkness in that happy age, after which unhappy darkness followed.

units.la: 7 Ibid. cum Petrarcham & Bocacium a morum sanctitate vitaque integritate laudari vidi.] Iniquus es, Bellarmine (non dico, ridiculus) qui leuitate aliqua aut infirmitate iuvetutis adspergis tota bono-rum vitam, aut eorum certè qui anteactum malu suu bona & honesta consequente administratione, vitæque mutatæ instituto deleuerunt. Nam ii [?] ab illo primo incendio Petrarchæ discesseris, quod iuuenis expertus est, neminem postea modestiorem ca-stioremve exstitisse, auctor est Hieronymus Squar-zafichus, & Gesualdus in vita illius, & omnes boni consentiunt, & ipse Petrarcha narrat quàm simplicissimè. Quapropter non malè de eo Latomus apud P. Iouium cecinit hos versus:
units.tr: 7 Ibid. When I saw Petrarch and Boccaccio praised for the holiness of their morals and the integrity of their lives.] You are unfair, Bellarmine (I do not say ridiculous), when you besmirch the whole life of good men with some levity or the weakness of youth, or at least of those who have wiped out their former wrongdoing by a good and honest administration and by a changed manner of life. For Girolamo Squarciafico reports, and Gesualdo in his life of him, and all good men agree, and Petrarch himself relates most simply, that after the first fire of Petrarch's youth, he was afterwards the most modest and chaste of men. Therefore Latomus, in Paolo Giovio, sang these verses about him not badly:

units.la: Qui tanta Hetrusci carminis dulcedine, Tamque æstuosis vexeris præconius Tuam puellam, vt nemo te non crederet Flagrare quantis nec vel Ætna incendiis, Atque idem amoris frigidus neglexeris Quem spectat omnis amans, vel in tenebris, scopu: Amasse Lauram, an Lauream te dixerim?
units.tr: You who with the sweetness of Tuscan song, and with such burning praise, celebrated your girl, so that everyone would believe you were aflame with fires greater than Etna's; and yet, cold in love, you neglected the mark at which every lover aims even in the dark: should I call you a lover of Laura, or of the laurel?

units.la: Incendium ætatis in Petrarcha probitas & castitas vitæ reliquæ exstinxit illico, nisi tu, Bellarmine, & tui similes velletis stilo maledico in posteritatem illud redardescere, ut solùm in vobis scilicet casti-tas & pudicitia esse videatur. De Ioanne Boccacio, iudicium idem: nihil enim ex vlla proba historia adferri potest, vnde probes morum sanctitatem & vitæ probitatem, prout tum vita fuit hominum ab illo abfuisse. At scripserunt amores, inquies, iste alienos, & ille suos. Agnosco: sed ille suæ ætati ser-vivit, quod postea expunxit vitæ sanctimonia, iste seculo servivit suo, quod hoc scribendi genere, iro-nico atque satyrico, magis informari putauit pos-se, quàm si directum coluisset scribendi modum.
units.tr: The fire of youth in Petrarch was at once extinguished by the probity and chastity of the rest of his life, unless you, Bellarmine, and men like you, wish by your malicious pen to rekindle it for posterity, so that chastity and modesty seem to exist only in yourselves. The judgement is the same concerning Giovanni Boccaccio: for nothing can be brought from any sound history by which you could prove holiness of morals and integrity of life, such as was not far from the men of his time. But you will say that he wrote of other men's loves, and the other of his own. I grant it. But the one served his age, which the sanctity of later life afterwards erased; the other served his own age, which he thought could be better informed by this ironic and satirical kind of writing than if he had cultivated a direct manner of writing.

units.la: Multum enim refert in agendo, quod ex Pindaro dicit Tullius ποτερον δίκας τεχας ὕψιον ἢ σχολικὰς ἀπει-τας colas. In seculo culpa, non in Boccacio fuit, qui seculo suo debitum, ut potuit, per mores seculi illius sui, non ut voluit, exsolvebat.
units.tr: For much depends on the manner of acting, as Cicero says from Pindar [ποτερον δίκας τεχας ὕψιον ἢ σχολικὰς ἀπει-τας colas]. The fault lies in the age, not in Boccaccio, who paid to his age what he could, through the manners of his own age, and not as he wished.

units.la: 8 Ibid. talibus videlicet sanctis Prophetis digni sunt Lutherani & Caluinistae. ] una voce respondemus ad ista omnia, CALVMNIA est respiciant in se ipsos Pontificij, & tacebunt. In hoc genere disputationum qui magis sapiunt, priores tacent. αὐτοχολωρεῖν[?] non est nostrum.
units.tr: 8 Ibid. such holy Prophets, namely, the Lutherans and the Calvinists are worthy of.] We answer all these things in one word: it is SLANDER. Let the Papists look at themselves and they will fall silent. In this kind of dispute, those who are wiser keep quiet. To be angry with oneself [αὐτοχολωρεῖν[?]] is not our business.

units.la: 9 Ibid. Istud, credo, Euangelium ab Antistite vestro Beza didicistis, ] falleris, Bellarmine. nescivit Euangelium adolescens Beza: didicit vir, & docet ad extremam senectam usque magno dolore vestro. quod autem adolescens fecit, aut primo juventutis flore, qua fide, quo iure nunc reponis viro & seni, qui jam annos quasi sexaginta & precibus coram Deo & professione religiosa coram universo mundo, & diligentia summa exstinxit sepelivitque pia mente maculas quas vos impie & inhumane cupitis suscitatas, totisque viribus revocatis ante ora & oculos omnium? Hoc non Bezę crimen est, deleuit jamdiu: vestrum crimen est, qui res ab ipso Beza, jam olim damnatas revocatis, sepultas refoditis, denique non potestis ferre, ut malum ἀ κειμένου[?] & ab ipso auctore sexcenties jugulatum non moveatur amplius, quod vulgo dici solet. Nō hominum, dirarum est hoc opus Eumenidū, quod faciunt vestri. Si exstant enim adhuc, per quos exstant, obsecro? non per Bezam, qui jam olim confixit atque eiurauit: non per nostros, qui Bezæ pietate virile senilemque amplectimur, & illa ipsa pie, quæ ille refugit damnatque refugimus: sed per vestros sycophantas exstant, patronos scilicet pietatis vestrę, qui leuia alienæ adolescentiæ carmina odiis puerilibus & veteratoriis artibus resuscitant, postquam tamdiu & religiosè ab ipso auctore sepulta sunt. Ita fecerunt iam aliquoties Colonienses vestri, vt ægrè auctori, malè Ecclesiæ facerent: duplices plane τυμβώρυχοι, qui & ossibus mortuorum & carminibus viuentium iam olim sepultis putribúsque sacrilegas iniiciunt manus.
units.tr: 9 Ibid. I believe you learned that gospel from your leader Beza,] You are mistaken, Bellarmine. The young Beza did not know the gospel; he learned it as a man, and he has taught it into extreme old age, to your great grief. But what the young man did, in the first flower of his youth, on what faith, by what right do you now lay against a man and an old man, who for nearly sixty years, both in prayer before God and in his public profession before the whole world, and with the greatest diligence, has by a devout mind wiped out and buried the stains which you wickedly and inhumanely wish to revive, and with all your strength you drag back before the eyes and faces of everyone? This is not Beza's crime; he blotted it out long ago. The crime is yours, who revive things long since condemned by Beza himself, dig up what was buried, and finally cannot bear that an evil which lay dead, and was slain by its own author six hundred times over, should not be stirred any more, as the common saying goes. This work is not of men but of dire Eumenides, which your people do. For if these things still exist at all, by whom do they exist, I beg you? Not by Beza, who long ago pierced them through and renounced them; not by us, who embrace Beza's piety as a man and an old man, and we reject what he shunned and condemned in that same piety. No, they exist through your sycophants, the patrons, namely, of your piety, who revive the light songs of another man's youth with childish hatreds and the tricks of hired hacks, after they have been so long and so devoutly buried by the author himself. Your Cologne men have already done this several times: they were doing harm to the author with difficulty and to the Church with ease. They are plainly double tomb-robbers, who lay sacrilegious hands both on the bones of the dead and on the songs of the living, long since buried and rotting.

units.la: Ibid. nisi vt formam Bethsabeæ impudicissimam (vt fecit) nobis depingeret. ]vtrumque falsum, & scriptum ita se habere, & ita fuisse consilium Bezæ. criminatio falsa, cuius nec tu aliquem dicas, ô Quintiliane, colorem, nec tu, Bellarmine, facias, etiamsi Quintilianus esses. Sed hîc verum est de te quod vulgò dici solet, οὐδεὶς χομήτης, ὅστις οὐ ψηνίζεται.
units.tr: Ibid. unless he depicted for us the most shameless form of Bathsheba (as he did).] Both claims are false, both the claim that the text reads so and the claim that this was Beza's intention. It is a false accusation, and you, O Quintilian, could not offer any colour for it, nor could you, Bellarmine, even if you were Quintilian. But here what the common saying says is true of you: [οὐδεὶς χομήτης, ὅστις οὐ ψηνίζεται] (there is no one who is not a fool in his own way).

units.la: Ibid. quos censura Ecclesiæ catholicæ legi ob impuritatem & corruptelam iuuentutis prohibet. ]Si ob impuritatem & corruptelam iuuentutis, cur ergo non prohibet illa Petrarchæ & Boccacij, quos ante damnauit eo nomine Aristarchus nouus? cur aliorum amatorios, lasciuos, spurcos libros auctorum amplius mille non prohibet? cur Bezæ amatorios, quos ipse damnauit quum primùm sapere cœpit, tanta diligentia cudi & recudi iubet? Cur etiam in amatoriis nō refingit quod lasciuū, turpe, & spurcū est, sed tantùm id quod monachos vel monachas, clerum & Ecclesiasticos tāgit? spurcitiā non sustulit, exempli causa, in Decamero Boccacij Ecclesiæ vestra, aut censura Ecclesiastica, sed tantùm eorum nomina qui spurcè fecisse in vestro ordine dicebantur. bantur. Sic enim auctor anonymus recte & verè annotavit, nomina eiusmodi expuncta esse, & alia substituta, sed integram spurcitiæ narrationem permansisse, si Nouellam 2. primi diei (quam totam, quia emendari ex animi sententia non poterat, expunxerunt) Nouellamque 6. diei 6. exceperis. Exempli causa, Nouella 4. eiusdem diei, quum inscriptio esset huiusmodi: Monachus lapsus in peccatum dignum punitione grauissima, honestè exprobrando Abbati suo eamdem culpam, se liberat à pœna: reposuerunt illi censores probi: Scholaris lapsus in peccatum, &c. exprobrando magistro suo eamdem culp. &c. narrationem cæteris in rebus intactam reliquerunt. Et hi boni Monachorum patroni in Scholaris sunt hoc pacto iniurij. Item nouella 1. diei 5. &c. quæ auctor ille anonymus obseruauit diligentissimè. Hem pietatem & sapientiam. Itane vero? impietatem, spurcitiam, turpitudinem censura vestra palam doceri sinet, modò suorum nomina dissimulata sint? Hi scilicet castitatis & pietatis Antistites, quorum censura id curat, vt impuritas & corruptela iuuentutis exstet in scriptis eiusmodi publicè, modò ne religiosæ illæ animæ in hanc-scenam dicantur prodiisse, aut consortes Ecclesia-stici.
units.tr: Ibid. which the censure of the Catholic Church forbids to be read on account of the impurity and corruption of youth.] If it forbids them on account of the impurity and corruption of youth, why then does it not forbid those of Petrarch and Boccaccio, whom the new Aristarchus condemned earlier on that very ground? Why does it not forbid the amatory, lascivious and filthy books of more than a thousand other authors? Why does it order Beza's love poems, which he himself condemned as soon as he began to be wise, to be printed and reprinted with such great diligence? Why also, in love stories, does it not recast what is lascivious, shameful and filthy, but only what touches monks or nuns, the clergy and churchmen? Your Church, or its ecclesiastical censure, did not remove the filth, for example, from Boccaccio's Decameron; it removed only the names of those who were said to have behaved filthily in your order. For the anonymous author has correctly and truly observed that such names were struck out and others put in their place, but the whole account of the filth remained intact, except for the second story of the first day (which they removed entirely, since it could not be emended to their satisfaction) and the sixth story of the sixth day. For example, the fourth story of the same day, whose title was as follows: A monk who has fallen into a sin deserving the most severe punishment, by honestly reproaching his abbot for the same fault, frees himself from punishment: those upright censors replaced it with: A scholar who has fallen into sin, etc., by reproaching his master for the same fault, etc. In other respects they left the narrative untouched. And these good patrons of the monks have wronged the scholar in this way. Likewise the first story of the fifth day, etc., which that anonymous author observed very carefully. Behold their piety and wisdom! So will your censure allow the filth, the shamelessness and the corruption to be openly taught, provided only that the names of its own people are concealed? These bishops of chastity and piety, whose censure takes care that impurity and corruption of youth exist publicly in writings of this kind, provided only that those devout souls are not said to have come forward on this stage, or to be fellow members of the Church.

units.la: 12 Art.3. cum Dantes factione Gibellinus eosferè Pontifices solum reprehendat, qui Gibellinis præter cæteros aduersabatur. Gibellinum fuisse Dantè supra negauimus in nota 5. festiuū autem illud est, Dantem reprehendere eos solum Pontifices qui Gibellinis aduersabantur. Atqui omnes Pontifices aduersabantur Gibellinis: nam factio VVelpha siue Guelpha Pontificum fuit, Imperatorum Gibellina: quæ
units.tr: 12 Art. 3. since Dante, being a Ghibelline by faction, reprehends almost only those Popes who were hostile to the Ghibellines above the rest.] We denied above, in note 5, that Dante was a Ghibelline. But that is a laughable claim, that Dante reprehends only those Popes who were hostile to the Ghibellines. Yet all the Popes were hostile to the Ghibellines: for the Guelf faction, or Welf, was that of the Popes, and the Ghibelline was that of the Emperors; which

units.la: ergo est fides,mi homo,istius exceptionis tuq;[?]quid est theatri nugas vendere,nisi hoc est?
units.tr: then is the faith, my good man, of this exception of yours? What is it but selling the trifles of the stage, unless this is what it is?

units.la: 13 Ibid. non sine magna animi perturbatione scripta, quum aulicis infensus esse cœpisset,] de tribus canticis respondet disputator. Atqui 1. alia multa sunt,quæ etiam adduxit auctor anonymus.2.etiam in his tribus Canticis scribendis aut nulla fuit, aut iusta perturbatio. Nullam fuisse dixerint alij,qui animum Petrarchæ semper fuisse compositissimum & sedatissimum ex omni historia cognoverint. Nos vt etiam dicamus fuisse iustam, quam Pontificis iniuria tum palam in publicum, tum etiam priuatè in sororem ipsam teste Squarzafi-cho, deinde verò in commoda & bona Petrarchæ tentata concitauerit,quum ex falso rumore mortis fuerunt alienatæ res omnes ipsius, tamen negamus ex eo sequi necessario, quòd perturbationis fel scripta illa infecerit, vt qui nouisset imperturbata scripta dare publico pro sua prudentia, & perturbationem animi apud se coquendam sibi reseruare, denique in nobili modestoque ingenio illo non potuisse perturbationem animi vim facere veritati,quin,eam imperturbatè perscriberet.
units.tr: 13 Ibid. written not without great disturbance of mind, since he had begun to be hostile to the courtiers,] The disputant replies concerning three songs. But first, there are many other things which the anonymous author also brought forward. Second, even in writing these three songs there was either no disturbance, or a just one. Others who have learned from the whole history that Petrarch's mind was always most composed and calm will say there was none. We, to say that it was just, since the Pope's injury then stirred up the gall of disturbance, both openly in public and also privately against his own sister, as Squarzafico testifies, and afterwards against Petrarch's goods and property, when all his possessions were alienated on the false rumour of his death, nevertheless deny that it follows of necessity that those writings were infected by the bitterness of that disturbance. For a man who knew how, by his prudence, to publish undisturbed writings, and to keep for himself the disturbance of his mind to be digested in private, and finally, in that noble and modest genius, could not let the disturbance of his mind do violence to the truth, so as not to describe it with composure.

units.la: 14 Art.4. Ut Prophetis insipientibus, qui sequuntur spiritum suum, & nihil vident.] verum quidem Propheta dicit,sed disputator non verè accommodat.Nam prædictionum istarum duo sunt genera: aliæ ex ratione communi sunt, aliæ ex revelatione singulari. Ezechiel de iis loquitur qui revelatio-nem singularem præ se ferebant, vt fallerent speciosius: illi autem boni viri & quicunque pij impietatem & iniustitiam viderunt Romani Papatus, ex ratione communi prædicunt certissimè. Nam ut rationis fuit communis & necessariae in lege, qui non crediderint & fuerint obsequuti legi, eos ex lege perituros, Leuit.26 & Deut.8.[?] item ut rationis communis est & necessariae ex natura Deum male perditurum malos, Matth. 21.41 sic etiam eo tempore, & inde ab eo tempore manet hoc constantissimum rationis communis caput & necessariae in Euangelio, male perituros eos ex Euangelio, qui non crediderint & obsequuti fuerint Euangelio, ac praesertim eos qui abutuntur specie & larua Euangelij ut subruant Euangelium, prout facit Papalis apostasia, quae pedetentim iamdiu ante illud tempus instituerat facere & architectari opus iniquitatis suae. Ex factis quae videbant illi, de euentis consequentia optima iudicabant boni viri communi illo prophetandi modo quem ante distinximus. Falsa itaque solutio disputatoris est.
units.tr: 14 Art. 4. like the foolish Prophets, who follow their own spirit and see nothing.] The Prophet does say this truly, but the disputant does not apply it truly. For there are two kinds of such predictions: some arise from common reason, others from singular revelation. Ezekiel speaks of those who put forward a singular revelation so that they might deceive more plausibly. But those good men, and all the godly, who saw the impiety and injustice of the Roman papacy, predict from common reason, most certainly. For just as it is a matter of common and necessary reason under the law that those who did not believe and did not obey the law would perish by the law (Lev. 26 and Deut. 8), and just as it is a matter of common and necessary reason from nature that God will destroy the wicked evilly (Matth. 21.41), so also at that time, and from then on, there remains this most constant head of common and necessary reason in the Gospel: that those will perish evilly by the Gospel who have not believed and have not obeyed the Gospel, and especially those who abuse the appearance and mask of the Gospel in order to overthrow the Gospel, as the Papal apostasy does, which had for a long time before that time been step by step beginning to do so and to build up the work of its iniquity. From the facts which they saw, the good men judged the consequences of the outcomes with the best judgement, by that common manner of prophesying which we distinguished before. The disputant's solution is therefore false.

units.la: 15 Ibid. Tentauerat quondam [?]Martinus Lutherus, horum omnium qui nunc in Ecclesiam catholicam debacchantur parens, futura praedicere. Utrumque falsum, Lutherum tentauisse futura praedicere, & eos qui Lutherum sequuntur in catholicam Ecclesiam debacchari. Prius calumniae est, po-sterius contumeliae. Contumeliae non respondemus, quam rei veritas elidit nobis tacentibus. Calumniam esse, locus ipse Lutheri clamitat potentissime. Nam quod Lutherus addita circumscriptione plurium conditionum expresserat, id disputator omittit, unicam solum conditione ex verbis illius & imperfectam exprimens: quod ille ratione communi dixerat, hic perinde obiicit atq; li reuelatione singulare cofingeret eamq; sibi arrogaret: quod ille denique [illegible, ~6 letters] proloquutus est indefinitè, sed acceptione determinata, vt vocant, ille vniuersè accipit, vt eo liberius calumniari possit. Non pronunciauit Lutherus vniuersè simpliciterque Papam, Cardinales, &c. in auras diffluxuros reipsa, sed in mentibus audientium, quos erat vocaturus significatione verbi: non in orbe terrarum vniuerso, sed in Germania sua: non in Germania denique tota, sed in Ecclesia sua, & quascunque huic in Germania coniungebat Deus. Vana est igitur disputatoris obiectio, & quaecunque ex ea tentat concludere.
units.tr: 15 Ibid. Martin Luther once attempted to foretell the future, he who is the parent of all those who now rage against the Catholic Church.] Both claims are false: that Luther attempted to foretell the future, and that those who follow Luther rage against the Catholic Church. The first is a calumny, the second an insult. We do not answer the insult, since the truth of the matter refutes it without our speaking. That it is a calumny, Luther's own passage cries out most powerfully. For what Luther expressed with the added limitation of several conditions, the disputant omits, expressing only a single condition, and that imperfectly, from his words. What Luther said by common reason, the disputant objects to as though it were a singular revelation which he was counterfeiting and claiming for himself. What Luther finally uttered indefinitely [illegible, about six letters], but with a determinate sense, as they say, the disputant takes universally, so that he can calumniate more freely. Luther did not pronounce universally and simply that the Pope, the Cardinals, etc., would dissolve into thin air in reality, but in the minds of the hearers whom he was going to call by the sense of the word; not in the whole world, but in his own Germany; not finally in all of Germany, but in his own Church, and whatever others God joined to it in Germany. The disputant's objection is therefore empty, and whatever he tries to conclude from it is likewise empty.

units.la: 16 Ibid. super hanc petram ædificabo Ecclesiam meam, ]hoc quidem Christus verissimè: sed falsum consequens, quod Bellarminus superædificat, ergo Romanam atque Papalem hanc super petram ædificatam esse in perpetuum. A toto in communi ad particulare non valet consequentia, etiam de ea Romana quæ vere Ecclesia est: quantominus valitura est ex homonymia, quum Ecclesia Rom. dicitur æquinocè, vt hic Bellarminus facit?
units.tr: 16 Ibid. upon this rock I will build my Church, Christ says this most truly. But the consequence that Bellarmine adds, namely that this Roman and Papal Church has been built upon the rock for ever, is false. An inference from the whole in general to a particular does not hold, even of that Roman Church which is truly a Church. How much less will it hold by equivocation, when the Roman Church is named ambiguously, as Bellarmine does here?

units.la: IN CAP. XIII.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: 1 Art.1. Pius V. Pontifex optimus & sanctissimus] imò sæuissimus, qui inde ex quo Papa renunciatus est, feris, præcipitibus, & sanguinariis consiliis operam dedit stigmatica sua vehementia: nec male anteà sermone vernaculo fra Scarpone appellatus. Carmina autem Petrarchæ aduersus vrbem Romam fuisse impiè scripta, quis pius dicat? Pium est, impietatem damnari: pium, publicè damnari & traduci publicam: quod Petrarcha fecit. Et quomodo impie fecerit, cuius pietatem Bellarminus infra cap. 21. defendit & laudat? Nempe hic zelus perturbatus loquitur, illic scientia.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. Pius V, the best and most holy Pontiff. Nay, the most savage, who from the time he was made Pope gave himself to savage, headlong and bloody counsels with his branded vehemence. He was not wrongly called fra Scarpone in the vernacular before this. But who would call it pious that Petrarch's poems against the city of Rome were written impiously? It is pious that impiety be condemned, and pious that it be condemned and exposed in public, which Petrarch did. And how could he have written impiously, when Bellarmine defends and praises his piety below in chapter 21? Clearly here zeal speaks in a disturbed way, and there learning speaks.

units.la: rhetorica & declamatoria haec verba sunt: negamus propositionem, & probationes illius.
units.tr: These are the words of rhetoric and declamation: we deny the proposition and its proofs.

units.la: non dicit auctor anonymus, Ecclesiae catholicae Praesules & Pastores, ut Bellarminus, sed Italico sermone, Podesta Papesca, id est, Papam potestatem: haec duo unum & idem negamus esse. Tum mendacium non esse illud docent res multorum annorum gestae, quum eos pro haereticis persecuti sunt qui Scripturam sacram sermone vernaculo habuerunt aut legerunt domi, & illud inter crimina in Actis publicis retulerunt, quod libri illi domi comperti essent. Hoc nefas tulisti, o Deus, & ego meis oculis ante annos quadraginta vidi in Gallia. Postremo saltem (ut alios taceam) fraterculo tuo (si dignus est) Bellarmine, Cofstero credes, qui in Enchiridio ad obiectionem loci illius Ioannis Scrutamini scripturas, in solutione his verbis vtitur: Neganda est consequentia: primo quidem quia Christus non indocta plebecula loquutus est, sed Sacerdotibus, Leuitis, & Pharisaeis, qui clauem acceperant scientiae, &c. quos constat non fuisse ex promiscua multitudine, sed principes viros, &c. Videsne, mi homo, negare Cofterum tuum, quod mandatum Christi pertineat ad indoctam (ut vocat) plebeculam & promiscuam multitudinem? & quae alia causa est, obsecro, cur neget praeceptum Christi ad plebem pertinere? Etsi negat falso. Nam Ioannes toto illo capite simpliciter de Iudaeis dicit communi appellatione, non autem de primoribus sin-gulariter. Erant quidem & primores in turba illa, quos etiam Christus alloquitur, at non ex primoribus solum turba, quam Christus compellabat. Sed vt demus primores fuisse solum, an propterea sequeretur praeceptum hoc ad laicos minime pertinere? nam quod rationis communis est, idem etiam commune est omnium: Hoc autem praeceptum rationis communis esse, docet Christus ipse, quum addit, quia vos videmini vobis in ipsis habere vitam aeternam. Haec solutio Cofteri profecto sapit omnino illam tyrannidem spiritualem, quam & auctor anonymus obiicit Pontifici, & me videre memini, quum adolescens in Gallia agerem. At huic certe responsioni non plane conuenit illa distinctio quam Bellarminus contr. lib.2.cap.14.posue-rat. Si tamen respipiscunt, aut saltem referunt pede ab institutis illa tyrannide & animarum carnificina, bene est: promoueat Deus, & prouehat in bonum.
units.tr: The anonymous author does not say, as Bellarmine does, the prelates and pastors of the Catholic Church, but in Italian Podesta Papesca, that is, the papal power. We deny that these two are one and the same. Next, the facts of many years show that this is not a lie, when people were persecuted as heretics for keeping or reading Holy Scripture in the vernacular at home, and when, among the crimes recorded in public acts, it was reported that such books had been found at home. O God, you have borne this wickedness, and I saw it with my own eyes forty years ago in France. Finally, to pass over others, you will believe your little brother Bellarmine (if he is worthy of the name), Costerus, who in his Enchiridion, answering the objection from that text of John, Search the Scriptures, uses these words in his solution: The consequence is to be denied: first, because Christ spoke not to an untaught common people but to priests, Levites and Pharisees, who had received the key of knowledge, etc., who are plainly not from the mixed multitude, but leading men, etc. Do you see, my friend, that your Costerus denies that Christ's command pertains to the untaught (as he calls them) common people and mixed multitude? And what other reason, I ask, is there for denying that Christ's precept belongs to the people? Yet he denies it falsely. For John, throughout that whole chapter, speaks simply of the Jews in a general term, not of the chief men alone. There were indeed chief men in that crowd, whom Christ also addressed, but the crowd Christ was addressing was not made up of chief men alone. But even granting that there were only chief men, would it follow that this precept does not pertain to the laity at all? For what belongs to common reason belongs to all in common. And that this precept belongs to common reason Christ himself teaches, when he adds, because you seem to yourselves to have eternal life in them. Costerus's solution certainly savours wholly of that spiritual tyranny which the anonymous author also charges against the Pope, and which I remember seeing when, as a young man, I was in France. But that distinction which Bellarmine had set down in the second book against controversy, chapter 14, does not agree plainly with this answer. Yet if they come to their senses, or at least turn their steps back from those practices of tyranny and of butchering souls, it is well. May God advance it and carry it forward to good.

units.la: 4 Art. 3. sacerdotes non lingua materna vbique ad populos concionentur. ] Vtinam facerent vbique atque fideliter. Sed non soluitur anonymi auctoris illius argumentatio. Nam quum lege praeceptum dicit vt Sacerdotes eloquantur, id est, praedicent populo suo lingua intellecta, [illegible, ~12 letters] praedicationem intelligit sermone & scripto: sermone, vt particulari & transeunte instrumento: scripto, vt communi atque permanente. Sic fecit Christus ipse, & scripturas exponens, & ad eas, n ad aliud quicquam, fideles reuocas, vt expressas diuinitus veritatis salutaris notas: sic fecerunt Apostoli: sic orthodoxi Patres. At Sacerdotu Ecclesiae Rom. quotusquisque sic facit? Sequentis solutionis eade ratio.
units.tr: 4 Art. 3. Priests do not preach to the peoples everywhere in their mother tongue. Would that they did so everywhere and faithfully! But the anonymous author's argument is not answered. For when he says that the law commands priests to speak, that is, to preach to their people in an intelligible language, [illegible] he understands preaching both by speech and by writing: by speech, as a particular and transitory instrument; by writing, as a common and lasting one. So Christ himself did, expounding the Scriptures and calling the faithful back to them and to nothing else, as the marks of saving truth expressed by God. So the Apostles did, and so did the orthodox Fathers. But how few of the priests of the Roman Church do so? The reasoning of the following answer is the same.

units.la: 5 Art. 4. cur quafo lingua minimè vulgari epistolas conscripserunt, si eas à vulgo legi voluerunt?] falsa obiectio. Sed distinctione opus. nam lingua aut vulgaris est, in vulgo trita, aut communis, licet non peraeque in vulgo trita. Romae vulgaris fuit Latina, communis Graeca, vt alibi ostendimus, & adeo communis, vt in vulgo multi eamdem colerent. In Aegypto vulgaris Aegyptia, Syra in Syria, in Arabia Arabica, in omnibus communis Graeca. aliud enim est τὸ κοινὸν, aliud τὸ ἰδιωτικόν. Quod itaque Paulus Romanis scripsit Graecè, fecit vt plures addificaret simul, cùm ea lingua Graecis & gentibus multis vernacula esset, multarumque praeterea tam communis quam quae maximè, etiam Romani populi, vt in controuersiam 1. ostendimus. Hebraeis verò non Hebraicè, sed Graecè scripserunt Apostoli, quia Hebraea lingua proprie dicta, per illud tempus nec vernacula, nec communis fuit, neutroque modo vulgaris, Graeca verò plerisque Hebraeorum communis fuit, atque etiam vernacula, ex qua Hellenistae dicti: nam Hebraei, ne ij quidem qui in Iudaea erant, bene sciebant Hebraicè, qui alibi, omnes Graeco sermone vt communi, aut etiam vulgari, vtebantur. horum autem numerus centuplo quàm illorum maior. De Parthis quod narrat, est insciëntiae: nam veteres, gentes exsulantes, diffractas quodammodo atque dissipatas vocabant Parthos, vt alibi ex Trogo Pompeio docuimus. Erat autem Iudaeorum gentis nomen maxima ex parte [illegible, ~12 letters], siue (vt dicuntur 1. Petr. 1. παρεπιδήμοις διασπορᾶς, id est ex vsu Orientalium, Parthi.
units.tr: 5 Art. 4. Why, I ask, did they write letters in a language that is not at all vernacular, if they wanted them to be read by the common people? A false objection. But a distinction is needed. For a language is either vernacular, that is, in common use among the people, or common, though not equally in common use among the people. At Rome the vernacular language was Latin, the common language Greek, as we have shown elsewhere, and so common that many among the people cultivated it. In Egypt the vernacular was Egyptian, in Syria Syriac, in Arabia Arabic, but in all of them Greek was the common language. For one thing is what is common [τὸ κοινὸν], another is what is private or of the people [τὸ ἰδιωτικόν]. Therefore, that Paul wrote to the Romans in Greek made it possible to edify more people at once, since that language was vernacular to the Greeks and to many nations, and besides it was as common, and even more so, among the Roman people too, as we showed in the first controversy. But the Apostles wrote to the Hebrews not in Hebrew but in Greek, because the Hebrew language properly so called was at that time neither vernacular nor common, and in neither way in common use; whereas Greek was common to most of the Hebrews and even vernacular, from which they were called Hellenists. For the Hebrews, even those who were in Judaea, did not know Hebrew well, while those elsewhere all used Greek as a common and even everyday tongue. And the number of these is a hundred times greater than that of the others. As for what he says about the Parthians, it is ignorance: for the ancients called exiled peoples, scattered and in a sense dispersed, Parthians, as we have shown elsewhere from Trogus Pompeius. Now the name of the Jewish nation was for the most part [illegible], or, as it is said in 1 Peter 1, sojourners of the dispersion [παρεπιδήμοις διασπορᾶς], that is, in the usage of the East, Parthians.

units.la: 6 Art.5 hoc praeceptum Apostolicum in 14. quae exstat Paulinis epistolis nō inuenitur, ]auctoris verba sunt iubet vt quisque nostrum scrutetur & examinet sanctam scripturam. Bellarminus negat. Nihil noua scriptura opus, aut Pauli epistola. Nam hæc ipsius sententia Rom.15.4. quæ ante scripta sunt, ad nostram doctrinam ante scripta sunt, vt per tolerantiam & consolationem Scripturarum spem habeamus. hunc finem, hoc opus annon omnibus præstituit Paulus? Item Rom. 16.26. mysterium Euangelij esse per Scripturas propheticas ex imperio æterni Dei ad obedientiam fidei omnibus Gentibus notificatum. item 1.Cor.14.1. ambite spiritualia, magis tamen vt prophetetis. &c. item 1. Thess.5.20. spiritum ne exstinguite: prophetias ne pro nihilo habete: id est (vt xᾶ λέγει Scriptura loquitur) spiritum fouete, & prophetias magni facite recolentes assiduè eas. & similia multa. nihil opus decimaquinta epistola ad ea probãda quæ in aliquot epistolis ex quatuordecim illis affirmantur. De epistola autem ad Romanos proximè diximus præcedente nota.
units.tr: 6 Art. 5. This Apostolic precept is not found in the fourteen Pauline epistles. The author's words are: he commands each of us to search and examine Holy Scripture. Bellarmine denies it. No new Scripture or Pauline epistle is needed. For this is Paul's own statement, Rom. 15.4: whatever was written before was written for our instruction, so that through patience and the comfort of the Scriptures we might have hope. Did not Paul set this purpose and this work before all? Likewise Rom. 16.26, that the mystery of the Gospel is made known through the prophetic Scriptures, by command of the eternal God, to all nations for the obedience of faith. Likewise 1 Cor. 14.1: desire spiritual gifts, but rather that you may prophesy. Etc. Likewise 1 Thess. 5.20: do not quench the Spirit; do not despise prophecies, that is (as the Scripture elsewhere speaks) cherish the Spirit and hold prophecies in high regard, reading them over constantly. And many similar passages. There is no need for a fifteenth epistle to prove what is asserted in some of those fourteen. But concerning the epistle to the Romans, we spoke just now in the preceding note.

units.la: 7 Art.6. vtrum ⋏Mahumethus id præceperit, aduersarius noster viderit.] Discedit Bellarminus ab anonymi illius auctoris mente. Non argumentatur, sed declarat similitudine quod priùs dixerat: scripturæ lectionem à Deo & seruis eius imperari, vt semper caueamus nobis ne ruamus in pelagus ignorantiæ credulitatem gignētis, cui omnis vanitas falsitásque facilè persuadetur. Hoc periculum demonstrat ab exemplo Mahumethi, dicens: Quòd si videre desideras, vtrùm id sit verum aut falsum quod dico tibi, aduerte solùm oculos ad eum modum quem magnus Christi inimicus ⋏Mahumed in stabilienda impia lege sua obseruauit: cuius præcipua intentio summaque cura fuit, vt populus persuaderet non attinere ad ipsos, ipsos, nec esse ipsorum legere Dei legem, sed hoc impro-borum Sacerdotum suorum solum officium esse. Hoc periculum explicat auctor ille, & ostendit insidiari piis ab Antichristo idem periculum, licet hi forte aut illi non cogitaverint. Et Sacerdotum est & vulgi, versari in lege Dei & Scriptura sacra dies & noctes, ne ignorantia credulitatem, credulitas vanitatem & falsitatem apportet, insidiante patre mendacij. Quamobrem sequentia Bellarmini omnia [illegible, ~8 letters] quod aiunt.
units.tr: 7 Art. 6. Whether Mahomet prescribed this, let our adversary see. Bellarmine departs from the mind of that anonymous author. He does not argue, but by a comparison he explains what he had said before: that reading Scripture is commanded by God and his servants, so that we may always beware lest we plunge into the sea of ignorance, which begets credulity, to which every vanity and falsehood is easily persuaded. The author shows this danger by the example of Mahomet, saying: But if you want to see whether what I tell you is true or false, turn your eyes only to the method which the great enemy of Christ, Mahomet, observed in establishing his impious law: his chief intention and greatest care was to persuade the people that it did not concern them, that it was not theirs to read the law of God, but that this was the sole duty of his wicked priests. That author explains this danger, and shows that the same danger lies in wait for the pious from Antichrist, though perhaps these or those have not thought of it. And it is the duty of priests and of the people alike to be occupied in the law of God and in Holy Scripture day and night, lest ignorance bring credulity, and credulity bring vanity and falsehood, the father of lies lying in wait. Wherefore all of Bellarmine's following points [illegible] as they say.

units.la: 8 Ibid. prauam illam consuetudinem, qua sibi diuinas literas omnes vendicabant, ] recte: nam usus cuique praecipitur, abusus interdicitur. De usu dicit auctor anonymus: de abusu Hieronymus. utrumque verum.
units.tr: 8 Ibid. that wicked custom, by which they claimed all the divine letters for themselves, ] rightly so: for use is enjoined on each person, and abuse is forbidden. The anonymous author speaks of use, Jerome of abuse. Both are true. ## In Chapter XIV.

units.la: In Cap. XIIII.

1 Art.1. omnia ad quinque capita revocari possunt.] sunt tamen loci aliquot in eo numero, qui ad usum horum capitum referri commodè non possunt. Sed ita Bellarmino visum est commodum. Nam exempli causa, ad quod horum capitum referri potest illud pag.16.ex cant.6.del Purgatorio?
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. All things can be referred to five heads.] There are, however, some passages in that number which cannot conveniently be referred to the use of these heads. But Bellarmine thought it convenient to do so. For example, to which of these heads can that passage on page 16 from Canto 6 of the Purgatorio be referred?

units.la: Ahi serua Italia, di dolore hostello, / Naue senza nocchiero in gran tempesta: / Non donna di provincia, ma bordello, &c.
units.tr: Ah, slavish Italy, hostel of grief,

units.la: id est, Eheu serua Italia, doloris hospitium, / Nauis sine nauclero in magna procella, / Non domina provincia, sed lupanar.
units.tr: that is, Alas, slavish Italy, the hostel of sorrow, a ship without a pilot in a great storm, not a lady of provinces but a brothel.

units.la: item pag.17.
units.tr: Likewise on page 17:

units.la: Ahi Gente, che dovresti esser devota, / Et lasciar seder Cesare in sella,
units.tr: Ah, people who ought to be devout

units.la: Se ben intendi ciò che Dio ti nota.
units.tr: and let Caesar sit in the saddle,

units.la: & quæ sequuntur. id autem est, Eheu gens quæ de-beres esse deuota, Et sinere Cæsarem sedere in throno. Si bene intelligeres id quod docet te Deus. & altera post pagina euidentissimè:
units.tr: if you understood well what God marks for you, and what follows. The meaning is: Alas, people who ought to be devoted, and who should allow Caesar to sit on the throne. If you understood what God teaches you. And on the other page, most plainly:

units.la: Soleua Roma, ch'el buon mondo feo, Duo Soli hauer, che l'vna & l'altra strada Facean vedere, & del mondo, & di Deo. L'vn l'altro ha spento, & è giunta la spada Col Pastorale, & l'vn & l'altro insieme Per vna forza, mal conuien che vada: Però che giunti l'vn & l'altro non teme. Se non mi credi, pon mente à la spiga: Ch'ogni herba si conosce per lo seme. Di hoggimai, che la Chiesa di Roma Per confonder in se due reggimenti Cade nel fango, & se brutta, & la soma.&c.
units.tr: Rome used to be the nurse of the good world, to have two suns, which showed each road, that of the world and that of God. One has put out the other, and the sword is joined to the pastoral staff; and the one and the other together, by one force, it is ill that they should go on, since joined they fear neither. If you do not believe me, look at the ear of grain: every herb is known by its seed. Now the Church of Rome, to confound two governments in herself, falls into the mud, and is foul and bears the burden, etc.

units.la: id est, Solebat Roma, quod mundum faciebat bonum Duos Soles habere, qui hanc & illam viam Facerent videre, & mundi & Dei. Alter alterum retudit, & adiunctus est gladius Pastoralis: & hic & ille simul Ex omni necessitate eat oportet male, Quia iunctorum nec hic nec ille timet. Si mihi non credis, animum adverte ad spicam, cum omnis herba cognoscatur ex suo semine. Deinceps dic Ecclesiam Romanam Eo quod confundit in se duo regimina, Cadere in lutum, & se corrumpere & rempublicam. & multa alia, quæ de Pontificia potestate utriusque gladij (ut vocant) adferuntur & consimilibus argumentis. Sed nos in cancellis, quos Bellarminus circumposuit, maneamus.
units.tr: That is: Rome used to make the world good by having two suns, which made the way of the world and of God visible. One has quenched the other, and the pastoral sword is joined to it: and this one and that one together must of necessity go badly, since, being joined, neither fears the other. If you do not believe me, attend to the ear of grain, since every herb is known by its seed. Henceforth say that the Roman Church, because it confounds two governments in itself, falls into the mire, and corrupts itself and the commonwealth. And many other things are brought forward about the Pontifical power over both swords (as they call them) and with similar arguments. But let us remain within the enclosure which Bellarmine has built around the subject.

units.la: 3 Art. 2. Quæ omnia falsa fabulosaque sunt. ] negatur, & nos iam supra contro 3. lib.4.cap.10.rem confirmauimus. Duo tamen errata in editionem libri Italici notandum est irrepsisse: unum, quod Photinum fuisse scribitur in heretico di Thessaglia, haereticum e Thessalia, pro eo quod est, di Thessalonica, e Thessalonica, vel Thessalonicensem: alterum, quod Anastasius III. Pontifex dicitur, (operarum errorem puto) pro Anastasio II. sed haec, ut vitiosa sunt, ab interpretibus sunt qui in opus Dantis commentarios ediderunt. Nam Christophorus Landinus in eum locum sic habet: Vidi una scritta che diceua, io guardo Anastasio Papa, &c. quae sic Latine reddidimus: vidi scripturam una qua diceret, ego observo Anastasium Papam. Photinus clericus Thessalia una cum Acacio, fuerunt haeretici, & docuerunt Spiritum sanctum non procedere a Patre, & Patrem esse maiorem Filio, itaque haeresin Anastasio Pontifici persuaserunt. Hic Romanus fuit, & sedit Theodorici Imperatoris tempore: qui quum haeresin illam aperte profiteretur & a multis Praelatis reprehensus esset, in tantam obstinationem venit ut eam vellet obtinere in Consistorio publico: sed euenit disputando ut ventris necessitate premeretur, & ad deponerandam aluum secederet, ubi impetu uno intestina omnia eruperunt, & ita periit. Non sine causa autem huic monumento apponit scripturam, quia denotat haeresin in summo Pontifice notam omnibus esse oportere, eo quod ij qui peccant quo excellentiores, eo notius est peccatum ipsorum. Unde Juvenalis, ut saepius di-ctum[?]
units.tr: 3 Art. 2. All these things are false and fabulous.] This is denied, and we have already confirmed the point above, controversy 3, book 4, chapter 10. It should be noted, however, that two errors have crept into the edition of the Italian book. One is that Photinus is written as a heretic "di Thessaglia", a heretic from Thessaly, when it should read "di Thessalonica", from Thessalonica, or Thessalonian. The other is that Anastasius III is called Pope (I think this is a printer's error) instead of Anastasius II. But these faults belong to the commentators who published notes on Dante's work. For Christoforo Landino on that passage says this: I saw a writing which said, "I watch Anastasius the Pope," etc. which we have rendered into Latin thus: I saw a writing which said, "I observe Anastasius the Pope." Photinus, a cleric of Thessaly, together with Acacius, were heretics, and taught that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father, and that the Father is greater than the Son; and they persuaded Pope Anastasius of this heresy. He was a Roman, and sat in the time of the Emperor Theodoric. When he openly professed that heresy and was rebuked by many prelates, he came into such obstinacy that he wished to maintain it in a public consistory. But it happened in the course of the dispute that he was seized with a pressing need of the belly, and withdrew to relieve his bowels, where all his intestines burst out in a single rush, and so he perished. The writing is placed on this monument not without reason, because it signifies that a heresy in the supreme Pontiff ought to be known to all, since those who sin the more eminent they are, the more notorious their sin becomes. Hence Juvenal, as has often been said:

units.la: Omne animi vitium tanto conspectius in seCrimen habet, quanto maior qui peccat habetur.
units.tr: Every vice of the mind has the more conspicuous guilt, the greater the one who sins is held to be.

units.la: Haftenus Landinus in eum locum. Nec secus posterior Landino Alexander Vellutellus in eumdem locum: Photinum, inquit, aiunt fuisse clericum & hæreticum in Thessalia, qui asserebat Spiritum sanctum non procedere a Patre, & Patrem esse maiorem Filio, atque hoc persuasisse Anastasio quarto, qui ut obstinatus in ista hæresi, volebat eam defendere in publico, & quæ sequuntur convenientia plane cum Landini verbis. Hinc suas notulas auctor desumpsit anonymus.
units.tr: Thus far Landino on that passage. Nor is Alessandro Vellutello, who came after Landino, any different on the same passage: They say, he writes, that Photinus was a cleric and heretic in Thessaly, who asserted that the Holy Spirit does not proceed from the Father, and that the Father is greater than the Son, and that he persuaded this to Anastasius the Fourth, who, being obstinate in that heresy, wished to defend it in public, and what follows, plainly agreeing with the words of Landino. From these notes the anonymous author has taken his own.

units.la: 4 Ibid. quomodo ergo fieri potest, ut ϵ[?]Anastasius ϵ[?]Acacium ad sedem revocare voluerit, quem iam olim defunctum esse constabat?] Gratianus dist. 19.c.Ana-stasius. Simpliciter dicit revocare: non intelligens, ut Bellarminus exponit, revocare in sedem mortuum, sed revocare nomen mortui in numerum orthodoxorum Episcoporum, prout in diptycha solebant referri, & publicè & diptychis pronunciari, ut controv.3.lib.4.cap.10. nota 10. ostendimus. Falsa itaque argumentatio.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. How then can it be that Anastasius wished to recall Acacius to his see, when it was well known that he had long since died?] Gratian, dist. 19, c. Anastasius, simply says recall: not understanding, as Bellarmine explains, to recall a dead man to his see, but to recall the name of a dead man into the number of orthodox bishops, as they were customarily recorded on the diptychs, and pronounced both publicly and from the diptychs, as we showed in controversy 3, book 4, chapter 10, note 10. The argument is therefore false.

units.la: 5 Ibid. in qua totis viribus persuadere nititur, ne nomen quidem ϵ[?]Acacii tolerandum esse?] primùm quæ-ritur, sinthe[?] veræ illæ epistolæ: nam cùm alia di-screpant, tum notatio temporis in fine illarum. dein-de esto sanè Anastasii epistola: at eam scripserit Anastasius quum adhuc saperet crederetque colle-garum suorum consiliis, postea verò desipuit, & in partes Photini abductus est. Sic ipse distinguit Pla-tina, ut alios taceam, in Anastasio II. dicens: ϵAna-stasius vero (ut quidam scriptores referunt) Anastasium Imp. excommunicavit, quòd ϵAcacio faveret: tametsi postea ipse ab ϵAcacio seductus[?] (id autem est, ut se-quentia docent, ab Acacianis) dum eum revocare clamculum tentat, clerum a se graviter alienavit: qui se a communione Pontificis tum maximè subtraxit, quòd etiam sine catholicorum consensu Photino Thessaloni-
units.tr: 5 Ibid. in which he strives with all his strength to persuade that not even the name of Acacius ought to be tolerated?] First, it is asked whether those letters are genuine, for they differ among themselves, and so does the dating at their end. Next, let us grant that the letter is Anastasius's; but he wrote it while he was still wise and trusted the counsels of his colleagues, and afterwards he lost his senses and was drawn over to the party of Photinus. Platina himself distinguishes it thus, to say nothing of others, writing of Anastasius II: But Anastasius (as some writers relate) excommunicated the Emperor Anastasius, because he favoured Acacius; although afterwards he himself was seduced by Acacius (that is, as the following words show, by the Acacians) and while he secretly attempted to recall him, he gravely alienated the clergy from himself: who then especially withdrew from communion with the Pontiff, because he had also, without the consent of the Catholics, given communion to Photinus, the deacon of Thessalonica, who then imitated the error of Acacius. Marianus Scotus, Sigebert and others say the same. Bellarmine, therefore, with this objection altogether [illegible].

units.la: [Note: the signs before Acacius and Anastasius are printed shorthand marks, transcribed as ϵ.] censi Diacono communicasset, qui tum Acacij[?] errorem imitabatur. Idem Marianus Scotus, Sigebertus, alij. Bellarminus itaque hac obiectione tota [illegible, ~8 letters].
units.tr: [Note: the signs before Acacius and Anastasius are printed shorthand marks, transcribed here as ϵ.] ...censed by the deacon Photinus, who then imitated the error of Acacius. Marianus Scotus, Sigebert and others say the same. Bellarmine, therefore, with this objection altogether [illegible].

units.la: 6 Ibid. Quod ergo ad Anastasium Imperatorem proprie pertinebat. hoc illi commentum placet. neutrum est fabula: nam Anastasium vtrumque, Imp. & Pontificem, male periisse scribunt distin-ctè historici.
units.tr: 6 Ibid. What belonged properly to the Emperor Anastasius. This invention pleases him. Neither is a fable: for the historians write clearly that Anastasius, both Emperor and Pontiff, perished miserably.

units.la: 7 Art.3. in eo tria splendida mendacia contineri. hæc non auctorem illum anonymum, sed Landinum & Vellutellum feriunt, quorum verba ante adduximus fide quàm optima, in nota 3. Quamobrem si quid falsi est, non ab hoc anonymo, sed ab illis unde exscripsit præstari debet. Certè apud Vellutellum emendari oportet locum, & hoc modo legi, & questo persuase ad Anastafiofecohdo, atque hoc persuasit Anastasio secundo. Cætera quæ audacter disputator furcillat, probari ab ipso non possunt.
units.tr: 7 Art. 3. that there are three splendid lies in it. These charges strike not that anonymous author but Landino and Vellutello, whose words we cited before, in note 3, as most faithful. Therefore, if anything is false, it must be answered for not by this anonymous author but by those from whom he copied. Certainly in Vellutello the passage must be corrected and read thus: and this persuaded Anastasius the Second, that is, he persuaded Anastasius the Second of this. The rest, which the disputant boldly ferrets out, cannot be proved by him.

units.la: 8 Art. 4. neque Dantes vere iudicauit. disputet sanè Bellarminus pro iudicio suo: verumtamen Dantes, qui celestinum illum vidit (ut rectè Vellutellus obseruauit) non temere eum hominem ignauum fuisse pronunciauit. Nihil de meo adferam: rem verbis Commentatorum explicabo. Landinus in argumento Cant. 5. Quum itaque intelle-xisset postea, ibi puniri ignorantes & eos qui vixerint ut bestiæ sine nomine aut fama, vidit alteram classem animarum, in qua agnouit Celestinum Papam, qui fecit magnam illam abdicationem Papatus. Rem totam Vellutellus exponit euidentius in eumdem locum: ille fuit frater Petrus Merone (siue, vt Landinus, de Maironi Sulmonensis, homo sanctæ vitæ, qui diu eremita fuerat in solitudine : sed quum ex obitu Nicolai III I. Cardinales diu versati essent in controuersia de electione noui Pontificis, tandem elegerunt istum, plane contra opinionem voluntatémque ipsius, quod ipsi videretur non posse se in eo statu bene operari salutem suam : quæ res quum innotuisset D. Benedicto Anagi-nensi Cardinali, qui post Celestinum Bonifacius VIII. Papa creatus est, industus est fraudulenter opera illius ad renunciandum Pontificatui, vt in Cant. 18. videbimus, vbi de eo agetur. Quamuis autem, vt diximus, istius vita fuerit sansta & laudabilis, vt ex eo confirmatur quod a Clemente V. post mortem canonizatus est & relatus in catalogum sanctorum : tamen quia sperabatur Ecclesiam per eum reformatum iri, quæ res per illud tempus desiderabatur non mediocriter, Poëta visum est, eum renunciando, Ecclesiámque in illo statu pessimo, vbi erat, relinquendo, defuisse multum officio suo, & exspestatione de ipso, & fecisse vt notaretur vitij, quod in sito loco Inferni puniretur, vbi eum ase fingit inuentum esse. Ignauum hominem fuisse oportuit iudicio Dantis, & corio elephanti tectum: quapropter à muscis & vespis cum suo sodalitio fingitur infestatus leuitatem certè & superstitionem eius non dubitauit Platina appellare. Siue autem à Clemente V. siue (vt alij volunt) ab Ioanne 22. canonizatus sit, festiuè canonizationi isti Dantes, (qui tum viuebat) illusisse videtur, dicendo:
units.tr: 8 Art. 4. nor did Dante judge truly. Let Bellarmine by all means argue for his own judgement; nevertheless Dante, who saw that Celestine (as Vellutello rightly observes) was not rashly pronounced by him to be a cowardly man, will not be moved. I will add nothing of my own: I shall explain the matter in the words of the commentators. Landino, in the argument to Canto 5: Since he had then understood that the ignorant are punished there, and those who lived like beasts without name or fame, he saw a second class of souls, in which he recognised Pope Celestine, who made that great renunciation of the papacy. Vellutello sets out the whole matter more plainly on the same passage: He was Brother Pietro da Morrone (or, as Landino has it, of Maironi of Sulmona), a man of holy life, who had long lived as a hermit in solitude. But when, after the death of Nicholas III, the cardinals had long been at odds over the election of a new Pontiff, they at last chose him, quite against his own opinion and wish, since he thought he could not work out his salvation in that state. When this became known to the Lord Benedict of Anagni, a cardinal, who was afterwards created Pope Boniface VIII, he was cunningly induced by his efforts to renounce the pontificate, as we shall see in Canto 18, where this will be treated. Although, as we have said, his life was holy and praiseworthy, as is confirmed by his canonisation after death by Clement V and his enrolment in the catalogue of saints, nevertheless, because it was hoped that the Church would be reformed through him, a thing greatly desired at that time, the Poet thought that by renouncing and leaving the Church in that most wretched state in which it was, he had fallen short of his duty and of the expectation placed in him, and had made himself an instance of the vice which is punished in that place of Hell where he is feigned to have been found. He had to be judged by Dante a coward, and clothed in an elephant's hide, which is why he is feigned to be harassed by flies and wasps with his company; Platina certainly did not hesitate to call his levity and superstition by name. Whether he was canonised by Clement V or (as others hold) by John XXII, Dante, who was then alive, seems to have mocked that canonisation wittily, saying:

units.la: Elle rigauan lor di sangue il volto:
units.tr: They were bathing their faces with blood,

units.la: Che mischiato di lagrime à lor piedi
units.tr: which, mixed with tears, was gathered at their feet

units.la: Da fustidiosi vermi era ricolto.
units.tr: by loathsome worms.

units.la: Illæ, inquit, muscæ & vespæ, rigabant eis sanguine vultum: vultum: qui sanguis mistus lacrymis ad pedes ipsorum à fastidiosis vermibus recolligebatur. Ita fuerunt, nempe Bonifacius VIII. musca aut vespa pungens, Clemens & Ioannes vermes sanguinem excipientes etiam ad miraculum vsque, vt postea Bellarminus narrat. ludicent prudentes & docti, vtra pars verius de Celestino sentiat: Dantes certe vir prudens & magnus sine praeiudicio sententiam tulit eius rei, quam suis oculis viderat. Ridiculum est, indigitari sanctos posse à tam impiis capitibus. Cardinalis Cameracensis, qui post annos amplius 150. vixit ab illo seculo, res auditas à superstitiosis & imperitis hominibus, non à certis visas idoneisque retulit. Certissimus testis Dantes.
units.tr: Those, he says, are the gadflies and wasps: they were bathing their faces with blood, which blood, mixed with tears, was gathered at their feet by loathsome worms. So, to be precise, Boniface VIII is the stinging gadfly or wasp, and Clement and John are the worms that catch the blood, even to the point of a miracle, as Bellarmine later relates. Let the wise and learned judge which side is nearer the truth about Celestine. Dante, at least, a wise and great man, without prejudice pronounced judgement on a matter he had seen with his own eyes. It is ridiculous that saints could be designated by such impious heads. The Cardinal of Cambrai, who lived more than 150 years after that age, reported things heard from superstitious and unlearned people, not things seen by reliable and competent witnesses. Dante is a most certain witness.

units.la: 9 Art.5. Dantes quidem non parum vituperat, sed ob vitam & mores. ] locus est de Simonia, in quo Pontifices istos omneis collocauit Dantes cant.19. inferni. Sed isti mores sunt Antichristo & damnata illa meretrice digni, quos Dantes obiicit, dicens: Et se non sofe, ch'ancor, &c. Profecto istos pontifices quos Dantes carpit, à pietate aut probitate nemo laudauit historicus. De clero, eadem ratio: quem damnata illa Simonia, ex-auctoratum effecit iamdiu.
units.tr: 9 Art.5. Dante indeed does not blame them very much, but for their life and morals. ] The passage is about simony, in which Dante placed all these Popes in Inferno, canto 19. But those morals are worthy of Antichrist and of that damned harlot, and Dante charges them with these, saying: And if it were not that I still... Certainly no historian has praised the piety or integrity of those popes whom Dante criticises. The same reasoning applies to the clergy, whom that accursed simony has long since struck off the roll.

units.la: 10 Ibid. in Domino collocata, nunquam tempefta-te sacrilegi schismatis dissipetur? ] ad haec omnia diu responsum est contr. 3.lib. 2. & contr. 4 lib.2.&3.
units.tr: 10 Ibid. placed in the Lord, never to be scattered by the storm of sacrilegious schism? ] All these points have been answered at length in Controversy 3, book 2, and Controversy 4, books 2 and 3.

units.la: II Ibid. Dantes factione Gibellinus ] criminatio falsa: vt ante in cap. 12. nota 5. ostendimus & sal-sum consequens.
units.tr: 11 Ibid. Dante, a Ghibelline by faction] This is a false accusation, as we showed earlier at chapter 12, note 5, and the consequence is false.

units.la: II Artic. 6. cur nobis non liceat eidem Danti, quem poëtam, non prophetam fuisse scimus, interdum etiam fidem non habere? ] argumentatio dispar, & inconsequens (vt vocant) ex particulari. Nam alia ratio eorum est quæ Poëta fingit, alia eorum quæ ex hypothesi & opinione communi refert, aut ex certa & singulari scientia. Non quicquid poëta dicit, figmentum poëticum est, sed vbi figmentum non est, testis profecto est aut communis famæ & alieni sermonis, aut compertæ veritatis. Constantini donationem ex hypothesi dixit communis famæ opinionisque: Pontificum seculi sui vitia dixit ex certa atque comperta veritate. Nam cui bono, si de illis scripsisset falsum? ac potius quomodo ipsi non fuisset damno, si crimina ficta & res falsas de eis perscripsisset?
units.tr: 11 Art. 6. Why should it not be permitted for us to suppose that this same Dante, whom we know to have been a poet and not a prophet, sometimes also was wrong? ] The argument is unequal and, as they say, inconsequent from a particular case. For there is one kind of thing a poet invents and another kind he reports from hypothesis and common opinion, or from certain and personal knowledge. Not everything a poet says is a poetic fiction; where there is no fiction, he is surely a witness either of common report and hearsay, or of established truth. Constantine's Donation he stated from hypothesis, as common report and opinion; the vices of the popes of his own age he stated from certain and established truth. For what would be the advantage to them if he had written falsely about them? Or rather, how would it not have harmed them if he had written up invented crimes and false facts about them?

units.la: In Cap. XV.
units.tr: In Chapter XV.

units.la: 1 Art.x. triumphat aduersarius, sed plane antevictoriam. ]imò verò ex victoria quam Dantes peperit. docebunt sequentia.
units.tr: 1 Art.x. The adversary triumphs, but only before victory. ] Indeed, it is from the victory which Dante has won. The following will show this.

units.la: 2 Ibid. Et se non fosse, ch'ancor lo mi vieta] Hæc verba lectoris causâ sic reddimus: Et absque eo fuisset quòd hoc adhuc me vetat Reuerentia summarum illarum clauium. Quas tu tenuisti in illa iucunda vita, V surus essem sermonibus adhuc gravioribus, Quod anaritia vestra mundum tristitia afficit, Calcando bonos, & sursum attollendo pravos. Summas claues appellat Dantes claues regni cælorum: quid enim regno cælorum superius? has claues tenent in Ecclesia omnes serui Christi: sibi soli Rom. Pontifex arrogat. neutrum exponit Dantes: sed tatum ait, nisi reuerentia teneretur illarum clauium, id est, vocationis illius & functionis Ecclesiasticæ, graviora se fuisse dicturum. At primum vtrum de vocatione communi feruorum Dei dicit, an de singulari illa prætenfa ( vt loquuntur ) Pontificis? deinde quàm prudenter grauiores sermones Bellarminus exponit contumeliosos? dicit enim, ne in Inferno quidem Dantes audeat contumeliosè illum alloqui. postremò qua consequentia illud eruitur, quòd non [?]Anti-christum, sed verum Christi vicarium fuisse illum cen-sebat Dantes? nulla est consequentia, nam prose-cto vel eo Antichristus est, quòd claues regni cælorum Antichristus, vt vicarius Christi, sibi arrogat, quisquis est aduersarius Christi. Ergo Christi ser-vus claues habet regni cælorum, vt Domini servus. Antichristus habet eas, vt prædo & inimicus Domini. Has claues reueretur pius etiam in manu An-tichristi, licet Antichristum horreat. Inanis igitur solutio.
units.tr: 2 Ibid.
