And if it were not that the reverence I still owe to that one holds me back] We render these words for the reader's sake as follows: And had it not been that the reverence owed to those highest keys, which you held in that pleasant life, still forbids me, I would be speaking with even weightier words, because your avarice afflicts the world with sorrow, trampling down the good and lifting up the wicked. Dante calls the highest keys the keys of the kingdom of heaven, for what is higher than the kingdom of heaven? All the servants of Christ hold these keys in the Church; the Roman Pontiff claims them for himself alone. Dante explains neither: he only says that, were he not restrained by reverence for those keys, that is, for that calling and ecclesiastical office, he would have spoken more severely. But first, does he speak of the common calling of the servants of God, or of that singular so-called office of the Pope? Second, how wisely does Bellarmine explain "weightier words" as "abusive"? For he says that Dante would not dare to address him abusively even in Hell. Lastly, by what sequence is it deduced from this that Dante thought he was not Antichrist but the true vicar of Christ? There is no such consequence. For surely he is Antichrist precisely because Antichrist, as the vicar of Christ, claims those keys for himself, whoever is the adversary of Christ. Therefore the servant of Christ holds the keys of the kingdom of heaven as a servant of the Lord; Antichrist holds them as a plunderer and enemy of the Lord. A pious man reveres these keys even in the hand of Antichrist, though he abhors Antichrist. The solution is therefore empty.

units.la: 3 Ibid. nullus vnquam veterum hunc locum [?]Apocalypsis de Rom. Ecclesia, aut summo eius Pontifice accipiendum esse docuit.] de Roma certè multi sunt interpretati, vbi Ecclesia & Pontifex. Miserè effugium disputator quærit hac solutione sua.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. No one of the ancients ever taught that this passage of the Apocalypse is to be understood of the Roman Church or of its supreme Pontiff.] Certainly many have interpreted it of Rome, where there is Church and Pontiff. The disputant seeks a wretched escape with this solution of his.

units.la: 4 Ibid. Tertullianus & Hieronymus supra citati,] nimirum capite 6. vbi de sententia eorum diximus.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. Tertullian and Jerome, cited above,] Of course, in chapter 6, where we discussed their opinion.

units.la: 5 Ibid. latius præsides religione diuina quàm dominatione terrena] de his omnibus locis iam ante vidimus contro. 3.lib.2.cap.2. & sequentibus.
units.tr: 5 Ibid. rulers more by divine religion than by earthly lordship] We have already seen all these passages earlier, in Controversy 3, book 2, chapter 2 and following.

units.la: In Cap. XVI.
units.tr: On Chapter XVI.

units.la: 1 Art.1. vas quod fuit & nō est, esse Romanam Ecclesiam] hæc procul dubio vera mens fuit Dantis: & ita Landinus & Vellutellus exponunt vno ore in suo commentario Landinus, recte[?] ponit vas non esse, quia ex quo ruptum est, non amplius est vas. Ergo non amplius Ecclesia est ut solebat esse, quia divisa est, & magna parte ex spirituali & virtutis plena facta est carnalis vitiosaque. Alter copiosius: nam, inquit, Ecclesia fuit, dum a rebus temporalibus abstinuit, & in sanctitate, parsimonia, & obedientia administrata est: sed postquam eo devenit ut vitiata & corrupta esset bonis temporalibus, non erat amplius, &c.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. The vessel that was and is not: that the Roman Church is this] Without doubt this was Dante's true meaning, and Landinus and Vellutellus both explain it in the same way. In his commentary, Landinus rightly says the vessel is not, because once it has been broken it is no longer a vessel. Therefore the Church is no longer what it used to be, since it has been divided, and for the most part it has been turned from spiritual and full of virtue into carnal and vicious. The other writes more fully: for, he says, the Church existed while it kept away from temporal affairs and was administered in holiness, frugality and obedience; but after it came to such a point that it was corrupted and spoiled by temporal goods, it was no longer the Church, etc.

units.la: 2 Ibid. scribit impius iste iuuenis per eam vocem significari Eucharistiam, ] mitiùs profecto agit auctor anonymus quàm Bellarminus referat. Eius haec verba sunt: Sed qui non habet culpam, credat, id est, pro certo habeat vindictam Dei non metuere, suppam, id est, offam, ut sunt ea quae fiunt in Missa ex hostia & vino, quae non possunt efficere ut [?]Maiestas Dei abstineat a sumenda vindicta de pastoribus adeo scele-ratis, &c. non dicit hanc ipsam offam esse, aut de hac ipsa Dantem proprie agere, sed hanc tantum in exemplum adfert: taquam si diceret, neque hac, neque alia vlla effici posse ut dormitet vindicta Dei, sed eam certo certius esse superventuram iis hominibus. Quapropter suum commentum oppugnat Bellarminus magis toto hoc cap. quàm auctoris illius dictum. Sentit enim simpliciter nulla offa, neque penita neque tincta fieri posse ut sistatur vindicta Dei, quae praesto est, nec sibi ab interventu rei vllius metuit, quin ius suum intrepidè & ineuitabiliter exsequatur.
units.tr: 2 In the same place this impious young man writes that this word signifies the Eucharist] The anonymous author in fact treats the matter more gently than Bellarmine reports. His words are these: But let him who has no guilt believe, that is, let him hold it for certain, that the vengeance of God does not fear a wafer, that is, a cake, such as those things which are made in the Mass from the host and wine, which cannot bring it about that the majesty of God refrains from taking vengeance on ministers so wicked, etc. He does not say that this very cake is meant, or that Dante is speaking properly of this very thing, but he brings it forward only as an example, as if he said that neither this nor any other thing can bring it about that the vengeance of God sleeps, but that it will most certainly overtake those men. Therefore Bellarmine attacks his own invention in this whole chapter more than the author's statement. For the author holds simply that no cake, whether unleavened or leavened, can bring it about that the vengeance of God, which is at hand, is stayed, nor does he fear any intervening thing that might prevent it from carrying out its right fearlessly and inevitably.

units.la: 3 Ibid. paulo post luce clarius ostendemus.] & nos confutabimus cap.19.
units.tr: 3 In the same place: we will show this more clearly than daylight after a little.] We too will refute it in chapter 19.

units.la: 4 Ibid. quamsibi prodesse parricida falsò atque impiè impiè credunt. ] hæc interpretatio pedibus trahatur per nos licet. Illa tamen plus habere videtur acuminis atque veritatis.
units.tr: 4 In the same place: what the parricide thinks will benefit himself, they believe falsely and impiously.] Let this interpretation be dragged along by the feet, so far as we are concerned. Yet that other one seems to have more keenness and truth.

units.la: In Cap. XVII.
units.tr: On Chapter XVII.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. Lutherum a Dante præsignificatum adversarius credit. ] totus hic locus est ænigmaticus, & in coniecturis poeticis positus: de quo non dicturus essem, nisi me ordo huius disputationis pertraheret. Antequam autem de re dicam, duo ponenda sunt: unum de vaticiniis: alterum de Poetæ verbis. Vaticiniorum alia ex ratione communi sunt, ut de prædictionibus ante diceba-mus in caput 12. nota 14. & 15. alia ex revelatione aut motu singulari. Exempli causa, in hac ipsa prædictione quæ agitur, exstat triplex interpreta-tio. Prima ex ratione communi, quam Landinus sequutus est, sic habet verbis ipsius in Commentario: Quia ad aquilam pertinet, inquit, dirigere & corrigere errores Ecclesiæ, addit aquilam non semper fore sine hærede, id est, sine Imperatore: nam quisquis factus est Imperator, hæres est aquilæ: & docet eo tempore fuisse aquilam sine hærede, quia licet Imperatores essent, tamen seruiebant Papa, & non audebant adhibitis Conciliis eum corrigere. Et sub finem eiusdem loci: Non ponit, inquit, hunc numerum pro numero annorum, sed quia quinquies centum notatur litera D. & quinque litera V. & decem litera X. quod est dux, dicit venturum ducem, id est, principem exercitus ablegatum a Deo, qui excidet scortum, & adulterium meretricis, id est, Papa & Curia Romana adulterata & omni vitio inquinata, cum Gigante illo (qui designat dominum temporalem,) qui delinquit, id est, peccat cum illa. Hæc communis Ladini interpretatio, ex ratione communi sumpta. Secunda interpretatio est ex motu singulari, quem aut opinio ingenerat, aut studium adulationis. Eiusmodi est Vellutelli & Bellarmini interpretatio. Nam Vellutellus accipit de Henrico Luxemburgico Imperatore, quòd opinionem apud se optimam concepisse Dantes de eo videretur: Bellarminus verò de Cane Scaligero, cui assentari Dantem hoc loco existimat. Tertia interpretatio ex revelatione est: nempe hæc dixisse Dantem non ex sensu aut motu suo, sed divino quodam impetu ad hæc scribenda ipsum adducente, sive intellexerit dictum, sive non intellexerit. Nam Deus utroque modo per servos suos revelationes suas communicat, quæ non nisi complemento solent intelligi, aut singulari declaratione divinitus accedente. Hæc auctoris anonymi interpretatio: qui Dantem, quamuis non intelligeret explicatè rei argumentum, divinitus tamen arbitratur actum ut ista scriberet, numerumque sibi incompertum traderet. Nunc ut Lector commodius judicet, cui forte non ita peruiæ sunt voces Italicæ, orationem Poetæ, de qua hic agitur, ad verbum exprimamus: Hoc ego, inquit, vi-deo certò, ac propterea id narro: Ad dandum ei tempus jam stella propinqua Secura ab omni contrapositione & omni resistentia sunt: Quo tempore unus quinquies centum decem & quinque Missus à Deo excidet scortum illud, Et Gigantem istum qui cum ipsa delinquit, De horum verborum interpretatione & sensu deinceps videbimus.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. The adversary believes that Dante foretold Luther.] This whole passage is enigmatic and rests on poetic conjectures. I would not speak about it were it not that the order of this discussion draws me on. Before I speak of the matter itself, two things must be set down: one concerning prophecies, the other concerning the words of the poet. Some prophecies arise from common reason, as we said earlier about predictions in chapter 12, note 14 and 15; others arise from revelation or a singular impulse. For example, in this very prophecy under discussion there is a threefold interpretation. The first, from common reason, is the one Landinus followed, and in his commentary he puts it thus: Because it belongs to the eagle, he says, to direct and correct the errors of the Church, he adds that the eagle will not always be without an heir, that is, without an Emperor: for whoever has been made Emperor is the heir of the eagle; and he teaches that at that time the eagle was without an heir, because although there were emperors, they nevertheless served the Pope and did not dare, with councils summoned, to correct him. And at the end of the same passage: He does not put this number for a number of years, he says, but because the letter D is marked for five hundred, and the letter V for five, and the letter X for ten, which makes DXV, he says that a leader will come, that is, a prince of the army sent by God, who will cast out the harlot and the adultery of the prostitute, that is, the Pope and the Roman Curia, corrupted and stained with every vice, together with that giant (who designates the temporal lord) who sins, that is, commits sin with her. This is Landinus' common interpretation, taken from common reason. The second interpretation comes from a singular impulse, which either opinion or a desire to flatter prompts. Such is the interpretation of Vellutellus and Bellarmine. For Vellutellus takes it of the Emperor Henry of Luxemburg, because Dante seems to have conceived a very good opinion of him; but Bellarmine takes it of Can Grande della Scala, whom he thinks Dante here sought to flatter. The third interpretation is from revelation: namely, that Dante said these things not from his own feeling or impulse, but from a certain divine rush that led him to write them, whether or not he understood what he said. For God communicates his revelations through his servants in both ways, and these are usually understood only when fulfilled, or by a singular declaration coming from God. This is the interpretation of the anonymous author, who thinks that Dante, although he did not explicitly understand the subject of the matter, was nevertheless moved by God to write these things and to hand down a number unknown to himself. Now, so that the reader may judge more conveniently, since perhaps the Italian words are not so familiar to him, let us express the words of the poet under discussion word for word: This, he says, I see with certainty, and therefore I tell it: At the time appointed for him, the star being near, safe from every opposition and every resistance: At which time one, sent by God, five hundred and ten and five, will cast out that harlot, and that giant who sins with her. We will look later at the interpretation and sense of these words.

units.la: 2 Ibid. per eum numerum non tempus sed personam significasse, hoc negat auctor anonymus: quum autem τὸ ξεινόμενον [?] ad probationem adducitur, non est nescius Bellarminus inconsequentem argumentationem esse, quia τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς petitur.
units.tr: 2 In the same place: that by that number he signified not a time but a person. The anonymous author denies this. But when the begging of the question [?] is brought forward as proof, Bellarmine is not unaware that the argument is inconsequential, because it assumes from the start what is to be proved.

units.la: 3 Ibid. sed tempus erit, quum quidam a Deo mis-sus adueniet, quo per numerum D. x v. significatur. hoc non dicit Dantes, sed loquitur aenigmaticè, ut sequens ipsius ἐπιδραματικὰ [?] ostendit, dicentis, Et forse che la mia narration buia, &c. Neque vero ex illis ipsius verbis probari potest, quae modo ad verbum expressissimus. Nam illa postea, vnus, quinquies centum decem & quinque, cur potius de nomine numerali & characteristico personae, quàm de tempore anni debeamus accipere, equidem non video. Profecto & hoc & illud convenire potest: sed illud, significari nomè Dux, puerile videtur quodammodo, ac non sapere acumen Dantis Aligerij, cuius alae volant sublimius. Illud abacum & ratiocinium magis spectat, hoc vero dignius vaticinio illius alti spiritus: quasi dicat, in quo tempore vnus, tempore inquam annorum quinquies centum quindecim, Missus a Deo, &c. ut nota 1. exposuimus vaticinium illius ad verbum.
units.tr: 3 In the same place: but there will be a time when a certain man sent by God will come, by which time is signified by the number D.XV. Dante does not say this, but speaks enigmatically, as his following [?] shows, saying: And perhaps my narration is obscure, etc. Nor can it be proved from those words of his which we have just expressed word for word. For as to why we should take those later words, one, five hundred and ten and five, as referring to the numeral name and character of a person rather than to the time of the year, I certainly do not see. Indeed both can apply, but that the name Dux [leader] is signified seems somewhat childish, and not in keeping with the keenness of Dante Alighieri, whose wings fly higher. The former regards calculation and reckoning more, but the latter is more worthy of the prophecy of that lofty spirit: as if he said, in which time one, the time, I say, of five hundred and fifteen years, sent by God, etc., as we set out his prophecy word for word in note 1.

units.la: 4 Ibid. in qua re imitari voluit Dantes locum illum cap.13. Apocal. hoc voluisse Dantem, probatio nulla est, nullaque ratio: neque vero ita esse Landinus, Vellutellus, aut alij animaduerterunt, quibus in visu fuit poema Dantis.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. in which matter Dante wished to imitate that passage of Rev. 13. There is no proof and no reason to show that Dante intended this. Nor have Landino, Vellutello or others noticed it, although they had Dante's poem before their eyes.

units.la: 5 Ibid. cur a vero per integrum biennium aberraf-set? non aberrat a vero qui verum narrat. Verum autem illud est, anno millesimo quingentesimo decimoquinto missionem Lutheri exstitisse, quum
units.tr: 5 Ibid. Why did he go astray from the truth for a full two years? He does not go astray from the truth who tells the truth. The truth is that Luther's mission took place in the year 1515, when

units.la: Doctor renunciatus est, postquam Roma rever-tisset: post biennium vero opus missionis suae fe-cisse palàm indulgentiis expugnandis. Quod dico, non ex opinione coniecturáue, non ex Lutheranorum(vt vocantur)scriptis, sed ex Surij ipsius verbis certum est demonstrare, qui in Appendice ad Io. Naucleri Chronica de Luthero ita scribit: Quum autem Saxoniae Princeps Fridericus V Vvittembergae nouam constituisset Academia, ad eam quoque Lutherus anno 1508. missus publicè prælegit Logicen & Physicen Aristotelis. Triennio post Romam ire compulsus cuiusdam litis componendae causa, ea transfacta redit Vvittembergam, & Doctor Theologiae factus, cùm esset disputator vehemens, &c. missionem anno 1515. habuit ordinariam, exercuit extra ordinem anno 1517. quum Leo X. quæstuarios suos & indulgentiarum propolas in Germaniam & alias Christiani orbis partes submisisset. Vera igitur Dantis, vera anonymi auctoris supputatio.
units.tr: he was declared Doctor after he had returned from Rome; but two years later he openly carried out the work of his mission by attacking indulgences. I say this is certain, not from opinion or conjecture, nor from the writings of the Lutherans (as they are called), but from the very words of Surius, who in his Appendix to John Naucler's Chronicle writes thus about Luther: When Frederick V, Prince of Saxony, had newly founded an academy at Wittenberg, Luther was sent there too in 1508, and lectured publicly on Aristotle's logic and physics. Three years later he was compelled to go to Rome to settle a certain lawsuit; when that was done he returned to Wittenberg, and, having been made Doctor of Theology, since he was a vehement disputer, etc. He had his ordinary mission in 1515, and exercised an extraordinary one in 1517, when Leo X had sent his quaestors and sellers of indulgences into Germany and other parts of the Christian world. So the reckoning of Dante is true, and the reckoning of the anonymous author is true.

units.la: 6 Ibid. cur etiam mille annos omisisset? ] En, quò Bellarminum, adducat inopia argumentorum? quasi vero nesciat numerum rotundatum non po-nè solum minui, verumetiam ante: quod notarij, quod vulgus ipsum obseruat promiscuè. Exempli causa, numerus plenus est 1515. hunc vero numerum annorum sic vulgo minuimus, prout & Iudaei solent, vt millenario omisso dicamus breuius & non incommodè, anno 515. elliptice imò etiam in rebus popularibus ac non obscuris dicamus etiam anno 15. vbi res inter agentes constat. Atque hanc ellipsin nonnumquam certis notis inter scribendum memini designari. Hic planè vigilans somniat.
units.tr: 6 Ibid. Why then did he also omit a thousand years? Look, here is where Bellarmine's lack of arguments leads him! As if he did not know that a rounded number is not only shortened but can also be cut down at the front, as scribes and ordinary people commonly do. For example, the full number is 1515, but in common speech we shorten this number, as the Jews also do, by dropping the thousand and saying more briefly and quite properly "the year 515". By ellipsis we may even say "the year 15" in ordinary and plain matters where the people concerned understand the reference. I recall that this ellipsis is sometimes marked by certain signs in writing. Here the watchful man is plainly dreaming.

units.la: 7 Ibid. vt per eum nuncium Lutherum ex monacho apostatam, ac priuatum hominem intelligeret?] non fuit Lutherus apostata, sed qui eiecerunt ipsum tyrannide sua, auctores sunt generalis illius apostasiae, de qua Paulus 2. Thessal. 2. non fuit priuatus homo, sed publica auctoritate praedicator & Doctor renunciatus, quod munus Deo auctore in Ecclesia publica fide exercuit. Sed ad rem. Negamus vocem illam missus de Imperatore a Poeta enunciari: hoc autem quid probari a nobis opus est, cum ipse quoque Bellarminus nobiscum neget de Imperatore fuisse dictam in sequente sua interpretatione? nam de Cane Scaligero hoc iubet accipi Bellarminus in fine capitis. Inanis igitur est argumentatio. Regeret fortasse Bellarminus se ex hypothesi auctoris illius anonymi sic argumentari. Hoc vero si dixerit, falsum dixerit: nam auctor ille primum suam interpretationem adfert καταφατικῶς[?] simpliciterque: postea vero [illegible, ~11 letters] duas alias adfert, siquis de Duce politico, ac non Euangelico, velit accipere. Harum vna est ipsius ex hypothesi Vellutelli, si de Henrici nomine accipiendum est, non Luxemburgicum illum, sed Nauarrenum hunc Condensemque accipi oportere: altera, ex hypothesi interpre-tum de illo seculo exponentium, Gigantis appellatione significari Philippum Pulchrum Francorum Regem, &c. haec nobis tacentibus commonstrant auctoris verba, quu ait: Et iste Gigas qui cum illa de-linquit, id est, rex Francia (vt Landinus exponit) fecit cum Clemente ignominiosas conuentiones multas, &c. Nullam profecto capturam his cassibus difputator assequuturus est.
units.tr: 7 Ibid. That by this messenger he understood Luther, an apostate from the monastery and a private man? Luther was not an apostate; rather, those who drove him out by their tyranny are the authors of that general apostasy of which Paul speaks in 2 Thessalonians 2. Nor was he a private man; he was appointed preacher and Doctor by public authority, and he discharged that office in the public Church of God's appointment. But to the point. We deny that the word sent is said by the poet of the Emperor. Why we must prove this is not clear, since Bellarmine himself, in his following interpretation, agrees with us that it was not said of the Emperor; indeed, at the end of the chapter he directs that it be taken of Can Grande della Scala. The argument is therefore empty. Bellarmine might perhaps reply that he argues this way on the hypothesis of that anonymous author. But if he says so, he says what is false. For that author first offers his interpretation affirmatively [καταφατικῶς] and simply; afterwards, however, [illegible, about eleven letters] he offers two others, in case anyone wishes to understand it of a political leader and not an evangelical one. One of these, on the hypothesis of Vellutello, is that if it must be taken of the name of Henry, then it is not that Luxembourg man but this Navarrese and Condé man who must be understood. The other, on the hypothesis of those who explain it of that century, is that by the name Giant is signified Philip the Fair, King of the French, and so on. These things the words of the author show, even though we say nothing: when he says, And this Giant who sinned with her, that is, the King of France (as Landino explains), made many shameful agreements with Clement, etc. Certainly the disputant will catch nothing with these snares.

units.la: 8 Ibid. Principem Verona intelligi, qui Canes Scaligerus nominabatur, ] negamus interpretationem: nec ita delipuisse Dantem virum grauem & sapientem credimus, vt se eousque in sermonem de rebus tantis, quod est imprudentiæ inuidiæque maximæ & periculosissimæ, iniiceret: præsertim cum res potentissimorum Principum maximè, Imperatoris, & Regis Galliæ ageretur.
units.tr: 8 Ibid. That the prince of Verona is meant, who was called Can Grande della Scala. We deny this interpretation. Nor do we believe that Dante, a grave and wise man, went so far astray that he would venture into speech about such great matters, which is the height of imprudence and of the most dangerous ill will, especially since the affairs of the most powerful princes, the Emperor and the King of France above all, were under discussion.

units.la: 9 Ibid. & nomen Canis exprimit, & ciuitatem eius describit, ] Non sum nescius hanc esse Vellutelli interpretationem quam Bellarminus hoc loco sequutus est. Sed non potest mihi quidem probari illa interpretatio, duabus maximè de causis. Vna est, quòd agit Dantes in eo loco de fuganda, exterminanda, & exstinguenda vniuersè auaritia, quam specie lupæ figurauerat, & in inferos etiam detrudenda, vnde ipsam primum diuisit in gentes inuidiam: nam hæc omnia simul proponit Dantes, quæ in vllum hominem cadere non possunt, aut rectè à mortuis (loquebatur autem cum eo Virgilius) viuenti tribui. Altera est, quòd magnus ille Canis obiit anno ætatis suæ 38. & illi ante octennium Dantes erat præmortuus, vt Vellutellus ipse ibidem annotauit. Fuit autem poema illud non vnius solum aut alterius anni, sed annorum complurium, vel ipso Dante in fine Cant. Paradisi teste: imperitum ergo est, ac non probabile commentum. Dantem, qui anno 3o. magni Canis obiit, & qui se annos aliquot in elaboratissimo illo opere occupauit, de illo vix adolescente in ipso limine operis res tam augustas cecinisse. Quid ergo sibi volebat Dantes sermone illo?aliquid certè Landinus dixit, sed non satis.Primùm itaque verba Dantis Latinè exprimam,deinde sensum eorum exponam paucis. Multa sunt animalia, inquit, illa quibus se coniugabit hæc lupa auaritiæ: Et plura adhuc futura sunt, donec lælaps seu vertagus Veniat, qui faciat eam mori cum dolore. Hic non cibabitur terra neque eleCtro,Sed sapientia, & amore,& virtute: Et natio eius futura est inter coaCtile & coaCtile. Vox Italica veltro à velocitate seu volatu ducta, proprie læPapa seu Pterelam & Vertagum acrem significat, cursui aptissimum & capiendæ feræ:vox peltro,electrum ex vario metallorum genere concinnatum: vox denique feltro, Græca origine, significat πλητὸν (quasi πλητὸν dixeris)opus coactile, vt pileorum & petasorum est, unde πλοντοὶ apud Iurecoss. dicti coactiliarij: quemadmodum & Galli appellant feutre, mutato l in u, quod Gallis ad euphoniam est vsitatissimum.
units.tr: 9 Ibid. And the name Dog both expresses him and describes his city. I am not unaware that this is Vellutello's interpretation, which Bellarmine has followed at this point. But that interpretation cannot, to my mind, be approved, for two chief reasons. The first is that in that passage Dante is speaking of driving out, banishing and utterly extinguishing avarice, which he had pictured under the form of the she-wolf, and of thrusting it down into hell, whence it first divided itself into the nations of envy. For Dante proposes all these things together, which cannot fall to any man, or rightly be attributed to one who is alive, since Virgil was speaking with him, and Virgil was dead. The second reason is that the great Can died in his thirty-eighth year, and Dante had died eight years before him, as Vellutello himself noted in that same place. Moreover, that poem was not the work of one year or of another, but of several years, as Dante himself testifies at the end of the Paradiso canto. It is therefore an inexperienced and improbable fiction to suppose that Dante, who occupied several years on that most elaborate work, and who died in the year the great Can died, sang of such lofty matters about him, a man scarcely grown, at the very threshold of the work. What then did Dante mean by that passage? Landino said something, certainly, but not enough. I shall first render Dante's words into Latin, and then briefly set out their sense. There are many animals, he says, with which she will couple, this she-wolf of avarice. And more are yet to come, until the greyhound or hound comes, who will make her die in pain. He will not feed on land or pewter, but on wisdom, love and virtue; and his nation shall be between felt and felt. The Italian word veltro, derived from swiftness or flight, properly means a swift greyhound, very apt for the chase and for taking wild game. The word peltro means electrum, a compound made from a varied kind of metals. Lastly, the word feltro, of Greek origin, means felt [πλητὸν] (you might say pilēton), a pressed work, as caps and hats are; whence the felt-makers are called plontoi [πλοντοὶ] by Iurecoss.; and as the French also call it feutre, changing l into u, which is very common in French for the sake of euphony.

units.la: Loquitur Dantes de Christo veniente per Euangelium suum, & instauratione Euangelij per seruos suos lupam illam auaritiæ, ac potius lethale monstrum fugaturo, exterminaturo,& in inferos vnde erupit, potenter deturbaturo. Allegorice autem omnia exprimit lupæ & vertagi similitudine, tamquam si dixisset (vt allegoriam in sensum proprium refundamus) Multi sunt homines,non homines sed pecudes, quibus lupa illa exitialis Auaritiæ adhærescet in perniciem ipsorum, Et plures adhuc futuri sunt, Donec Christus Iesus seruator noster,vt Vertagus acer adueniat instructus Euangelio pacis, vt eam ad mortem tristem adigat.Hic adferens Euangelium suum non pascetur agris aut diuitiis, quàs lupa deuorat,sed sapientia,& amore vel charitate Christiana, & virtute diuina: & gens siue natio seruorum eius, id est, pij administri eius calceati praeparatione Euangelij pacis, non est delicias actura in terra aut electro, sed vitam asperam seuerámque victura in pellibus & coactili o-pere ad iter faciendum & iniuriam depellendam commodo. Nam propterea subiicit Poeta: Questi la caccierà per ogni villa, &c. his fugabit eam lupam per omnem vicum, Donec ipsam remiserit in infernum. Eò unde inuidia primùm ipsam dididerat. Hæc germana Dantis, pij & sapientis & grauis Poetæ, sententia. Quamobrem in sequentibus omnibus disputator οὐδὲν πρὸς ὥρας [?]. Coniungantur his quæ dicit Ioannes Apoc.13.& 18. de nundinatione & auaritia Ecclesiam occupatura, & in orbem inundatura ex meretricis gremio: plana hæc omnia futura sunt.
units.tr: Dante speaks of Christ coming through his Gospel, and of the restoration of the Gospel through his servants, who will put to flight that she-wolf of avarice, or rather that deadly monster, will destroy it utterly, and will powerfully thrust it down into the hell from which it broke out. He expresses all these things allegorically, by the likeness of the she-wolf and the greyhound, as if he had said (to turn the allegory back into its literal sense): Many are the men, not men but beasts, to whom that deadly she-wolf of avarice will cling to their destruction. And more are yet to come, until Christ Jesus, our Saviour, comes like a fierce greyhound, armed with the Gospel of peace, to drive her to a grievous death. Bringing his Gospel, he will not be fed on fields or riches, which the she-wolf devours, but on wisdom, and on love or Christian charity, and on divine virtue; and the nation or people of his servants, that is, his godly ministers, shod with the preparation of the Gospel of peace, will not live in delights on land or pewter, but will live a hard and austere life, in skins and in felt work, suited to the journey and to warding off injury. For this reason the poet adds: Questi la caccierà per ogni villa, etc., that is: He will chase her through every village, until he has sent her back into hell, whence envy first drove her. This is the true meaning of Dante, a godly, wise and grave poet. Therefore, in everything that follows, the disputant is talking nothing to the point [οὐδὲν πρὸς ὥρας]. Let these things be joined with what John says in Revelation 13 and 18 about trafficking and avarice that will seize the Church and flood the world out of the bosom of the harlot: all these things are yet to come plainly.

units.la: IN CAP. XVIII.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER XVIII.

units.la: Art.1. venias peccatorum auditoribus pollicentur, cum Pontificis testimonium nullum proferre possint. hoc ita nec Landinus dixit. nec Dantes angustè sensit. Hic enim Poeta grauissimus in Cantico 29. pio & arguto illo, postquam de vanitate & indignitate cucullatorum dixisset, his verbis vtitur: Sed ea auis in ore cucullæ siue capitij nidulatur, Quam si vulgus vidisset, visura esset Indulgentiam, de qua confidit sibi. Qua tanta illusio in terra creuit, Vt sine probatione vllius testimonij ad omnem promissionem concurrent. Hac re pinguefacit porcum sanctus Antonius, Et a'y præterea, qui adhuc magis sunt porci. Soluendo moneta sine charactere. Non dicit Dantes de testimonio bullato Pontificis, sed de testimonio diuino per nō[?] per Euangelium & Scripturam sacram, quæ character est fidei nostræ & diuinæ indulgentiæ, & sine qua moneta nulla iusta est. Nec vero amplius his Landinus dicit, aut verbum ullum facit de Pontifice, quod tamen adspergit Bellarminus ipsius interpretationi. Bullarum quidem meminit: sed quid bullæ, nisi bullæ? Dei, non hominis signum ad certam salutaremque indulgentiam est necessarium.
units.tr: Art. 1. The Papists promise pardons to the hearers of their sermons, although they can produce no testimony of the Pontiff. Landinus did not say this, and Dante did not understand it narrowly. For this most weighty poet, in the twenty-ninth canto, with that pious and lively wit, after speaking of the emptiness and unworthiness of the hooded friars, uses these words: But that bird nests in the mouth of the cowl or hood, which if the crowd saw, they would see the indulgence in which they trust. Such great deception has grown on earth that without any proof of testimony they flock to every promise. For this reason Saint Anthony fattens his pig, and others even worse than pigs. Paying in coin without the stamp. Dante does not speak of the Pontiff's sealed testimony, but of the divine testimony through the Gospel and Holy Scripture, which is the stamp of our faith and of divine indulgence, and without which no coin is valid. Nor does Landinus say anything more than this, or make any mention of the Pontiff, although Bellarmine attributes this to his interpretation. He does indeed mention bulls, but what are bulls except bulls? For a sure and saving indulgence, the sign of God, not of man, is necessary.

units.la: IN CAP. XIX.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: 1 Art.1. respondimus ad ea, quæ ex Dante protulit aduersarius. ] primùm respondit malè, vt hactenus ostendimus: secundò non respondit ad omnia, sed suo commodo Volsellis pugnauit (vt cum Varrone loquar) putatorem, non disputatorem agens.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. We have replied to those things which the adversary brought forward from Dante. ] First, he replied badly, as we have shown so far; secondly, he did not reply to everything, but, to suit himself, fought with Volsellus (to use Varro's words), acting as a pruner rather than a disputant.

units.la: 2 Ibid. sed etiam plane hæreticum & impium esse. ] negatur, & ad singula respondebimus.
units.tr: 2. Ibid. but also plainly heretical and impious. ] This is denied, and we will answer each point.

units.la: 3 Art.2. De sancto Petro sic loquitur Dantes: ] & nos etiam sic loquimur: sed consequens Pontificiorum falsum est, si Petro datæ sunt claves regni cælorum, ergo ipsi soli, ac non aliis Coapostolis & seruis Dei communiter. istud consequens neque Dantes dixit, neque nos concedimus. Contra leges Logicorum est, si à toto in modo siue communi argumentatio fiat de particulari negatiuè: vt controuersia 3.lib.i & 2.sæpe ostendimus.
units.tr: 3. Art. 2. Dante speaks thus of Saint Peter: ] We also speak in this way. But the Papists' inference is false: if the keys of the kingdom of heaven were given to Peter, then they were given to him alone, and not in common to the other apostles and servants of God. Dante did not state this inference, and we do not concede it. It is against the rules of the logicians when an argument moves from the whole, in a general way, to a negative particular, as we have often shown in Controversy 3, Book 1 and 2.

units.la: 4 Art.3. locum sanctum de cælo stabilitum, vbi successor Petri sedem habet? ] hoc nusquam dicit Dantes: sed Bellarminus turbat, vt hoc dicere videatur ille. Iubebatur Dantes per inferos Virgilius sequi re[?] sat diffidens, & duobus exemplis vtitur, quibus probare instituit non esse sibi iustas vires ad suscipiendum expeditionem tantam: Aeneas, quem descendisse ad inferos Virgilius narrat. Aeneid.6.& Pauli Apostoli, qui in caelum tertium, in Paradisum legitur ascendisse, 2. Cor.12. se viribus nec Aeneam esse, nec Paulum. Prius illud exponit his verbis: Tu dici, che di Siluio lo parente, &c. id est, Tu dicis, Siluij parentem Corruptibilem adhuc, id est, Aeneam quum adhuc mortalis esset, ad incorruptibile Seculum abiisse, & itafuisse vt perciperet sensu, nimirum in inferis. Itaque si aduersarius omnis mali, Deus puta, Vrbanus fuit cogitando altum effectum. Qui proditurus erat ab ipso, & qui, & qualis: Non videtur homini intelligenti indignum, illum fuisse alma Romae & imperii in caelo empyreo patre electum: Quae Roma, & quod imperium (vt verum dicamus) Fuerunt stabilita ad locum sanctum, vbi sedet successor maximi illius Petri. Sensus est, Aenea vi quadam singulari fuit instructus vt inferos viseret: vnde etiam sapientibus viris videtur credibile, eum patrem a Deo fuisse datum Romanae vrbis atque imperij: hactenus de consilio & decreto Dei poetica argumentatione. Sequentia vero non dicuntur ex decreto Dei, sed ex humano instituto, quum addit: Quae Roma, & quod imperium fuerunt stabilita, nunc videlicet, humano instituto, non autem diuino, ad locum sanctum vbi sedet, &c. id est, vt habeatur locus sanctus, vbi sedeant successores Petri. Exponit Dantes sequentibus, dicens, Per quae fuerant andata, &c. hac profectione, inquit, Aeneae an inferos, cuius tu das eigloriam, Virgilij, intelliguntur res, quae fuerunt occasiones, id est, occasiones attulerunt. Victoria ipsius, & sta{†}stationis Papalis. Ex figmento poetico nectitur consequens poetice. Quid hac argumentatione facias, Bellarmine? ego, inquit Dantes, nec tantus sum, nec ad res tantas. Quod si quis tamen perui-caciter volet contendere, sedem Petri Romæ esse, hæc certa est responsio, communiter sedem Petri dici pro eo quod est, Petri Apostolorúmque & seruorum Dei. Nam etiam propterea illi Paulum adiungit Dantes sequentibus, vt omnes veteres secerunt, loquentes σωτηρίας, & habet etiamnum scripta multa Pontificum, signa, atque nomisma-ta, de quibus ipse Bellarminus egit contr. 3. lib. 1. cap. 27. Vincunt tamen Pontificij ex eo quod figu-ratè dictum est sfσωτηρίας, conclusionem proprie simplicitérque eruentes, quia causa pia & lu-cratiua est, in Romano foro: in cœlesti, vos autem non sic, Matth. 20. 26. Negamus itaque Bellarmini dictum.
units.tr: 4. Art. 3. A holy place established in heaven, where the successor of Peter has his seat? ] Dante nowhere says this; Bellarmine distorts his words so that he seems to say it. Dante, being somewhat distrustful, was told to follow Virgil through hell, and he uses two examples by which he sets out to prove that he does not have the strength to undertake so great a journey: Aeneas, whom Virgil narrates as having descended to the underworld (Aeneid 6), and the Apostle Paul, who is read to have been caught up to the third heaven, into Paradise (2 Cor. 12). He says that he is neither Aeneas nor Paul in strength. He explains the first in these words: You say that of Silvio's parent, etc., that is, "You say that the parent of Silvius, still corruptible, that is, Aeneas while he was still mortal, went to the incorruptible world, and so was able to perceive with his senses," namely in the underworld. Therefore, if the adversary of all evil, God, that is, was thinking on the lofty effect, the one who was to come from him, and who and of what kind he was, does not seem unworthy to an intelligent man that he was chosen in the Empyrean heaven as the father of Rome, the nourishing city, and of the empire. This Rome and this empire (to speak the truth) were established for the holy place where the successor of that greatest Peter sits. The meaning is that Aeneas was endowed with a special power to visit the underworld; hence it seems credible even to wise men that he was given by God as the father of the city and empire of Rome. So far this is a poetic argument about the counsel and decree of God. But what follows is not said from God's decree, but from human institution, when he adds: This Rome and this empire were established, now clearly by human institution, not by divine, for the holy place where he sits, etc., that is, so that there might be a holy place where the successors of Peter sit. Dante explains this in what follows, saying: Through which had gone, etc. "By this journey," he says, "of Aeneas to the underworld, of whose glory you speak, of Virgil, are understood the things which were the occasions," that is, which brought about the occasions: the victory of that same one, and the establishment of the Papal see. From a poetic fiction a consequence is poetically drawn. What will you do with this argument, Bellarmine? "I," says Dante, "am neither so great nor equal to such great things." But if anyone should still stubbornly wish to contend that the see of Peter is at Rome, this is the sure reply: the see of Peter is commonly spoken of as the see of Peter and of the apostles and servants of God. For this reason Dante also joins Paul in what follows, as all the ancients did, speaking of salvation [σωτηρίας]; and there are still many writings, seals and coins of the Pontiffs, about which Bellarmine himself treated in Controversy 3, Book 1, chapter 27. Nevertheless the Papists conquer from the fact that salvation [σωτηρίας] was said figuratively, drawing out the conclusion as if it were said properly and simply, because the cause is pious and profitable in the Roman marketplace; but in the heavenly one, but you are not so (Matt. 20.26). We therefore deny Bellarmine's statement.

units.la: § Art. 4. qua reuerentia Dantes Pontificem etiam mortuum prosequatur, ] vide supra in cap. 15. nota 2. modestior erat prudentiorque Dantes, quàm vt seculum illud tenebricosum de ea causa commoueret.
units.tr: § Art. 4. With what reverence Dante treats even a dead Pontiff, ] See above on chapter 15, note 2. Dante was more modest and more prudent than to stir up that dark age on that matter.

units.la: 6 Art. 5. † iniuriam illi factam, Christo factam indicari?] Prosopopœia est poetica Hugonis Iapeti in posteritatem suam inuehentis auaritiæ infamis nomine: cuius inter alia exempla illud est Philippi Pulchri Francorum Regis, qui Bonifacium VIII. multauit male. In hac autem narratione Hugo decorum seruans, & in argumento quod agitur prudenter subsistens, nihil plane dicit de criminibus Bonifacij, sed tantùm cum indignatione adsert quæcunque ad grauandum crimen auaritiæ (de quo illic erat agendi locus) in Rege Philippo pertinebant, cætera, quia non erant loci illius, reticet.
units.tr: 6. Art. 5. † That the injury done to him is shown to be done to Christ?] It is a poetic prosopopoeia of Hugh Capet, inveighing against his posterity with the infamous name of avarice. Among other examples of this is that of Philip the Fair, King of the French, who wrongly punished Boniface VIII. In this narrative Hugh, keeping to what is fitting and prudently remaining within the subject in hand, says nothing at all about the crimes of Boniface, but only with indignation brings forward whatever pertained to aggravating the crime of avarice (for which that was the place to speak) in King Philip, and passes over the rest, because it was not appropriate to that place.

units.la: Ad crimen autem Philippi [illegible, ~10 letters] proponendum & indignitatem exaggerandam istius auaritiæ, tria ordine proponit, factum Philippi, sensum mentis siue conscientiæ, & consilium eius. Factum Dantes exponit his verbis: Videbam Anagniam intrare florem lily, &c. Sensum mentis siue conscientiæ exponit ex hypothesi communis opinionis, quam etiam Rex Philippus habebat pro vera, quòd Pontifex Rom. esset vicarius Christi, eóque peccabat longè atrocius, cùm ita contestaretur ex aduerso ipius conscientiæ, dum ait: Fit vicario suo Christum esse captum: quod exaggeratur sequentibus poetica exegesi, dicendo: vidi ipsum Christum altera vice deridere: Vidi renouari actum & fel, Et inter vinos latrones occidi, tamquam si diceret, Philippum & alios Bonifacij aduersarios tam fuisse reum, qui contra sensum veniret suæ conscientiæ, quàm si Christum ipsum cum Iudæis persequutus esset. Tandem consilium sequitur, quum ait, Vidi nouum Pilatum adeo crudelem. Vt hoc ipsum non satiaret, &c. Factum affirmat Dantes, sensum non affirmat, nisi ex hypothesi receptæ opinionis, & quæ in ipso Philippi animo inlidéret, ex quo atrocius crimen eius esse dicit contestante ipius conscientia. Non sequitur [illegible, ~12 letters]. Pathetica autem illa oratio, quæ postsubiungitur, non ad hoc solum, sed ad omnia auaritiæ exempla pertinet, quæ Hugo ante in cantu illo adduxerat.
units.tr: In order to set out the crime of Philip [illegible, ~10 letters] and to magnify the enormity of this avarice, he sets out three things in order: the deed of Philip, the sense of his mind or conscience, and his counsel. Dante sets out the deed in these words: I saw the flower de luce enter Anagni, etc. He sets out the sense of his mind or conscience on the hypothesis of the common opinion, which King Philip also held to be true, that the Roman Pontiff is the vicar of Christ; and therefore he sinned far more atrociously, since his own conscience bore witness against him, when he says: He makes Christ himself captive in his vicar. This is magnified in what follows by a poetic exegesis, saying: I saw Christ himself mocked a second time; I saw the vinegar and gall renewed, and he killed between living thieves, as if he were saying that Philip and the other opponents of Boniface were so guilty that they went against the sense of their own conscience, as if they had persecuted Christ himself with the Jews. Finally the counsel follows, when he says: I saw a new Pilate so cruel that this did not satisfy him, etc. Dante affirms the deed, but does not affirm the sense except on the hypothesis of the received opinion, which pressed upon Philip's own mind, from which he says his crime was more atrocious, his own conscience bearing witness. [illegible, ~12 letters] does not follow. But that passionate speech which is added afterwards pertains not only to this, but to all the examples of avarice which Hugh had earlier brought forward in that canto.

units.la: {7} Art.6. summu officium, sacrosque ordines cum prauis moribus in Bonifacio Dates[?] agnoscat?] verba sunt Guidonis Comitis, vel potius Sinonis, cant.27.de inferno, qui Franciscanus, factus conqueritur de impietate Bonifacij VIII. quod ipsum ad novas & gravissimas fraudes sollicitavisset. Ex hypo-thesi verba sunt, & κατὰ[?] pronunciata, non valet consequentia ex istiusmodi sermone simpliciter.
units.tr: Art. 6. "the highest office, and the holy orders, with corrupt morals in Boniface"; the words are those of Count Guido, or rather of Sinon, Canto 27 of Hell, who, having become a Franciscan, complains of the impiety of Boniface VIII, who had urged him to new and very grave frauds. The words are spoken hypothetically and in character [κατά], and the inference cannot simply be drawn from such speech.

units.la: 8 Art.7. & continuo in genua procubuisse, ] fecisse narrat Dantes, utrum bene aut male, non dicit: ex narratione facti nihil sequitur. Praeterea aut ex officio, aut ex perturbatione animi, insperata rei novitate fecerit, quae trahi in exemplum non debet. Atque haec posterior causa videtur fuisse ex verbis sequentibus. Subiicit enim Dantes: Drizza le gam be, & leuati su, frate: &c. id est, Erige crura, & exsurge, frater, Respondit ille, ne erres, conservus sum Tecum, &c. Non est igitur consequentiae bonae argumentatio.
units.tr: 8 Art. 7. And at once fell to his knees, Dante reports that he did this, but he does not say whether well or badly. Nothing follows from the report of an act. Moreover, he either did it from duty, or from agitation of mind at the unexpected novelty of the event, which ought not to be taken as an example. This latter cause seems to be the true one, from the words that follow. For Dante adds: Straighten your legs and rise up, brother, that is, "Raise your legs and stand up, brother." He answered: "Do not err, I am a fellow servant with you," etc. So the argument is not a sound inference.

units.la: 9 Art.8. Mi ridizzo[?] con le parole sue.] Et qui-vis etiam Episcopus summus sacerdos, summus Pontifex, summus Pastor in iure canonico appel-latur. Nempe respectu vario appellatur summus, aut in sua Ecclesia, aut in dioecesi, aut in Ecclesia universa in hac proprie summus Pontifex Chri-stus, non homo quisquam est. Veteres Rom. Pon-tificem summum respectu Patriarchij vel dioece-seos Patriarchalis suae appellabant. Sic Agape-tum Dantes.
units.tr: 9 Art. 8. I smile at his words. Any bishop whatever is called in canon law the highest priest, the highest Pontiff, the highest Pastor. Indeed, he is called highest in various respects: either in his own church, or in his diocese, or in the universal Church. In this last sense, properly, the highest Pontiff is Christ, no mere man. The ancients called the Roman Pontiff the highest with respect to his Patriarchate or Patriarchal diocese. So Dante calls Agapetus.

units.la: 10 Art.9. Nel santo officio.] sanctum officium est omnium Episcoporum & servorum Dei in Ecclesia ipsius: quid hoc magis ad Potifice Rō. quā ad alios?
units.tr: 10 Art. 9. In the holy office. The holy office belongs to all the bishops and servants of God in his Church. What is this more to the Roman Pontiff than to others?

units.la: 11 Art.10. Quesito vi basli[?] a vostro salvamento.] Elegans locus, pietatem grauitatémque Christianam sapiens. Dicit Dantes: Estote Christiani ad vos commouendos tardiores, Ne estote sicut penna ad omnem ventum, Et ne creditote quod aqua vos quaevis lavet: Habetote vetus & nouum testamentum. Pastor ille Ecclesia, qui vos ducit, Hic vobis sufficit ad salutem ve-stiram[?]. Bona fide, mi Bellarmine, putaresne haec verba ad Pontificem Rom. pertinere? Pium est, de Christo accipi, quia opus est ipsius proprium quarto modo: de vllo homine siquis accipit, derogat Christo officium suum. Nos fieri negamus posse.
units.tr: 11 Art. 10. Be not slow to save yourselves. An elegant passage, wise in Christian piety and gravity. Dante says: "Be Christians, slower to move yourselves; do not be like a feather at every wind, and do not believe that any water washes you. Have the Old and the New Testament. That pastor of the Church who leads you is enough for your salvation." Good faith, my Bellarmine: would you think these words pertain to the Roman Pontiff? It is right to understand them of Christ, because it is his proper work in the fourth manner; if anyone takes them of any man, he takes from Christ his office. We deny that this can be done.

units.la: de-finitio est spei sumpta ex Magistro sentent. lib. 3. distinct.16. Eo discrimen est, quod Magister dicit meritis praecedentibus: Dantes vero prudentius dicit & sanctius: Spes est exspectatio certa futurae gloriae, quam producit Gratia divina & praecedens meritum. Spem enim Christianam nostram non aliud praecedit meritum quam Christi Seruatoris nostri: atque huc respexit Dantes, in cuius mente capienda Bellarminus non mediocriter fallitur. Demonstrant apud Dantem ibidem verba sequentia, quū[?] Psalmus Dauidis adducitur.
units.tr: This is a definition of hope taken from the Master of the Sentences, Book 3, distinction 16. The difference is that the Master says "by preceding merits," whereas Dante says more prudently and more holily: "Hope is the certain expectation of future glory, which divine grace and preceding merit produce." For no merit precedes our Christian hope except that of Christ our Saviour; this is what Dante had in view, and Bellarmine is not a little mistaken in grasping his mind. The words of Dante that follow, where a Psalm of David is cited, show this.

units.la: diserte hic locus agit de dono liberi arbitrii, prout fuit in ipsa creatione hominis a Deo attributum: hoc autem quis unquam negavit nostrum?
units.tr: Here the passage clearly treats of the gift of free will, as it was bestowed by God on man in his very creation. But who among us has ever denied this?

units.la: Haec quidem verba sunt Dantis in persona Virgilii: sed Bellarminum oportebat eorum meminisse quae interroganti poetae Virgilius respon-derat paulo ante. Nam quaesiuerat Dantes, dicen-do: Ma cio m'ha fatto di dubbiar pin[?] pregno, &c. quae hic[?] ferme ad verbum reddimus. Sed hoc me fecit ad dubitandum grauidiorem, Quod si amor foris offertur nobis, Et anima non incedit cum altero pede: Si in directum, aut in distortum incedit, non est ipsius meritum. Et ille mihi, Quantum ratio hic videt, Dare tibi possum ego: inde vlterius respice Tantum ad Beatricem (Theologiam intelligit) quae est opus fidei. etsi postrema haec verba mendo vacare non puto, & legi oportere, quae operatur fide,che pro ch'e. Iniquè facit Theologus, qui ex verbis constrictis rationis humanae angustia argumentatur Theologice, contra ipsum praeceptum Dantis. Aliter contemplatur liberum arbitrium homo naturalis solo rationis suae instrumento, aliter Theologus, quod poeta ille distinxerat diligentissime, & tam apertis verbis. Non considerant vterque liberum arbitrium secundum idem. Est igitur conclusio falsa. De reipsa in tomum 4. videbitur.
units.tr: These are indeed Dante's words, spoken in the person of Virgil; but Bellarmine ought to have remembered what Virgil had answered the questioning poet a little before. For Dante had asked, saying: But this has made me more troubled with doubt, etc. which we render here nearly word for word. But this made me more burdened with doubt, that if love is offered to us from outside, and the soul does not walk with the other foot: if it walks straight or crooked, it is not its merit. And he said to me: As far as reason sees here, I can give you; beyond that look only to Beatrice (he means Theology) which is a work of faith. Yet I do not think these last words are free of error, and it should be read, "which works through faith," che for ch'e. The theologian acts unfairly who argues theologically from the narrow limits of human reason, against the very precept of Dante. Natural man considers free will in one way, with only the instrument of his reason; the theologian in another. The poet had distinguished this most carefully and in such plain words. Neither of them considers free will in the same respect. The conclusion is therefore false. The matter itself will be seen in volume 4.

units.la: 15 Art.13. Alio loco signum Crucis approbat. ] locus est Cant. 2. nos lignum crucis nec horremus, nec improbamus, sed superstitiosum vsum & indignum illius, qui in Papatu obtinet. De hoc signo postea contro. 7.lib.2.cap.29. videbimus.quàm vere sua illa somnia huic probationi adsuat, ipse viderit.
units.tr: 15 Art. 13. In another place he approves the sign of the Cross. The passage is Canto 2. We neither shudder at the wood of the cross nor disapprove of it, but we disapprove of the superstitious use of it, and its unworthy use, which prevails in Papacy. We shall see about this sign later, in controversy 7, book 2, chapter 29. How truly he fits his dreams to this proof, he himself will have to judge.

units.la: 16 Art.14.[?] Alio loco inuocationem sanctorum de-scribit, ] describit quidem, & narrat ex hypothesi recepta Purgatorij, sed non propterea probat, vt nota 8. dicebamus, narrat se audisse, at probare se non dicit iudicio suo.
units.tr: 16 Art. 14. In another place he describes the invocation of saints. He does describe it, and he narrates it from the received hypothesis of Purgatory, but he does not on that account prove it. As we said in note 8, he reports that he heard it, but he does not say that he proves it by his own judgement.

units.la: 17 Artic. 15. de intercessione B. Virginis Mariae.] utroque loco visum unicum est: praeterea visum est Bernardi, quem in hoc argumento fuisse nimium & hyperbolicum nouerunt omnes: poftre-mo vt non negamus intercessionem viuentium pro viuentibus, ita nec pro praefentibus intercef-fionem praefentium & coram postulata audien-tium.Erat autem in visione Dantes Bernardo praesens, & Bernardus propius aberat a Virgine. Dispar itaque ratio est, & nihil ad firmamentum Pontificij abusus pertinens. hic enim praefens praesentem, audiens audientem coram dicitur appellare:illi etiam toto caelo absentes appellant, & audire aflerunt,nos negamus,vt controu. 7.lib.1.cap. 15.& feq.ostendetur.
units.tr: 17 Art. 15. On the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary. In both places there is only a single vision. Besides, it is Bernard's vision, and everyone knows that Bernard was excessive and hyperbolic on this subject. Finally, as we do not deny the intercession of the living for the living, so neither do we deny the intercession of those present for those present, asked and hearing face to face. But in the vision Dante was present to Bernard, and Bernard was nearer to the Virgin. The reasoning is therefore different, and has nothing to do with supporting the papal abuse. For here one present is said to address one present, a hearer a hearer face to face; whereas those others call upon from wholly absent places, and claim to hear. We deny this, as will be shown in controversy 7, book 1, chapter 15 and following.

units.la: quid fiat in vulgo narrat Dantes, non quid probet, vt nota 8.didtum, nos iuris documenta, non opinionum exempla quaerimus.
units.tr: What is done among the common people Dante relates, not what he proves, as noted in note 8. We seek documents of law, not examples of opinions.

units.la: fallit disputator aequiuocatione : non enim agit Poeta de imaginibus in materia expressis, pictis,sculptisve in modum aspectabilem, sed de imaginibus quae repraesentantur animis nostris per praedicationem verbi,cuius proxime meminerat. Duo,inquit,genera sunt imaginum, vel potiùs modi repraesentandis imaginibus sanctorum : vnus, a Deo in Scriptura & verbo ipsius, alter, ab Ecclesia in praedicatione verbi. Demonstrat quod dicimus contextus feries & argumentatio Dantis. Ait enim ad verbum:Sic loqui conuenit ad vestrum ingenium, Quia a solo sensato apprehendit Id quod facit postea intelle-ctu dignum, Propterea Scriptura condescendit facul-tati vestrae, & pedes & manus Attribuit Deo : & aliud intelligit: & sanctla Ecclesia eum aspectu humano Gabrielem & Micaelem vobis repraesentat, Et a-lium, tum, qui Tobiam restituit sanum. Non agit de repræsentatione materiæ, sed Scripturæ & prædicationis illius. Inanis itaque probatio.
units.tr: The disputant deceives by equivocation. For the Poet is not speaking of images expressed in matter, painted or sculpted in a visible form, but of images represented to our minds through the preaching of the word, which he had mentioned just before. There are two kinds of images, he says, or rather two modes of representing the images of saints: one from God in Scripture and his word, the other from the Church in the preaching of the word. The sequence of the context and Dante's argument show what we say. For he says, word for word: It befits speech to suit your capacity, since it apprehends from the sense alone what afterwards it makes worthy of understanding. Therefore Scripture condescends to your faculty, and attributes feet and hands to God, and means something else; and holy Church represents to you Gabriel and Michael with human appearance, and the other one who restored Tobias sound. He does not treat of the representation of matter but of Scripture and of that preaching. Therefore the proof is empty.

units.la: 20 Art. 18. de votis, quæ sine Pontificis auctoritate commutari nequeunt, ] Loquitur ibi dantes de rebus votiuis & offerendis ex obligatione voti, non de personis votiuis, vt ostendit legalis distinctio, quare verbis proximè præcedentibus attulerat. Nihil autem proprie votiuum est, nisi quod est in potestate nostra, vt controu. §. lib 2. cap. 15. & sequentibus ostendimus. Neque verò de auctoritate Pontificis Rom. dicit, sed vniuersè minister[?] j Ecclesiastici, quod clava alba. id est, regni cælorum, & sacerdotali veste designatur. Sensus est, qui res suas obstrinxit deo, ne arbitratu suo mutato, sed ex consilio Ecclesiæ & fidelium dei seruorum qui in ea sunt, a voto sese absoluito. Quid hæc ad Pontificem magis, quàm ad Nolanum Episcopum? Alioquin personas ex dono & vocatione dei colentes virginitatem laudamus cum Apostolo, & bene ex officio facere iudicamus, quum dono vtuntur & obsequuntur vocationi dei. Virginitatem minimè contemnimus, sed eam quæ ambitiosè, atque superstitiosè & contumeliosè in deum sine doni & vocationis diuinæ conscientia quæritur, improbamus.
units.tr: 20 Art. 18. On vows, which cannot be changed without the authority of the Pontiff. Dante speaks there of votive things and of offerings made from the obligation of a vow, not of votive persons, as the legal distinction he had set out in the words immediately before shows. Nothing is properly votive except what is in our power, as we show in controversy §, book 2, chapter 15 and following. Nor does he speak of the authority of the Roman Pontiff, but in general of the minister of the Church, which is indicated by the white club, that is, the kingdom of heaven, and by the priestly vestment. The sense is: one who has bound his goods to God, not to change them at his own pleasure, but to release himself from the vow by the counsel of the Church and of the faithful servants of God who are in it. What does this bear on the Pontiff more than on the Bishop of Nola? Otherwise, we praise, with the Apostle, persons who cultivate virginity from the gift and calling of God, and we judge that they act well from duty, since they use the gift and obey the calling of God. We in no way despise virginity, but we disapprove of that which is sought ambitiously, superstitiously and reproachfully toward God, without awareness of the divine gift and calling.

units.la: 21 Articul. 19. qui virginem Deo dicatam ex monasterio sanctæ clarę rapuerunt, ] factum narrat dantes, non laudat, aut damnat: quid hoc ad probationem argumenti? exemplum refert, non iudicium suum.
units.tr: 21 Art. 19. who carried off a virgin dedicated to God from the convent of holy Clare,] He is recounting a deed, not praising or condemning it. What does this have to do with proving the argument? He reports an example, not his own judgement.

units.la: 22 Art.20. color che son contenti Nel foco,]Non debuit reticere Bellarminus antecedens verbum, Et vederai color che f.&c. id est, Et videbis eos qui continentur Foco, quia sperant venire, Quandocunque fuerit, ad beatas gentes. visum ergo est poeticum, & ex hypothesi communis sententiae, quam refert Dantes poeticè, argumentum operis totius proponitur commodissimè: ipsum de inferno, de Purgatorio, & de Paradiso carmen canturum esse. quod-nam genus hoc probationis est?
units.tr: 22 Art. 20. the colours who are content in the fire,] Bellarmine ought not to have passed over the preceding words, And you will see the colours who are held in the fire, that is, "And you will see those who are held in the fire because they hope to come, whenever it may be, to the blessed nations." This is therefore a poetic passage. On the hypothesis of the common opinion, which Dante reports poetically, the subject of his whole work is most conveniently set forth: that he will sing of hell, of purgatory and of paradise. What kind of proof is this?

units.la: 23 Art.21. Alio loco de suffragiis pro defunctis,] nempe loquitur Dantes, ut poeta, poeticè ex communis erroris hypothesi: fingens priore loco Arnaldum Provincialem poetam, posteriore verò Oderisium Agobbium Miniatorem in Purgatorio enuncian-tes ista, & subsidium alienarum orationum Pur-gatorialibus animis afferri imperantes.
units.tr: 23 Art. 21. In another place, concerning suffrages for the dead,] Dante speaks here as a poet, and poetically, on the hypothesis of a common error: in the earlier place he imagines Arnaldus Provincialis, a poet, and in the later place Oderisi of Gubbio, an illuminator, in Purgatory, pronouncing these things and ordering that the help of other people's prayers be brought to the souls in purgatory.

units.la: 24 Art. 22. de duobus gloriosissimis Ducibus Mi-norum & Prædicatorum.] & hæ narrationes sunt ex hypothesi opinionis in vulgo receptæ, & inuale-scentis superstitionis, cuius incrementa si vidisset magnus ille poeta Dantes ut nos videmus, parcior fuisset in laudando ortu eius, & cunas ipsas pro sua pietate oppugnasset. Nam ut nemo repente pessi-mus, sic nihil fere repente pessimum: etiam sa-pientissimos quosque fallunt principia mali, pro-gressus docent.
units.tr: 24 Art. 22. concerning the two most glorious leaders of the Minorites and the Preachers.] These narratives are based on the hypothesis of an opinion received among the common people and of a superstition that was growing. If that great poet Dante had seen its growth as we see it, he would have been more sparing in praising its birth, and in his piety he would have attacked its very cradle. For as nothing is suddenly most wicked, so there is hardly anything most wicked suddenly: the beginnings of evil deceive even the wisest, and its progress shows this.

units.la: 25 Art.23. de approbatione regulæ S. Francisci per Apostolicam sedem.] horum & sequentium ratio est eadem cum præcedente nota. dignum verò pa-tella[?] operculum, quod vulgo dici solet. Innocentius III. in somnis viderat ruentem S. Ioannis Lateranensis ædem, nisi duo quidam vili habitu eam sustensustentassent. Venit ad eum S.Franciscus, inquiunt Landinus & Vellutellus, ut ipsi religionem suam auctoraret: quem recognoscens Papa, eum ipsum esse in somnis à se visum, confirmavit ei religionem suam Papali bulla, & omnia postulata i-psius indulsit. Ex somnio somniantis Papæ scilicet religionis auctoritas. Si tanti est somnium dormientis, quanti futurum est placitum & decisio vigilantis?
units.tr: 25 Art. 23. concerning the approval of the rule of St Francis by the Apostolic See.] The reasoning for this and the following points is the same as for the preceding note. A worthy lid for a dish, as the common saying goes. Innocent III had seen in a dream the church of St John Lateran falling, unless two men of mean appearance had propped it up. St Francis came to him, say Landini and Vellutello, to have his order approved. The Pope, recognising him as the man he had seen in his dream, confirmed his order by papal bull and granted all he asked. So the authority of a religious order rests on the dream of a dreaming Pope. If a sleeper's dream is worth so much, what will be the worth of the decision and pleasure of a waking man?

units.la: 26 Ibid. Item: Diseconda[?] corona redimita Super Honorio] id est, potestatem habuit ministrandi sacramenta, & dignitatem habendi sacerdotalem, ut ait Landinus. Hoc vero quo iure? nam iure divino oves sunt, non Pastores, & prioris Ecclesiæ usus: quo autem modo? factionibus & rixis indignissimis, quum pro suo iure ordinarij (ut vocant) adver-sus istam instrulionem[?] Monachorum diu multumque decertarent. his legibus in Ecclesia vivitur scilicet.
units.tr: 26 Ibid. Again: the second crown, wreathed above Honorius] That is, he had the power of administering the sacraments and the dignity of holding priesthood, as Landini says. But by what right? For by divine right they are sheep, not ministers, and this is contrary to the practice of the earlier Church. And by what means? By the most unworthy factions and quarrels, while for their so-called ordinary right they long and fiercely contended against that establishment of monks. So evidently this is the law by which people live in the Church.

units.la: 27 Art.24. Item de primis sociis sancti Francisci.] locus est in eodem Cantico qui supra, non in 12. est autem narratio illa tota verbis Thomæ Aquinatis expositæ θεοπρεπωμιτικῶς[?], ut Dates nō[?] suū sensum, sed locum publicum exponeret: Cuius rei vel hoc argumentum est luculentissimum, quòd factionibus Franciscanorum & Dominicanorum inter ipsos illudens. Thomam Aquinatem introducit buccinatorem vel enconiasten S. Francisci, & contrà Bonaventuram præconem S. Dominici, Cant. 12. Aliud est sensum Dantis adferre, aliud mimesin[?] vel prosopopœiam alterius. Sensum Dantis audia-mus Cant. 18. de Paradiso, sub finem cælites appel-lantis ad misericordiam his verbis.
units.tr: 27 Art. 24. Again, concerning the first companions of St Francis.] The passage is in the same Canto as above, not in the twelfth. That whole narrative is set out in the words of Thomas Aquinas, [θεοπρεπωμιτικῶς], in an imitative and prosopopoeic manner, so that Dante might expound not his own sense but a commonplace. The clearest proof of this is that he mocks the factions of the Franciscans and the Dominicans among themselves. In Canto 12 he introduces Thomas Aquinas as the trumpeter or panegyrist of St Francis, and against him Bonaventure as herald of St Dominic. It is one thing to bring forward Dante's own sense, another to bring forward another's mimicry or prosopopoeia. Let us hear Dante's own sense in Canto 18 of Paradise, near the end, where he calls on the heavenly beings to show mercy in these words:

units.la: O militia del ciel, cui io contemplo, Adora per color che sono in terra Tutti sviati dietro al malo esemplo. Gia si solea con le spade far guerra: Ma hor si fa togliendo hor qua, hor quinci Lo pan, ch'e' pio padre a nessun serra. &c.
units.tr: O host of heaven, which I contemplate, pray for those on earth who have all gone astray after the bad example. Once men used to wage war with swords, but now it is done by taking, now here, now there, the bread which the loving father locks up from no one, etc.

units.la: id est, O militia coeli, quam ego contemplor. Adora, vel precare pro us qui sunt in terra, Omnes exorbitantes post malum exemplum. Olim solebat gladiis belligerari: Sed iam fit bellum tollendo modo huic, modo illi Panem, quem pius pater nemini occludit & sexcenta alia eiusmodi, pietatem & scientiam & animum dantis non obscure testificantia.
units.tr: That is: O host of heaven, which I contemplate. Pray, or intercede, for those who are on earth, all who have wandered after the bad example. Once they used to wage war with swords, but now war is made by taking away the bread, now from this one, now from that one, which the loving father shuts up from no one; and six hundred other things of this kind, which plainly testify to his piety, his learning and the mind of the speaker.

units.la: IN CAP. XX.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER XX.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. ut videlicet Romanam curiam multorum vitiorum accusent.] ac proinde etiam non excusent Pontificem, ut caput Romanae curiae.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. namely that they accuse the Roman court of many vices.] And so they do not excuse the Pope either, as the head of the Roman court.

units.la: 2 Ibid. non Pontificum, aut sedis Apostolicae dignitatem imminuant.] quasi vero vitia Pontificum non minuerent dignitatem ipsorum. Sed hoc illud est quod dicit Papa Symmachus c.non nos.dist.40. vel potius Ennodius praeco redemptus a Symmacho: quis sanctum dubuet esse, inquit, quem apex tantae dignitatis attollit? in quo si d.sint bona acquisita per meritum, sufficiunt quae a loci praedecessore testantur: aut enim claros ad haec fastigia erigit, aut qui eriguntur illustrat. Scilicet cathedram sanctificavit Petrus, quam illi oletarent, & tamen ab ea sanctificaren-tur, fieréntque odore ipsorum sordes. Et tu, bone [?]antes, hic non exclames ut Cant. 27. de paradiso? Q difesa di Dio perche pur giaci? veni, o domine Ie-
units.tr: 2 Ibid. they diminish not the dignity of the Popes or of the Apostolic See.] As if the vices of the Popes did not diminish their dignity! But this is what Pope Symmachus says in c. Non nos, dist. 40, or rather Ennodius, the herald hired by Symmachus: who, he says, can doubt that the one whom the summit of so great a dignity raises up is holy? If good deeds acquired by merit are in him, what his predecessor in that place has borne witness to is enough; for either he raises men of distinction to these heights, or he adorns those who are raised up. Clearly Peter sanctified the chair, which they were supposed to stink up, and yet they were sanctified by it, and by their smell the filth was made fragrant. And you, good [?] saints, do you not here cry out, as in Canto 27 of Paradise? Why, O defence of God, do you still lie? Come, O Lord Je-

units.la: su, &c. su,& salutem adfer Ecclesiae tuae.
units.tr: su, etc. su, and bring salvation to your Church.

units.la: § Ibid. atque Apostolis eius, Petro & Paulo.] Petrarcham ipsum audiamus: nam dignus est lectu locus. Respondet Francisco-Bruno Pontificis Secretario, qui ipsum reprehenderat, in hunc modum: Quid vis dicam, aut respondeam? In hoc quidem & in reliquis haud inuitus consilio tuo sistem: ne quid tamen occulam amico tali, siue ego securior, siue tu cautior, nihil tam formidolosum video: seu actiue formidolosum sumitur, seu passiue. Dices mihi. B. veritas odium parit. P. Scio, & expertus scio: odium tamen illud amabile viris fortibus arbitror, etiam, si propter veri studium morien-dum esset, optabile: sed non id periculum est in praesenti certamine. Tutius est interdum belligerare cum multis, quam cum uno: alter alterum exspectans, maluit sua alia quam se alienae vindicem iniuriae. Fuit mihi cum uno istorum nominatim, atque inscriptis, lis pergrauis, & euasi, & agebatur de me solo: hic de tota agitur Ecclesia: honestissima autem bella sunt quae pro repub. fusci-piuntur. B. Nihilne igitur times? P. & quid timeam ord[?]te, cui nihil dari, modicum posset auferri? de his loquor quae fortuita nuncupantur: mea enim mihi nullus eripiet, non senescens tantum & inermis Presbyter, sed nec in-menis tyrannus, nec armatus praedo. B. At negari potest, si quid optaueris. P. Plane mihi negetur Episcopatus quae petendum duxero: imo vero plane mihi detur vt torqueat, & si hac in parte delirauerim, graui ac sollicito mu-nere fera & insolita plectatur ambitio: proinde modo Papam non offenderem, quem non tam propter Papa-tum (obseruua istud, Bellarmine) quam propter eximiam raramque virtutem, & quae illam probant gesta magnifica, perpetuo mihi amadum venerandumque dele-gi, & quem suis reprehensionibus delectatum, alienis multa cum sua laude coniunctis irasci non est verisimiles[?], de caeteris quid ad me? B Non potentiam nosti, non opes.
units.tr: § Ibid. and to his Apostles, Peter and Paul.] Let us hear Petrarch himself, for the passage is worth reading. He answers Francesco Bruno, the Pope's secretary, who had rebuked him, in this manner: What do you want me to say, or to answer? In this matter, as in the rest, I am not unwilling to follow your advice; yet I will not hide anything from such a friend, whether I am the more confident or you the more cautious. I see nothing so fearful: whether fearful is taken actively or passively. You will say to me: "Truth begets hatred." I know it, and I know it from experience. Yet I think that hatred is lovable to brave men, and even desirable if one had to die for the love of truth. But that is not the danger in the present contest. It is sometimes safer to wage war with many than with one; each waiting for the other preferred to defend his own rather than to avenge another's wrong. I once had a very grave lawsuit with one of them, named and written down, and I came through it, and it concerned me alone. Here the whole Church is at stake; and the most honourable wars are those waged for the commonwealth. B. Then do you fear nothing? P. And why should I fear for what has nothing to give, and could lose only a little? I speak of those things called accidental: for no one will take from me what is mine, not a grown-old and unarmed priest, nor an unarmed tyrant, nor an armed robber. B. But it can be denied, if you wish for something. P. Let the bishopric be plainly denied me, since I have thought it not worth seeking; indeed let it plainly be given me so that it may torment me, and if I have gone mad in this respect, let my ambition be punished by a wild and unusual, heavy and anxious office. Therefore, provided I did not offend the Pope, whom I have chosen to love and revere always, not so much for the papacy (note this, Bellarmine) as for his outstanding and rare virtue, and for the splendid deeds that prove it, and since it is not likely that he who is pleased with his reproofs will be angry with things joined to his great praise, what else is it to me? B. You do not know his power, nor his wealth. P. But I know his character too: I know them, and I know myself; and I do not attack men but the vices of men. B. Meanwhile you spare your own.

units.la: P Sed & mores noui: scio illos, & me scio, neque homines, sed vitia hominum insector[?]. B Interim tuis parcis.
units.tr: P. By Hercules, I hate no one more deeply, and I accuse no one more sharply; but I am dealing with it within myself, with this one and that other.

units.la: P Nulla hercle odi altius, nulla acrius arguo: sed id mecum ago, hoc cum altero.
units.tr: B. But that is not yours to do:

units.la: B Non est autem tuum:
units.tr: But it is not yours.

units.la: P Quomodo non est meum quod est omnium? nisi forte Saracenorum siue Iudaeorum, qui nostris gaudent & tripudiant ruinis.
units.tr: How is it not mine, when it belongs to everyone? Unless perhaps it belongs to the Saracens or the Jews, who rejoice and dance over our ruin.

units.la: B At nequicquam niteris: frustra autem niti, ait Crispus, neque aliud se fatigando nisi odium quaerere, extrema dementia est.
units.tr: But you struggle in vain. To struggle in vain, says Crispus, and to seek nothing by one's labour but hatred, is the height of madness.

units.la: P Ego vero nonnihil, immo plurimum quaero: Euaporo animum, & tristitiam questu leuo, posteritati me approbo, & excuso: bonis placeo, & (nisi fallor) Deo, malis certe displiceo: & quoniam verecundia aut conscientia nihil est, aculeos saltem doloris infigo, sed non inscius[?] quam sint multi mali, & quam pauci boni: libro nempe, non numero. Parumne tibi igitur haec videntur?
units.tr: I do indeed seek something, and a great deal. I relieve my spirit and lighten my sadness by complaining. I win the approval of posterity and make my excuses. I please good men and, unless I am mistaken, God; I certainly displease the wicked. And since shame or conscience means nothing to them, I at least drive in the sting of my pain. Yet I am not unaware how many are wicked and how few are good; I count books, not men. Do these things seem too little to you?

units.la: B Quid tibi autem est iniuria illatum, ut sic oderis?
units.tr: B: But what injury has been done to you, that you hate them so?

units.la: P Nihil mihi, sed Rom. urbi, sed Ecclesiae, sed Petro & Paulo, sed Christo: cuius etsi ius-fa[?] non impleam, nomine glorior.
units.tr: P: None to me. But to the city of Rome, to the Church, to Peter and Paul, to Christ. Although I do not fulfil his law, I glory in his name.

units.la: Neque vero omnes, immo equidem nullum odi: quosdam vero & dilexi, quibusdam & diligi visus sum, & quid eorum amor valeat, si utilitas & blanditia essent, probe didici.
units.tr: Nor do I hate everyone; indeed I hate no one. Some I have loved, and to some I have seemed loved, and I have learned well what their love is worth when it is only usefulness and flattery.

units.la: B Sed ah nescis plus saepe parum odii nocere, quam amoris plurimum prodesse?
units.tr: B: But do you not know that a little hatred often does more harm than much love does good?

units.la: P Nihil penitus scio, nihilque velim scire quo timidior fiam: qui nihil cupit, & nihil metuit.
