Ut quorundam animantium magnitudo terribilis ac nocendi potens, sic quorundam ipsa paruitas atque impotentia tuta est, & violentia inaccessa. Quid unquam musca aquila nocuit? quid formica leo? haec dixi ut me intelligas, &c. Haec bona fide Petrarchae verba, quae literis B.& P.additis illustraui, ut obiectiones Brunià[?] solutionibus Petrarchæ commodiùs haberentur distinctæ, quod lectoribus adiumento esset. Multa profectò his verbis insunt, quæ disputatoris causam minimè adiuuant.
units.tr: P: I know nothing at all, and I would not wish to know anything that would make me more timid, for he who desires nothing and fears nothing is safe. As the size of some creatures is terrifying and able to do harm, so the very smallness and powerlessness of others is safe, and their weakness is beyond attack. What has a fly ever harmed in the eagle's presence? What has an ant done to the lion? I have said this so that you may understand me, and so on. These are Petrarch's words, cited in good faith; I have illustrated them by adding the letters B and P, so that the objections of the Bellarmine dialogue may be kept more conveniently apart from Petrarch's replies, which will be a help to readers. Indeed, many things in these words do not help the disputant's cause at all.

units.la: 4 Ibid. si amicus sit vicario Iesu Christi?] hæc quidem verba sunt Petrarchæ, sed mutila. Nam Innocentius sextus, quum nondum esset Pontifex, odium pergraue in Petrarchā priuata de causa conceperat, & criminationem temere imbiberat de eo, quòd magus esset, prout tum ferme iniquitate seculi illius habebantur qui literarum scientiâ præstabant, Hieronymi Squarzaficho teste in vita illius. Hoc igitur malum respiciens Petrarcha, quòd leuatum officio bonorum animaduertebat, prudenter honores oblatos recusans vtitur verbis aptis ad gratiarum actionem honestam, cum modesta criminis antecedentis commemoratione.
units.tr: 4. Ibid. if he were a friend of the vicar of Jesus Christ? These are indeed Petrarch's words, but cut short. For Innocent VI, before he became pope, had conceived a serious hatred against Petrarch for private reasons, and had rashly taken up the accusation that he was a magician, as learned men were then commonly regarded in that unjust age, according to Girolamo Squarzafico in his life of him. Petrarch, observing this evil, and seeing that it had been lightened by the good offices of good men, wisely declined the honours offered him, and uses words suited to an honourable expression of thanks, with a modest reminder of the earlier accusation. Bellarmine concludes badly from this, since the words are spoken and reported in a divided sense, as they say. The consequence is false.

units.la: Ecce nunc, inquit, iterum aliis atque aliis de eadem re & literis pulsor & nunciis, quibus & stupor meus crescit & gaudium. Nam quis, quæso, non stupeat, simulque non gaudeat, si amicus sit vicario Iesu Christi, qui me magicum non tantùm suspicari, sed affirmare sileat? & quæ sequuntur. Vicarium Iesu Christi dicit ex communi vsu, cætera ex rei veritate & conscientia. Sed male Bellarminus concludit ex eo quod κατὰ[?] dictum, & relatum diuiso sensu, vt loquuntur. Consequentia falsa.
units.tr: Behold now, he says, again I am pressed by letters and messengers on the same matter, which both increase my astonishment and my joy. For who, I ask, would not be astonished, and at the same time rejoice, if he were a friend of the vicar of Jesus Christ, who keeps silent about suspecting me of being a magician, let alone asserting it? and what follows. He calls him the vicar of Jesus Christ according to common usage, and the rest according to the truth of the matter and his conscience. But Bellarmine concludes wrongly from what was said, and reported in a divided sense, as they say. The consequence is false.

units.la: 5 Ibid. veritatis vitæ vicarius es in terris.] hæc ita de Pontifice prædicantur, vt aliorum quoque Dei seruorum communia sint, etiam magistratuum: nam Dei minister est tuo bono, inquit Apostolus Rom.13.4. singularem illam prærogatiuam Ponti-ficis Rom. negamus esse, vt contro.[?] nullam esse toto orbe terrarum civitatem, ubi magis religio ac devotio erga res divinas conspiciatur, affirmat. ] hæc omnia Petrarcha dedit loco & tempori, & (quod amplius est) argumento instituto orationis suæ. Volebat enim Urbanum Pontificem Avenione evocare, & Romæ Italiæque restitui homo Italus Pontificem. Sic argumentum suum exornat quàm maximè potest, oratorie. Multis probarem, nisi me scirem Theologiæ & veritati eius operam dare oportere, sepolita Romæ & Avenionis, Tiberis & Rhodani, Italiæ & Galliæ comparatione, quam ibi pro argumento Petrarcha adhibuit, cùm tamen de ipso male merita non esset Gallia. Sed neque hic nobis insanire lubet. Negatur ex eiusmodi oratione consequi ea quæ Bellarminus intendit.
units.tr: 5. Ibid. You are the vicar of the truth and of life on earth. These things are said of the pope in such a way that they are common also to the other servants of God, even to magistrates: for he is God's minister for your good, says the Apostle, Rom. 13.4. We deny that this singular prerogative belongs to the Roman pontiff, when he affirms that there is no city in the whole world where religion and devotion towards divine things are more evident. Petrarch gave all these things to the place, the time, and (what matters more) the argument of his speech. For he wished to summon the pope Urban from Avignon, and to have the pope, an Italian, restored to Rome and Italy. So he adorns his argument as richly as he can, in the manner of an orator. I could prove this at length, were I not aware that I must devote myself to theology and its truth, by burying Rome and Avignon, the Tiber and the Rhône, and the comparison of Italy and France, which Petrarch brings in there as an argument, although France had not deserved ill of him. But we have no wish to rave here either. It is denied that the things Bellarmine intends follow from such a speech.

units.la: Nulla, inquit, homini in vicarium Dei sui causa sufficiens est offensionis. ] vicarium Dei dicit, ut nota 5. Cæterum dignus locus est quem integrum apponamus: nam de Columnensibus Italis, non de Rege Galliæ hos sermones habet in hunc modum:
units.tr: No cause, he says, is sufficient for a man to take offence at the vicar of his God. He calls him the vicar of God, as noted at 5. But the passage is worth setting out in full, for he speaks in this way not of the king of France but of the Italian Colonna family:

units.la: Etsi enim nulla homini in vicarium Dei sui causa sufficiens sit offensa, tamen revera linguae ille licentioris, & altioris (si dici fas est) animi vir, quàm Domini vicarium deceret humillimi, quicquid passus est, non sine causa quidem ab hostibus est passus, utique magnis atque insignibus viris longa & graui persecutione lacessitis atque afflictis, quòd iam sic ad extrema perductis, ut aut grande illis aliquid audendum, aut funditus corruendum esset, ac propterea tam grauius nihil metuentibus, quibus mors aerumnarum finis, nō accessio videretur. Nec tamen ea res sine magni alterius hostis auxilio ac fauore: nec tunc etiam aperta vi, sed noctu-rnis insidiis acta est.
units.tr: For although no cause is sufficient for a man to take offence at the vicar of his God, yet in truth that man, of a more reckless tongue and a higher spirit (if it is right to say so), whatever he suffered was not indeed suffered without cause at the hands of his enemies. He was assailed and afflicted by a long and grievous persecution, by great and distinguished men, who had been brought to such extremities that they had either to dare something great or be utterly ruined. Therefore, fearing nothing, they regarded death, which is the end of troubles, as no addition to them, and so they were the more dangerous. Nor was this done without the help and favour of another great enemy; nor was it done then by open force, but by nocturnal ambushes.

units.la: 8 Ibid.sed obsequium insuper & obedientiam debemus.] hæc omnia eiusdem sunt generis. Loquitur Petrarcha ex vsu communi & opinione recepta, non probas quod dicit, sed supponês quod dicebatur & habebatur vulgo. Alioquin enim quomodo Pontifex Rom. ad illud fastigium ascenderit non diuina auctoritate, sed humana arte atque instituto, Satanæ dolis, & mundi imprudentia, satis in controuersiam 3.&4. exposuimus.
units.tr: 8. Ibid. but we owe, moreover, submission and obedience. All these things are of the same kind. Petrarch speaks according to common usage and received opinion. He does not prove what he says, but assumes what was said and held by the people. For otherwise, how the Roman pontiff rose to that height not by divine authority but by human art and contrivance, by the wiles of Satan and the imprudence of the world, we have set out sufficiently in Controversies 3 and 4.

units.la: 9 Ibid.sed etiam de cæteris omnibus fidei nostræ ca-pitibus.] hæc non sunt huius instituti: neque enim Petrarcham testem capitum fidei, sed impietatis quæ Romæ obtinet appellamus. Etsi videamus quid possint disputatoris argumenta.
units.tr: 9. Ibid. but also concerning all the other articles of our faith. These matters do not belong to this undertaking. For we do not call Petrarch a witness to the articles of faith, but to the impiety that prevails at Rome. Yet let us see what the disputant's arguments can do.

units.la: 10 Ibid.& missas deuotissimè celebrauerit.] de monastica vita diximus in controu. 5.lib.2.de missa in tom 3. videbimus. ex vsu seculi, non ex certa scientia loquutus est Petrarcha. Etsi quid mirum, si & temporum iniuria, & suæ infirmitatis conscientia, & mundi contemptu siue religioso, siue superfti-tiofo(hoc enim vitium ferme adnasci solet) se in solitudines & secessus contulerunt boni?
units.tr: 10. Ibid. and celebrated Mass most devoutly. We have spoken of the monastic life in Controversy 5, book 2, and we shall see about the Mass in volume 3. Petrarch spoke according to the custom of his age, not from certain knowledge. And yet what wonder is it, if good men withdrew into solitudes and retreats, both from the wrongs of the times, from the consciousness of their own weakness, and from contempt for the world, whether religious or superstitious (for this vice is usually inborn)?

units.la: 11 Ibid. orat pro anima Pontificis defuncti.] esto sanè: ad Christum orat, non alium quemquam. Quo autem modo priora seculaa pro defunctis orauerint, controu. 6.& 7. exponimus.
units.tr: 11. Ibid. he prays for the soul of the deceased Pontiff. Granted, certainly: he prays to Christ, and to no one else. How the earlier centuries prayed for the dead we set out in Controversies 6 and 7.

units.la: 12 Art.1.B.Virginem ac Sanctos cateros magna deuotione implorat.] hæc omnia ex vsu illo superstitioso & peruulgato seculi: cui Petrarcha siue prudens cesserit (vt multi faciunt) siue imprudens crediderit, præiudicare non potest veritati.
units.tr: 12. Art. 1. He implores the Virgin and the other Saints with great devotion. All these things come from that superstitious and widespread usage of the age. Petrarch, whether he yielded to it prudently, as many do, or believed it imprudently, cannot prejudice the truth.

units.la: 13 Ibid. Vedra Bologna,& poi la nobil Roma.] Quæ hic de Rom. Pontifice dicuntur, ex vsu in publicum iamdiu inuecto dicuntur. Quod vicarius Christi appellatur, aut fit communi, aut singulari modo. Si communi, bene est: de eo diximus nota 5. sinau-tem singulari, vt fit hoc tempore, negamus.
units.tr: 13. Ibid. Verona, Bologna, and then noble Rome. What is said here about the Roman pontiff is said in accordance with a usage long since introduced into public life. That he is called the vicar of Christ is either said in a common sense or in a singular sense. If in a common sense, it is well; of that we spoke at note 5. But if in a singular sense, as is the case now, we deny it.

units.la: ] factionum Italicarum verba sunt, quum rueret Imperatorum in Italia auctoritas. Liberius vero paulo ante illam, quum res integriores essent, asseruerat ex iure, & veritate Dantes Cant. 6. de Purgatorio, & alibi.
units.tr: These are the words of the Italian factions, when the authority of the emperors in Italy was collapsing. Earlier, however, when things were still more intact, Dante had asserted it more freely, from right and truth, in Canto 6 of the Purgatorio, and elsewhere.

units.la: ] falsum: non agit Petrarcha de Romana urbe, sed de Ecclesia Dei in urbe Rom. hospitante. hoc visurus est facile, quisquis, sine praeiudicato expendet ipsa Petrarchae verba quę Bellarminus adducit.
units.tr: This is false. Petrarch is not speaking of the city of Rome, but of the Church of God dwelling in the city of Rome. Anyone who weighs Petrarch's own words, which Bellarmine adduces, without prejudice will see this easily.

units.la: ] narratio est, non iudicium Petrarchae: quis autem nescit aeque mala ac bona narrari posse?
units.tr: It is a narrative, not a judgment, by Petrarch. But who does not know that bad things can be narrated just as well as good ones?

units.la: ] ex communi errore & opinione Petrarcha eo deuenit, ut Virginis aduocationem imploraret. Quod errores suos deplorauit, factum bene: quod non sine errore deplorauit, abductus communi errore, humanum factum est hominis, quod accipimus humaniter, atque ignoscimus. Et certe expediuit sese ab hoc errore Petrarcha quodammodo vi veritatis & conscientiae, quum illud carmen inter alia perscriberet: quo Bellarminus ipse imprudens claudit hoc ipsum caput. Nam Deum solum appellat in utroque carmine: sed posterius dignum est quod omnes intelligant. Postquam eundem planxit errores & amores suos, & addit: Tu, the vedi i miei mali indegni & empi, &c. quos versus ad verbum ita reddimus. Tu, qui vides mea mala indigna & impia, Rex cœli inuisibilis, immortalis, Succurre animæ aberranti & fragili, Eiusque defectum tua gratia adimple: Adeo vt si vixerim in bello & in procella, Moriar in pace & in portu: & fistatio Fuit vana, saltem sit discessus honestus, Ad hoc pauculum vitæ, quod mihi procedit. Et ad moriendum, dignetur esse tua manus præsto: Tu scis bene, quod in alio non habeo spem. hæc ad verbum, quæ sanctissime Petrarcha pronunciauit, spem suam in Deo solo testatus esse, ac non in alio vllo.
units.tr: Through common error and opinion, Petrarch came to implore the Virgin's intercession. That he deplored his errors was a good thing. That he deplored them not without error, carried along by the common error, is a human failing of a man, which we accept humanely and pardon. And certainly Petrarch in some measure freed himself from this error by the force of truth and conscience, when among other things he wrote that poem with which Bellarmine himself, unwittingly, closes this very chapter. For in both poems he addresses God alone, but the later one is worth everyone's attention. After he had lamented the same errors and loves of his, he adds: You, who see my unworthy and impious evils, etc. We render these verses word for word as follows: "You, who see my unworthy and impious evils, invisible and immortal King of heaven, succour a wandering and frail soul, and fill its lack with your grace; so that, even if I have lived in war and storm, I may die in peace and in harbour; and if my delay was in vain, let at least my departure be honourable, for the little life that is left to me. And for dying, may your hand deign to be at hand; you know well that I have no hope in another." These are the words in which most holy Petrarch declared that his hope is in God alone, and in no other. ## In Chap. XXI.

units.la: In Cap. XXI.

1 Art. quæ in eo libro Italico continentur quem scripsit de vita & moribus Pont. ] si liber est ipsius: quod non est credibile. Nam neque Paulus Vergerius, Hieronymus Squarzafichus eum agnoscunt in vita ipsius, neque veritati historiæ & genio Petrarchæ respondet. Quamobrem nihil probatur sequenti-bus, ex libro supposititio[?]. Profecto eu Pontificem vir integer laudare non potuit, qui tantopere infa-niuit amore sororis ipsius: & ipsum magnificis promissis, etiam galeri Cardinalitij & Gerardum fratrem sollicitauit, vt ea impure potiretur: quæ res fecit vt Petrarcha ex comitatu Pontificio fugeret, scripta morali cantilena quæ incipit, Io non vo pin[?] cantare como solea, &c. testes Philelphus & Squarzafichus.
units.tr: 1 Art. which are contained in that Italian book which he wrote on the life and morals of the Popes: if it is his book, which is not credible. For neither Paulus Vergerius nor Hieronymus Squarzafichus acknowledges it as his, and it does not agree with the truth of history or with Petrarch's character. Wherefore nothing is proved by what follows from a spurious book. Certainly an upright man could not have praised that Pope, who raved so madly with love for his sister, and who, with magnificent promises, even solicited for him the cardinal's hat and his brother Gerard, so that he might possess her impurely. This matter led Petrarch to flee the papal court, writing a moral song that begins I no longer want to sing as I used to, etc. The witnesses are Philelphus and Squarzafichus.

units.la: 2 Art.2.sed de vitiis tantum quæ tum vigebant, ea dicere: quasi vero etiam doctrinæ non essent vitia. Deinde an error tibi vitium est? dicit autem Petrarcha, Albergo di dolor, madre d'errori Sonetto 92. id est, hospitium doloris, erroris mater. item Sonetto 108. Fontana di dolore, albergo dira, Schola d'errori, & tempio d'heresia, Gia Roma, hor Babylonia falsa & ria, &c. id est, fons doloris, hospitium irae, Schola erroris, & templum hæreseos, Ante Romaniam Babylonia falsa & nequam, &c. lic alia multa.
units.tr: 2 Art. 2. but he speaks only of the vices that were then prevailing, as if doctrine were not also a vice. Then, is error not a vice for you? Petrarch says: An inn of sorrow, mother of errors, Sonnet 92, that is, an inn of grief, mother of error. Likewise Sonnet 108: Fountain of sorrow, cruel inn, school of errors and temple of heresy, once Rome, now false and wicked Babylon, etc., that is, fountain of sorrow, inn of anger, school of error and temple of heresy, once Rome, now false and worthless Babylon, etc. And many other such things.

units.la: 3 Ibid. ut scriberet Rom. Pontificem Antichristum falsum, aut Ecclesiam ipsam Rom. Id certè non obscurè cecinit Petrarcha in sex illis carminibus (Sonetta vocat) quæ tantopere Sixtus V. improbauit, ut aliqua expungi ex scriptis illius duxerit oportere. Affirmauit palàm Sixtus, quod mutata sententia (nam carmina exstincta putat) Bellarminus negare audet. Hoccine probitatis est? ubi pudor, ii ita non pudet disputare?
units.tr: 3 Ibid. that he wrote that the Roman Pontiff is the false Antichrist, or the Roman Church itself. Petrarch certainly sang this not obscurely in those six poems (he calls them sonnets) which Sixtus V so greatly disapproved of that he judged some of them should be struck out of his writings. Sixtus plainly affirmed it, and that Petrarch later changed his opinion (for he thinks the poems were suppressed), yet Bellarmine dares to deny it. Is this honesty? Where is shame? Are they not ashamed to argue in this way?

units.la: 4 Ibid. sacrosanctissimam sedem appellat.] de his duobus argumentis diximus in caput 2o nihil sequitur ex æquiuocatione recti, nihil ex falso ueri.
units.tr: 4 Ibid. he calls it the most holy see. We have spoken of these two arguments in chapter 2: nothing follows from an equivocation about what is right, and nothing from what is false about what is true.

units.la: 5 Ibid. nefarium illud bellum in summum catholicæ Ecclesiæ Past[?]] quòd nefarium vocat, perturbationi animi ignoscimus: quòd negat, iniquè facit. Nam Petrarcha ipse ad hoc opus apertè Galliam excitat, cantico illo 2. cuius principium est. L'auara Roma haura l'ultimo scacco, S'io non m'inganno. Et tu, mia Francia, dei O darlo a quella volta, o cieca sei, &c. id est, Auara Roma habitura est ultimum casum, Nisi fallor, & tu, mea Francia, debes Aut dare illum) hoc est, præstare) hoc istu, aut cæca fueris, &c. Si his moribus uiuitur, ubi fides? si pugnatur his telis, ubi iustitia?
units.tr: 5 Ibid. that impious war against the supreme Catholic Church: that he calls it impious we pardon as a disturbance of mind; that he denies it, he does unjustly. For Petrarch himself openly stirs up France to this undertaking, in his second canzone, whose beginning is: Greedy Rome will suffer the last check, unless I am mistaken. And you, my France, must either give it to that side, or you are blind, etc., that is, greedy Rome is about to fall at last, unless I am mistaken, and you, my France, must either bring this about (that is, furnish it), or you will be blind, etc. If life is lived by such customs, where is faith? If the fight is waged with such weapons, where is justice?

units.la: 6 Art.3. Pium V. Pontificem nullam fecisse Petrarcha iniuriam,] saltem quam Petrarcha senserit: at sensit posteritas, senserunt boni, quibus se probari & placere voluit, vt ex epistola eius ad Brunum cap. 20. nota 3. ostendimus. iniuriam ergo Petrarchae fecit, qui posteritati fecit, cui se Petrarcha probari voluit. Sequentia σοφίσματα[?] sunt, & coniectura contraria elidi possunt, si cui referendum esse, par pari videbitur. Negamus Petrarcham fuisse facturum: sed contrà intonaturum in Romam gravius, quo in deterius abiit Pontifex & Roma tota, ex eo tempore.
units.tr: 6 Art. 3. that Pius V did Petrarch no wrong: at least not as Petrarch perceived it. But posterity perceived it, and the good perceived it, those to whom he wished to be approved and pleasing, as we have shown from his letter to Bruno, chapter 20, note 3. He therefore did wrong to Petrarch, who did wrong to posterity, to whom Petrarch wished to be approved. The following are sophisms [σοφίσματα], and the contrary conjecture can be rebutted, if it is to be referred to whoever it may be; equal will be matched against equal. We deny that Petrarch would have done so; rather, he would have thundered more severely against Rome, into which the Pope and all Rome have gone downhill since that time.

units.la: 7 Art.4. Iudicem enim aduersarius fecit, haereticum esse: negamus sequi ex falsis, aut ambiguis aut secundum quid dictis probationibus: has autem omnes sic esse, euidenter supra in caput 20. docuimus. Sequens antithesis, vbi in nos inuehit non solum est declamatoria, sed falsa & sycophantica. Singula in suis locis refellimus: non placet hic actum (quod aiunt) agere. αὐτὸς αὖ πυθμὴν ὁδός[?].
units.tr: 7 Art. 4. For he made the adversary a judge that he is a heretic: we deny that it follows from proofs that are false, ambiguous, or true only in a certain respect; and that all of these are so, we have clearly taught above in chapter 20. The following antithesis, in which he inveighs against us, is not only declamatory but false and sycophantic. We refute each point in its own place; it does not please us to do here what they call "doing the same thing again" [αὐτὸς αὖ πυθμὴν ὁδός].

units.la: In Cap. XXII.
units.tr: In Chapter XXII.

units.la: 1 Art.1. sed addit hoc ipsum manifestum argumentum esse veritatis fidei ac religionis, quae Romae colitur. prius membrum agnoscimus, sed illam circumscriptione, quae Romae colitur, negamus veram esse: auctoris verba adferri oportuit. Aliud est Christiana religio, cuius certa aeternitas, aliud Romana, cuius certa semper est mutabilitas, & nunc comperta mutatio.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. but he adds that this very thing is a manifest argument of the truth of the faith and religion which is cultivated at Rome. We acknowledge the first clause, but we deny that the religion cultivated at Rome, under that qualification, is true. The author's own words ought to have been quoted. Christian religion is one thing, whose eternity is certain; Roman religion is another, whose mutability is certain and whose change is now a matter of record.

units.la: 2 Ibid. & ad sacrosancta illa mysteria plane indignus accessit. nos quidem res diuinas omneis religiosè procurari & enunciari iubemus: sed haec quaestio quam risit Boccacius, vtrum Confessio & extrema vnctio sacramenta sint, quod negamus, & tomo 3. confutabimus. De monasticis argumento diximus controuersia 5.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. and he approached those most holy mysteries in a wholly unworthy way. We indeed order that all divine things be handled and spoken of with reverence. But this question, which Boccaccio laughed at, whether Confession and extreme unction are sacraments, we deny, and we will refute it in volume 3. We have spoken about monastic matters in controversy 5.

units.la: 3 Art.2. Causa est in promptu, nescit enim vulgus c. quasi vero non potuerit alia ratione prospici, quàm abolendis, expungendis, aut corrumpendis libris. Ῥῶμα mi homo, narras, ac non ἰάματα. nam quis non hac occasione roget, quid est? quid dixit? aut quid commeruit? Equidem vt nunquam probaui lapsus hominum eiulgari, quod contra charitatem est: ita nec probare possum lapsus hominum publicos dissimulari, quorum dissimulatio damnosa publico futura est: illos tegere, priuatæ charitatis est, hos retegere, opus est publicæ charitatis, & fortitudinis verè Christianæ. Vtinam verò non fuisset data copiosa à Pontificiis sacerdotibus atque monachis per tot secula occasio.
units.tr: 3 Art. 2. The cause is ready to hand, for the common people do not know... As if it could not have been provided for by some other means than by abolishing, erasing or corrupting books. "You tell me of wounds [ῥῶμα], my good man, and not of remedies [ἰάματα]." For on this occasion who would not ask: what is it? what did he say? or what has he deserved? Indeed, just as I have never approved of publicising men's lapses, which is contrary to charity, so I cannot approve of public lapses being hushed up, since their concealment will be harmful to the public. To cover up private lapses belongs to private charity; to expose public ones is a task of public charity and of truly Christian courage. Would that the Papist priests and monks had not given so many centuries a copious occasion for this!

units.la: 4 Art. 3 ne facinoris aspeƈtus eos, qui idem ipsum cernerent, vlla ex parte laderet. agebat Constantinus de iis criminibus quæ salua ratione publici possunt contegi. nam etiam Imperator & iustus ac prudens magistratus ea castigare & potest & debet sine publica nota, propter grauiorem (vt nostri vocant vulgo) consequentiam. Eadem Cypriani ratio. Inanis est itaque argumentatio, quam belle sibi ex particulari Bellarmino videtur adstruere.
units.tr: 4 Art. 3 lest it should in any way harm those who saw the very deed. Constantine was dealing with those crimes which can be covered up without harm to the public good. For even an emperor, and a just and prudent magistrate, can and must punish such things without public disgrace, on account of the graver consequence (as our people commonly call it). The reasoning of Cyprian is the same. The argument is therefore empty, which he seems to build so neatly for himself from the particular case of Bellarmine.

units.la: 5 Art. 4. de precibus pro defunctis, de sacrificio Missæ plane catholicè scribit. ] sed ista omnia nihil pertinent ad causam quæ agitur: non enim quæstio iuris est proprie, sed facti, quam auctor anonymus ex illis auctoribus probatam voluit: nempe Romam, & Romanam curiam, & caput ipsius Babylonis illius, quam Scriptura descriplit, vitiis quà doctrinæ, quà morum, quà disciplinæ atque ordinis Ecclesiastici abundare.
units.tr: 5 Art. 4. he writes about prayers for the dead and the sacrifice of the Mass quite in a catholic manner. But all these things have nothing to do with the matter in hand. For the question is not properly one of right but of fact, which the anonymous author wanted proved from those writers: namely, that Rome, and the Roman curia, and the head of that very Babylon which Scripture describes, abound in vices of doctrine, of morals, of discipline and of ecclesiastical order.

units.la: In Cap. XXIII.
units.tr: In Chapter XXIII.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. & eorum multitudines agmina quædam Antichristum præcurrentia esse credamus. ] & antece- dens falsum, & consequens. Utrumque negamus, ad probationes transeamus.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. and we should believe their multitudes to be troops going before Antichrist. Both the antecedent is false and the consequent. We deny both. Let us pass on to the proofs.

units.la: 2 Art. 2. nuncium Dei a Dante prædictum] vide supra in cap. 17.
units.tr: 2 Art. 2. the messenger of God foretold by Dante. See above, in chapter 17.

units.la: 3 Ibid. multoque deteriores, quam fuerint in Papatu.] iniquum est, sermones demegoricos ita præcise rapiʼnam quis nescit multa in sermonibus figuratè dici, quæ si ad viuum reseces, cum veritate pugnare videbuntur? sed elto. Lutherus de communi loquitur, & de primis temporibus illis quibus edidit Postillas suas: neque simpliciter de eo queritur, quòd Ecclesiæ (vt Bellarminus vocat) Lutheranæ sint deteriores Pontificiis, sed quòd homines illi qui ad Lutheri doctrinam transiuerant, mutationem religionis in effrænè morum licentiam conuertissent. Alia est ratio Ecclesiæ, alia hominum multorum in Ecclesia vitiis & malis moribus indulgentium: quam rem præcedentibus cap. cùm Bellarminus toties distinxerit, quid est cur obliuiscatur in hoc loco, & particularem hominum conditionem cum Ecclesia confundat? negamus sequi.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. and far worse than they were in the Papacy. It is unfair to snatch at sermons, which are figurative, so precisely. Who does not know that many things are said figuratively in sermons, which, if you cut them down to the quick, will seem to clash with the truth? But let that pass. Luther speaks of the common people and of those early times in which he published his Postils. Nor does he simply complain that the Lutheran churches (as Bellarmine calls them) are worse than the Papists, but that those men who had passed over to Luther's teaching had turned the change of religion into unbridled licence of morals. The condition of the Church is one thing; that of many men indulging in vices and bad morals within the Church is another. Since Bellarmine has so often distinguished these in the preceding chapters, why does he forget this here and confuse the particular condition of men with the Church? We deny the inference.

units.la: 4 Art. 3. Is in concione 4. super caput 21. Lucæ sic habet:] de homine nihil dicimus: qua in re inimicum animum suum disputator prodit, & nihil causam adiuuat. hoc tantùm dico vt ante, Iacobum Andreę de hominum vitiis particularibus, non de Ecclesia dicere. Inconsequens igitur argumentatio.
units.tr: 4 Art. 3. In sermon 4 on chapter 21 of Luke he has this: We say nothing about the man. In this matter the disputant betrays his hostile spirit and does nothing to help his cause. I say only, as before, that James Andreae spoke of the particular vices of men, not of the Church. The argument is therefore inconsequent.

units.la: 5 Art. 4. Is in epistola ad Vulturium Neocomum:] Erasmo cum aquilis res fuit, non cum Vulturiis: istum Vulturium Erasmus non nouit. Subieɖitiɨ est & ψευδώνυμος[?] epistola, vel ipso Erasmo teste, qui librum Epistolarum suarum ita Frobenio tradidit excudendum, ut alias quasvis epistolas pro nō suis haberi iusserit publico scripto suo in Epistolas inserto: quo testimonio quid certius? Neque verò illa epistola spiritum lenem Erasmi spirat, aut stilum comprobat. Falsa probatio.
units.tr: 5 Art. 4. He, in the letter to Vulturius Neocomus: Erasmus had dealings with eagles, not with vultures; Erasmus did not know this Vulturius. The letter is supposititious and pseudonymous, by the testimony of Erasmus himself, who handed the book of his Letters to Frobenius to be printed, and ordered by a public notice inserted among the Letters that any other letters were not to be regarded as his. What could be more certain than this testimony? Nor does that letter breathe the gentle spirit of Erasmus or agree with his style. A false proof.

units.la: IN CAP. XXIIII.
units.tr: IN CHAPTER XXIV.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. contemni sine ulla auctoris iniuria potuisset.]rhetoricatur hic Bellarminus. Nos verba dantem sinamus: ad rem ipsam accingimur. Quod autem carmina auctoris anonymi Bellarminus satyras dicit, indignationi & æstui animi eius ignoscimus.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. could have been despised without any injury to the author. Bellarmine indulges in rhetoric here. Let us allow him his words; we come to the matter itself. As for Bellarmine calling the verses of the anonymous author satires, we pardon the indignation and heat of his mind.

units.la: 2 Art. 2. sub Christo in terris caput omnium Chri-stianorum est Pontifex maximus: sub i.] negamus u-trumque, & simile, quia dispar, & ordinem, quia mundi, non Ecclesiæ, humanus, ac non diuinus est, prout controu. 3. libro 1. ca. 5. & sequentibus ostendimus.
units.tr: 2 Art. 2. under Christ on earth the head of all Christians is the supreme Pontiff; under... We deny both, and the like, because the comparison is unequal, and the order, being of the world and not of the Church, is human and not divine, as we have shown in controversy 3, book 1, chapter 5 and following.

units.la: 3. Ibid. ut capite constituto schismatis tolleretur occasio.]de Chrysostomi loco diximus controu. 3. lib.1. cap.12.nota 56.& seq.de loco Hieronymi, lib.1.ca. 8. nota ultima eiusdem controversiæ: de utroque, cap.25.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. so that with the head appointed the occasion of schism might be removed. We have spoken of the passage of Chrysostom in controversy 3, book 1, chapter 12, note 56 and following, and of the passage of Jerome in book 1, chapter 8, last note of the same controversy. Of both, see chapter 25.

units.la: 4 Art.3. quid inter vicarium & successores discrimi-nis esset, videre non potuit.] imò verò Bellarminus animo tam perturbato fuit quum carmen illud legeret, ut nec quid auctor ille dicat animadvertere satis potuerit, nec quid respondeat. Hæc illius au-ctoris verba:
units.tr: 4 Art. 3. he could not see what difference there is between a vicar and successors. Indeed Bellarmine was so disturbed in mind when he read that poem that he could scarcely notice what that author says, nor what he replies. These are that author's words:

units.la: Ei lascio i suoi per fidi Ambasciadori De la sua gratia:&[?] non per Successori De la sua gloria. E furto. Et cio chi crede Heretico Heretico non é.&c. id est, Ipse reliquit suos in legatos vel nuncios fidos Suæ gratiæ, & non in successores Suæ gloriæ. Furtum est: & hoc qui credit, Haereticus non est. Non dicit auctor ille successores Christi, quod iste tantopere exagitat, sed successores gloriæ Christi, videlicet qui hic in Ecclesia militante non personæ Christi simpliciter, sed gloriæ personæ Christi successerint. Quòd si nolet Pontifex successor dici gloriæ illius, ergo dicatur licet successor gloria mundi: quemadmodum solenniter in Papæ Rom. inauguratione obseruari solet. Nam praecedit eo die κονπορόφως Pontifici stupas in summo conto praeferens ante oculos illius, in quas postea ardente tæda immittit ignem, proclamans alta voce hanc formulam, Sic transit gloria mundi, Pater sancte. Haec Pontificalis Romani verba, tit. de consecratione & coronatione summi Pontificis: Ante Pontificem immediatè Minister ceremoniarum praecedit cum duabus arundinibus: super alteram stuppam, super alteram vero candelam ardentem portans: & quum Pontifex capellam sancti Gregorii exierit, ceremoniarius ad eum conuersus ignem stuppa mittit, & genu flexus alta voce dicit, Pater sancte, sic transit gloria mundi: quod tertio facit distinctè aequali spatio, antequam perveniant ad portam capellae. Haec illa est gloria, cui succeedit Pontifex, vicarius Christi scilicet: quam gloriam non Christi aut vicarij (vt falsò praedicant, & auctor anonymus vocauit συγχωρητικῶς) sed mundi esse optimè verissimèque Ceremoniarius ille pronunciat.
units.tr: I leave to his faithful ambassadors his grace, and not to successors his glory. It is theft. And whoever believes this is not a heretic. That is: he left his own as faithful legates or messengers of his grace, and not as successors of his glory. It is theft, and whoever believes this is not a heretic. That author does not say successors of Christ, which this man harps on so much, but successors of Christ's glory: namely, those who in the militant Church have succeeded not simply to the person of Christ but to the glory of Christ's person. But if the Pontiff is unwilling to be called successor of that glory, then let him be called successor of the glory of the world, as is solemnly observed at the inauguration of the Roman Pope. For on that day a man goes before the Pontiff carrying tow on a long pole before his eyes, into which afterwards he puts fire with a burning torch, proclaiming aloud this formula: Thus passes the glory of the world, Holy Father. These are the words of the Roman Pontifical, title on the consecration and coronation of the supreme Pontiff: Immediately before the Pontiff goes the master of ceremonies, with two reeds: on one, tow; on the other, a lighted candle. And when the Pontiff has left the chapel of St Gregory, the master of ceremonies turns to him, sets fire to the tow, and kneeling says in a loud voice, Holy Father, thus passes the glory of the world; which he does three times, distinctly and at equal intervals, before they reach the door of the chapel. This is that glory to which the Pontiff, that is, Christ's vicar, succeeds. The master of ceremonies pronounces most rightly and truly that this glory belongs not to Christ or to his vicar (as they falsely proclaim, and as the anonymous author called it, by way of concession [συγχωρητικῶς]), but to the world.

units.la: {§} Artic. 4. nisi radicem & matricem Catholicæ Ecclesia, quae sola Romana est] negantur haec omnia, & confutata sunt controu. 3. lib.1. & 2. & 4.de Cypriani locis his omnibus videndum controu. 3. lib. 1. cap. 12. nota 52. & sequentibus. de loco Irenaei, controu.1.lib.3. cap.8.nota 2.
units.tr: {§} Art. 4. unless the root and mother of the Catholic Church, which is the Roman alone. All these things are denied, and they have been refuted in controversy 3, books 1, 2 and 4. For the passages of Cyprian, all these are to be seen in controversy 3, book 1, chapter 12, note 52 and following. For the passage of Irenaeus, controversy 1, book 3, chapter 8, note 2.

units.la: 6 Art.5.sed etiam seruum feruorum Dei libenter appellet.] nepe κατ' ἀντιφρασιν[?] Romanis praeconibus frequētatā. Recte Bellarminus dicit hoc in loco, si tale testimonium in epistolis Paulinis non habere, si verbum habendi postrema illa significatione quā Aristoteles tradebat acceperit: nam habet, qui vtitur, & contrà auarus dum omnia habet, habet nihil. Sed si ea omnia quae Paulus dicit 2.Thess.2. Antichristi sunt, & eadem sunt hodie competuntque Rom.Pontifici, profectò Bellarminus fallitur iudicio suo. vide controu. 3. lib.3. cuius proprium est hoc argumentum. Luthero nihil competit eiusmodi, nec probari potest: sed Bellarminus dat verba, dum exercet iras.
units.tr: 6 Art. 5. "but he gladly calls himself the servant of the servants of God." That is, by antiphrasis [κατ' ἀντίφρασιν], a phrase much used by Roman heralds. Bellarmine rightly says here that such a testimony is not found in the Pauline epistles, if one takes the word "to have" in that last sense which Aristotle gave it: for he who uses a thing has it, and the miser, though he has everything, has nothing. But if all those things which Paul says in 2 Thessalonians 2 belong to Antichrist, and are the same today and fit the Roman Pontiff, then Bellarmine is certainly mistaken in his own judgment. See controversy 3, book 3, whose proper subject this argument is. Nothing of that sort fits Luther, nor can it be proved; but Bellarmine fobs us off with words while he vents his anger.

units.la: 7 Art.6.imperando, castigando etiam, & corrigenda seruiat.] Non temere exagitat auctor anonymus, sed institutā nominis illius humilis cum dominio, quo Papa vtitur, comparatione. Sic enim ille:
units.tr: 7 Art. 6. "by commanding, even by punishing, and he should serve by correcting."] The anonymous author is not rashly attacking here, but is making a comparison between the humble title he adopted and the lordship which the Pope exercises. For he says:

units.la: Se feruo sei de i ferui del signore, Onde tanta superbia, che comandi A i Principi, a i Signori, a i Re piu grandi, Et di Sopra ti vindichi l'honore? &c.id autem est, Si seruus es feruorum Domini, Vnde tanta superbia, vt imperes Principibus, Dominis, Regibus maximis, Et Supremi tibi vindices honorem? Haec argumentationis ratio: Qui seruus feruorum est, idem non potest simul esse dominus dominantium ratione vlla: Tu, Romane Papa, tua ipsius confessione seruus feruorum rum es: qua igitur ratione summus es omnium, & summis dominaris? Si dominium circumscriptum & limitatum (vt vocant) effet, fortasse speciem habitura effet defensio: at incircumscriptum est: nam Papa secundum Innocentium habet plenitudinem potestatis, secundum Bonifacium dominus est v-triusque gladij, & Sol est mundi. Solutio itaque Bellarmini falsa, qui exempla & distinctiones adfert dominiis limitatis solum conuenientes, cum dominium Papę sit merum & limitationis expers. vide supra in cap.3.nota 5.
units.tr: "You are a servant of the servants of the Lord; whence such pride, that you command princes, lords, and the greatest kings, and claim for yourself the honour above all?" The line of argument is this: he who is a servant of servants cannot in any way at the same time be lord of lords. You, Roman Pope, by your own confession are a servant of servants; by what reasoning then are you the highest of all, and rule over the highest? If your dominion were circumscribed and limited (as they call it), perhaps the defence would have some appearance. But it is unlimited: for the Pope, according to Innocent, has the fullness of power; according to Boniface, he is lord of both swords, and he is the sun of the world. Bellarmine's solution is therefore false, for he brings forward examples and distinctions that suit only limited dominions, whereas the Pope's dominion is pure and free of any limitation. See above, in chapter 3, note 5.

units.la: 8 Ibid.sibique a populis supplicari patiebatur.] in-consequens argumentatio ex dispari. nam eadem non est ratio Christi quæ Pontificis. Christi utrumque dominium est, à natura, diuina, incircumscri-ptum, à voluntate & œconomia, circumscriptum ad salutem nostram: itaque hoc respectu dicebat, non veni ut facia voluntatem meam, &c. quid tale Pontifici?
units.tr: 8 "And allowed himself to be entreated by the peoples." The argument is an inconsequent one from unlike cases. For the case of Christ is not the same as that of the Pontiff. Christ's dominion is twofold: by nature, divine and unlimited; by will and economy, circumscribed for our salvation. Hence in this respect he said, "I came not to do my own will," and so on. What of the kind applies to the Pontiff?

units.la: 9 Art. 7. de primario Ecclesiæ fundamento, quod à nullo pendeat.] negatur distinctio, & probationes illius omnia ante confutata controu.[?] 3. lib. 1. cap. 10: expensisque omnes veterum Patrum loci, quos Bellarminus ex abundanti in hunc locum accumulat?
units.tr: 9 Art. 7. concerning the primary foundation of the Church, that it depends on no one. The distinction is denied, and its proofs have all been refuted before, in controversy 3, book 1, chapter 10; and have all the passages of the ancient Fathers been weighed, which Bellarmine heaps up in excess on this point?

units.la: 10 Art. 8. prodit se cuiusdam quinti Euangelij disci-pulum ac sectatorem esse.] & Bellarminus se prodit non inscium calumniæ, ex animi perturbatione ducens argumenta, nō ex rei & veritatis fide. Quid est Euangelium quintum, obsecro, nisi quod pro-cudit Roma? nam de indulgentiis Rom. in Euan-gelio Christi nullum verbum.
units.tr: 10 Art. 8. "he shows himself to be a disciple and follower of some fifth Gospel." Bellarmine also shows himself not unaware of calumny, drawing his arguments from disturbance of mind rather than from faithfulness to the matter and truth. What is a fifth Gospel, I beg you, except what Rome produces? For there is not a word about Roman indulgences in the Gospel of Christ.

units.la: 11 Ibid. humiles piscatores, ex Bethsaida vico Galilæa.] exemplum dispar: nam illos vocauit ipse Christus, at Sixtum V.& Pium V.vocauit & instituit mundus:ut de vocationibus Pontificalibus di-ctum est controu.4.
units.tr: 11 Ibid. "humble fishermen from Bethsaida, a village of Galilee." The example is unlike: for Christ himself called those men, but the world called and appointed Sixtus V and Pius V, as was said about papal vocations in controversy 4.

units.la: 12 Ibid. Non sapit illi quod Apostolus ait: ]falsum: nam sapit illi optime quod ait Apostolus, sed Sixto illi, Pio, & similibus non sapiunt τὸ ἀποστολικὸν [?].
units.tr: 12 Ibid. "It does not taste to him what the Apostle says." False: for what the Apostle says tastes very well to him, but to Sixtus, Pius, and their like the apostolic spirit [τὸ ἀποστολικὸν] does not taste.

units.la: 13 Ibid. Non probat aduersarius consilium Dei, ] negatur: probat enim consilium Dei religiosissime, sed non probat consilium Romae istius scortantis cum Principibus terrae, nec probat argumentationem Bellarmini, ex particulari exemplo & adeo dispari nectentis conclusionem suam.
units.tr: 13 Ibid. "The adversary does not approve the counsel of God." This is denied: for he approves the counsel of God most devoutly, but he does not approve the counsel of that harlot of Rome who fornicates with the princes of the earth; nor does he approve Bellarmine's argument, which links its conclusion to a particular and so unlike example.

units.la: 14 Ibid. Credo etiam Mosem contemnet, qui ad pr.] hæc fides nec Euangelij, nec veritatis, nec charitatis est: ergone ab Antichristo, a patre mendacij, & ab hoste est humani generis?ita profecto sapit poculum meretricis magnæ, unde Bellarminus istam haurit fidem. Nos illi optamus a Domino, ut vere sapiat.
units.tr: 14 Ibid. "I think also that he will despise Moses, who to..." This faith belongs neither to the Gospel, nor to truth, nor to charity. Is it therefore from Antichrist, the father of lies, and the enemy of the human race? Indeed that is the taste of the cup of the great harlot, from which Bellarmine drinks this faith. We pray the Lord that he may truly be wise.

units.la: 15 Ibid. viam sibi ad summos honores patefecisse.] eadem argumentandi fiducia ex diuerso. laudat a-nonymus auctor, laudant boni eos qui pietate, virtute fide ex loco humili ad summos honores sibi parauerunt viam: sed duo negat ille, tum istos Pontifices hac via virtutis & laudis sibi honores parauisse, tum Pontificatum Rom. iustum legitimumque honorem esse. Pius V. artibus, Sixtus V. carnificina & feritate saeuissima commendationem adeptus est.
units.tr: 15 Ibid. "to have opened for themselves a way to the highest honours." The same reckless argument is used in reverse. The anonymous author praises, and good men praise, those who by piety, virtue, and faith have made for themselves a way from a humble station to the highest honours. But he denies two things: first, that these Pontiffs gained their honours by this way of virtue and praise; second, that the Roman Pontificate is a just and lawful honour. Pius V obtained commendation by artifice, and Sixtus V by butchery and most savage cruelty.

units.la: 16 Ibid. Qua cum ita sint, aut solus aduers.] ex falsis antecedentibus conclusio falsa.
units.tr: 16 Ibid. "Since these things are so, either the adversary alone..." A false conclusion from false premises.

units.la: 17 Ibid. ex monasteriis ad summum Pontificatus fastigium omnibus aetatibus fuisse promotos? ] nos negamus:nam falsum est omnibus aetatibus fuisse monasteria, vel Hieronymo teste, vt controuersiæ 5. lib.2.ostendimus. tum posteriorum seculorum monasteria sanctimoniæ priorum respondere, aut respondisse iamdiu: postremo optimos, sapientissimos, vtilissimos fuisse Pontifices qui ex illis lacunis emerserunt, quæ hodie Ecclesiam & mundum totum inficiunt fœtore suo.
units.tr: 17 Ibid. "...have all been promoted from monasteries to the summit of the Pontificate in all ages?" We deny it: for it is false that there were monasteries in all ages, even by the testimony of Jerome, as we have shown in controversy 5, book 2. Moreover, the monasteries of later centuries do not correspond to the sanctity of earlier ones, or have not corresponded for a long time; and lastly, that the Pontiffs who emerged from those pools, which today infect the Church and the whole world with their stench, were the best, wisest, and most useful.

units.la: 18 Ibid. Monachus certè fuerat S. Dionysius.] æ-quinoce:nam aliud est Monachus secessum quaerès extra ordinem vt persecutiones fugiat & Deo seruiat, aliud ex voto ordinariam faciens monasticen & necessariam: illos qui fuerunt olim, laudamus, hos, qui fingunt sibi monasteria ad meritum, improbarnus. non fuit Dionysius de isto genere.
units.tr: 18 Ibid. "Certainly Saint Dionysius had been a monk." An equivocation: for it is one thing to be a monk who seeks seclusion outside the ordinary order, to flee persecution and serve God; it is another to make monastic life an ordinary and necessary thing by vow. We praise those of former times, but we condemn those who devise monasteries for merit. Dionysius was not of that kind.

units.la: 19 Ib. Monachus fuerat S. Gregorius, id est, pietatis & literarum sacrarum studiosus, quibus & se & alios in secessu informaret. Atq; hi Monachi tū nō erat de clero, vt ipse Bellarmin agnouit aliquoties controuersia 5. finaute[?] ad clerū promoti essét, Monachi & Clerici siue Monachi & Leuitę dicebätur, vt Gregorie appellat Platina. Eadè Adeodati & Agathonis, & aliorū ratio, qui minore superstitione, maiore sanctimonia & studio exercuerunt monasticen, sed ab ista otiosa & superstitiosa plurimum dissidete, quę posteà in peius ruit cū ipso seculo. Nō ita sunt monachi huius seculi, qui has laudes veterū iustas ne per somnium quidem cogitant decerpere. Non sequitur quicquā ex particulari, & diuerso tempore.
units.tr: 19 Ibid. "Saint Gregory had been a monk," that is, a student of piety and sacred letters, by which he might form himself and others in retirement. And these monks were then not of the clergy, as Bellarmine himself acknowledged several times in controversy 5; but once they were promoted to the clergy, they were called monks and clerics, or monks and Levites, as Platina calls Gregory. The same reasoning applies to Adeodatus, Agatho, and others, who practised monastic life with less superstition and greater holiness and zeal, but who differed greatly from that idle and superstitious life which afterwards declined for the worse along with the age itself. The monks of this age, who do not even dream of plucking away the just praises of the ancients, are not like that. Nothing follows from a particular case at a different time.

units.la: 20 Ibid. satis eum contra venenatas detractorum linguas communiebant.] de hoc Gregorio dictum satis controuersiæ 3.lib.4.cap.13.
units.tr: 20 Ibid. "they fortified him sufficiently against the poisonous tongues of detractors." Concerning this Gregory, enough has been said in controversy 3, book 4, chapter 13.

units.la: 21 Ibid. vt ipsòfe Pontificatu sponte abdicauerit.] de hoc Celestino videndum supra cap.14. Sed quid tā multis opus est? Monachos veteres meliores fuisse recentioribus plurimùm, nemo nescit: omnino tamen fuisse & bonos & malos, licet plureis malos. Sed vtut sit, illud dictū Augustini in hoc tempore est verissimum, quo vsus est in libro de opere monachorum, vt bonus choraules malus est symphoniachus, ita bonū monachū esse concionatorē & clericum malum. Nihil ergo ex particulari cōficit Apologetes, vt antè diximus: præsertim cū monasteriis nunc (vt ita dicamus) malum sit epidemicū, ignorātia, audacia, feritas, impietas: quod experientia quotidiana docet, sola verò Dei manus gratiosè curare potest, & suo tēpore (spero & oro) factura est.
units.tr: 21 Ibid. "so that he himself voluntarily resigned the Pontificate." On this Celestine, see above, chapter 14. But why do we need so many examples? Everyone knows that the monks of old were much better than the more recent ones; yet there were certainly both good and bad, though the bad were more numerous. However that may be, the saying of Augustine is most true in this present matter, which he used in his book On the Work of Monks: as a good flute-player is a bad symphony-player, so a good monk is a bad preacher and a bad cleric. Therefore the Apologist builds nothing from a particular case, as we said before; especially since monasteries now suffer (so to speak) from a plague of ignorance, audacity, savagery, and impiety, which daily experience teaches, and which only the hand of God can graciously cure; and in its own time (I hope and pray) it will do so.

units.la: 22 Art.9.ex monasteriis ad Episcopatū assumpti fuerint.] at non monasteriis, vt nunc sunt, otiosis, atque vitiosis, sed veris pietatis sanctimoniæ, eruditionis aliis, phrontiiteriis, gymnasiis, scholiis, & ludis literariis, vt controuersia §.[?]docuimus, nec ipse Bellarminus simpliciter negare ausus est. Iusta asceteria laudamus, quibus prisci Patres, etiam seueriùs, pòst successores fuperftitiofiùs vsi sunt: sed superstitiosa otij atque vitij domicilia, quæ hoc tēpore sūt plurima, laudare nō possumus. Incōsequēs est ex dispari argumentatio, vt sæpius dictum.
units.tr: 22 Art. 9. "were taken from monasteries to the episcopate." But not from monasteries as they now are, idle and vicious, but from true monasteries of piety, sanctity, and learning, which were schools, gymnasia, and academies, as we showed in the section of controversy; nor did Bellarmine himself dare to deny this outright. We praise the ancient retreats, which the early Fathers used even more strictly, and which their successors used more superstitiously; but we cannot praise the superstitious dwellings of idleness and vice, which at this time are very numerous. The argument from unlike cases is inconsequent, as has often been said.

units.la: 23 Art. 10. semetipsum in inferna demergit.] hæc rugiens dicat, non Christianus Leo. Huic nos, vt homini & auctoritatis nomine & ambitione propria in causa sua prurienti, humaniter ignoscimus: Christi verò solius principatum spiritualem in Ecclesia ipsius agnoscimus, cui nos adhærere bonum est, ac non humanis præiudiciis. Regi autem huic æterno, incorruptibili, invisibili[?], soli sapienti Deo honor sit & gloria in secula secu-lorum. Amen.
units.tr: 23 Art. 10. He plunges himself into hell.] These are the words of a roaring lion, not of a Christian Leo. We pardon him humanely, as a man who, both in the cause of his own authority and through his own ambition, is itching in his own case; but we acknowledge the spiritual sovereignty in the Church to belong to Christ alone, and it is good for us to cling to Him, and not to human prejudices. Let honour and glory be to that eternal, incorruptible, invisible King, to God alone, the wise one, for ever and ever. Amen.

units.la: IN ROBERTI BELLARMINI CONTROVERSIAM VI: QVÆ ET TERTIA EST tomi 2. de Ecclesia quę est in Purgatorio.
units.tr: IN ROBERTI BELLARMINI CONTROVERSIAM VI: WHICH IS THE THIRD, IN VOLUME 2 ON THE CHURCH, THAT IS IN PURGATORY.

units.la: IN PRÆFATIONEM. I. ART. I.
units.tr: ON THE PREFACE. I. ART. I.

units.la: De ea disputandum est, quæ degit infrà terram:] dicendum fuerat, quæ dicitur, aut quę putatur degere infra terram. Nos Ecclesiam proprie dictam negamus infrà terram esse. Eiusdem generis sunt quæ sequuntur proximè, Fideles iam defunctos, necdum beatos, & corpore & animo esse infra terram, diuersis in locis, Negamus.
units.tr: We must dispute about that which dwells below the earth: it ought to have been said "that which is said, or is thought, to dwell below the earth." We deny that the Church, properly so called, is below the earth. Of the same kind are the words that follow immediately: that the faithful already dead, not yet blessed, are below the earth both in body and in soul, in diverse places, we deny.

units.la: Liber prior, de Purgatorio: IN CAPVT I.
units.tr: Book I, On Purgatory: CHAPTER I.

units.la: 1. Art.2. Multi iusti affliguntur, non vt purgentur, sed vt exerceantur & probentur. Hæc duo non sunt [illegible, ~8 letters] purgari, & probari: quemadmodum & auru, cuius simile Siracides vsurpauit, eadem purgatur, & probatur igne per aurificem: atque haec duo in piis concurrunt simul: quis enim adeo pius est in hac vita, cui non sit purgatione opus? impiorum ratio diuersa est. Et quid aliud, obsecro, docent Paulus Rom. 5.3. & 8.17. & Iacob. 1.2. & 1. Petr. 1.6. haec itaque Bellarmini ratio infirma est: non enim verba haec sunt contradicentia, neque positio vnius (vt cum Iurecos. dicamus) est remotio alterius in hoc argumento.
units.tr: 1. Art. 2. Many righteous are afflicted, not that they may be purged, but that they may be exercised and proved. These two are not [illegible, ~8 letters] to be purged and to be proved. Just as gold, to which Siracides compared them, is purged and proved by fire in the goldsmith's hands, so these two come together in the pious. For who in this life is so holy that he has no need of purging? The case of the impious is different. And what else, I ask, do Paul (Rom. 5.3 and 8.17), James (1.2) and 1 Peter (1.6) teach? Therefore Bellarmine's argument is weak. For these words do not contradict one another, nor does the positing of one (as we say with Jurecos.) mean the removal of the other in this matter.

units.la: 2. Art. 3. De hoc est tota controuersia. recte: nos etenim negamus & locum istum esse, & in eo fieri opus purgationis istius.
units.tr: 2. Art. 3. On this the whole controversy turns. Rightly so. For we deny both that this place exists and that the work of that purging is carried out in it.

units.la: In CAPVT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: 1. Art. I. Primus omnium qui aliquid sensit contra Purgatorium videtur fuisse Aerius, Negatur: nam Christus, Apostoli, Euangelistę, & primum illud seculum nesciuit Purgatorium hoc, vt suo loco in confutandis Bellarmini propositionibus ostendemus. Si sciuissent, non certe dissimulauissent illi fidelissimi certissimique totius consilij diuini interpretes. De Aerij autem istius doctrina videbitur lib. 2. cap. 15. & seq.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. The first of all who felt anything against Purgatory seems to have been Aerius. This is denied. For Christ, the Apostles, the Evangelists and the first age did not know this Purgatory, as we will show in its proper place when refuting Bellarmine's propositions. Had they known it, those most faithful and most certain interpreters of the whole counsel of God would certainly not have concealed it. The teaching of this Aerius will be seen in book 2, chapter 15 and following.

units.la: 2. Art. 5. Idem postea docuerunt Albigenses, posteà, inquis? atqui Albigenses (si vera est Bellarminea illa temporis circumscriptio) istis omnibus simul praecesserunt. Nam Dominicus obiit tempore Alexandri II. Pontificis, vt scribit Petrus Damianus in vita illius ad Alexandrum, qui vixit eodem tempore & legatione functus est apud Henricum IIII. vt refert Schaffnaburgensis in historia anni 1069.interfuit autem Dominicus disputationibus aduersus Albigenses habitis frequentissime cum Didaco Prę[?]-fule Oxoniensi, siue Exomensi, (vt MS. habet) in Hispania claro. Volaterranus Oxoniensem vocat, legendum vbique Oxomensis. Hispani Ofmam vocant: a qua non procul abest locus Eremi a S. Dominico habens nomen, quod ibi egerit poenitentiam plurimum. Fallitur ergo Bellarminus in Chronologia. Quod de inferno ipsis tribuitur, calumnia est.
units.tr: 2. Art. 5. The same thing was taught afterwards by the Albigenses. Afterwards, you say? But the Albigenses (if Bellarmine's reckoning of time is correct) preceded all of these together. For Dominic died in the time of Pope Alexander II, as Peter Damian writes in his life, addressed to Alexander, who lived at the same time and served as legate to Henry IV, as Schaffnaburgensis reports in his history of the year 1069. Moreover, Dominic very frequently took part in the disputations held against the Albigenses with Diego Prefule of Oxford, or Exomensis (as the manuscript has), famous in Spain. Volaterranus calls him Oxoniensis; it should everywhere be read Oxomensis. The Spaniards call the town Osma, and not far from it is the hermitage that bears St. Dominic's name, because he did much penance there. Bellarmine is therefore wrong in his chronology. What is ascribed to them concerning hell is a calumny.

units.la: 3. Art. 6. Videtur confundere Huffitas cum V al-denfibus. ]Videtur male: nam distinguit hos ab illis evidentissime: sed hoc illorum commune fuisse dicit: Sic enim ille: ab Ecclesia Catholica recedentes, impiam Valdensium sectam atque infamiam amplexi sunt. Huius pestifera ac jampridem damnata factionis dogmata sunt: Rom. Praesulem reliquis Episcopis parem esse &c.
units.tr: 3. Art. 6. He seems to confuse the Hussites with the Waldensians. He seems wrong, for he distinguishes these from those very clearly, but says that this was common to them. For he speaks thus: Departing from the Catholic Church, they embraced the impious sect and infamy of the Waldensians. The dogmas of this pestilent and long-condemned faction are: that the Roman bishop is equal to the other bishops, and so on.

units.la: 4. Art. 7. Et existimare purgatorium esse locum te-nebricosum & laborum plenum, ] Haec sententia Graecis falso tribuitur; nisi commode distinxeris, ut lib. 2.cap.10.obseruabimus: quia de poena damni (vt vocant) non de poena sensus agebant Graeci, quū Purgatorium concederent: nam ubique repugnat Graeci in actionibus Ferrariensis & Florentini Concilij, si vnum locum exceperis, qui proculdubio corruptus est, & suum vlcus inspicientibus aperit. Sic enim Graeci Latinis de Purgatorio confirmantibus respondent: Quacunque, Patres amplissimi, protulistis atque citastis, Orientalis Ecclesia profitetur, quoniam inter Graecos vulgo legitur male, quamuis) & Latinos paruam fit differentia. Demonstrant proxime sequentia, quum subiiciunt continuo: Vestram ergo sententiam literis tradite, quod ipsi quoque saluri fumus: Vt in quonam a vobis differamus, palam fiat. Accipit autem ille interpres quoniam pro, quòd, ex abusu illius seculi. Sic enim promiscuè vertebant ἐν[?].Imò verò exstat Græcè & Latinè singularis libellus περὶ τοῦ καθαρτηρίου[?] πυρός, de igne Purgatorio, in Concilio Ferrariensi (ut probabile est) habitam orationem continens, in quo ἀρνοῦνται[?] Græci & dogma istud negant, & locorum Scripturæ interpretationem confutant, quibus Latini abutuntur. Purgatorium itaque & ignem & locum Græci, καὶ τὸ πῦρ καὶ τὸν τόπον[?], quod aiunt, negauerunt. vide plura infrà cap. 15. nota 21.
units.tr: 4. Art. 7. And to think that purgatory is a dark place full of toil. This opinion is falsely attributed to the Greeks, unless you distinguish properly, as we shall observe in book 2, chapter 10. For when the Greeks conceded Purgatory, they were speaking of the penalty of loss (as they call it), not the penalty of sense. For everywhere the Greeks resist the Latins in the proceedings of the Council of Ferrara and Florence, except for one passage, which is undoubtedly corrupt and reveals its sore to those who look closely. For thus the Greeks answer the Latins who confirm Purgatory: Whatever, most distinguished Fathers, you have put forward and cited, the Eastern Church professes, since there is little difference between Greeks and Latins (commonly read badly, though). What follows immediately demonstrates this, when they add at once: Therefore put your opinion in writing, so that we too may be saved; so that it may become plain in what respect we differ from you. That translator takes quoniam for quod, owing to the usage of that age. For they translated promiscuously... Indeed there exists, in Greek and Latin, a single little book On the purgatorial fire [περὶ τοῦ καθαρτηρίου πυρός], containing a speech delivered at the Council of Ferrara (as is probable), in which the Greeks deny [ἀρνοῦνται] this dogma and refute the interpretation of the Scripture passages by which the Latins abuse it. Thus the Greeks denied Purgatory, the fire and the place [καὶ τὸ πῦρ καὶ τὸν τόπον], as they say. See more below, chapter 15, note 21.

units.la: 5. Art. 8. Quanquam Lutherus ipse valdè varius fuit.] quæ de aliis affirmantur, suo loco singula videbimus: quæ de Luthero sequentibus proximè notis singulatim expendentur.
units.tr: 5. Art. 8. Although Luther himself was very inconsistent. What is affirmed of others we shall examine each in its place; what is said of Luther will be weighed one by one in the following notes.

units.la: 6. Ibid. Facilè persuadeor in Scripturis de eo fieri mentionem.]Mutilantur Lutheri verba. Sic enim ille: Ego, inquit, qui credo fortiter, imò ausim[?] dicere, scio purgatorium esse, facilè persuadeor in Scripturis de eo fieri mentionem, quemadmodum illud Matthæi inducit Gregorius in Dialogo, non remittitur neque in hoc seculo, nec in futuro, volens peccata quædam remitti in Purgatorio. Admitto & illud 2. Mac. 12. Sancta est & salubris cogitatio pro defunctis exorare, &c. Sed hoc volo, quòd in universa Scriptura non habeatur memoria Purgatorij, quæ posset stare in contentione & convincere. Nam & liber Machabæorum, cum non sit in canone, pro fidelibus potens est, contra pertinaces nihil facit: & dictum Gregorij facillimè eluditur, quòd neque, hic neque in futuro peccatum remittatur, id est, nunquam. & quæ sequuntur. Nec homo repente exuit professione Christiana quicquid humani habet, nec Monachus quicquid habet Monachi. Lutherus diu fuerat monachus, & fermentum monasticum diu imbiberat, ut ipse profitetur saepe. Id autem prout non uno die imbiberat, ita nec uno deonerauit aut exspuit die, sed cum tempore: prout viam simplicitatis Christi ex Scripturis paulatim didicit. Quod ergo se credere, scire, persuaderi dicit de Purgatorio, id a fermento Monachorum est, cui plane renunciauit postea: etsi non plane fieri mentionem illius dicit, sed tantum obscure & per quasdam consequentias. Quod autem stare in contentione & conuincere posse negat, id dicit verissime, quod dictum tamen disputator pro sua fide sic Luthero tribuit, ut si postmodum mutata sententia illud affirmasset, ac non eodem tempore. Etenim verum est fundamentum illud, quo altera post responsione utitur: non posse Ecclesiam plus tribuere auctoritatis & firmitatis libro, quam per seipsum habeat: non confirmare, aut meliorem reddere. quidni etiam de dogmate dicatur idem? Ingressus autem est Lutherus primum in certamen de indulgentiis anno 1517. Haec vero disputatio post biennium fuit Lipsiae habita: quo adhuc tempore sibi vir bonus de multis rebus in monasterio haustis videbatur confirmatissimus, quas longo post interuallo ex Scripturis vidit sibi discendas esse. Consulatur praefatio, quam Lutherus ipse tomis operum suorum praefigi voluit: ubi Lectores meminisse iubet ac misericordia affici quod fuerit miser monachus: ut sua illa scripta coram Deo & mundo eiuraret, quae nouitius aut perturbatus conscripserat. Principes, Magistratus, Iureconsultos non pudet legibus posterioribus, prout tempore & usu cognouerunt, priores abrogare: & hominem pudeat aliquam inscientiam sua meliore veri scien-tia abrogare? & alios non pudeat inscientiam præ-cedentem iis obiicere qui ex animo ad scientiam transfiuerunt?
units.tr: 6. Ibid. I am easily persuaded that mention of it is made in the Scriptures. Luther's words are mutilated. For he says: "I who believe firmly, indeed dare to say, I know that purgatory exists. I am easily persuaded that mention of it is made in the Scriptures, just as Gregory in his Dialogue cites that saying of Matthew, it is not forgiven either in this age or in the age to come, wishing that certain sins be forgiven in purgatory. I also admit that passage of 2 Maccabees 12, It is holy and wholesome to pray for the dead, etc. But this I maintain: that in the whole of Scripture there is no record of Purgatory which could stand in contention and convince." For the book of Maccabees, since it is not in the canon, is powerful for the faithful but does nothing against the obstinate; and Gregory's saying is very easily eluded, since it is not forgiven neither here nor in the future means never. And what follows. Nor does a man at once strip off everything human in his Christian profession, nor a monk everything he has of the monk. Luther had been a monk for a long time and had long soaked up the monastic leaven, as he himself often professes. But just as he did not soak it up in a single day, so he did not discharge or spit it out in a single day, but over time, as he gradually learned from the Scriptures the way of Christ's simplicity. Therefore what he says he believes, knows and is persuaded of concerning Purgatory comes from the leaven of the monks, from which he plainly renounced himself afterwards, although he says he does not plainly make mention of it, but only obscurely and through certain consequences. But that he denies it can stand in contention and convince, he says most truly. Yet the disputant, for the sake of his own faith, attributes this saying to Luther in such a way as if he had afterwards changed his opinion and affirmed that, and not at the same time. For that foundation which the other uses in his later reply is true: that the Church cannot give a book more authority and firmness than it has in itself, and cannot confirm it or make it better. Why should not the same be said of a dogma? Luther first entered the conflict over indulgences in 1517. This disputation, however, was held at Leipzig two years later, at which time the good man still seemed to himself most assured about many things he had drunk in in the monastery, which after a long interval he saw must be unlearned from the Scriptures. Let the preface be consulted, which Luther himself wished to be prefixed to the volumes of his works, where he bids readers remember and feel pity that he was a wretched monk, so that he might renounce before God and the world those writings which he had composed as a novice or in a disturbed state. Are princes, magistrates and jurists not ashamed to repeal earlier laws in favour of later ones, as they have come to know through time and use? And is a man ashamed to set aside some earlier ignorance by his better knowledge of the truth? And is the other not ashamed to throw earlier ignorance in the face of those who have sincerely passed over to knowledge?

units.la: 7. Art. 9. Habentur inter articulos a Leone dam-natos in fine.] Nempe hæc obiecit Leo damnauitq; sed alia confinxit Leo, alia Lutherus sine mutatione iam ante docuerat: cuiusmodi illud est quod præcedente nota ex verbis Lutheri adduximus, Purga-torium non posse probari ex Scripturis. Nihil hic profecto varius Lutherus fuit.
units.tr: 7. Art. 9. Among the articles condemned by Leo at the end are these. Certainly Leo objected these things and condemned them, but Leo also invented other things, and Luther had taught others without change long before. Of this kind is what we cited in the preceding note from Luther's words, that Purgatory cannot be proved from the Scriptures. Surely Luther was in no way inconsistent here.

units.la: 8. Art. 10. Per omnia etiam probo.] Hæc omnia Lutherus postea scripsit, quàm melius atque diligentius ex Scripturis sacris ἐμπνευσάντων[?]. Hoc ab homine Christiano fieri nemo θεοδίδακτος[?] reprehensurus, nemo homo miraturus, nemo nisi impius damnaturus est: etenim quo argumento faciat quisquam aut argumenti specie?
units.tr: 8. Art. 10. Per omnia etiam probo.] Luther wrote all these things later, after examining them better and more carefully from the holy Scriptures [ἐμπνευσάντων?]. No Christian will rebuke this, no one will be surprised by it, and no one but an impious man will condemn it, for what argument or semblance of argument could anyone bring against it?

units.la: 9. Art. 11. Satisfactionem & discrimen peccati mortalis a veniali.] hæc quàm verè dicantur, in tom.3. & 4.videbitur.
units.tr: 9. Art. 11. Satisfactionem & discrimen peccati mortalis a veniali.] How truly these things are said will be seen in volumes 3 and 4.

units.la: 10. Art. 13. In ipsius Platonis operibus] rectè sanè: sed Augustinus de Platonicis, non de Platone dicebat.Multa autem Platonici dixerunt,quæ non sensit unquam Plato:multa Stoici & Academici,quæ nunquam Zeno aut Aristoteles:multa etiam Christiani (nam homines sunt) quæ nunquam Christus Propheta noster inculpatissimus.
units.tr: 10. Art. 13. In ipsius Platonis operibus] Rightly so, certainly. But Augustine was speaking of the Platonists, not of Plato himself. The Platonists said many things that Plato never thought; the Stoics and Academics said many things that Zeno or Aristotle never did; and Christians too (for they are men) have said many things that Christ, our most blameless Prophet, never taught.

units.la: In Cap. III.
units.tr: In Chapter III.

units.la: 1 Art.1. Primum igitur Purgatorium esse.) nos Pur-gatorium[?] negamus esse, & probationes eius consu-tabimus. Art.2. Quinto hoc esse de fide.) nos & istas omneis conclusiones negamus, & auctoritatem loci. Ius negationis sequentibus exponemus.
units.tr: 1 Art.1. Primum igitur Purgatorium esse.) We deny that Purgatory exists, and we will refute its proofs. Art. 2. Quinto hoc esse de fide.) We also deny all these conclusions and the authority of the passage. We will set out the grounds of our denial in what follows.

units.la: Art.10. Librum Machabæorum non esse canonicum apud Iudæos, sed apud Christianos esse.) distinctione opus. Nam apud Iudæos nullo modo fuit canonicus, nec diuino canone, nec Ecclesiastico proprie aut æquiuocè dicto: apud Christianos vero nec diuino canone est canonicus, nec fuit Ecclesiastico primùm: sed procedente tempore in Ecclesia paulatim receptus est, & per gradus auctoritatis prouexit temerè, falsóque[?] diuinis adæquatus est, & indigitatus humano censu, appellatione æquiuoca: ut in controuersiam i. ostendimus,
units.tr: Art.10. Librum Machabæorum non esse canonicum apud Iudæos, sed apud Christianos esse.) A distinction is needed. Among the Jews the book was in no way canonical, neither by the divine canon nor by the ecclesiastical canon, whether taken properly or equivocally. Among Christians it is not canonical by the divine canon, and at first it was not canonical by the ecclesiastical canon either; but as time went on it was gradually received in the Church, rose by degrees to authority, was rashly and falsely made equal to the divine books, and was given a status by human judgment under an equivocal name, as we showed in Controversy 1.

units.la: Ibid. Legit hunc librum in Missa, & legebat iam olim.) non sequitur, Ecclesia legit, ergo diuinus est: nec sequitur, Ecclesia Rom. legit, ergo universa: nec denique sequitur, Ecclesia legit à 500. aut 600. annis, ergo & prisca illa, quæ accepit à Deo, non ante fecit libros canonicos. Nam pia Ecclesia fuit: est autem impium factum, si qui homo vel Ecclesia li-brum dicatur facere canonicum. Hoc quarto modo proprium deitatis est, prout Lutherus, etiam novi-tius cap. præcedentis nota 6. affirmavit.
units.tr: Ibid. Legit hunc librum in Missa, & legebat iam olim.) It does not follow: the Church reads it, therefore it is divine. Nor does it follow: the Roman Church reads it, therefore the whole Church does. Nor finally does it follow: the Church has read it for five or six hundred years, therefore that ancient Church, which received its books from God, did not earlier make books canonical. For the Church was pious; but it would be impious to say that any man or Church makes a book canonical. This is the fourth respect in which something belongs properly to deity, as Luther affirmed, even as a novice, in note 6 of the preceding chapter.

units.la: Ibid. Ne ullus liber legeretur in Ecclesia sub nomine diuinorum librorum, nisi canonicus esset.] de hoc canone vide in contr. 1. lib. 1. cap. 9. nota 6. & cap. 10. nota 6.
units.tr: Ibid. That no book should be read in the Church under the name of the divine books unless it were canonical.] On this canon see in Controversy 1, book 1, chapter 9, note 6, and chapter 10, note 6.

units.la: Ibid. Innocentius 1. in epist. ad Exuperium, c. ult.) huius Innocetij nec magna fuit eruditio, si eius sunt quæ dicuntur esse (ut recte Erasmus censuit) nec erudita epistola: cur ergo sit authentica? Sed his omis-sis, agit Innocentius de canone Ecclesiastico, & dicto æquiuocè, vt paulò ante fuerat actum in Concilio Carthag.3. nihil sequitur ex Homonymia.
units.tr: Ibid. Innocentius 1. in epist. ad Exuperium, c. ult.) The learning of this Innocent was not great, if the writings ascribed to him are his (as Erasmus rightly judged), nor is the letter learned. Why then is it authentic? But setting that aside, Innocent treats of the ecclesiastical canon, and of a term used equivocally, as had been done a little earlier at the Third Council of Carthage. Nothing follows from the homonymy.

units.la: 7 Ibid. Sed Ecclesia pro canonicis habet.) vide con-tro.1.lib.1.cap.15.nota 3.
units.tr: 7 Ibid. Sed Ecclesia pro canonicis habet.) See Controversy 1, book 1, chapter 15, note 3.

units.la: 8 Art.11. Patres a nobis citatos lib.1. de verbo Dei, cap.15.) ne actum agamus, ibidem respondimus, ex-posuimusque auctoritatem illorum.
units.tr: 8 Art.11. Patres a nobis citatos lib.1. de verbo Dei, cap.15.) To avoid repeating ourselves, we responded there and explained their authority.

units.la: 9 Art.13. Perfide agit Pseudomartyr.) ἐξ ἀρχῆς [illegible, ~10 letters] mi homo bona verba.
units.tr: 9 Art.13. Perfide agit Pseudomartyr.) From the very beginning [ἐξ ἀρχῆς] [illegible, ~10 letters] my good man, fair words.

units.la: 10 Ibid. Ex solo hoc libro argumenta petat ad probandum, orandum esse pro mortuis.) Atqui non dicit Augustinus se probationem adducere ex libro canonico: nam & aliunde probationes sui generis afferri possunt. Tum quodnam hoc sit probationum genus, ex ipso Augustino in controu.1. satis superque ostendimus.
units.tr: 10 Ibid. Ex solo hoc libro argumenta petat ad probandum, orandum esse pro mortuis.) But Augustine does not say that he is bringing a proof from a canonical book alone, for proofs of another kind may also be brought from elsewhere. As to what kind of proof this is, we have shown quite sufficiently from Augustine himself in Controversy 1.

units.la: 11 Ibid. Aerium in numero haereticorum, quia negauerat orationes pro defunctis.) Falsum. Sic enim Augustinus scribit: Aerius, quum esset Presbyter, doluisse fertur, quod Episcopus non potuit ordinari; & in Ariano-rum haeresin lapsus propria, quoque dogmata addidisse nonnulla, dicens orare vel offerre pro mortuis oblationem non oportere, &c. Haereticum fuisse Augustinus dicit, quia fuit Arrianus, caetera vero dogmata haereticum addidisse, vt schisma faceret in Ecclesia probabilius, quae dogmata non faciebant haereticum, sed ab haeretico excitabantur, vt probabiliter haeresin & schisma defenderet. Nusquam dicit eum fuisse in numero haereticorum ideo positum, quia orationes pro defunctis negauerat.
units.tr: 11 Ibid. Aerium in numero haereticorum, quia negauerat orationes pro defunctis.) False. For Augustine writes: Aerius, when he was a presbyter, is said to have been grieved that he could not be made a bishop; and having fallen into the heresy of the Arians, he added some doctrines of his own, saying that one ought not to pray for the dead or offer the oblation for them, etc. Augustine says he was a heretic because he was an Arian.
