The other doctrines he added as a heretic, in order to make a schism in the Church more plausible. Those doctrines did not make him a heretic; rather, they were stirred up by a heretic, so that he might plausibly defend heresy and schism. Nowhere does Augustine say that Aerius was placed among the heretics because he had denied prayers for the dead.

units.la: 12 Ibid. Ex quo apparet insignis fraus Martyris.) Itáne vero? fraus Martyris? at nos audiamus Augustini verba ἀλλά, vt videamus Bellarminii fidem, Et hanc quidem scripturam, inquit, quæ appellatur Machabæorum, non habent Judæi, sicut legem & Prophetas & Psalmos, quibus Dominus testimonium perhibet tanquam testibus suis, dicens, oportebat impleri omnia quæ scripta sunt in lege & Prophetis & in Psalmis de me: sed recepta est ab Ecclesia non inutiliter, si sobrie legatur vel audiatur: maxime propter illos Macha-bæos, qui pro Dei lege sicut veri martyres, &c. Profecto non Iudæos Ecclesiæ opponit Augustinus ea mente quam Bellarminus confingit ὁμωνύμως, sed Ecclesiam priscam quæ fuit Iudæorum in testamento vetere, opponit Ecclesiæ noui testamenti suo tempore existenti. Non potest autem Ecclesia librum facere canonicum ex non canonico: multo minus Ecclesia noua facere, ut quod non est canonicum sit canonicum Ecclesiæ veteris. Et bona fide, negabis-ne, Bellarmine, sic locum accipi oportere? atqui Augustinus ipse interpretatur de quibus Iudæis affirmet, dicens se non de Iudæis secundum literam aut carnem agere, sed de Iudæis secundum spiritum, & vere Iudæis, quum Dominum ipsum adducit Ecclesiæ caput testimonia Scripturæ illius, non libri Machabæorum adducentem. Cætera diximus in controu.I.
units.tr: 12 Ibid. Ex quo apparet insignis fraus Martyris.) Really? A notable deceit of the Martyr? But let us hear Augustine's own words, so that we may see Bellarmine's good faith: And this writing, he says, which is called that of the Maccabees, the Jews do not have, as they do not have the Law and the Prophets and the Psalms, to which the Lord bears witness as to his own witnesses, saying: it was necessary that all things written in the Law and the Prophets and the Psalms concerning me should be fulfilled. But it has been received by the Church, not uselessly, if it is read or heard soberly; especially on account of those Maccabees who, for the law of God, like true martyrs, etc. Indeed, Augustine does not set the Jews against the Church in the sense that Bellarmine invents [ὁμωνύμως]. Rather, he sets the ancient Church, which was that of the Jews under the Old Testament, against the Church of the New Testament existing in his own time. But the Church cannot make a non-canonical book canonical; much less can the new Church make what is not canonical into canonical for the old Church. Bellarmine, will you in good faith deny that the passage must be taken in this way? Augustine himself explains which Jews he means, saying that he is not speaking of Jews according to the letter or the flesh, but of Jews according to the spirit, and truly Jews; and when he cites the testimonies of that Scripture, as the head of the Church, it is not the book of the Maccabees that he is citing. We have said the rest in Controversy 1.

units.la: Ibid. Ne putemus imitandum factum Iudæ Patriarchæ, qui incestum perpetrauit.) Nec vera interpretatio, nec par locorum ratio. Interpretatione Grammatici melius quàm Sophistæ dabunt. Sobrie, inquiunt, id est, prudenter iudicioque certo, ut quum Plautus in Persa rem sobrie & frugaliter accurari dicit. Nam sobrius opponitur ebrio, qui briam, grande vas vini sic olim dictum Arnobio, exhaus-crit[?], eoque iudicij vim & prudentiæ vsum amiserit. Sobrie humana scripta omnia audiri à nobis oportet & legi: at diuinis & canonicis etiam inebriari, [illegible, ~9 letters] religiosum est, illa legamus necesse est adhibita prudentia & lima iudicij, hæc fide prudentiam iudiciumque captiuum rapiente secundum Deum. Qui secus interpretatur, [illegible, ~4 letters]. Dispar itaque est comparatio libri & loci Genesæos, qui est canonicus & [illegible, ~6 letters] ἀξιος, cum 2. Machab. libro: qui liber, vel auctore teste, limæ iudicij humani permissus est.
units.tr: Ibid. Ne putemus imitandum factum Iudæ Patriarchæ, qui incestum perpetrauit.) Neither the interpretation nor the comparison of the passages is sound. Grammarians will give a better explanation than the Sophists. "Soberly," they say, means prudently and with sure judgment, as when Plautus in the Persa says a matter is handled soberly and thriftily. For sober is opposed to drunk; one who has emptied a bria, a great vessel of wine, as Arnobius once called it, has lost the power of judgment and the use of prudence. All human writings must be heard and read by us soberly; but to be made drunk even on divine and canonical books is [illegible] religious. Those we must read with prudence and the file of judgment; these we must read in faith, which seizes captive prudence and judgment for God. Whoever interprets otherwise [illegible]. The comparison, therefore, between this book and the passage of Genesis, which is canonical and [illegible] worthy, is unequal to the Second Book of Maccabees, a book which, by its author's own testimony, was submitted to the file of human judgment.

units.la: Hæc Martyr ignorauit scilicet. Non deceptus est, mi homo: sed intempestiuè noluit mouere quæ nihil ad rem attinebant. non fuit illius loci, quæstionem moueri, de errore vulgi, qui sine damno veritatis diuinæ potuit dissimulari.
units.tr: Evidently this Martyr was unaware of this. He was not deceived, my good man; he merely chose, untimely, not to raise matters that had nothing to do with the point. It was not the place to raise the question of the error of the common people, which could be passed over without harm to divine truth.

units.la: Male. nam quicquid est canonicum, ex quo à Deo profectum est, semper est canonicum: quod aliquando non fuit canonicum, id ab homine vllo, ac ne ab vniuersa quidem Ecclesia auctoritatem obtinere potest canonis: hoc quidem humano censu [illegible, ~5 letters], sed nunquam est canonicum; si canonicum proprie dixeris, vt supra nota 12.
units.tr: Wrong. For whatever is canonical, since it has come from God, is always canonical. What at some time was not canonical cannot obtain the authority of canon from any man, or even from the whole Church. In human reckoning this may be [illegible], but it is never canonical, if you speak of canonical properly, as in note 12 above.

units.la: distinctionem, & comparationem negamus: vt lib.1.controu.1.cap.15.nota 13.
units.tr: We deny the distinction and the comparison, as in Book 1, Controversy 1, chapter 15, note 13.

units.la: Negatur 1. pro eadem quæstione has duas habuisse. Nam pro adiunctis quæstionibus, & quidem necessariò adiunctis habuerunt conuenienter naturæ: aliud autem est habere pro adiunctis, aliud pro unica. Secundo ut demus ita opinionem fuisse posterioribus seculis, tamen non eo sequeretur ita fuisse in vulgo inde à Machabæorum tempore, ad quorum tempora hæc historia pertinet. Hæc itaque distinctio & falsa & inutilis est. Quid, quòd de Essenis plane contrarium Iosephus lib. 2. de bello Iudaico, cap. 7. affirmauit? Opinio quippe, inquit, apud illos firmata consistit, corruptibilia quidem esse corpora, materiamque eorum non esse perpetuam; animas autem immortales semper manere, & de æthere subtilissimo commeantes, quasi carceribus, ita corporibus implicari, velut quas illecebra naturalis attraxerit: quum vero fuerint à carnalibus releuatæ vinculis, quasi de seruitute longissima liberatas, ita illico lætari eas sublimesque ferri, & quæ sequuntur. Sic enim Ruffinus minime male ex Græco auctore interpretatus est. Nec plus igitur veritatis inest sequentibus, quæ ex fundamento isto eruuntur.
units.tr: We deny, first, that they held these two views about the same question. For they held them as accompanying questions, indeed necessarily accompanying ones, in keeping with nature; but to hold something as accompanying is one thing, and to hold it as the only thing is another. Second, even granting that the opinion was held in this way in later centuries, it would not follow that it was held this way among the common people from the time of the Maccabees, to whose times this history belongs. This distinction, therefore, is both false and useless. And what of the fact that Josephus, in Book 2 of The Jewish War, chapter 7, affirmed the plain opposite about the Essenes? For the opinion among them is firmly established: that bodies are corruptible and their matter is not everlasting, but souls remain immortal forever, coming from the most subtle ether and bound in bodies as in prisons, drawn as if by some natural allurement; but when they have been released from the fleshly chains, as if freed from a very long servitude, they rejoice and are carried aloft, and what follows. For Rufinus translated the Greek author quite faithfully. Therefore the consequences drawn from this foundation contain no more truth than the foundation does.

units.la: 18 Ibid. Et qui vnum fatebantur, fatebantur alterum.) si universè dicuntur ista, dicuntur falsò; ut Essenorum exemplo modò ostendimus: si particulariter, nihil sequitur ex particulari, ut loquuntur.
units.tr: 18 Ibid. And those who confessed the one also confessed the other.) If these words are taken universally, they are false, as we have just shown from the example of the Essenes. If they are taken particularly, nothing follows from the particular, as they say.

units.la: 19 Art.17. Posset enim alioqui negari consequentia.) posset quidem negari (nam quid imperitia aut malitia non audeat?) sed negaretur falsò. nam & argumentationes à proprio, ab accidentibus & adiunctis perpetuis ac necessariis ductæ[?] necessariam habent consequentiam. Est autem hoc proprium animæ personaliter corpus suum sustentantis, ut sua conditione hac aspergat corpus, idémque est adiunctum sive accidens perpetuum corporis ex veritate iustitiæ Dei.
units.tr: 19 Art. 17. For otherwise the consequence could be denied.) It could indeed be denied (for what will ignorance or malice not dare?), but it would be denied falsely. For arguments drawn from what is proper to a thing, from its accidents, and from its perpetual and necessary attributes, have a necessary consequence. Now it is proper to the soul that it sustains its own body personally, so that by its condition it animates the body, and this is a perpetual attribute or accident of the body, arising from the truth of God's justice.

units.la: 20 Ibid. Deus erit Deus viuentium, etiamsi mortui non resurgant, quandoquidem animi ipsi viuunt.) non sequitur.nam animi, quamuis iacente corpore, sibi viuunt & suo corpori, quamuis separato, & manet illius ad hoc(ut ita dicam) affectio, qua suum corpus, peccato diuulsum, veritate iustitiæ diuinæ receptu-rus est, per modum adiuncti necessarij. Sequetium itaque par ratio in hunc modum.
units.tr: 20 Ibid. God will be the God of the living, even if the dead do not rise, since the souls themselves live.) It does not follow. For the souls, though the body lies dead, live to themselves and to their body, even when separated from it; and there remains in them that disposition (so to speak) by which the body, torn apart by sin, is to be received back in the truth of divine justice, as a necessary attribute. Therefore the same reasoning holds for the following, in this way.

units.la: 21 Ibid. Quia proderit ad gloriam animæ acquirendam.) si causaliter acquirendam sentit, propositio falsa est, sin ut antecedens, non autem ut causam, profuturam putat, hoc bene intellectum non fumus præfracte negaturi.
units.tr: 21 Ibid. Because it will profit to acquire the glory of the soul.) If he means that it acquires glory as a cause, the proposition is false; but if he means that it will profit as an antecedent, and not as a cause, we shall not stubbornly deny this when it is rightly understood.

units.la: 22 Ibid. Si mortui non resurgunt, inde sequi animas esse mortales.) nihil sequitur ex antecedente falso, ut supra nota 17. ostendimus.
units.tr: 22 Ibid. If the dead do not rise, it follows that souls are mortal.) Nothing follows from a false antecedent, as we showed above in note 17.

units.la: 23 Art.18 In textu Graeco non haberi particulam, ergo.) verum est, non exstare οὐ in Graeco, ut habetur hodie. Sed aut exstitit olim, estque restituendum ex translatione Latina, quam vocant Hieronymi: aut apponendum vidit Hieronymus, cuius versio tantidem est ac Græca lectio, si Bellarmino fidem habemus sequentibus, & contr.1.lib.2.cap.9. & 10. Sane si quis in totum illum contextum penitius introspexerit, facile comperturus est aut particulam illam desiderari, aut (quod similius vero) ineptam atque [illegible, ~12 letters] totam illam consequutionem esse; auctoremque, mente, lingua, manu titubasse, quum ita scriberet. Statuit enim interpres ille totum antecedentem versum cum iis quæ præcesserant longius, cofstruen-dum esse; & totum illum alterum, [illegible, ~40 letters] esse discludendum notis paren-thesios, thefeos, vt sequentia cum prioribus cohærerent, quæ alioquin turpiter hiulea sunt. Ac propterea adiecit, ergo. Quid autem Bellarminus sua translatio-ne? adiicit vocem quæ (non exstat autem in Græco) vt istud membrum faciat παρένθετον, & particulam ἐν[?] exponit ideo quæ interpretatio purioribus Græcis plane inaudita est in consequutione eiusmodi. Alterum oportet fecisse male, aut illum qui inepte scripserit, aut hüc qui pro auctoritate infercit & interpretatur alieno vsu.
units.tr: 23 Art. 18 That the particle "therefore" is not found in the Greek text.) It is true that οὐ is not found in the Greek as it is read today. But either it was there once and must be restored from the Latin translation which they call Jerome's, or Jerome saw something to be added, and his version amounts to the same as the Greek reading, if we trust Bellarmine in what follows, and in the first controversy, book 2, chapters 9 and 10. Certainly, if anyone examines that whole passage more closely, he will easily discover either that the particle is missing, or (what is more likely) that the whole consequence is absurd and unfitting, and that the author, in mind, language and hand, faltered when he wrote it that way. For that translator decided that the whole preceding verse must be construed together with what came before at some length, and that the whole of the other part (illegible) must be set apart by parenthesis marks, so that the following sentences would cohere with the earlier ones, which otherwise are shamefully gapped. And for this reason he added therefore. But what does Bellarmine do with his translation? He adds the word which (though it is not in the Greek) to make that clause a parenthesis [παρένθετον], and he explains the particle [ἐν?] as for this reason; an interpretation which is wholly unknown to purer Greek writers in a consequence of this kind. One of the two must have erred: either the man who wrote it awkwardly, or this one who, on the strength of authority, thrusts in the word and interprets it by a foreign usage.

units.la: 24 Ibid. Neque est insolitum historicis, aliquid interdum colligere ex rebus gestis, quod ad imitationem & bonos mores pertineat. ] De historicis sacris, falsum: nam iustas tenuerunt historiae leges, de quibus Tullius lib.1.de oratore.de aliis,distinguendum.Nam si periti fuerunt historici, aut præfati sunt se historiam aucturos exoterica illa disciplina & veniam deprecati sunt, aut imperitiæ arguuntur suo ipsorum merito.
units.tr: 24 Ibid. Nor is it unusual for historians sometimes to draw from events something that pertains to imitation and good morals.) As regards sacred historians, this is false: for they kept to the just laws of history, concerning which Cicero, On the Orator, book 1. As for others, a distinction must be made. For if the historians were skilled, they either declared beforehand that they would enlarge the history with that esoteric teaching, and asked pardon for it; or they are convicted of ignorance by their own fault.

units.la: 25. Art. 19. Cum satis aperte colligatur ex iis quæ hic habentur.] Negatur colligi. Nam si mortuis loca deputarentur solum tria a Pontificiis, vera esset consequentia ex ipsorum hypothesi, quam tamen hypothesin negamus: sed cum plura ab eis statuantur, (vt postea disputator ipse non obscure statuit lib. 2. cap.7.) non valet consequentia ex insufficiente enumeratione: si nec in coelo, nec in inferis sunt, esse igitur in Purgatorio. Plura autem statui ab eis loca testis est Zacharias Lilius in suo orbis breviario: nimirum inferos, in quibus poenæ: limbum puerorum, vbi non est Dei visio: Purgatorium, vbi poenæ, sed cum diuina gratia: & Limbum sanctorum Patrum: supra quæ omnia Paradisus est cælestis gloriæ.
units.tr: 25. Art. 19. Since it is sufficiently clearly inferred from what is stated here.) It is denied that it is inferred. For if only three places were assigned to the dead by the Papists, the consequence would be valid from their own hypothesis, which hypothesis we nevertheless deny. But since they set down more (as the disputant himself later plainly sets down, book 2, chapter 7), the consequence from an insufficient enumeration does not hold: if they are neither in heaven nor in hell, then they are in Purgatory. That they set down more places is attested by Zacharias Lilius in his Breviary of the World: namely, hell, in which are punishments; the limbo of children, where there is no vision of God; Purgatory, where there are punishments, but with divine grace; and the limbo of the holy Fathers; and above all these is the heavenly Paradise of glory.

units.la: Consulatur Bellarminus ipse lib. 2. cap. 6. & 7. qui plura etiam loca non dubitauit concedere. Frustra igitur sequentia.
units.tr: Let Bellarmine himself be consulted, book 2, chapters 6 and 7, where he did not hesitate to concede several more places. Therefore what follows is in vain.

units.la: 26. Ibid. Iussisse pro eis orari & sacrificari, vt a peccatis soluerentur: Non dicit a pœnis, sed a peccatis: sunt autem secundum Pontificios, etiam carceres ad custodiam, ac non ad pœnam, dati. Est itaque futilis hæc tota argumentatio, & vitiosa ex insufficiente (vt vocant) enumeratione, cuius firmamenta in superioribus euersa sunt.
units.tr: 26. Ibid. That he commanded prayers and sacrifices to be offered for them, that they might be loosed from sins: He does not say from punishments, but from sins. Yet according to the Papists, prisons are also given for custody, and not for punishment. Therefore this whole argument is futile and faulty, arising from an insufficient (as they call it) enumeration, whose foundations have been overthrown above.

units.la: 27. Art. 20. Quia forte ignorabant legis prohibitionem, Quasi vero ignorantia legalis & publici iuris excusare posset. Nam illi de anathemate suffurati erant, id est, de rebus quæ sacratæ fuerant idolis Iamniæ, vt referthistoria. Lex autem habetur. Deutero. 13. 17.
units.tr: 27. Art. 20. Because perhaps they did not know the prohibition of the law. As if legal ignorance and ignorance of public law could excuse! For those men had stolen things under the ban, that is, things that had been consecrated to the idols of Jamnia, as the history relates. The law is found in Deut. 13. 17.

units.la: 28. Ibid. Ditescendi cupiditate, quæ venialis esse potest: Atqui ne ex iure quidem Pontificio venialis est huiusmodi cupiditas: prout ex dist. 25. c. vnum. §. quæ autem, & c. qualis, non obscure confirmari potest. non fuit leuis cupiditas hominum contingentium anathema.
units.tr: 28. Ibid. The desire to be enriched, which can be venial: Yet not even by Papist law is such a desire venial, as can be made clear from dist. 25, c. unum, §. quae autem, and c. qualis. It was no slight desire of men who had touched the anathema.

units.la: 29. Ibid. Et quoad culpam remissum illis fuisse, Prius incertæ coniecturæ est, posterius distinctionis falsæ, vt tomo 3. videbitur. Et vnde probetur doluisse eos & pœnituisse, cum ne morientes quidem anathema à se abiecerint? nam inuenta fuisse anathemata sub tunica eorum cuiusque ipse auctor refert. 2. Mac. 12. 40. Quapropter sequens Psalmi locus nihil ad rem: agit enim Psaltes de iis qui viuentes conuertebantur, isti vero ne morientes quidem ab anathemate abstinebant.
units.tr: 29. Ibid. And that as regards guilt, it was forgiven them. The former is an uncertain conjecture, the latter rests on a false distinction, as will be seen in volume 3. And how is it proved that they grieved and repented, when they did not even cast off the anathema while dying? For the author himself reports that anathemas were found under the tunic of each one of them, 2 Mac. 12. 40. Therefore the following verse of the Psalm has nothing to do with the matter: the Psalmist is speaking of those who were converted while living, but these men did not abstain from the anathema even when dying.

units.la: 30. Ibid. Considerasse eos, qui cum pietate obdormiuerant, uerant,optimá habere repositam gratiam.] hoc si de illis existimauit Iudas, falsus fuit, vt modo ostendimus: sinautem de piis qui ante in bello sacro occiderant, nihil ad causam istorum pertinet. Quid autem ex vtrauis sententia consequatur?
units.tr: 30. Ibid. That they considered those who had fallen asleep in piety as having the best grace laid up.] If Judas thought this of them, he was mistaken, as we have just shown. But if it concerns the pious who had earlier fallen in the holy war, it has nothing to do with the case of these men. But what follows from either opinion?

units.la: antecedens locus opinionis est, non autem fidei; consequens igitur τὸ ἐξ ἀφῆς αὐτῆ [?]. nam quicquid sine fide fit, peccatum est, Rom. 14. 23. & orationi fidei, ac non alteri, promissiones fiunt Iac. 5. 15. & sequentib.
units.tr: The antecedent is a matter of opinion, not of faith; the consequent therefore [τὸ ἐξ ἀφῆς αὐτῆ?] is of the same kind. For whatever is done without faith is sin, Rom. 14. 23; and the promises are made to the prayer of faith, and not to another, Jas. 5. 15 and following.

units.la: Sed vtram consequentiam Bellarmine, afferis? nam certum oportet dici. At nos 1. vtramque consequentiam negamus, & ante confutauimus. 2. antecedens prius distinguimus, orabant enim pro mortuis in solatium viuorum, non in auxilium mortuorum, vt cum Augustino loquar: posterius negamus, laudari orationem pro defunctorum peccatis in Scriptura sacra diuinitusque authentica.
units.tr: But which consequence do you assert, Bellarmine? For it must be stated as certain. We, first, deny both consequences, and have refuted them before. Second, we distinguish the antecedent: for they prayed for the dead as a consolation for the living, not as a help to the dead, to speak with Augustine; the consequent we deny: that the praising of prayer for the sins of the departed is found in Holy Scripture, which is divinely authentic.

units.la: vtrumque concedimus de Scriptura libri Machabaeorum: nam diuinae auctoritatis non est. Sequentia itaque nos minime commouent.
units.tr: We concede both points about the Scripture of the books of the Maccabees: for it is not of divine authority. Therefore what follows does not move us in the least.

units.la: Hoc vero non est absurdum, sed ipsissima veritas, si orandi verbum proprio sensu acceperis, vt vulgo solet accipi. Prisci autem Patres aut figurate loquuti sunt, ex quo propria consequentia non potest erui; aut de poena solum damni (vt vocat) loquuti sunt, quod eos mortuos carere visione Dei statuerentur aut denique solatium illud humanitus superstitibus indulserunt toleranConsulatur Bellarminus ipse lib. 2. cap. 6. & 7. qui plura etiam loca non dubitauit concedere. Frustra igitur sequentia.
units.tr: This, however, is not absurd, but the very truth, if you take the word "pray" in its proper sense, as it is commonly taken. But the early Fathers either spoke figuratively, from which a proper consequence cannot be drawn; or they spoke only of the punishment of loss (as they call it), since they held that the dead lack the vision of God; or finally they granted that comfort to the living, out of human tolerance. Let Bellarmine himself be consulted, book 2, chapters 6 and 7, where he did not hesitate to concede several more places. Therefore what follows is in vain.

units.la: 26. Ibid. Iussisse pro eis orari & sacrificari, vt a peccatis soluerentur: Non dicit a poenis, sed a peccatis: sunt autem secundum Pontificios, etiam carceres ad custodiam, ac non ad poenam, dati. Est itaque futilis haec tota argumentatio, & vitiosa ex insufficiente (vt vocant) enumeratione, cuius firmamenta in superioribus euersa sunt.
units.tr: 26. Ibid. That he commanded prayers and sacrifices to be offered for them, that they might be loosed from sins: He does not say from punishments, but from sins. Yet according to the Papists, prisons are also given for custody, and not for punishment. Therefore this whole argument is futile and faulty, arising from an insufficient (as they call it) enumeration, whose foundations have been overthrown above.

units.la: 27. Art. 20. Quia forte ignorabant legis prohibitionem, Quasi vero ignorantia legalis & publici iuris excusare posset. Nam illi de anathemate suffurati erant, id est, de rebus quae sacratae fuerant idolis Iamniae, vt refert historia. Lex autem habetur. Deutero. 13. 17.
units.tr: 27. Art. 20. "Because perhaps they did not know the prohibition of the law." As if ignorance of the law and of public right could excuse anyone! For those men had stolen from the anathema, that is, from the things that had been consecrated to the idols of Jamnia, as the history relates. The law is found in Deutero. 13. 17.

units.la: 28. Ibid. Ditescendi cupiditate, quae venialis esse potest: Atqui ne ex iure quidem Pontificio venialis est huiusmodi cupiditas: prout ex dist. 25. c. vnum. §. quae autem, & c. qualis, non obscure confirmari potest. non fuit leuis cupiditas hominum contingentium anathema.
units.tr: 28. Ibid. "Out of a desire for gain, which can be venial." Yet not even by Papal law is such a desire venial, as can be clearly confirmed from dist. 25, c. unum, §. quae autem, and c. qualis. It was no slight desire of the men who touched the anathema.

units.la: 29. Ibid. Et quoad culpam remissum illis fuisse, Prius incertae coniecturae est, posterius distinctionis falsae, vt tomo 3. videbitur. Et unde probetur doluisse eos & poenituisse, cum ne morientes quidem anathema a se abiecerint? nam inuenta fuisse anathemata sub tunica eorum cuiusque ipse auctor refert. 2. Mac. 12. 40. Quapropter sequens Psalmi locus nihil ad rem: agit enim Psaltes de iis qui viuentes conuertebantur, isti vero ne morientes quidem ab anathemate abstinebant.
units.tr: 29. Ibid. "And as to guilt, forgiveness was granted them." The former is an uncertain conjecture, the latter a false distinction, as will be seen in vol. 3. And how is it proved that they grieved and repented, when they did not cast away the anathema even as they died? For the author himself reports that anathemas were found under the tunic of each of them (2 Macc. 12.40). Therefore the following verse of the Psalm is irrelevant: the Psalmist speaks of those who were converted while still living, but these men did not refrain from the anathema even in death.

units.la: 30. Ibid. Considerasse eos, qui cum pietate obdormiuerant, uerant, optimá habere repositam gratiam.] hoc si de illis existimauit Iudas, falsus fuit, vt modo ostendi-mus: sinautem de piis qui ante in bello sacro occi-derant, nihil ad causam istorum pertinet. Quid au-tem ex vtrauis sententia consequatur?
units.tr: 30. Ibid. "Having considered that those who had died in piety had laid up grace in the best way." If Judas thought this about them, he was mistaken, as I have just shown. But if he thought it about the pious men who had earlier fallen in the holy war, it has nothing to do with the cause of these men. But what follows from either view?

units.la: 31 Ibid. Incertum fuisse statum illorum & propterea licuisse pro eis orare, etiamsi damnati fuissent.) antecedens locus opinionis est, non autem fidei; consequens igitur τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς αὐτῆ [?]. nam quicquid sine fide fit, peccatum est, Rom. 14.23. & oratione fidei, ac non alteri, promissiones fiunt Iac. 5.15. & sequentib.
units.tr: 31. Ibid. "The state of those men being uncertain, and therefore it was permitted to pray for them, even if they had been condemned." The antecedent is an opinion, not a matter of faith; the consequent is therefore [τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς αὐτῆ?]. For whatever is done without faith is sin (Rom. 14.23), and promises are made through prayer of faith, not otherwise (James 5.15 and following).

units.la: 32. Art. 21. Ergo Purgatorium est in alia vita.) Sed vtram consequentiam Bellarmine, afferis? nam certum oportet dici. At nos 1. vtramque consequentiam negamus, & ante confutauimus. 2. antecedens prius distinguimus, orabant enim pro mortuis in solatium viuorum, non in auxilium mortuorum, vt cum Augustino loquar: posterius negamus, laudari orationem pro defunctorum peccatis in Scriptura sacra diuinitusque authentica.
units.tr: 32. Art. 21. "Therefore Purgatory is in the other life." But which consequence do you assert, Bellarmine? For one must state what is certain. We deny both consequences, and have refuted them before. (2) We distinguish the antecedent: they prayed for the dead for the comfort of the living, not for the help of the dead, to use Augustine's words. The latter we deny: that prayer for the sins of the dead is praised in holy and divinely authentic Scripture.

units.la: 33 Ibid. Et Scriptura erraret laudando eiusmodi orationem.) vtrumque concedimus de Scriptura libri Machabaeorum: nam diuinae auctoritatis non est. Sequentia itaque nos minime commouent.
units.tr: 33. Ibid. "And Scripture would err in praising such a prayer." We concede both, regarding the Scripture of the Maccabees, for it is not of divine authority. Therefore what follows does not move us at all.

units.la: 34 Ibid. Quorsum enim oratio pro illis, qui aut non egent, aut iuuari non possunt?) Hoc vero non est absurdum, sed ipsissima veritas, si orandi verbum proprio sensu acceperis, vt vulgo solet accipi. Prisci autem Patres aut figuratè loquuti sunt, ex quo propria consequentia non poterit erui; aut de poena solum damni (vt vocat) loquuti sunt, quòd eos mortuos carere visione Dei statuerentur aut denique solatium illud humanitus superstitibus indulserunt tolerantes,non approbantes infirmitatem illorum. Sed de hac re controu.7.& tomo 4.videbitur.
units.tr: 34. Ibid. "For why pray for those who either do not need it or cannot be helped?" This is not absurd but the very truth, if you take the word "pray" in its proper sense, as it is commonly taken. The early Fathers, however, either spoke figuratively, from which no proper consequence can be drawn; or spoke only of the penalty of loss (as it is called), since they supposed the dead lack the vision of God; or finally they granted that comfort to the living in a human way, tolerating their weakness without approving it. But this matter will be seen in Controversy 7 and vol. 4.

units.la: 35 Art. 22. partim à testimonio infallibili scriptoris sacri.]negamus utrumque argumentationis locum.
units.tr: 35. Art. 22. "Partly from the infallible testimony of the sacred writer." We deny both parts of the argument.

units.la: 36 Ibid.omnes qui cum Iuda erant, ad preces con-uersos.] nempe publica de causa, ne iudicium illud Dei amplius exardescere in populum, sed ira illius desineret, ut Deuter.21.7. & seq.& alibi. Non ergo causa mortuorum, sed uiuentium reliquiarum maxime sunt conceptæ orationes istæ.atque hoc commonstrant sequentia.
units.tr: 36. Ibid. "All who were with Judas turned to prayer." Namely, for a public cause: lest that judgment of God blaze out further against the people, but his wrath might cease (Deut. 21.7 and following, and elsewhere). Therefore these prayers were offered chiefly not for the sake of the dead but for the surviving remnant, and the following words show this.

units.la: 37 Ibid.nomine omnium in Hierusalem, ad sacrificia pro mortuis,] Iudas aut Ecclesia non misit ut of-ferretur sacrificium pro peccatis illorum, ut expia-rentur ipsi; quæ sententia nihil commune habet cum lege Dei: sed misit ut offerretur sacrificiū pro peccato Ecclesiæ totius ad expiationem ipsius ex le-ge,Leuit. 4.13. Quod enim auctor aliter accipit interpretaturque sequentibus, id erroris est humani; cum nec auctoritate Dei nitatur in lege, nec bonorum exemplis qui ad illam usque ætatem uixerunt.
units.tr: 37. Ibid. "In the name of all in Jerusalem, for sacrifices for the dead." Judas or the Church did not send that a sacrifice be offered for the sins of those men, that they might be expiated; that opinion has nothing in common with the law of God. He sent that a sacrifice be offered for the sin of the whole Church, for its atonement, according to the law (Lev. 4.13). For what the author takes and interprets otherwise in what follows is human error, since it rests neither on the authority of God in the law nor on the examples of good men who lived up to that age.

units.la: 38 Ibid.tamquam sanctam, piam, & religiosam.) at nos istam negamus esse Scripturam sacram, ut ante: licet eam Pontifices in magno Missali suo lectione in anniuersario defunctorum, & in Concilio Tridentino indigetauerint.
units.tr: 38. Ibid. "As holy, pious, and religious." But we deny that this is Holy Scripture, as before, although the Papists have declared it so in their great Missal in the reading for the anniversary of the dead, and the Council of Trent has done likewise.

units.la: 39 Ibid.laudatur, quod fortiter, & viriliter egerit, non quod pie & sancte.] addendum fuerat ad euidentiam, ex cæco humano sensu, qui lib.1. de ciuit. Dei copiose exponitur: nam factum istud Raziæ illic Augustinus in toto cap. simpliciter & absolute ci-tra ullam tergiuersationem improbat, auctorem vero patitur utcunque excusari humanis praesum-ptionibus.
units.tr: 39. Ibid. "He is praised because he acted bravely and manfully, not because he acted piously and holily." It should have been added for clarity, drawing on the blind human sense that is fully set out in book 1 of De civitate Dei. For there Augustine, throughout that chapter, condemns the deed of Razis simply and absolutely, without any evasion, but allows the author to be excused in some measure by human presumptions.

units.la: non sequitur ex disparí. Nam hoc quidem Augustinus dicit de Samsone, & verum est; quia vocatione tum communi publica ut iudex, tum singulari diuina ut typus Christi & vindex Ecclesiae, instructus fuit, ut sua morte hostes publicos traderet mortiti per fidem. Hebr.ii. In Razia vero quid monstrari potest eiusmodi?
units.tr: It does not follow from the dissimilar. For Augustine says this of Samson, and it is true, because he was equipped with a calling both common and public, as judge, and singular and divine, as type of Christ and avenger of the Church, so that by his death he might hand over the public enemies, having been put to death through faith (Heb. 11). But in Razis what of that kind can be shown?

units.la: similium [?] allegorice, & eo allegoriarum modo, quae nec probabiliter nec verisimiliter aliquid confirmare possunt. Verissime olim Chrysostomus in 5. cap. Esaiae: non permisit, inquit, ut penes auditorem esset auctoritas accommodandi a se dicta, quibus vellet rebus aut personis: sed Scriptura ipsa praeuertens seipsam interpretata est. hac in re boni Patres multi luxuriati sunt, delectantes magis quam docentes aut probantes sermonem suum.
units.tr: [Similar?] by allegory, and by that manner of allegories which can confirm nothing probably or plausibly. Chrysostom long ago said most truly, on chapter 5 of Isaiah: "He did not permit," he says, "that it should be in the hearer's power to apply what was said to whatever things or persons he wished; but Scripture itself, anticipating us, interpreted itself." In this matter many good Fathers ran riot, delighting more than teaching or proving their discourse.

units.la: negamus hunc sensum loci illius esse; ut taceam librum esse Apocryphum, & lectionibus incertis inde a prisco seculo variantem. Illud enim ἐπὶ τάφον δικαίων [?], vel supersepulturam iusti per hypallagen dictum est, pro eo quod est, super iustos etiam postquam de vita decesserunt, in posteris ipsorum: quo sensu dicebat Naomi nuribus suis, exerceat erga vos Iehoua benignitatem, quemadmodum exercuistis erga mortuos & erga me, Ruth.i.8. nam qui mortuorum necessariis benefacit, mortuis ipsis dicitur benefacere. Confirmat nostram hanc interpretationem oppositum membrum, neque dis[?] peccatoribus, siue (vt in Latino contextu legitur) & noli ex eo manducare & bibere cum peccatoribus. nam hæc omnino ad viuentes, non ad mortuos respiciūt: quapropter & antecedens membrum viuentibus accommodari necesse est.
units.tr: We deny that this is the sense of that place, not to mention that the book is Apocryphal and has varied in its readings since ancient times. For that phrase [ἐπὶ τάφον δικαίων?], "upon the grave of the just," is said by hypallage, or "over the burial of the righteous," meaning "upon the just even after they have departed this life, among their descendants." In this sense Tobit said to his daughters-in-law, "May Jehovah deal kindly with you, as you have dealt with the dead and with me" (Ruth 1.8). For whoever does kindness to the needs of the dead is said to do kindness to the dead themselves. The opposite member confirms our interpretation: "nor with sinners," or as the Latin text reads, "and do not eat from it and drink with sinners." For these all refer entirely to the living, not the dead; therefore the preceding member must also be applied to the living.

units.la: 43 Ibid. consuetudo quæ & olim in Ecclesia fuit, & nunc etiam est, vt affines defunctis conuiuium faciant, ambigue dictum, aut falsò. Nam olim cum sepul-chreta essent familiaria, vt omnes historiæ docent; non solebant lugentes ipsi conuiuium exhibere, sed amici lugentium eos couiuuali[?] munere consolari, siue ad monumentum ipsum, siue in loco prædió-que religioso illius. Quapropter in Græco legitur, ἐκχέον τοὺς ἄρτες σου ἐπὶ τὸν τάφον τῶν δικαίων[?], effunde panes tuos, id est, cibaria tua super monumentum iustorum, non autem dicit, super monumentum meum, quia filio suo officium erga bonos quoslibet poste-rósque ipsorum præscribebat. Atque hunc fuisse iustum in prisca Ecclesia morem ostendit Ieremias 16.7. nam charitatis officium est. Contrà verò Ethnicorum mos fuit, vt lugentes ipsi parentalibus suis quàm superstitiosissimè occupati exhiberent aliis silicernia, etiam religiosis suis & sacerdotibus ad quam iniquam & impiam consuetudinem Christianos Bellarminus reuocat verbis seq. Hæc itaque omnia quæ dicit, negamus cum verbo Dei, ratione naturæ, & historiæ veteris illius fide conuenire. De oratione pro defunctis postea videbitur: de qua & Chrysostomus in eo loco dicit verissime qui mox adducitur.
units.tr: 43. "The custom which was both formerly in the Church and is now also, that relatives hold a feast for the dead" is stated ambiguously, or falsely. For formerly, when tombs were familiar places, as all histories teach, the mourners themselves did not usually provide the feast; rather, the friends of the mourners comforted them with a meal, either at the monument itself or in the place sacred to it. Therefore the Greek reads [ἐκχέον τοὺς ἄρτες σου ἐπὶ τὸν τάφον τῶν δικαίων], "pour out your bread," that is, your food, "upon the tomb of the righteous," not "upon my tomb," because he prescribed to his son a duty toward good men of any kind and their descendants. That this was the just custom in the early Church, Jeremiah 16.7 shows, for it is a duty of charity. On the contrary, it was the custom of the heathen for the mourners themselves, most superstitiously busy with their parental rites, to provide funeral feasts for others, even for their religious men and priests. To this wicked and impious custom Bellarmine recalls the Christians in the words that follow. Therefore we deny all these things he says, since they do not agree with the word of God, the reason of nature, or the faith of that ancient history. Prayer for the dead will be discussed later, and Chrysostom speaks most truly about it in the passage quoted next.

units.la: 44 Ibid. cur Presbyteros, vt pro eis velint orare, obsecras? reprehendit hos mores in isto loco Chrysostomus: ii[?] reprehendit, cur laudauisset To-bias. bias? qui certè aliud sibi voluit. Cur ergo disputator laudat? Reprehendi à Chrysostomo, ex verbis ipsius omnes, me tacente, cognoscent. Sic enim ille, postquàm de huius vitæ afflictionibus dixisset: Nihil autem huiusmodi de futuris rebus scribitur, quin imò totum oppositum, aufugit, inquit, dolor, tristitia, gemitus: & rursum, ab Oriente atque Occidente venient, & recumbent in sinu Abrahæ, Isaac, & Iacob: & alibi, thesaurus sunt quæ illic sunt, spirituales, inexstinguibiles fulgidæque lucernæ, cælestis vita. Cur ergo defunctum exagitas? cur committis ut timeant mortem alii atque formident? cur causam præbes ut nonnulli Deum incusare audeant, quòd mala nobis tanta inuexerit? imò vero cùm post mortem tuorum pauperes conuocas? cur Presbyteros, ut pro eo velint orare, obsecrare? Non ignoro te responsurum, ut defunctus quietem adipiscatur, ut propitium iudicem inueniat. his ergo de rebus flendum atque vlulandum arbitraris? nonne vides, quàm maximè ipsis repugnas? nam cùm illum abiisse in prata florentia putes, ingentes tamen aduersus ipsum fluctus suscitas tempestatis. & quæ sequuntur. Ethnicos, reprehendit Christianorum, aut infirmos ritus atque imprudentes quid mihi ex istis colligas? hæc profecto à monitore imperito & ignorante puto esse, cui disputator fidem habuit inconsulto loco. Nam Chrysostomus certè alia omnia.
units.tr: 44 Ibid. why do you beg the priests to pray for him? Chrysostom reproves these customs in this passage. He reproves ... why he commended Tobias? Yet Tobias certainly meant something else. Why then does the disputant praise him? Everyone will recognise, without my help, that Chrysostom reproves it, from his own words. For after describing the afflictions of this life, he says: Nothing of this kind is written about future things; on the contrary, the opposite is true: pain, sadness and groaning flee away. And again: they will come from East and West and recline in the bosom of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. And elsewhere: the treasures that are there are spiritual, inextinguishable and shining lamps, a heavenly life. Why then do you harass the dead man? Why do you cause others to fear and dread death? Why do you give some the occasion to dare to accuse God, because he has brought us such great evils? Indeed, why do you summon the poor after the death of your people? Why do you beg the priests to pray for him? I do not doubt that you will reply that the dead man may attain rest and find a gracious judge. Do you then think that we must weep and wail over these things? Do you not see how far you contradict yourself? For while you think he has gone away into flowering meadows, you nevertheless stir up huge waves of tempest against him. And what follows. You gather from these things the customs of the heathen, or of weak and unwise Christians? I think these things come from an unskilled and ignorant adviser, whom the disputant trusted, without consulting the place. For Chrysostom certainly says otherwise.

units.la: 45 Ibid. & deinde transfit ad commendationem mortuorum, ut in litera patet. ] negatur: nam etiam spectant ad viuentes adiuncta omnia, antecedentia & consequentia. illa autem verba sunt figurate dicta, ut nota 42. & 43. ostendimus.
units.tr: 45 Ibid. And then he passes on to the commendation of the dead, as is clear from the text. ] Denied: for all the surrounding material, preceding and following, also bears on the living. Those words, moreover, are spoken figuratively, as we showed in notes 42 and 43.

units.la: 46 Art. 24. tamen credibile est, præcipuè facta esse ad iuuandas animas defunctorum. ] falsum. Iabefitæ enim ieiunauerunt luctus & calamitatis publicæ, ut fit, conscientia, 1. Sam. 31.13. Dauid similiter ob luctum publicum ieiunauit: scriptum est enim, ieiu-nauerunt, vsque ad vesperam propter Saulem, & propter Ionathanem filium eius, & propter populum Iehoua, denique propter familiam Isräelis, quòd cecidissent gladio. 2. Sam. 1. 12. Quòd autem de Abnero lugens Dauid ieiunio vsus est, fecit maximè, ut studium suum testificaretur, luctúsque sui veritatem; & se à suspicione cædis purgaret publicè: quod verba ipsius confirmant luculentissimè 2.Sam.3.28.& narratio auctoris versu 36. bonum visum est in oculis populi totius:& versu 37. agnoscebant enim totus populus eius & totus Israel die illo non esse profectum à Rege, ut morte afficeretur Abner filius Ner. Consulantur loci. Nos hìc non coniecturas, sed probationes certas adferimus, ad quas non adeò respexit Beda.
units.tr: 46 Art. 24. Yet it is credible that they were done chiefly to help the souls of the dead. ] False. For the Jabeshites fasted out of grief and public calamity, as is usual, conscience-bound, 1 Sam. 31.13. David likewise fasted for public mourning: for it is written, they fasted until evening for Saul, and for Jonathan his son, and for the people of Jehovah, and finally for the family of Israel, because they had fallen by the sword. 2 Sam. 1.12. But that David, mourning for Abner, used fasting, he did mainly to bear witness to his own zeal and the truth of his grief, and to clear himself publicly of suspicion of murder. His own words confirm this most clearly, 2 Sam. 3.28, and the author's narrative at verse 36: it seemed good in the eyes of all the people, and at verse 37: for all his people and all Israel recognised that day that it had not been from the king that Abner son of Ner was to be put to death. Let the passages be consulted. Here we bring not conjectures but certain proofs, to which Bede did not sufficiently attend.

units.la: 47 Ibid. quòd irrationabile fuisset, in signum doloris, septem dies ieiunare.]Atqui ieiunauisse illos in signum doloris, falsum est, si postremum exemplum exceperis. Ieiunare in signum doloris solùm, hypocritarum est: pij ieiunant in exercitium pietatis, humilitatis, & resipiscentiæ, ad consequendam misericordiam, & liberationem à malo, si causa religiosa est, aut ampliorem communicationem boni; siue diarium, siue hebdomadis vnius, ut 4.Esdrę aliquoties, siue complurium exstiterit, ut Dan. 10. 2. & Nehem. 1.4. sin causa politica est, ad signum & testificationem solam potest pertinere, ut in luctu Danidis de cæde Abneri factum est. Nihil ergo sequitur ex causa falsa, aut insufficiente causarum enumeratione.
units.tr: 47 Ibid. that it would be unreasonable to fast seven days as a sign of grief.] But that they fasted as a sign of grief is false, if you except the last example. To fast merely as a sign of grief belongs to hypocrites. The godly fast as an exercise of piety, humility and repentance, to obtain mercy and deliverance from evil, if the cause is religious, or a fuller communication of good; whether for a day, or for a week, as in 4 Ezra several times, or for several weeks, as in Dan. 10.2 and Neh. 1.4. But if the cause is political, it can pertain only to a sign and a bare testimony, as happened in David's mourning for the slaying of Abner. Nothing therefore follows from a false cause, or from an insufficient enumeration of causes.

units.la: 48 Ibid. & præterea eum suffragiis non[?] egere,] nihil sequitur ex dispari. Nam hinc quo medio probes acta esse ieiunia ad iuvandas animas defuncto-rum, quia Dauid puero vivo ieiunauit orauitque, non autem mortuo? Contra vero illud ex eo sequutu-rum est, non esse pro defunctis iuvandis ieiunia obseruanda, nec eos iuvari ieiuniis, cum Dauid non ieiunauerit.
units.tr: 48 Ibid. and moreover that he had no need of suffrages,] Nothing follows from an unlike case. For from what means would you prove that fasts were performed to help the souls of the dead, because David fasted and prayed while the boy was alive, but not when he was dead? On the contrary, it would follow from that that fasts are not to be observed for helping the dead, nor are they helped by fasts, since David did not fast for the dead.

units.la: 49 Ibid. ut essent participes precum & sacrificiorum, quæ ibi offerebantur. ] negatur. Nam id nusquam Scriptura dicit: tum quæ preces & sacrificia, aut à quibus tum offerebantur in Chananæa[?], quum sepeliri in ea poscerent? vide infrà cap. 15. nota 16. & lib.2.cap.19.nota 9.
units.tr: 49 Ibid. that they might be partakers of the prayers and sacrifices that were offered there. ] Denied. For Scripture nowhere says this: what prayers and sacrifices, or by whom, were then offered in Canaan, when they asked to be buried in it? See below, chapter 15, note 16, and book 2, chapter 19, note 9.

units.la: 50. Art.25. Sit puniri fuere post hanc vitam, ad correctionem tamen & emendationem. ] Hæc Augustino tribuuntur falsò: Cassiodori sunt: quemadmodum bene distinguuntur interlineari Glossa. negatur interpretatio.
units.tr: 50. Art. 25. That they are punished after this life, yet for correction and amendment. ] These things are falsely attributed to Augustine: they are Cassiodorus's, as the interlinear gloss rightly distinguishes. The interpretation is denied.

units.la: 51. Ibid. Et talem me reddas, cui iam emendatorio igne non opus sit, &c. ] Adulterata lectio. Sic enim apud Augustinum est: & talem me reddas, cui iam emendato igne non opus sit, &c. Illud, emendato, est tertij casus, & construitur cum voce antecedente cui: tanquam si diceret, talem me reddas, quem iam emendatum & liberatum à peccatis in hac vita, non sit opus tradi in ignem æternum, &c. hanc germanam esse lectionem Augustini (ut nihil de fide meliorum exemplarium & MSS. dicam) arguunt adiū-ēta[?] omnia. Nam de Purgatorio in tota illa enarratione altum silentium[?]. De recentioribus auctoribus quod adfertur, unica negationis litura expungimus.
units.tr: 51. Ibid. And make me such a one that I have no further need of the cleansing fire, etc. ] A corrupted reading. For in Augustine it is thus: and make me such a one, for whom, now cleansed by fire, there is no need, etc. The word "cleansed" is in the dative case and agrees with the preceding word "for whom", as if he said: make me such a one, whom, now cleansed and freed from sins in this life, it is not necessary to hand over to eternal fire, etc. That this is Augustine's genuine reading (not to mention the testimony of better copies and manuscripts) is shown by all the surrounding material. For in that whole exposition there is deep silence about Purgatory. As for the recent authors quoted, we strike out the single negation.

units.la: 52. Art. 26. Per aquam, ut abluantur peccata: per ignem, ut exurantur. ] Hæc allegorici dicti expositi[?]. est allegorica: qua tribulationes grauissimæ cum inundatione aquarū, & incendio ignis ardentis comparantur, ut fit plurimum. Neque de baptismi aqua dicebat Dauid, qui nondum erat, neque de igne Purgatorij, qui nondum fuerat somniatus (loquitur autem Ecclesia de rebus in hac vita toleratis, non subeundis post mortem) neque Origenes in Num. 25. quicquam dicit eiusmodi. Ambrosius de igne tribulationum purgante in hac vita electos Dei loquitur planissimè, verba exponens Ecclesiæ dicentis, igne nos examinasti, & de probationibus quas in hac vita tulerat expostulantis: hi, inquit, etsi per ignem examinabuntur, dicent tamen, transiuimus per ignem & aquam, id est, euadent profitebunturque se euasisse per gratiam Dei) aliy in igne remanebunt, &c. Idem verò in Psalm. 118. serm. 3. agit de baptismo passionis siue tribulationis in hac vita, quo & Christus baptizatus est pro nobis, & nos baptizamur in Christo, complantati in mortem & sepulturam ac perpes-siones illius. Rom. 6. & 2. Cor. 4. & 2. Tim. 2. & ad illam salutarem aquam Christi, & ignem Spiritus respicit, quum verba illa enunciat. Demonstratur id verbis sequentibus: quis est, inquit ille, qui in hoc igne baptizat? non Presbyter, non Episcopus, non Ioannes, qui ait ego vos baptizo in pœnitentiam, &c. sed ille de quo Ioannes ait, qui venit post me, fortior me est, &c. Ne plura, sententiam suā paulò post euidenter ostendit Ambrosius dicēs: Qui ergo per ignem transierit intrat in requiem: transiit a materialibus atque mundanis ad illa incorruptibilia atque perpetua. Alius iste ignis quo exuruntur peccata non voluntaria, sed fortuita: quem parauit[?] seruulis suis Dominus Iesus, ut eos ab ista commemoratione quæ permixta est mortuis, emundet: alius ille
units.tr: 52. Art. 26. Through water, that sins may be washed away; through fire, that they may be burnt up. ] This is an allegorical saying, explained as such. It is allegorical, in which very grievous tribulations are compared with a flood of waters and the burning of a blazing fire, as commonly happens. David was not speaking of the water of baptism, which did not yet exist, nor of the fire of Purgatory, which had not yet even been dreamed of (the Church, moreover, speaks of things endured in this life, not to be undergone after death); nor does Origen in Numbers 25 say anything of the kind. Ambrose speaks very plainly of the fire of tribulation that purges the elect of God in this life, expounding the words of the Church saying, you have tested us by fire, and complaining of the trials she had undergone in this life: these, he says, though they will be tested by fire, will nevertheless say, we passed through fire and water, that is, they will escape and will confess that they escaped by the grace of God; others will remain in the fire, etc. Moreover, in Psalm 118, sermon 3, he treats of the baptism of suffering or tribulation in this life, with which Christ was baptised for us, and we are baptised in Christ, planted together in his death and burial and sufferings, Rom. 6, 2 Cor. 4, and 2 Tim. 2; and when he utters those words he has in view the saving water of Christ and the fire of the Spirit. This is shown by the words that follow: who is it, he says, who baptises in this fire? Not a priest, not a bishop, not John, who said, I baptise you unto repentance, etc., but he of whom John said, he who comes after me is stronger than I, etc. In short, Ambrose clearly shows his own opinion a little later, saying: He therefore who has passed through fire enters into rest: he has passed from material and worldly things to those incorruptible and perpetual things. That other fire, by which sins that are not voluntary but accidental are burnt up, which the Lord Jesus has prepared for his servants, to cleanse them from that remembrance which is mingled with the dead: that other

units.la: ) ignis, quem deputavit diabolo & Angelis eius, &c. Priorem ignem docet commorationis istius esse, posteriorem vero stationis malorum in futuro seculo. Hæc Bellarminum oportuit animadvertere: non autem verba Ambrosij ad præsumptam illam de Purgatorio sententiam detorquere.
units.tr: "The fire which he prepared for the devil and his angels, etc." Ambrose teaches that the former fire belongs to this temporary sojourn and the latter to the punishment of the wicked in the age to come. Bellarmine ought to have noticed this, and not twisted Ambrose's words toward his presumed opinion about Purgatory.

units.la: 53. Art.27. Hunc locum exponit de pœna Purgatorij B. Augustinus]Exponit quidem de pœnis purgatoriis, sed non de pœnis Purgatorij: prout ipse disputator paulò post agnoscit sub finem cap. Præterea exponit istud ἐλλαμπτικῶς[?], non autem ἀφοριστικῶς[?], ut ipse demonstrat sequentibus, alias interpretationes adferens. Nam propterea sic ait ibidem post aliquot versus: Nisi forte sic eos dicendum est emundari à sordibus, & eliquari quodammodo, quum ab eis mali per pœnale iudicium separantur, &c. & rursum capite seq. evidentius, quum ait: Video quippe alterum sensum, ne dies pristinos & annos priores carnalium sacrificiorum, & quæ sequuntur. Probabiliter suadere nō potest huiusmodi argumentatio.
units.tr: 53. Art. 27. Augustine expounds this passage of the punishment of Purgatory. He does expound it of purgatorial punishments, but not of the punishments of Purgatory, as the disputant himself later admits at the end of the chapter. Moreover, he expounds it illustratively [ἐλλαμπτικῶς], not definitively [ἀφοριστικῶς], as he shows himself in what follows, where he offers other interpretations. For shortly after some lines he says: "Unless perhaps it must be said that they are cleansed from filth and in some way melted down, when the wicked are separated from them by penal judgment, etc." And again, more clearly, in the next chapter, when he says: "I see indeed another sense, lest the former days and former years of carnal sacrifices, and what follows." Such an argument cannot persuasively establish anything of the kind.

units.la: 54. Art.28. Per confessionem peccatum arefieri, ut igne Purgatorio post hanc vitam absumi possit, & ex hoc loco probat.]illa verba, post hanc vitam, sunt Bellarminei glossematis. Hæc ad verbum Basilius habet: Si igitur per confessionem detexerimus peccatum, iam succrescens gramen arefecimus, dignum plane quod depascatur ac devoret purgatorius ignis, &c. Esse autem ignem illum in hac vita confirmat proxime sequentibus, quum in illa Esaiæ verba, quia propter indignationem iræ Domini succensa est terra omnis, his verbis utitur: declarat in gratiam & beneficium animæ, terrena ipsa tradi depascenda igni punitivo: quemadmodum & ipse Dominus subindicat dicens, ignem veni mittere ig terram : & quid volui, nisi ut accendatur ? de igne in terra omnino agit, & affirmat Christus, non de fictitio Purgatorij vaporario.
units.tr: 54. Art. 28. That sin is dried up through confession, so that it can be consumed by purgatorial fire after this life, and he proves this from this passage. The words "after this life" are Bellarmine's gloss. Basil has the words word for word: "If therefore we have revealed the sin through confession, we have already dried up the grass that was springing up, a fit thing indeed to be grazed upon and devoured by purgatorial fire, etc." That Basil means this fire to be in this life he confirms in the sentences immediately following, where, on the words of Isaiah, "because of the indignation of the wrath of the Lord all the earth is set on fire," he says: he declares that for the grace and benefit of the soul, the earthly things themselves are handed over to be consumed by punitive fire, just as the Lord himself hints when he says: "I came to send fire on the earth, and what do I wish but that it be kindled?" He is speaking entirely of fire on the earth, and Christ affirms it, not of the fictitious steam-bath of Purgatory.

units.la: 55. Art. 29. Iram[?] Domini portabo hic, vel in Purgatorio.] De Hieronymo, falsum: nam loquitur de igne castigationum siue punitiuo (ut Basilij interpres vertit) in hoc seculo, non de illo praesumpto in futurum Purgatorio: quod docent adiuncta omnia. Quae postea veluti ex Glossa ordinaria adduntur, ei tribuuntur falsò: non enim ab ea sunt haec verba, sed ab altera parte expositionum Nicolai de Lyra, quae inscribuntur Moralitates Bibliae, & allegoriis alienis, ineptis, falsisque diffluunt. Negamus auctoritatem earum, & huius ipsius interpretationis.
units.tr: 55. Art. 29. "I will bear the wrath of the Lord here or in Purgatory." This is false, as attributed to Jerome. For he speaks of the fire of chastisements, or punitive fire (as the translator of Basil renders it), in this age, not of that supposed Purgatory in the future; all the surrounding material shows this. What is added afterwards, as if taken from the Ordinary Gloss, is falsely attributed to it. These words are not from the Gloss but from the other part of the expositions of Nicholas of Lyra, entitled Moralities of the Bible, which overflow with allegories that are foreign, silly and false. We deny the authority of those and of this very interpretation.

units.la: 56. Art. 30. Cum eo descendit post mortem suam.] Et hanc quoque negamus interpretationem. De Limbo alibi videbitur.
units.tr: 56. Art. 30. "He descended with him after his death." We deny this interpretation too. The matter of Limbo will be considered elsewhere.

units.la: 57. Ibid. Quia isti rectius[?] dicuntur vincti.] Imo[?] nec recte, nec vere hi, aut illi.
units.tr: 57. Ibid. "Because these are more rightly called bound." Nay, neither these nor those are called so rightly or truly.

units.la: 58. Ibid. Hic vero consolatur.] Principium petitur: nam Purgatorium, & limbum istum negamus esse, huic vero hypothesi negatae disputator superstruit.
units.tr: 58. Ibid. "But here he comforts." This begs the question: we deny that Purgatory and that Limbo exist, and the disputant builds upon this denied hypothesis.

units.la: 59. Ibid. & multos eorum inde liberasse.] Haec falsò. Etenim Augustinus Epist. 99. ad Euodium in eam sententiam inuehit magis quam probat, reiicit magis quam accipit. Postquam enim de variis illis multorum sententiis dixit, quae eo spectare videbantur, & interpretationes in locum Petri hoc sensu adductas confutauit, suam ipsius statuit quam modestissime, & ad eam transfit his verbis: Considera tamen ne forte totum illud quod de conclusis in carcere spiritibus qui[?] diebus Noe non crediderant, Petrus A-
units.tr: 59. Ibid. "and delivered many of them thence." This is false. For Augustine, in Letter 99 to Evodius, inclines toward that opinion more than he proves it; he rejects it more than he accepts it. After speaking of the various opinions of many who seemed to aim at this, and refuting the interpretations of Peter's words brought forward in this sense, he set out his own view, most modestly, and passes to it with these words: "Consider however whether perhaps all that Peter the Apostle says of the spirits shut up in prison, who had not believed in the days of Noah, does not pertain at all to hell, but rather to those times whose form, transferred to these

units.la: postolus dicit, omnino ad inferos non pertineat, sed ad illa potiùs tempora, quorum formam ad hac re-uertora transfluuir, &c. Verùm de hac re tota an plius deinceps Bellarminus cogitauit, ex quo controuersiam scripserat. Nam de interno loqui Petrum, non de Purgatorio, defendit in ea vehementissi ne lib. 4. cap 13. & illudit Augustini interpretamento: hic vero contra statuit, in inferno, id est in Purgatorio. Memorem magis esse opportuit. In libro 11. in Genesin cap.35. nullum habetur verbum de Purgatorio, sed de inferno solum, quo descendisse animam Christi Augustinus asserit, siue præsentia essentiæ (nam vtrumuis in medio relinquit) siue præsentia virtutis suæ. Hæc autem quid habent commune cum Purgatorio? Locum denique totum Zachariæ alioqui pertinere contextus ipse ostendit euidentissimè.
units.tr: times, passes over, etc." But Bellarmine afterwards thought about this whole matter more than once, since he had written the controversy. For in the fourth book, chapter 13, of that very vehement work, he defends the view that Peter speaks of hell, not of Purgatory, and mocks Augustine's interpretation; yet here he decides the opposite, "in hell, that is, in Purgatory." He ought to have been more mindful of this. In book 11 on Genesis, chapter 35, there is no word about Purgatory at all, but only about hell, into which Augustine asserts that the soul of Christ descended, whether by the presence of his essence (for he leaves either in suspense) or by the presence of his power. But what have these to do with Purgatory? Finally, the context itself most evidently shows that the whole passage of Zechariah pertains to something else.

units.la: 60. Art. 31. & B. Hieronymus in hunc locum. ] Et hæc Malachiæ verba negamus ad Purgatorium pertinere, sed ad totum opus & tempus Euangelij, crucisque Euangelio coniunctæ. Nec aliter accepit Origenes, vt verba ipsius commonstrant dicentis, sicut fornax probat aurum, sic homines tentatio. Veniendum est ergo omnibus ad ignem, veniendum est ad ad conflatorium. Sedet enim Dominus, & conflat, & purgat filios Leui, & quæ sequuntur. Ambrosius, Augustinus, Hieronymus itidem: quorum verba super uacaneum fuerit adducum, cum disputator ipse proximè sequentibus verbis agnoscat, pœnam illam purgatoriam non esse eam de qua nunc agitur, nam illam, de qua Patres videlicet ipseque Malachias, purgare vi-uentes, se autem agere de pœna mortuorum.
units.tr: 60. Art. 31. And Blessed Jerome on this passage. We deny that these words of Malachi pertain to Purgatory, but rather to the whole work and time of the Gospel, and to the cross joined to the Gospel. Origen did not understand it otherwise, as his own words show, saying: "As the furnace tests gold, so temptation tests men. All must therefore come to the fire; all must come to the smelting-house. For the Lord sits and smelts and purges the sons of Levi, and what follows." Ambrose, Augustine and Jerome likewise; it would be superfluous to adduce their words, since the disputant himself, in the words immediately following, acknowledges that "that purgatorial punishment is not the one now under discussion, for that one, of which the Fathers and Malachi himself speak, purges the living, whereas I am treating of the punishment of the dead."

units.la: 61. Ib. Tamè inde rectè infertur Purgatorij.] Recte inferri negamus posse iusto medio, aut analogia.
units.tr: 61. Ib. "Yet it is rightly inferred of Purgatory from this." We deny that it can be rightly inferred either by the golden mean or by analogy.

units.la: 62. Ibid. Nec erit tempus purgationis ulterius, ut nunc est post mortem ante iudicium. ] petit τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς[?], quod in controuersia est. Turbat autem disputator omnia, ut aequatur quod vult. Est purgatio universalis, est & singularis. Universalis consideratur modo absolute secundum totalitatem suam (ut ita loquamur) principio, processu, termino in omnibus membris purgandis universè & singulariter per Christum, de qua Malach. 3. modo secundum aliquam ipsius partem, inprimis autem secundum terminum ipsius. Est autem in universali purgatione terminus duplex: unus in universitate, atque hic consummabitur in secundo aduentu Christi, 1. Cor. 15. alter in singulis universitatis, atque hic in singulis piis secundum animam consummatur statim a morte ipsorum, prout prisci Patres ex sacra Scriptura crediderunt. Haec omnia conturbat disputator, ut nihil non dixisse videatur. Est autem inconsequens ab universali absolute ad universale secundum quid, vel contra: nec magis consequi potest ab universali secundum illud argumentatio. Irenæus de universali absolute dicit, quod est verissimum: Bellarminus hoc ad confictam purgationem rapit secundum tempus & locum, de quo in Scripturis nullum verbum. Patres de purgatione etiam poenali in hac vita loquuti sunt. Bellarminus de purgatione poenali post hanc vitam somniat, & ab huius exemplo de illa argumentatur, contra Scripturam, fidem, & analogiam.
units.tr: 62. Ibid. "Nor will there be any further time of purgation, as there is now after death and before judgment." He begs the question [τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς], which is the point in controversy. The disputant, moreover, confuses everything so that it may square with what he wants. There is a universal purgation and there is also a particular one. The universal is considered in one way absolutely, according to its totality (so to speak): its beginning, progress and end, in all the members to be purged, universally and individually, through Christ, of which Malachi 3 speaks; and in another way according to some part of it, and above all according to its end. In the universal purgation there is a twofold end: one in the whole universe, and this will be completed at the second coming of Christ (1 Cor. 15); the other in the individuals of the whole, and this is completed in each of the pious according to the soul immediately after their death, as the early Fathers believed from holy Scripture. The disputant confounds all of this, so that he seems to have said nothing at all. Moreover, it is an invalid inference to pass from the universal absolutely to the universal in some respect, or the reverse; nor can an argument follow from the universal in that respect any more than from the other. Irenaeus speaks of the universal absolutely, which is most true; Bellarmine drags this over to his invented purgation as to time and place, of which there is not a word in the Scriptures. The Fathers spoke of penal purgation even in this life. Bellarmine dreams of penal purgation after this life, and from the example of that he argues about it, against Scripture, faith and analogy.

units.la: IN CAP. IV.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER IV.

units.la: Art.1. colligunt sancti Patres quaedam peccata remimittit in futuro seculo per orationes & suffragia Ecclesiæ.] At 1. non omnes ita colligunt, vt postea videbitur. 2. qui ita colligunt ex eo loco, male collegerunt. De singulis suo ordine postea videbitur.
units.tr: Art. 1. The holy Fathers infer that certain sins are forgiven in the future age through the prayers and suffrages of the Church.] First, not all of them infer this, as will be shown later. Second, those who do infer it from that passage have inferred it wrongly. Each point will be considered in its place later.

units.la: 2. Ibid. & omnes gloss, vt ordinaria, interlinearis, &c.] Augustini locum interpolatum esse à nonnullis veteramentariis, & verborum serie, & veterum MSS. aliorumque probatiorum fide ostenditur. Nam pleraque illa verba lib. 21. cap. 24. de ciuit. Dei, abesse Vives annotauit ab antiquis libris Brugensibus & Colonienfibus MSS. & ab eo quod olim Friburgi excusum est, quorum tamen incorruptior fides: nempe redolent alienam manum. Eiusdem locus libr. 6. in Iulianum cap. 5. nihil dicit eiusmodi, remitti in futuro seculo per orationes & suffragia Ecclesiæ: de inferenda hac conclusione Augustinus ibi nullum verbum. Remitti electis in hoc & in futuro seculo peccata sua religiosè credimus, nec eorum vllum hic remitti quod non remittatur illic: sed ea peccata quæ inhærent homini ad extremum vsque spiritum, magis remitti dicimus in futuro seculo, quia remissionem absolutam in effectu (vt ita dicimus) sortiuntur, quum homo ex hac vita soluitur, simulque cum hac vita dissoluitur vitiositas ipsius. Hoc sibi Augustinum velle demonstrant sequentia ipsius verba, quum latronis exemplum adfert dicentis, Memento mei, quum veneris in regnum tuum. vide postea in articulum 7. Sequentium omnium postea suo loco confutabitur auctoritas.
units.tr: 2. Ibid., and all the glosses, the ordinary gloss, the interlinear gloss, etc.] That the passage of Augustine has been interpolated by some of the older translators is shown from the sequence of the words and from the faith of old manuscripts and other more reliable witnesses. For Vives noted that most of those words in book 21, chapter 24, of The City of God are absent from the old Bruges and Cologne manuscripts and from the edition once printed at Freiburg, and their more trustworthy testimony smells of a foreign hand. The passage of Augustine in book 6 against Julian, chapter 5, says nothing of this kind, that sins are forgiven in the future age through the prayers and suffrages of the Church; Augustine says not a word there about drawing this conclusion. We devoutly believe that the elect have their sins forgiven both in this age and in the age to come, and that none of them is forgiven here which is not also forgiven there. But we say that those sins which cling to a man until his last breath are forgiven more fully in the future age, because they obtain complete remission in effect (as we may say) when a man is released from this life, and at the same time the sinfulness of his nature is dissolved along with this life. That Augustine means this is shown by the words that follow, where he cites the example of the thief saying, Remember me when you come into your kingdom. See later under article 7. The authority of all the rest will be refuted in its place later.

units.la: 3. Art. 2. Esse exaggerationem, quum dicitur ite in ignem æternum.] Inconsequens ex dispari. Nam, vt par esset ratio, Bellarminum oportebat dicere vi- uentibus, ite in ignem hunc & in æternum, quod verè impiis dicit Christus:non autem mortuis,ite in ignem æternum,solùm. Tum dispar est affirmantis & negantis propositionis ratio,vt pòst exponitur.
units.tr: 3. Art. 2. That it is an exaggeration when one says, Depart into everlasting fire.] This is an inconsequent inference from a dissimilar case. For if the reasoning were to be the same, Bellarmine ought to have said to the living, "Depart into this fire and into everlasting fire," which Christ truly says to the wicked; but not to the dead, merely Depart into everlasting fire. Moreover, the reasoning of an affirmative proposition and of a negative one is different, as will be explained later.

units.la: 4. Ibid. Qualis est, cùm fit partitio, & vni membro nihil respondet. ] Negamus exaggerationem hanc ineptam esse : nam vtrique membro aliquid suum respondere postea demonstrabitur in art.7.perinde enim est ac fiquis diceret ἐμφατικῶς[?], iste homo nec fecundùm corpus, nec fecundùm animam vacabit pœna: quod emphaticum est & ad præcidendam omnem tergiuerfationem commodissimum.
units.tr: 4. Ibid. What sort of thing is it, when a division is made and nothing corresponds to one member?] We deny that this exaggeration is inept; for it will be shown in article 7 that something corresponds to each member. It is just as if someone said emphatically, "This man will go unpunished neither in body nor in soul," which is emphatic and most suitable for cutting off every evasion.

units.la: 5. Art.3. Respondeo eodem modo.] Et nos quoque eodem modo soluimus.
units.tr: 5. Art. 3. I answer in the same way.] We too answer in the same way.

units.la: 6. Art.4. Quia ibi completur eorum remissio] Hæc distincti nihil ad rem facit.Quid enim? an non & peccata illa quæ dicuntur venialia remittuntur etiam in alio seculo, & ibi completam remissionem habent? nam quod semel remisit,id semper remittit Deus, cuius æterna est & constans remissio atque ἀεὶ πυιλντος[?].
units.tr: 6. Art. 4. Because their remission is completed there.] This distinction has nothing to do with the matter. For what? Are not those sins which are called venial also forgiven in another age, and do they not there have complete remission? For what God has once forgiven, he always forgives; his remission is eternal and constant, and [always the same].

units.la: 7. Art.5. Vt oratio crescat.] Hæc argumentatio ex hypothesi Pontificiorum ducitur: quam ego quidem præstare nolo.
units.tr: 7. Art. 5. So that prayer may increase.] This argument is drawn from the hypothesis of the Papists, which I for my part am unwilling to grant.

units.la: 8. Art.6. In Purgatorio remitti etiam culpas, saltem veniales: ] negamus Purgatorium esse, ergo & remissionem in eo fieri.
units.tr: 8. Art. 6. In Purgatory, sins are forgiven too, at least venial ones.] We deny that there is a Purgatory, and therefore that remission takes place in it.

units.la: 9. Ibid. Falsum est, loqui Christum de sola culpa. ] Agnoscimus: sed Caluinus hanc argumentationem ἀποσκευαστικῶς[?] non ex sensu suo protulit, sed ex Pontificiorum hypothesi: qui iamdiu peccatorum pœnam in Purgatorio lui, hic culpam remitti docuerunt. Hinc ergo conclusit iusta consequentia Caluinus, siue loquatur Dominus de remissione culpæ. solum,fiue culpæ & pœnæ simul,tamen ea verba nihil ad Purgatorium stabiliendum facere, ad quod solius pœnæ communiter remissio ex sententia Magistrorum nostrorum pertinet. Cæterum vt ostendat Caluinus istam non propriam, sed hypotheticam solutionem esse, mox alteram solutionem adfert In-ftit.lib.3.cap.5.§.7.dicens, Ne tamen adhuc nobis chstrepant, planiorem habebunt solutionem,&c. vbi refert eam ipsam solutionem quam disputator ante Martyri tribuit articulo 2.
units.tr: 9. Ibid. It is false that Christ speaks of guilt alone.] We grant this. But Calvin did not put forward this argument from his own view, but from the hypothesis of the Papists, who have long taught that the punishment of sins is paid in Purgatory and guilt is remitted here. Calvin therefore concludes with a sound inference, whether the Lord speaks of the remission of guilt alone or of guilt and punishment together, that those words have no bearing on establishing Purgatory, to which, according to the opinion of our teachers, the remission of punishment alone is commonly assigned. Moreover, to show that this is not Calvin's own solution but a hypothetical one, he soon offers another solution in the Institutes, book 3, chapter 5, section 7, saying, Yet lest they still make a noise against us, they will have a plainer solution, etc. There he reports the very solution which the disputant earlier attributed to Martyr in article 2.

units.la: 10. Ibid. Neque quantum ad culpam, neque quantum ad pœnam. ] Hactenus verus est disputatoris hic sensus: distinctionem verò sequentem nunquam per omnia probaturus est: Negamus itaque.
units.tr: 10. Ibid. Neither as to guilt nor as to punishment.] So far the disputant's sense is true here; but he will never prove the following distinction in every respect. So we deny it.

units.la: 12 Art. 7. nonne illi qui aut venialium purgatione indigebunt, aut solius pœnæ debitores erunt? ] vtrumque hoc dictum negamus, tum esse homines qui venialium purgatione indigeant post hanc vitam, tum alios esse qui solius pœnæ debitores sint: nemo enim secundum Deum rationemque debitor est pœnæ, quin idem sit culpæ reus. Quinam ergo sunt, inquies, quibus remittitur in futuro seculo? nempe ij quos in hac sua enumeratione omisit disputator, vt ab insufficiente enumeratione argumentando falleret. Nam peccatoribus remittuntur peccata sua aut in hoc seculo, dum adhuc viuunt, aut in futuro seculo, id est, quando soluuntur ex hoc corpore peccati mortis, & abeunt ex hoc seculo in venturum illud. Mortis enim momentum commune nobis est terminus seculi vtriusque; huius a quo morientes abeunt, & illius in quod transeunt. Quæ autem per momentum illud dicitur fieri remissio, non tribuitur seculo peregrunti huic) quod ineptum esset} sed illi permanenti in quod deueniunt morientes. Remittitur homini in morte, quod non fuerat remissum in vita: quod autem non remittitur in vita, si in morte remittitur, id recte in seculo ven-turo, potius quàm in hoc, remitti dicitur. Exempli causa, naturalis vitiositas hominis non nisi morte dissoluitur, & planè post mortem remissa est. vide quae diximus supra nota 2.
units.tr: 12. Art. 7. Are not those who will need the cleansing of venial sins, or who will be debtors of punishment alone?] We deny both of these statements: that there are people who after this life need the cleansing of venial sins, and that there are others who are debtors of punishment alone. For no one, according to God and reason, is a debtor of punishment without being also guilty of the sin. Who then, you will ask, are those to whom remission is granted in the future age? Namely, those whom the disputant omitted from his own enumeration, so that by an insufficient enumeration he might deceive in his argument. For sins are remitted to sinners either in this age, while they are still living, or in the future age, that is, when they are released from this body of sin and death and depart from this age into the one to come. For the moment of death is a boundary common to us of both ages: the one from which the dying depart, and the one into which they pass. But the remission which is said to take place at that moment is not attributed to this age, which is passing (that would be absurd), but to that age which abides, into which the dying arrive.
