Remission is granted to a man at death which had not been granted in life; and what is not remitted in life, if it is remitted in death, is rightly said to be remitted in the age to come rather than in this one. For example, a man's natural sinfulness is dissolved only by death, and is clearly forgiven after death. See what we said above in note 2.

units.la: 12 Ibid. qui n. hinc cum iniustitia decedunt, certè in iudicio non absoluentur. ] Ambiguè. Decedunt omnes homines cum iniustitia: Christum excipio, qui non est homo ἀλης[?], & nescuit in se quid peccatum esset, 1.Petr.2. Sed eorum classes duae: nam alii sic decedunt cum iniustitia, ut & iniustitia decedat ab ipsis; alii verò sic decedunt, ut non decedat ipsorum iniustitia, sed cum ipsis semper maneat haereatque. Priores electi sunt, posteriores reprobi & damnati: Priores in iudicio absoluentur & consistent, prout hic iam absoluti sunt; posteriores verò nunquam. Nihil ex ambiguo sequitur.
units.tr: 12. Ibid. For those who depart from here in unrighteousness will certainly not be acquitted in judgment.] This is ambiguous. All men depart in unrighteousness, except Christ, who is not a man free from sin by nature, and who knew no sin in himself (1 Peter 2). But there are two classes of them. For some depart in unrighteousness in such a way that the unrighteousness also departs from them; but others depart in such a way that their unrighteousness does not depart, but always remains and clings to them. The former are the elect, the latter the reprobate and damned. The former will be acquitted in judgment and will stand, just as they are already acquitted here; the latter never. Nothing follows from the ambiguity.

units.la: 13 Art. 9. sed tamen sequi secundum regulam prudentiae, ] quasi verò Dialecticorum regulae à regula prudentiae differant. & quaenam sunt regulae prudentiae, nisi λογικῆς, cuius Organū auctores tradiderunt distinctionem itaque negamus.
units.tr: 13. Art. 9. But yet it follows by the rule of prudence,] As if the rules of the dialecticians differed from the rule of prudence! And what are the rules of prudence, except those of logic, whose instrument the authors have handed down? So we deny the distinction.

units.la: 14 Ibid. quia alioqui faceremus Dominum ineptissimè loquutum. ] negamus sequi. Nam contrà prudentiae lex est in dicendo duplex; nempe ut simplicia efferantur simpliciter, generatim, ac velut incuriosius; & ut ea quae vehementiam & motum desiderant efferantur aggesto sermone, singulari enumeratione, & accuratione emphatica: prout hic fecit Dominus, grauem denunciationem grauiter exaggeras, & adversus omnes tergiversationes circumuniens prudentissimè. Quapropter sequentia nihil ad causam. vide plura infrà cap. 10. nota 44.
units.tr: 14. Ibid. For otherwise we would make the Lord speak most inepty.] We deny that it follows. For in speaking, the law of prudence is twofold: namely, that simple matters be stated simply, in general terms, and rather carelessly; and that matters which call for vehemence and feeling be stated with an accumulated discourse, a particular enumeration, and an emphatic precision. This is what the Lord has done here, most prudently heightening a grave denunciation gravely and encircling every evasion. Therefore what follows has nothing to do with the case. See more below in chapter 10, note 44.

units.la: 15 Ibid. non autem loqueretur inepte, si diceret, neque in aula Hispaniæ, neque in aula Brabantiæ.] atqui plane eadem hic loquutio est: non remittetur ei, sive non est ei remissurus Deus neque in hoc seculo, neque in futuro, id est, nec in terra, nec in cœlo; vel nec hic, nec illic: quia videlicet utrobique iudicat & præstat remissionē Deus. Quamobrem ineptit Bellarminus, quum alterum illud exemplum ineptum adfert, neque in aula Hispaniæ, neque in aula Franciæ, quia non regnabat Philippus in utraque aula, Deus autem regnat in utroque seculo, & remittit pro bona voluntate sua. Ex dispari quid concludas?
units.tr: 15. Ibid. But he would not speak foolishly if he said, neither in the court of Spain nor in the court of Brabant.] Yet this is plainly the same way of speaking: it will not be forgiven to him, or God will not forgive him, neither in this age nor in the future, that is, neither on earth nor in heaven; or neither here nor there, because God clearly judges and grants remission in both. Therefore Bellarmine is wrong when he brings forward that other example, which is itself inept, neither in the court of Spain nor in the court of France, because Philip did not reign in both courts, whereas God reigns in both ages and grants remission according to his good pleasure. What do you conclude from a dissimilar case?

units.la: 16. Ibid. Non bene sequi ex negativo affirmativum, sed approbavit.] Dissimile: nam hæc negatio est categorica, & adversativam hanc categoricam sua vi continet, regnum meum non est de hoc mundo, sed de mundo seculove altero in quo iustitia habi-tat:illa vero quæ agitur, copulatiua est, negans de u-troque seculo. Inepte facit, qui diversi enunciati eandem esse rationem putat.
units.tr: 16. On the same passage: "It does not follow from a negative to an affirmative, but he has approved it." Dissimilar: for this negation is categorical, and by its own force it contains the categorical adversative, "my kingdom is not of this world," which refers to the other age or world in which righteousness dwells. But the proposition under discussion is copulative, denying the one age and the other alike. He acts foolishly who thinks that a different statement has the same reasoning.

units.la: 17. Ibidem. Proinde non opponuntur sicut se-culum præsens & futurum:] verum id quidem est, non eo modo opponi: sed opponuntur alio modo. Nam oppositionum modus aut est proprius & simplex, aut figuratus & dictus πλαγίως ἢ γνωμικῶς [?], quum aliud per consequens ex alio intelligitur, manente integro oppositionis sensu. Proprie, id est, propriis verbis opponuntur seculum præsens & futurum, evidentibusque: impro-prie vero, id est, figuratis ἀπὸ νεύματος ἢ συνεκδοχῆς [?]. μετωνυμίας verbis, fit seculi praesentis, ubi nunc degi-gi nus, cum inferno oppositio, ubi tum damnati trahendent. Haec vero oppositio non magis inepta est quàm illa Homeri in principio Iliados ἀ, πολλὰς ἰφθίμους ψυχὰς ἄιδι προΐαψεν ἡρώων αὐτοὺς δ' ἐλώρια τεῦχε κύνεσσιν [?], &c. aut illa Virgilij Georgic. 4. nec fertilis illa iuuencis, Nec pecori opportuna seges, nec commoda Bacho, & sexcenta alia.
units.tr: 17. On the same passage: "Therefore they are not opposed as the present age and the future." This is true, that they are not opposed in that way; but they are opposed in another way. For the mode of opposition is either proper and simple, or figurative and called by the Greek term indirect or by way of gnome, when one thing is understood by consequence from another while the sense of the opposition remains intact. The present age and the future are opposed properly, that is, in proper words and plainly; but improperly, that is, by figurative expressions of metonymy or synecdoche, the opposition of the present age, in which we now live, is set against hell, where the damned then dwell. This opposition is no more absurd than that of Homer at the beginning of the Iliad, "many mighty souls he sent to Hades, heroes, and made them a prey for dogs," etc., or that of Virgil in the fourth Georgic, "nor is that land fertile for cattle, nor a crop suited to the herd, nor fit for Bacchus," and countless other examples.

units.la: 18 Art. II. non debere exponi Matthaeum per Marcum, sed potius Marcum per Matthaeum. falsum. Nam alter est interpres alterius promiscuè pro ratione locorum: praesertim vero posterior est interpres prioris, ut Marcus est posterior Matthaeo. Quod autem Matthaeus dixit μεγαλοφυῶς[?], id simpliciter Marcus expositum, nunquam.
units.tr: 18. Article 2. "Matthew ought not to be explained by Mark, but rather Mark by Matthew." False. For each is the interpreter of the other, indiscriminately, according to the circumstances of the passages; especially the later is the interpreter of the earlier, as Mark is later than Matthew. But that Matthew said something magnificently, Mark never simply expounded it.

units.la: 19 Ibid. et constat Matthaeum copiosius scripsisse, non sequitur, ergo evidenti rem esse illius sermonem & interpretamentum alterius: nam saepe quoque vsurpat ut brevitas copiam superet evidentia, prout est huius aut illius sermo facilis. Contingens est propositio, & particularis, quae iustam efficere argumentationem non poterit.
units.tr: 19. On the same passage: "and it is agreed that Matthew wrote more fully," does not follow: therefore the thing is clearly his discourse and the explanation of the other. For he often also uses brevity, so that evidence surpasses fullness, as this or that discourse is easy. The proposition is contingent and particular, and will not be able to produce a valid argument.

units.la: 20 Ibid. & Marcum fecisse quasi compendium ex Evangelio Matthaei. Inconsequens: nam suam quoque euidentiam habent compendia. Tum bene est, compendium esse affirmamus: ergo quod abundantius Matthaeus dixerat, non remittetur ei, neque in hoc neque in futuro seculo, compendiosè Marcus enunciauit dicens, nunquam remittetur, vel non remittetur in seculum. Imò verò, vtut compendium dicatur esse, Marcus apertis verbis ἐξηγεῖται[?], quum addit, sed reus aeternae damnationis futurus est.
units.tr: 20. On the same passage: "and Mark made, as it were, a summary of the Gospel of Matthew." Inconsistent: for summaries also have their own clarity. Then, granting that it is a summary, what Matthew had said more fully, "it shall not be forgiven him, neither in this world nor in the world to come," Mark stated in brief, saying "it shall never be forgiven," or "it shall not be forgiven for ever." Indeed, however it is called a summary, Mark explains it in plain words when he adds, "but he is liable to eternal damnation."

units.la: 21 Ibid. Marcus autem proprie pro toto spatio huius seculi seculi & futuri. ] Illudit Bellarminus argutiis. Non est nescius eas voces quæ indistincte enunciantur & sonant per se, distingui pro subiecti, aut prædicati, aut adiunctorum modo. Sic quum Scriptura dicit in seculum, aut æternitatem absolute sonat, vbi res diuinæ aguntur, aut æternitatem secundum quid, id est, modo rei illius quæ agitur respondentem. Quum igitur dicebat Petrus, non lauabis mihi pedes in seculum, agit de seculo vel vita sua, acsi diceret, dum viuam: quum autem dicit Marcus, non remittetur in seculum, agit de seculo Dei, quod seculum κατα[?] χρηστικῶς[?] dictum nihil aliud est quam æternitas. Fallit igitur disputator ἀλλ᾽ τὸ κυρίως λεγόμενον[?].
units.tr: 21. On the same passage: "But Mark properly, for the whole space of this age," of the age and the future. Bellarmine plays with subtleties. He is not unaware that words which are uttered indistinctly and sound of themselves are distinguished according to their role as subject, predicate, or adjuncts. Thus when Scripture says "for ever," it sounds absolutely, of eternity, where divine matters are treated; or it sounds of eternity in a qualified sense, that is, corresponding to the mode of the matter being treated. Therefore when Peter said, "you shall never wash my feet," he speaks of the age or his life, as if he said, while I live; but when Mark says, "it shall not be forgiven for ever," he speaks of the age of God, which age, taken in an approved sense, is nothing other than eternity. The disputant therefore is mistaken, but what is properly said is...

units.la: 22. Ibid. Indicauit in alio seculo dimitti aliqua peccata. ] De antecedente disiunctiua nihil opus est laboremus, quia inanis est per se, nec aliter quàm inanibus coniecturis quicquam affirmari potest de ea. Hæc autem disiunctiua adæquè falsa est, aut ineptè exponi à Matthæo verba Christi, aut indicari peccatorum remissionem in alio seculo fieri. Prius non est verum: nam Matthæum dicemus verba Christi exposuisse ἐμφατικῶς[?] apposita enumeratione, quemadmodum Virgilius non ineptè cecinit Georgic. 1. Tum Sol pallentes haud vnquam discutit vmbras: Nec cum inuectus equis altum petit æthera, nec cum Præcipitem Oceani rubro lauit æquore currum. &c similia. Posterius non esse verum supra inde ab articulo 8. & nota 13. satis superque ostendimus.
units.tr: 22. On the same passage: "He indicated that some sins are forgiven in another age." Nothing need be laboured on the disjunctive antecedent, because it is empty in itself, and nothing can be affirmed about it except by empty conjectures. But this disjunctive is equally false: either Matthew explained the words of Christ absurdly, or it is shown that the remission of sins takes place in another age. The former is not true: for we shall say that Matthew explained the words of Christ emphatically, by an apposite enumeration, just as Virgil sang not absurdly in the first Georgic, "Then the sun never dispels the pale shadows, nor when carried on horses it seeks the high heaven, nor when it bathes its headlong chariot in the red sea of Ocean," and similar things. The latter is not true, as we have sufficiently and more than sufficiently shown above, from article 8 and note 13 onwards.

units.la: 23. Art. 12. Neque Marcus phrasi Hebraica vtitur, sed proprie loquitur. ] Vtrumque falsum. Nam Matthæum phrasi Hebraica vti, quum ait, neque in hoc seculo, neque in futuro, & Paraphrasçon Chaldaicarum, quæ sunt vetustissimæ, & perpetuus Hebræorum vsus ostédit העולם הזה ואת העולם הבא [?] id est, seculum hoc seculúmque futurum passim nominantium [illegible, ~9 letters]. Inoleuit autem hæc phrasis maximè, ex quo Sadducæi orti sunt, qui rationem alterius illius seculi totam expungebant, vt expressa hac distinctione veré atque emphaticé tæter illorum error repercuteretur vsitata hac loquendi formula, quemadmodum & infidelium in Gentibus. Sic enim in testamento nouo seruata fuit hæc oppositio, quum apud Iudæos diceretur, Marc. 10.30. Luc. 18.30.& 20.34. itémque apud Ethnicos, Ephef. 1.21. nihil tam fuit translatitium, quàm istud est.
units.tr: 23. Article 12. "Mark does not use a Hebrew phrase, but speaks properly." Both false. For that Matthew uses a Hebrew phrase, when he says, "neither in this age nor in the future," and the Chaldee paraphrases, which are most ancient, and the constant usage of the Hebrews show it, [calling] "this age and the age to come" [העולם הזה ואת העולם הבא], that is, this age and the future age, by those who name them everywhere, [illegible]. This phrase became especially established from the time when the Sadducees arose, who wholly denied the account of that other age; so that by this distinction being expressed, their foul error might be truly and emphatically repelled by this customary formula of speech, just as also the unbelief of the Gentiles. For in the New Testament this opposition was preserved in this way, when it is said among the Jews, Mark 10:30, Luke 18:30 and 20:34, and likewise among the Gentiles, Ephesians 1:21. Nothing was so commonplace as that.

units.la: Marcum verò non esse vsum phrasi Hebraica disputator non negaret, nisi cæco contradicendi studio raperetur. Nam illud Petri, in æternum siue in seculum, Ioan. 13. Hebraicam esse loquutionem confessus est: eandem adhibuit Marcus. tam hic profes[?]so Hebræa phrasi vsus est, quàm magister ipsius Petrus. Quòd si dicat quisquam Petrum de temporaria æternitate loqui, Marcum non item, nugas agit: nam vtrumque Hebraicum est, & Hebraica ratione dicitur, quam supra nota 21. ostendimus.
units.tr: But the disputant would not deny that Mark did not use a Hebrew phrase, unless he were carried away by a blind zeal for contradiction. For Peter's words, "for ever," or "into the age," John 13, he admitted to be a Hebrew expression: Mark used the same. Here the teacher, Peter himself, used a Hebrew phrase no less than his own master did. But if anyone should say that Peter speaks of a temporary eternity and Mark does not, he is talking nonsense: for both are Hebrew and are spoken in the Hebrew manner, which we showed above in note 21.

units.la: Sed cur in hac nona solutione omisit disputator alteram phrasim Hebraicam à tribus Euangelistis in argumento hoc vsurpatam? Non est enim (opinor) nescius Hebræum sermonem adeò euphemismo & suauitati studere, vt res pronunciatu vel auditu duras [illegible, ~6 letters] enunciet: vt exempli causa, non erit innocens, perinde est ac si dixeris, condemnabitur: non habebit innocentem, perinde atque condemnabit. Exod. 20. non remittet, sed puniet; non remittetur, id est, punietur.
units.tr: But why in this ninth solution did the disputant omit the other Hebrew phrase, used in this matter by the three Evangelists? For (I suppose) he is not unaware that the Hebrew language so greatly favours euphemism and gentleness, that it states harsh things in softer terms, in pronunciation or hearing: for example, "he will not be innocent" is the same as if you said, "he will be condemned"; "he will not hold him innocent" is the same as "he will condemn him." Exodus 20: "he will not forgive," but will punish; "it will not be forgiven," that is, he will be punished.

units.la: Proinde quum Christus ita loquutus est, lenioribus verbis pronunciauit sententiam acerbis-
units.tr: Therefore when Christ spoke in this way, he pronounced in gentler words the most bitter sentence,

units.la: [The last word of this line is printed in heavier type and is partly lost in the scan.] simam, eos qui ita blasphemauerint, punitum iri cum in hoc, tum vero (quod grauius) in venturo seculo, nec vnquam aut vsquam effugituros seuerum iudicium Dei. Atque haec verissima erit illius loci interpretatio. Quicquid ergo ex hoc loco arguentur Pontificij, vel eo nomine peccant, qui iod proprias conclusiones volunt astruere ex figurato loquendi modo. Ad alia veniamus.
units.tr: [The last word of this line is printed in heavier type and is partly lost in the scan.] that those who have so blasphemed would be punished both in this age and, what is more grievous, in the age to come, and would never and nowhere escape the severe judgment of God. And this will be the truest interpretation of that passage. Whatever the Papists therefore argue from this passage, they err on this account, who wish to establish proper conclusions from a figurative mode of speaking. Let us come to other matters.

units.la: IN CAPVT V.
units.tr: IN CHAPTER V.

units.la: 1. Art. 1. Ex eo statuunt [Catholici duo Ecclesiastica dogmata, Purgatorium, & venialia peccata] Negamus tum haec esse Ecclesiastica dogmata, vt vide ur Pontificiis, tum verbis Apostoli 1. Cor. 3. confirmari.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. From this they establish [the Catholics' two ecclesiastical dogmas, Purgatory and venial sins] We deny both that these are ecclesiastical dogmas, as the Papists seem to think, and that they are confirmed by the words of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 3.

units.la: 2. Art. 2. Idem repetit quaest. 1. ad Dulcitium. Difficilem esse agnoscimus, non in se (nam verbum lucis est) sed nobis in luce adhuc caecutientibus, ac ferme gestientibus lucem videre solum.
units.tr: 2. Art. 2. He repeats the same in question 1 to Dulcitius. We acknowledge that it is difficult, not in itself (for it is the word of light), but for us, who are still dimly sighted in the light and almost eager merely to see the light.

units.la: 3. Art. 4. Vtitur Apostolus in hac sententia similitudine duorum Architectorum, imo duorum operariorum, quorum vnus est ἀρχιτέκτων, architectus siue architecton: alter vero τέκτων ἐποικοδομῶν, structor superaedificans fundamento quod ille posuit. Hoc se velle docet Apostolus claris verbis. Hic primus Bellarmini error.
units.tr: 3. Art. 4. The Apostle uses in this sentence the likeness of two architects, or rather of two workmen, of whom one is an architect [ἀρχιτέκτων], and the other a builder [τέκτων ἐποικοδομῶν], a structor who builds upon the foundation that the first has laid. The Apostle teaches clearly that this is what he means. Here is Bellarmine's first error.

units.la: 4. Ibid. Alter vero super simile fundamentum, secundus error: non enim super simile fundamentum aedificare dicitur operarius, sed super vnum & idem. Nam nemo potest fundamentum aliud (ἄλλον, non ἀλλοῖον) statuere praeter id quod positum est, quod est Iesus Christus. Quod si quis superaedificet super hoc fundamentum, ἐπὶ τῷ θεμελίῳ [?] &c. vnum dicit fundam[?] mentum numero,non autem differens.1.Cor.3.ver-su 11.&12.
units.tr: 4. Ibid. But the other upon a similar foundation, is his second error: a workman is not said to build upon a similar foundation, but upon one and the same. For no one can lay another foundation [ἄλλον, not ἀλλοῖον, a different kind] besides the one that has been laid, which is Jesus Christ. But if anyone builds upon this foundation [ἐπὶ τῷ θεμελίῳ] etc., the Apostle calls it one foundation in number, not one differing in kind. 1 Cor. 3:11–12.

units.la: 5. Ibid. Eámque tegit fœno & stipulis. ] Non hoc solùm modo,sed quocunque modo inani atque periturò parietes fornaceos,stramineos,cratitios,congestos tumultuariè,denique materia aut forma alienaconstructos,& tecta œdificio Dei fecundùm materiam aut formam indigna significat. Iste est itaque tertius Bellarmini error.
units.tr: 5. Ibid. and covers it with hay and straw. He signifies not only this, but any way at all that is empty and perishable: walls of furnace-brick, of straw, of wattle, heaped up in a disorderly way; in short, anything built of material or form foreign to the foundation, and a roof unworthy of God's building in its material or form. That is therefore Bellarmine's third error.

units.la: 6. Art.5. & breui tempore totam consumi, ] aut partem illius,id est opus quodcunque in ea domo fuerit ex ligno,fœno,stipula concinnatum.De sequentibus suo loco videbitur.
units.tr: 6. Art. 5. and in a short time all is consumed, or a part of it, that is, whatever work in that house has been made of wood, hay or straw. What follows will be considered in its place.

units.la: 7. Art. 7. Omnes superædificare super fidei fundamentum vel opera bona, vel mala. ] aliud est proprie interpretari locum, aliud exponere analogica accommodatione atque alludere. Non interpretatur illic Augustinus Paulum,sed tantùm ex analogia operariorum & administrorum Dei ratiocinatur de singulis Christianis, qui etiam pro sua conditione quisquè operantur Deo.
units.tr: 7. Art. 7. All build upon the foundation of faith either good works or bad. It is one thing to interpret a passage properly, and another to expound it by an analogical application and to allude to it. Augustine does not interpret Paul there, but only reasons, from the analogy of workmen and the ministers of God, about individual Christians, each of whom works for God according to his own condition.

units.la: 8.Art.8. Architectos hīc ab Apostolo non vocari,n. ] non agit Apostolus hoc loco de architectis solùm, sed τῶν οἰκοδομῶν[?], de structoribus quibusuis & administris Dei in Ecclesia ipsius : vt nota 3. ostendimus.
units.tr: 8. Art. 8. Here the Apostle is not calling architects, The Apostle in this place speaks not only of architects, but of builders [τῶν οἰκοδομῶν], of builders of every kind and of the ministers of God in his Church, as we showed in note 3.

units.la: 9. Art.9. Vtraque expositio est bona, ] sed hæc primaria & propria, illa secundaria & accommodata longiùs per quandam analogiam, ex qua nihil tamen necessariò possis concludere. Sequentia negamus, vt nota 1.de assertione Purgatorij & peccatorum venialium.
units.tr: 9. Art. 9. Both expositions are good, but this one is primary and proper, the other secondary and accommodated more remotely by a certain analogy, from which, however, you can necessarily conclude nothing. We deny the consequences, as in note 1 on the assertion of Purgatory and venial sins.

units.la: 10. Art. II. Quia Apostolus dicit,Salvus erit quasi pe[?] perignem. Hæc ratio non est necessaria, vt postea videbimus. Verumtamen de re conuenit.
units.tr: 10. Art. 11. Because the Apostle says, He will be saved, yet as through fire. This argument is not necessary, as we shall see later. Nevertheless, we agree on the matter itself.

units.la: Hæc propositio est quidem verissima: sed assumptio falsa, nimirum salutis nomen in malam partem ab iis accipi qui ita exponunt, saluus[?] erit, id est, nunquam penitus consumetur. Nam cùm salutis duæ sint partes, vindicatio à malo atque interitu, & boni vitæque communicatio: nomine salutis aut vtraque pars intelligitur pro prie, aut altera solùm [illegible, ~9 letters]. Viderunt hoc Hebraei interpretes, qui plurimis in locis feruandi verbum interpretati sunt vindicare à malo, aut etiam opem vindicando ferre. Sed hæc nihil ad nos, qui non hæremus isti Græcorum interpretationi.
units.tr: This proposition is indeed most true, but the assumption is false, namely that those who explain it thus take the name of salvation in a bad sense: he will be saved, that is, will never be utterly destroyed. For since salvation has two parts, deliverance from evil and destruction, and the communication of good and of life, by the name of salvation either both parts are understood properly, or the other alone [illegible, about nine letters]. The Hebrew interpreters saw this, who in very many places rendered the verb "to keep" as "to deliver from evil," or even "to bring help by delivering." But these things are nothing to us, who do not cling to that Greek translation.

units.la: hanc interpretationem postea difficultate 5. (vt Bellarminus distinguit) confutabimus.
units.tr: We will refute this interpretation later, in difficulty 5 (as Bellarmine distinguishes it).

units.la: sic ab omnibus negamus intelligi, & negamus proprie intelligi: licet analogicè extendatur quodammodo interpretatio.
units.tr: We deny that it is understood in this way by everyone, and we deny that it is understood properly, although the interpretation is in some measure extended by analogy.

units.la: Negamus Chrysostomum vllam Purgatorij meminisse. Priore loco hoc tantum dicit, mortuos deflendos esse qui in peccatis sunt mortui, & omnia pietatis officia erga eos atque pro eis occupanda, dum hic viuentes sunt mortui: qui verò piè sunt mortui, eorum memoriam piè colendam atque prosequendam. Sed hæc duo Bellarminus confundit imprudens, vt infrà cap. 10. & lib.2.cap.15. & sequentibus demonstrabimus. fteriore nihil dicit amplius:sed tantum explicat regulam quam statim proposuerat in principio orationis suæ his verbis:lugeamus peccatores non tantum defunctos,verum & viuentes : de iustis autem gaudeamus,non modò superstitibus , verum & mortuis. Hoc homiliæ totius argumentum. de Purgatorio ne γῶ [?] quidem.
units.tr: We deny that Chrysostom mentions any Purgatory. In the earlier passage he says only that the dead who are dead in sins are to be mourned, and that all the offices of piety towards them, and on their behalf, are to be undertaken while those who are living here are dead; but those who have died in piety are to have their memory honoured and pursued with piety. But Bellarmine rashly confuses these two things, as we shall show below in chapter 10 and in book 2, chapter 15 and following. In the latter passage he says nothing further, but only explains the rule which he had at once laid down at the beginning of his discourse in these words: Let us mourn the sinners, not only when they are dead, but also while they live; but let us rejoice over the righteous, not only when they survive, but also when they are dead. This is the argument of the whole homily. Not even a word about Purgatory.

units.la: 15. Ibid. Peccata venialia concedit Homil. 24 in Matth. ]Et nos concedimus esse piis venialia, sed longe diuersa mente,vt tomo 4. videbitur.non aliter in eo loco dicit Chrysostomus.
units.tr: 15. Ibid. He concedes venial sins in Homily 24 on Matthew. We too concede that there are venial sins in the pious, but with a very different meaning, as will be seen in volume 4. Chrysostom says nothing different in that place.

units.la: 16. Art. 13. & commenta, quæ pugnant cum verbo Dei.]vel potius (vt dicamus paucis) πολλῶν κενῶν ἐπι-λογισμῶν [?], omnem inanem structuram præter verbum Dei impositam fundamento vero,tum quæ curiosa, inutilis,superuacanea, tum vero quæ adulterina,aut falsa,aut damnosa quocunque modo. Quamobrem hæc interpretatio optimam sextæ sententiæ partem complectitur,quam post disputator probat. Nam Caluini , aliorumque sententiam hic refert angu-stius.
units.tr: 16. Art. 13. and inventions, which are contrary to the word of God. Or rather, to say it in a few words, of many empty reasonings: every vain structure laid upon the true foundation apart from the word of God, both what is curious, useless and superfluous, and what is adulterated, false or harmful in any way. Wherefore this interpretation embraces the best part of the sixth opinion, which the disputant afterwards proves. For he reports the opinion of Calvin and others here in a narrower form.

units.la: 17. Artic. 14. Quia hæretici non seruantur per ignem purgatorium , ] Primum non sequitur ex falsa loci interpretatione , quam difficultate 5. confutabimus. deinde nec sequitur ex particulari : nam hæreticum nullum seruari , aut omnem seruari, falsum est, quosdam vero seruari, & quosdam non seruari (nimirum eos qui non retinent caput,Coloss.2.19.)verisimum.vide contro.4. lib.3. cap.4.
units.tr: 17. Art. 14. Because heretics are not saved through purgatorial fire. First, this does not follow from the false interpretation of the passage, which we shall refute in difficulty 5. Second, it does not follow even from the particular case: for it is false that no heretic is saved, or that every heretic is saved; but that some are saved and some are not (namely those who do not hold fast the head, Col. 2:19), is true. See controversy 4, book 3, chapter 4.

units.la: 18 Ibid. hæretici non ædificant super fundamentum, quod est Christus, nisi nomine tenus. ] de his, verum;de illis,falsum: inconsequens ex particulari, vt modò dicebamus.eadem ratio sequentium.
units.tr: 18. Ibid. Heretics do not build upon the foundation, which is Christ, except in name only. Of these it is true; of those it is false: an inconsequence drawn from the particular, as we were just saying. The same reasoning applies to what follows.

units.la: 19 Ibid.eiusmodi Doctores saluos futuros per ignem purgatorium.] Ambrosius de doctoribus vanæ & corruptę doctrinæ(sic enim vocat)loquitur promissione: de igne autem Purgatorij in futuro sæculo,nullum verbum.
units.tr: 19. Ibid. Such teachers will be saved through purgatorial fire. Ambrose speaks of teachers of vain and corrupt doctrine (for so he calls them) with a promise; but about the fire of Purgatory in the future age, not a word.

units.la: 20 Ibid.quidam autem, inquit, hæc de hæreticis intelligunt, &c.]satis est, quòd hæc ab Hieronymo iuxta tropologiam(vt ipse loquitur adducta sunt.
units.tr: 20. Ibid. But some, he says, understand these things of heretics, etc. It is enough that these things were adduced by Jerome according to tropology, as he himself says.

units.la: 21 Art.15.ita B. Augustinus lib. de fide & operibus. cap. 16.] verba Augustini adduci oportebat, non detorqueri. Sic exponere Augustinum, & de operibus supererogationis quicquam negamus dicere. Consulatur locus: est enim longior, quàm vt hic exscribi possit. Quapropter sententiam illam veram negamus esse, & quæ ex ea nectuntur sequentibus.
units.tr: 21. Art. 15. So Blessed Augustine, book On Faith and Works, chapter 16. The words of Augustine ought to have been quoted, not twisted. To expound Augustine in this way, we deny that he says anything about works of supererogation. Let the passage be consulted: it is longer than can be copied out here. Wherefore we deny that that sentence is true, and that what is drawn from it in what follows is true.

units.la: 22 Art. 16. qua bona est, sed alia est melior.] bona, id est, minimè mala: verumtamen non est huius loci propria, sed tantùm accommodata per quamdam analogiam petitam longiùs, vt supra nota 7.distinximus.
units.tr: 22. Art. 16. which is good, but another is better. Good, that is, by no means bad; yet it is not proper to this passage, but only applied by a certain analogy drawn from further afield, as we distinguished in note 7 above.

units.la: 23 Art.18. qui primi in aliqua regione fidem prædicant, dicuntur Apostoli eius regionis.]sed æquiuoca est appellatio, quæ ad solos illos Apostolos ἀποστόλους pertinet qui Christum viderunt in carne, & mandata ab eo acceperunt.
units.tr: 23. Art. 18. Those who first preach the faith in some region are called the apostles of that region. But the appellation is equivocal: it pertains only to those apostles [ἀποστόλους] who saw Christ in the flesh and received commands from him.

units.la: 24 Ibid. non quidem hæretica vel mala, sed tamen curiosa, inutilis, superuacanea] nos vtrumque doctrinæ genus simul comprehendi affirmamus, vt nota 16. antè monuimus. Quæ autem sequuntur de merito & de peccatis venialibus, in tomo 4. videntur. ita B.Augustinus libro de fide & operibus, cap. 16.] ignem doloris Augustinus vocat, idque diuerso aliquantum sensu. Sed non mora-mur ista.
units.tr: 24. Ibid. not indeed heretical or evil, but nevertheless curious, useless, superfluous. We affirm that both kinds of doctrine are comprehended together, as we warned earlier in note 16. What follows about merit and venial sins is seen in volume 4. So Blessed Augustine, in book On Faith and Works, chapter 16, calls it "the fire of grief," and in a somewhat different sense. But we will not linger on these matters.

units.la: ex quo apparet certum quemdam & definitum diem significari,] Conceditur, nisi dies hic dicatur aequiuoce, aut indefinite: aequiuoce, pro luce quae noctì atque tenebris eius opponitur: indefinite vero siue per emphasin, pro eo quod est dies ipse, id est tempus reuelans omnia, vt vulgo dici solet. quo sensu olim Pindarus, ἡμέραι δ' ἐπίλοιποι μάρτυρες ζοφώντες [?], siue tralatione ex re forensi sumpta, pro eo quod est dies cognitionis legitimae & iudicij in Ecclesia per Spiritum ex verbo ipsius. Sic enim postea Apostolus ἀνθρώπινον ἡμέραν diem humanum vocat, 1.Cor.4.3. Ego interpretationem aequiuocam magis probo, vt nomine ἡμέρας diei intelligatur φῶς, lux, de qua Apostolus Ephes.5.13. lux Christi faciens omnia nobis manifesta, nimirum verbo & Spiritu suo, qui vere praelucens ignis est.
units.tr: Whence it appears that a certain and definite day is signified, It is granted, unless this day is said equivocally or indefinitely: equivocally, for the light that is opposed to night and its darkness; indefinitely, or by emphasis, for what is the day itself, that is, the time that reveals all things, as is commonly said. In this sense Pindar once wrote of days remaining as shadowy witnesses [ἡμέραι δ' ἐπίλοιποι μάρτυρες ζοφώντες]; or else by a figure taken from legal affairs, for the day of lawful knowledge and judgment in the Church, through the Spirit, from his word. For afterwards the Apostle calls it "human day," 1 Cor. 4:3. I prefer the equivocal interpretation more, so that by the name of day is understood light [φῶς], of which the Apostle speaks in Eph. 5:13: the light of Christ, making all things manifest to us, namely by his word and his Spirit, who is truly a shining fire.

units.la: aliud est pronomen ἐπιδεικτικόν, οὗτος [?], quo Paulus vtitur 2.Tim. in his tribus locis cap.1. & 4. aliud articulus ὁ. Illic semper ἐκεῖνο τῆς ἡμέρας vocat cum demonstratione; hic vero cum emphasi & citra demonstrationem. Ex diuerso nihil sequitur. Nec refert, quòd ὁ vel τῆς accipitur nonnunquam ἐπιδεικτικῶς. nos-enim huic loco negamus conuenire; & probamus vel eo argumento, quòd tantopere variant auctores in eius interpretatione. Quod si ἐπιδεικτικῶς accipitur, vt fit, tum vero ἡ ἡμέρα & ἐκείνη ἡμέρα differunt vt hic dies & ille dies: prius de praesente aut propinquo, posterius de absente aut longinquo e-nunnunciatur. sic enim dies hic illi quàm rectissimè opponitur.
units.tr: The demonstrative pronoun οὗτος [?] is one thing, and it is the pronoun Paul uses in 2 Timothy in these three places, chapters 1 and 4. The article ὁ is another. There he always calls it "that day" [ἐκεῖνο τῆς ἡμέρας] with demonstration, but here with emphasis and without demonstration. Nothing follows from the contrary. Nor does it matter that ὁ or τῆς is sometimes taken demonstratively, for we deny that this fits this passage, and we prove it by this argument, that the interpreters vary so greatly in explaining it. But if it is taken demonstratively, as it is, then "the day" [ἡ ἡμέρα] and "that day" [ἐκείνη ἡμέρα] differ as this day and that day do. The former is said of the present or near, the latter of the absent or distant. For in this way "this day" is most correctly set against "that day."

units.la: 28 Art.24. præsens tempus non dicitur in Scripturis dies Domini, sed dies nostra, ] aut etiam hic vel hæc dies, sicut contrà tempus alterius vitæ ac potius iudicij magni dicitur dies Domini vel dies ille oppositione euidentissima, ut proximè dicebamus.
units.tr: 28 Art.24. The present time is not called in Scripture the day of the Lord, but our day, ] or even "this day," and so on, just as, on the contrary, the time of the other life, or rather of the great judgment, is called the day of the Lord, or "that day," by the most evident contrast, as we were just saying.

units.la: 29 Art. 26. posse intelligi de tempore futuro post hanc vitam. ] atqui Augustinus non tantum posse exponi dicit, sed affirmatè exponit diem doloris lib.de fide & operibus,& in Enchiridio ad Laurentium, siue diem tribulationis, lib. 21. de ciuit. Dei, cap.26. dies enim, inquit, Domini declarabit: dies vtique tribulationis, quoniam in igne, inquit, reuelabitur. Eand[?]que tribulationem ignem vocat, &c. sic non obscurè hanc interpretationem illi alteri de die iudicij anteponit.
units.tr: 29 Art. 26. It can be understood of future time after this life. ] Yet Augustine not only says it can be explained so, but expressly explains "the day of sorrow" in his book on faith and works, and in the Enchiridion to Laurence, or "the day of tribulation," in book 21 of The City of God, chapter 26: for the day, he says, of the Lord will declare it: the day, that is, of tribulation, since it will be revealed, he says, in fire. He also calls that tribulation fire, and so on. Thus he plainly prefers this interpretation to that other one about the day of judgment.

units.la: 30 Art.28. quorum mihi videtur verissima sententia, ] nos negamus,& rationes confutabimus.
units.tr: 30 Art.28. Of which the most true opinion seems to me ] We deny this, and we will refute the arguments.

units.la: 31 Artic. 29. vbique in Scripturis dies Domini significat diem vltimi iudicij. ] Falsum. dicitur etiam de die visitationum iudiciorumque particularium in hac ipsa vita, idque apud Prophetas frequentissimè, vt Esai.2.12. & 13.6. & 9.Ezech.13. 5. & 30.3.Ioel 1.15. & 2 11. Amos 5.18. & 20. Abdi.15. Sopho.1.7. & 14. Sed & diem Dominicum Ioannes Apoc.1.10. appellauit quid ergo consequaris, mi homo, antecedente falso?
units.tr: 31 Artic. 29. Everywhere in Scripture the day of the Lord signifies the day of the last judgment. ] False. It is also said of the days of visitations and of particular judgments in this very life, and that very often among the Prophets, as in Isaiah 2:12 and 13:6, Ezekiel 9 and 13:5 and 30:3, Joel 1:15 and 2:11, Amos 5:18 and 20, Obadiah 15, Zephaniah 1:7 and 14. But John also called it "the Lord's day" in Revelation 1:10. So what do you gain, my good man, from a false premise?

units.la: 32 Art. 30. quo designatur vna quædam certa dies, ] hoc ante confutauimus nota 26.
units.tr: 32 Art. 30. By which one certain day is designated. ] We refuted this before, in note 26.

units.la: 33 Art. 31. quia dicit Ἀπόστολος, dies Domini declarabit, ] falsum. verba sunt Apostoli, ἡ γὰρ ἡμέρα [?] dies enim declarabit: vox, Domini, quum interiicitur, glossema adnatum est, ut in editione vulgata: sed hoc glossema non exemplaria Græca, non Syrus, aut Arabs agnoverunt. Sequentia itaque nihil ad quæstionem faciunt: nam Apostolus cap. 4. de præstituto tempore loquitur universè; tum singulari, quo Deus res abditas illustrat ad demonstrationem gloriæ suæ & probationem servorum suorum, quum ipsi visum est; tum universali, quo venturus est ad iudicandum vivos & mortuos, 2. Cor. 5. 10.
units.tr: 33 Art. 31. Because the Apostle says, the day of the Lord will declare it, ] False. The words of the Apostle are for the day will declare it [ἡ γὰρ ἡμέρα δηλώσει]; the word "of the Lord" is an insertion, a gloss that has crept in, as in the Vulgate edition. But the Greek copies, the Syriac, and the Arabic do not acknowledge this gloss. So what follows has nothing to do with the question. For the Apostle, in chapter 4, speaks in general of the appointed time, and in a particular sense, when God makes hidden things clear for the demonstration of his glory and the proving of his servants, when it seems good to himself; and in a universal sense, when he will come to judge the living and the dead, 2 Cor. 5:10.

units.la: 34 Art. 32. quia sequitur: quia in igne revelatur.] non sequitur ex homonymia, mutato prædicatio-nis genere: nam ignem figuratè dictum accipit pro-prie.
units.tr: 34 Art. 32. Because it follows: because it is revealed in fire. ] It does not follow from an ambiguity, by changing the kind of predicate. For he takes "fire," which is said figuratively, in its proper sense.

units.la: 35 Ibid. 2. Petr. 3. elementa ignis ardore tabescent.] hi omnes loci alieni à quæstione sunt: nam agunt aut de splendore gloriæ ipsius maiestatisque divinæ, aut de iudicio universali & ultimo; Apostolus contrà de particulari & antecedente declaratione Dei in Ecclesia sua testimonium dantis doctrinæ servorum suorum in utramvis[?] partem.
units.tr: 35 Ibid. 2 Pet. 3. The elements will melt with the heat of fire. ] All these passages are foreign to the question. For they deal either with the splendour of his glory and divine majesty, or with the universal and final judgment. The Apostle, on the contrary, speaks of the particular and present declaration of God in his Church, which bears witness to the doctrine of his servants, in either direction.

units.la: 36 Ibid. non[?] potest intelligi per hanc diem, nisi dies ultimi iudicij[?]] negatur, & Caietanus recte cum aliis negat, ut dictum ante.
units.tr: 36 Ibid. It cannot be understood by this day, except the day of the last judgment. ] This is denied, and Cajetan rightly denies it with others, as said before.

units.la: 37 Ibid. illa dies erit notissima propter iudicium acerrimum & maximum, quod in illa exercebitur.] Negatur propositio ex falsa interpretatione. Illa enim propositio, ἡ γὰρ ἡμέρα δηλώσει[?], non significat diem illam fore notissimam, ut hic interpretatur; sed potius diem illam effecturam ut innotescat quale sit opus unius cuiusque administri in Ecclesia Dei. Diem autem appellat lucem & vim illius à Spiritu Dei in verbo expositam & suo tempore revelatam, ut Paulus loquitur Philip. 3. de qua optimè Nazianzenus oratione 15.ad patrem & Basilium dixit:d?bilitatem oculorum ,sol, cordis imbecillitatem Deus aduenientes coarguit,& aliis quidem lux,aliis vero ignis est,vnicu- que pro materia & qualitate subiecta.Inanis igitur est hæc disputatoris argumentatio.
units.tr: 37 Ibid. That day will be most notable because of the most severe and greatest judgment which will be carried out in it. ] The proposition is denied, because of a false interpretation. For that proposition, for the day will make it known [ἡ γὰρ ἡμέρα δηλώσει], does not mean that the day will be most notable, as he here interprets it; rather it means that the day will bring it about that the quality of each minister's work in the Church of God becomes known. But he calls the day the light and power of that which is set out by the Spirit of God in the Word and revealed in its time, as Paul speaks in Philippians 3. On this point Nazianzen, in his fifteenth oration to his father and to Basil, said well: The sun reproves the weakness of the eyes, God the weakness of the heart as they approach; and to some it is light, to others fire, according to the matter and the quality of the subject. So this argument of the disputant is empty.

units.la: 38 Art. 33.falsum erit, vt illi qui per ignem transfie- runt.] expositionem istâ negamus:nam dies siue lux & ignis simul sunt, quemadmodum in omni substantia simul sunt forma & formalis actus ipsius:hę res distinctæ, at non separatæ sunt, eóque simul agunt in subiectis omnibus pro ratione ipsorum. In hunc modum fit manifestum opus vniuscuiusque,vt dicit Paulus:nam dies siue lux manifestum facit,quia lux hæc ab igne est, quo reuelatur siue dies & lux illa proprie & immeditatè, siue opus vniuscuiusque mediatè etiam per lucem: nam igne reuelatur illo quem proximè ex Nazianzeno ostendimus.Non sequitur ex æquiuoca acceptione vocis, dies, & ambigua membri totius explicatione.
units.tr: 38 Art. 33. It will be false, as with those who passed through fire. ] We deny this explanation. For the day, or light, and fire are at once together, just as in every substance form and its formal act are together. These things are distinct, yet not separated, and so they act together in all subjects according to their nature. In this way the work of each one is made manifest, as Paul says: for the day, or light, makes it manifest, because this light is from the fire, by which the day, or that light, is revealed, properly and immediately, or the work of each one is revealed mediately too, through the light. For it is revealed by fire, as we showed just above from Nazianzen. It does not follow from an equivocal use of the word "day" and from an ambiguous explanation of the whole clause.

units.la: 39 Art. 34. & iterum postea in vltimo iudicio publicè.] hæc solutio vera esset aduersus Caietanum & alios, si daretur veram esse proximè præcedentem interpretationem: sed ea confutata est, quapropter solutio hæc nihil ad causam.
units.tr: 39 Art. 34. And again afterwards in the last judgment publicly. ] This solution would be true against Cajetan and others, if the interpretation immediately before were granted to be true. But it has been refuted, so this solution has nothing to do with the case.

units.la: 40 Art. 35. quandoquidem noster interpres vertit, reuelabitur.]atqui non ita legit Ambrosius, non interpres Syrus,non exemplaria, non auctores Græci. Vulgatus ille interpres non est instar omnium, nec esse apud bonos debet. Quod autem verbo præsente Apostolus vtitur,id co factum est,quia actum ordinarium ignis illius notādum duxit, vt thesi hypothesis de quibus agitur confirmaret. Morum opus,inquit,igne revelabitur.cur autem ? quia quod revelatur,revelatur igne.
units.tr: 40 Art. 35. Since our translator renders it, will be revealed. ] But Ambrose does not read it so, nor does the Syriac translator, nor the copies, nor the Greek authors. That Vulgate translator is not the equal of all, nor should he be held in esteem among good men. The Apostle's use of the present tense is because he thought it necessary to note the ordinary action of that fire, so as to confirm by the hypothesis the thesis under discussion. The work of morals, he says, will be revealed by fire. Why? Because what is revealed, is revealed by fire.

units.la: 41 Ibid. ut,virum non cognosco,Luc.1.] hoc exem-plum alienum est à regula,& torquetur male: vide interpretationem loci,controu.5.lib.2.cap.22.
units.tr: 41 Ibid. As, I do not know a man, Luke 1. ] This example is foreign to the rule and is wrongly twisted. See the interpretation of the passage, controversy 5, book 2, chapter 22.

units.la: 42 Ibid. intelligunt Paulum de iudicio particu-lari:] eo videlicet quod facit Deus in Ecclesia vi-ventium.
units.tr: 42 Ibid. They understand Paul of the particular judgment: ] that is, of course, what God does in the Church of the living.

units.la: 43 Art.36.quis fit ignis,qui in die Domini uniuscu-iusque opus probabit.] Nos de hac quæstione mini-mè laboramus, tum quia per se expedita est satis, tum quia non est huius loci ex mente Apostoli,sed ex antegressis Bellarmini suppositionibus. Nobis autem secundùm Paulum quæstio esse debet, quis sit ignis,qui die,id est,luce sua vel tempore suo probabit opus uniuscuiusque. Hanc quæstionem absolu-ta hac Bellarmini difficultate expediemus: volen-te Domino.
units.tr: 43 Art. 36. What kind of fire it is, which will prove each one's work in the day of the Lord. ] We do not trouble ourselves at all about this question, both because it is sufficiently settled in itself, and because it does not belong to this place according to the mind of the Apostle, but rather to the earlier suppositions of Bellarmine. But for us, according to Paul, the question ought to be what sort of fire it is which, in the day, that is, by its light or at its time, will prove the work of each one. With the help of the Lord, we will settle this question by answering this difficulty of Bellarmine's.

units.la: 44 Art. 38.de illo qui emendabit eos qui per ignem salvi erunt.] agunt Patres de igne illo castigationis, sive punitivo(ut Basilius vocat supra cap.3.nota 54.) sive purgatorio,quo hic castigantur & emendantur electi Dei. ignem tribulationis Augustinus vocat, lib.21.de civit.Dei,cap.26. Quæ autem hic de futuro Purgatorio & igne illius adtexuntur, germanæ gerræ.
units.tr: 44 Art. 38. Concerning him who will cleanse those who will be saved through fire. ] The Fathers are speaking of that fire of chastisement, or punitive fire (as Basil calls it above, chapter 3, note 54), or purgatorial fire, by which God's elect are here chastised and cleansed. Augustine calls it the fire of tribulation, in book 21 of The City of God, chapter 26. But what is added here about a future Purgatory and its fire is pure nonsense.

units.la: 45 Art.39. non est ignis purgans vel affligens, sed probans & examinans. Est quidem Spiritus Dei ignis probans & examinans:sed hic 1.negamus Paulum de ultimo illo Dei iudicio agere, ut Caietanus & alij. 2. negamus in ultimo illo iudicio probari igne & examinari eos quibus Christus dicturus est, venite benedicti Patris mei, &c. 3. si iste ignis non est purgans & affligens, ergo non est ignis Purgatorij. Quid ergo ad Purgatorij probationē attinet? nam & hic quoque ignis iudicij & probationis diuinæ exercet vim suam, dum viuimus.
units.tr: 45 Art. 39. It is not a cleansing or afflicting fire, but a proving and examining one. ] Indeed the Spirit of God is a proving and examining fire. But here, first, we deny that Paul is speaking of that last judgment of God, as Cajetan and others do. Second, we deny that in that last judgment those to whom Christ will say come, blessed of my Father, etc., are proved and examined by fire. Third, if this fire is not cleansing and afflicting, then it is not the fire of Purgatory. What then has this to do with proving Purgatory? For here too the fire of divine judgment and proving exercises its power, while we live.

units.la: 46 Ibid. ad illos ignes quos transituri sumus, dicat, vide humilitatem meam, &c.] de ignibus fornacis tribulationum Ambrosius loquitur, quos Deus accedit suis exercendis iudicio suo. Demonstrant quod dicimus adiuncta omnia: illa enim interpretatur verba Ecclesiastici 2. Omne quod tibi applicitum fuerit accipe & in dolore sustine, & in humilitate tua patientiam habe: quoniam in igne probatur aurum & argentum, homines vero receptibiles in camino humiliatio nis: siue (vt Ambrosius vertit) homines acceptabiles in fornace humilitatis. quæ verba quisquis ad probationem huius vitæ pertinere non videt, nihil videt.
units.tr: 46 Ibid. to those fires through which we are about to pass, let him say, see my humility, etc.] Ambrose is speaking of the fires of the furnace of tribulations, through which God by his judgment tests his own people. All the surrounding words show what we say. He is explaining the words of Ecclesiasticus 2: Whatever is brought upon you, accept it, and endure it in grief, and have patience in your humiliation; for gold and silver are tried in fire, but acceptable men in the furnace of humiliation, or, as Ambrose translates, acceptable men in the furnace of humility. Whoever does not see that these words concern the testing of this life sees nothing at all.

units.la: 47 Ibid. Lyranus, Caietanus, & alij in hunc locum.] Sedulius de examine iudicij diuini, quod fit in hac vita, loquitur vt Ambrosius: Posteriorum interpretationes, etsi variant, iustas negamus esse.
units.tr: 47 Ibid. Lyranus, Cajetan, and others on this passage.] Sedulius, like Ambrose, speaks of the examination by divine judgment that takes place in this life. Though the later interpretations differ from one another, we deny that they are sound.

units.la: 48 Art.40. non aliter potest intelligi, quomodo ignis probat eos qui aurum & argentum ædificarunt,] falsum: nam ignis Spiritus Dei per verbum etiam in hac vita probat doctrinam seruorum eius; prout Apostolus dicit 1. Cor.14.32. spiritus Prophetarum Prophetis subiici.
units.tr: 48 Art.40. In no other way can it be understood how fire tests those who built with gold and silver.] False. The fire of God's Spirit, working through the word, tests the teaching of his servants even in this life, as the Apostle says in 1 Cor. 14:32: the spirits of the prophets are subject to the prophets.

units.la: 49 Art.41. quia hæc expositio optime conuenit verbis Apostoli,] negamus. Nam & Bellarminus ipse, vt ostendat conuenire, mox incipit ab occupatione: quod certè non fuisset facturus, si optimè conueniret.
units.tr: 49 Art.41. because this explanation agrees very well with the words of the Apostle,] We deny it. Bellarmine himself, to show that it agrees, at once begins with a diversion, which he certainly would not have done if it agreed so well.

units.la: 50 Ibid. tamen non transierunt ab oculis Dei,] imò ne probatio quidem operum aut iudicium, aut præ-mium transfit in oculis Dei, cui omnia sunt præsen-tissima. Agit autem Apostolus de eo quod manet in se reipsa, non de eo quod manet in oculis Dei; ut contrario membro ostenditur τὰ [illegible, ~8 letters]. Non e-nim de opere agit quà ardet, ac detrimentum pati-tur operarius eius in conspectu Dei consilióve i-psius, sed effectu & reipsa in se. Quid hîc Bellarminum iuvat tam frigidè [illegible, ~9 letters], & iocularitèr?
units.tr: 50 Ibid. yet they have not passed from the eyes of God,] Indeed, not even the testing of works, nor judgment, nor reward, passes from the eyes of God, to whom all things are most present. But the Apostle is speaking of what remains in itself in reality, not of what remains in the eyes of God, as the contrasting clause shows [τὰ, illegible]. For he is not speaking of the work as it burns, and its worker suffers loss in the sight or counsel of God, but of the outcome and the reality itself. What does Bellarmine gain here by such a cold and jesting [illegible]?

units.la: 51. Ibid. Cuncta quæ fiunt adducet Deus in iudicium,] Hæc de omni cognitione & iudicio Dei pronun-ciavit Sapiens promiscuè tam in hac quàm in futura vita: nullam videlicet impietatem aut ἀπ' ἑαυτοῦ sive hîc (ubi exercet castigátque suos) sive illic, ubi iudiciorum divinorum est consummatio, effugere cognitionem Dei aut iudicium posse: quemadmodum ante expositum verba Apostoli, 1. Cor. 4. 5. A communi indiuiso) ut vocant) non est bona consequentia ad diuisum concludens. Sequens autem glossema de bonis operibus ignem iudicij divini sustinentibus, & mercede eorum meritoria reiicimus, & tomo 4. iuvante Domino confutabimus.
units.tr: 51. Ibid. Whatever is done God will bring into judgment.] The Wise Man pronounced this about every knowledge and judgment of God, indiscriminately, both in this life and in the life to come: that no impiety can escape the knowledge of God or his judgment by its own power [ἀπ' ἑαυτοῦ], whether here, where he exercises and chastises his own, or there, where divine judgments are brought to completion. So also before, in the words of the Apostle, 1 Cor. 4:5. To conclude about the divided from a common, undivided (as they call it) premise is not a good inference. We reject the following gloss about good works bearing the fire of divine judgment and their meritorious reward, and with the Lord's help we will refute it in the fourth volume.

units.la: 52. Art. 42. Quia iudicium Dei rectissime vocatur ignis] De omni iudicio Dei verissimè dictum, non de ultimo illo solùm. Nihil itaque agit Bellarminus, quum hoc argumento contendit Paulum de iudicio vltimo agere. Quid ergo (ut promissum præstemus) sibi hæc verba volunt? Cuiusque opus manifestum fiet, &c. Primùm voces distinguamus, ut ex eis commodiùs aperiamus sensum Apostoli. Voces sunt, o-pus, dies, ignis. Opus doctrinæ vel ministerij do-ctrinalis agi hoc loco inter nos convenit. Dies aut lucem significat superueniențem operi, aut tempus quo opus profertur in lucem, ex forensi usu, ut 1.Cor.4.3. Ignis aut Deum significat, aut Spiritu Dei & vim divinam illam, qua perlustrantur omnia, illustrantur bona, & consumuntur mala. Etenim Deus noster ignis consumens est, Deut.4.24. & Hebr.12.29. Sensus igitur hic est simplicissimus: cuiusque operis manifestum fiet: id est, qualitas & modus doctrinae cui fuerit operatus, utrum proba sit, necne. dies enim declarabit, id est, lux illa doctrinae, quam Deus verbo praefert, velut face salutari & διαυγέστατο[?], aut certe aliquod tempus conuentus legitimi ad iudicium congregati & illustrati per Spiritum: in quo religiose conuocato aequum est secundum Deum & naturam, ut Prophetarum spiritus Prophetis subiiciantur, 1.Cor.14.32. nam per ignem revelabitur, quod latet, id est, per Deum, vel potius per Spiritu Dei, postea vero ubi productum fuerit quod latere videbatur, cuiusque opus quale sit, ignis probabit, id est, Deus vel Spiritus Dei explorabit in Ecclesia ex verbo suo per servorum suorum ministerium. Haec via ordinaria in Ecclesia Dei, quam decet Apostolus, & confirmat sequentibus. Propterea enim subiicit: ꝗ[?]An nescitis vos esse templum Dei, in quorum Ecclesia diem solet Dominus dicere iudiciumque facere: @[?] Spiritum Dei habitare in vobis, id est, ignem illum revelantem, probantem, & iudicantem omnia ex verbo veritatis? si quis templum Dei violat, id est, Ecclesiam impietate doctrinae perdit volens, hunc perdet Deus: sed alios seruabit & opus ipsorum, quorum opus manserit examinatum verbo: alios seruabit denique, & opus ipsorum exustum perdet. Deinde vero interiectis pauculis versibus eodem pertinentibus, cap.4.dicit: Dominus is est qui me iudicat, &c. tum seipsum, quà Apostolus, & communi sorte aliorum Prophetarum eximens, tum alios sisti iubens in Ecclesia cognitioni & iudicio Dei; modò ne temere quisquà humano iudicio suo anteuertat Deum, cùm Prophetæ in hac cognitione iudicióque nihil sint nisi administri Christi.
units.tr: 52. Art. 42. Because the judgment of God is most rightly called fire.] This is most truly said of every judgment of God, not only of that last one. So Bellarmine accomplishes nothing when he contends from this argument that Paul is speaking of the last judgment. What, then, do these words mean (to make good our promise)? Each one's work will be made manifest, etc. First let us distinguish the terms, so that we may more easily open up the Apostle's meaning from them. The terms are: work, day, fire. It is agreed among us that work here means the work of teaching, or the teaching ministry. Day signifies either the light that comes upon the work, or the time when the work is brought into the light, in the forensic sense, as in 1 Cor. 4:3. Fire signifies either God, or the Spirit of God and that divine power by which all things are searched, good things are illuminated, and evil things are consumed. For our God is a consuming fire, Deut. 4:24 and Heb. 12:29. The sense here is therefore most simple: each one's work will be made manifest, that is, the quality and manner of the doctrine to which he has laboured, whether it is sound or not. For the day will declare it, that is, that light of doctrine which God brings forth in his word, like a saving torch and most clear [διαυγέστατο?], or at least some time of a lawful assembly gathered for judgment and enlightened by the Spirit. In such an assembly, convened in a godly manner, it is right, according to God and nature, that the spirits of the prophets be subject to the prophets, 1 Cor. 14:32. For it will be revealed by fire what lies hidden, that is, through God, or rather through the Spirit of God. Afterwards, when what seemed hidden has been brought to light, fire will test of what sort each one's work is, that is, God or the Spirit of God will examine it in the Church, from his word, through the ministry of his servants. This is the ordinary way in the Church of God, which the Apostle prescribes and confirms in what follows. For he therefore adds: Do you not know that you are the temple of God, in whose Church the Lord is accustomed to appoint a day and make judgment? And that the Spirit of God dwells in you, that is, that fire which reveals, tests and judges all things by the word of truth? If anyone violates the temple of God, that is, wishes to destroy the Church by the impiety of doctrine, God will destroy him. But he will save others and their work, whose work has remained tested by the word; and finally he will save others, while their work, burnt up, he will destroy. Then, after a few intervening verses bearing on the same matter, in chapter 4 he says: It is the Lord who judges me, etc. Here he exempts himself, as an apostle, from the common lot of the other prophets, and commands others to be brought before the examination and judgment of God in the Church, provided only that no one rashly anticipates God with his own human judgment, since the prophets in this examination and judgment are nothing but ministers of Christ.

units.la: Art.43. etiam aliam posuerunt, de qua infrà dicemus. de Augustino, falsum: vt aliquoties ante monuimus.
units.tr: Art.43. They have also put forward another, of which we shall speak below.] About Augustine, false, as we have warned several times before.

units.la: Art 44. dum quis conuertitur, id est, docetur revocaturque ad veritatem, pro qua lignum, fænum, stipulam, in ædificio Domini posuerat.
units.tr: Art 44. while someone is converted, that is, is taught and called back to the truth, for which he had laid wood, hay and stubble in the building of the Lord.

units.la: Ibid. & sic per ignem salui fiunt. dicendum fuerat ex verbis Apostoli, & sicut per ignem salui fiunt. nam altera illa loquutio sermonem Apostolicum perteruolat. Sequētia à iudicio charitatis sunt, quod humanum iudicium Martyris postea disputator conatur elidere.
units.tr: Ibid. and so they are saved through fire.] It should have been said from the words of the Apostle: and yet so as through fire they are saved. For that other wording flies far from the Apostolic sense. What follows comes from the judgment of charity, which the later disputant tries to overturn, against the human judgment of the martyr.

units.la: Art.45. quia illud iudicium fit solum in morte, adhuc viuente homine, vel putest fieri etiam post mortem. Negatur: nam disputator τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς petit. Non agit Apostolus de iudicio particulari aut vniuersali Dei solius proprie, sed de iudicio Dei & Ecclesiæ, siue Dei per Ecclesiam facto, vt commonstrant sequētia, quæ nota 52. destrinximus. Quod autem de iudicio in hora mortis dicitur à Martyre, id non ex propria vi loci Pauli dicitur, sed ex analogia. De iudicio post mortem, nullum verbum. Ergo locus Pauli est de iudicio Dei in causa viuentis Ministri per Ecclesiam & in Ecclesia faciendo. Quapropter sequentia omnia nihil ad causam plane. hoc enim iudicium Ecclesiasticum nec in morte fieri, nec post mortem potest.
units.tr: Art.45. because that judgment takes place only at death, while the man is still living, or it can take place even after death.] Denied, for the disputant begs the question from the beginning. The Apostle is not speaking strictly of the particular or universal judgment of God alone, but of the judgment of God and the Church, or of God's judgment made through the Church, as the following words show, which we marked in note 52. What the martyr says about judgment at the hour of death is not drawn from the proper force of Paul's passage, but from analogy. Of judgment after death, there is not a word. Therefore Paul's passage concerns God's judgment on a living minister, made through the Church and in the Church. Hence all the following arguments are plainly beside the point, for this ecclesiastical judgment can neither take place at death nor after death.

units.la: 57 Ibid. peto, quo modo agetur cum illis qui superā-dificarunt lignum, fœnum, stipulas, & moriuntur repen-te,] respondeo, abscondita sunto Domini Dei nostri, Deut.30. quanquam dicimus ex analogia. Deum qui in Ecclesia & per iudicium Ecclesiæ facit viuentibus gratiam, eandem morientibus & mortuis in Christo & per Christum facere, cùm fundamētum hoc positum semper tenuerint.
units.tr: 57 Ibid. I ask, how will it be with those who build on wood, hay and stubble, and die suddenly?] I answer: the secret things belong to the Lord our God, Deut. 30. Yet we say, by analogy, that God, who in the Church and through the Church's judgment shows grace to the living, does the same for the dying and the dead in Christ and through Christ, since they have always held fast to this foundation once laid.

units.la: 58 Ibid. nec possunt etiam saluari, nisi admittatur Purgatorium; ] admittimus omnino purgatorium, gratiam Dei in Christo per sanguinem eius mundantem nos ab omni peccato : quod Bellarminus cap.1. confessus est. aliud purgatorium, ἄτοπον[?].
units.tr: 58 Ibid. Nor can they be saved unless Purgatory is admitted;] We wholly admit a purgatory: the grace of God in Christ, which through his blood cleanses us from all sin, as Bellarmine confessed in chapter 1. Another purgatory, which is absurd [ἄτοπον], we do not admit.

units.la: 59 Art.46. ignis ille, de quo Paulus loquitur, afficiet pœna proprie & vere,] negatur, si de pœna in persona dixeris; non autem de pœna in re & opere, quæ proprie appellatur multa siue mulcta. In illum autem modum Bellarminus accipit quem negamus, ut ostendit sequentibus.
units.tr: 59 Art. 46. That fire of which Paul speaks will afflict with punishment properly and truly: I deny this if you mean punishment in the person. But it is not denied of punishment in the thing and the work, which is properly called a fine or forfeit (multa sive mulcta). Bellarmine understands it in the sense we deny, as he shows in what follows.

units.la: 60 Ibid. quàm ζημιοῦσθαι θανάτῳ, morte multari:] inconsequens ex homonymia. Nam ζημία proprie mulctam in re siue opere significat; ζημιοῦσθαι θανάτῳ, per abusionem dictum est. Etymologicum magnum audiamus: Ζημία, ἡ τῶν ὄντων [illegible, ~20 letters] τὸ ζῶν μείω-σις, ἡ τὰ κτήματα [illegible, ~25 letters] ἡ τῶν ζῷων μείωσις, περὶ τὸ μειούμενον. Hæc prima etymologia, sequitur altera: ἡ παρὰ τὸ ζῆν τῶν γινομένων [?] τὸ ἐπαρμένα. Tertia denique, ἡ ἡμία τῆς οὐσίας, ἡ πολιτική. Suidas vero ait, ζημία, στέρησις. Sic omnes Græci, pro priuatione, aut læsio-ne. Atque hinc Plinius lib.16. nat.hist. cap.26. de nucibus pineis, Quæ se in arbore, inquit, ipsa diuisere, Zamia vocantur, lædúntque cæteras nisi detrahantur. quò respexisse videtur Plautus quū diceret in Aulu-laria pauper Euclio, Nemini credo qui large blādu'st, dives pauperi: Vbi manum iniicit benignè, ibi onerat a-liquam Zamiam. Aliud ergo est mulctabitur; dam-num patietur; aliud, poenas dabit: quæ disputator co-fundit tamen. Mulcta in re aut in opere est ciuiliter solùm, poena in persona corporaliter. In Purgatorio, si quod est (negamus autem) poenam, ac non multam oportet dici: nam quid præter seipsum in Purgatorium inferat moriens?
units.tr: 60 Ibid. rather than to be punished with death, to be fined with death: this is an inconsequence arising from a double meaning. For zēmia (ζημία) properly signifies a fine in the thing or the work, and zēmioūsthai thanatōi (ζημιοῦσθαι θανάτῳ) is said by abuse. Let us hear the Etymologicum Magnum: zēmia is the diminution of beings [ζημία, ἡ τῶν ὄντων ... μείωσις] ... the diminution of living things [τὸ ζῶν μείωσις], or the diminution of possessions ... the diminution of animals, concerning what is diminished. This is the first etymology, and a second follows: the loss of things that come into being [ἡ παρὰ τὸ ζῆν τῶν γινομένων]. Finally a third: the loss of substance, the civic sense. Suidas says zēmia is deprivation [ζημία, στέρησις]. So all the Greeks use it for privation or harm. Hence Pliny, Natural History book 16, chapter 26, on pine nuts: those which split apart on the tree itself are called zamiae, and they harm the others unless they are removed. Plautus seems to have had this in mind when, in the Aulularia, the poor Euclio says: I trust no one who flatters generously; when a rich man lays his hand on a poor man kindly, he loads him with some zamia. So to be fined (mulctabitur) is one thing, to suffer loss (damnum patietur) another, and to pay penalties (poenas dabit) a third; the objector nonetheless confuses them. A fine in the thing or the work is only civil, while punishment in the person is bodily. In Purgatory, if there is such a thing (which we deny), it ought to be called a fine, not a punishment: for what does the dying man bring into Purgatory apart from himself?

units.la: 61 Ibid. similitudo transeuntis per ignem significat pœnam ac dolorem:] Negatur: nam ignis iste de quo agitur, non est pœnalis in personam, sed exploratorius in opus doctrinæ; vt ante dixerat Apostolus, per ignem reuelatur, & vniuscuiusque opus quale sit, ignis probabit, vtrum sit mansurum, aut periturum igne illo. Non homo transit per ignem, sed opus ipsius: homo autem non punitur, sed dolet; non quòd ab igne torreatur, sed quòd suum opus igne illo exustum videat, & se operam illam in Ecclesia perdidisse nullo suo ipsius aut Ecclesiæ (quod sperabat) commodo. Hic autem non est pœnalis dolor, vt postea agnoscit disputator in 4. sua argumentatione. Sequentium eadem ratio.
units.tr: 61 Ibid. the likeness of one passing through fire signifies punishment and pain: I deny this. For the fire of which we are speaking is not penal for the person but a testing fire for the work of doctrine, as the Apostle had said before: by fire it shall be revealed, and fire shall try what sort each man's work is, whether it will remain or perish in that fire. It is not the man who passes through the fire but his work. The man is not punished but grieves, not because he is scorched by the fire, but because he sees his work burnt up by it, and that he has laboured in vain in the Church, with no benefit to himself or to the Church, as he had hoped. This grief is not penal, as the objector later admits in his fourth argument. The same reasoning applies to what follows.

units.la: 62 Art. 47. quia Apostolus opponit hunc transitum per ignem mercedi:] transitum non personæ (vt Bellarminus putat) pœnalem; sed operis seu doctrinæ eius. Ex ambiguo nihil recte concludi potest. Quid autem sit ambigui, sequentibus proximè ostendemus.
units.tr: 62 Art. 47. because the Apostle sets this passing through fire against reward: a passage not penal for the person (as Bellarmine thinks), but for the work or its doctrine. Nothing can rightly be concluded from an ambiguous term. What is ambiguous we will show shortly below.

units.la: 63 Ibid. est aliqua pœna præter iacturam operum, & præter confusionem quam ex se adfert.] Vtrumque indistincte[?] atque imperfectè dicitur. Merces non significat ipsum bonum opus ( est enim boni operis merces, non opus bonum hominis) neque lætitiam tantùm significat ex bono opere; sed fructùm gloriæ Dei, ædificationisque publicæ in veritate, & laudem illius, id est, approbationem publicam Dei in Ecclesia eius Spiritu & verbo. Quapropter hanc mercedem postea Apostolus vocat laudem; ubi hunc sermonem concludit, 1. Cor. 4. 5. sicut & 2. Cor. 8.18. Ex contrario autem damnum sive detrimentum, ζημία, non est opus ipsum inane, non sola iactura & vacuitas ab illo fructu quem servi Dei auferunt percipiuntque; sed etiam censura & nota publica per Spiritum Dei in Ecclesia operi seu ministerio hominis impressa, qua opus improbatur, homo vero confunditur ad salutem emendationémq; ipsius. Inconsequens igitur enthymema est.
units.tr: 63 Ibid. there is some punishment beyond the loss of works and beyond the confusion which it brings of itself: both points are stated indistinctly and imperfectly. Reward does not mean the good work itself (for the reward is of a good work, not the good work of a man), nor does it mean only joy arising from a good work. It means the fruit of God's glory and of public edification in the truth, and his praise, that is, God's public approval in his Church by his Spirit and Word. That is why the Apostle afterwards calls this reward praise, where he concludes this discourse (1 Cor. 4. 5.), as also in 2 Cor. 8. 18. On the contrary, loss or detriment (zēmia, ζημία) is not the empty work itself, nor merely the lack of and emptiness from that fruit which the servants of God are deprived of and do not receive. It is also the censure and public mark impressed by the Spirit of God in the Church on the work or ministry of a man, by which the work is disapproved and the man himself is put to shame, for his salvation and amendment. The enthymeme is therefore inconsequent.

units.la: 64 Art.48. At Paulus dicit, detrimentu patietur ergo, &c. Assumptio hæc παραλογίζεται[?] ex elenchi ignoratione. Nàvtrumq;[?] verù est, homine eiusmodi iudicio & detrimentum capere & lucrù: detrimentum operis anteacti, quo mulctatur, adeò ut totum pereat abdicetúrque iudicio Dei & Ecclesiæ; lucrum vero eruditionis in melius & informationis in futurum tempus. Quid? non-ne sic frequenter vsuenit tironibus & inscitis operariis, ut eodem iudicio magistri sive artificis & detrimentum operis capiát & eruditionis vel scientiæ lucrum?
units.tr: 64 Art. 48. But Paul says, he shall suffer loss, therefore, etc. This assumption is a paralogism arising from ignorance of the elenchus. Both are true: a man under such judgment both suffers loss and gains. He suffers the loss of the work he has done, for which he is fined, so that all of it perishes and is rejected by the judgment of God and the Church. But he gains in learning, to become better, and in instruction for the time to come. What then? Does it not often happen to apprentices and unskilled workmen that, by the same judgment of the master or craftsman, they both suffer loss of their work and gain in learning or knowledge?

units.la: 65 Art.49. quia sequeretur, omnes qui salvantur salvari quasi per ignem, ] Non sequitur ratione ulla. Nam primùm illa verba, οὕτως ὡς διὰ πυρός[?], verum tamen quasi per ignem, ad membrum remotius pertinent, ζημιωθήσονται[?], damnum vel detrimentum patie-tur operis sui: tamquam si diceret, eodem igne quq[?] opus factum est manifestum, reuelatum,& probatum(vt supra dicebat Apostolus) eodem consumetur tamquam storea aut matta imperiti atque inepti artificis, qui operis sui iacturam facit. Illa vero verba, αὐτὸς δὲ ζωώσεται, ipse vero seruabitur, κατὰ ᾰ̓πόλλυ per anticipationem interiecta sunt παρενθήκη, ne damnato & reprobato opere damnatus etiam reprobatúsque operarius esse videretur, aut ipse animum forte abiiceret: ac si obiiceretur, quid ergo fiet misero? nonne pereunte opere & operarius periturus est? de hoc, inquit Paulus, operario equidem non dixerim: contra enim seruabitur auctore Spiritu Dei in Ecclesia ipsius. Hanc traiectionem notauit Theodoretus apud Oecumenium, dicens: οὕτως δὲ ἀναγκαῖως ἀκριβῶς ἐρμηνεύει τὴν τῶν γραμμάτων διάνοιαν. εἴπερ τὸ ἔργον τοῦτο διὰ πυρὸς ἀνὴρ τὸ κατὰ τοῦτο ἐκεῖνο τὸ ἔργον ζῶν τὸ πῦρ, αὐτὸς δὲ σώζεται. Secundo siquis contendat ad propinquius membrum pertinere, quod ego quidem non puto; tamen vt demus ita esse, dicimus non ad hoc solum, sed ad vtrumque membrum pertinere in hunc modum: detrimentum patietur opus, ipse vero seruabitur; verumtamen vtrumque hoc quasi per ignem, id est, eodem illo iudicio & cognitione Spiritus Dei in Ecclesia ipsius, quod iudicium per quamdam similitudinem ignem appellauimus. Postremo in verbo seruandi fallit disputator à dicto κατὰ τὴν. Non enim hoc loco agitur de salute hominis proprie atque vniuersè, quà Christianus est (etsi omnino eum seruari affirmamus qui caput & fundamentum retinet) sed de salute operarij quà operarius. hic operarius, inquit (vt verbis Pauli vtamur 1. Cor. 9. 27.) ἵνα μὴ ἀδόκιμος γένωμαι, postquam aliis praedicauit dicauit μνώματι[?] seruato fundamento, non fiet reprobus operarius sententia Dei in Ecclesia sua; sed seruabitur, id est, salua & integra functione, quum iudicium Dei atque Ecclesiæ acceperit, censebitur adhuc in numero seruorum Dei, & auctore Domino vtiliter legitiméque in ædificatione Ecclesiæ occupabitur.
units.tr: 65 Art. 49. because it would follow that all who are saved are saved as though through fire: this does not follow by any reasoning. For first, those words thus as through fire [οὕτως ὡς διὰ πυρός] apply to the more remote member, he shall suffer loss [ζημιωθήσονται], that is, the loss of his work, as if he said: by the same fire by which the work is shown to be manifest, revealed and tested (as the Apostle said above), it will be consumed like the straw or mat of an unskilled and inept craftsman who suffers the loss of his work. The words but he himself shall be saved [αὐτὸς δὲ σωθήσεται] and yet so as by fire are inserted by way of parenthesis, by anticipation, so that the work is condemned and rejected but the workman does not seem to be condemned and rejected too, or perhaps lose heart. It is as if someone objected: what then will happen to the poor man? Will not the workman also perish when the work perishes? Paul answers: I would not say this of the workman. For he will be saved, by the authority of the Spirit of God in his Church. Theodoret, cited in Oecumenius, noted this transposition, saying: thus he precisely and necessarily explains the sense of the words: if this work is burnt through fire, then the fire by which that work is tested is the same, but the man himself is saved [οὕτως δὲ ἀναγκαῖως ἀκριβῶς ἐρμηνεύει τὴν τῶν γραμμάτων διάνοιαν ... αὐτὸς δὲ σώζεται]. Secondly, if anyone insists that it refers to the nearer member, which I do not think, still, granting that it is so, we say that it refers not to this alone but to both members in this way: the work shall suffer loss, but he himself shall be saved; yet both are as through fire, that is, by that same judgment and knowledge of the Spirit of God in his Church, which judgment we have called fire by a certain likeness. Lastly, the objector errs in the word saved, taking it from the phrase according to [κατά]. For this passage is not concerned with the salvation of the man properly and universally, as he is a Christian (although we firmly affirm that he is saved who keeps the Head and the foundation), but with the salvation of the workman as a workman. Here the workman, says Paul, using his own words in 1 Cor. 9. 27: lest I myself should become a castaway [ἵνα μὴ ἀδόκιμος γένωμαι], after he has preached to others, while the foundation is kept, will not become a reprobate workman by the sentence of God in his Church. Rather he shall be saved, that is, safe and whole in his office; when he has received the judgment of God and the Church, he will still be counted among the servants of God, and, by the Lord's authority, he will be usefully and lawfully employed in building up the Church.
