units.la: 66 Ibidem. si ignis, de quo Paulus loquitur, est iudicium Dei, omnes saluabuntur quasi per ignem. ] non sequitur ex diuerso: nam aliud est iudicium Dei hic per Spiritum & verbum in Ecclesia ipsius & coniuncta cognitione Ecclesiæ, aliud iudicium Dei vltimum in resurrectione per se. Vtriusque ratio plurimum differens. Quamobrem sequens obiectio & responsio nihil ad nos.
units.tr: 66 Ibid. if the fire of which Paul speaks is the judgment of God, all shall be saved as through fire: this does not follow from the opposite. For the judgment of God here, by the Spirit and Word in his Church and by the joint knowledge of the Church, is one thing; the final judgment of God at the resurrection, by itself, is another. The grounds of the two differ greatly. Therefore the following objection and reply have nothing to do with us.

units.la: 67 Art.5o. hæc est palinodia scilicet, quam [?]sommiat Pseudo martyr Petrus.] de palinodia apud alios nihil dicit Martyr: nam de sensu[?] ipsorum in morte dicit, non diu ante mortem. Certè multa sentiunt de vanitate fiduciæ suæ morientes Pontificij multi, de quibus viuentes per somnium ne cogitauerunt qui dein, quum extra certamen verbis vanitatis considerent. Humaniter autem de illis sentiebat Martyr, quod Bellarminus vetat hac prudente sua affirmatione. De Bernardo saltem non ex opinione, sed Gulielmi Abbatis fide hoc Martyr rectè affirmauit. Sic enim ille refert lib. 1. de vita Bernardi, ca. 13.
units.tr: 67 Art. 50. this is the palinode, namely, which the pseudo-martyr Peter brings up: Martyr says nothing of the palinodes of others. For he speaks of their feelings in death, not long before death. Certainly many Papists, dying, feel the vanity of their confidence, which while living they scarcely thought of, even in their dreams, and they reflect on it when they are outside the contest, with words of vanity. Martyr judged these men humanely, which Bellarmine forbids by his prudent assertion. About Bernard, at least, Martyr rightly affirmed this, not from opinion but on the faith of Abbot William. For so William reports in book 1 of the Life of Bernard, chapter 13.

units.la: Quum Bernardus extremum iam trahere spiritum videretur, in excessu mentis suæ ante tribunal Domini sibi visus est præsentari. Adfuit autem & Satan ex aduersario, improbis eum accusationibus pulsans. Vbi vero ille omnia fuerat prosequutus, & viro Dei pro sua fuit parte di-
units.tr: When Bernard seemed to be drawing his last breath, in an ecstasy of mind he seemed to himself to be brought before the judgment seat of the Lord. Satan too was present, the adversary, assailing him with wicked accusations. When he had set out everything, and it was the man of God's turn to answer for his part,

units.la: cendū[?], nihil territus aut turbatus ait, Fateor nō sum dignus ego, nec propriis possum meritis regnum obtinere cœlorum. Caterum duplici iure illud obtinens Dominus meus, hæreditate scilicet patris, & merito passionis, altero ipse contentus, alterum mihi donat: ex cuius dono iure illud vendicans, non confundor. & similia, quibus Bernardus omissa ratione monachatus, Missæ, &c. ostendit se in solo Christi merito conquiescere.
units.tr: (he had to speak), nothing frightened or disturbed him, and he said: "I confess that I am not worthy, nor can I obtain the kingdom of heaven by my own merits. But my Lord, who holds it by a twofold right, namely by inheritance from the Father and by the merit of his passion, is content with the one and gives me the other. Claiming it by the right of that gift, I am not confounded," and similar words, by which Bernard, setting aside any reckoning of his monastic life, Masses, and so on, showed that he rested in the merit of Christ alone.

units.la: 68 Art.51. inueniuntur ædificasse lignum, fœnum, aut stipulam.] hanc sententiam, qua Purgatorium locu-lorum, non animarum, statuitur, negamus, itemque probationes eius.
units.tr: 68 Art.51. they are found to have built wood, hay, or stubble.] We deny this opinion, by which a Purgatory is set up as a place and not as a state of souls, and likewise its proofs.

units.la: 69 Ibid. aliud peccata omnia passione purgasse.] Cyprianus agit de perpessionibus huius vitæ, quæ nihil ad purgationem futuri seculi pertinent: nam purgantur filij Dei igne tribulationum, dum in hac vita sunt, castigantur que: ut ci[?] putator ipse agnoüit cap.1. Sic autem Cyprianum sentire docet argumentum & totus contextus epistolæ: nam de pœnitentium conversione & reconciliatione cum Ecclesia loquitur. de Purgatorio isto commentitio ne apex quidem est.
units.tr: 69 Ibid. that by his suffering he purged all other sins.] Cyprian is speaking of the sufferings of this life, which have nothing to do with the purging of the future age: for the sons of God are purged by the fire of tribulations while they are in this life, and are chastened, as the author himself acknowledged in chapter 1. That Cyprian thinks this is shown by the argument and the whole context of the letter, for he speaks of the conversion and reconciliation of penitents with the Church. Of that invented Purgatory there is not even a trace.

units.la: 70. Art. 52. Idem habet ferm. 20. in Psal. 118.] prior locus agit de igne examinis diuini in Ecclesia per verbum, vt nota 19. dicebamus: posterior de igne tribulationum, vt nota 46. demonstrauimus.
units.tr: 70. Art. 52. He has the same in Sermon 20 on Psalm 118.] The former passage speaks of the fire of the divine test in the Church through the Word, as we noted at note 19; the latter of the fire of tribulations, as we showed at note 46.

units.la: 71 Art.53. & lib.2. in Iouinianum vltra medium.] Primus locus de igne tribulationum in hac vita loquitur euidentissimè. Secundus locus alludit ad verba Pauli, non eorum adfert interpretationem: agit enim de suppliciis hominum omnium propter opera ipsorum, non de examine doctrinæ prædicatæ, quod agit Paulus. Ex allusione consequi nihil potest. vide infra in cap.10.not. 52. Locus tertius nihil habet ferme quam verba ipsa Apostoli, nec quicquam eorum explicat.
units.tr: 71 Art.53. and in book 2 against Jovinian, beyond the middle.] The first passage speaks most evidently of the fire of tribulations in this life. The second alludes to the words of Paul but does not offer their interpretation: for it deals with the punishments of all men on account of their works, not with the testing of the preached doctrine, which is what Paul deals with. Nothing can follow from an allusion. See below in chapter 10, note 52. The third passage contains almost nothing but the Apostle's own words, and explains none of them.

units.la: graviorem tamen est ille ignis, quam quicquid potest homo pati in hac vita. De priore loco, quę corruptum Bellarminus adfert, diximus in caput 3. nota 51. Posterior eiusdem plane est argumenti. Nam Augustinus instituit comparationem ignis æterni cum igne tribulationum purgatorio in hac vita, non cum igne, quem futurum somniant Purgatorij. Atque hoc ostendunt ultima illius verba lucu-lentissimè.
units.tr: Yet that fire is more grievous than anything a man can suffer in this life. About the former passage, which Bellarmine cites in a corrupt form, we spoke at chapter 3, note 51. The latter is plainly of the same nature. For Augustine sets up a comparison between eternal fire and the fire of tribulations in this life as a purgatory, not with the fire which they dream of as the future fire of Purgatory. The final words of that passage show this most clearly.

units.la: Agnoscimus inde a Gregorij sæculo in citerioribus Ecclesiis plurimum obtinuisse nescio quo humanitatis studio & probabilitatis specie: sed tamen hoc ipsum non ita affirmatè dixit Gregorius, sed lenius ac velut [illegible, ~10 letters]. Testis Gregorius ipse, atque ex eo Gratianus dist.26.c.qualis. quū ait: qualis hinc quisque egreditur, talis in iudicio apparebit vel representabitur. postea vero hoc verè magis quàm fuerè dictum, quasi humanitate quadā corrupturus (ne dicam, corrupturus) subiicit: Sed tamen de quibusdam levibus culpis esse ante iudicium purgatorius ignis credendus est, &c. Nos verò in hac causa & Gregorij, & sequentiū auctoritatem negamus, dicentes cum Augustino universè quod ille speciatim respectu quorundam pronunciauit Enchirid. cap.67. qui hoc credunt, & tamen catholici sunt, humana quadam benevolentia mihi falli videntur. Dicit quidem non esse incredibile, sed credendum non dicit, qua-uis errori multorum aperte obniti nolit pro sua modestia & publicæ pacis studio.
units.tr: We acknowledge that from the age of Gregory onward this view has gained great ground in the Churches of the West, through I know not what zeal for kindness and a semblance of probability. Yet Gregory himself did not state it so positively, but more gently, and as it were [illegible, ~10 letters]. Gregory himself is the witness, and from him Gratian, dist. 26, c. "qualis", when he says: "Whatever sort of person goes out from here, such will appear, or be shown, at the judgment." Afterwards, however, he said this more truly than before, as if he were about to correct it, with a kind of humaneness (not to say a corruption), adding: "Yet it must be believed that for certain light faults there is a purging fire before the judgment," and so on. But we, in this matter, deny the authority both of Gregory and of those who follow him, saying with Augustine in general what he pronounced in particular concerning certain people in the Enchiridion, chapter 67: "Those who believe this, and yet are Catholics, seem to me to be deceived by a certain human kindness." He indeed says that it is not incredible, but he does not say that it must be believed, although for his own modesty and his zeal for public peace he is unwilling to resist openly the error of many.

units.la: 74 Art.56. illud parum tamquam plumbum igne resoluitur & purgatur, &c.] Loquitur Origenes de igne tribulationum punitiuo & purgatorio in hac vita, vt euincunt praecedentia. Hæc verba illius: Sicut fornax probat aurum,sic homines iustos tentatio. Veniendum est ergo omnibus ad ignem ,veniendum est ad conflatorium, videlicet istud tentationis. Sedet enim Dominus,& conflat,& purgat filios Leui. Sed & illuc quum venitur, nempe in fornacem tentationis seu conflatorium, si quis multa opera bona, & quæ sequuntur.vide supra cap.3.nota 60. Secundus locus eiusdem homil. 14. in Leuiticum eodem plane est argumento. Tertius locus homil.12.in Ieremiá non modò reticet Purgatorium,sed euertit funditus. Nam duo statuit tempora Origenes: primum,quod est operum & tribulationum perpessionum q; in hac vita; & secundum in altera,quod est coronæ: Primum quippe,inquit,propter iniustitias tormenta perpetimur,deinde propter iustitiam coronamur. Sed quia locus est longior, Lectorè piū nolumus hoc loco morari interpretatione: Origenem audiamus agentem de verbis Ierem.16.18. quibus temporales poenas Iudeis & Israelitis pronunciat ante infligendas quàm promissiones Euangelicæ præstentur. Istum locum,inquit,cum cateris editionibus conferentes inuenimus positū, Et tribuā [?] illis primum duplices iniustitias eorum: ut ostendatur quia etsi ex posterioribus factis, nimirum diuinæ gratiæ, digni effecti sunt beatitudine Dei; attamen quia aliquando peccauerunt,& humanis vitiis non carebant,primum oportet eos recipere sua delicta. Et vide si non sit vera ratio. Quis peccata non recipit nempe ille qui post credulitatem (malim, fidem) & baptismum audierit Dominum dicentem, dimissa sunt tibi peccata, nec vltra peccauerit. Sensus est, huic non sunt illae duplices iniustitiae, de quibus Propheta dicit. Si autem post lauacrum & veniam delictorum rursus ad pristinas sordes fuerimus reuersi, & adhuc imperfecto sensu ab Apostolorum vestigiis recedentes aut iniusta gesserimus aliqua, aut certe in ipsa iustitia sint aliqua nata peccata, quid nobis fiat consideremus: vtrum ne egredientes de praesenti saeculo, si habuerimus vitia vel virtutes, recipiemus pro virtutibus praemia, & dimittentur nobis ea quae scientes peccauimus, an plectemur pro delictis, neque recipiemus praemia pro virtutibus. Sed neutrum horum verum est, quia & pro peccatis torquebimur, videlicet primum in hac vita, & pro iustitia in illa recipiemus praemia quae meremur ἀξιούμεθα. Si enim post fundamentum Iesu Christi non solum in tuo corde aurum, & argentum & lapidem pretiosum (si tamen habes aliquid auri vel argenti) superaedificaueris, verum & ligna, foenum & stipulam: quid tibi vis fieri, quum anima seiuncta fuerit a corpore? utrum nam ingredi vis in sancta cum lignis tuis, cum foeno & stipula, ut polluas regnum Dei, an propter lignum, foenum, & stipulam foris residere, & pro auro, argento, & lapide pretiosò nihil mercedis accipere? Sed neque hoc aequum est. Quid igitur sequitur, nisi ut primum propter ligna ignis tibi detur, qui consumat foenum, lignum, vel stipulam? Deus quippe noster apud eos qui possunt intelligere diuina, ignis dicitur esse consumens: & quum dicit Propheta, Deus noster ignis consumens est, non appositum quid consumat, tibi derelinquens de manifestioribus intellectum. Neque enim id quod ad imaginem & similitudinem suam permanet, ignis ille consumit, non proprias creaturas, sed superaedificata ligna, foenum, stipulam. Locus est difficilis(de loco Ieremiæ dicit) & ad interpretandum nunquam[?] fudorus egens, ut cum primis secunda consentiant. Repromissiones legitimas, & post prospera repente tristia prædicantur: Et retribuam, inquit illis primum duplices iniustitias eorum. Necessario appositum est, primum. Primum quippe propter iniustitias tormenta perpetimur, deinde propter iustitiam coronamur. Neque enim e contrario ante tribuenda sunt iusta, & sic reddenda peccata, vt cessantibus bonis vitia æterna permaneant: sed ante recipiemus mala, & deinde bona, vt sublatis vitiis virtutes permaneant in æternum. & quæ sequun-tur. In his profecto omnibus de Purgatorio futuro vestigium nullum: sed tantum de pœnis purgatoriis quæ in hac vita infliguntur, antequam in possessionem vitæ æternæ transmittamur morte.
units.tr: 74 Art.56. that little, like lead, is melted and purged by fire, etc.] Origen is speaking of the punitive and purging fire of tribulations in this life, as the preceding passages make clear. His words are these: "As the furnace tests gold, so temptation tests righteous men. All must therefore come to the fire, must come to the crucible, that is, to the temptation of trial. For the Lord sits and refines and purges the sons of Levi. But also when one comes there, namely into the furnace of temptation or the crucible, if anyone has many good works, and so on." See above, chapter 3, note 60. The second passage of the same Homily 14 on Leviticus is plainly of the same subject. The third passage, from Homily 12 on Jeremiah, not only is silent about Purgatory but utterly overturns it. For Origen sets up two times: the first, which belongs to works and to the sufferings of tribulations in this life; and the second, in the other life, which is that of the crown: "For first, he says, we suffer torments on account of our iniquities; then we are crowned on account of our righteousness." But because the passage is rather long, we do not wish, dear reader, to linger over the interpretation here; let us hear Origen treating the words of Jeremiah 16:18, by which he announces temporal punishments to the Jews and Israelites before the promises of the gospel are fulfilled. "Comparing this passage," he says, "with the other editions, we find it set down: 'And I will repay them first for their double iniquities,' so that it may be shown that, although by their later deeds, namely of divine grace, they have been made worthy of the blessedness of God, yet because at some time they sinned and were not free from human vices, they must first receive their sins. And see whether this is not the true reasoning. He who, after faith and baptism, has heard the Lord saying, 'Your sins are forgiven you,' and has not sinned again, does not receive sins." The sense is that such a person does not have those double iniquities of which the prophet speaks. "But if after the washing and the forgiveness of sins we have returned again to our former filth, and still with an imperfect understanding, departing from the footsteps of the Apostles, have done some unrighteous things, or certainly some sins have been born even in righteousness itself, let us consider what will happen to us: whether, when we depart from the present age, if we have vices or virtues, we shall receive rewards for our virtues, and those sins which we committed knowingly will be forgiven us, or whether we shall be punished for our offences and shall not receive rewards for our virtues. But neither of these is true, because we shall both be tormented for our sins, namely first in this life, and for our righteousness in that other life we shall receive the rewards which we deserve [ἀξιούμεθα]. For if upon the foundation of Jesus Christ you have built not only gold and silver and precious stone in your heart (if indeed you have any gold or silver), but also wood, hay, and stubble: what do you wish to happen to you when the soul is separated from the body? Do you wish to enter into the holy places with your wood, hay, and stubble, so as to defile the kingdom of God; or to sit outside on account of the wood, hay, and stubble, and receive no reward for the gold, silver, and precious stone? But neither of these is fair. What follows, then, except that first fire is given you on account of the wood, so that it may consume the hay, the wood, or the stubble? For our God, among those who can understand divine things, is said to be a consuming fire; and when the prophet says, 'Our God is a consuming fire,' he does not add what it consumes, leaving you to understand the more obvious things. For that fire does not consume what remains according to his image and likeness, not his own creatures, but the wood, hay, and stubble built upon them. The place is difficult," (he says of the passage in Jeremiah) "and needs an interpreter who is never at a loss, so that the second things may agree with the first. Lawful promises and, after prosperous things, sad ones are suddenly announced: 'And I will repay them first for their double iniquities.' The word 'first' is necessarily added. For first we suffer torments on account of iniquities, then we are crowned on account of righteousness. For the righteous things are not to be given before, and so the sins repaid, so that when good things cease, the vices remain for ever; but we shall first receive evils, and then goods, so that when vices are removed, virtues may remain for ever." And what follows. In all these things there is certainly no trace of a future Purgatory, but only of purgatorial punishments which are inflicted in this life, before we are sent on by death into possession of eternal life.

units.la: 75. Ib. Basilius hunc locu[?] intellexisse de igne Purgatorio:]
units.tr: 75. Ibid. Basil understood this passage to refer to the purgatorial fire:

units.la: Utrüque falsum. Nec ipse Oecumenius Paulū sic interpretatus est de futuro Purgatorio, sed de examine quod in hac vita vita fit, vt verba ipsius ostendunt & locus Malachiæ: postea vero Photij adfert interpretatione, quaaliena[?] a loco esse disputator ipse affirmauit: τὸ σωθήσεται, inquit, [?] ἐκ ἀφανισθήσονται εἰς τὸ μὴ ὂν χωρήσει, ὥσπερ αἱ ἐν [?] αὐτῶν αἱ πονηραί, & quæ sequuntur. Tandem vero Basilij sententiam adferens, dicit: ἐν τῇ [illegible, ~6 letters] Βασιλείου [illegible, ~12 letters] ἐξ αὐτοῦ ἐκλέγατο. id est, in Esaiæ interpretatione sanctus Basilius bis recordatus huius dicti de purgatione accepit ipsum. nihil amplius. De purgatione, inquit Bellarminus, videlicet nostri Purgatorij. Fabulæ. Basilium ipsum appello (si placet) Oecumenij interpretem. Sic autem ille in Esaiæ 5. de doctrina & administris eius hunc locum euidenter explicauit, vt nullum de Purgatorio verbum fecerit.Alter locus eius(si bene obseruaui)non exstat.Et quàm festiuum est Bellarmini interpretamentum?de purgatione:ergo inquit, nostri Purgatorij purgatione : quasi verò alia non esset vlla, nec traderetur purgatio. Nam Purgatorium negamus esse,purgationes verò alias profitemur. Non sequitur à genere ad speciem:quòd si non sequitur ad speciem veram, quid de ficta & commentitia dicturi sumus?Sed hæc satis.
units.tr: Both claims are false. Oecumenius himself did not interpret Paul in this way, of a future Purgatory, but of the trial that takes place in this life, as his own words and the passage from Malachi show. Later he brings in an interpretation from Photius, which the disputant himself admits is foreign to the passage: "the word 'will be saved' [σωθήσεται], he says, 'does not go off into non-being, as do the wicked among them'," and so on. Finally, setting out Basil's opinion, he says that in Basil's interpretation of Isaiah the saint twice recalled this saying about purging and took it from him, nothing more. "About purging," says Bellarmine, "namely of our Purgatory." Fables! I call Basil himself (if you please) an interpreter of Oecumenius. For in Isaiah 5 he explained this passage clearly of the doctrine and its ministers, and made no mention of Purgatory at all. His other passage (if I have observed rightly) does not exist. And how absurd is Bellarmine's gloss: "about purging, therefore of the purging of our Purgatory"? As if there were no other purging, and none were taught. For we deny that Purgatory exists, but we profess other purgings. It does not follow from genus to species; and if it does not follow to a true species, what shall we say of a fictitious and invented one? But enough of this.

units.la: 76. Ibid. ἐν ᾧ καθεὶζόντα τὰ ψυχαί, καθάπερ χρυσῶν ἐν τῷ χωνευτηρίῳ:] Primùm hæc verba nusquam apud Theodoretum exstant, nec suo tempore extitisse Græci testabantur in Concilio Ferrariensi: secundò vt sint Theodoreti,nomine ψυχῶν intelliguntur homines ἀνθρωπῶν[?] ex Scripturæ vsu, & prædicantur ista de purgatorio tribulationum igne, quæ piis in hac vita accidunt. Sunt enim verba hæc sumpta ex Sapi. 3.5. vbi agitur de tribulationibus quas piorum animæ in hac vita pertulerunt. Nihil ergo sequitur ex vocis homonymia.
units.tr: 76. Ibid. "in which the souls sit, like gold in the crucible":] First, these words are nowhere to be found in Theodoret, and the Greeks testified at the Council of Ferrara that they did not exist in his time. Second, even if they are Theodoret's, by "souls" men are understood, according to the usage of Scripture, and these things are said of the purgatorial fire of tribulations, which befall the pious in this life. For these words are taken from Wisdom 3:5, where the subject is the tribulations which the souls of the pious endured in this life. Nothing therefore follows from the ambiguity of the word.

units.la: 77. Art. 58.[?] Necessario diuersi ignes esse debent.] necessario, inquis? nempe ex hypothesi diuersarum interpretationum quas ante comportasti atque commentus es.Atqui nos eas confutauimus: ergo inane est consequens ex antecedente falso. Et quis vnquā fando audiuit tam multas homonymias in vna eademque sententia ab homine prudente vsurpatas esse?itaque negamus hanc responsionem totam.
units.tr: 77. Art. 58. "Necessarily there must be different fires."] Necessarily, you say? Indeed, from the hypothesis of the different interpretations which you assembled and invented before. But we have refuted them; therefore the consequence is empty, following from a false antecedent. And who has ever heard of so many equivocations in one and the same sentence being used by a prudent man? So we deny this whole answer.

units.la: 78. Ibid. Sed allegans allusio mihi videtur esse in verbis Pauli.] Hæc verò non allusio,sed illusio dicenda est. Ne mireris,Lector: nos vnum ignem in verbis Pauli hac sententia tota agnoscimus, quia alucet nobis in eo videndo veritas simplicitásque Christi: Bellarminus multos ex vno construit, quia fumum cupit excitare qui tenebras offundat veritati & simplicitati cognitionis nostræ. Negamus iustam esse illam sequentem metaphrasin, quatot ignes, puta conflagrationis, iudicij, & purgationis, ex vno igne & vno in loco accenduntur.
units.tr: 78. Ibid. "But an allusion seems to me to be in the words of Paul."] This is not an allusion but should be called an illusion. Do not be surprised, reader: we recognise one fire in the words of Paul throughout this sentence, because the truth and simplicity of Christ shine for us in seeing it. Bellarmine builds many out of one, because he wants to raise a smoke that clouds the truth and the simplicity of our knowledge. We deny that the following metaphor is just, that as many fires (of conflagration, of judgment, and of purgation) are kindled from one fire and in one place.

units.la: 79. Art. 59. Non esse insuetum B. Paulo in eadem sententia vti varie aliquo nomine:
units.tr: 79. Art. 59. That it is not unusual for St Paul to use one name in various ways in the same sentence:

units.la: hæc propositio falsa est, præterquàm in rebus typicis & sacramentalibus. Hæc vnica est exceptio in testamento vetere & nouo obseruata, ad quam prius exemplum pertinet, quo Deus Pater fecilse Christum, qui non nouerat peccatum, pro nobis peccatum dicitur, 2. Corinth. 5. hoc Sacramentali genere loquutionum pleni sunt Scripturæ libri.
units.tr: This proposition is false, except in typical and sacramental matters. This is the one exception observed in the Old and New Testament, and to it belongs the first example, where God the Father is said to have made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us (2 Corinthians 5). The books of Scripture are full of this sacramental kind of speech.

units.la: 8o. Ibid. Rom. 8. De peccato damnauit peccatum.] Negatur hic varie peccatum accipi. Nam proprie illud membrum, ῥῶ ἀμαρτίας, & de peccato, ad antecedentia pertinet in hanc sententiam. Deum misisse Filium suum in similitudine carnis peccati, idque pro peccato: & ita distingui meminit Oecumenius. plana est sententia. Quod siquis tamen peruicaciter ad sequentia contendat pertinere, tamen etiam hoc modo negabitur variam esse nominis significationem: quemadmodum nec generis variat significatio, quum de hac & de illa specie distincte enunciatur. Itaque sensus futurus est, quem Chrysostomus, Theodoretus, & alij attulerunt: Deum condemnauisse in carne peccatu peccans etiam de peccato commisso, nempe τῷ ἐνεργοῦντι ἀεὶ τῆς ἐνεργείας, efficiens peccatum damnauisse de peccatis quæ effecit. Sic constans semper manet atque vnica significatio.
units.tr: 80. Ibid. Romans 8: "He condemned sin through sin."] It is denied here that sin is taken in different senses. For the clause "concerning sin" [περὶ ἁμαρτίας] properly belongs to what precedes in this sentence: that God sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and that as an offering for sin; and Oecumenius recalls the distinction in this way. The sense is plain. But if anyone stubbornly insists that it belongs to what follows, even so it will be denied that the meaning of the word varies; just as the meaning of a genus does not vary when it is stated distinctly of this species or of that. So the sense will be that which Chrysostom, Theodoret and others have brought forward: that God condemned sin in the flesh, the sin being committed also with regard to the sin committed, namely by the one who always works the working [τῷ ἐνεργοῦντι ἀεὶ τῆς ἐνεργείας], that is, by effecting, condemned sin in the sins which it effected. Thus the meaning remains constant and single.

units.la: 81. Art.60. Quod iudicium cum sit iustissimum, omnino aliqua poena eum afficit. ] Negatur argumentatio: Fallit enim ex elenchi ignoratione. Paulus agit de iudicio quod hic facit Spiritus Dei ex verbo per Ecclesiam ipsius: disputator verò de iudicio Dei futuro in altero seculo: quam sententiam ante confutauimus.
units.tr: 81. Art. 60. "Since this judgment is most just, it must inflict on him some punishment."] The argument is denied, for it fails through ignorance of the point at issue. Paul speaks of the judgment which the Spirit of God here carries out through the word, by his Church; the disputant speaks of God's future judgment in the other age. This opinion we have refuted before.

units.la: 82. Art. 61. Quo peruenit ad aliquem locum is qui transfit per ignem. ] Interpretationem negamus. Nō.n. dicit Apostolus, ὡς διὰ πυρός[?], sed simplicissimè, οὕτω δὲ ὡς διὰ πυρός[?]. Deinde verò hoc membrum ad verbum remotius pertinere docuimus ex Theodoreto suprà nota 65. Tum de igne futuro dici negauimus, & Bellarmini sententiam confutauimus inde à nota 43. saepius.
units.tr: 82. Art. 61. "To which he who passes through fire comes to some place."] We deny the interpretation. For the Apostle does not say "as through fire" [ὡς διὰ πυρός], but simply "yet so as through fire" [οὕτω δὲ ὡς διὰ πυρός]. Then we have shown that this clause refers rather remotely to the verb, from Theodoret, cited above at note 65. Moreover we have denied that it is said of future fire, and we have refuted Bellarmine's opinion, often, from note 43 onward.

units.la: 83. Ibid. Ad eum modum quo decet gloriosum esse Filium Patris unigenitum. ] Dispar est huius loci ratio, & friget interpretatio. Disparem locum esse vel eo euincitur, quòd verba Ioannis propria sunt, haec allegorica, ac non unius solum metaphorae: item quòd illa de proprietate personae Filij, haec de actionibus transeuntibus enunciantur, & similia. Frigere interpretationem res ipsa loquitur. Non enim satis est dici id quod Bellarminus adfert: sed ita dici oportuit, vidimus eum gloriosum diuina gloria: vt qui Filius est Patris unigenitus. Illud ὡς, sicut vel quasi non est similitudinis, sed veritatis & simplicis affirmationis: quemadmodum suo sermone Hebrei, & Graeci, & Latini obseruarunt hanc particulam accipi frequentissime.
units.tr: 83. Ibid. "In the manner which befits the Son of the Father, the only-begotten, to be glorious."] The reasoning of this passage is unlike, and the interpretation is weak. That the passages are unlike is shown even by this: John's words are proper, these are allegorical and not of one metaphor only; likewise, the former are said of the property of the person of the Son, these of transitive actions, and so on. That the interpretation is weak the matter itself makes plain. For it is not enough to say what Bellarmine brings forward; it had to be said thus: "we have seen him glorious with the divine glory," as he who is the only-begotten Son of the Father. That ὡς, "as" or "as if," is not of likeness but of truth and plain affirmation, as Hebrews, Greeks and Latins have observed in their own speech, that this particle is very often taken in this way.

units.la: IN CAP. VI.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER VI.

units.la: 1. Art.1. Hic locus aperte conuincit quod volumus. ] Negamus, & probationes confutabimus.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. This passage plainly proves what we want. ] We deny it, and we will refute the proofs.

units.la: 2. Art.2. Ita & Baptismus prodesset. de hac revidebitur lib.2.cap.15.& seq.
units.tr: 2. Art. 2. So also Baptism would profit. This will be reviewed in book 2, chapter 15 and following.

units.la: 3. Art.13. & pro mortuo sublatus fuit, vel pro mortuo lotus sepultusque fuit, etiamsi viueret. At hoc sensu non potest accipi praepositio Graecorum ὑπέρ. Graece autem scribebat Apostolus.
units.tr: 3. Art. 13. and was lifted up for the dead, or was washed and buried for the dead, even though he was alive. But the Greek preposition ὑπέρ cannot be taken in this sense. The Apostle, however, was writing in Greek.

units.la: 4. Art.14. Quid facient, qui orant, ieiunant, gemunt, affligunt se pro mortuis, si mortui non resurgunt? hac interpretationem genuinam negamus esse. Probationes audiamus.
units.tr: 4. Art. 14. What will they do who pray, fast, groan, and afflict themselves for the dead, if the dead do not rise? We deny that this is the genuine interpretation. Let us hear the proofs.

units.la: 5. Art.15. Luc.12. Baptismo habeo baptizari. Id quidem verum est baptizari accipi pro affligi: sed duobus modis disputator fallitur. Primum enim aliud est affligi ab alio quopiam, aliud seipsum affligere. Scriptura autem nusquam baptizandi verbum vsurpauit in causa eorum qui affligunt animas suas: sed de eis solum enunciat qui per alios affliguntur, & quasi merguntur aliena violentia. In hunc modum dicebat Christus, potestis bibere calicem, quem ego bibiturus sum, aliena opera praebitum, & baptismo quo ego baptizor, per summam iniuriam aliena mersus baptizari? Itemque illud apud Lucam, baptismo habeo baptizari, non autem meipsum baptizare, & in profundum illud barathrum mergere: nam propterea ibidem Christus subiicit, & quomodo constringor vsque quo perfectum sit? Seipsum cruci non affixit, nō afflixit Christus, sed afligendum affligendumque pro nobis tradidit: seipsum non mersit, sed mergi passus est pro nobis. Ex Scripturis triplex solum est Baptismus, aquae, Spiritus, & crucis siue martyrij: nemo se baptizat ipse aqua, nemo Spiritu: ergo nec cruce siue martyrio. Secundo aliud est baptizari illis modis modis ex Scripturę vsu:aliud secundùm accommo-dationem extensionémque allegoricam, qua Patres vsi sunt absque auctoritate Scripturę,vt Christianos animos ad refipiscentiam & adiumenta eius ἀναγωγ-ικῶς[?] proritarent. Negamus illam Patrum loquutionem ex Scripturis esse : imò ( vt ad rem veniamus propiùs) negamus hunc locum 1.Cor.15.ab vllo Pa-trum in hanc sententiam adductum esse. Itaque sal-sa probatio.
units.tr: 5. Art. 15. Luke 12. I have a baptism to be baptized with. It is true that "to be baptized" can mean "to be afflicted." But the disputant is misled in two ways. First, to be afflicted by someone else is one thing, and to afflict oneself is another. Scripture nowhere uses the word "baptize" of those who afflict their own souls. It speaks only of those who are afflicted by others and, as it were, sunk by another's violence. In this way Christ said, "Can you drink the cup that I am to drink?", meaning a cup handed to him by another's work, and "the baptism with which I am baptized", meaning one who is plunged by another's great injury. Likewise that passage in Luke, "I have a baptism to be baptized with", does not mean baptizing oneself and plunging oneself into that deep abyss. This is why Christ adds right there, "and how am I constrained until it is accomplished?" Christ did not fix himself to the cross or afflict himself. He gave himself up to be afflicted for us. He did not plunge himself under; he suffered himself to be plunged for us. Scripture recognises only a threefold baptism: of water, of the Spirit, and of the cross or martyrdom. No one baptizes himself with water, and no one with the Spirit; therefore neither does anyone baptize himself with the cross or martyrdom. Second, it is one thing to be baptized in these modes according to the usage of Scripture, and another thing according to the extended allegorical application which the Fathers used, without the authority of Scripture, to spur Christian souls on to repentance and its aids. We deny that this manner of speaking of the Fathers comes from Scripture. Indeed (to come closer to the matter) we deny that this passage, 1 Cor. 15, was ever cited by any of the Fathers in this sense. Therefore the proof is false.

units.la: 6. Ibid. Vocant pœnitentiam afflictionem Baptismum laboriosum,& secundam tabulam. ] non afflictionem istam externam, sed pœnitentiam ipsam. Et quidni priore nomine vocent Sacramentali modo, cum sit baptismus pœnitentiæ, Matth. 3. 11. & Marc. 1. 4. & pœnitentia sit perpetui baptismi nostri in Christo Iesu ? Rom. 6. posterior appellatio debetur Patrum allegoriis, de qua in tomum 3. videbitur.
units.tr: 6. Ibid. They call repentance affliction, a laborious baptism, and a second plank. ] Not that external affliction, but repentance itself. And why should they not call the former by that name in a sacramental way, since it is the baptism of repentance (Matt. 3:11; Mark 1:4), and repentance is the perpetual baptism of ours in Christ Jesus (Rom. 6)? The latter designation is owed to the allegories of the Fathers, which will be seen in volume 3.

units.la: 7. Ibid. Lacrymis, inquit, se baptizat.] Id est, tingit, mergit, abluit. quis negat fieri, quum hominem vere pœnitet mali sui? & propterea dicuntur lacrymarum rivi aut fluenta in Scripturis, quibus rigantur boni, vt Psalm. 6. 7. & alibi. de argumento sequentis loci dictum est nota 5.
units.tr: 7. Ibid. He baptizes himself, he says, with tears. ] That is, he dips, plunges, and washes. Who denies that this happens when a man truly repents of his evil? For this reason streams and floods of tears are spoken of in Scripture, by which the good are watered (Ps. 6:7 and elsewhere). The argument of the following passage has been dealt with at note 5.

units.la: 8. Ibid. Scio & quintum, lacrymarum & pœnitentia.] Allegoricè, vt nota 5. dicebamus, & oratoria, non autem simplicè propriáque accommodatione.
units.tr: 8. Ibid. I know also a fifth, of tears and repentance. ] Allegorically, as we said at note 5, and rhetorically, not by a simple and proper application.

units.la: 9. Art. 16. Ipsa pœna Purgatorij à Scriptura & Patribus vocatur baptisma:] Negatur: & quænam est, a-mabo, analogia inter Baptismum & pœnam Purga-torij?
units.tr: 9. Art. 16. The very pain of Purgatory is called baptism by Scripture and the Fathers. ] Denied. And what, pray, is the analogy between Baptism and the pain of Purgatory?

units.la: 10. Ibid. Spiritu sancto in hac vita: igne vero in futura:] hoc nusquam dicit Hieronymus: sed hæc illius verba, quæ Hieronymus non de suo sensu, sed alieno[?] magis enunciat, postquam probabiliorem adduxisset: siue quia in præsenti,Spiritu baptizamur: & in futuro,igne: Apostolo quoque huic sensui congruete,uniuscuiusq; opus quale sit,ignis probabit. Nō dicit, in præsenti,aut in futuro seculo,quod Bellarminus soniat[?]: sed in præsenti quum dicit,ad actionem præsentem Baptismi administrati respicit: in futuro autem, ad efficaciam ex baptismo consequuturam, quæ donatur ignis appellatione. Nam infans, exempli causa, quum baptizatur, communionem Spiritus accipit: quū vero baptizatus in Christo viuit, igne purgatur regiturque,id est,luce & efficacia accepti Spiritus, per iudicium ipsius contestans baptizati hominis conscientiæ:hæc efficacitas iudiciumque Spiritus ignis appellatur. Etsi hæc non est sententia Hieronymi: sed à Basilio est, qui mente suam apertius explicat dicens: αὐτὸς ὑμᾶς βαπτίσει ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ καὶ πυρί. τὸ δὲ πυρὸς βάπτισμα τῶν ἐν τῇ χρίσει λέγων, καὶ δὴ φησιν ὁ Σωτήρ, ἐκάστου τὸ ἔργον ἐπὶ τὸ πῦρ αὐτὸ δοκιμάσει καὶ πάλιν ἡ ἡμέρα δηλώσει [?]. id est, ille vos baptizabit in Spiritu sancto & igne: baptisma ignis vocans probationem quæ fit in iudicio (ad verbum:non dicit autem, futuro) id est, iudicio mentis Christianæ iam prius illustratæ communione Spiritus in baptismo: quemadmodum dicit Apostolus, uniuscuiusque opus quale sit,ignis probabit ipsum,siue per Spiritum intus in ipso,siue foris per ministerium aliorum prælucens: & rursum,nam dies palam faciet,quia reuelatur igne; nimirum Spiritus Dei efficaciter omnia illustrantis. Igne ergo vocat illa efficacitate Spiritus iudicia siue priuata cuiusque,siue communia Ecclesiæ illustrantem. Quòd & Bellarminus huic interpretationi credidit, quid causæ est cur huic loco quartum huius libri caput non asignauerit? cur primũ probationum locum, hoc omissò, ex Matth.12. placuit adducere? Bedæ ignosco, vel potius seculo iam obuoluto hac tenebrarum nube & fumo Purgatoriali, quum ita incertus scriberet.
units.tr: 10. Ibid. By the Holy Spirit in this life, by fire in the future. ] Jerome nowhere says this. These are rather his words, which he does not put forward in his own sense but reports in another's, after he had first adduced a more probable view: "either because in the present we are baptized with the Spirit, and in the future with fire; the Apostle also agrees with this sense: each one's work, of whatever sort it is, fire will test." He does not say "in the present age" or "in the future age", as Bellarmine babbles. When he says "in the present", he looks to the present action of the baptism administered. "In the future", however, he looks to the efficacy that follows from baptism, which is given the name of fire. For an infant, for example, when baptized, receives communion of the Spirit. But when the baptized person lives in Christ, he is purged and ruled by fire, that is, by the light and efficacy of the Spirit received, which, through its judgment, bears witness to the conscience of the baptized man. This efficacy and judgment of the Spirit is called fire. Yet this is not Jerome's own view. It comes from Basil, who explains his mind more openly, saying: "He himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and in fire" [αὐτὸς ὑμᾶς βαπτίσει ἐν πνεύματι ἁγίῳ καὶ πυρί]. Calling it the baptism of fire, he means the testing that takes place in judgment. And the Saviour says, "each one's work by fire will test it", and again, "the day will declare it." That is, the judgment of the Christian mind, already enlightened beforehand by communion of the Spirit in baptism. (He does not say "future" here.) As the Apostle says, "each one's work, of whatever sort it is, fire will test it", either through the Spirit within a man or from outside through the ministry of others shining before him; and again, "for the day will make it plain, because it is revealed by fire", that is, by the Spirit of God, who efficaciously illuminates all things. So he calls by the name of fire those judgments, whether private of each person or common of the Church, which the efficacy of the Spirit illuminates. Since Bellarmine too believed this interpretation, why did he not assign this passage to the fourth chapter of this book? Why did he choose to bring forward first the proof-text from Matthew 12, leaving this one out? I pardon Bede, or rather the age already wrapped in this cloud and smoke of Purgatory, since he wrote so uncertainly.

units.la: 11. Ibid. Vocat ignem Purgatorij in alia vita vltimum baptisma.] falsum. sic vocat Nazianzenus ignem æternum, in quem maligni & impœnitentes coniiciuntur cum diabolo & Angelis eius, vt docet consequutio sermonis illius, & in eum locum Nicetas expósuit. Nam postquam Nouatianos ad resipiscentiam prouocauit, illico subiicit: εἰ δὲ μὴ, τῷ ἑαυτῷ προ-πευσάμενον[?]. Τυχὸν ἐκεῖ τῷ πνεύματι βαπτισθήσονται[?] τῷ πλευσματι[?] βαπτισθῆναι τῷ ὑπομονητικῷ καὶ μακροθύμῳ[?], ὡς ἐδει ὡς χρόνου τῶν ὕλων[?], καὶ ἀναλαμβάνεται κακίας κουφότητα[?]. Sin minus, inquit, erant via suam fortasse illic baptizabuntur igne illo vltimo, baptizmate illo laboriosiore atque longiore, quod exedit materiam vt gramen, & absumit omnis malitiæ leuitatem. Hæc qui de igne Purgatorij accipiunt, dum Nouatianis impœnitentibus aperiunt Purgatorium, plane sapiunt Origenem, salutem danatis post tempus promittentes. Sequens itaque conclusio, ἐλίκτα, καὶ οὐδὲν ὑμεῖς[?].
units.tr: 11. Ibid. He calls the fire of Purgatory in the other life the last baptism. ] False. Gregory Nazianzen calls the eternal fire by that name, into which the malicious and impenitent are cast together with the devil and his angels, as the sequence of that discourse shows, and Nicetas expounded it on that very passage. For after he had called the Novatians to repentance, he at once adds: "But if not, perhaps there they will be baptized with that last fire, a more laborious and longer baptism, which eats up matter like grass and consumes all the lightness of malice." Those who take this of the fire of Purgatory, while they open Purgatory to the impenitent Novatians, plainly savour of Origen, who promises salvation to the damned after a time. Therefore the following conclusion is false.

units.la: 12. Art. 17. Quia hæc expositio maximè quadrat cum sequentibus.] Negamus quadrare: nam sequentia Pauli verba ad argumentationem eandem pertinet, vt ostendit particula καὶ. Disputator vero sic facit alterum argumentationis locum.
units.tr: 12. Art. 17. Because this exposition agrees best with what follows. ] We deny that it agrees. For the following words of Paul belong to the same argument, as the particle "and" [καί] shows. The disputant, however, makes the second place of argument in this way.

units.la: 13. Art. 18. Eadem est cum illa 2. ⁊Mach.12. si mortui non resurgunt, superfluum est & vanum orare pro mortuis:] Negatur: nam Pauli dictum verum est: Lafonis vero Cyrenæi & epitomarij illius falsa asse[?] tio, ut supra cap.3. ostendimus.
units.tr: 13. Art. 18. It is the same as that second one, 2 Macc. 12: if the dead do not rise, it is superfluous and vain to pray for the dead. ] Denied. Paul's saying is true. But the assertion of Lafonis the Cyrenian and of that epitomiser is false, as we showed above in chapter 3.

units.la: 14. Art. 19. Sed à consuetudine Iudæorum,] Quasi vero etiam ab incredulis reiici non æquè potuisset exemplū Iudæorum: deinde verò negamus Iudæos fecisse, qui quidem bene fuerunt instituti, aut ex authenticis libris ullum exemplum, auctoritatem, rationémve adferri posse. Narrat disputator somnia vigilantium.
units.tr: 14. Art. 19. But from the custom of the Jews. ] As if the example of the Jews could not equally well have been rejected even by unbelievers! Moreover, we deny that the Jews did this, since they were indeed well instructed; nor can any example, authority or reason be adduced from authentic books. The disputant recounts the dreams of waking men.

units.la: 15. Art. 20. Cùm testimonium ex libris Machabæorum exponeremus. ] Dicendum fuerat, ex libro Machab. sed plurale melius sonat scilicet, rem verò confutauimus supra cap.3. nota 17. & seq. Falsa igitur conclusio. Dices, Et quænam igitur est loci Paulini sententia? Respondeo, errauit Bellarminus calculo, & interpretatione. Calculo: nam plures loci illius interpretationes extant. Interpretatione: quia nec Paulum, nec Chrysostomum & Theophylactū interpretatur bene. Possem de Oecumenio & Photio dicere: sed isti tam obscurè in eum locum scripserunt, ut quæstiones videatur ferere, qui ex eis probationem petit. Sunt igitur aliæ interpretationes: nam verbum βαπτίζεσθαι[?], aliis est baptizari, aliis affligi, aliis ablui solemni lotionum usu quæ in cadauera humana fuerunt obseruata, siue à Iudæis, siue à Gentibus. Præpositio ὑπὲρ[?] aliis est super, aliis pro: sed istud, pro, varie exponitur, pro iuuandis mortuis, mortuorum loco: pro afferenda & probanda mortuorum causa qui mortem pro Christiana fide & spe resurrectionis oppetierint, & similia. Vocem denique mortuorum alij proprie acceperunt, alij figurate. Qui proprie, aut de corporibus mortuis acceperunt, quod verbis Pauli non satis conuenit, ut Bellarminus recte obseruauit, aut de personis, fi[?]e omnibus universe, sive (quod melius) electis, & qui in fide remissionis peccatorum, resurrectionis carnis, & vitæ æternæ in Christo sunt vita functi.
units.tr: 15. Art. 20. When we were expounding the testimony from the books of the Maccabees. ] It should have said "from the book of the Maccabees", but the plural sounds better, namely... the matter we refuted above in chapter 3, note 17 and following. The conclusion is therefore false. You will ask, "What then is the sense of the Pauline passage?" I answer that Bellarmine erred in his reckoning and in his interpretation. In reckoning, because several interpretations of that passage exist. In interpretation, because he interprets neither Paul nor Chrysostom and Theophylact well. I could say something about Oecumenius and Photius, but they wrote so obscurely on that passage that anyone who seeks proof from them seems to be seeking questions. There are therefore other interpretations. For the verb [βαπτίζεσθαι] some take as "to be baptized", others as "to be afflicted", and others as "to be washed by the solemn custom of washings which were observed for human corpses, whether by Jews or by Gentiles." The preposition [ὑπέρ] some take as "over", others as "for". That "for" is variously explained: for helping the dead, in the place of the dead; for pleading and proving the cause of the dead who suffered death for the Christian faith and the hope of resurrection; and the like. Finally, some took "the dead" properly, others figuratively. Those who took it properly, either of dead bodies, which does not fit Paul's words well, as Bellarmine rightly observed, or of persons, whether all universally or (what is better) the elect, and those who have departed this life in faith in the remission of sins, the resurrection of the flesh and eternal life in Christ.

units.la: Qui figurate, aut pro fide resurrectionis mortuo-rum acceperunt, aut (quod certius) pro fide Chri-stiana tota, cuius signaculum est in confessione Christianæ fidei credere nos remissionem peccato-rum, resurrectionem carnis, & vitam æternam, ut Chrysostomus disertissime, & breviùs post eum Theophylactus explicauit. Nam cætera se dissimulare propter auditores, qui nondum ad baptismum venerant, Chrysostomus aperte pronunciat. Etsi ergo accepit ille, baptizari pro mortuis, pro eo quod est baptizari pro corporibus nostris (quæ mortua futura sunt) in spem resurrectionis futuræ, ut idem exprimit evidentissime in 1. Cor. 10. homil. 23. tamen substantia interpretationis illius est, agere Paulum de baptismo communi nostro in fidem Christia-nam & spem resurrectionis futurę. Quid ergo? nem-pe argumentatur Apostolus ab eo quod faciunt pij, postquam argumentationes à resurrectione Chri-sti, prædicatione Dei per seruos suos, & fide communi Ecclesiæ piorúmque in ea attulisset. Quid faciunt pij? baptizantur, inquit, pro mortuis, id est, pro fide resurrectionis mortuorum, in qua tam multi sunt mortui, & se ipsi pro eis, id est, pro contestanda communi eorum & sua fide paratos mori profitentur in Christo, ut mortuorum primitiis. Atque in hunc sensum duplex est argumentatio: prior, cur illi se curant baptizari? quo fine? euentu? posterior, cur Ecclesia baptizat? qua fide? quo iure? Atque hæc pia est interpretatio: cui nihil aliud aduersari videtur posse, quàm illud, quod de quibusdam videtur Paulus agere, non de communi Baptismi Christia- ni lege. Quanquam & hoc responderi potest, com- munem seculorum omnium doctrinam in Ecclesia de resurrectione mortuorum affirmari à præsente vsu Ecclesiæ, per recentem Christi institutionem, veritatemq; & complementu illius obsignato. Alte- ra tamen mihi magis probatur interpretatio de cru- ce & afflictionibus Christianorum, qui pro defen- sione & assertione Christi piorumque in Christo dormiétium perpetiebantur omnia ab infidelibus.
units.tr: Those who have taken it figuratively have understood it either as the faith of the resurrection of the dead, or (what is more certain) as the whole Christian faith, whose seal is the confession that in the creed we believe in the forgiveness of sins, the resurrection of the flesh, and eternal life. Chrysostom explained this most eloquently, and Theophylact more briefly after him. For Chrysostom plainly says that the other matters were passed over because of the hearers, who had not yet come to baptism. So although he took baptized for the dead to mean baptized for our bodies, which are destined to die, in hope of the future resurrection, as he expresses most clearly in his homily 23 on 1 Cor. 10, nevertheless the substance of that interpretation is that Paul is speaking of our common baptism into the Christian faith and the hope of the future resurrection. What then? Plainly the Apostle argues from what the godly do, after he had brought forward arguments from the resurrection of Christ, from God's preaching through his servants, and from the common faith of the Church and of the godly within it. What do the godly do? They are baptized, he says, for the dead, that is, for the faith of the resurrection of the dead, in which so many are dead; and they profess that they themselves are ready to die in Christ for them, that is, to bear witness to their common faith and their own, as the firstfruits of the dead. In this sense the argument is twofold: the first, why do they take care to be baptized? To what end, with what outcome? The second, why does the Church baptize? On what faith, by what right? This is a godly interpretation, to which nothing seems able to be opposed except that Paul appears to be speaking of certain people, not of the common law of Christian baptism. Yet this too may be answered: the common doctrine of all ages in the Church concerning the resurrection of the dead is affirmed by the Church's present practice, through the recent institution of Christ, and its truth and completion is sealed by that practice. Still, the other interpretation, concerning the cross and the afflictions of Christians, who suffered everything from unbelievers in defence and assertion of Christ and of the godly who sleep in Christ, seems to me more acceptable.

units.la: Alioqui, ait Apostolus, si non est resurrectio mortuorum, quid facturi sunt, qui baptizantur pro illis mortuis, id est, affliguntur, pro defensione resurrectionis Christi & Sanctorum omnium qui iam obdormierunt in Christo? Si omnino mortui non resurgunt, vlli, cur baptizantur pro illis mortuis, & crucem sufferunt in communione Christi pro illis mortuis & fide eorum afferenda? Confirmat hanc interpretationem sequens hypothesis du- plex. Vna ab exemplo & facto Apostolorum omnium: cur etiam nos periclitamur omni momento? altera à singulari Pauli, Diebus singulis morior, &c. quem ordinem prudentissimè Chrysostomus obseruauit. Nam illa thesis, resurrectionem mortuorum probari pietate illorum qui nullam refugiunt crucem vt fidem suam & communem piorum obsignent perpesionibus etiam cruentæ mortis: confirmatur communi Apostolorum atque seruorum Dei hypothesi, & ipsius Pauli singulari quàm potentissimè.
units.tr: Otherwise, says the Apostle, if there is no resurrection of the dead, what will those do who are baptized for those dead, that is, who are afflicted for the defence of the resurrection of Christ and of all the saints who have already fallen asleep in Christ? If the dead do not rise at all, why are they baptized for those dead, and why do they endure the cross in the fellowship of Christ for those dead and for the maintenance of their faith? The following twofold supposition confirms this interpretation. The first is drawn from the example and practice of all the Apostles: why are we also in danger every hour? The second is drawn from Paul's own singular case: I die daily, and so on, an order which Chrysostom observed most wisely. For that thesis, that the resurrection of the dead is proved by the piety of those who shrink from no cross, so as to seal their faith and the common faith of the godly even by sufferings of bloody death, is confirmed by the common supposition of the Apostles and servants of God, and by Paul's own singular case, as powerfully as possible.

units.la: IN CAPUT VII.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER VII.

units.la: 1, Art.3. Eam simpliciter non esse probabilem.]
units.tr: 1, Art. 3. That it is simply not probable.

units.la: Hoc verum esse negamus: nam recte Chrysostomus interpretatur, & ex mente Christi.
units.tr: We deny that this is true: for Chrysostom interprets rightly, and in accordance with the mind of Christ.

units.la: 2. Ibid. & magna ex parte hunc sermonem esse metaphoricum:] hanc interpretationis viam negamus. De Hilario quod dicit, falsum est: nam vtitur quidem hac loquutione, in omni vitæ nostra via: sed eodem sensu quo vulgo dicitur, toto vitæ curriculo. Alioquin & puram interpretationem loci seruat Hilarius, vt propriam, & alteram subiungit latiorem analogicè: quod Bellarmino obseruare oportuit. Alij aut non sunt interpretati, sed alluserunt, vt postea common-strabimus, aut allegorico sensu allato proprium non excluserunt, quod iniquum foret: aut denique, vt re-centiores, ad solam allegoriam hæc Christi verba retulerunt, quod imprudens & ludicrum.
units.tr: 2. Ibid. And for the most part this saying is metaphorical:] We deny this way of interpreting it. What he says about Hilary is false: for Hilary does indeed use this expression, in every way of our life, but in the same sense in which it is commonly said, through the whole course of life. Moreover Hilary keeps the plain interpretation of the passage as the proper one, and then adds a wider, analogical one; Bellarmine ought to have noticed this. Others either did not interpret at all but merely played with the text, as we shall show later, or, having offered an allegorical sense, did not exclude the proper one, which would be unfair; or finally, like the more recent writers, they referred these words of Christ to allegory alone, which is careless and frivolous.

units.la: 3. Ibid. Quod non soleat Dominus tam serio docere & instruere humanam prudentiam,] Prudentiam, inquis? at iustitiam hic docebat & asserebat Christus contra præstigiarum Pharisaicarum figmenta: qua de iustitia dixerat prius ibidem versu 20. Alia est iustitiæ causa, quam lex docuerat verè, & Pharisæi corruperant: alia humanæ prudentiæ. Falsa igitur defensio.
units.tr: 3. Ibid. That the Lord does not usually teach and instruct human prudence so seriously,] Prudence, you say? But here Christ was teaching and asserting justice, against the Pharisaic juggling tricks; concerning that justice he had said before, in the same place, verse 20. The cause of justice is one thing, which the law had truly taught and the Pharisees had corrupted; the cause of human prudence is another. The defence is therefore false.

units.la: 4. Si loqueretur de humano iudicio.] & hoc falsum. Nam agebat Christus de iustitia secundum veritatem legis: qua nihil gravius, si veritatem fidei exceperis. Et quanto gravius, obsecro, videtur illud Matth. 6. 2. Amen dico vobis, receperunt mercedem suam? & similia multa. Deinde quàm prudenter iste exempla hominum & facta illegitima profert, vt eleuet iustitiæ diuinæ ex lege veritatem? hic [illegible, ~3 letters] scilicet,
units.tr: 4. If he were speaking of human judgement.] This too is false. For Christ was speaking of justice according to the truth of the law, than which nothing is weightier, if you except the truth of faith. And how much weightier, I beg you, does that saying of Matt. 6. 2 seem: Amen I say to you, they have received their reward? and many similar sayings. Then how wisely does this man bring forward examples of men and unlawful deeds, in order to exalt the truth of divine justice from the law? Here [illegible, about three letters], of course.

units.la: 5. Art. 4. Pro is autem qua habentur Luca 12. nul[?] lo modo recipi posse:] negamus hoc dictum,& proba-tiones eius.
units.tr: 5. Art. 4. But for those things which are found in Luke 12, in no way can it be accepted:] We deny this statement, and its proofs.

units.la: 6. Ibid. ¶At Luc.12. Dominus loquitur de futuro iudicio:] non sequitur, si vno aut altero in loco loquitur de iudicio futuro, ergo totâ oratione de eo loqui & singulas partes eius. Præterea non sunt illa eiusdem sermonis. Nam sermonis illius Christi principium est à versu 54. quum ait Lucas, dicebat autem etiam turbâ, Quum videritis nubem exorientem,&c. Ergo ne de futuro quidem iudicio in toto illo ser-mone loquitur. Nam sermo ille postremus Christi duas habet vniuersè partes: vnam, de agnoscendo aduentu Christi & tempore Euangelij: alteram, de agnoscenda vera iustitia & regula vitæ ex veritate legis, quam Pharisæi corrumpebant. Hoc vtroque nomine turbas communiter reprehendit Christus, & ad sensum meliorem fidei & resipiscentiæ Chri-stianæ reuocat secundum Deum. Falsa igitur se-quentia.
units.tr: 6. Ibid. But in Luke 12 the Lord speaks of the future judgement:] It does not follow that, because in one or another place he speaks of the future judgement, therefore he speaks of it in the whole discourse and in each of its parts. Moreover these are not parts of the same discourse. For the beginning of that discourse of Christ is at verse 54, where Luke says: And he also said to the crowds, When you see a cloud rising, and so on. Therefore he does not even speak of the future judgement throughout that whole discourse. For this final discourse of Christ has, taken altogether, two parts: one concerning recognising the coming of Christ and the time of the Gospel; the other concerning recognising true justice and the rule of life from the truth of the law, which the Pharisees were corrupting. On both counts Christ rebukes the crowds in general, and calls them back to the better sense of Christian faith and repentance according to God. The sequence is therefore false.

units.la: 7. Ibid. Liberandi se à creditore antequam ad iudi-cium veniatur.] Argumentatio falsa ex falsa loci interpretatione, quem locum proximè præcedente nota exposuimus.
units.tr: 7. Ibid. To free oneself from the creditor before one comes to judgement.] The argument is false, arising from a false interpretation of the passage, which we explained in the immediately preceding note.

units.la: 8. Ibid. Rectè intelligi per viam, vitam: per iudicem, Deum, &c.] Negatur: nam primùm ex suo sensu Chrysostomum sequuntur: deinde verò sensum alienum referunt. Sic enim Theophylactus prius quidem ex sententia sua, inquit, [illegible, ~24 letters], &c. demonstrat etiam inculpatam pacem, &c. Secundò autem ad sententiam aliorum transit, dicens, [illegible, ~18 letters], &c. nec se-cus Euthymius.
units.tr: 8. Ibid. That by the way one rightly understands life, and by the judge God, etc.] Denied: for first they follow Chrysostom in his own sense, and then they report another's sense. For Theophylact first, indeed, from his own opinion, says [illegible, about 24 letters], etc., he also shows a blameless peace, and so on. Secondly, however, he passes to the opinion of others, saying [illegible, about 18 letters], etc. Euthymius does the same.

units.la: 9. Art. §. & Hieronymus in epist. 8. ad Demetriadem.] Origenes quàm miserè hunc locum exponit, & [illegible, ~8 letters], ne Bellarminus quidem non videt: quid ergo efficiat eius auctoritas? Origenis vestigia pressit Ambrosius, eodem pelago allegoriarum mersus plus satis: etsi allegoriam illius noua cumulat allegoria. De Euthymio & Theophylacto falsum, vt nota 8.diximus. Hieronymus ad Demetriadem rhetoricatur, alludens quidem ad hunc locum, sed non ex professo (vt loquuntur) interpretans. Aliud est [illegible, ~8 letters], aliud [illegible, ~8 letters]. Nec temerè iudicium suum Erasmus suspendit de hac epistola.
units.tr: 9. Art. §. And Jerome in letter 8 to Demetrias.] How wretchedly Origen expounds this passage, and [illegible, about 8 letters], even Bellarmine does not see: what then does his authority achieve? Ambrose trod in Origen's footsteps, plunged in the same sea of allegories more than enough, although he piles up new allegory upon allegory. What is said of Euthymius and Theophylact is false, as we noted in note 8. Jerome in his letter to Demetrias uses rhetorical display, alluding indeed to this passage, but not expounding it professedly, as they say. One thing is [illegible, about 8 letters], another [illegible, about 8 letters]. Nor did Erasmus rashly suspend his judgement about this letter.

units.la: 10. Ibid. Coa[?]tius, est error impressorum, & debet legi, cautius.] Nobis vero pluris est librorum omnium veterum consentiens auctoritas, quàm Bellarmini sententia. Sic destituuntur, non restituuntur bonorū libri. Quinetiam ipse Hieronymus auctor est idoneus licentię isti coercendę. Nam sententiam suam primum his verbis attulit: Ex praecedentibus autem & consequentibus manifestum est sensus: quòd nos Dominus atque Saluator noster, dum in illius seculi via currimus, ad pacem & ad concordiam cohortetur, &c. Postea vero concludens hanc interpretationem, quam suam esse probauit, & transiturus ad alias quas improbat, sic ait: Cum hac manifesta sit & consequens intelligentia, plerique arbitrantur de carne dictum & anima, &c. Tres alias interpretationes accumulans: in quibus ne probabile quidem est laudandis aut coparandis eum occupare sese voluisse. Deinde esto sane, dixerit cautius: nonne est etiam cautela mala, ac non laudabilis? Nihil profecto apud bonos & prudentes atque intelligentes viros assequetur disputator bellis istis cautelis suis.
units.tr: 10. Ibid. Coa[?]tius is a printer's error, and it ought to be read cautius.] For us, however, the consenting authority of all the old books is worth more than Bellarmine's opinion. So the books of good authors are deprived, not restored. Indeed Jerome himself is a suitable witness against this licence. For he first set out his opinion in these words: From what goes before and what follows, the sense is plain: that our Lord and Saviour, while we run in the way of this age, exhorts us to peace and to concord, and so on. Later, however, concluding this interpretation, which he proved to be his own, and about to pass to the others which he rejects, he says: Since this meaning is plain and consistent, many think that it was said of flesh and soul, and so on. He then piles up three other interpretations, among which there is not even a probable one which he wished to occupy himself in praising or comparing. Next, granted that he said cautius: is not caution also a bad thing, and not commendable? Certainly the disputant will achieve nothing before good and wise and intelligent men with these cautions of his in his wars.

units.la: II. Art. 6. Respondet Hieronymus,
units.tr: II. Art. 6. Jerome replies,

units.la: Sed alludens apud virginem rhetoricè, non apud doctos neruosè argumentans, vt supra nota 9. dicebamus.
units.tr: But he is arguing by allusion before a girl, rhetorically, not by sinewy argument before the learned, as I said above at note 9.

units.la: 12. Art. 7. Alterum hominem, qui nimirum nos laesit, aut nos illum.] Posterius verò est in hoc quidem loco: nam Christus ei qui offendit alterum consulit: vt totus ille sermo docet euidentissimè. De eo qui offensus est agit Christus. Matth. 18. 15.
units.tr: 12. Art. 7. The other man, who of course has wronged us, or we him.] The latter applies in this place. For Christ advises the one who has given offence to another, as that whole discourse teaches very plainly. Christ is speaking of the one who has been offended. Matt. 18.15.

units.la: 13. Ibid. Et cum quo semper possumus concordare, dum via durat:] Illa vox semper, adtexitur praeter me-tem & argumentum Christi: nec verò conuenire potest cum altera voce cito, qua Christus vtitur dicendo, compone cum aduersario tuo cito, &c. Matt. 5. 25.
units.tr: 13. Ibid. And with whom we can always agree, while the way lasts:] That word always is added beyond the meaning and argument of Christ, and it cannot agree with the other word quickly, which Christ uses when he says, make terms with your adversary quickly, etc. Matt. 5.25.

units.la: 14. Art. 8. Quia non proprie vnus homo tradet alterum Deo iudici:] Responsio hæc aliena est, & falsa. Aliena: nam Christus non agit de Deo iudice, sed de iudice humano simpliciter, qui inter ἀντιδίκους interponit iudicium suum. Falsa: nam etiam vnus homo alterum potest, imò alios tradere Deo iudici iusta expostulatione sua, prout ἀντίδικοι possunt tradere aduersarios suos, & figuratè dicuntur posse.
units.tr: 14. Art. 8. Because one man does not strictly hand another over to God the judge:] This answer is foreign and false. Foreign, because Christ is not speaking of God as judge, but of a human judge in general, who interposes his own judgment between the [antidikous] (adversaries). False, because even one man can hand another over, indeed many others, to God the judge by his just complaint, just as [antidikoi] (adversaries) can hand over their opponents, and are figuratively said to be able to do so.

units.la: 15. Art. 9. Aduersarium esse Dei legem, siue Deum ipsum,] negamus hanc iustam esse interpretationem loci. Nam 1. (vt verbis vtar Hieronymi) consequens intelligentia plane diuersa est. 2. Dei lex per se est bona, sancta, iusta, & boni sancti iustique index atque administra. Deus est dominus: conscientia, internus testis: nihil horum est hominis aduersarium, nisi per accidens, id est, nisi homo ipse sibi prius aduersetur & saluti suae. 3. allegorica interpretatio nec anteponi genuinae debet, nec eam potest euertere. hac Ambrosius, Beda, &c. vsi sunt. Anselmum aliter interpretari ipse disputator annotauit supra artic. 7. sed Anselmus sibi non satis constat in sua illa interpretatione. Augustinus lib.i.de serm. Dom.in mo-te, quantum hic fluctuet allegoriis quisquis legere volet, statim animadversurus est. aliis in locis allu-dit ἀλληγορίζων[?], non interpretatur accurate hoc præ-ceptum Christi. Gregorij & Bernardi eadem ratio. hi omnes dicunt quod verum est de re quodammodo, sed non quod huius loci verum sit interpretamentum.
units.tr: 15. Art. 9. That the adversary is God's law, or God himself,] we deny that this is a just interpretation of the passage. For, (to use Jerome's words) first, the consequent understanding is plainly different. Second, God's law is in itself good, holy, just, and is the index and administrator of what is good, holy and just. God is the Lord; conscience is the inner witness. None of these is a man's adversary, except by accident, that is, unless the man himself first opposes himself and his own salvation. Third, an allegorical interpretation ought neither to be preferred to the genuine one nor can it overturn it. Ambrose, Bede, and others used this. The disputant himself noted above at art. 7 that Anselm interprets otherwise, but Anselm is not wholly consistent with himself in that interpretation. Whoever wishes to read Augustine's first book on the Sermon on the Mount will at once notice how much he wavers among allegories. In other places he alludes allegorically [allegorizōn?] and does not interpret this precept of Christ accurately. Gregory and Bernard have the same reasoning. All of these say what is true of the matter in some way, but not what is the true interpretation of this passage.

units.la: 16 Art.10. vt etiam recordaretur reconciliari cum Deo, sive cum eius lege.] negatur hoc sibi Christum eo in loco voluisse. Quid enim? annon is qui affert munus suum ad altare opera etiam daturus fuisset suæ cum Deo reconciliationi? non potest profecto ista interpretatio cum verbis antecedentibus conve-nire.
units.tr: 16. Art. 10. That he should also remember to be reconciled with God, or with his law.] It is denied that Christ meant this in that place. For what? Would not the man who brings his gift to the altar also be about to give, by his works, his reconciliation with God? Certainly that interpretation cannot agree with the preceding words.

units.la: 17 Ibid. Lucæ 12.non possumus intelligere,nisi legem Dei,aut conscientiam.] hoc falsi evicimus supra nota 6.
units.tr: 17. Ibid. Luke 12. We cannot understand except God's law or conscience.] We have shown this to be false above at note 6.

units.la: 18 Art.11. convenient omnes iudicem esse [Christum:] omnes quidem iudicem agnoscunt Christum qui Christiani sunt;sed non omnes conveniunt huc locum agere de iudice Christo. Nam Chrysostomus, Hieronymus; Theophylactus, Euthymius, alij sunt aliter interpretati; quorum expositio est cum mente Christi consentiens.
units.tr: 18. Art. 11. All agree that the judge is [Christ]: All who are Christians acknowledge Christ as judge, but not all agree that this passage is about Christ as judge. For Chrysostom, Jerome, Theophylact, Euthymius and others have interpreted it differently, and their exposition agrees with the mind of Christ.

units.la: 19. Art.12. utrumque est probabil[?]] imo vero utrumque allegoricum, & a mente Christi & veritate rei alienissimum.
units.tr: 19. Art. 12. Each is probable] Indeed each is allegorical, and most alien both to the mind of Christ and to the truth of the matter.

units.la: 20 Art. 13. carcerem esse infernum, in quo tamen multa sunt mansiones, alia pro damnatis, alia pro his qui purgantur.] negamus ista omnia: & aliena esse a consilio Christi. tum ipsa consequentia argumen-tationis ostendit, tum optime viderunt annotaquerúntquɔ illi Patres quorum nomina modò attuli-mus.
units.tr: 20. Art. 13. That the prison is hell, in which nevertheless there are many mansions, some for the damned and others for those who are being purged.] We deny all of these things, and that they are foreign to the purpose of Christ. The very sequence of the argument shows this, and those Fathers whose names I have just mentioned observed it very well.

units.la: Art.14. per nouissimum quadrantem intelligi minuta peccata, & hoc alienum à mente Christi, vt iidem Patres scitè obseruarunt. Sed & Augustinus (quem iste slagellat postea) interpretationem alteram meliorem adsert dilemmaticè, quæ hic dissimulatur malè. Sic enim ille lib.1.de sermone Dom. in monte: De soluendo autem, inquit, nouissimo quadrante, potest non absurdè intelligi, aut pro eo positum quod nihil relinquitur impunitum, sicut loquentes etiam dicimus vsque adsœcem, quum volumus exprimere aliquid ita exactum vt nihil relinqueretur: vel vt significarentur, &c. est autem verissima ꝗ illa interpretatio.
units.tr: Art. 14. That by the last farthing are meant small sins, and this is foreign to the mind of Christ, as those same Fathers shrewdly observed. But Augustine too (whom this man afterwards flails) offers a better alternative interpretation by way of a dilemma, which here is badly concealed. For he says in the first book of his On the Sermon on the Mount: Concerning paying the last farthing, it can not absurdly be understood either as put for the sense that nothing is left unpunished, just as we also say "down to the dregs" when we want to express something so exact that nothing is left over; or to signify, etc. And that interpretation is most true.

units.la: Ibid. an hæc solutio fiat in gehenna, an in Purgatorio? Vtrumque negamus, quia repugnat germanæ Christi & loci totius sententiæ; vt supra diximus agi de humana fratrum reconciliatione, quam in hac vita fieri natura, charitas, iustitia, & pietas iubent & ita accipi exempla iubent sequentia.
units.tr: Ibid. Whether this payment is made in gehenna or in Purgatory? We deny both, because they conflict with the genuine sense of Christ and of the whole passage; as we said above, the passage is about the human reconciliation of brothers, which nature, charity, justice and piety bid us make in this life, and the examples that follow bid us take it so.

units.la: Ibid. cognouit eam Joseph. &c. Hanc interpretationem Augustinus nō affirmatè attulit, sed dilemmaticè; & veriorem priore membro dilemmatis posuerat, vt nota 21.retulimus. quamobrem de ea minimè laboramus.
units.tr: Ibid. Joseph knew her, etc. Augustine did not assert this interpretation outright but by way of a dilemma; and he had put the truer one in the first part of the dilemma, as we reported at note 21. Therefore we are not at all concerned about it.

units.la: Art.16. Tertia hæc sententia est omnium verissima. negamus hoc dictum, & probationes illius.
units.tr: Art. 16. This third opinion is by far the truest. We deny this statement, and its proofs.

units.la: Ibid. manendum in carcere Purgatorij adsummum, vsque ad refurrestionem. locus est apud Tertullianū lib.de anima ca.35. Sed heus tu, an nō vides Tertullianū agere ex hypothesi falsæ interpretationis, quā fabricat erat Carpocrates, vt principio capitis pitis retulerat? Ex illa ipsa interpretatione summus ille argumentandi artifex Carpocratem suo iugulat gladio; non suam interpretationem adferens, quam expressit magis lib. de patientia cap. 12. sed Carpocratianam elidens de suo. Demonstrant eiusde verba lib. de anima, cap. vltimo, similiter dicentis [illegible, ~12 letters]: in summa, quum carcerem illum, quod Euangelium demonstrat, inferos intelligimus, & nouissimum quadrantem modicum quoque deliquum mora resurrectionis illic luendum interpretamur, &c. Præterea nõne vides ponere Tertullianum poenam illam in mora resurrectionis, id est, non in supplicio animæ simpliciter, sed in poena damni, ut vocant, per quam anima abest tum à visione diuinæ gloriæ, tum ab unione personali & coniunctione corporis, quod tandiu ab anima abesse cogitur & luere malum futuræ resurrectionis mora? Hoc certe Tertullianum sensisse ipse aperte clamat ibidem cap. vltimo, quum etiam continuò subiicit, nemo dubitabit animam aliquid pensare penes inferos, salua resurrectionis plenitudine, per carnem quoque. Sensus enim est, eo pensare hominem, quod & anima suo corpore manet orbata tamdiu, & corpus anima sua destitutum iacet. Quid ex his illius verbis amplius poterit exprimi?
units.tr: Ibid. Remaining in the prison of Purgatory at most until the resurrection. The passage is in Tertullian, On the Soul, chapter 35. But look here: do you not see that Tertullian is arguing from the hypothesis of the false interpretation which Carpocrates devised, as he had related at the beginning of the chapter? From that very interpretation that great master of argument runs Carpocrates through with his own sword, not bringing forward his own interpretation, which he set out more fully in On Patience, chapter 12, but refuting the Carpocratian one from his own resources. The words of the same author in On the Soul, last chapter, similarly saying [illegible, about twelve letters]: in sum, since we understand that prison, which the Gospel shows to be Hades, and interpret the last farthing as even a slight debt of delay of resurrection to be paid there, etc. Moreover, do you not see that Tertullian places that punishment in the delay of the resurrection, that is, not in the punishment of the soul simply, but in the so-called punishment of loss, by which the soul is absent both from the vision of divine glory and from personal union and conjunction with the body, which it is compelled to be without for so long, paying the penalty of the delay of the future resurrection? Certainly Tertullian openly declares in the same last chapter that this is what he thought, when he immediately adds: No one will doubt that the soul weighs something in the realm below, though the fullness of the resurrection is preserved, through the flesh as well. For the sense is that a man pays by this: the soul remains bereft of its body for so long, and the body lies deprived of its soul. What could be expressed more clearly from those words of his?

units.la: 26. Art. 17. aliud peccata omnia passione purgasse.] vide supra in caput 5. nota 69.
units.tr: 26. Art. 17. That his passion purged all sins.] See above on chapter 5, note 69.

units.la: 27. Art. 18. designatur non inde exiri posse, nisi reddat quisque nouissimum quadrantem.] quid hic nobis cum Origene; qui etiam daemonum restitutionem affirmabat, regressumque damnatorum ad vitam æternam? Iecit fundamenta Purgatorij hac sua hæresi, ipsum exstruxerunt ab hæresi illa Pontifices: negamus in hac causa vllam esse auctoritatem il-lius.
units.tr: 27. Art. 18. It is signified that one cannot come out from there unless each pays the last farthing.] What have we to do here with Origen, who also affirmed the restoration of the demons and the return of the damned to eternal life? By this heresy of his he laid the foundations of Purgatory, and the Pontiffs built it up from that heresy. We deny that there is any authority of his in this cause.

units.la: 28 Art. 19. per fluuium igneum transfibunt, &c.] hæc omnia pronunciat Eusebius de iudiciis Dei quæ in hac vita exercentur ad purgationem & castigationem nostri. Demonstrant sequentia, quæ hic omittuntur, quum ait: per fluuium igneum, de quo Prophetic̄us ferm̄ commemorat, & fluuius rapidus qui currebat ante eum, per vada feruentibus globis horrenda transfibunt. Est enim Propheticus ille sermo Dani.
units.tr: 28. Art. 19. They will cross through a river of fire, etc.] Eusebius pronounces all these things about the judgments of God, which are exercised in this life for our purging and correction.
