The following words, which are omitted here, demonstrate this, when he says: through a river of fire, of which the prophetic discourse of Daniel makes mention, and a rapid river which ran before him, they will cross through the shallows amid dreadful, fiery globes. For that prophetic discourse is Daniel's.

units.la: 7. vbi Deus effingitur res Monarchiarum mundi & Ecclesiæ ipsius dirigens iudicio suo in hoc ipso seculo quàm potentissimè. Nam si ad tempus post mortem respexeris, dicit idem auctor ibidem paulo ante de illo tempore: ideo expiatura erit illic inextinguibilis concrematio, quicquid hic non studuerit sanare correptio. Et in conclusione eiusdem homiliæ: Et ideo charissimi, conuertamus nos ad meliora, dum in nostra sunt potestate remedia: Curramus, dum lucem habemus, nec præsentia salutis tempora negligamus: hinc moriendo peccatis exstinguamus mortem, hinc vitam meritis vitæ comparemus. his certè nihil commune est cum Bellarmini affirmatione.
units.tr: 7. Where God is depicted directing the affairs of the monarchies of the world and of the Church itself by his judgment, as powerfully as possible, in this very age. For if you look to the time after death, the same author says a little earlier in the same place about that time: therefore the unquenchable burning will there make expiation for whatever correction here has not troubled to heal. And in the conclusion of the same homily: And so, dearly beloved, let us turn ourselves to better things while the remedies are in our power. Let us run while we have the light, and let us not neglect the present times of salvation. Here, by dying, let us extinguish death through sins; here let us win life by the merits of life. Nothing in these has anything in common with Bellarmine's assertion.

units.la: 29 Art. 20. quum tamdiu exercetur noxius pœnis, vt communi supplicia erroris expendat. Et non videt Bellarminus Ambrosiū de pœnis peccatori in hac vita contingentibus agere? Latinum hominem appello, Grammaticulum & literatorem infimæ fortis, quid illa verba sibi velint: vt quadrantis oblatione illic (de balneo loquitur) vnusquisque lauandi accipit facultatem, ita hic accipit eluendi, quia vnusquisque peccatum, & quæ sequuntur. Quid est hic, obsecro, nisi in hac vita, vbi mortaleis castigat igne afflictio-num num & expurgat Deus? Quisquis profecto exponit hic, id est, in futuro illo seculo, aut aliud agit, aut futurum seculum non credit.
units.tr: 29 Art. 20. While the wrongdoer is so long punished, that he may pay for the penalties of common error. Does Bellarmine not see that Ambrose is speaking of punishments that befall sinners in this life? I appeal to any Latin speaker, any schoolboy of the lowest rank, to say what these words mean: just as by the offering of a quadrant one there receives the opportunity of washing (he is speaking of the bath), so here one receives the chance of cleansing, because each one sin, and what follows. What, I ask, is "here" in this passage, if not this life, where God chastises mortals with the fire of affliction and purges them? Whoever explains here as meaning that future age either is doing something else or does not believe in the future age at all.

units.la: 30 Art. 21. donec etiam minuta peccata persoluas.] Hieronymus ex aliena sententia, quam improbat, his verbis utitur, ut supra nota 10. oportendimus: quam re n a disputatore videri, aut certe non dissimulari oportuit, ut bona fide agere diceretur. Incosequens igitur argumentatio. Quae sequuntur, de communi sunt errore labentis seculi, cui Bernardus cessit. Ignoscimus.
units.tr: 30 Art. 21. until you have paid even the smallest sins. Jerome uses these words to state the opinion of another, which he rejects, as I noted above at note 10. The opponent should have shown this, or at least not hidden it, if he wanted to be said to argue in good faith. So the argument that follows is inconsequential. What follows is the common error of the declining age, to which Bernard gave way. We pardon it.

units.la: 31 Art. 22. soluet vltimum quadrantem, & consequenter exibit inde.] Haec solutio nihil ad nos, qui alteram Augustini interpretationem quam priore loco attulerat, id est, παροιμιώδη illam afferimus, ut nota 21. & 22. dicebamus. Quam interpretationem prius concludens dixerat: Donec soluas autem quod dicitur est, minor si non eam significat poenam quae vocatur aeterna. Unde enim soluitur illud debitum, ubi iam non datur poenitendi & correctionis locus? Postea vero ἀγγελικῶς subiicit alterum illum interpretationis modum quem Bellarminus reprehendit: Ita enim fortasse hic positum est, Donec soluas, quomodo in illo ubi dictum est, fede a dexteris meis, & quae sequuntur. Prius illud affirmate Augustinus dicit, hoc vero posterius συμπτωτικῶς, de interpretationis modo.
units.tr: 31 Art. 22. he will pay the last farthing, and consequently will come out from there. This solution has nothing to do with us. We bring forward the other interpretation of Augustine, which he had given in the earlier place, that is, the proverbial one [παροιμιώδη], as I said at notes 21 and 22. Concluding that interpretation first, he had said: "Until you pay" is said, however, if the lesser sense does not mean that punishment which is called eternal. For from where is that debt paid, when there is no longer any place for repentance and correction? Afterwards, however, he adds, in the angelic manner [ἀγγελικῶς], the other mode of interpretation, which Bellarmine finds fault with: "Until you pay" is perhaps put here in the same way as in that place where it is said, "Sit at my right hand," and what follows. Augustine states the former assertion firmly; the latter he gives incidentally [συμπτωτικῶς], as a matter of the mode of interpretation.

units.la: 32. Art. 23. sed propter debitum pecuniarium coniicitur in carcerem donec soluat.] Diffinctio falsa. Agit enim Christus de offensis personalibus, non de aere alieno debitisve pecuniariis. Probatur. 1. generali argumento & quaestione tota: nam quaestio est de interpretatione praecepti, Non occides, quod praeceptum a corruptionibus Pharisaeorum aliorumque vindicat: quid autem huic præcepto cum re pecuniaria? 2. verbis ipsis Domini, quū dicit, siquid frater tuus habet aduersum te: nam illud, habere aliquid contra alterum, non enunciatur de re pecuniaria, sed de offensis personalibus proprie: similiter que illud, διαλλαγήτω reconciliator. quod omnes ferme Patres in locum hunc agnouerunt. Nec refert quod dicitur, vltimum quadrantem. Nam dictum est μεσιτ[?]ας. præterea quàm multæ sunt personales offensæ, quæ etiam pecuniaria æstimatione eluuntur? Non enim omnis offensa capitalis est, aut digna corporali supplicio. Hæc vero Draconis lex, non Christi futura effet. Negamus itaque distinctionem, & totam consequutionem illius.
units.tr: 32. Art. 23. but on account of a money debt he is cast into prison until he pays. A false distinction. Christ is speaking of personal offences, not of debts of money or other financial obligations. This is proved: (1) by the general argument and the whole question. For the question is about the interpretation of the precept You shall not kill, which he defends against the corruptions of the Pharisees and others. What has money to do with this precept? (2) By the Lord's own words, when he says if your brother has anything against you. For to have something against another is not said of money matters but properly of personal offences. Likewise with be reconciled [διαλλαγήτω], which nearly all the Fathers have recognised in this passage. Nor does it matter that he says the last farthing, for the word used is "mediator" [μεσίτας]. Moreover, how many personal offences are also wiped away by a monetary valuation? Not every offence is capital or deserving of bodily punishment. But that would be the law of Draco, not what Christ would enact. So we deny the distinction and the whole inference drawn from it.

units.la: In Cap. VIII.
units.tr: In Chapter VIII.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. agi de pœna iniungenda in foro Dei, vt patet ex illo, reus erit gehennæ ignis.] negatur restrictio, agitur de pœna communiter respectu diuini & humani fori. Est autem inconsequens à communi indiuiso (vt loquuntur) ad diuisum argumentatio. Confirmatur hæc sententia nostra hypothesi, vel quæstionis ipsius specie. Nam pro eo quod Lege scriptum erat, non occides, & occisorem iudicio damnari iubebatur; contrà veteribus, siue à veteribus dicebatur, non occides; qui autem occiderit, reus erit iudicio: id est, nemo nisi qui ex facto occidisset, trahi in iudicium poterat; plena erant licentiæ & ἀτιμίας omnia. Christus itaque veritas & vindex diuinæ legis, à fermento Iudæorum purgaturus & asserturus eam, ostendit vel iniquam iram, conuicium, & contumeliam, εἰ τὸ ἀκριβὲς [?] & summum ius Legis respe-xeris, xeris, omni iudicio priuato & publico, humano & diuino damnari oportere, prout quod semel vno iudicio iniquum est, id semper & omni iudicio iniquum habendum est. nam iudiciorum diuersitate non subiantia iuris (quod semper & vbique vnum est) sed ordo solum & circumstantiæ variantur. Nō statuit Christus diuersa iudicia, aut eorum iurisdictionem modumque disterminat; sed tantum omni iudicio iram, conuicium, contumeliam damnatam esse confirmat, eoque abstinere omnes ab ea oportere; si qui contrà venerint, eos iubet quamprimum operam reconciliationi dare. Omne autem iudicium distinguit in forum foli & cœli, humanum diuinumque: ac humanum quidem, quia ordines suos habet, distinguit in minus, ὑρίσιν, & maius, σωσ́ρι ον, diuinum vero (quod semper idem est) ab vltimo supplicio eius determinat gehennæ ignis appellatione. Et quàm belle consequitur à parte ad totum? si hæc pars de iudicio diuino agit, ergo & locum totum de eo agere; hoc nullæ docent aut probant Logicorum leges.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. that the punishment to be imposed in God's court is being discussed, as is clear from that: "shall be liable to the fire of hell." The restriction is denied; the punishment is discussed in general, with respect to both the divine and the human court. The inference from the common undivided (as they say) to the divided is inconsequential. Our view is confirmed by our own hypothesis, or by the very kind of question. For whereas the Law said, "You shall not kill," and the killer was commanded to be condemned by judgment, on the contrary it was said to the ancients, or by the ancients, "You shall not kill; but whoever kills shall be liable to judgment." That is, no one could be dragged into court except one who had actually committed a killing; and everything was full of licence and dishonour [ἀτιμίας]. Christ, therefore, as the truth and the avenger of the divine law, about to purge it of the leaven of the Jews and to vindicate it, shows that anger, insult and contumely, if you look to the exact and supreme right of the Law, must be condemned by every judgment, private and public, human and divine; for what has once been judged unjust by one judgment is to be held unjust by every judgment always. For the difference of courts does not change the substance of the law (which is always and everywhere one), but only the order and the circumstances. Christ does not establish different courts, nor does he define their jurisdiction and mode; he only confirms that anger, insult and contumely are condemned by every judgment, and that all must abstain from them. If anyone has acted contrary to this, he orders them to seek reconciliation as soon as possible. Moreover, he distinguishes every judgment into the court of the earth and the court of heaven, human and divine. The human court, because it has its own ranks, he distinguishes into the lesser, judgement [κρίσιν], and the greater, council [συνέδριον]; the divine court, which is always the same, he defines by the most extreme penalty, by the name "the fire of hell." And how neatly does one infer from part to whole? If this part treats of divine judgment, then the whole passage treats of it too. No laws of logic teach or prove this.

units.la: 2 Ibid. exponit omnia tria de pœnis animarum post hanc vitam.] locū hunc apud Augustinum reperire nondum potui.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. he explains all three as concerning punishments of souls after this life. I have not yet been able to find this passage in Augustine.

units.la: 3 Ibid. aliis autem vtpote leuioribus peccatis pœnas leuiores, ac proinde temporales.] negatur. Nā Christus non dicit, solum, in vnoquoque membro, & singulare (vt in dispescedis iurisdictionibus obseruatur) iudiciorum præscribit modum; sed tantum Pharisaicum fermentū abstergat, docens, omne malum omni iudicio damnatum esse. Dicitis, inquit, aut dixerunt maiores vestri & tradiderunt vobis, eum demum qui occiderit, teneri iudicij; qui non occ derit, non teneri, sed citra iudicium posse peccatum suum apud homines & Deum ipsum eluere. Toto coelo (quod aiunt) erratis, hominum peccatis contra veritatem iudicij humani & diuini omnis indulgentes.{r} Non enim solum is tenetur iudicio qui homi-nem occiderit, verumetiam qui fratri suo, id est, homini iratus fuerit temere; idque auctoritate publici humani & diuini iuris sancitū est. Et ita deinceps. Distinguuntur quidem à Christo peccatorum & poenarū gradus: sed aliud est in remotione seu confutatione distinguere (tū enim ex confutantis verbis nihil ponitur necessariò) aliud in positione, vt vocant, & affirmatione, qua res distinctè circumscribi solet. Remouet Christus Iudaeorum axiomata distinctè, non autè distinctè definit sua; sed κατὰ τὸ συναθροισμὸν [?] statuit haec mala omni iudicio damnabilia esse, contra quam Iudaei tradiderant. Augustinum Bellarminus non satis assequutus est: nam haec à verbis & mente Augustini absunt. Consulatur lo-cus.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. but for the lesser sins, as being lighter, lighter punishments, and therefore temporal ones. Denied. For Christ does not say, in each member and singly (as is observed in the distribution of jurisdictions), what mode of judgments is to be prescribed; he only wipes away the Pharisaic leaven, teaching that every evil is condemned by every judgment. "You have been told," he says, "or your ancestors have said and handed down to you, that only he who kills is liable to judgment; he who does not kill is not liable, but can wipe away his sin before men and God himself without any judgment." You are wrong, as they say, by the whole heaven, indulging human sins against the truth of human and divine judgment. For not only is he liable to judgment who kills a man, but also he who is angry with his brother, that is, with a man, without cause; and this is sanctioned by the authority of public human and divine law. And so on. Christ certainly distinguishes degrees of sins and punishments; but to distinguish in refuting is one thing (for then nothing necessarily is put forward from the words of the one refuting), and to distinguish in positing, as they call it, and affirming, by which a matter is usually circumscribed distinctly, is another. Christ rejects the axioms of the Jews distinctly, but he does not define his own distinctly; rather, by way of summary [κατὰ τὸ συναθροισμὸν], he establishes that these evils are condemnable by every judgment, contrary to what the Jews had handed down. Bellarmine has not sufficiently grasped Augustine; for these points are far from the words and mind of Augustine. Let the passage be consulted.

units.la: 4. Art. 2. nec enim lex vetus aliam mortem comminabatur hominibus, vt patet Exodi 21.] nempe ciui-liter, prout de ciuilibus iudiciis agitur Exodi 21. & seq. verūtamen falsum est, non aliam morte denunciari lege: nam & maledictionem diuinā mortem-que aeternam comminatur, Leuit. 26. Deut. 27. & 28. & seq. & alibi passim.
units.tr: 4. Art. 2. for the old law did not threaten men with another death, as is clear from Exodus 21. Namely, civilly, as civil judgments are treated in Exodus 21 and following. Yet it is false that the law threatened no other death: for it also threatens divine curse and eternal death, Leviticus 26, Deuteronomy 27 and 28 and following, and elsewhere throughout.

units.la: 5 Ibid. & multo magis homicidia puniri morte aeterna.] Primum haec obiectio est voluntaria, vt cum Scholasticis loquar, id est, ab ipso ficta, non à nobis prolata. Secundò autem ex falso antecedente & falsum exsurgit consequens. negantur omnia, & iure.
units.tr: 5 Ibid. and much more so that homicides are punished with eternal death. First, this objection is voluntary, to use the language of the Schoolmen, that is, made up by himself, not brought forward by us. Second, from a false antecedent a false consequent arises. All of it is denied, and rightly so.

units.la: 6. Art.. 4. hunc locum intelligi de pœnis post hanc vitam.] Augustinus nihil eiusmodi, ut notà iudicebamus. Contrà enim hæc illius verba eodem in loco: hic autem omnia divino iudicio dimittuntur, ubi finis damnatorum est gehenna ignis. de aliis suo loco videbimus capitib. seq.
units.tr: 6. Art. 4. that this place is to be understood of punishments after this life. Augustine says nothing of the kind, as I noted. On the contrary, these are his words in the same place: but here all things are committed to the divine judgment, where the end of the damned is the fire of hell. We shall see about the others in their place, in the following chapters.

units.la: 7 Ibid. posse deduci pœnas aliquas post hanc vitam purgatorias esse: nam hinc habemus quædam peccata non mereri nisi pœnam temporalem. Utrumque falsum, antecedens & consequens. Antecedens falsum esse constat ex nota 3. consequens est inconsequens. Ne plura, omnis ἀνομία est per se damnata: omne peccatum est ἀνομία: damnatum igitur per se. Quod autem aliter pensantur, siue condonata, siue effecta temporali pœna, id non ex se aut merito suo habent, sed beneficio gratię remittentis malum, imputantis bonum, & hominem cum actu ipsius acceptantis. Sed de his in tomo 4. videbitur.
units.tr: 7 Ibid. That some punishments after this life may be deduced to be purgatorial, for from this we have that certain sins deserve only temporal punishment. Both parts are false, the antecedent and the consequent. That the antecedent is false is clear from note 3. The consequent does not follow. To say no more, every ἀνομία is in itself damnable, and every sin is ἀνομία, so it is damnable in itself. That such sins are weighed differently, whether they are forgiven or their temporal punishment is remitted, does not come from themselves or from their own merit, but from the grace of the one who remits the evil and imputes the good, and from the man's acceptance of this by his own act. But this will be seen in volume 4.

units.la: 8. Ibidem. damnabitur ad pœnas æternas, qui non merebatur nisi temporales.] talia esse peccata negamus: ergo & homines ei [?] talibus peccatis negamus mori. hæc igitur omnia sunt aranearum telæ.
units.tr: 8. Ibid. He will be condemned to eternal punishments who deserved only temporal ones. We deny that there are such sins. Therefore we also deny that men die with such sins. All of this, then, is spiders' webs.

units.la: 9. Art. 5: ex quibus sequitur, homines post mortem iuvari precibus sanctorum.] Negamus sequi. Id quidem sequitur, homines beneficos post mortem recipi, id est, agnosci & excipi ab eis quos affecerint beneficiis; prout mortui dicuntur mortuos excipere, Esai. 14. 9. & Ezech. 32.[?] sed iuvari eos id vero non sequitur ratione ulla. Hæc itaque propositio, & sequens falsa est.
units.tr: 9. Art. 5: From these it follows that men are helped after death by the prayers of the saints. We deny that it follows. It does follow that beneficent men are received after death, that is, that they are recognised and welcomed by those whom they have benefited, just as the dead are said to receive the dead, Isa. 14. 9 and Ezek. 32. But that they are helped by this does not follow by any reasoning. Therefore this proposition, and the one that follows, is false.

units.la: 10. Art. 6. salvari propter opera illa bona quæ fecerunt.] hoc nemo nostrum dicturus est: quemadmo-dum nec illud sequens, bona opera facta ex bonâ[?] intentione meritoria esse.
units.tr: 10. Art. 6. They are saved on account of those good works which they did. None of us will say this, any more than the following claim, that good works done from a good intention are meritorious.

units.la: 11. Ibid. ad id cogunt verba illa: facite amicos, qui recipiant. ] Negatur cogere: nam recipiunt etiam qui non iuvant: imo in hac vita saepe accidit, ut recipiant in numerum suum ordinemque inviti & nolentes. Non ergo sequitur necessario; si recipiunt, iuvant.
units.tr: 11. Ibid. Those words compel us to this: make friends who will receive you. We deny that they compel it. For those who receive also include those who do not help; indeed, in this life it often happens that people receive others into their company and their order even against their will and unwillingly. It therefore does not follow necessarily that if they receive, they help.

units.la: 12. Ibid. ut bonorum intercessione salvantur qui elee-mosynas faciunt; ] haec non sunt Hieronymi verba, sed disputatoris glossemata. Duos quidem coniungit Scripturae locos, Galat. 6. & Luc. 16. sed de hoc esse-ctu nullum verbum.
units.tr: 12. Ibid. That those who give alms are saved by the intercession of the good. These are not Jerome's words but the glosses of the disputant. He does indeed join two passages of Scripture, Gal. 6 and Luke 16, but says nothing at all about this effect.

units.la: 13. Ibid. qui suis precibus nos iuvant, & iuvabunt quum mortui fuerimus. ] nihil istorum Ambrosius, haec bona fide sunt ipsius verba: facite vobis amicos de iniquo mammona, ut largiendo pauperibus angelorum nobis caeterorumque sanctorum gratiam compare-mus. nihil amplius. Quid Augustinus? multa quidem verba facit de hoc argumento lib. 21. de civit. Dei, cap. 27. sed nihil omnino dicit eiusmodi. uterq; vero quum sanctos nominat eo loco, ad pios respicit proprie qui in hac vita sunt, quorū gratiam, id est, favorem & studium sanctis officiis pietatis chari-tatisque iubemur omnes comparare. Quam argutae scopæ sunt. quæ ex locis eiusmodi verrentes eruunt Purgatorium!
units.tr: 13. Ibid. Who help us by their prayers, and will help us when we have died. Ambrose says none of this; these are his own words, quoted in good faith: make for yourselves friends from the unrighteous mammon, so that by giving to the poor we may win for ourselves the grace of the angels and of the other saints. Nothing more. What of Augustine? He indeed says much on this subject in book 21 of The City of God, chapter 27, but he says nothing of the kind at all. Both writers, when they name the saints in that place, look properly to the pious who are in this life, whose grace, that is, whose favour and zeal for the holy duties of piety and charity, we are all bidden to win. How clumsy are the brooms that sweep such passages and dig out Purgatory from them!

units.la: 14. Art. 7. Dominus ipse explicat. ] antecedens quidem concedimus, sed negamus consequens, ut nota II.dictum.
units.tr: 14. Art. 7. The Lord himself explains. We grant the antecedent, but deny the consequent, as was said in note 11.

units.la: 15. Art. 8. & isti sunt, inquit, qui recipiuntur in æterna tabernacula precibus amicorum. ] liberalis paraphrastes hic est, sed Augustinus parcior: qui post-quam de sceleratis non recipiendis in æterna taber-
units.tr: 15. Art. 8. And these, he says, are the ones who are received into the eternal tabernacles through the prayers of friends. This is a generous paraphrase, but Augustine is more sparing. After he had spoken of the wicked not being received into the eternal tabernacles,

units.la: [The text ends here; the catchword "nacula" stands in the bottom margin.] nacula dixisset,hæc verba subiicit: Est itaque quidam vitæ modus: nec tam mala, vt his qui eam viuunt nihil prosit ad capessendum regnum cælorum largitas eleemosynarum, quibus etiam iustorum sustentatur inopia, & fiunt amici qui in tabernacula æterna suscipiant; nec tam bona vt ad tantam beatitudinem adipiscendam eis ipsa sufficiat, nisi eorum meritis quos amicos fecerint, misericordiam consequantur. Hæc ille, vbi de sanctis quidem suscipientibus loquitur in æterna tabernacula; sed de sanctis agentibus in hac vita, quorum sustentatur inopia; & qui fiunt amici in tabernacula æterna suscepturi eos qui cum necessitatibus sanctorum communicant, denique dextram fraternitatis coram Deo iungunt migraturis in illam meliorem vitam. Quod si placebit tamen de mortuis pertinaciter exponere, annuimus eos recipere quoscunque in consortium beatæ vitæ intromittit Deus per gratiam: & recipere in æterna tabernacula, vt supra diximus nota 9.sed iuuare, præstare, & similia non dicit Christus.
units.tr: tabernacles he adds these words: There is therefore a certain manner of life, neither so bad that to those who live it the generosity of almsgiving, by which even the want of the just is sustained, and by which friends are made who will receive them into the eternal tabernacles, is of no benefit towards attaining the kingdom of heaven; nor so good that it suffices of itself for attaining such great blessedness, unless they obtain mercy through the merits of those whom they have made friends. So he writes; here he speaks of the saints who receive into the eternal tabernacles, but of the saints who act in this life, whose want is sustained, and who become friends who will receive into the eternal tabernacles those who share with the needs of the saints; and finally they join the right hand of brotherhood before God with those who are departing to that better life. But if it is still pleasing to expound stubbornly on the dead, we agree that they receive whomever God admits into the fellowship of blessed life through grace, and receive into the eternal tabernacles, as we said above in note 9. But Christ does not say to help, to furnish, or anything similar.

units.la: 16. Art. 9. Ad hunc locum nihil respondet Petrus Martyr,]non fuit cur responderet; cum nec ista di-cat Augustinus, nec adhuc quisquam exstitisset qui adeo male de Augustino mereri in eo argumento fuisset ausus.
units.tr: 16. Art. 9. Peter Martyr makes no reply to this passage. There was no reason for him to reply, since Augustine does not say these things, and no one had yet arisen who had dared to deserve so ill of Augustine on this subject.

units.la: 17. Ibid. Epulonem in gehenna esse dicunt, proinde Petrus Martyr in ventum pugnat. ]satis est tamen ad causam Martyris, si vel vnus esse in Purgatorio dicatur: quod disputator non negat plane. Et certe si in inferis non est recordatio Dei, vt ipse Bellar. minus agnoscit alibi; non est mirum si qui Epulonem illum, qui Dei & Mosis & legis recordatur, non fuisse tum in inferno crediderint. Sed viderint qui ista[?] curiosè rimari solent.
units.tr: 17. Ibid. They say Epulo is in gehenna, so Peter Martyr fights against the wind. ] It is enough for Martyr's case, however, if even one soul is said to be in Purgatory, and the disputant does not clearly deny this. And certainly, if there is no remembrance of God in hell, as Bellarmine himself admits elsewhere, it is no wonder that those who think Epulo, who remembers God, Moses and the law, was not then in hell believed so. But let those look to it who are accustomed to pry too closely into such matters.

units.la: 18. Art.10. nisi crederet post hanc vitam posse remitti peccata,] & nos remitti post mortem credimus, ac non solùm remitti posse: verumtamen eo sensu quem ante ostendimus cap.4 nota 2. & 11. sequentia verò negamus, & libro 2. Deo dante, confutabimus.
units.tr: 18. Art. 10. unless he believed that sins can be forgiven after this life,] We too believe that sins are forgiven after death, and not merely that they can be forgiven. Yet we deny the following in the sense I have already shown in chapter 4, note 2 and note 11, and with God's help I will refute it in book 2.

units.la: 19. Ibid. hinc probat aliqua peccata remitti post mortem.] falsum: vt ibidem supra cap.4 nota 2. dicebamus.
units.tr: 19. Ibid. from this he proves that some sins are forgiven after death.] False, as I was saying in the same place above, chapter 4, note 2.

units.la: 20. Art.11. quòd cùm non posset intelligi de damnatis, necessariò videtur accipiendum de iis qui purgabatur [?],] Non sequitur vlla necessitate, 1. ex homonymia vocis inferorum, de qua diximus in controu. 2. deinde verò ex insufficiente enumeratione, quod in disiun-ctiuis propositionibus est vitiosum. Nam alias præ-terea numerari à Pontificiis inferorum partes diximus supra in caput 3. nota 25. & idem postea limbum Patrum fuisse tradit, quem à Purgatorio distinguit artic.14. & libro 2. aliquoties.
units.tr: 20. Art. 11. that since it could not be understood of the damned, it must necessarily be taken of those who were being purged,] It does not follow by any necessity: first, from the ambiguity of the word "hell", which I discussed in the controversy; second, from an insufficient enumeration, which is a fault in disjunctive propositions. For I have said above, in chapter 3, note 25, that the Papists also list other parts of hell; and the same author afterwards teaches that there was a limbo of the Fathers, which he distinguishes from Purgatory in article 14 and several times in book 2.

units.la: 21. Ibid. liberasse eos qui per ignorantiam peccauerunt, nec tamen à Dei fide recesserunt.] nec verba Epiphanij, nec mente disputator expressit satis. Sed hoc vnum satis est ad refellendam argumentationem, quòd Bellarminus restringit ὁμωνύμως vocè inferorum, quam Epiphanius vniuersè ponit. Nam propterea inferos opponit mundo, vt locus inuisibilis animarum simpliciter intelligeretur (sic vocat Irenæus lib.5. cap.vlt.) quum ait, τὰς μὲν [?] γινώσκουσι καὶ μὴ πλανηθῆναι ὑπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς θεότητος, ἐγκειμένοις [?] ἀμνησίαν [?] ἐν ἀδῇ [?] κατεχομένοις, τὰς μὲν ἐν κόσμῳ διὰ μαρτυρίας, τὰς δὲ ἐν ᾅδου [?] ἐλπίδι καὶ σωτηρίας [?]. venisse Christum iis qui olim noverant ipsum ac non aberrauerant a deitate ipsius, sed propter lapsus in inferno detenti fuerant, facturum[?] gratiam ἀμνηστίας[?] vel remissionis peccatorum, iis quidem qui adhuc degebant in mundo, per respicientiam, iis vero qui in inferno, per misericordiam & salutem. Nihil sequitur ex homonymia.
units.tr: 21. Ibid. that he freed those who sinned through ignorance, yet did not fall away from faith in God.] The disputant has expressed neither Epiphanius' words nor his meaning adequately. But this one point is enough to refute the argument: Bellarmine restricts the word "hell" equivocally, whereas Epiphanius uses it universally. For he opposes hell to the world precisely so that the invisible place of souls is understood simply (Irenaeus calls it this in book 5, last chapter), when he says: [τὰς μὲν γινώσκουσι καὶ μὴ πλανηθῆναι ὑπὸ τῆς αὐτῆς θεότητος, ἐγκειμένοις ἀμνησίαν ἐν ᾅδῃ κατεχομένοις, τὰς μὲν ἐν κόσμῳ διὰ μαρτυρίας, τὰς δὲ ἐν ᾅδου ἐλπίδι καὶ σωτηρίας]. That is, that Christ came to those who had long known him and had not strayed from his deity, but had been held in hell because of their lapses, to grant amnesty or forgiveness of sins: to those who were still living in the world, through repentance; and to those who were in hell, through mercy and salvation. Nothing follows from the ambiguity.

units.la: 22. Ibid. nō potest intelligi de doloribus ipsius Christi,] falsum: nam propterea verba sequentia adhibuit Petrus, iuxta quod impossibile erat teneri eum ab illis, siue detineri: soluit enim virtute diuina sua, vt Petrus ibidem asserit, mortemq; superauit morte. Idem agnouit Augustinus ep.99.
units.tr: 22. Ibid. cannot be understood of the sufferings of Christ himself,] False. For Peter added the words that follow for this reason, since it was impossible for him to be held by them, or detained: for by his divine power he loosed the pains, as Peter there asserts, and overcame death by death. Augustine too recognised this in letter 99.

units.la: 23 Ibid. hodie mecum eris in Paradiso.] inconsequens: nam dolores crucis, mortis, & inferorum vnum in Christo sunt, licet ratione distinguantur, & recte. Quamobrem sequentia frustra sunt, & conclusio falsa.
units.tr: 23 Ibid. "Today you will be with me in Paradise."] Inconsequential. The pains of the cross, of death, and of the underworld are one in Christ, though they are rightly distinguished in thought. So what follows is pointless, and the conclusion is false.

units.la: 24. Art.12. nec dabis sanctum tuum videre corruptionem.] vide contr.2.lib.4.cap.8.
units.tr: 24. Art. 12. "Nor will you let your Holy One see corruption."] See the second controversy, book 4, chapter 8.

units.la: 25. Artic.13. Vtitur hoc loco B. Augustinus lib.12. de Gen.cap.33. sed Augustinus vniuersè dicit, iste accipit æquiuocè. frustra est.
units.tr: 25. Art. 13. Here Augustine, in book 12 of the Literal Commentary on Genesis, chapter 33, is used. But Augustine speaks in general terms, and this writer takes the words equivocally. It is pointless.

units.la: 26. Ibid. per eos qui sub terra, non possunt intelligi nisi animæ Purgatorij.] falsum. & ipse Bellarminus euertit hanc interpretationem sequente artic. De limbo fabulam negamus, vt lib.2. & controuersia seq. demonstrabitur.
units.tr: 26. Ibid. "Those who are under the earth" cannot be understood except as the souls in Purgatory.] False. Bellarmine himself overturns this interpretation in the following article. We deny the fable of Limbo, as will be shown in book 2 and the following controversy.

units.la: 27. Art.14. loquitur enim de tempore, quod præcessit Christi mortem.] negatur: nam hæc interpretatio profluit ex falsa & præpostera visionis illius interpretatione. Sed nolumus hic lōgiores esse, ne extra propositam quæstionem delabamur. Eiusdem autē generis est sequens affirmatio, qua Christus morte sua aperuisse dicitur mysteria libri usque ad illam diem clausa: ambigua & æquivoca omnia: ut con-troversiæ 2. lib.4.cap.12. ostendimus.
units.tr: 27. Art. 14. For he speaks of the time that preceded Christ's death.] Denied. This interpretation flows from a false and inverted understanding of that vision. But we do not wish to be longer here, lest we wander away from the question proposed. Of the same kind is the following assertion, that by his death Christ is said to have opened the mysteries of the book, which were closed until that day. All of these are ambiguous and equivocal, as we showed in the second controversy, book 4, chapter 12.

units.la: IN CAP. IX.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER IX.

units.la: r.[?] Art.1. sumitur ex Conciliis & Ecclesia consuetudine. Negamus Purgatorium a Conciliis & prisca Ecclesia illa probatum esse.
units.tr: r.[?] Art. 1. It is taken from the Councils and the custom of the Church. We deny that Purgatory was approved by the Councils or by the early Church.

units.la: 2. Ibid. si autem aliquorum pomeridiano tempore defunctorum commendatio facienda est, solis orationibus fiat. ] Argumentatur disputator consequentia non bona, & illudit homonymiis. Non sequitur, si ora-tionibus, ergo pro mortuis orationes fuisse habitas. Nam & pro adstantibus, & pro Ecclesia habebantur; præsertim si Episcoporum, aut clericorum, aut idoneorum hominum exitus minari aliquid Ecclesiis videretur. Homonymiæ sunt variæ, quas optimè demonstratura est canonis Græci comparatio. Sic enim habet in ipsa editione Parisiensi:
units.tr: 2. Ibid. "But if the commemoration of some who died in the afternoon is to be made, let it be made by prayers alone." The disputant argues by a bad inference and plays on ambiguous terms. It does not follow that, if prayers, therefore prayers for the dead were offered. For prayers were also offered for those present and for the Church, especially if the departure of bishops, clergy, or worthy men seemed to threaten something to the churches. There are various ambiguities, which the comparison with the Greek canon will clearly demonstrate. For it reads thus in the Paris edition:

units.tr: [illegible in the scan]

units.la: Latina sic habent c. sacramenta altaris. de consecr. dist. 1. Sacramenta altaris non nisi a ie-iunis hominibus celebrentur, excepto uno die anniver-sario quo Cæna Domini celebratur. Nam si aliquorum pomeridiano tempore defunctorum, sive Episcoporum si-ne clericorum: hoc additur Tomo 1. Conciliorum) sive caeterorum commendatio facienda est, solis oratio-nibus nibus fiat,si illi qui faciunt iam pransi inueniantur. Prima homonymia, seu æquiuocatio est, quòd vocem Sacramenta, quæ pro omnibus rebus, sermonibus, actionibusque sacris sumitur, quæ in communione sacra religiosè obseruantur, accipit Bellarminus angustè pro iis quæ Sacramenta dicuntur vulgo, quorum tamen communioni & introitus & confessio & orationes ad eam pertinentes & canon & postcommunio adhærebant; nam propterea Græci verterunt [?]ἁγια[?]. Secunda est,quòd vocem Comendationis accipit pro oratione quæ fit apud Deum pro commendatione & salute mortui. Sed aliud est [?]παρὰ[?]δεσις,vt rectè verterunt Græci. Nam etsi [?]τὸ παρὰδοσις[?] in hoc argumento id quod Latini componere dixerunt,& mandare humo siue sepulturæ,& [?]παρὰ[?]δοσιν,depositionem siue funerationem, siue recentioribus (quia mandatio vox inaudita erat) comendationem, qua mortui corpus comendatur, componitur,traditurque terræ in spe resurrectionis,significare quibusdã visum est: melior tamen est omnino fimpliciórque Suidæ interpretatio dicentis: [?]παρὰδοσεως γὰρ ἡ ἐν ἀγγελίᾳ πρὸς τοὺς πατρὰς φασὶ γὰρ, ἑλάξων[?] [?]παραδόσιν[?], id est, dicitur etiam [?]παραδόσεως[?] relatio fuit denunciatio apud Patres. dicunt enim, accepi relationem.Sic enim accipitur in Conciliis passim: vt exempli causa, Concilij Carthag.3. can.28. qui in Græca editione est canon 23. sic habetur, [?]εἰ μὴ ἀπ' αὐτῶν τὰ προτα[?]δόντ[?] ἀποδίδωμι[?] [?]ἀπολύτ[?] [?]ἑτέρω[?] [?]παραδόσιν[?], id est,formata, aut comendationem & similia multa. hæc autè relatio in corporibus sanctorum efferendis fiebat publicè tum sermone, tum annotatione & perscriptione, cuius Cyprianus frequenter meminit: & comendatio ex eo dicebatur, quod commendaretur mentibus & actis Ecclesiæ defunctiChristiani nomen, cuius postea ex ordine & suo tempore fiebat ἀνάμνησις siue commemoratio. Aliud enim est commendatio, aliud commemoratio in actis prisçæ antiquitatis illius. Tertia ambiguitas potius quàm æquiuocatio est, quòd nomen orationum interpretantur de orationibus siue supplicationibus quæ ab Ecclesia pro defunctis in pœna sensus Purgatoriali tabescentibus habebantur: cùm ἐ diuerso orationes istæ aut ad pœnam damni solùm respicerent, vt seq. exponemus, aut pro superstitibus, id est, adsistentibus & Ecclesia tota haberetur primum in Ecclesia prisca; deinde verò longo interuallo orationes pro mortuis purgandis accesserint priuato errore, qui in publicum tàdè receptus est. Demóstrat Origenes lib. 3. in Iobum dicens: Nunc verò nos nō natiuitatis die celebramus, cùm sit dolorum atque tentationum introitus, sed mortis die celebramus, vtpote omnium dolorum depositionem atque omnium tentationum effugationem: diem mortis celebramus, quia non moriuntur, hi qui mori videntur. Propterea & memorias sanctorum facimus, & parentum nostrorum vel amicorum in fide morientium deuote memoriam agimus, tam illorum refrigerio gaudentes, quàm etiam nobis piam consummationem in fide poscimus. Sic itaque non diem natiuitatis celebramus, quia in perpetuum viuent ÿ qui moriuntur: celebramus autem, religiosos cum Sacerdotibus conuocantes, fideles vnà cum clero inuitantes, adhuc egenos & pauperes, pupillos & viduas saturantes, vt fiat festiuitas nostra in memoriam requiei (non dicit in requiem, siue orationem pro requie) defunctis animabus, quarum memoriam celebramus, nobis autem efficiatur in odorem suauitatis in conspectu æterni Dei. Artificio que hinc profectum est, quòd in Breuiario Rom. officio pro defunctis duo habentur orationum genera: quorum prius ad superstites Ecclesiamque respicit, posterius orat pro mortuis: illud prisca Ecclesia, hoc recentioris & superstitione adnascente factum. His positis, ad rationem Carthaginiensis illius canonis veniamus. Obseruabatur pro tempore mortis cuiusque in Africa tempus depositionis & commendationis illius. Quum itaque tempore matutino efferebantur deponebanturque piorum corpora, eo quòd Ecclesiæ conuentus adesset funeri, sacra synaxis & oblationes & orationes simul habebantur: quum autem pomeridiano, minimè habebantur. Id alij superstitiosè rati contumeliosum in defunctos esse nisi post meridiem quoque fieret, vrgebant vt etiam eadem obseruarentur in depositione eorum qui pomeridianis horis efferebantur.
units.tr: The Latin text reads thus, in the decree Sacramenta altaris, De consecratione, distinction 1: The sacraments of the altar are not to be celebrated except by fasting people, except on the one anniversary day on which the Lord's Supper is celebrated. For if the commemoration of some who died in the afternoon, whether bishops, without clergy (this is added in the first volume of the Councils) or others, is to be made, let it be made by prayers alone, nibus fiat, if those who perform it are found to have already dined. The first ambiguity, or equivocation, is that Bellarmine takes the word "sacraments," which in general is used for all sacred things, words, and actions observed religiously in the holy communion, narrowly, for those things commonly called sacraments. Yet the introit, the confession, the prayers pertaining to communion, the canon, and the postcommunion also belonged to that communion. For this reason the Greeks translated it as [ἅγια] (holy things). The second is that he takes the word "commendation" for the prayer offered to God for the commendation and salvation of the dead. But paradosis [παράδοσις] is something else, as the Greeks translated it rightly. For although some have thought that paradosis in this matter means what the Latins expressed by "to commit to the ground" or "to burial," and paradosin [παράδοσιν], a "depositing" or "funeral," or in more recent usage (since "mandatio" was an unfamiliar word) a "commendation," by which the body of the dead is commended and committed to the earth in hope of the resurrection, the interpretation of Suidas is by far the better and simpler, saying: "For paradoseos [παραδόσεως] is the report, given in the proclamation before the Fathers; for they say, 'I received the report' [παράδοσιν]." That is, the word paradosis means the report or announcement made before the Fathers. This is how the word is understood everywhere in the Councils, for example in canon 28 of the Third Council of Carthage, which is canon 23 in the Greek edition, where it reads: "unless from them... [a report] is given to another," that is, a formal statement, or commendation, and many similar things. This report was made publicly over the bodies of the saints when they were carried out, both by speech and by a written record and entry, of which Cyprian often speaks. The commendation was so called because the dead person was commended to the minds and acts of the Church, and the name of the Christian, which afterwards was recited in its order and at its proper time, was made into a memorial or commemoration. For in the records of that early antiquity, commendation is one thing and commemoration another. The third ambiguity is less an equivocation than a confusion: he interprets the name "prayers" as prayers or supplications offered by the Church for the dead who languish in the pain of Purgatorial sense. Yet these prayers either, on the contrary, looked only to the pain of loss, as we shall explain below, or were offered for the survivors, that is, for those present, and were held by the whole Church, first in the early Church. Later, after a long interval, prayers for the dead to be purged came in through a private error, which was then gradually received into public use. Origen shows this in book 3 on Job, saying: But now we do not celebrate the day of birth, since it is the entrance into sorrows and temptations, but we celebrate the day of death, as the putting off of all sorrows and the driving away of all temptations. We celebrate the day of death, because those who seem to die do not die. Therefore we also keep the memories of the saints, and we devoutly commemorate our parents and friends who die in the faith, rejoicing in their refreshment, and asking for ourselves a pious end in the faith. Thus we do not celebrate the day of birth, because those who die live forever; we celebrate it by calling together the devout with the priests and inviting the faithful along with the clergy, and by feeding the needy and poor, orphans and widows, so that our festival may be in memory of the rest of the departed souls (he does not say "into rest," or a prayer for rest), whose memory we celebrate, and that it may become for us a fragrant odour in the sight of the eternal God. From this arose the practice, found in the Roman Breviary, that in the office for the dead there are two kinds of prayers: the first looks to the survivors and the Church, the second prays for the dead. The first belongs to the early Church, the second came from a later time and arose from growing superstition. With this in place, let us come to the reasoning of that Carthaginian canon. In Africa the time of burial and commendation was observed according to the time of each person's death. Therefore, when the bodies of the pious were carried out and buried in the morning, since a gathering of the Church was present at the funeral, the sacred synaxis, the offerings, and the prayers were held at the same time; but when it was in the afternoon, they were not held at all. Others, thinking this superstitiously an insult to the dead unless it was done also after noon, urged that the same observances be kept at the burial of those who were carried out in the afternoon hours.

units.la: Itaque Concilio placuit, & recte, ne sacramenta & quæ ad officium altaris(vt vocât)pertinent, eo tempore liceret obseruare, orationes haberi probauit.
units.tr: Therefore the Council decided, and rightly, that the sacraments, and what pertains to the office of the altar (as they call it), should not be allowed at that time, but it approved that prayers be held.

units.la: Quas orationes? inquies. Certè aut pro superstitibus, aut pro defunctis. Pro superstitibus habitas fuisse & probatas, ante ostendimus. Pro mortuis purgandis expiandisque tum demum haberi coeperūt, quum sententiæ de mortuorum statu inclinarunt primùm particulari errore, deinde communi. Dum ergo sententia fuit, pios in paradisum & gloriam eius (quod ex verbo Dei credimus) auolare, non fuit oratum pro illis, sed pro superstitibus, pro defunctis vero gratiæ Deo habitæ, & commendatio Ecclesiæ facta. Postea successit altera sententia, quam optimè (vt alios taceam) expresit Augustinus in Psalmum 36.quum ait: Tuus certè dies vltimus longè abesse non potest. Ad hunc te præpara: qualis enim exieris de hac vita, talis reddéris illi vita. Post vitam istam paruam nondum eris vbi erunt sancti, quibus dicetur, venite benedicti Patris mei, percipite regnum quod vobis paratum est ab initio mundi. Nondum ibi eris: quis nescit? Sed iam poteris ibi esse, vbi illum quondam vlcerosum pauperem dies ille superbus & sterilis in mediis suis tormentis vidit a longe requiescentem. In illa requie positus, certe secura expectatis iudicij diem, &c. Haec sententia vbi obtinuit, coeptum est orari pro defunctis, non ad remissionem peccatorum, aut poenarum leuamentum (nam credebant requiem) sed ad refrigerium & consolationem eorum in resurrectionis & gloriae futurae & visionis diuinae exspectatione. Atque hic status est, quem Scholastici καταχρηστικῶς poenam dani appellarunt, positam in carentia visionis Dei & perfectae illius gloriae, quam sancti receptis corporibus in coelo sunt possessuri, vt contro. 7.lib.1.cap. 2. amplius videbitur. Tandem vero inuadente illa falsa opinione de Purgatorio & poenis illius, quas poenas sensus dixerunt, tum omnes, quasi mappa missae (quod aiunt) in orationes omnigenas pro defunctis sine iudicio, & modo, & fine effusi sunt. Prisca itaque Ecclesiae orationes ad Purgatorium negamus pertinere: quod hic semel copiosius oportuit explicari, ne deinceps actum saepius cogamur agere. 3. Ibid. In Concilio iv. Carthag. cap. 79.] huius plane eadem ratio, quam superiore nota expressimus. 4 Art. 2. Oblationes factas, vt oraretur pro defunctis: ] Vtrumque falsum: neutro enim loco fit oratio num pro defunctis mentio. Canone 34. hoc tantum dicitur, nulla pro illis in oblatione commemoratio fiat, neque {y} ... neque cum Psalmis ad sepulturam eorum cadauera deducantur. Id est, nullus honor eorum nomini aut cadaueri ab Ecclesia publicè habeatur. Canone vero 39. oblationum & rerum oblatarum per fidelium commemorationes fit mentio: de orationibus, aut defunctorum statu ne ɣρν quidem.
units.tr: What prayers? you will ask. Surely either for the survivors or for the dead. That prayers were held and approved for the survivors we have shown above. Prayers for the dead to be purged and expiated began to be held only when opinions about the state of the dead first inclined toward a particular error, and then toward a general one. So while the opinion was that the pious flew straight to paradise and its glory (as we believe from the Word of God), prayer was not made for them, but for the survivors; for the dead, thanks were given to God and the commendation of the Church was made. Afterwards another opinion followed, which Augustine, to pass over others, expressed very well in his commentary on Psalm 36, when he says: Your last day certainly cannot be far off. Prepare yourself for it: for as you leave this life, so will you be rendered to that life. After this small life you will not yet be where the saints are, to whom it will be said, "Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world." You will not yet be there: who does not know this? But already you will be able to be there, where that rich man, once a sore-ridden beggar, saw from afar, in the midst of his torments, the other resting. Placed in that rest, you will surely await securely the day of judgment, etc. When this opinion prevailed, it began to be prayed for the dead, not for the forgiveness of sins or the lightening of penalties (for they believed in rest), but for the refreshment and consolation of the dead while they awaited the resurrection, future glory, and the vision of God. And this is the state which the Schoolmen, catachrestically, called the pain of loss, consisting in the absence of the vision of God and of that perfect glory which the saints, once they receive their bodies, will possess in heaven, as will be seen more fully in the seventh controversy, book 1, chapter 2. At last, when that false opinion about Purgatory and its penalties, which they called penalties of sense, took hold, then everyone, as they say, like a napkin dropped at Mass, poured out prayers of every kind for the dead without judgment, measure, or end. We therefore deny that the prayers of the early Church pertain to Purgatory; this had to be explained more fully here once, lest we be forced to do the same thing again and again. 3. Ibid. In the Fourth Council of Carthage, chapter 79: the reasoning here is plainly the same as what we expressed in the previous note. 4. Art. 2. Offerings made so that prayer might be said for the dead: Both claims are false, for in neither passage is there any mention of prayer for the dead. In canon 34 it is only said that no commemoration of them is to be made in the offering, nor are their bodies to be escorted to burial with psalms. That is, no public honour is to be paid by the Church to their name or their body. In canon 39 there is mention of offerings and gifts offered by the commemorations of the faithful; there is not even a hint about prayers or the state of the dead.

units.la: 5. Art. 3. Pro spiritibus defunctorum loco competentim Ecclesia ad Dominum deprecetur. Hic locus non exstat in actis Cabilonensis Concilij 1. sed Concilij 2. sub Carolo Magno habiti: quo tempore iam in Occidentali Ecclesia inualescebat lucratiua illa opinio de Purgatorio, & animarum statu. Negamus autoritatem illius. Sequens, id est, Aurelianense Concilium 2. nihil dicit de orationibus pro mortuis, sed tantum de oblationibus mortuorum, id est, quas mortis causa morituri pij donauerant: hoc autem nihil ad rem quæ agitur.
units.tr: 5. Art. 3. For the spirits of the dead, the Church should pray to the Lord in a fitting manner. This passage is not found in the acts of the first Council of Chalon, but in those of the second Council, held under Charlemagne, when that profitable opinion about Purgatory and the state of souls was already gaining ground in the Western Church. We deny its authority. The following decree, that of the second Council of Orléans, says nothing about prayers for the dead, only about the offerings of the dead, that is, those which pious people had given on account of their death while they were about to die. But this has nothing to do with the matter under discussion.

units.la: 6. Art. 4. Etiam pro suspensis in patibulo esse orandum & sacrificandum. Responsio duplex: vna, hæc acta fuisse, quum iam illo graui errore Ecclesia teneretur: altera, Concilium illud VVormatiense non agere de orationibus pro mortuis, sed pro iis qui sunt damnati & rapiuntur ad mortem, id est, pro morituris morientibusve. Rem ita se habere demonstrant non solum quæstionis verba tempore præsente enunciata, de his qui in patibulis suspendiuntur pro suis sceleribus: sed etiam, idque maximè verba definitionis, vel synodalis responsi: quæ sic habent plane: Si omnibus de peccatis suis puram confessionem agentibus, & digne pœnitentibus communio in fine secundum canonicum iussum danda est, cur non etiam eis qui pro suis peccatis pœnam extremam persoluunt? Scriptum est enim, non vindicat Deus bis in id ipsum. Nam Dominus ait, in quocunque die conuersus fuerit peccator, peccata eius non reputabuntur ei: & iterum, nolo mortem peccatoris, sed ut conuertatur & viuat. Salutem ergo homini adimit, quisquis mortis tempore poenitentiam denegat: & desperat de misericordia Dei qui eam ad subuenientendum[?] morienti sufficere vel in momento non credit posse. Latro ergo perdidisset in cruce premium ad Christi dextram pendens, si illum unius horae poenitentia non iuuisset. Nam quum esset in poena, poenituit, & per unius sermonis professionem habitaculum paradisi Deo promittente promeruit, &c. Pro morituris oblatione, orationem, communionem, id est, Ecclesiasticam reconciliationem & pacem procurandam minime negamus, quod Concilium VVormatiense aperte probat: sed eorum qui iam sunt mortui diuersa ratio.
units.tr: 6. Art. 4. Prayer and sacrifice must also be made for those hanged on the gallows. There is a twofold answer. First, these acts were made when the Church was already held by that grave error. Second, the Council of Worms is not concerned with prayers for the dead, but with those who have been condemned and are led to death, that is, with those about to die or dying. That this is the true state of the matter is shown not only by the words of the question as it was put at that time, concerning those who are hanged on gibbets for their crimes, but still more by the words of the definition, or synodal reply, which read quite plainly: If communion is to be given at the end, according to the canonical command, to all who make a pure confession of their sins and repent worthily, why should it not also be given to those who pay the final penalty for their sins? For it is written, God does not punish twice for the same thing. For the Lord says, on whatever day the sinner is converted, his sins shall not be counted against him; and again, I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live. Therefore whoever denies repentance at the time of death takes away salvation from a man, and whoever does not believe that God's mercy is enough to help a dying man even in a moment, despairs of that mercy. The thief hanging on the cross would then have lost the reward at Christ's right hand, if the repentance of a single hour had not helped him. For when he was in punishment he repented, and by the confession of a single word he merited, God promising, a dwelling in paradise, and so on. We by no means deny that for those about to die an offering, prayer and communion should be procured, that is, ecclesiastical reconciliation and peace, as the Council of Worms plainly proves; but for those who are already dead, the reasoning is different.

units.la: 7. Art. 5. Dicitur sacrilegium, fraudare animas defunctorum orationibus, &c.] Nihil eiusmodi: Haec ipsa sunt verba Symmachi: valde iniquum & ingens sacrilegium est, ut quacunque vel pro remedio peccatorum, vel salute, vel requie animarum suarum unusquisque venerabili Ecclesiae contulerit aut certe reliquerit, ab his a quibus haec maxime seruari conuenit, id est, Christianis & Deum timentibus hominibus, & super omnia a principibus & primis regionum, in aliud transferri vel converti. Non agit Symmachus de orationibus, sed de oblationibus siue fundationibus (ut vocant) & donationibus mortis causa in Ecclesiae, pauperum, & aliorum pios usus factis. Aliud est oblatio a viuente facta siue instituta, aliud oratio pro mortuis. Ex disparato non valet consequentia.
units.tr: 7. Art. 5. It is called sacrilege to defraud the souls of the dead of prayers, etc.] Nothing of the kind. These are the very words of Symmachus: It is a most unjust and great sacrilege that whatever each man has given or left to the venerable Church, either for the remedy of his sins, or for the salvation or rest of his soul, should be diverted or turned to other uses by those by whom it ought most of all to be kept, that is, by Christians and men who fear God, and above all by princes and the chief men of the regions. Symmachus is not speaking of prayers, but of offerings or foundations (as they are called) and gifts made on account of death for the pious uses of the Church, of the poor and of others. An offering made or established by a living person is one thing; a prayer for the dead is another. The conclusion does not follow from things that are unlike.

units.la: 8. Art. 6. Ex Graecorum Synodis a Martino Bra-carensi Episcopo collectis, can. 69.] Nihil eiusmodi: nam hæc ipsa verba sunt canonis, vt habentur etiam dist. prima. de confecr. c. non oportet clericos: nec licet Christianis prandia ad defunctorum sepulchra deferre, & sacrificare mortuis. Quis oculatus non videt interdici Ethnicorum superstitionibus, quas tenuiores, si forte, aut infirmiores Christiani obibant interdum spe commodi, aut conuersationis specie? nihil profecto istorum ad rationem Purgatorij Pontificalis pertinet. Nam mos fuit Gentilium ad sepulchra curare silicernia mortualesque cœnas, & parentare seu litare manibus mortuorum, & sacrificare ipsis: huius rei plenæ sunt historiæ, etiam ἀσεβῶν[?] impiarum exemplis ad expiandos manes: & Bellarminus ipse agnoscit controu. 7. lib. 2.
units.tr: 8. Art. 6. From the synods of the Greeks, collected by Martin, bishop of Braga, canon 69.] Nothing of the kind. For these are the very words of the canon, as they are also found in Distinction 1, On Consecration, the chapter non oportet clericos: Nor is it lawful for Christians to carry meals to the tombs of the dead, or to sacrifice to the dead. Who with his eyes open does not see that this forbids the superstitions of the heathen, which weaker or feebler Christians sometimes practised, hoping for some gain or out of a show of fellowship? None of this truly pertains to the reasoning of the Papists' Purgatory. For it was the custom of the Gentiles to tend the tombs with funeral banquets and memorial feasts, to pour libations to the spirits of the dead, and to sacrifice to them. Histories of this are full, even with examples of the rites of the impious [ἀσεβῶν] for appeasing the shades; and Bellarmine himself acknowledges it in Controversy 7 of book 2.

units.la: 9. Ibid. Sacram Eucharistiam in os ingerere conantur[?]. Antecedens falsum, & consequens inconsequens. Hæc verba canonis: μὴ δὲ τοῖς σώμασι τῶν ζώντων τῆς ἀγιείας μὴ παλαιῶν· γάρ πάντα γὰρ, λάβετε, φάγετε τὰ ἐκ τῶν νεκρῶν σώματα οὐδὲ λαβεῖν δυνάμεθα, οὐδὲ φαγεῖν[?]. id est, nemo corporibus morientium Eucharistiam communicet. Scriptum est enim, accipite, comedite: mortuorum autem corpora non possunt accipere, nec comedere. Latina versio in tomo 2. Concil. posuit, nemo mortuorum corporibus Eucharistiam comm. &c. Agit Concilium de iis qui agunt animam (hi enim sunt ψυχοπομπῶν[?]) & quorum nec spiritus, nec corpus in illa violenta separatione est functionum istarum capax. Quapropter iidem mortui appellantur verbis sequentibus, quia momentum illud communis est vitæ & mortis terminus: eoque respectu iidem viuentes & mortui communiter appellantur. Vetat ergo Concilium, ne cum iis qui eousque perducti sunt communicetur Eucharistia: quæ res quid facit[?] ad causam Purgatorij? Atque hanc sententiam vidit & assecutus est Joannes ille Constantinopolitanus Patriarcha apud Harmenopulum in Epitome S.Canonum sectione 2. tit.6. ubi de hoc casu agitur evidentissime. Deinde vero, ut de mortuis demus agi, prohibetur abusus & superstitio illa: ex hac autem prohibitione recte confici non potest argumenta-tio, qua Purgatorium confirmetur: Id tantum sequeretur, imperitos & superstitiosos homines ita statuisse. An vero pii judicio valentes hac probatione acquiescent?hocipsum in causa pari Bellarminus negavit ante, idque recte, cap.6. artic.3. Falsa igitur & inanis argumentatio.
units.tr: 9. Ibid. They try to thrust the holy Eucharist into the mouth. The antecedent is false, and the consequent does not follow. The words of the canon are: Let no one give the Eucharist to the bodies of the dead. For it is written, take, eat; but bodies of the dead can neither take nor eat [μηδεὶς τοῖς σώμασι τῶν νεκρῶν τὴν ἁγίαν εὐχαριστίαν μεταδιδότω· γέγραπται γάρ, λάβετε, φάγετε· τὰ δὲ σώματα τῶν νεκρῶν οὔτε λαβεῖν οὔτε φαγεῖν δύναται]. The Latin version in volume 2 of the Councils renders it, Let no one give the Eucharist to the bodies of the dead, and so on. The Council is speaking of those who are dying (for these are the ones who are conducting souls [ψυχοπομπῶν]) and whose spirit and body, in that violent separation, are not capable of these functions. For this reason the same people are called dead in the following words, because that moment is the common boundary of life and death, and in that respect those who are living and those who are dead are commonly called by the same name. The Council therefore forbids that the Eucharist be communicated to those who have been brought to that point. What bearing has this on the cause of Purgatory? This is also the view seen and adopted by that John, Patriarch of Constantinople, in Harmenopulus's Epitome of the Sacred Canons, section 2, title 6, where this case is treated most clearly. Further, even if we grant that the dead are meant, that abuse and superstition is forbidden; but from this prohibition no argument can rightly be drawn to confirm Purgatory. The only thing that would follow is that ignorant and superstitious men held such a view. But will men of sound judgment accept this proof? Bellarmine himself denied the same thing earlier, in a like case, and rightly so, in chapter 6, article 3. The argument is therefore false and empty.

units.la: 10. Art. 7. Nam in omnibus fit oratio pro defunctis.] Non sequitur, ergo pro iis qui sunt in Purgatorio o-rationem factam. Nam etiam pro iis oratum est qui plenam Dei visionem assequuti nondum videbantur, ut opinio veterum obtinebat: quod nota 2. di-cebamus. Tum (ut ad singula veniamus) Lateranense Concilium cap. 66. de exsequiis mortuorum dicit, quas nemo bonus negat: de Purgatorio nullum ver-bum. Florentinum atque Tridentinum recentiora sunt, nec veritati possunt praescribere: utrumque æ-stu inconsiderato Purgatorij æstuavit. Liturgiarum commentum non est tam vetus quam fingitur: ut ex singularum verbis commonstrari potest: omnes sunt partus supposititij, & ἀνυστήγραφοι[?]. Sed hæc alij sæpe. Tum quid aliud postulant omnes, quam ut animæ fidelium defunctorum requiescant in pace? Purgatorij nulla mentio: non enim agnoverunt Græci. Dices, nempe requiescant in pace, quum petitur, in-telligimus requiem in pace à pœnis Purgatorij. Nos vero negamus, id Græcos sibi voluisse: & in ConciConcilio Florentino ipsi negauerunt, licet de nomine Purgatorij noluerint contendere, quum ad disceßum omnia pararentur. Pax duplex est: vna, a rebus intrinsecis: altera, ab extrinsecis. Mortuos crediderunt veteres venire quidem in locum pacis a rebus exteris, & ab omni malo immunes esse: sed quia plenitudine gloriæ & visione Dei carere putabant ad diem vsque iudicij, propterea illos arbitrabantur æstuare desiderio gloriæ & visionis diuinæ: pacémque illis & refrigerium & lucem exoptabant in pia illa sita, commendantes eos precibus suis Domino. Hoc argumento dicebant illi quod in Litaniis legitur: requiem æternam da eis Domine, & lux æterna luceat eis: Requiescant in pace, & similia. De pace vero a malis exteris, & pœna quam vocant sensus, vt pœnis Purgatorij, & consimilibus, nulla apud Græcos mens, nulla mentio: Latinorum est inuentum, idque recentius. Quàm autem illa Concilia sint generalia, ante in controu. 4. dicebamus.
units.tr: 10. Art. 7. For prayer is made for the dead in all.] It does not follow that prayer was offered for those who are in Purgatory. For prayer was also offered for those who were not yet thought to have attained the full vision of God, as the opinion of the ancients held; which we noted in note 2. Then, to take the points one by one: the Lateran Council, chapter 66, on funeral rites for the dead, which no good man denies, says nothing of Purgatory. The Council of Florence and the Council of Trent are more recent, and cannot prescribe to the truth; both were heated by the rash fervour about Purgatory. The fiction of the liturgies is not as old as it is pretended, as can be shown from the words of each; all are spurious offspring and bear no known author's name [ἀνυστήγραφοι]. But many others have often said these things. Then what else do they all ask, except that the souls of the faithful departed may rest in peace? There is no mention of Purgatory, for the Greeks did not recognise it. You will say that when we ask that they may rest in peace, we understand rest in peace from the punishments of Purgatory. But we deny that the Greeks meant this, and at the Council of Florence they themselves denied it, although when everything was being prepared for their departure they were unwilling to contend about the name of Purgatory. Peace is twofold: one from intrinsic things, the other from extrinsic. The ancients believed that the dead do indeed come into a place of peace, free from external troubles and immune from every evil; but because they thought the dead lacked the fullness of glory and the vision of God until the day of judgment, they supposed that they burned with longing for glory and the divine vision. They prayed for peace, refreshment and light for them in that pious place, commending them to the Lord by their prayers. By this argument those men said what is read in the litanies: Grant them eternal rest, O Lord, and let eternal light shine upon them; may they rest in peace, and similar words. But there is no thought or mention among the Greeks of peace from external evils, or of the punishment which they call sensible, such as the punishments of Purgatory and the like. This is an invention of the Latins, and a fairly recent one. How far those councils are general, I said before in Controversy 4.

units.la: II. Art. 8. Quæ affectio fidei & pietati repugnat.
units.tr: II. Art. 8. Which affection is repugnant to faith and piety.

units.la: Hæc repetitio verbis Martyris non plane respondet: sed ad rem.
units.tr: This repetition does not fully answer the Martyr's words, but it does address the matter.

units.la: 12. Art. 9. Locum suum habet etiam commendatio defunctorum. Nempe ex secunda illa sententia Augustinus loquitur, quam supra nota 2. & 10. protulimus verbis ipsius. Illa autem sententia nihil Purgatorij sapit. De loco 2. Mac. 12. diximus supra cap. 5.
units.tr: 12. Art. 9. The commendation of the dead also has its place. Certainly it is the second opinion mentioned above that Augustine is speaking of, which we set out in his own words in notes 2 and 10. But that opinion has no flavour of Purgatory. We discussed the passage in 2 Maccabees 12 above, in chapter 5.

units.la: 13. Art. 10. In solennibus precibus Ecclesiæ, quæ leguntur ex libro, & maturo iudicio compositæ sunt, & a Concilio Episcoporum approbatæ, quomodo poterit idfieri? Nempe vt illud priuato, sic etiam hoc publico & communi errore, quo & Concilia humana non raro labuntur. Neque vero hunc errorem esse dissitetur Augustinus ipse, quando copiosa oratione habita pro Monica matre sua libro 9. Confessionū cap. vltimo hæc verba subiicit: Et credo iam feceris quod te rogo: sed voluntaria oris mei approba Domine. sic errorem illum excusat non religionis auctoritate, sed humanitatis officio, cui gratia Domini sit indulgentia, ut petit.
units.tr: 13. Art. 10. In the solemn prayers of the Church, which are read from a book, composed with mature judgement and approved by a council of bishops, how can this happen? Certainly in the same way as in private error, so in this public and common error, into which even human councils not infrequently fall. Nor does Augustine himself deny that this was an error, when, after a lengthy prayer offered for his mother Monica, he adds these words at the end of Book 9 of the Confessions: And I believe you have already done what I ask you; but, Lord, approve the free offerings of my mouth. Thus he excuses that error not by the authority of religion but by the duty of human kindness, to which the indulgence of the Lord's grace is granted, as he asks.

units.la: 14. Art. 11. Ecclesiam esse columnam & firmamentum veritatis, 1. Tim. 3.] Non sequitur) ut controu. 4. lib. 3. cap. 14. ostendimus.
units.tr: 14. Art. 11. "The Church is the pillar and ground of the truth," 1 Tim. 3.] It does not follow, as we showed in controversy 4, book 3, chapter 14.

units.la: 15. Ibid. Insania esse disputare contra id quod universa Ecclesia facit.] non sequitur à dicto secundum quid, ut vocant, simpliciter: non sequitur ex particulari universè. Illic enim Augustinus agit de rebus mediis & per se liberis in conscientia, non de omnibus rebus universè.
units.tr: 15. Ibid. "It is madness to dispute against what the whole Church does."] It does not follow from a statement made with qualification, as they say, to an unqualified one; it does not follow from the particular to the universal. For Augustine there is speaking of matters that are indifferent and free in themselves and in conscience, not of all things universally.

units.la: 16. Ibid. portæ inferi non prævalebunt adversus eā.] Neque hoc sequitur, Ecclesia si errat, ergo ruit: neque illud, si errat, ergo verę fidei & iustæ pietati adversatur: nec istud denique, si errat in particulari, ergo ruit universè. Inconsequentia omnia, ut obseruauimus controu. 3. lib. 1. cap. 19. & controu. 4. lib. 2. cap. 2. Quapropter disputator in sequentibus φλυαρεῖ[?].
units.tr: 16. Ibid. "The gates of hell shall not prevail against it."] Nor does it follow: if the Church errs, therefore it falls; nor that: if it errs, therefore it is opposed to true faith and righteous piety; nor finally this: if it errs in a particular matter, therefore it falls universally. All these are non sequiturs, as we observed in controversy 3, book 1, chapter 19, and controversy 4, book 2, chapter 2. Therefore the disputant in what follows talks nonsense [φλυαρεῖ].

units.la: 17. Art. 12. & alia causa, inquit, citra Purgatorium esse potuit, ut pro defunctis in Ecclesia preces fierent.] & verè id quidem. Nam preces fiunt non solum pro curando & auersando malo, verumetiam pro bono amplificando promouendoque: siue publico, ut quum oramus, veniat regnum tuum, ad perfectionem universam regni Dei & Ecclesiæ attendentes; siue priuato, ut quum pro eo oramus qui nondum asse-quutus est gloriæ plenitudinem. Fuit autè communis illa Patrum multorum sententia, pios nondum ad gloriam coelestem venire morte, sed loco suo in sinu Abrahæ quiescere carentes visione Dei, &c. vt nota 2. dicebamus.
units.tr: 17. Art. 12. "And another cause, he says, could exist apart from Purgatory, for prayers to be made for the dead in the Church."] And indeed that is true. For prayers are made not only for averting and removing evil but also for increasing and advancing good: whether publicly, as when we pray "Thy kingdom come," looking to the full perfection of the kingdom of God and the Church; or privately, as when we pray for one who has not yet attained the fullness of glory. Moreover, it was the common opinion of many of the Fathers that the pious do not go to heavenly glory at death, but rest in their place in the bosom of Abraham, lacking the vision of God, and so on, as we said in note 2.

units.la: Ibid. Proinde commentitia Petri Martyris solutio est. ] Negamus sequi ex eo quod ἀμαρτία distinctum. nam Augustinus ita ex hypothesi loquitur, sive per suppositionem secundæ illius Patrum sententiæ quam modo diximus: mortuos (exceptis martyribus) quiescere in sinu Abrahæ carentes visione Dei gloriæque plenæ illius, desiderioque ferentes complementi eius. In hanc demum sententiam & orare mortuos, & pro mortuis orari tradiderunt. Non sequitur autem, si pro mortuis eo statu oratum est, ergo pro inquilinis Purgatorij & pœnis ipsorum Ecclesiam orauisse.
units.tr: Ibid. "Therefore the solution of Peter Martyr is a fabrication."] We deny that it follows from what has been distinguished as [ἀμαρτία]. For Augustine speaks in this way hypothetically, that is, on the supposition of that second opinion of the Fathers which we have just mentioned: that the dead (excepting the martyrs) rest in the bosom of Abraham, lacking the vision of God and that full glory, and feeling a longing for its completion. It was in this sense that they taught both that the dead pray and that prayers are offered for the dead. But it does not follow that, if prayer was offered for the dead in that state, therefore the Church prayed for the inhabitants of Purgatory and their punishments.

units.la: Art. 14. Sed magis vt orent ipsi pro nobis.] Propositi consequens non est necessarium, quia piorum defunctorum omnium par non est ratio ex Patrum illorum sententia, atque adeo Bellarmini ipsius lib. 2. cap. 7. infra, qui inferos, Purgatorium, limbum puerorum, limbum Patrum, & quintum præterea locum ἀνώνυμον definiuit esse, præter Paradisum, quo immigrant animæ morientium. De oratione autem sanctorum pro nobis, in controuersiam seq. vi-debitur. Cæterum optarem explicationem fuisse solutionem Martyris. Sed veritatis hæreamus disputatoris nostri.
units.tr: Art. 14. "But rather that they may pray for us."] The consequence of the proposition is not necessary, because the reasoning from those Fathers' opinion does not apply equally to all pious dead; and so it is also the view of Bellarmine himself, in book 2, chapter 7 below, who defines hell, Purgatory, the limbo of children, the limbo of the Fathers, and, besides these, a fifth place [ἀνώνυμον], nameless, apart from Paradise, into which the souls of the dying migrate. The prayers of the saints for us will be considered in the following controversy. Otherwise I would have wished for an explanation rather than Martyr's solution. But let us cling to the truth of our disputant.

units.la: Art. 15. Neque videtur vllo modo conuenire, vt quis petat quod iam habet:] Falsum. dicimus enim, Panem nostrum quotidianum da nobis hodie: item, qui credit in Filium, habet vitam æternam: credimus autem, & vitam habentes petimus. & similia mult nam etiam idipsum quod habemus, idem etiam in vsum verti, continuari, augeri, confirmari petimus: & siquid est præterea eiusmodi.
units.tr: Art. 15. "Nor does it seem in any way fitting that someone should ask for what he already has."] False. For we say, "Give us this day our daily bread"; likewise, "he who believes in the Son has eternal life"; yet we believe, and though having life we ask for it. And there are many similar cases; for even what we have, we also ask to be turned to use, continued, increased, confirmed; and whatever else is of this kind.

units.la: atqui hoc ipsum est quod sibi vult Martyr vtens putandi verbo precatur illis, inquit, Ecclesia id quod putat iam eos consequutos, id est, videns eos partem assequutos esse, ita eos censet ac si totum assequuti essent plane. id illis exoptat compleri quod restat complendum: nempe vt qui requiescunt in pace securi, perveniant ad gloriam optatam.
units.tr: Yet this is precisely what the Martyr means in using the verb "to think" in the phrase "the Church prays for them," he says, "the Church regards them as having already obtained what it thinks they have obtained," that is, seeing that they have obtained a part, it judges them to have obtained the whole entirely. It wishes for them that what remains to be completed be completed: namely, that those who rest in peace in security may arrive at the glory they desire.

units.la: Hæc distinctio falsa est. Sciebat Ambrosius esse in cœlo Theodosium, & credebat. Sed quia duplicem eorum statum in cœlo statuebant Patres qui in fide vixerant: vnum, in quiete exspectante gloriam: alterum, in gloria (nam priorem confessoribus, posteriorem martyribus assignabant) sic Theodosium in cœlo credebat esse, vt in quiete & tranquillitate piorum consisteret, non in gloriæ plenitudine, aut martyrum prærogatiua. Demonstrant id quod dicimus verba pleraque Ambrosij: vt quum dicit, manet ergo in lumine Theodosius, & sanctorum cœtibus gloriatur, & quæ sequuntur. Item antea, Absolutus igitur dubio certamine fruitur nunc augusta memoria Theodosius luce perpetua, tranquillitate diuturna, &c. Hæc enim attributa duo sunt illius defunctorum status, dum resurrectio beata expectatur: vt ante nota 2. & 10. dicebamus.
units.tr: This distinction is false. Ambrose knew that Theodosius was in heaven, and believed it. But because the Fathers who had lived in the faith laid down a twofold state of these in heaven, one of rest awaiting glory, the other of glory (for they assigned the former to confessors and the latter to martyrs), so he believed Theodosius to be in heaven in such a way as to remain in the rest and tranquillity of the pious, not in the fullness of glory or the privilege of the martyrs. Most of Ambrose's words demonstrate what we say, as when he says, "Theodosius therefore remains in the light and glories in the assemblies of the saints," and what follows. Likewise earlier: "Freed therefore from the doubtful struggle, the august memory of Theodosius now enjoys perpetual light and lasting tranquillity," etc. For these are the two attributes of that state of the dead while the blessed resurrection is awaited, as we said before in notes 2 and 10.

units.la: Epiphanius vero nusquam dicit in Ecclesia orari pro sanctis, Fallitur Bellarminus plurimùm. Hæc enim ipsa verba sunt Epiphanij in contextu Græco: ἐπὶ τὰ ... ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ... [illegible, ~20 letters] τῇ ἀὴ εἴη τούτου [?] πνεύματος [?] ... [illegible, ~20 letters] ... ἀπ(ε)λθόντες [?] ζῶσι [?], καὶ ἐν ἀνυπαρξίᾳ [?] οὐκ εἰσὶν, ἀλλὰ εἰσι καὶ ζῶσι [?] πρὸς τῇ δεσπο-τῇ [?], καὶ ὅπως ἀὴ τὸ σημνότατον κήρυγμα [?] διηγήσωνται [?], ὡς ἐλπὶς ἔχειν [?] ... [illegible, ~30 letters] ... ὠφελεῖ δὲ καὶ ἡ ... ... [illegible, ~25 letters] ... ἐν κόσμῳ ἡμᾶς οὕτως σφάλλεσθαι ἀκουσίως [?] καὶ ἑκουσίως [?], ἵνα τὸ συντελέσθηναι σημαινθη [?]· καὶ γὰρ [?] διηγῶν ποιοῦμεθα τῶν μνημῶν [?], καὶ γὰρ ἀμαρτωλῶν. &c.id est, quàm proximè ad verbum.
