Deinde verò de eo quòd nomina dicuntur defunctorum, quid hoc institutum fuerit praestabilius? quid hoc opportunius & admirabilius? tum quòd qui adsunt credunt defunctos viuere, neque esse in ἀνυπαρξίᾳ conditione eorum quæ desiuerunt esse, sed eos esse & viuere apud Dominum, idque ut honestissima illa praedicatio enarrari possit, ipsem esse iis qui orant pro fratribus ac si in peregrinatione exsisterent: tum quòd oratio facta pro illis prodest, etsi omnino criminibus non abrumpit, saltem ut significetur status perfectior, quia dum in mundo sumus, saepe voluntarie & inuoluntarie labimur. Etenim pro iustis mentionem facimus, & pro peccatoribus. Ac pro peccatoribus quidem, sunt recurrentes, ὑπόμνοι, respicientes ad misericordiam Dei, pro iustis vero & patribus, & Patriarchis, Prophetis & Apostolis, & Euangelistis, & Martyribus, & Confessoribus, Episcopis & Anachoretis, & ordine vniuerso, vt Dominum Iesum Christum separemus ab a[?]iorum hominum ordine propter honorem qui debetur ipsi & ut gloriam reddamus ipsi,&c. Sensus est, fieri defunctorum commemorationem, & oblationem orationémque pro illis ad publicam fidei, spei,cha-ritatis,& ordinis significationem:fidei de illis,quòd creduntur viuere,quamuis vita functi:spei de viuen-tibus, quòd sperat eos in statum eundem post mortem peruenturos & victuros in Domino: charitatis in omnes, qua non eorum quidem peccata alleuantur, sed perfectior status designatur quàm hîc fit, cùm peccatorum per misericordiam Dei, tū iustorum per gratiam: ordinis denique, vt status i-psorum superior nostro,sed longè inferior statu & conditione Christi ostendatur Seruatoris nostri. Quis, obsecro, apex in his omnibus verbis deprehendi potest, qui vel fumum redoleat Purgatorij? Agitur certè abEpiphanio de oratione pro mortuis quibuscunque, si Christum exceperis, oratione autem non efficace erga mortuos, sed apud viuos significante coram Domino in Ecclesia eius. Nihil hic feritur Purgatorio, sed in Papatu metitur prolixissimè.
units.tr: "But Epiphanius nowhere says that prayers are offered in the Church for the saints."] Bellarmine is greatly mistaken. For these are the very words of Epiphanius in the Greek text: [ἐπὶ τὰ ... ἐν τῇ ἐκκλησίᾳ ... ] [the rest of the Greek is illegible in the scan] Next, concerning the naming of the dead: what institution could be more worthy of praise? what could be more fitting and more admirable? Then, because those present believe that the dead live, and are not in the state of non-existence of things that have ceased to be, but that they are and live with the Lord; and so that that most honourable proclamation may be told, that they themselves are present to those who pray for their brethren as if they were still on pilgrimage. Then, because prayer offered for them benefits them, although it does not wholly break off their sins, at least so that a more perfect state may be signified; for while we are in the world we often fall, both voluntarily and involuntarily. Indeed we make mention of the righteous, and of sinners [ἀμαρτωλῶν]. For sinners we make supplication, ὑπόμνοι, looking to the mercy of God; but for the righteous, and the fathers, and patriarchs, prophets, apostles, evangelists, martyrs, confessors, bishops and hermits, and the whole order, that we may set the Lord Jesus Christ apart from the order of other men, on account of the honour due to him, and that we may render glory to him, etc. The sense is that the commemoration of the dead, and the offering and prayer for them, are made as a public sign of faith, hope, charity and order: of faith concerning them, that they are believed to live, though they have departed this life; of hope concerning the living, that they hope the departed will come to the same state after death and live in the Lord; of charity toward all, by which the sins of the dead are not indeed lifted up, but a more perfect state is marked out than that which exists here, since sinners are helped by the mercy of God and the righteous by grace; and finally of order, so that their state is shown to be higher than ours but far below the state and condition of Christ our Saviour. What trace, I beseech you, can be detected in all these words that even smells of the smoke of Purgatory? Epiphanius is certainly speaking of prayer for the dead in general, Christ excepted, but of prayer that is not effective toward the dead, rather one that signifies before the Lord, among the living, in his Church. Nothing here favours Purgatory; but this is measured out at great length in Papacy.

units.la: 24. Ibid. & addit:peccatorum quidem vt illis à Deo misericordiam imploremus: ] Hæc interpretatio tota est aliena à verbis & mente Epiphanij: cuius verba & mentem proximè fide optima retulimus. Nam de fidelibus defunctis agitur, quorum hi peccatores illi iusti comparatè pro ratione anteactæ vitæ appellantur: pro vtrisque offertur sacrificium, vt vocant,& gratiæ aguntur Domino: nam & gratiarum actio species orationis est, quam Bellarminus ipse art.sequente sacrificium gratiarum actionis vocat,i-[?]ique Martyrem vellicans,
units.tr: 24. Ibid. & addit: "peccatorum quidem, ut illis a Deo misericordiam imploremus": This interpretation is wholly foreign to the words and meaning of Epiphanius, whose words and meaning we rendered very faithfully just above. For he is speaking of the faithful dead, of whom the one group are called sinners and the other righteous, in comparison with one another and according to the manner of their past life. The sacrifice, as they call it, is offered for both, and thanks are given to the Lord, for the thanksgiving is itself a kind of prayer. Bellarmine himself, in the following article, calls it a sacrifice of thanksgiving, and in doing so he is nipping at the Martyr.

units.la: 25. Art. 16. Ex liturgia Gracorum, de qua Epiphanius loquitur, ] & unde constat hanc esse Graecorum liturgiam de qua Epiphanius loquitur, quae exstat apud Chrysostomum? nam particularis est Chryso-stomi liturgia, si vera est inscriptio.
units.tr: 25. Art. 16. Ex liturgia Gracorum, de qua Epiphanius loquitur, ] And how do we know that this is the Greek liturgy of which Epiphanius speaks, the one that is found in Chrysostom? For the liturgy in Chrysostom's name is a particular one, if its title is genuine.

units.la: 26. Ibid. Quorum supplicationibus respice nos Deus.] de hac re videbitur, Deo dante, controversiae 7.li-bro 1.cap.18.
units.tr: 26. Ibid. Quorum supplicationibus respice nos Deus.] This matter will be considered, God willing, in the seventh controversy, book 1, chapter 18.

units.la: 27. Ibid. & quiescere eos facito vbi videtur lumen vultus tui. ] Haec oratio est prisca Ecclesiae ex hypo-thesi secundae illius sententiae Patrum, de qua nota 2. & 10. dicebamus. Nam sanctos vel fideles defun-ctos primum crediderunt videre Deum seu vultum Dei, postea vero creditum est non videri quidem ab illis Deum, sed lumen vultus Dei, vt ibidem ex-positum. pro his ergo sic habebatur publica olim oratio. vide nota 22.
units.tr: 27. Ibid. & quiescere eos facito vbi videtur lumen vultus tui. ] This prayer is an ancient one of the Church, on the hypothesis of that second opinion of the Fathers, which we noted at notes 2 and 10. For at first they believed that the holy or faithful dead see God, or the face of God; later it was believed that God is indeed not seen by them, but the light of God's face, as explained there. Therefore a public prayer of this kind was once used for them. See note 22.

units.la: 28. Ibid. Quae omnino talis est, qualem Cyrillus, Epiphanius & Augustinus describunt.] Falsum: nam hodierna Pontificiorum liturgia pro ratione trium temporum Ecclesiae, quae ante nota 2. distinximus, fuit concinnata. vide supra nota 10. de Augustino supra nota 19. de Epiphanio nota 23. & 24. de Cyrillo [?] pite seq. videbitur.
units.tr: 28. Ibid. Quae omnino talis est, qualem Cyrillus, Epiphanius & Augustinus describunt.] False. For the present liturgy of the Papists was devised according to the three periods of the Church, which we distinguished before at note 2. See above note 10. On Augustine, see above note 19; on Epiphanius, notes 23 and 24; on Cyril, what follows will show.

units.la: IN CAP. X.
units.tr: IN CAP. X.

units.la: 1. Art. 1. Longam orationem describit pro defunctis fieri solitam. ] Opus est [illegible, ~12 letters], & recentioris{§}-ui: quod nec Eusebius lib.3. hist. Eccl.nec Hieronymus in catalogo scriptorum agnoscunt, & quod multis argumentis probari potest, nec Apostolicum esse, quia errores habet, nec Clementis illius, qui[?] nouitia habet multa, quæ post aliquot demum secula in Ecclesiam irrepserunt, ut sæpe dictum.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. Longam orationem describit pro defunctis fieri solitam. ] There is need of [illegible, about 12 letters], and of a more recent ... which neither Eusebius in book 3 of his Ecclesiastical History nor Jerome in his catalogue of writers acknowledges, and which can be proved false by many arguments: it is not apostolic, because it contains errors, nor is it of that Clement who ... has many novelties, which crept into the Church only after some centuries, as is often said.

units.la: 2. Ibid. Eúmque in luce statuat, & regione viuorum.]
units.tr: 2. Ibid. Eúmque in luce statuat, & regione viuorum.]

units.la: Et hunc Dionysij librum foetus recentioris esse confirmant plurima cum alia, tum quæ à Photio in Bibliotheca narrantur, quæ Theodorus Presbyter conatus est ut potuit eludere. Deinde agitur illic de eo qui est ἄρτι κεκοιμημένῳ, recens mortuus, cuius animam è corpore emigrantem sanctis orationibus prosequuntur pij, ut illam Deus in pace & luce statuat, ὡς κόλπως Ἀβραὰμ, καὶ Ἰσαὰκ, καὶ Ἰακὼβ, &c. quæ secunda fuit priscorum Patrum sententia, ut cap. 9. nota 2. dicebamus. Postremo non sequitur, orant ut eum in luce statuat, ergo orant ne sit in Purgatorio. Nam etiam fieri argumentatio potest, ergo orare eos ne ad inferos abeant. atque hoc verius: nam de Purgatorio in Scripturis nullum verbum.
units.tr: Both the more recent origin of this book of Dionysius is confirmed by many things, besides those which are related by Photius in the Bibliotheca, and which Theodore the Presbyter tried as best he could to evade. Next, it deals there with one who is "ἄρτι κεκοιμημένῳ" [just fallen asleep], recently dead, whose soul, as it departs from the body, the pious accompany with holy prayers, that God may set it in peace and light, "ὡς κόλπους Ἀβραὰμ, καὶ Ἰσαὰκ, καὶ Ἰακὼβ" [into the bosom of Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob], and so on. This was the second opinion of the ancient Fathers, as we noted at chapter 9, note 2. Finally, it does not follow that because they pray that he may be set in light, therefore they pray that he may not be in Purgatory. For the same argument could equally be made: therefore they pray that he may not go down to hell. And this is the more correct inference, for there is not a word about Purgatory in the Scriptures.

units.la: 3. Ibid. Respondet, sentire omnino.] Primum non est Athanasij: nam quomodo Epiphanium Episcopum Cypri & alios recentiores auctores Athanasius, qui prior fuit tempore, adduxisset? Tum non quæsivit auctor ille de quibusdam animis vniuersè, sed de animis peccatorum solùm, quorum pœnas alleuari statuit pietate aliena, non autem peccata purgari, & pœnas tolli: quod hic conatur adstruere. Postremò negamus veram esse auctoris illius sententiam, & postea ex Augustini testimoniis aliquot hoc & sequente libro cofutabitur. Nam hoc quoque ex parte Bellarminus ipse supra cap. 9. artic. 12. confessus est.
units.tr: 3. Ibid. Respondet, sentire omnino.] First, it is not Athanasius's: for how could Athanasius, who was earlier in time, have cited Epiphanius, bishop of Cyprus, and other more recent authors? Next, that author did not inquire about certain souls in general, but only about the souls of sinners, whose punishments he held could be lightened by the piety of others, not that sins are purged and punishments removed, which is what he here tries to establish. Finally, we deny that the opinion of that author is true, and afterwards it will be refuted from several testimonies of Augustine, in this book and the following one. For Bellarmine himself confessed this in part above, in chapter 9, article 12.

units.la: 4. Ibid. Basilius in liturgia orationem instituit pro mortuis.]
units.tr: 4. Ibid. Basilius in liturgia orationem instituit pro mortuis.]

units.la: Nempe in eam sententiam, quam cap. 9. nota 2. & 10. dicebamus. nam ista fuit secunda opinio Patrum. Non sequitur autem, ergo esse Purgatorium, aut ergo esse mortuos in Purgatorio. Nam etiam ibidem expresse opponit lucem viuentium inferni poenis, & ab his absolui mortuos, & in illa manere petit. Etsi Basilij opus quis nobis confirmet esse, ex uno exemplari Syro, non autem Graeco, in tanta hominum licentia speciosos titulos mentientium?
units.tr: Indeed in the sense which we noted at chapter 9, notes 2 and 10; for that was the second opinion of the Fathers. But it does not follow that therefore there is a Purgatory, or that the dead are in Purgatory. For in the same place he expressly sets the light of the living against the pains of hell, and asks that the dead be released from these and remain in that light. Yet who will confirm for us that the work is Basil's, when it survives in one Syriac copy and not in Greek, in such great licence of men who put false and showy titles on things?

units.la: 5. Art. 1. Ibidem orat pro anima eiusdem Caesarij.
units.tr: 5. Art. 1. Ibidem orat pro anima eiusdem Caesarij.

units.la: Prior Nazianzeni locus nihil ad rem facit. Agitur enim de iis qui moriuntur, ac non de mortuis iam olim. Sic enim habet verba Graeca: αὐτῷ ... de praemorientibus dicit, non de praemortuis. Similem fallaciam vide cap.9. nota 6. Posterior locus de Caesario agit συνεκδυχικῶς, quem statim ab oratione habita elaturi erant de more (nam oratio ante cadauer habebatur) & humi deposituri coram Domino: tanquam si diceret, suscepta in caelis anima etiam hoc corpus in terris suscipe suo tempore excitandum. Quid hoc ad Purgatorium, obsecro?
units.tr: The earlier passage of Nazianzen has nothing to do with the matter. For it is about those who are dying, not those who have long been dead. For the Greek words say "αὐτῷ" [to him] ... he speaks of those who are about to die, not of the dead. See note 6 of chapter 9 for a similar fallacy. The later passage concerns Caesarius "συνεκδυχικῶς" [by synecdoche]: he was to be carried out, as was customary, straight after the oration delivered (for the oration was given before the corpse), and laid in the ground before the Lord; as if he were saying, "Let the soul received in heaven receive also this body on earth, to be raised at its proper time." What has this to do with Purgatory, I ask you?

units.la: 6. Ibidem. In vanitate & iniquitate vitam meam.
units.tr: 6. Ibid. In vanity and iniquity have I spent my life.

units.la: Haec dicebat Ephrem ex hypothesi secundae illius Patrum sententiae: quae fideles mortuos extra malum: sed in expectatione perfecti boni, ac non in plenitudine versari statuit, vt ante distinguebamus. Sequentium vero plerorumque eadem ratio.
units.tr: Ephrem said this on the basis of the second opinion of the Fathers, which holds that the faithful dead are outside evil but dwell in the expectation of the perfect good, not in its fullness, as we distinguished earlier. The later writers, for the most part, follow the same reasoning.

units.la: 7. Art. 3. Pro quibus offertur obsecratio sancti illius & tremendi sacrificij.
units.tr: 7. Art. 3. For those for whom that holy and dreadful sacrifice of supplication is offered.

units.la: Haec quoque Cyrilli, auctoris non adeo certi (de Hierosolymitano dico) auctoritas ex hypothesi secundae illius sententiae enunciata est, qua defuncti non plena vita & Dei visione frui, sed in regione quadam viuentium & luce exspectare vitam credebantur: & alij quidem plus, alij vero minus: qui status comparatione coelestis illius vitae etiam exsulium quoddam appellatur. Sic enim Cyrillus ibidem continuo explicat, dicens: Exemplo vobis demonstrare volumus: scio enim multos dicere, quid iuuat animam in peccatis, id est, peccatricem, ex hoc mundo decedentem, etiamsi in hoc sacrificio mentio illius fiat? An enim si rex aliquis eos a quibus offensus est in exsulium pepulerit, postea vero illorum propinqui coronam aliquam considerantes pro iis qui sunt in supplicio, id est, exsulio, vt praecesit proxime, exsulibus eidem offerant, nonne condonationem aliquam supplicium ipsis dederit? Ad eundem modum & nos pro defunctis preca-tiones adhibentes, quamuis sint peccatores, non quidem coronam plectimus: sed Christum pro nostris peccatis mactatum offerimus, vt & nobis & illis eum qui est benignissimus propitium reddamus. Statuit nimirum Cyrillus defunctos non esse in malo, id est, in poenis Purgatorij, vt ipse adfirmat: sed esse in exsulio quodam, siue priuatione & carentia (vt loquuntur) boni, in poena damni ac non sensus: atque in eo statu versantes communibus Ecclesiae precibus adiuuari. Nos vero & statum eiusmodi negamus esse, prout & ipse Bellarminus sequente controuersia negat libro primo cap. 2. & veras orationes esse quae fiunt ex suppositione illius.
units.tr: This statement of Cyril's, from an author not especially certain (I mean the Jerusalemite), is also made on the basis of that second opinion, according to which the dead were believed not to enjoy full life and the vision of God, but to await life in a certain region of the living and in light, some more and some less. Compared with that heavenly life, this condition is even called a kind of exile. For Cyril himself immediately explains this in the same place, saying: We wish to show you by an example. For I know that many ask, what good does it do a soul that is in sins, that is, a sinful soul, departing from this world, even if mention of it is made in this sacrifice? If some king had driven into exile those by whom he had been offended, and afterwards their relatives, considering some crown for those who are in punishment, that is, in exile, as was said just before, offered it to the exiles, would he not have granted them some remission of their punishment? In the same way we, offering prayers for the dead, although they are sinners, do not indeed weave a crown, but offer Christ slain for our sins, so that we may make Him, who is most kind, propitious both to us and to them. Cyril clearly held that the dead are not in evil, that is, in the punishments of Purgatory, as he himself affirms, but are in a certain exile, or privation and lack (as they say) of good, in the punishment of loss and not of sense, and that those who are in that condition are helped by the common prayers of the Church. We, however, deny that such a state exists, just as Bellarmine himself, in the following controversy, denies it in book 1, chapter 2, and denies that the prayers made on the supposition of it are true prayers.

units.la: 8. Ibi. vt fieret particeps multarum orationum.] haec abEusebij verbis absunt longissime. Sic enim ille ad verbum: τῆς τῶν ἁγίων ψυχῶν ... [Greek text, partly illegible]
units.tr: 8. Ibid. That he might be made a partaker of many prayers. These words are very far from Eusebius's words. For he says, word for word: <bl>of the holy souls</bl> ... [Greek text, partly illegible]

units.la: 8. Ibi. vt fieret particeps multarum orationum. [?]μία γεγυνὼς, ὡς ἂν καὶ μετὰ πλήθους ἀξιωθῇ τῶν ὑπὸ [?] ἐπὶ τὴν [?] τῶν ἀποστόλων [?] σωφρονέστερον [?] εὐχῶν. excellente, inquit, fidei promptitudine vel alacritate profpi-ciens ut suum tabernaculum (corpus dicit) post mortem fieret consors vel particeps alloquutionis Apostolorum, tamquam si etiam post obitum censeretur dignum orationibus quae ibi conficiendae erant in honorem Apostolorum. id est, ut quodammodo vel secundum quendam significationis modum corporalem participaret verbum Dei & preces Ecclesiae in loco nomini Apostolorum consecrato. falsum igitur refert Bellarminus. Tum ut demus id sibi Eusebium voluisse, an ergo propter ea sequetur agi de orationibus habendis in eorum gratiam quos ignis torret Purgatorij?
units.tr: 8. Ibid. That he might be made a partaker of many prayers. [Greek text, partly illegible] Becoming excellent, he says, advancing in promptness or eagerness of faith, so that after death his tabernacle (he means the body) might become a partner or sharer in the address of the Apostles, as if he were counted worthy, even after death, of the prayers which were to be offered there in honour of the Apostles. That is, that in some way, or by some manner of signifying bodily, he might share in the word of God and the prayers of the Church consecrated in the place of the Apostles' name. Bellarmine therefore reports falsely. Yet even granting that Eusebius meant this, does it follow from it that we are speaking of prayers to be offered on behalf of those whom the fire of Purgatory torments?

units.la: 9. Aërium haereticum facit, quia hoc negabat. Prior locus Epiphanij quicquā nō habet eiusmodi. Sic enim ille ad verbū; ἐπὶ δὲ τῶν [?] πλαδτπαντων, [?]ηνυθη [?] μνήμης ποιοῦνται, περὶ δὲ [?] [?] καὶ εἰκονισμάς [?]. Super defunctis aute[?], nominatim commemorationes faciunt, quum orationes habent & cultus & oeconomias, siue dispositiones. Nihil amplius Epiphanius, omnia, vt ante, ex hypothesi fecundae illius Patrum sententiae. Hoc autem quid ad Purgatorium? aut vbi nomen, vel indicatio illius? Secundus locus falso adducitur. Non enim dicit Epiphanius eo fuisse Aërium haereticum, quod istud negaret; sed hoc simpliciter affirmat, Aërium haereticum negauisse orationes pro defunctis; nempe quod animas: in locum suum abire ex morte statueret. Sed de hac re lib.2. cap.75. & seq. videbitur.
units.tr: 9. He makes Aërius a heretic because he denied this. The first passage of Epiphanius contains nothing of the kind. For he says, word for word: [Greek text, partly illegible] Concerning the dead, however, they make commemorations by name, and when they offer prayers and rites and arrangements, or dispositions. Epiphanius says nothing more; everything, as before, is on the basis of that second opinion of the Fathers. But what has this to do with Purgatory? Where is the name of it, or any indication of it? The second passage is wrongly cited. For Epiphanius does not say that Aërius was a heretic because he denied this; he simply affirms that Aërius, a heretic, denied prayers for the dead, namely because he held that souls go at death into their own place. But this matter will be seen in book 2, chapter 75 and following.

units.la: 10. Art. 4. Ne fatigemur mortuis auxilium ferre, preces pro illis offeretes. haec omnia & sequetia testimonia dicuntur ex hypothesi secunde illius senten-tiæ, quam Patres attulerunt, vt supra cap. 9. nota 2. & 10. exposuimus, & proxime nota 7. illu’strauimus. Hanc vero sententiam ne ipse quidem Chryfostomus constanter adfirmauit; sed ea tamquam recepta in vulgus interdum vsus est: nam aliter idem sermone de latrone, itemque sermonib. de cruce & latrone loquutus est.
units.tr: 10. Art. 4. Let us not weary ourselves in bringing help to the dead, offering prayers for them. All these statements and those that follow are made on the basis of that second opinion of the Fathers which we set out above in chapter 9, note 2, and chapter 10, and illustrated just now in note 7. Yet not even Chrysostom himself affirmed this opinion consistently; he sometimes used it as one commonly received among the people. For in another sermon he speaks differently about the thief, and likewise in sermons on the cross and the thief.

units.la: 11. Ibid. Non temere ab Apostolis hæc sancita fuerunt.] ὑπὸ τῶν ἀποστόλων, à tempore inde Apostolorum; non autem ἀπὸ aut παρὰ. sic loquitur Chrysostomus ex opinione vulgi. Sed & hoc & sequentia ex eadem hypothesi, de qua proxime diceba-mus.
units.tr: 11. Ibid. These things were not decreed lightly by the Apostles. [Greek: by the Apostles], from the time of the Apostles onward; not [Greek: from] or [Greek: beside]. Chrysostom speaks in this way according to popular opinion. But this and what follows rest on the same supposition we were just discussing.

units.la: 12. Ibid. orasse pro animabus parentum suorum Arcadij & Eudoxiæ iam defunctorum.] hæc Theodoreti verba. cap. 36. οὕτως ἐπιδεὶς τὴν ἀδρυαν καὶ τὰς ὀφθαλμούς καὶ τὸ μέτωπον, ἱκετείαν ὑπὲρ τῶν γεγυνηκότων ἀπεσωμενοι, συγγνώμαν τοῖς ἐξ ἀγνοίας ἡδικηκόσιν ἀντεδοῦναι. hic, inquit, adiectis capsa & oculis suis & fronte, supplicationem pro parentibus obtulit, rogans vt iis qui per ignorationem iniuria eum affecerant ignoscerent. Symbolica hæc fuit actio & solatium viuentis Theodosij: quia enim parentes iunioris Theodosij Arcadius & Eudoxia cum aliorum, tum vel maxime Gainæ scelerati instigatione grauissimis iniuriis Chrysostomum affecisset, placuit Theodosio, tamquam germano ipsorum filio, ossa Chrysostomi defuncti nomine parentum suorum humano quodam modo parentare, inutili quidem secundum rem, at non secundum significationem ceremonia: quemadmodum in causis capitalibus interdum vsuenit, vt iniquis iudicibus eorumque heredibus solemnia eiusmodi imperen-turtur ad publicam significationem eiurationeque alicuius facti. hoc Theodosius iunior fecit voluntarie: sed quid ad Purgatorium ista? nam nec Chrysostomus eos tenere vinctos in Purgatorio poterat; nec vero sanctus ille vir, si potuisset, voluisset unquam.
units.tr: 12. Ibid. He prayed for the souls of his parents Arcadius and Eudoxia, already dead. These are the words of Theodoret, chapter 36: [Greek text] Here, he says, with his hands, eyes and forehead raised, he offered a supplication for his parents, asking that they might pardon those who had wronged him through ignorance. This was a symbolic action and a comfort to the living Theodosius. For when Arcadius and Eudoxia, the parents of the younger Theodosius, had wronged Chrysostom most grievously, both through the instigation of others and especially of the wicked Gainas, it pleased Theodosius, as their own son, to perform for the dead Chrysostom's bones, in the name of his parents, a kind of human parental honour. It was a useless thing in fact, but not in meaning as a ceremony, just as in capital cases it sometimes happens that solemn rites of this kind are imposed on unjust judges and their heirs, to make a public declaration and renunciation of some deed. The younger Theodosius did this voluntarily. But what has this to do with Purgatory? For Chrysostom could not hold them bound in Purgatory, nor would that holy man, even if he could, ever have wished to.

units.la: 13. Art. 5. non parum conducunt etiam iis qui in gravibus delictis mortui sunt. id est, in ipso facto (ut vocant) & delictorum grauium perpetratione. Sunt autem haec omnia ex hypothesi secundae illius sententiae Patrum, de qua cap. 9. nota 2. & 10. & hoc capite saepius diximus.
units.tr: 13. Art. 5. They also help, not a little, those who have died in grave sins. That is, in the very deed (as they call it) and the commission of grave sins. All these statements rest on that second opinion of the Fathers, which we have often discussed in chapter 9, note 2, and chapter 10, and in this chapter.

units.la: 14. Ibid. Gregorij Nysseni, & aliorum. de oratione quidem pro mortuis Damascenus profert testimonia Patrum in eam sententiam quam hactenus exposuimus: sed nulla ratione ex eo sequitur, aut Purgatorium, aut defunctos in Purgatorio esse: quod ignorauerunt Graeci. Apud Palladium quaedam loculum qui hic adducitur: sed non inuenio. Numeri corrupti sunt; restituet disputator, quum volet.
units.tr: 14. Ibid. Of Gregory of Nyssa, and of others. Damascene indeed brings forward testimonies of the Fathers on prayer for the dead, in the sense which we have so far set out; but from this it does not follow in any way either that Purgatory exists or that the dead are in Purgatory, which the Greeks did not know. A certain passage from Palladius is cited here, but I cannot find it. The numbers are corrupt; the disputant will restore them when he wishes.

units.la: 15. Art. 6, libro de exhortatione castitatis procul a medio. Oblationes pro mortuis primo in loco Tertullianus appellauit, quae ex fundatione sunt (ut vocant) & instituto mortuorum, vel legatione testamentaria, sive ad sacra & synaxes, sive ad eleemosynas mortuis erogandas: quod etiam B. Rhenanus in eum locum annotauit, ac propterea Inquisitio Hispanica (si Deo placet) vtrobique deleri iubet. Hanc interpretationem demonstrat sequentia, quae etiam oblationes pro natalitiis adtexuntur, vt in eum locum obseruauimus. Secundo autem & tertio loco agit de oratione pro mortuis ex hypothesi olim recepta, & secundum rationem illam quam supra cùm alibi sæpe, tum nota 6.& sequentibus ex-pressimus.
units.tr: 15. Art. 6. In the book on the exhortation to chastity, far from the middle. Tertullian first called by the name of offerings for the dead those that come from endowment (as they say) and from the appointment of the dead, or from a testamentary bequest, whether for sacred rites and assemblies or for alms to be distributed for the dead. B. Rhenanus also noted this on that passage, and for this reason the Spanish Inquisition, God willing, orders both passages to be deleted. The following words, in which offerings for birthdays are also added, confirm this interpretation, as we observed on that passage. In the second and third places, however, he speaks of prayer for the dead on the basis of the opinion once received, and according to that reasoning which we have expressed above, both often elsewhere and in note 6 and the following notes.

units.la: 16. Art.7.non est quo pro dormitione eius apud vos fiat oblatio , aut deprecatio aliqua. ] hic locus aperte ostendit oblationes aut deprecationes illas olim non fuisse factas ad liberandum animas à malo aut pœnis Purgatorij(nam qua fide aut charitate sancti illi Patres fuissent, atque adeo iussissent eos qui in Purgatorio sunt ibidem contabescere, quando commodè liberari p[illegible, ~2 letters]sunt?)sed tantùm ad vsum, conso-lationem, exemplum, & symbolica institutionem uiuentium. Itaque vt oblationes illæ ad contestatio-nem publica significandam fuerunt imperatæ, sic ad detestationem quamdam ostendendâ fuerunt veri-tæ; nec tamen vllam salutis aut boni spiritualis ia-cturam iis importarunt quorum factum hoc signo fuit publicè detestationi. Enimuerò quo iure miser qui clericum tutore dixerit, à salute & regno cœlo-rum excludatur? Quòd si pro ipsis inimicis Christus orari iubet; quis orandum pro eis qui ignorantia, aut infirmitate aliqua, aut necessitate contra istum canonem veniunt, negauerit?
units.tr: 16. Art. 7. There is no reason for an offering or any petition to be made for his repose among you.] This passage clearly shows that those offerings or petitions were not made in the past to free souls from the evil or the penalties of Purgatory. (For with what faith or charity would those holy Fathers have been, and would they have ordered those who are in Purgatory to waste away there, when they could be readily set free?) They were made only for the use, consolation, example and symbolic instruction of the living. Just as those offerings were ordered to signify public testimony, so they were made to show a certain public detestation, and yet they brought no loss of salvation or of any spiritual good to those whose act was marked by that public sign of detestation. Indeed, by what right would someone be shut out from salvation and the kingdom of heaven for calling a cleric his guardian? And if Christ bids us pray even for our enemies, who would deny that prayer should be offered for those who through ignorance, some weakness or necessity act against that rule?

units.la: 17. Art.8.& sacrificia se oblaturum pollicetur. ] hæc omnia pronunciauit Ambrosius ex eadem hypothesi quam sæpius diximus, quòd animas in re-quie, non in gloria esse statueret, & varios esse requiei illius gradus : nam propterea orabant vi-uentes, & refrigerium illis exoptabant in exspe-ctatione gloriæ, non autem in pœnarum vllarum perpessione quas de Purgatorio fabulantur. Eadem locorum sequentium Hieronymi, Paulini,& Augu-stini ratio.
units.tr: 17. Art. 8. And he promises that he will also offer sacrifices.] Ambrose pronounced all these things from the same hypothesis we have often mentioned, namely that he held that souls are in rest, not in glory, and that there are various degrees of that rest. For this reason the living prayed and longed for refreshment for them while they waited for glory, not for any suffering of the penalties which they invent about Purgatory. The same reasoning applies to the following passages of Jerome, Paulinus and Augustine.

units.la: 18. Art.9.sicut aqua exstinguit ignem,ita eleemosyna peccatum.]nempe offerentis eleemosyna & peccato renunciantis. nam fi ad defunctum respexeris, eius sanctæ familia dicitur ab Hieronymo, offa veneranda, cineres quiescentes. in his quomodo peccatum, aut incendium eius reliinxeris?
units.tr: 18. Art. 9. As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.] Namely, the almsgiving of the one who offers it, who renounces sin. For if you look to the dead person, Jerome calls his body the holy family, a venerable bone, resting ashes. How, in these, will you find sin or its fire?

units.la: 19. Art.10. anima uxoris defunctæ fatis fecerit, corpori lachrymis, anima eleemosynis. ] nempe quas illa viuens erogari de suo, & suo nomine mandauerat, ita fit satis mortuo, licet non sentiat, dum præstatur mandatum ipsius.
units.tr: 19. Art. 10. The soul of the wife who has died has made satisfaction, the body with tears, the soul with almsgivings.] Namely, the almsgivings which she, while living, had ordered to be distributed from her own goods and in her own name. In this way the dead person is satisfied, even though he does not perceive it, while her command is carried out.

units.la: 20. Ibid. commendans eamdem animam Amando Episcopo.] hæc omnia, vt supra nota 17.
units.tr: 20. Ibid. Commending the same soul to Bishop Amandus.] All these things are as stated above in note 17.

units.la: 21. Art.11. locum suum habet etiam commendatio mortuorum.] nempe ad requiem ipsorum hærentium (vt credebatur) in exspectatione diuinæ gloriæ: quod ante dictum centies.
units.tr: 21. Art. 11. The commendation of the dead also has its place.] Namely, for the rest of those who (as was believed) remain in expectation of the divine glory. This was said a hundred times before.

units.la: 22. Ibid. qui cum defunctis a fidelibus exhibetur, eum prodesse non dubium est.] Mutilatus locus: sic enim ait Augustinus, eum prodesse non dubium est iis qui, quum in corpore viuerent, talia sibi posit hanc vitam prodesse meruerunt, id est, qui dum viuerent, pietatem, sanctimoniam, & integritatem vitæ coluerunt etiam a morte commendabilem. Hæc autem omnia de pœna damni solum, ac non sensus præstita olim, affectum quidem & significationem affectus viuentium probant; sed non probant effectu veritatemq; rei quam imaginantur affectu suo: vt dicetur postea lib.2. cap.15. & sequentibus.
units.tr: 22. Ibid. Which, when it is shown by the faithful to the dead, is undoubtedly of benefit to them.] The passage is mutilated. For Augustine says: it is undoubtedly of benefit to those who, while they were in the body, merited that such things could benefit them after this life, that is, who while living cultivated piety, holiness and integrity of life, which is commendable even after death. But all these things, offered in the past, prove only the penalty of loss, not of sense, and they prove the affection and the expression of affection of the living; but they do not prove the truth of the thing which they imagine by their affection, as will be said later in book 2, chapter 15 and following.

units.la: 23. Ibid. tract.84. in Ioan. quæst.2. ad Dulcitium,] hi omnes loci conueniunt plane cum iis quæ nota 17. & alibi sæpe posuimus. Sequentia de Aerio ante Hegauimus nota 9.
units.tr: 23. Ibid. Tractate 84 on John, question 2, to Dulcitius.] All these passages agree plainly with what we have put forward in note 17 and often elsewhere. The following passages about Aerius were discussed above in note 9.

units.la: 24. Art.12. pro eis Domino preces fundunt.] hæc testimonia atque sequentia, tertij sunt illius seculi, quo superstitio & error obtinuit plurimum, ut capitis 9.nota 2.distinximus. Confudit autem hoc seculum ista duo doctrinæ capita, de sanctorum requie in expectatione gloriæ malo carentium & ad gloriam perfectam anhelantium, pro quibus orabatur prius; & de pœnis Purgatorialibus in eadem expectatione subeundis, pro quibus orant Pontificij. Nos prius toleramus, posterius negamus, omniaque de eo testimonia.
units.tr: 24. Art. 12. They pour out prayers to the Lord for them.] These testimonies and those that follow belong to the third century, when superstition and error held the greatest sway, as we pointed out in chapter 9, note 2. This age, however, confused two heads of doctrine: the rest of the saints, who are free from evil and wait for perfect glory, for whom prayer was offered earlier; and the penalties of Purgatory, to be undergone in that same waiting, for which the Papists pray. We accept the former and deny the latter, and we deny all testimonies about it.

units.la: Art. 13. non pro eorum spiritibus vel eleemosy-nam faceret, vel Deo sacrificium offerret.] non sequitur ex imperfecta causarum enumeratione. Dicendum enim fuerat; nisi catholica Ecclesia crederet fide-libus defunctis augeri & promoveri bona (quod antecedens Ecclesia statuebat) aut dimitti peccata & mala aboleri, quod in subsequente Ecclesia obtinuit. Negatur ergo auctoritas.
units.tr: Art. 13. He would not make an almsgiving for their spirits, nor offer a sacrifice to God.] This does not follow from an incomplete enumeration of causes. For it should have been said: unless the Catholic Church believed that good things are increased and advanced for the faithful dead (which the earlier Church held), or that sins are forgiven and evils removed, which the later Church maintained. The authority is therefore denied.

units.la: Art. 14. qua defunctis tanta a viuis beneficia impenduntur.] negamus omnia hæc testimonia; verumtamen ea distinctione servata, quam proxima nota posuimus. Nam ab errantibus dicta sunt.
units.tr: Art. 14. By which such great benefits are bestowed on the dead by the living.] We deny all these testimonies, but with the distinction observed which we set out in the preceding note. For they were spoken by those who were in error.

units.la: Art. 15. simul omnes errare non possunt, quin Ecclesia universa erret & pereat.] falsum, nisi distinctione adhibita: nempe si error est fundamentalis, & quasi iugulum Ecclesiæ petens ac ipsum salutis caput. Nam errore quouis non Christianus, non Ecclesia perit; sed eo demum errore qui absolute perniciosus atque exitialis est. Illo errore Ecclesia vel tota in terris militans errare potest; hoc vero minimè.
units.tr: Art. 15. All together they cannot err without the whole Church erring and perishing.] This is false unless a distinction is applied: namely, if the error is fundamental, and attacks like a throat-cutter the very head of salvation. For the Christian and the Church do not perish through any error whatever, but only through that error which is absolutely pernicious and deadly. The Church militant on earth, whole, may err in that error; but in this one, by no means.

units.la: Art. 16. ante m.ccc. annos usu receptum fuit, precationes fierent pro defunctis,] hæc non Caluini, sed aduersariorum obiicientium verba, ad quæ copiosè respondet sequentibus eodem in loco. Melius hic referri oportuit multa Caluini, quæ Bellarminus dissimulat.
units.tr: Art. 16. Before 1300 years had passed it was received in use that prayers should be made for the dead.] These are not the words of Calvin but of the adversaries who raise the objection, to which he replies fully in the following passages in the same place. It was right to cite here the many things of Calvin which Bellarmine passes over.

units.la: 29. Ibid. Sed omnes fateor, in errorem abreptifuerunt. ] Omnes, inquis? atqui hoc Caluinus non dicit vniuersè. hæc enim illius verba. Certè quisquis mediocri prudentia pollet, facilè agnoscit quicquid de hac re legitur apud veteres, publico mori & vulgi impe-ritia fuisse datum. Abrepti etiam ipsi, fateor, in errorem fuerunt. &c. nusquam vox omnes comparet.
units.tr: 29. Ibid. But I confess they were all carried away into error.] All, you say? But Calvin does not say this universally. For these are his words: Certainly whoever has moderate prudence readily recognises that whatever is read about this matter among the ancients was given over to the common folly and ignorance of the people. They themselves, I confess, were also carried away into error, and so on. The word all appears nowhere.

units.la: 30. Ibid. & nullum fuisse ex antiquis qui restite-rit, ] de errore Ecclesiæ responsum est nota 27. nullum autem fuisse qui restiterit, id nunquam, dixit Caluinus, aut scripsit. Et quàm multa hic Caluino adfingit! quàm multa præterit! Consulat lector prudens & pius.
units.tr: 30. Ibid. And that there was none of the ancients who resisted,] An answer about the error of the Church has been given in note 27. But that there was none who resisted, Calvin never said or wrote. And how many things does he here add to Calvin! How many does he pass over! Let the prudent and pious reader consider this.

units.la: 31. Art. 17. At hoc mendacium est; aperte enim ci-tati Patres dicunt iuuari animas. ] non est mendacium, si quid distinctè dicitur, & affirmatur negaturque diuerso respectu. Priscos illos Patres verum est, qui quidem meliùs fuerunt instituti, dixisse, orasse veteres pro mortuis, non vt cos iuuarent, sed vt ostenderent erga eos pium affectum, &c. contrà vero id quoque certum est eos qui non vsqueadeò veritatem rei cognouerunt, orationem pro mortuis defendisse, quòd iuuari animas eorum crederent. Etsi ne hoc quidem prætereundum est, quum iuuari animas cœperunt credere, intellexisse de adiumento in bonum; postea vero inualescente errore Purgatorij, intellexisse de adiumento ad liberationem à malis illius. Priorem sententiam toleramus; posteriorem pernegamus, quia aduersatur gratiæ &c. veritati Christi salutaris nostri. Cætera agnosci-mus.
units.tr: 31. Art. 17. But this is a lie; for the Fathers cited clearly say that souls are helped.] It is not a lie, if something is said distinctly and affirmed and denied in different respects. It is true that those earlier Fathers, who were indeed better instructed, said that the ancients prayed for the dead, not so as to help them, but to show a pious affection towards them, and so on. On the other hand, it is also certain that those who did not so fully understand the truth of the matter defended prayer for the dead because they believed that their souls were helped. Yet this too must not be passed over: when they began to believe that souls were helped, they understood it of help towards good; but later, when the error of Purgatory grew strong, they understood it of help towards deliverance from its evils. We accept the former opinion; the latter we utterly reject, because it is opposed to grace, etc., and to the saving truth of Christ our Saviour. We acknowledge the rest.

units.la: 32. Art. 18. priuato quodam affectu omnibus probari voluit.]Caluinus sic ait, pro natura affectu probari aliis voluit, sic cætera, quæ hic suo commodo Bellarminus refert.
units.tr: 32. Art. 18. He wished to prove it by a certain private affection, to be approved by all.] Calvin says thus: he wished to prove it to others by natural affection, and so on for the rest, which Bellarmine here reports to suit his own purpose.

units.la: 33. Art. 19. Et tamen isti ipsi ad orationem pro defunctis hortantur.] sed ad eam orationem minime, quæ liberatura ex pœ-is Purgatorij, aut adiutura liberationem ex eis videretur: ut supra nota 7. & cap. 9. nota 2[?]. & 10. ostendimus.
units.tr: 33. Art. 19. And yet these same men urge prayer for the dead.] But not at all to that prayer which would be thought to free from the penalties of Purgatory, or to help in deliverance from them, as we have shown above in note 7, and in chapter 9, note 2[?], and in chapter 10.

units.la: 34. Ibid. hanc esse ⟨Apostolicam traditionem,] hæc omnia proxime cap. 9. confutauimus suo ordine.
units.tr: 34. Ibid. That this is the Apostolic tradition,] All these things were refuted in their order just above, in chapter 9.

units.la: 35. Ibid. non dubium esse quin iuventur anima,] Augu-stinus de adiumento dicit in stabiliendo promo-vendoq; bono; non autè in curandis & depellendis malis; quia hæc non sentiunt post vitam hanc fideles mortui: ut ante sæpius distinximus.
units.tr: 35. Ibid. That there is no doubt that the soul is helped,] Augustine speaks of help in establishing and advancing good, not in curing and driving away evils, because the faithful dead do not feel these after this life, as we have often distinguished before.

units.la: 36. Ibid. in toto libro non est vna syllaba, quæ dubium vel insinuet de quo (Caluinus loquitur,) affirmatio audax: nam bona pars libri, eo excepto quod de sepultura dicitur, magis est problematica, quàm axiomatica; & ita cedit plerumque communi sententiæ, ut tamen reuellat modestissimè. Exemplum esto è principio cap. 5 quum dicit, Quum ergo fidelis mater fidelis filij defuncti corpus desiderauit in basilica martyris poni, siquidem credidit eius animam meritis martyris adiuuari, hoc quod ita credidit supplicatio quædam fuit & hæc profuit, siquid profuit. hæc postrema verba ἐπανορθωσὶν[?] Augustini docent communi illi opinioni obnitentem. Sic alia plurima, præsertim inde à medio libri.
units.tr: 36. Ibid. In the whole book there is not one syllable that hints at doubt about what (Calvin says) is a bold assertion. For a good part of the book, apart from what is said about burial, is more problematic than axiomatic, and it so often yields to the common opinion while quietly undermining it with great moderation. Take as an example the beginning of chapter 5, where he says: Since, then, a faithful mother desired that the body of her faithful dead son be laid in the basilica of a martyr, believing indeed that his soul was helped by the merits of the martyr, this supplication which she made in such belief was a certain kind of prayer, and it helped, if it helped at all. These last words show Augustine resisting that common opinion. The same is true of very many other passages, especially from the middle of the book onwards.

units.la: 37. Ibidem.est enim familiare (aliuno[?] reprehendere, ridere sanctos.] calūnia. Sāctos alioquin stare in hac vita, & cadere, & resurgere quis negat? nul-lum profecto peccatum, nein sanctis quidem lauda-dile.
units.tr: 37. Ibid. For it is familiar (to some) to criticise and laugh at the saints. Calumny. Who denies that the saints otherwise stand in this life, and fall, and rise again? Certainly there is no sin, not even one to be praised in the saints.

units.la: 38. Art.20. est intoleranda impudentia, vel imperitia.] negatur: sequentibus confutabitur.
units.tr: 38. Art. 20. It is intolerable impudence or ignorance. Denied; it will be refuted in what follows.

units.la: 39. Ibid. docent animas quorundam sanctorum egere refrigerio, & iuvari orationibus viventium.] non sequitur, ergo Purgatorium esse], ut capite 9. ostendimus nota 2. & deinceps. nam ista ex hypothesi suntdicta illius sententiae quam Bellarminus negat controu. 7. lib. 1. cap. 1. & seq.
units.tr: 39. Ibid. They teach that the souls of certain saints need refreshment and are helped by the prayers of the living. It does not follow, therefore, that there is a Purgatory, as we showed in chapter 9, note 2, and following. For these statements are made on the hypothesis of that opinion which Bellarmine denies, Controversy 7, book 1, chapter 1 and following.

units.la: 40. Art.21. sunt apertissima loca in Patribus ubi asserunt Purgatorium;] de priscis Patribus, negamus recentiorum auctoritati non habemus fidem.
units.tr: 40. Art. 21. There are most plain passages in the Fathers where they assert Purgatory. Concerning the ancient Fathers, we deny it. We do not give credence to the authority of more recent writers.

units.la: 41. Ibid. vel post obitum per expurgantis ignis fornacem expiatus, ad pristinam vellet redire felicitatem.] Negamus haec de Purgatorio Pontificio accipi oportere. Nam ipse Nyssenus ante aliquot paginas in eadem oratione mentem piorum negat hoc modo post mortem affici, quum ait: Quando mens extra prælium quod in connexione atque conflictu sibi invicem oppositorum elementorum committitur, constituta fuerit, tum angi ac discruciari definit. & quae sequuntur. Quid ergo est quod sibi Nyssenus voluit? nempe illud ipsum quod ante in caput 3. evidenter ostendimus, erudiri homines ut pristinam illam felicitatem inte-gritatémque in qua protoplastus fuerat conditus, exoptent sibi, alios verbo doctrinae salutaris, alios opere afflictionum: ac eos quidem qui emendantur doctrina, in curriculo ipso vitae huius emendari: qui vero afflictionibus, eos emendari etiā in ipsis mor[?] tis angustiis, & post mortem emendatos esse. Vbi ergo est expurgantis ignis fornax?in hac vita:quan- do exitur ex ea?in obitu. nā post obitum plane ex- piatus est,quum ab illa expiantis ignis fornace libe- ratus viuit in Domino.Hæc Gregorij Nyffeni sen- tentia,quam Sifanus interpres reddidit incommo- dius.Eadem quoque ratio sequentis loci.
units.tr: 41. Ibid. or, purified after death by the furnace of the cleansing fire, would wish to return to his former happiness. We deny that these words ought to be taken of the Papist Purgatory. For Nyssen himself, a few pages earlier in the same oration, denies that the minds of the pious are affected in this way after death, when he says: When the mind has been set outside the battle which is waged in the joining and clash of mutually opposed elements, then it ceases to be distressed and tormented. And what follows. What, then, did Nyssen mean? Surely just what we showed clearly before in chapter 3: that men are taught to desire for themselves that former happiness and integrity in which the first-formed man was created, some by the word of saving doctrine, others by the work of afflictions. Those who are amended by doctrine are amended in the very course of this life; but those who are amended by afflictions are amended even in the straits of death itself, and are made clean after death. Where, then, is the furnace of the cleansing fire? In this life. When is one led out of it? At death. For after death one is plainly cleansed, when, freed from that furnace of the cleansing fire, he lives in the Lord. This is the sense of Gregory of Nyssa, which the translator Sifanus rendered rather inconveniently. The same reasoning applies to the following passage.

units.la: 42. Ibid. aliis,inquit,post hanc vitam purgatorio i- gne materia labes abstergentibus. ] mutilatus locus li- cet eadem mente cum superioribus.Plenior est ille Nyffenj stilus,& locus copiosior, quàm vt huc to- tus adferatur:sed hoc illud est quod statuit,alios do- ctrinæ salutaris fide iam expiari,alios deinceps ex- piatum iri purgatorio afflictionum igne, quo ad mortem vsque, atque adeo in morte ipsa expian- tur virtute Dei. Sic exponit ipse Gregorius verbis sequentibus, quum rationem hanc continuò subii- cit: non enim in perpetuum apud naturam permanet alienarum rerum cupido, &c. quæ verba non nisi ad hanc naturam & præsentem vitam pertinere pos- sunt.
units.tr: 42. Ibid. Others, he says, after this life, by the purgatorial fire, wipe away the stain of matter. The passage is mutilated, though in the same sense as the preceding ones. Nyssen's style is fuller, and the passage too extensive to quote here in full. But this is what he lays down: some are already cleansed by faith in saving doctrine, others are to be cleansed afterwards by the purgatorial fire of afflictions, which lasts until death, and indeed they are cleansed in death itself by the power of God. Gregory himself explains this in the words that follow, when he at once adds this reason: For the desire for things belonging to others does not remain in nature for ever, etc. These words can refer only to this nature and to the present life.

units.la: 43. Art.22. vide etiam eumdem ferm.20. in Pfalm. 118. ] agit vtroque in loco Ambrosius de tribulatio- nibus huius vitæ, quibus homines ad emendationè prouocantur ,aut in perniciem dantur præcipites. Nam propterea de fidelibus dicit ad vitam hanc re- spiciens ,salui erimus per fidem. fides enim est præ- sentis vitæ,quę saluum facit.De Psalmo 118.diximus suprà cap.5.nota 46.
units.tr: 43. Art. 22. See also the same, sermon 20, on Psalm 118. In both places Ambrose is speaking of the troubles of this life, by which men are provoked to amendment or are handed over headlong to destruction. For he says of the faithful, looking to this life: We shall be saved by faith. For faith belongs to the present life, and it is this that saves. We discussed Psalm 118 above in chapter 5, note 46.

units.la: 44. Art.3. sed nec vlla post mortem purgatoria tor- menta patitur. ] non sequitur, ergo post mortem poenas purgatorias esse temporaleis vllas. Nam in- consequēs est ex negatione affirmatio,vt suprà cap. 4. ostendimus. Et ratio est euidens: nam id tantum recte adfirmamus quod est; e contrario vero negamus recte tum illud quod non est, tum illud quod dicitur esse & non est. Post mortem gratia aut poena aeterna est; purgatoria vero & temporalis nulla, licet dicatur esse. Utrumque de infantibus recte Augustinus negat, & τὸ ὂν ἀληθῶς [?], καὶ τὸ ἀξίως λεγόμενον [?]. Sed non sequitur, ergo id quod est ἀξίως λεγόμενον [?], ideo esse ἀληθῶς ὄν [?]. Exemplū esto, si quis animam humanam dixerit nec in suo corpore, nec in alieno per metempsychosin Pythagoream, aut metensomatosin Empedoclceam vivere solitariam, verum dicit: nam vivit in corpore ut principium vitae, motus, & quietis illius. Sed qui ex eo infert, ergo metempsychosin & metensomatosin esse, perbellas nugas agit.
units.tr: 44. Art. 3. But he does not suffer any purgatorial torments after death. It does not follow that there are therefore no temporal purgatorial punishments after death. For, as we showed above in chapter 4, from the denial an affirmation does not follow. And the reason is plain: we rightly affirm only what is; conversely, we rightly deny both what is not, and what is said to be but is not. After death there is eternal grace or eternal punishment; but purgatorial and temporal punishment there is none, although it is said to exist. Augustine rightly denies both of these concerning infants, and [what truly is] and [what is said worthily]. But it does not follow that what is said worthily [axiōs legomenon] is therefore truly being [alēthōs on]. Take this example: if someone says that the human soul does not live a solitary life either in its own body or in another by the Pythagorean metempsychosis or the Empedoclean metensomatosis, he speaks truly, for it lives in the body as the principle of its life, motion and rest. But whoever infers from this that there is metempsychosis and metensomatosis is talking very silly nonsense.

units.la: 45. Ibid. purgatos, aeterni ignis supplicijs non tradendos.] haec verba a farctura sunt, non ab Augustino: ut supra cap.4.nota 2. ostendimus, ex Vivis testimonio.
units.tr: 45. Ibid. Those who are cleansed are not to be handed over to the punishments of eternal fire. These words are a stuffing, not Augustine's, as we showed above in chapter 4, note 2, on the testimony of Vives.

units.la: 46. Ibid. de quo Apostolus inquit, falsum erit, sic tamen quasi per ignem.] stilus redundantior, & magis phraseon quarumdam quàm rerum pigmentis luxurians arguit homilia non esse Augustini: prout etiam Erasmus vidit. Est seculi posterioris φράσεως [?]. Quod si ex testimoniis Scripturae, quae ille ἐμμανὴς [?] adduxit, iudicium placeat fieri; aut de praesentibus afflictionibus purgatoriis verba eius oportet intelligi, aut fateri pessime adduci Prophetarum locos, Dan. 7. & Ezech. 24. nihil autem ex diverso probari potest.
units.tr: 46. Ibid. Of which the Apostle says: it will be so, yet as through fire. The style is too full and luxuriant, and abounds more in the colouring of certain phrases than of matters, which shows that the homily is not Augustine's; Erasmus also saw this. It is of the phraseology of a later century. And if judgment is to be made on the scriptural testimonies which he, like one out of his mind, adduces, then either his words must be understood of present purgatorial afflictions, or we must admit that the passages of the Prophets, Daniel 7 and Ezekiel 24, are very badly cited. Nothing, however, can be proved from the opposite side.

units.la: 47. Ibid.ω post hanc vitam habebit vel ignem purgationis, vel poenam aeternam.] Primum opus illud Augustini est neophyti, vt ipse testatur libro I. retract. cap. 10. propterea non debet illius tanta esse auctoritas, ac eorum scriptorum est quae exercitatus aut veteranus scripsit. Secundo & hoc observandum, distinctionum alias esse plane affirmatiuas, aliias synchoreticas & per concessionem dictas ex hypothesi eorum quibuscum agitur. sic autem loquitur Augustinus suppositá opinione quae iam tu in vulgus dissiminabatur paulatim, non affirmata sententia tamquam sua: prout ex verbis eiusdem proxime sequentibus, & ex cap. 23. & 27. ibidem cognoscitur, vbi flammeá illam frameam Gen. 3. exponit allegorice. Haec optima omnium solutio est atque facillima. Dici praeterea potest, committi à Bellarmino fallaciam compositionis & divisionis (vt vocant) in Augustini verba. Sic enim vocibus integris legenda esse & interstinguenda; quae paulo altius repetá vt legentes intelligant. In ista ergo perplexitate, cuius vultus non sudet, vt manducet panem suum? quod omnibus diebus vitae nostrae passuri sumus, id est, huius vitae quae transitura est. Et hoc illi dictum est qui coluerit agrum suum, quem ipsa patitur donec revertatur in terram ex qua sumptus est, id est, donec finiat vitam istam. Qui enim coluerit agrum suum intentus (vulgo legitur interius) & ad panem suum quamuis cum labore pervenerit, potest usque ad finem vitae huius huc labore patiri, post hanc autem vitam non est necesse vt patiatur. (& vbi igitur pro istis Purgatorium?) Sed qui forte agrum non coluerit, & finis eum opprimi permiserit, habet in hac vita maledictionem terra sua in omnibus operibus suis, & post hanc vitam. Habebit vel ignem purgationis, vel panam aeternam: ita nemo euadit istam sententiam. Sed agendum est, vt saltem in hac tantum vita sententiatur. Prout ergo Augustinus principio dixerat, cuius vul-tus non sudet, &c. ita iam concludit dicens, habebit vel ignem purgationis, vel poenam aeternam nimirum quisque Adami filius. Forte etiam (quod me iadiu memini obseruare)locus corruptus est, & reponendus verborum ordo in hunc modum:habet vel maledictionem terra suae [?] in omnibus operibus suis, vel ignem purgationis, & post hac vitam habebit poenam aeternam. quae lectio iisdem Augustini locis quos ante attigi-mus, videtur confirmari. Pius lector & prudens viderit.
units.tr: 47. Ibid. After this life he will have either the fire of purgation or eternal punishment. This first work of Augustine's is that of a novice, as he himself testifies in book 1 of the Retractations, chapter 10; therefore its authority ought not to be as great as that of writings which a practised or veteran author wrote. Second, this must also be observed: some distinctions are plainly affirmative, others are concessive and made by way of concession, on the hypothesis of those with whom one is dealing. Augustine speaks in this way on the supposition of an opinion which was by then gradually being spread among the common people, not as an affirmed opinion of his own; as is known from the words of the same passage that immediately follow, and from chapters 23 and 27 of the same work, where he explains allegorically the flaming sword of Genesis 3. This is the best and easiest solution of all. It may further be said that Bellarmine commits the fallacy of composition and division (as they call it) in Augustine's words. For the words must be read and punctuated as whole units, going back a little further so that readers may understand: In that perplexity, whose face does not sweat, that he may eat his bread? This we shall suffer all the days of our life, that is, of this life which is to pass away. And this was said to him who tilled his field, which the earth itself suffers until it returns to the earth from which it was taken, that is, until this life is finished. For he who tilled his field, intent (commonly read as interius) and having reached his bread with labour, can endure this labour in this life until its end; but after this life he need not suffer it. (And where, then, is Purgatory in place of these things?) But he who perhaps did not till his field, and whom the end was allowed to overwhelm, has in this life the curse of his earth in all his works, and after this life he will have either the fire of purgation or eternal punishment. Thus no one escapes that sentence. But we must act so that he is condemned in this life alone. So, as Augustine had said at the beginning, whose face does not sweat, etc., so now he concludes, saying: he will have either the fire of purgation or eternal punishment, namely every son of Adam. Perhaps also (as I remember I observed long ago) the passage is corrupt, and the order of the words should be restored in this way: he has either the curse of his earth in all his works, or the fire of purgation, and after this life he will have eternal punishment. This reading seems to be confirmed by the same passages of Augustine which we touched on before. Let the devout and prudent reader judge.

units.la: 48. Ibid. gravior tamen erit ille ignis, quàm quicquid potest homo pati in hac vita. ]Haec Augustinus de igne aeterno enunciat, quem cum igne tribulationum huius vitae purgatorio (vt vocant) comparat. vide supra in cap. 5. nota 72.
units.tr: 48. Ibid. Yet that fire will be more severe than anything a man can suffer in this life. ] Augustine says this about eternal fire, which he compares with the fire of the trials of this life, the so-called purgatory. See above, in chapter 5, note 72.

units.la: 49. Art. 24. non dubitat de poena animarum, sed de modo & qualitate. ]Negamus hanc distinctionem, quia est commentitia, vt mox dicebamus.
units.tr: 49. Art. 24. He does not doubt the punishment of souls, but its mode and quality. ] We deny this distinction, because it is invented, as we said a moment ago.

units.la: 50. Ibid. dubitat, an ignis purgatorius sit idem & substantia cum igne gehennae. ] illud artifex hac responsione. Augustinus enim toto illo capite verba Pauli exponit de igne tribulationum huius vitae. Tandem vero ex hypothesi inualescentis iam tum, sed nondum obtinentis sententiae, ita scribit: Post istius sane corporis mortem, donec ad illum veniatur qui post resurrectionem corporum futurus est damnationis & remunerationis vltimus dies, si hoc temporis interuallo spiritus defunctorum eiusmodi ignem dicuntur perpeti quem non sentiant illi qui non habuerunt tales mores & amores in huius corporis vita, vt eorum ligna, & fœnu, & stipula consumatur, alij vero sentiant qui eiusmodi secum adificia portauerunt, siue hic tantum, siue & hic &c. ibi, sive ideo hic ut non ibi secularia, quamuis a damnatione venialia, concremantem igne transitoria tribulationis inueniant, non redarguo, quia forsitan verum est. Potest quippe ad istam tribulationem pertinere etiam ipsa mors carnis, quae de peccati primi perpetratione coepta est, & secundum cuiusque aedificium tepore suo ab unoquoque suscepta. Possut & persecutiones Ecclesiae, etc.
units.tr: 50. Ibid. He doubts whether purgatorial fire is the same in substance as the fire of hell. ] Bellarmine handles this with the following answer. For Augustine, throughout that whole chapter, expounds the words of Paul as referring to the fire of the trials of this life. Finally, however, from a hypothesis that was already gaining ground but had not yet prevailed, he writes as follows: After the death of this body, until the day comes for him who is to come after the resurrection of bodies, the last day of judgement and reward, if in this interval of time the spirits of the dead are said to suffer a kind of fire which those do not feel who did not have such morals and loves in the life of this body, that their wood, hay and stubble are consumed, but others feel it who have carried such buildings with them, whether here only, or both here and there, etc. ...; or because here, so that they are not there, worldly things, though venial in comparison with damnation, they find burning them with the transitory fire of tribulation, I do not refute, because perhaps it is true. For indeed this tribulation may include even the death of the flesh itself, which began with the commission of the first sin, and is undergone by each person according to his building, in its own time. Persecutions of the Church may also belong to it, etc.

units.la: Nonne vides, mi homo, Augustinum agere de igne, quo sive ibi tantum, sive & hic & ibi, sive ideo hic ut non ibi exercentur spiritus seruandorum, de igne concremante transitoria tribulationis, de igne cui accensetur ipsa mors carnis, cui tribulationes Ecclesiae? Haec autem ad illum aeternum ignem minime pertinent. Nec refert, quod eo in loco Augustinus proxime aeterni ignis meminerat: nam ἀναίρεσιν sive per remotionem oppositi (quod illi auctori folenne est, & interdum ad obscuritatem usque) tantum meminerat, cum tamen institutus sermo de igne probante haberetur in toto illo capite. Nam haec proxime antecedentia illius verba de loco Pauli 1.Cor.3. dicentis: Si autem salui fient, profecto & ad dexteram stabunt, & cum ceteris audient, venite benedicti Patris mei, possidete paratum vobis regnum, non ad sinistram, ubi illi erunt qui salui non erunt, & ideo audient, discedite a me maledicti in ignem aeternum. Nemo quippe ab illo igne saluabitur, quia in supplicium aeternum ibunt illi omnes, ubi vermis eorum non morietur, & ignis non exstinguetur quo cruciabuntur die ac nocte in secula seculorum. Hac ergo remotione vel negatiua (ut vocant) posita, continuo ad sermonem Augustinus redit de igne probationis, prout verba eius quam fidelissime retulimus, & distertis verbis effugium Bellarmineum obstruit.
units.tr: Do you not see, my friend, that Augustine is speaking of a fire by which, whether there only, or both here and there, or because here so that not there, the spirits of those who are to be saved are tested; of the fire that consumes the transitory things of tribulation; of the fire to which death of the flesh itself is set alight, and to which the tribulations of the Church belong? But these have nothing to do with that eternal fire. Nor does it matter that in that passage Augustine had just mentioned eternal fire: for he mentioned it only by [ἀναίρεσιν], that is, by removal of the opposite (a figure customary with that author, and at times carried to obscurity), whereas the discussion in the whole chapter was about the fire that tests. For the words immediately preceding are those on the passage of Paul in 1 Cor. 3, saying: But if they are saved, certainly they will stand also at the right hand, and will hear with the rest, "Come, blessed of my Father, possess the kingdom prepared for you", not at the left, where those will be who are not saved, and who therefore will hear, "Depart from me, accursed, into eternal fire." For no one will be saved from that fire, since all those will go into eternal punishment, where their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched, by which they will be tormented day and night for ever and ever. With this removal, or negative (as they call it), set down, Augustine at once returns to his discussion of the fire of testing, as I have reported his words as faithfully as possible, and with plain words he blocks Bellarmine's escape route.

units.la: 51. Ibid. quo hic vri solent, cum rebus valde dilectis carere coguntur, ] haec distinctio pugnat cum Augustini verbis. Nam aliud est ignis purgatorius de quo ille dicit, aliud ignis doloris de amissione rerum temporalium, quem iste comminiscitur. Ignis purgato-rius (quem Augustinus queri posse, & aut inueniri aut latere pronunciat, condonans aliquid errori publico) est, hęredū[?] est vitæ; ignis ille doloris de amis-sione temporalium, hic infirmitatis est; illic impietatis, quam damnat, non purgat Deus.
units.tr: 51. Ibid. by which men are usually burned here, when they are compelled to go without things they love very much, ] This distinction conflicts with Augustine's words. For one thing is purgatorial fire, of which he speaks, and another is the fire of grief over the loss of temporal things, which this author invents. Purgatorial fire (which Augustine declares can be asked about, and either found or hidden, granting something to the common error) belongs to the inheritance of life; that fire of grief over the loss of temporal things belongs to weakness. The former is of impiety, which God condemns rather than purges.

units.la: 52. Art.25. moderatam arbitramur & mixtam clementiæ sententiam iudicis. ] de igne tribulationum dicit Hieronymus, quo hic purgantur & probantur iusti, ut Bellarminus ante cap.1. confessus est. vide in cap.5. nota 71.
units.tr: 52. Art. 25. We judge the sentence of the judge to be moderate and mingled with mercy. ] Jerome speaks of the fire of tribulations, by which the righteous are here purged and tested, as Bellarmine confessed before chapter 1. See chapter 5, note 71.

units.la: 53. Art.26. alij flammis expiantur expurgatoriis, alij sententiam aeternae subeant damnationis. ] haec sententia est tertia corruptioris seculi, ut ante cap.9. nota 2.& 10. distinximus. negamus auctoritatem illius.
units.tr: 53. Art. 26. Others are cleansed by purgatorial flames, others undergo the sentence of eternal damnation. ] This opinion is the third of the more corrupt age, as we distinguished before, chapter 9, notes 2 and 10. We deny the authority of it.

units.la: 54. Art.27. id ignis decoquat & resoluat, ut effician-tur omnes aurum purum. ] de igne tribulationis in hac vita loquitur, ut supra cap.3. nota 60.& cap.5. nota 74. docuimus.
units.tr: 54. Art. 27. That fire may burn away and dissolve it, so that all are made pure gold. ] He speaks of the fire of tribulation in this life, as we taught above, chapter 3, note 60, and chapter 5, note 74.

units.la: 55. Art.28. vitiique levitatem absumit. ] vide supra cap.6. nota 11.
units.tr: 55. Art. 28. and takes away the lightness of vice. ] See above, chapter 6, note 11.

units.la: 56. Art.29. ipse autem saluus erit quasi per ignem. ] haec Basilius de igne tribulationum in hac vita pronunciat, quemadmodum &Esaias vaticinabatur. vi-de sup.cap.3. nota 54.
units.tr: 56. Art. 29. But he himself will be saved as if through fire. ] Basil declares this of the fire of tribulations in this life, just as Isaiah also prophesied. See above, chapter 3, note 54.

units.la: 57. Art.30. per vada feruentibus globis horrenda trā-sibunt. ] vide supra cap.7. nota 28.
units.tr: 57. Art. 30. Through the fords they will cross the dreadful glowing masses. ] See above, chapter 7, note 28.

units.la: 58. Art.31. & repurgantur, sicut aurum in conflatorio. ] ut sup. cap.5. nota 76.
units.tr: 58. Art. 31. and are purified again, as gold in the crucible. ] As above, chapter 5, note 76.

units.la: 59. Ibidem. qui transfit per ignem, & à concretis leuioribus maculis expiatur. ] vt supra cap. 5. nota 75.
units.tr: 59. Ibid. who passes through the fire, and is cleansed of the lighter stains that cling to him. ] As above, chapter 5, note 75.

units.la: 60. Ibid.nisi modico quoque delicto[?] mora resurrectio-nis expenso.] vide supra cap. 7. nota 25.
units.tr: 60. Ibid. unless the delay of the resurrection is weighed against even a small offence. ] See above, chapter 7, note 25.

units.la: 61. Ibid.aliud peccata omnia passione purgasse.] vide supra cap. 7. nota 26.
units.tr: 61. Ibid. that another has purged all sins by his suffering. ] See above, chapter 7, note 26.

units.la: 62. Artic. 32. (Christianos, si in peccato praeuenti fuerint, saluandos esse post poenas?] concedimus: nam Hieronymus loquitur de poenis quas in hac vita Christiani perferunt. Neque refert, quod scribat Hieronymus, praeuenti fuerint: quo verbo Bellarminus hic, opinor, abuti cogitat, vt hoc dicto ad rationem futuri seculi putetur pertinere. Nam Hieronymus diuerso plane sensu id verbum accipit, sequu-tus videlicet Paulum Galat. 6.1.
units.tr: 62. Art. 32. Are Christians, if they have been overtaken by sin, to be saved after punishments? ] We grant it: for Jerome speaks of the punishments which Christians endure in this life. Nor does it matter that Jerome writes overtaken: Bellarmine, I suppose, here intends to misuse that word, so that the saying may be thought to pertain to the reckoning of the age to come. For Jerome takes that word in a plainly different sense, following, of course, Paul in Gal. 6.1.

units.la: 63. Artic. 33. refrigeret animam eius stillicidiis misericordia sua per orationes vestras, &c.] vide supra nota 17.
units.tr: 63. Art. 33. may his mercy cool his soul with drops, through your prayers, etc. ] See above, note 17.

units.la: 64. Ibid.alia poenali acerbitate, alia purgatoria clementia exerceri puto. hoc Boëthij testimonium atque sequentia ad illud seculum corruptius pertinent, quo tertia illa sententia falsa obtinuit, de qua supra cap. 9. nota 2. & 10. Negamus itaque horum testimoniorum aliquam auctoritatem esse, quia opiniones humanas adsuunt diuinis rebus praeter auctoritatem Scripturae sacrae: nam nihil vltra hanc scire (vt cum Tertulliano dicam) omnia sciro est.
units.tr: 64. Ibid. I think they are exercised by one kind of penal bitterness and another purgatorial mercy. This testimony of Boethius, and what follows, pertain to that more corrupt age in which that third false opinion prevailed, of which above, chapter 9, notes 2 and 10. We therefore deny that any of these testimonies has authority, because they add human opinions to divine matters, apart from the authority of holy Scripture: for to know nothing beyond this (as I say with Tertullian) is to know everything.

units.la: 65. Ibid. & quodam purgatorio igne purganda.] Confutatum supra cap. 4.
units.tr: 65. Ibid. and to be purged by a certain purgatorial fire. ] Refuted above, chapter 4.

units.la: 66. Art. 38. Perstringentur igne atque amburentur, &c.] Hæc duo testimonia loco nō suo Bellarminus infert inferciuit,prout ab [illegible, ~6 letters] aliquo repente fubmis-sa sunt.Lactantij locus quam auctoritatem obtinere possit,nemo ignorat qui cum iudicio librum illum 7.legerit:adeo fabulis circumfluit, & portentosis e-tiamque haereticis opinionibus.negamus igitur.Tu nihil Purgatorium pontificium iuuat. Nam Purga-torium iudicio vltimo praeire tradunt Pontificij, Lactantius subsequi. Dicit enim: sed & iustos quum iudicauerit, etiam igni eos examinabit. Tum quorum peccata vel pondere vel numero praevaluerint,&c. Inanis igitur probatio.
units.tr: 66. Art. 38. They will be scorched and burned with fire, etc. ] Bellarmine has thrust these two testimonies into a place not their own, as they were put forward suddenly by someone [illegible]. As to what authority the passage of Lactantius can have, no one who has read that seventh book with judgement is ignorant: it is so full of fables and monstrous, even heretical, opinions. We therefore deny it. Indeed it does not help the Papist purgatory at all. For the Papists teach that Purgatory precedes the last judgement, while Lactantius places it after. For he says: But also when he has judged the righteous, he will examine them even by fire. Then those whose sins have outweighed them, either by weight or by number, etc. The proof is therefore empty.

units.la: 67. Art.39. In quo subeunda sunt gravia illa expian-da a peccatis animae supplicia.]Aliud est,si nos secun-dum nos conditionemque nostram, & iudicium i-tem diuinum secundum se absolute considerabi-mus, quam si comparate secundum rationem gra-tiae & iustitiae gratiosae Dei. Absolute nemo homo est, quem grauia illa supplicia subire non oporte-ret: comparate vero secundum ordinem gratiae & oeconomiae diuinae, plane contra accidit. Hilarius priore modo loquitur, iste ad posteriorem rapit fallens elenchi(vt vocant)ignorationem. Quemadmodum etiam,exempli causa,illud Psaltae dictum, non iustificabitur in conspectu tuo vlla caro, absolute efti[?]ve-riffimum, secundum rationem vero ordinemque οἰκονομίας illius gratiosae omnis caro iustificatur quae est censetur que in Christo Iesu.Hoc sibi velle Hilarium demonstrant quae proxime praecesserunt. Meminit Propheta, inquit, arduum esse & naturae humanae periculosissimum, Dei desiderare iudicia. Cum enim nemo viuens in conspectu ipsius mundus sit, quomodo desiderabile eius potest esse iudicium? An cum ex omni verbo otioso rationem simus praestituri, diem iudicij concupiscimus, in quo nobis est ille indefessus ignis obeundus? &c. Aliam quercum Bellarminus excutiat oportet, siglandem Purgatoriam nobis probaturus est.
units.tr: 67. Art. 39. In which those grievous punishments, to atone for the sins of the soul, are to be undergone. ] It is one thing if we consider ourselves according to ourselves and our condition, and the divine judgement likewise in itself absolutely, and another if we consider it comparatively, according to the reckoning of the grace and gracious justice of God. Absolutely, there is no man who ought not to undergo those grievous punishments; comparatively, however, according to the order of grace and the divine economy, the very opposite happens. Hilary speaks in the former sense, and this author snatches at the latter, committing the fallacy of ignoratio elenchi (as they call it). Just so, for example, the saying of the Psalmist, no living flesh shall be justified in your sight, is absolutely most true; but according to the reckoning and order of that gracious economy of Christ, all flesh that is in Christ Jesus is justified and is counted so. That Hilary meant this is shown by what immediately precedes. The Prophet remembers, he says, that it is difficult and most dangerous to human nature to desire the judgements of God. For since no one living is clean in his sight, how can his judgement be desirable? Or when we are to render account for every idle word, do we long for the day of judgement, in which that tireless fire must be faced by us? etc. Bellarmine must examine another oak, if he is to prove to us a purgatory of the sort he wants.

units.la: IN CAPUT II.
units.tr: CHAPTER II.

units.la: I. Art.I. Quædam peccata sunt venialia, soláque temporali pœna digna. ] Distinguenda hæc propositio. Nam venialia dicuntur per se, aut per accidens, id est, per gratiam & misericordiam Dei, peccatum delentis, & hominem actionemque illius acceptatis in Christo Iesu. Nullum peccatum per se veniale est, mortalia omnia: contrà verò peccata omnia sunt electis venialia per gratiam, omnia reprobis mortalia per se & per iustitiam Dei homines actionesque ipsorum per se considerantis in ipsis. Itaque & assumptio falsa est, nisi hæc eadem distinctio observetur.
units.tr: I. Art. 1. Some sins are venial, and deserve only temporal punishment.] This proposition needs distinguishing. Sins are called venial either in themselves or by accident, that is, through the grace and mercy of God, who blots out sin, and who accepts the man and his action in Christ Jesus. No sin is venial in itself; all sins are mortal.
