On the other hand, all sins are venial to the elect through grace, and all are mortal to the reprobate in themselves and through the justice of God, who considers the men and their actions in themselves. So the assumption is false too, unless this same distinction is observed.

units.la: 2. Art.2. Hic describitur peccatum, veniale ex imperfectione actus. ] Negatur: nec Iacobus ullam venialis peccati mentionem facit, nec de quolibet peccato dicit promiscuè, sed de peccato illo tentationis, quod homines illi [illegible, ~9 letters] reiicere in Deum sua impietate solent. Non sequitur ex particulari universè, non ἐν τὸ κατά τι λεγομένου ἁπλῶς[?]. Hoc ut intelligatur, age, paucis expendamus Iacobi locum. Dixerat primum: beatus est vir, qui sustinet tentationem, ac non deprimitur frangitúrve illa: quoniam probus compertus accipiet coronam vitæ, quam promisit Dom.nus iis qui diligunt ipsum. Ab hac propositione salutari, ex contrario Iacobus instituit de iis dicere, qui sustinent tentationem, sed crimen vitij sui in Deum plerumque transferunt, quando tentationi cedunt. Hos damnat duobus modis, κατ' ἀναίρεσιν [?] καὶ θέσιν [?], remotione & affirmatione contraria. Remotio est blasphemiæ illius, quū dicit, Nemo quum tentatur, dicat, à Deo tentor: ratio, quia Deus in se, extra se, & in creaturas suas est omnis malæ tentationis expers. nam Deus, inquit, tentari malis non potest, nec quemquam tentat. Quid ergo est? inquies. Affirmat quid sit tentatio mala Iacobus sequentibus, totúmque processum illius exponit conuenientissimè secundùm principia, vel causas, actiones, & euenta illius. De principiis vel causis ait: Sed vnusquisque tentatur, dum à propria cupiditate abstrahitur inescaturque. Tentationis, inquit, malæ (nam de hac solùm agitur, ex præcedente versu,) principia sunt tria, subiectum, obiectum, & ordinatio vnius ad alterum. Subiectum est vnusquisque homo, & τὸ ἐνθυμητικὸν [?] proprium, siue concupiscentiuum ipsius, vt Tertullianus nominat. Obiectum est hoc quidem in loco non quicquid concupisci potest simpliciter, sed quicquid rationem habet τῷ λελογισμένῳ [?], inescantis concupiscentiam. Ordinatio vero vnius ad alterum est tanquam à coitu siue congressu primo concupiscentiæ & obiecti, vbi concurrit duplex actus ad generationem peccati in mala tentatione positi: vnus concupiscentiæ simplex, quà se ipsa abstrahit à bono: alter mouentis obiecti ad malum, quo inescatur concupiscentia, abripiturque tentatione mala, mouens se proprio motu voluntatis, & mota à suo obiecto. Sequuntur actiones μεταφορικὰς [?] enunciatæ, conceptus & partus. Prior generationem significat, vt fiat peccatum: posterior constitutionem, quà peccatum fit in esse, vt loquuntur vulgo. Deinde cupiditas, inquit, posteaquam concepit, parit peccatum, id est, facit vt sit in esse quod erat in fieri, vt ita loquamur. Postremo autem hic euentus ille est, quod peccatum illud tentationis male συνπλεκτον, perductum in actum, siue intus, siue foris etiam peractum gignit mortem. Non negat igitur Iacobus omne peccatum gignere mortem, aut affirmat peccata quaedam esse per se venialia: sed tentationem distinguit a peccato, & ordinem peccati ex tentatione adversus blasphemos demonstrat luculentissime: non autem peccati cuiusuis in genere: quod Bellarminus conatur adstruere. Frustra autem de imperfectione actus argumentatur, nam vt partus concupiscentiae est peccatum (vt loquuntur) totalitate essentiae, ita conceptus concupiscentiae est peccatum totalitate virtutis siue potentiae, gradu, non statu aut natura sua ab illo differens: ac proinde natura & statu damnatum, mortale, non veniale dicendum est.
units.tr: 2. Art. 2. Here sin is described as venial from imperfection of the act.] Denied. James makes no mention of venial sin at all, and he does not speak of every sin indiscriminately, but of that sin of temptation which men [illegible] are accustomed to transfer to God by their impiety. What holds of a particular case cannot be inferred universally; it is not the case that what is said of a part is said simply [ἐν τὸ κατά τι λεγομένου ἁπλῶς]. To understand this, let us briefly weigh James's passage. He had said first: Blessed is the man who endures temptation, and is not crushed or broken by it; for when he has been approved he will receive the crown of life, which the Lord has promised to those who love him. From this wholesome proposition James draws, by way of contrast, a statement about those who endure temptation but very often shift the blame for their own vice onto God when they give way to temptation. He condemns these in two ways, by negation and by affirmation [κατ' ἀναίρεσιν καὶ θέσιν], by removing and by asserting the contrary. The negation is of that blasphemy when he says: Let no one, when he is tempted, say, "I am tempted by God"; the reason being that God, in himself, outside himself, and in his creatures, is free from all evil temptation. For God, he says, cannot be tempted with evils, nor does he tempt anyone. What then is it? you will ask. James, in the verses that follow, states what evil temptation is, and sets out the whole process of it most fittingly according to its principles, or causes, actions, and outcomes. Concerning the principles or causes he says: But each one is tempted when he is drawn away and enticed by his own desire. The principles of evil temptation (for only this is under discussion, from the preceding verse) are three: the subject, the object, and the ordering of the one to the other. The subject is each man, and his own faculty of reasoning [τὸ ἐνθυμητικὸν], or his concupiscible part, as Tertullian calls it. The object here is not whatever can simply be desired, but whatever has a reasoned appeal [τῷ λελογισμένῳ] to the desire that entices. The ordering of the one to the other is, as it were, the first coming together or meeting of desire and object, where two acts concur to generate sin in evil temptation: one is the simple act of desire, by which it draws itself away from the good; the other is the moving object that draws desire toward evil, by which desire is enticed and carried off by temptation, the object moving itself by its own motion of will, and moved by its object. Then follow the actions, expressed metaphorically: conception and birth. The former signifies the generation, so that sin may come about; the latter the constitution, by which sin comes into being, as people commonly say. Then desire, he says, after it has conceived, gives birth to sin, that is, makes what was in becoming to be in being, so to speak. Finally, the outcome is this: that sin, once conceived in that evil entanglement and brought into act, whether inwardly or outwardly, by the act also brings forth death. James therefore does not deny that every sin brings forth death, nor does he affirm that some sins are venial in themselves. Rather, he distinguishes temptation from sin, and most clearly demonstrates the order by which sin arises from temptation, against blasphemers; but not of any sin whatever, as Bellarmine tries to maintain. Moreover, the argument from imperfection of the act is vain; for just as the birth of desire is sin (as they say) in its whole essence, so the conception of desire is sin in its whole power or faculty, differing from the other only in degree, not in its status or nature. Accordingly, by its nature and status it must be called damnable and mortal, not venial.

units.la: 3. Ibid. Iacobus explicat processum peccati secundum se.] negatur. nam peccatum qua est secundum se, rationem habet communem omni peccato. Iacobus vero non agit de peccato secundum rationem communem, sed qua peccatum a tentatione est: non ergo processum peccati secundum se Iacobus explicat.
units.tr: 3. Ibid. James explains the process of sin in itself.] Denied. For sin, as it is in itself, has a rationale common to every sin. But James is not treating of sin according to its common rationale, but as it arises from temptation. Therefore James does not explain the process of sin in itself.

units.la: 4. Ibid. Tentationem concupiscentiae, quae sine peccato esse potest,] Distinguendum tentationis nomen. Nam tentatio est aut πειρασμος, aut πειρα, vt in controuersiam 2. diximus. Illa est in motu obiecti aut impellentis causae, vt quum diabolus monens omnia tentaret Christum immotum, Matt. 4. haec in motu subiecti voluntarij, & se accommodantis voluntarie mouenti causae, vt quum Satanas in Iudam ingressus dicitur, Luc. 22. 3. Quapropter negamus sequenquentia omnia, & confutabuntur planiùs controuersiæ 2.generalis libro 1.in tomo 4.Deo dante.
units.tr: 4. Ibid. Concupiscent temptation, which can exist without sin,] The term temptation needs distinguishing. For temptation is either peirasmos or peira, as we said in controversy 2. The former lies in the motion of an object or an impelling cause, as when the devil, moving all things, tempted Christ, who stood unmoved (Matt. 4). The latter lies in the motion of a voluntary subject, who voluntarily accommodates himself to the moving cause, as when Satan is said to have entered into Judas (Luke 22.3). Wherefore we deny all the following, and they will be refuted more fully in controversy 2, general book 1, in volume 4, God willing.

units.la: 5. Ibid. Accedente nimirum pleno consensu generat mortem. ] Et hæc antecedentia negamus omnia, & negamus consequens. Non enim sequeretur, etiamsi ista daremus omnia, ergo venialia remitti in Purgatorio futuri seculi: Eadem rationum sequentium conditio & modus: quod hic semel dictum vo-lumus.
units.tr: 5. Ibid. Clearly, with full consent, it generates death.] We deny all of these antecedents, and we deny the consequent. For it would not follow, even if we granted all these things, that venial sins are forgiven in the Purgatory of the future age. The condition and manner of the following arguments is the same; we wish this to be said once here.

units.la: 6. Art. 3. Hic describitur veniale ex levitate mate-ria, ] Negatur. non ex materia aut forma est, quod veniale peccatum est: sed per accidens, & ex accidente gratia fit veniale: alioquin veniale non posset dici proprie, ut docet ratio, & natura vocis. Sequentia itaque nihil ad rem.
units.tr: 6. Art. 3. Here venial is described from lightness of matter,] Denied. A sin is not venial from its matter or form, but by accident, and it becomes venial by an accident of grace; otherwise it could not properly be called venial, as reason and the nature of the word teach. The following therefore has nothing to do with the matter.

units.la: 7. Art.4. Spiritum contribulatum per pœnitentiam. ] Primùm non est Augustini opus, licet auctoris veteris. Secundò non iuvat Bellarmini causam. Id.e-nim solùm dicit quod ante nota1.dicebamus: nempe omnia peccata esse piis venialia, qui virtutem & sapientiam Dei agnoverunt: impiis verò non esse venialia, quibus certa pœna debetur hic & in futuro seculo: idque ex natura bonitatis Dei, quæ & iustum amat, & improbum amantémque violentiæ odit, Psal.11.5. ideóque depluit super ipsum iudicia sua.
units.tr: 7. Art. 4. A contrite spirit through repentance.] First, this is not the work of Augustine, though it is of an ancient author. Second, it does not help Bellarmine's cause. For it says only what we said before in note 1: namely, that all sins are venial to the pious, who have acknowledged the power and wisdom of God, but are not venial to the impious, who are owed a certain punishment here and in the future age. This follows from the nature of the goodness of God, which loves the just and hates the wicked and those who love violence (Ps. 11.5), and therefore rains down upon him his judgments.

units.la: 8. Art.5. Intelligibile non est, quomodo verbum otiosum ex natura sua dignum sit perpetuo odio Dei, & sempiternis flammis: ] certè non est intelligibile, nisi idem[?] qui dixit doceat per Spiritum. Iis vero quos Spiritus ille veritatis docet, intelligibilia sunt hæc: primùm, omnem ἁμαρτίαν[?] per se maledictam esse, omne autem peccatum ἁμαρτίαν[?] esse: secundò, ab ἁμαρτίᾳ[?] illud proficisci, quòd maledictus est quisquis non præstiterit verba Legis faciendo ea, Deut.27.26. tertiò, verba Legis esse, diliges Iehovam Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, & ex toto animo tuo, & ex totis viribus tuis, Deuter.6.5. quartò, quisquis otiosum verbum pronunciat, eum ipso facto contra se testari, se nec Deum diligere ex toto corde suo, &c. (otiatur enim) nec proximum suum ut seipsum, cùm ratio proximi iubeat: ut sermones nostri (quod ait Apostolus Ephes.4.) sint boni [illegible, ~12 letters]. Postremò, quisquis igitur otiosum verbum pronunciat, hunc reum esse naturae peccati sui coram iudicio Dei: hoc qui non intelligit, eum sanctè dicimus, nec perfectionem Dei satis intelligere, nec naturam peccati, nec suam conditionem ipsius.
units.tr: 8. Art. 5. It is not intelligible how an idle word, by its nature, deserves the perpetual hatred of God and eternal flames:] Certainly it is not intelligible, unless the one who said it teaches it through the Spirit. To those whom that Spirit of truth teaches, these things are intelligible: first, that every sin [hamartia] is in itself accursed, and every sin is a hamartia; second, that it follows from hamartia that whoever does not perform the words of the Law by doing them is accursed (Deut. 27.26); third, that the words of the Law are: You shall love Jehovah your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your strength (Deut. 6.5); fourth, whoever utters an idle word bears witness against himself by the very fact that he does not love God with all his heart, etc. (for it is idle), nor his neighbour as himself, since the reason of the neighbour commands it; so that our speech, as the Apostle says (Eph. 4), may be good [illegible]. Finally, whoever therefore utters an idle word is guilty of the nature of his sin before the judgment of God. Whoever does not understand this, we say, does not understand the perfection of God sufficiently, nor the nature of sin, nor his own condition.

units.la: 9. Ibid. Persequeretur eum, quem amicum paulo ante habuerat: Omnino dispar ratio: nam hominis ad hominem est analogia: & quæ hominis ad Deū? non sequitur ex dispari. Sic falsa conclusio ex falsis antecedentibus.
units.tr: 9. Ibid. He would persecute the one whom he had held as a friend shortly before: The reasoning is wholly unlike. For there is an analogy between man and man, but what is the analogy between man and God? Nothing follows from an unlike case. So a false conclusion follows from false premises.

units.la: 10. Ibid. Igitur tale peccatum deleri in morte non potest. negatur consequens: nam omne peccatum electorum Dei & in vita & in morte deletur: post mortem deletum permanet. Ratio est, quia in vita & morte semen Dei est in ipso, post mortem Deus in ipso est & ipse in Deo. vide 1.Ioan.3.9.
units.tr: 10. Ibid. Therefore such a sin cannot be blotted out in death. I deny the consequent. For every sin of God's elect is blotted out both in life and in death, and after death it remains blotted out. The reason is that in life and in death the seed of God is in him; after death God is in him and he is in God. See 1 John 3.9.

units.la: 11. Ibid. Cum septies in die cadat iustus, ut dicitur Prouerb. 24. Æquiuocè: nam Sapiens agit de casu afflictionum, iste de casu peccati. Sic inconsequens argumentatio.
units.tr: 11. Ibid. For the righteous man falls seven times a day, as is said in Proverbs 24. This is an equivocation. For the Wise Man is speaking of falling into afflictions, while this author is speaking of falling into sin. So the argument does not follow.

units.la: 12. Art.6. Potest fieri, & sæpe fit, ut in tota vita aliquis non satisfecerit plenè pro temporali illa pœna: Negamus assumptionem istam, hoc posse fieri, aut vn-quam fieri: petitur [illegible, ~6 letters], hic Deus temporaleis pœnas exigit, qualeis & quantas vult, illic vero æternas. De satisfaciendi verbo, posito pro eo quod estluere[?] in tomum 3. volente Deo, videbitur. Præterea ex præmissis conclusio est inconsequens propter insufficientem enumerationem. Sic enim Bellarminus statuit, quisquis dat has pœnas Domino, aut in vita, aut post mortem dare:omittit autem aliquid tertium: nam etiam in morte dat pœnas, qui communis est terminus mediusque inter hoc & futurum sæculum. Sic postea art.12.
units.tr: 12. Art. 6. It can happen, and often does happen, that someone in the whole of his life does not fully satisfy for that temporal punishment. We deny this assumption, that it can happen or ever happen. [Illegible] ... Here God exacts temporal punishments, of what kind and how great he wills, but there eternal ones. Concerning the word "satisfy", taken for what ... will be seen in volume 3, if God wills. Moreover, the conclusion from the premises does not follow, because the enumeration is insufficient. For Bellarmine lays down that whoever gives these penalties to the Lord gives them either in this life or after death; but he omits a third case. For a man also pays penalties in death, which is the common and middle boundary between this age and the age to come. So too later, in art. 12.

units.la: 15. Art. 8. Simul est agnoscenda vera pœna & satisfactio debita culpæ præteritæ ex iustitia. Varie hic Bellarminus fallit. Primum enim Calvino adfingit quæ ab ipso non dicuntur: nam illa verba præcedente art. posita, & proinde cum non sint ista pœna ex iustitia luenda, &c. apud Calvinum eo loco non exstant, nec alibi exstare puto. Secundo, non agit ibi Calvinus de omnibus iudiciorum divinorum causis universe (de his enim agit copiose eodem libro, cap. 8. & sequentibus) sed de iis solum quæ ad hominem afficiendum pœnitentia vel affectum pertinent: cuius respectu omne iudicium Dei aut vindictæ, iudicium, aut castigationis dicendum est. Aliæ autem præter ea sunt causæ, quæ ad Deum, quæ ad proximum pertinentes. Non sequitur ex parte universe: non simpliciter, ex eo quod κατά τι dicto. Tertio nec Calvinus negat, nec vero negamus pœnam esse: sed prout iudicium est, ita & pœna esse ex iudicio statuimus. Est autem iudicii castigatorium, ergo & pœna castigatoria, sive pœnalis castigatio: non pœna satisfactoria, sive pœnalis satisfactio, nisi [illegible, ~8 letters] acceperis. Nam satisfactio proprie importat ex parte utraque analogiam, sumentis & luentis poenam, ut proprie fiat satis: quę analogia nullo modo in rebus nostris probari apud Deum potest. Solius Christi est satisfactio. Postremò ambigua & insidiosa loquutio illa est, satisfactio debita culpæ præteritæ ex iustitia. Nam etsi debetur poena, tamen non est satisfactio, aut poena satisfactoria. Tū etsi debetur ex iustitia, tamen aliud est iustitia Dei absolutè, aliud iustitia in Christo, quę coniunctam habet dispensationem gratiæ & satisfactionem infinitam Christi, qui nobis factus est à Deo Patre iustitia, 1. Cor. 1.& 2.Cor.5. Illi nunquam satisfaciunt impij, sed semper luunt: huic non satisfaciunt electi: sed eius modulum sibi impositum in Christo perferunt, conquiescentes in satisfactione illius, & portant mortificationem Domini Iesu in corpore suo, ut etiam vita Iesu manifesta fiat in eodem ipsorum corpore, 2.Cor. 4.10. Quamobrem Bellarminus operam ludit sequentibus: nam has poenas esse piorum minimè negamus, sed satisfactiones negamus esse.
units.tr: 15. Art. 8. At the same time the true punishment and the satisfaction owed for past guilt from justice must be acknowledged. Bellarmine is misleading here in several ways. First, he attributes to Calvin things that Calvin does not say. For those words, and therefore since these are not punishments to be paid from justice, etc., which he puts in the preceding article, are not found in Calvin in that place, nor, I think, anywhere else. Second, Calvin is not there treating of all the causes of God's judgments in general (for he treats of these at length in the same book, chapter 8 and following), but only of those which pertain to afflicting man with repentance or feeling. With respect to this, every judgment of God must be called either a judgment of vengeance or a judgment of chastisement. But there are other causes besides these, which pertain to God and to our neighbour. It does not follow from a part to the whole; it does not follow simply from what is said in a certain respect. Third, Calvin does not deny that it is a punishment, nor do we deny it; but insofar as it is a judgment, we hold that it is also a punishment arising from the judgment. It is therefore a punishment of correction, that is, a penal correction, not a satisfying punishment, or penal satisfaction, unless you understand it in some other sense. For satisfaction properly implies an analogy on both sides, of the one who receives and of the one who pays the penalty, so that satisfaction is properly made; and this analogy can in no way be proved before God in our case. Satisfaction belongs to Christ alone. Lastly, that phrase satisfaction owed for past guilt from justice is ambiguous and deceptive. For although a punishment is owed, it is still not satisfaction, nor a satisfying punishment. Then, although it is owed from justice, the justice of God considered absolutely is one thing, and the justice in Christ is another, which has joined to it the dispensation of grace and the infinite satisfaction of Christ, who was made justice to us by God the Father (1 Cor. 1 and 2 Cor. 5). The wicked never satisfy, but always pay; the elect do not satisfy in that sense, but bear the measure laid upon them in Christ, resting in his satisfaction, and they bear the mortification of the Lord Jesus in their body, so that the life of Jesus may also be made manifest in the same body of theirs (2 Cor. 4.10). Wherefore Bellarmine is wasting his effort in what follows, for we do not deny that these are punishments of the godly, but we deny that they are satisfactions.

units.la: 14. Ibid. Quia blasphemare fecisti nomen Domini. Hæc verba rationem reddunt poenalis castigationis, non satisfactionem probant: quod Bellarmino probandum fuit.
units.tr: 14. Ibid. Because you have caused the name of the Lord to be blasphemed. These words give the reason for a penal correction; they do not prove satisfaction, which was what Bellarmine had to prove.

units.la: 15. Art.9. Mors est vera poena peccati originalis, Antecedens distinguimus, negamus consequens. Mortem si vniuersè dicit præsentem & futuram, hæc vera poena & totalis est originalis peccati: sinautem hanc aut illam seorsim, poena partialis est: si oppositè atque comparatè, mors præsens vix poena dicenda est, sed appendicula quædam, & alterius æternæ significatio. Demonstratur quod dicimus verbis Apostoli Rom.6.23. mortem opponentis vitæ, quū ait: stipendia peccati mors: donum autem Dei est vita æterna in Christo Iesu Domino nostro. Consequens itaque negatur a communi indiuiso. Illud autem commune indiuisum non luunt homines iusti: sed per mortem hanc temporalem ad vitam æternam transeunt satisfactione iustitiæ diuinæ in Christo, cum ipsi nihil omnino ad satisfactionem afferant. Sequentia itaque iis euertuntur quæ nota 13. attulimus. Quid, quod de pœnis aduentitiis extra ordinem Caluinus agit: non autem de naturalibus & ordinariis? nihil sequitur ex dispari.
units.tr: 15. Art. 9. Death is the true punishment of original sin. We distinguish the antecedent and deny the consequent. If he means death in general, present and future, then this is the true and total punishment of original sin; but if he means this or that part of it separately, it is a partial punishment; if he means it in contrast and comparison, then present death can hardly be called a punishment, but rather a small appendage and a sign of the eternal death that follows. What we say is shown by the words of the Apostle in Romans 6.23, who sets death against life when he says: For the wages of sin is death, but the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord. The consequent is therefore denied from the common undivided term. But men who are justified do not pay that common undivided penalty; rather, through this temporal death they pass into eternal life by the satisfaction of divine justice in Christ, while they themselves contribute nothing at all to the satisfaction. Thus what follows is overturned by those things which we brought forward at note 13. And what of this: Calvin treats of penalties that come by chance, outside the ordinary course, and not of the natural and ordinary ones? Nothing follows from an unlike case.

units.la: 16. Ibid. Quomodo potest esse mors flagellum paternum ad peccatum cauendum institutum?) Caluinus agit de iudiciis quæ in via exercentur, non in termino & vltima linea illius. dispar ratio est. Tum an Bellarminus ignorat esse peccatum internum, & esse externum? Profecto autem qui in flagello sunt mortis, ij saltem interno actu abstinere à peccato docentur, licet externi actus præripiatur ipsis commoditas præueniente morte.
units.tr: 16. Ibid. How can death be a fatherly scourge instituted to guard against sin? Calvin treats of judgments which are exercised on the way, not at the end and final line of it. The reasoning is unlike. Again, does Bellarmine not know that there is internal sin and external sin? Indeed, those who are under the scourge of death are at least taught to abstain from sin in their inner act, even though the opportunity of the external act is snatched from them by death coming first.

units.la: 17. Art. 10. Eorum qui puniti sunt morte violenta, cum eis remissum esset peccatum,] nempe mors istorum fuit pœnalis communiter, & singulariter. Communiter, qua mors fuit, quæ communis omnium: singulariter, qua ob singularem causam eos præuenit mors tempore, & modo: nam serius veniret, & sine ignominiosa diuinæ iræ significatione. Mors autem vltima linea rerum est, aiebat ille, ex qua male de castigationibus in via obuenientibus struitur argumentatio: nam ratio dispar. Frustra igitur exempla sequentia.
units.tr: 17. Art. 10. Of those who were punished with a violent death, although their sin had been forgiven: the death of these men was penal, in general and in particular. In general, insofar as it was death, which is common to all; in particular, insofar as death anticipated them in time and manner for a special reason, for otherwise it would have come later and without the shameful sign of divine wrath. But death, he says, is the final line of things, and from it a faulty argument is built against chastisements that come on the way; for the case is unlike. Therefore the examples that follow are of no use.

units.la: 18. Ibid. Iussit occidi multa millia de populo sine ulla delectu.] Falsum: nam eos iussit occidi solum q[?] palàm post increpationè publicà in sua idololatria perstantes deprehenderentur: ut evidenter illa Mo-ysis verba Exod.32.29.commonstrant, consecrate ministerium vestrum hodie Iehoua, &c. hæc manifesta executio & significatio vindictæ Dei.
units.tr: 18. Ibid. He ordered many thousands of the people to be killed without any distinction. False. For he ordered only those to be killed who were openly found to persist in their idolatry after a public rebuke, as the clear words of Moses in Exodus 32.29 show: Consecrate your ministry today to the LORD, etc. This was the plain execution and manifest sign of God's vengeance.

units.la: 19. Ibid. Multos eorum qui indignè communicabant, morte à Deo punitos fuisse.] Etsi ad hæc omnia exempla & consimilia ex parte ea pertinent quæ proximè dicebamus, in eis tamen singularis quædam consideratio est obseruanda: nempe aliam esse rationem præsentis mortis absolutè, aliam prænunciatæ sententiæ, & suo tempore exsequendæ. Quæ antè diximus, ad mortem absolutè pertinent, quam pœnalem esse agnouimus duobus modis nota 17. hæc autem exempla mortis sunt prænunciatæ, aut verbo & sententia, vt Num.14. & 1.Reg.13. aut exemplo & facto, vt 1.Cor.11. & suo tempore secundùm sententiam consequutæ. Non est autem disputator nescius reos sententia iudicis damnatos censeri mortuos ciuiliter, quamuis diu vitam hanc[?] trahant naturaliter, & mortem prænunciatam ad castigationem esse, illatam verò ad pœnam pertinere, vt suprà cumscripsimus. Ita fuit multorum morte, quos Deus meditationem mortis & resipiscentiam & fructus dignos resipiscentiæ partim sententiæ dictione, partimque exemplis funerum frequentium & minis præsentissimis docere voluit. Quamobrem huius argumentationis vniuersa ratio omnibus modis est dispar. Sequentia in Bellarmino nihil probà necessariò: sed nolumus extra oleas, quod aiunt.
units.tr: 19. Ibid. Many of those who communicated unworthily were punished with death by God. Although, as far as they go, all these examples and similar ones pertain to what we were just saying, there is nevertheless a particular consideration to be observed in them: namely, that the reason for death as present absolutely is one thing, and the reason for a sentence pronounced in advance and to be carried out in its time is another. What we said before pertains to death absolutely, which we have acknowledged to be penal in two ways (note 17). But these examples are of death foretold, either by word and sentence, as in Numbers 14 and 1 Kings 13, or by example and deed, as in 1 Corinthians 11, and following the sentence in its time. Nor is the disputant unaware that those condemned by the sentence of a judge are considered civilly dead, although they naturally drag out this life for a long time, and that a death foretold is for chastisement, while a death inflicted pertains to punishment, as we have set out above. So it was with the death of many, whom God wished to teach the meditation on death, repentance, and fruits worthy of repentance, partly by the pronouncement of sentence and partly by the examples of frequent funerals and very present threats. Therefore the whole reasoning of this argument is unlike in every respect. What follows in Bellarmine proves nothing necessarily; but we do not wish to go beyond the bounds, as they say.

units.la: 20. Art. II. Sic seruatur misericordia & veritas.] Hæc omnia Augustini vltrò accipimus, & credimus. Nam varie sunt Dei iudiciorum causæ: sed quâ eos
units.tr: 20. Art. II. So mercy and truth are preserved. We accept and believe all of this from Augustine without reservation. The causes of God's judgments are various, but

units.la: ipsos respiciut in quos exercet iudicaDeus, omnino aut vindictæ sunt, aut castigationis iudicia (vt recte Caluinus in argumento de pœnitentia tradidit) aut vtrumque diuerso respectu coniunctum habent.
units.tr: as regards the very people on whom God executes judgment, they are altogether either judgments of vengeance or judgments of correction (as Calvin rightly taught in his treatise on repentance), or they have both, joined together in different respects.

units.la: 21. Art.12. In articulo mortis conuertuntur, quando nullam possunt agere pœnitentiam: ] Si conuertuntur, agunt igitur pœnitentiam : nam pœnitentiæ partes sunt auersio a malo & conuersio ad bonum. In proprie ergo Bellarminus loquitur, oppositum statuens in appositio, vt vocant. Dicet de pœnitentiæ professione & demonstratione agere. Ergo nihil concludit, quia illæ sunt partes essentiales pœnitentiæ: professio autem & demonstratio sive externa significatio actus materialis est circumstantiæ, sine quo vera est coram Deo pœnitentia. Non sequitur a negatione signi negatio veritatis. Itaque falsum & consequens.
units.tr: 21. Art. 12. They are converted at the point of death, when they can perform no repentance. If they are converted, then they do perform repentance, for the parts of repentance are turning away from evil and turning to good. Bellarmine therefore speaks improperly, setting up a contrary in what the rhetoricians call an apposition. He says that they perform a profession and demonstration of repentance. Therefore he concludes nothing, because those are not the essential parts of repentance. A profession and demonstration, or outward signification, of the act is an external circumstance, without which repentance is true before God. A denial of the sign does not follow as a denial of the truth. So the inference is false.

units.la: 22. Ibid. Ergo pro actualibus debet inueniri alia pœnitentia. ]Negatur consequens, neque ex antecedente iusto medio probari potest. Nam etiam sine pœnitentia delentur peccata, pro quibus Christus factus est nobis redemptio a Deo Patre, 1. Cor. 1.
units.tr: 22. Ibid. Therefore another repentance must be found for actual sins. The consequent is denied, and it cannot be proved from the antecedent by any sound middle term. For sins are blotted out even without repentance, for which Christ was made our redemption by God the Father (1 Cor. 1).

units.la: 23. Ibid. Naturali morte puniret peccata magna & parva, multa & pauca.] de morte distinguendum, vt supra nota 15. alioquin vtrumque falsum. Nam Deus nec morte naturali punit peccata omnia & quæuis nostra: nec si faceret, iniuste agere, aut prouidentia erum nostrarum carere dicendus esset, quia etiam mortem hanc suæ condiunt circumstantiæ, vt nota 7. dictum.
units.tr: 23. Ibid. By natural death God would punish great and small sins, many and few. We must distinguish concerning death, as I noted above at note 15; otherwise both claims are false. For God does not punish all sins and every one of our sins by natural death, nor, if he did, would he be said to act unjustly or to lack providence over our affairs, since he also tempers this death with its own circumstances, as I said in note 7.

units.la: 24. Art.13. A communi opinione omnium gentium.] error comuni non valet consequentia: à sapientibus discitur sapientia: sunt autem sapientes in his rebus quos Deus docuit sapientiam, Iob.28.Matth.11.27.
units.tr: 24. Art. 13. From the common opinion of all nations. A common error does not make a valid argument. Wisdom is learned from the wise, but those are wise in these matters whom God has taught wisdom (Job 28; Matt. 11:27).

units.la: · 25.Ibid. Patet ex lib.2. cMacchabæorum[?], cap. 12.]
units.tr: 25. Ibid. It is evident from 2 Maccabees, chapter 12.

units.la: Non est liber sapientis instituti in diuina sapientia, sed est misera epitome ex auctore misero Iasone Cyrenaeo, quem propter confusionem numerorum, & difficultatem historię ipse reprehendit epitomarius, 2.Mac.2.25. sed de hac re libro 1.controuersiæ 1.
units.tr: That book is not the work of a man wise in the divine wisdom. It is a poor epitome of the wretched author Jason of Cyrene, whom the epitomist himself criticises for the confusion of his numbers and the difficulty of his history (2 Macc. 2:25). I deal with this matter in book 1 of this controversy.

units.la: 26. Ibid. Iudæos consuevisse orare pro mortuis, non tamen pro illis quise interimunt.] Auctor non ita vetus, sed error peruetus: quia Pharisæorum & Iudæorum iam olim dogma fuit [illegible, ~10 letters] animas æter-nis retrudi carceribus, alias autem facultatem remis-sendi[?] percipere, vt ait Iosephus lib. 18. antiq. Iudaic. cap.2. & pluribus exponit Epiphanius Panarij lib.1. propterea orabant pro mortuis. Hæc non rem, sed errorem probant. Prauum autem usum & lex Scripturæ & ratio vincit, dist.10. c.usus, & c.consuetudinis.
units.tr: 26. Ibid. The Jews customarily prayed for the dead, but not for those who have been put to death. The author is not so old, but the error is very old. For it was already long ago a doctrine of the Pharisees and Jews that the souls of the wicked are shut up in eternal prisons, while others obtain the power of being released, as Josephus says in book 18 of the Antiquities of the Jews, chapter 2, and Epiphanius sets out at length in book 1 of the Panarion. That is why they prayed for the dead. These facts prove not the thing itself but the error. Scripture and reason overcome a bad practice (Distinction 10, the chapters "Usus" and "Consuetudinis").

units.la: 27. Art.14 Egit Lethæo purgatos flumine, &c.] Hæc omnia consensum hominum insipientium in erro-re probant, non rei veritatem.
units.tr: 27. Art. 14. He drove them, purged, through the river Lethe, etc. All these things prove the agreement of foolish men in error, not the truth of the matter.

units.la: 28. Art. 15. Vix possunt aliunde prouenire, quàm à naturali lumine omnibus hominibus communi.] Hæc indistincte nimis disputator profert. Tria distingui oportet, principia, ratiocinationem, & opus inde exurgens. Principia sunt lumen ipsum, ratiocinatio actus est seu motus luminis, operi eorum accensentur determinationes & conclusiones nostrę per ratiocinationem ex principiis elicitæ. Cum autem nihil sit nisi tenebræ, Ioan.1. lumen illud principiorum tenebricosum est, id est, commune, obscurum, corruptum in tenebris mentis nostræ, cæca ratiocinatio:de-terminationes & conclusiones, præsertim quæ res diuidivinas & seculi venturi spectant, cæcissimę. Principiis conueniunt omnes, qua sunt naturæ primigeniæ rudera, & notiones communes ab ea insitæ: sed ratiocinatione variant, determinationibus &conclusionibus differunt maxime. Proveniunt quidem hæc à naturali lumine, sed à corrupto obscuroque corruptissima & obscurissima:idque in rebus solum naturalibus, quas natura hominis non potest transcendere. Atqui hæc de ratione futuri seculi supernaturalia sunt, divina sunt, quæ ut capiat homo, naturam hanc suam transcendat, necesse est, & à Deo ipso doceatur, ut ipse quoque Aristoteles agnoscit. Metaphysic. i. Frustra igitur in hoc argumento naturalis hominum consensus nobis obducitur, in quo natura hæc tota cæca est.
units.tr: 28. Art. 15. They can hardly come from anywhere but the natural light common to all men. The disputant here sets things out in too undifferentiated a way. Three things must be distinguished: the principles, the reasoning, and the work that arises from them. The principles are the light itself; the reasoning is the act or motion of that light; the work of these is the determinations and conclusions we draw from the principles through reasoning. Since nothing is but darkness without light (John 1), that light of principles is dim: it is general, obscure, and corrupted in the darkness of our mind, and our reasoning is blind. The determinations and conclusions, especially those concerning divine matters and the age to come, are utterly blind. All men agree on the principles, which are the ruins of original nature and the common notions implanted by it; but in reasoning they vary, and they differ most in their determinations and conclusions. These do indeed come from the natural light, but from a light that is corrupted and obscure, and they are most corrupt and obscure; and this holds only in natural matters, which human nature cannot go beyond. But the things concerning the nature of the age to come are supernatural and divine. For a man to grasp them he must transcend this nature of his own, and he must be taught by God himself, as Aristotle himself acknowledges (Metaphysics, book 1). So in this argument the general consent of men is brought against us in vain, since in these matters all of nature is blind.

units.la: 29. Ibid. Varia sunt, & diversa pro Gentium varie-tate. ] & ita sunt illæ de Purgatorio sententię, quia sunt conclusiones naturę nostrę in supernaturali-bus errantis temere.
units.tr: 29. Ibid. They are various and diverse, according to the variety of the nations. So too are those opinions about Purgatory, since they are conclusions of our nature rashly wandering in supernatural matters.

units.la: 30. Ibid. Oportet dicere esse confessionem luminis naturalis: ] Negatur: confessio est tenebrarum naturalium in supernaturalibus rebus futuri seculi errantium, & ludentium in errore suo: quam nec Scriptu-ra agnoscit, nec primi illi Patres Ecclesiæ priscæ, ut capitibus antecedentibus est confirmatum.
units.tr: 30. Ibid. It must be said that it is a confession of natural light. This is denied. It is a confession of natural darkness, wandering in supernatural matters of the age to come and playing in its own error. Neither Scripture acknowledges it, nor did those first Fathers of the early Church, as has been confirmed in the preceding chapters.

units.la: 31. Ibid. Eiusdem n. providentiæ divinæ cognitio do-cuit Purgatorium, quæ docuit infernum & paradisum. ] Negatur: nam hęc docent natura & Scriptura: illud opinio ex tenebris involans in mentes hominum, aut sibi in peccato indulgentium, aut lucrum ex a-liena superstitione colligentium.
units.tr: 31. Ibid. The knowledge of the same divine providence taught Purgatory, which also taught hell and paradise. This is denied. For nature and Scripture teach the latter; the former is an opinion flying out of darkness into men's minds, either of men indulging themselves in sin or of men gathering profit from another's superstition.

units.la: 32. Art. 16. Et per eas transitum ad præmia pro iis qui sunt mediocriter mali vel boni. ] Hęc omnia usque adeò naturalia sunt, vt Christum obliterent & gratiam salutarem eius. Illud est Christianum Theologum agere scilicet.
units.tr: 32. Art. 16. And through them a passage to rewards for those who are moderately bad or good. All these things are so entirely natural that they obliterate Christ and his saving grace. That is what a Christian theologian ought to avoid.

units.la: Quas apparitiones cum viri grauissimi retulerint, non immerito veras fuisse credimus. ]Nos vero minimè credimus. Etenim hominum illorum qui apparitiones istas retulerunt, alij graues fuerunt somno, alij graues errore isto qui iâ olim inualuit, alij denique dæmonum illusionibus (qui huic scenæ quàm lubentissimè operam côdonant) imprudentes licet, prægrauati. Quòd si visiones & apparitiones miraculosæ fuerunt, quæ tandem proferuntur documenta veritatem miraculorum istorum contestantia.
units.tr: Since very serious men have related these appearances, we rightly believe they were true. We certainly do not believe it. For of those men who related these appearances, some were heavy with sleep, some heavy with that error which has long prevailed, and others, though unwary, were overwhelmed by the illusions of demons (who most gladly lend their help to this stage-play). But if the visions and appearances were miraculous, what documents are then produced that attest the truth of these miracles?

units.la: Art. 23. Neque etiam ipsos deceptos fuisse, cùm habərent spiritum discretionis, & essent amici Dei]Primùm habuisse omneis illos spiritu discretionis unde constat? Secundò habuerint sanè, consequens tamen non est necessarium ex actu contingente. Neque enim est semper necessarium, vt qui habet spiritu discretionis & est amicus Dei, non decipiatur: sed hoc demum est necessarium, quisquis habet spiritum discretionis eoque semper vtitur, & quisquis est perfectè amicus Dei, eū nunquam decipi. Hoc autem de illis nec Bellarminus quidem affirmauerit: nā(vt rectè dicitur in glossa Decretalium) non semper credendum est viro sancto.
units.tr: Art. 23. Nor were they themselves deceived, since they had the spirit of discernment and were friends of God. First, from what source is it known that all of them had the spirit of discernment? Second, they may indeed have had it, but the consequence does not follow necessarily from a contingent act. For it is not always necessary that one who has the spirit of discernment and is a friend of God should not be deceived. It is necessary only that whoever has the spirit of discernment and uses it always, and whoever is perfectly a friend of God, should never be deceived. Bellarmine himself would not affirm this of those men, for (as is rightly said in the gloss on the Decretals) one must not always believe a holy man.

units.la: Art.24. Homines sœcordes facit in peccatis cauedis, & bonis operib. faciedis.]Negamus doctrinâ hac quę tollit Purgatoriū perniciosā esse, hominesq; socordes facere. An propterea Apostoli fuerūt socordes, aut Ecclesia Apostolica, cp Purgatorium nesciuerit?
units.tr: Art. 24. It makes men careless in avoiding sins and in doing good works. We deny that this doctrine, which removes Purgatory, is harmful or makes men careless. Were the Apostles therefore careless, or the Apostolic Church, because it did not know of Purgatory?

units.la: Ibid. Quandoquidem in morte, siue pauca siue multa peccata habuero, omnia delebuntur.]hęc mali serui infidelis verba, non animæ Christianæ: quid ista ad pios?
units.tr: Ibid. For at death, whether I have few or many sins, all will be blotted out. These are the words of an unfaithful wicked servant, not of a Christian soul. What have such words to do with the pious?

units.la: 37. Ibid. per debita pœnitentia opera ibi diluendum, certè diligentior cautiorque euadit. hæc mercenariorum seruorum ignorantium beneficium Christi, non ingenuorum filiorum Dei verba sunt, liberalem Christi educationem & gratiosam Patris adoptionem in Christo profitentium. Fallit Bellarminus τὸ πρὸς τὴν μὴ ἄπον ὡς ἄπον [?]. Sed hæc tomo 4. videbuntur.
units.tr: 37. Ibid. If by the due works of repentance one is to be cleansed there, one certainly becomes more diligent and cautious. These are the words of hired servants who are ignorant of the benefit of Christ, not of the freeborn sons of God, who profess their liberal upbringing in Christ and their gracious adoption by the Father in Christ. Bellarmine commits the fallacy of treating what is not absurd as absurd [τὸ πρὸς τὴν μὴ ἄπον ὡς ἄπον]. But these matters will be seen in volume 4.

units.la: In Cap. XII.
units.tr: In Chapter XII.

units.la: 1. Art.3. Non enim expri nitur quando adueniet hæreditas Domini. Auctorem istius argumentationis nominari oportuit: non est à nobis, nec à nobis præstari debet. Dauid certè aliud dicit plane. Argumentatio falsa, & solutio allegorica: neutrum in disputandi ratione iustum.
units.tr: 1. Art. 3. For it is not stated when the inheritance of the Lord will come. The author of this argument ought to have been named. It is not ours, and we ought not to be made responsible for it. David clearly says something different. The argument is false and the solution allegorical; neither is fair in the method of disputing.

units.la: 2. Art.5. Nisi per ea quæ hic gesserunt meruerint ut iuuari possent. Negatur responsio tota, & restrictiones illius. Nam hortatio ad omneis universè homines pertinet, ergo & hortationis argumentum. Alioqui quàm insulsum esset, si hortationem universalem ratione particulari Sapiens probare diceretur? atque hoc sibi voluit Hieronymus. Gregorius petit τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς [?]. Negamus auctoritatem eius, ut diximus in cap.10.
units.tr: 2. Art. 5. Unless by what they did here they have merited to be helped. The whole response is denied, along with its restrictions. The exhortation applies to all men universally, so the argument drawn from the exhortation does too. Otherwise how silly would it be to say that the Wise Man proves a universal exhortation by a particular reason? This is also what Jerome meant. Gregory begs the question [τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς]. We deny his authority, as we said under chapter 10.

units.la: 3. Art.7. Aliquando cadit, & ibi manet ac putrescit vbi cecidit. Ex diuerso nihil sequitur in utrauis parte: nam nec locus ad causam hanc facit, nec solutio ad locum. Quamobrem hoc totum nihil ad nos. Hoc dicit Sapiens, si quis cui benefecerit, presto esse benedictione Dei: qui facit, ut beneficia collata pullulent suo loco, sicut faciunt plantæ humi depositæ. hoc series contextus docet, prout alibi exposuimus: Sequentia similiter principium petunt, & festiuæ sunt allegoriæ. Negamus.
units.tr: 3. Art. 7. Sometimes it falls, and there it remains and rots where it fell. From the opposite, nothing follows on either side: the place does not bear on this cause, and the solution does not bear on the place. Therefore this whole point is nothing to us. The Wise Man says that if anyone has done good to another, the blessing of God is at hand, which makes the benefits conferred sprout in their place, just as plants do when set in the ground. The sequence of the context teaches this, as we have explained elsewhere. What follows similarly begs the question, and the allegories are frivolous. We deny it.

units.la: 4. Ibid. Constat enim Patres in eo loco non manifesse perpetuo. De his partim sequente libro, partimque controuersia seq. videbitur.
units.tr: 4. Ibid. For it is agreed that the Fathers did not speak manifestly and continuously in that place. Part of this will be seen in the following book, and part in the following controversy.

units.la: 5. Art. 9. Respondeo dupliciter: Sed obseruet lector neutram responsionem meminisse illius vocis, omnium, quam Propheta bene expresserat.
units.tr: 5. Art. 9. I answer in two ways: But let the reader observe that neither answer remembers that word, all, which the Prophet had expressed well.

units.la: 6. Ibid. Non recordari iniquitatum nihil aliud esse, quam non seruare inimicitiam cum eo qui peccauit. Negatur exclusiua. Nam & hoc & amplius hoc significat ex vsu Scripturæ sacræ, per metalepsin Hebræis frequentatam. Vt enim scire duplex est, εἰκὸν [?] καὶ [illegible, ~10 letters], ita & recordari.
units.tr: 6. Ibid. Not to remember iniquities is nothing other than not to keep enmity with the one who has sinned. The exclusive is denied. For this, and something more, is what the word signifies from the usage of Holy Scripture, by a metalepsis frequently used by the Hebrews. For just as knowing is twofold, [εἰκὸν] and [illegible], so too is remembering.

units.la: 7. Ibid. Recordari iustitiarum esset remunerare bona merita. Non sequitur ex disparitate iustitiæ & peccati dispar in nobis ratio. Sed de hac re controuer. 4. [illegible, ~5 letters] videbitur. Inanis itaque argumentatio.
units.tr: 7. Ibid. To remember righteousnesses would be to reward good merits. It does not follow from the disparity between righteousness and sin that our reasoning must be disparate. But on this matter the fourth controversy [illegible] will be seen. The argument is therefore empty.

units.la: 8. Art. 10. Recordari iniquitatum esse quidem punire, sed punire in æternum: Negatur restrictio: nec vero ita accipitur 1. Reg. 17. 18. & alibi. Male restringitur per circunstantiam temporis id quod dicitur simpliciter. Eiusdem quoque modi est sequens interpretatio: quam vel eo nomine improbamus, quod rem enunciatam simpliciter atque communiter, negamus secundum quid aut particulariter restringi oportere, nisi ratio subiecti aut prædicati adiunctorumque necessitatem faciendi illud attulerit.
units.tr: 8. Art. 10. To remember iniquities is indeed to punish, but to punish for ever: The restriction is denied; nor is it so understood in 1 Reg. 17. 18 and elsewhere. What is said simply is wrongly restricted by a circumstance of time. The following interpretation is of the same kind, and we reject it for this reason: we deny that a matter stated simply and generally must be restricted in a qualified or particular sense, unless the nature of the subject or predicate and the necessity of the accompanying circumstances require it.

units.la: 9. Ibid. opera bona impiorum non fraudari temporali mercede, dicendum fuerat, non semper; nam contingens propositio est. fit prout dispensat Deus· Enimuero quænam sunt bona impiorū opera? coram Deo nulla sunt, quia nulla vnquam simpliciter bona: sed bona censentur humanitus, ἀξιως, & comparatione solum. horum ergo etiam gratuita merces, siquando remuneratur Deus, non propter bonitatem operum ipsorum, sed propter bonitatem suam demonstrandam confertur: nec aliter sentiunt Patres.
units.tr: 9. Ibid. the good works of the wicked are not defrauded of temporal reward, it should have been said: not always, for it is a contingent proposition. It happens as God dispenses. But what are the good works of the wicked? Before God there are none, since none is ever simply good; they are reckoned good only by human judgment, [ἀξίως], and by comparison. Therefore their gratuitous reward too, whenever God does remunerate it, is bestowed not on account of the goodness of the works themselves but to demonstrate God's own goodness. The Fathers think no differently.

units.la: 10. Ibidem. colligitur ex illis verbis Luc. 16. recepisti bona in vita tua. ] male colligitur ex homonymia vocis ὁπλάσεις, percepisti; non autem recepisti: quod Græci norunt. Confutatur autem sequente membro, cui unum & idem verbum commune est. dicit enim Christus, fili, memento te bona tua percepisse in vita tua, & Lazarum similiter mala. & quæ mala recepisse Lazarum in hac vita, mi homo, dixeris?
units.tr: 10. Ibid. It is gathered from those words of Luke 16, You have received your good things in your life. It is wrongly gathered from the ambiguity of the word [ἀπέλαβες], "you have received," and not "you have received back," as the Greeks know. It is refuted, however, by the following clause, which shares one and the same verb. For Christ says, "Son, remember that you received your good things in your life, and Lazarus likewise evil things." And what evil things, my friend, would you say Lazarus received in this life?

units.la: 11. Art. 12. duo tantum loca remanebunt, paradisus & gehenna. ] Purgatorium finem acceptarum negamus: quod enim nunquam est, nunquam fine accipit. duo tantum loca esse post hanc vitam, sive ante iudicium sive post illud, agnoscimus: nec plura Christus. Alioquin ubi probationem adfert sententiæ suæ, dixisset Christus, esuriui enim, & dedisti mihi quod ederem, & quod insuper luendum fuit, luitis in Purgatorio: & item sequentibus Matth. 25. 35. fortasse paralepsin Bellarminus dicet inesse Christi verbis: sed revera in tota Scriptura est perpetua paralepsis Purgatorij, perpetuum silentium. Quid, quod veteres illi qui primi purgationem posuerunt, ij post iudicium putabant superuenturam ? vide supra cap. 10. nota 66. Quam sua-ue est Pontificiis in meridie vitę philosophari Pur-gatorium!
units.tr: 11. Art. 12. only two places will remain, paradise and hell. We deny that Purgatory receives an end: for what never exists never receives an end. We acknowledge that there are only two places after this life, whether before the judgment or after it, and Christ mentions no more. Otherwise, when he brings forward proof of his statement, Christ would have said: "For I was hungry, and you gave me something to eat; and what had to be paid over and above, you pay in Purgatory," and likewise in the following verses of Matthew 25. 35. Perhaps Bellarmine will say that a paralepsis lies in Christ's words; but in truth there is a perpetual paralepsis of Purgatory throughout Scripture, a perpetual silence. What of the fact that those ancient men who first posited purgation thought it would come after the judgment? See above, chapter 10, note 66. How pleasant it is for the Papists to philosophise about Purgatory in the noon of life!

units.la: 12. Ibid.non condemnatur, modo etiam addat cæte-ra quæ requiruntur.] datur conditio bene intellecta: sed ex mente Bellarmini negatur. Nec valet simile in causa dispari sine dissimili: nā salutem solus Christus adfert, sola fides percipit in Christo; sed arboris [illegible, ~6 letters] multæ efficiunt concurrentes causæ. Quid? nonne creatio opus est Dei solius, nec cum re ulla creata communicabile? multo igitur magis salus est Dei solius opus in Christo Iesu, Ephes. 2. 8. prius agnoscit Magister lib. 2. sentent. dist.1. & tota Scholasticorum caterua, posterius Scriptura clamat.
units.tr: 12. Ibid. he is not condemned, provided he also adds the other things which are required. A condition well understood is given, but according to Bellarmine's meaning it is denied. Nor does the comparison hold in an unlike cause without a dissimilar one. For salvation is brought by Christ alone, and faith alone receives it in Christ; but the fruit of a tree is produced by many concurring causes. What then? Is not creation the work of God alone, not communicable to any created thing? Much more, therefore, salvation is the work of God alone in Jesus Christ, Eph. 2. 8. The Master of the Sentences acknowledges the former in book 2, distinction 1, and the whole band of Schoolmen with him; the latter Scripture proclaims.

units.la: 13. Ibid. neque continuo qui salvus erit per fidem, sine Purgatorio salvus erit.] negatur: probationem vero quam disputator adtexit, supra in caput 5. confutavimus.
units.tr: 13. Ibid. nor will he who is saved through faith necessarily be saved without Purgatory. Denied. The proof which the disputant appends we refuted above, under chapter 5.

units.la: 14. Artic. 13. potuisse fuisse in plenam satisfactionem reputari.] satisfactionem, inquit? negamus, vt ante cap. 11. nota 13. & seq. imputatur iustitia & satisfactio Christi, non est a nobis vlla. Sola illa recordatio Christi salutaris est, de qua dicebat latro Luc.23.42. Domine, memento mei, cum venerit in regnum tuum.
units.tr: 14. Art. 13. could have been reckoned as full satisfaction. Satisfaction, he says? We deny it, as before, chapter 11, note 13 and following. The righteousness and satisfaction of Christ are imputed to us, and there is nothing of ours in it. That single remembrance of Christ is saving, of which the thief said, Luke 23. 42, "Lord, remember me when you come into your kingdom."

units.la: 15. Ibid. priuilegia paucorum legem non fecerunt.] negamus priuilegium fuisse: nam communis rationis enunciatum est. Testatur id priscorum Patrum sententia, qui ex hoc loco adstruxerunt, caelos prius occlusos fuisse, ab hoc tempore mortis Christi aditum in caelum Patribus atque defunctis omnibus patuisse. sed de hac re in controuersia 2. lib. 4. diximus,& contr.seq.videbitur.Non ergo privilegium fuit.
units.tr: 15. Ibid. the privileges of a few have not made the law. We deny that it was a privilege, for it is a statement of common reason. The opinion of the ancient Fathers bears witness to this, who from this passage argued that the heavens had been shut before, and that from the time of Christ's death the way into heaven lay open to the Fathers and to all the dead. But we have spoken of this matter in the second controversy of book 4, and the following controversy will treat it further. So it was not a privilege.

units.la: 16. Art.15. nihil peccati contrahere ex eiusmodi motibus.] falsa interpretatio,cū verbis Apostoli & argumēto pugnans. Nō enim dicit, nihil peccati; sed potius, nihil condemnationis.& argumentum est non de concupiscentia, sed de conscientia regeneratio-nis nostrae & pacis cum Deo in Christo. Recte i-gitur de Purgatorio dicitur. nam si nulla (vt vult Apostolus) nunc est condemnatio iis qui sunt in Christo Iesu, nec Purgatorialis igitur condemnatio est. Sequentia falsa sunt,& confutabuntur in tomo 4. Deo dante.
units.tr: 16. Art. 15. to contract no sin from such motions. A false interpretation, clashing with the words of the Apostle and with his argument. For he does not say "no sin," but rather "no condemnation." And the argument concerns not concupiscence but the assurance of our regeneration and of our peace with God in Christ. Rightly, then, is it said concerning Purgatory: for if there is now (as the Apostle wills) no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus, then there is no purgatorial condemnation either. What follows is false, and will be refuted in the fourth tome, God willing.

units.la: 17. Art. 16. patere domum cœlestem post mortem: non patere ante mortem.] responsio falsa. Non enim quærit Apostolus, utrum pateat illud domicilium, nec ne; sed ex eo se & pios omnes cōsolatur, quod dissoluto huius domus nostrae tabernaculo habe-mus illud alterum domicilium, ac non tabernaculum habemus, inquam, iure, possessione, & vsu præ-sentissimo ex facto: ex tabernaculo statim veniunt pij in domicilium suum, nec sunt illis vmbris Poëtarum similes, de quibus fabulata est antiquitas, inops inhumataque turba, &c. Aeneid.6. Fallit disputatorem vocis ἐάν significatio. Non enim dicit Apostolus conditionaliter, si terrestris huius domus nostrae tabernaculum dissolutum fuerit (quis enim dissolui nescit?) sed potius circumscribit tempus; quum terrestris huius domus nostrae tabernaculum dissolutum fuerit, aedificium ex Deo habemus, domum non manufactam, &c. decedente tabernaculo succedit domus. Ἐὰν[?] est idem quod ἐὰν. & ita Chrysostomus ibidem expo-nit, dicens: Etenim ne externum tuum hominem corrumpi audiens animo discrucieris, hoc asserit, ὅτι [?] πνευματικῶς τὸ τοῦτο ἡμῶν [?], τότε μᾶλλον χαρῆσαι, quod quum i-stud plene atque omnino acciderit, tum maxime gaude-bis, atque ad meliorem regionem concedes. Stat igitur firma certaque obiectio, quam Bellarminus nequit effugere.
units.tr: 17. Art. 16. the heavenly home is open after death, not open before death. The response is false. For the Apostle does not ask whether that dwelling is open or not; rather, from this he comforts himself and all the godly, that when the tabernacle of this our house is dissolved, we have that other dwelling, and we have it, I say, by right, by possession, and by the most present enjoyment from the fact itself. From the tabernacle the godly come at once into their own dwelling, and they are not like those shades of the poets, of whom antiquity told fables, "a helpless and unburied crowd," etc., Aeneid 6. The disputant is deceived by the meaning of the word [ἐάν]. For the Apostle does not speak conditionally, "if the tabernacle of this our earthly house shall be dissolved" (for who does not know that it will be dissolved?); rather he fixes the time: "when the tabernacle of this our earthly house shall be dissolved, we have a building from God, a house not made with hands," etc. As the tabernacle decays, the house succeeds it. [ἐὰν] is the same as [ἐάν], and so Chrysostom expounds it in the same place, saying: "For lest you, hearing that your outward man is corrupted, be tormented in mind, he asserts that [ὅτι πνευματικῶς τὸ τοῦτο ἡμῶν], then rather you will rejoice, when this has happened fully and entirely, and will depart to a better region." The firm and certain objection therefore stands, which Bellarmine cannot escape.

units.la: 18. Ibid. contrarium potius indicare, quum ait, si tamen vestiti & non nudi inueniamur. ] negatur hoc indicari illis verbis Apostoli. Ex adiunctis intelligenda sunt, non ex voluntariis somniis. Dixerat Apostolus, in hoc suspiramus, expetentes superinduere domicilium nostrum, quod e coelis est. Cur autem ἐπενδύσασθαι [?], superinduere vel superindui? siquidem etiam induti; nimirum tabernaculo terrestris huius domus nostrae, nō nudi inueniamur. id autem est, sive deprehendamur viuentes in die illo & transmutemur in caelum ascendentes consociato adhuc corpore & animo nostro, sive morte praeueniamur diem illum. Sic enim loquutus erat 1.Cor.15. 51. non omnes quidē obdormiemus, tabernaculum videlicet exuentes; sed omnes mutabimur, &c. itemque 1. Thess.4. 15. & sequentib. nos vivi qui reliqui erimus in aduentu Domini, &c. Demonstrant interpretationem hanc sequen-tia, quum dicit Apostolus: nos enim qui sumus in isto tabernaculo, gemimus grauati: in quo constituti non cupimus eo exui, sed superindui, &c. haec facilis & plana sententia, quam nebulis glossematum nō patiemur obscurari: adeo perspicua sunt omnia atque conspicua in Pauli verbis. Sequentia itaque nihil ad Andromacha-cham, quod aiunt.
units.tr: 18. Ibid. rather indicates the contrary, when he says, if indeed we are found clothed and not naked.] It is denied that those words of the Apostle indicate this. They must be understood from their context, not from voluntary dreams. The Apostle had said, in this we groan, longing to put on over our dwelling which is from heaven. But why to put on over [ἐπενδύσασθαι] or to be clothed over? Since indeed we have been clothed too, namely with the tabernacle of this earthly house of ours, so that we shall not be found naked. This means either that we are found alive on that day and are changed, ascending into heaven with our body and soul still joined, or that we are anticipated by death before that day. For the Apostle spoke in this way in 1 Cor. 15:51, we shall not all indeed sleep, that is, putting off the tabernacle, but we shall all be changed, etc., and likewise in 1 Thess. 4:15 and following, we who are alive and remain at the coming of the Lord, etc. The words that follow show this interpretation, when the Apostle says: for we who are in this tabernacle groan, being burdened; in which we do not wish to be stripped, but to be clothed over, etc. This is an easy and plain sense, which we will not allow to be obscured by the mists of glosses; everything in Paul's words is so clear and conspicuous. Therefore what follows has nothing to do with the so-called Andromachan argument.

units.la: 19. Ibid. vt ipse idem ait 1. ad Corinth. 3. ] confutatum supra cap.5.
units.tr: 19. Ibid. as the same man says in 1 Cor. 3.] Refuted above in chapter 5.

units.la: 20. Art. 19. qui remissionis & purgationis locum inueniunt niunt in futuro seculo, nihil recipiunt nisi quod gesserunt in corpore:] utrumque negamus; & subiectum, esse qui purgationis locum inveniunt in futuro seculo; & praedicatu ipsum, homines eiusmodi (si qui sunt) nihil recipere nisi quod gesserunt in corpore, ac proinde illud quum vivèrent, in corpore fuisse meritos: ut quidem hodie à Pontificiis accipitur merendi verbum.
units.tr: 20. Art. 19. who find a place of remission and purgation in the future age receive nothing except what they did in the body.] We deny both: the subject, that there are people who find a place of purgation in the future age; and the predicate, that people of this kind (if there are any) receive nothing except what they did in the body, and therefore that they merited while living in the body, in the sense in which the Papists today understand the word merit.

units.la: 21. Ibid.id meruerunt in hac vita recte vivendo, ut etiam post hanc vitam a Domino exaudirentur.] & ταυτολογεῖ[?] disputator, & falsu dicit τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς postulans. Negamus ista omnia, & libro 2. confutabimus.
units.tr: 21. Ibid. they merited this in this life by living rightly, so that they might be heard by the Lord even after this life.] The disputant tautologizes [ταυτολογεῖ] and falsely begs the question [τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς]. We deny all of this, and will refute it in book 2.

units.la: 22. Ibid. Dionysium libro de Ecclesiastica hierarchia, cap. ultimo, parte tertia;] de hoc Dionysij loco dixi-mus supra cap. 10. nota 2.
units.tr: 22. Ibid. Dionysius in the book On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, last chapter, part three.] We spoke about this passage of Dionysius above in chapter 10, note 2.

units.la: 23. Ibid. & libro de cura pro mortuis, cap. 1.] idem est uterque Augustini locus, cùm in posteriore ex professo repetat priloris[?] verba: & nihil ad argumentum facit, quia tum æquivocè accipitur merendi verbum (nam aliter olim Patres intelligebant quâ hodie Pontificij, ut ostendemus in tomum 4.) tum diversa est plane Bellarmini hypothesis ab Augustini mente. Nam Augustinus ita scribebat respiciens ad communem illam & invalescentiam tum in Ecclesia sententiam, quòd animæ defunctorum piorum non fruerentur visione Dei, sed luce visionis & tranquillitate à malo, exspectantes diem resurrectionis quo visione Dei fruerentur. In eo statu animæ æstuantis desiderio visionis beatæ, requiè precabantur & refrigerium defunctis superstites; non ut liberarentur à malo, sed ut levarentur morte illius tædio, dum resurrectionem sui corporis, & plenam visionem Dei exspectabant prout supra; cap.9. & 10.ostendimus. Hic illius curae pro mortuis, & orationum fundamentum, quo respiciebat Augustinus quum ista scriberet. Demonstrant Augustini verba in Enchiridij cap. 109. quod proxime praecessit, dicentis:
units.tr: 23. Ibid. and in the book On care for the dead, chapter 1.] The two passages of Augustine are the same, since in the later he deliberately repeats the words of the former. It has nothing to do with the argument: the word merit is taken equivocally there (for the Fathers once understood it differently from the Papists today, as we will show in tome 4), and Bellarmine's hypothesis is plainly different from Augustine's mind. Augustine wrote this looking to the common and then prevailing opinion in the Church, that the souls of the pious dead do not enjoy the vision of God, but enjoy the light of the vision and tranquillity from evil, awaiting the day of resurrection on which they would enjoy the vision of God. In that state, with souls longing eagerly for the blessed vision, the living who survived prayed for rest and refreshment for the dead; not that they might be freed from evil, but that they might be relieved of the tedium of death, while they awaited the resurrection of their body and the full vision of God, as we have shown above in chapters 9 and 10. This is the foundation of that care for the dead and of prayers, to which Augustine looked when he wrote these things. The words of Augustine in Enchiridion chapter 109, which immediately precedes, show this, saying:

units.la: Tempus autem quod inter hominis mortem et ultimam resurrectionem interpositum est, animas abditis receptaculis continet, sicut unaquaeque digna est vel requie vel aerumna, pro eo quod fortuita est in carne quum vueret.
units.tr: The time, however, which is interposed between a man's death and the final resurrection, keeps souls in hidden receptacles, as each one is worthy of rest or of distress, according to what it did in the flesh while it lived.

units.la: Postea enim continuo sequitur cap.II. Neque negandum est defunctorum animas pietate superstitum viventium releuari, quum pro illis sacrificium Mediatoris offertur, vel eleemosyna in Ecclesia fiunt: sed eis haec prosunt, qui quum vueret, ut haec sibi postea prodesse possent, meruerunt. &c. meruerunt autem, id est, τῆς ἀξίας ἐνεργῶν[?] dignitatem hanc assequuti sunt, non vi sua operumve suorum, sed diuina ordinatione per gratiam opera fidei & praemia dispensantem.
units.tr: For immediately afterwards, in chapter 11, there follows: Nor is it to be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of the living who survive, when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them, or alms are given in the Church; but these benefit only those who, while they lived, merited that these things could profit them afterwards, etc. Merited, however, means that they attained this dignity [τῆς ἀξίας], not by their own power or their own works, but by divine ordination, which dispenses the works of faith and their rewards through grace.

units.la: Ab hac hypothesi distat quam plurimum disputatoris sententia, qui animas purgari post mortem in Purgatorio a malo statuit (non in bono promoveri in suis receptaculis) poenarum perpessione & alienae curae officiis: contra quam Augustinus concludit eodem in loco, dicens: Quum ergo sacrificia sive altaris, sive quarumcunque eleemosynarum pro baptizatis defunctis omnibus offeruntur, pro valde bonis gratiarum actionis sunt, pro non valde malis propitiationes sunt, pro valde malis, etsi nulla sunt adiumenta mortuorum, qualescunque vivorum consolationes sunt. Quibus au-tem prosunt, aut ad hoc prosunt ut sit plena remissio, nimirum damnationis in moram & minus demen-sum lucis, aut certe tolerabilior fiat ipsa damnatio, quae modo diximus. Nam de damnatione in poena, quia aeterna est, accipi Augustinus ipse vetat sequentibus. Gregorij auctoritatem in hoc argumento sæpe antea negauimus.
units.tr: The disputant's opinion, which holds that souls are purged after death in Purgatory from evil by undergoing punishments and by the offices of others' care (and are not advanced in good in their receptacles), is very far from this hypothesis. Against this Augustine concludes in the same place, saying: Therefore when sacrifices, whether of the altar or of any alms, are offered for all the baptized dead, they are thanksgivings for the very good, they are propitiations for the not very bad, and for the very bad, though they are no help to the dead, they are whatever consolations for the living. But they profit those to whom they do profit, either to this end, that there may be full remission, namely of the delay of damnation and of a lesser measure of light, or at least that the damnation itself may become more tolerable, which we have just described. For Augustine himself forbids us to understand this of damnation in punishment, because it is eternal, in what follows. We have often denied the authority of Gregory in this argument before.

units.la: 24.Ib. quæ seminauerit homo, hæc & metet Galat. 6.] negamus istam locorum interpretationem, nihil enim Scriptura docet eiusmodi.
units.tr: 24. Ib. whatever a man sows, this he will also reap. Gal. 6.] We deny this interpretation of the passage, for Scripture teaches nothing of that kind.

units.la: 25. Art.21. [?]arnodo enim, id est a fine huius iudicij de quo nunc loquor.] Falsa interpretatio: nondum enim de iudicio vltimo in eo loco agitur, & series prophetiæ contra ostendit, vt aliquando in eum librum exposuimus.
units.tr: 25. Art. 21. For from the end, that is, from the end of this judgment of which I now speak.] A false interpretation: the passage is not yet about the last judgment, and the sequence of the prophecy shows the contrary, as we have expounded in that book at another time.

units.la: 26. Ibid. qui simpliciter moriuntur in Domino, neque aliquid purgandum secum ferunt.] negatur distinctio. nam simpliciter agit Apostolus de iis qui moriuntur in Domino. Moriuntur autem in Domino, quoscunque dedit ipsi Pater; vt contrà non moriuntur in Domino quicunque non fuerunt ordinati ad vitam æternam.
units.tr: 26. Ibid. who simply die in the Lord and bring nothing to be purged with them.] The distinction is denied. For the Apostle speaks simply of those who die in the Lord. Those die in the Lord whom the Father has given to him; just as, conversely, those do not die in the Lord who were not ordained to eternal life.

units.la: 27. Ibid. in Domino ratione caritatis quam secum ferunt, partim non in Domino ratione peccatorum, quæ nihilominus secum ferunt.] vtrumque negamus, & modum subiecti, & prædicationem totam. Negamus decedere quemquam cum peccatis venialibus, ita vt peccata venialia luere eum post mortem oportet pœna aliqua temporali: negamus eos partim mori, partimque non mori in Domino, quos Bellarminus asserit.[illegible, ~4 letters]diluta sunt & vana quæ dicit omnia.
units.tr: 27. Ibid. in the Lord by reason of the love they carry with them, partly not in the Lord by reason of the sins which they nevertheless carry with them.] We deny both the mode of the subject and the whole predication. We deny that anyone departs with venial sins, so that he must expiate those venial sins after death by some temporal punishment. We deny that they partly die in the Lord and partly do not, as Bellarmine asserts. All that he says is weak and empty.

units.la: 28. Ibid. eosdem homines in hac vita partim esse dicit filios Dei, partim filios huius seculi.] Non est par ratio. Nam in vita Christianus quisque vtrumque hominem in se gerit, veterem & nouum: in morte vero, vna cum corpore peccati deponit alterum, totus aut vetus est, aut nouus. ac vetus quidem dat totus poenas, novus vero totus extra poenas est in requie & luce Domini, ut loquuntur Patres. Ex dispari non valet consequentia.
units.tr: 28. Ibid. he says that the same men in this life are partly sons of God, partly sons of this age.] The comparison does not hold. For in this life every Christian bears both men within himself, the old and the new; but in death he puts off the one together with the body of sin, and the remaining man is wholly either old or new. The old man is wholly given over to punishments, while the new man is wholly free from punishments, in rest and in the light of the Lord, as the Fathers say. From an unlike premise the consequence does not follow.

units.la: IN CAP. XIII.
units.tr: IN CHAPTER XIII.

units.la: 1. Art. 2. loqui eum de satisfactione pro culpa, quae praecedit iustificationem. ] negatur distinctio ista satisfactionis, & Cypriani verborum restrictio. De distinctione nota seq.videbitur. Cyprianum de omni pia satisfactione & poenitentia agere homine Christiano dicta, res ipsa loquitur. Quid enim Demetriano cum istis argutis & commentitiis distinctionibus? huic Cyprianus totum officium explicat Christianum: ideoque postquam verba auctoris Sap.5. expressisset, ad locum venit publicae hortationis, dicens: Erit tunc sine fructu poenitentia, & dolor poenae, & inanis ploratio, & inefficax deprecatio. In aeternam poenam fere credunt, qui in vitam aeternam credere noluerunt. Securiati igitur & vita, dum licet, pronidete. Offerimus vobis animi & consilii nostri salutare munus: & quia odisse non licet nobis, & sic Deo plus placemus dum nullam pro iniuria vicem reddimus, hortamur dum facultas adest, dum adhuc aliquid de seculo superest, Deo satisfacere, & ad veram religionis candidam lucem de profundo tenebrosae superstitionis emergere. Non invidemus commodis vestris, nec beneficia divina celamus. O diis vestris benevolentiam, reddimus, & pro tormentis ac supplicis quae nobis inferuntur, salutis iter demonstramus. Credite, & vivite: & qui nos ad tempus persequimini, in aeternum gaudete nobiscum. Quando isthinc excessum fuerit, nullus iam locus poenitentiae est, nullus satisfactionis effectus. Hic vita aut amittit amittitur aut tenetur, hic saluti æternæ cultu Dei & fru-ctu fidei promittetur.&c.totum profecto feruandi hominis officium per totam vitam proponit obseruandum, non tricis distinctionum impedit subtiliter imperitos.
units.tr: 1. Art. 2. that he speaks of satisfaction for guilt which precedes justification.] This distinction of satisfaction is denied, and so is the restriction of Cyprian's words. The distinction will be examined in the following note. That Cyprian is speaking of all pious satisfaction and repentance performed by a Christian is shown by the matter itself. For what has Demetrianus to do with these subtle and invented distinctions? Cyprian sets out to him the whole duty of the Christian. Therefore, after quoting the words of the author at Wisdom 5, he comes to the passage of public exhortation, saying: Then repentance will be without fruit, and the grief of punishment, and empty weeping, and ineffectual entreaty. Those who would not believe in eternal life are almost certain to believe in eternal punishment. Therefore, while it is allowed, take thought for your security and your life. We offer you the saving gift of our mind and counsel. And since we may not hate, and so we please God more, since we return no requital for injury, we exhort you, while the opportunity is present and something of the world still remains, to make satisfaction to God and to emerge from the deep darkness of superstition into the pure white light of true religion. We do not envy your advantages, nor do we hide the divine benefits. We return goodwill to your gods, and for the torments and punishments inflicted on us we show the way of salvation. Believe, and live; and you who persecute us for a time, rejoice with us for ever. When you have departed from here, there is no longer any place for repentance and no effect of satisfaction. Here life is either lost or kept; here eternal salvation is promised through the worship of God and the fruit of faith. etc. Indeed he sets out for the whole course of life the entire duty of saving a man, to be observed throughout life, and he does not, by the snares of subtle distinctions, entangle the unskilled.

units.la: 2. Ibid. duplicem ponunt satisfactionem. Vnam ante iustificationem, qua Deus placatur de congruo. ]Negamus hæc a Patribus prisc is esse: auctorem laudari oportuit. Tum negamus vllam satisfactionem esse ante iustificationem nostri in Christo Iesu. Postremo negamus Deum placari de congruo vlla vlius satisfactione citra satisfactionem Christi: hæc enim fundamentum est totius (quam vocant) congruentiæ.
units.tr: 2. Ibid. They posit a twofold satisfaction. One before justification, by which God is appeased in a fitting manner.] We deny that these things come from the ancient Fathers; the author ought to have been cited.
