Next, we deny that there is any satisfaction before our justification in Christ Jesus. Last, we deny that God is appeased in a fitting manner by any satisfaction of anyone apart from the satisfaction of Christ; for this is the foundation of the whole of what they call congruity.

units.la: 3. Ibid. de qua Daniel 4. peccata tua eleemosynis redime.] Primum falsa est loci interpretatio, vt in tomum 3.& 4. dicturi sumus, volente Domino: secundo autem falsa est loci accommodatio, vt ipse quoque Bonauentura aperte pronunciat in lib.3. sentent. q.18. dicens: Mereri dicitur tripliciter, vno modo simpliciter abusiue, alio modo partim proprie & partim improprie; tertio modo simpliciter proprie. Simpliciter abusiue dicitur mereri, qui facit aliquod opus de genere honorum, tame facit illud malo modo, id est, mala intentione, sicut ille qui dat eleemosynam cum murmure. Talia enim opera aliquando remunerantur a Deo ex immensa largitate, sicut innuitur de Nabuchodonosor. Ille vero meretur partim proprie, partim abusiue, qui facit opus de genere bonorum & bona intentione, veruntamen nō ex charitate: sicut aliquis peccator facit opera de genere bonorum & propter Deum, in quibus de congruo se disponit ad gratiam. Ille vero meretur simpliciter proprie qui facit bonum opus, & bona intentione, & ex charitate.
units.tr: 3. Ibid. Concerning which Daniel 4: redeem your sins by almsgiving.] First, the interpretation of the passage is false, as we shall say when we come to volumes 3 and 4, the Lord willing; second, the application of the passage is false, as Bonaventure himself plainly declares in book 3 of the Sentences, distinction 18, saying: To merit is said in three ways: in one way, simply and improperly; in another way, partly properly and partly improperly; in a third way, simply and properly. A man is said to merit simply and improperly who does some work of the kind that is good, but does it in a bad manner, that is, with a bad intention, like one who gives alms with a grumble. For such works are sometimes rewarded by God out of immense generosity, as is hinted in the case of Nebuchadnezzar. But he merits partly properly and partly improperly who does a work of the kind that is good, with a good intention, yet not out of charity; as a sinner does works of the kind that are good and for God's sake, by which he disposes himself in a fitting manner for grace. But he merits simply and properly who does a good work, with a good intention, and out of charity.

units.la: Et primum quidem meritum dicitur meritum interpretatiuum: secundum dicitur meritum congrui: tertium dicitur meritum condigni. Vides, Bellarmine, quid vesfter Bonauentura dicat de illo exemplo Nabuchodonosoris? meritum esse negat nisi abusiue: meritū congrui esse negat, sed interpretatiuum solum. Cū Bonauentura itaque, bona pace tua, negamus interpretationem tuam.
units.tr: And the first kind of merit is called interpretative merit; the second is called merit of congruity; the third is called merit of condignity. You see, Bellarmine, what your Bonaventure says about that example of Nebuchadnezzar? He denies that it is merit except improperly; he denies that it is merit of congruity, but holds it to be merely interpretative. So with Bonaventure, with all due respect to you, we deny your interpretation.

units.la: 4. Ibid. alteram post iustificationem, qua Deo ex condigno satisfit pro poena. Deo satisfieri ab homine Ἀγ negamus per se, nisi καταχρηστικῶς, abusiue, vt antè in caput II. expositum. Satisfieri autem ex condigno potest qui affirmat, aut nescit quid sit ex condigno mereri vel satisfacere ex Scholasticorum disciplina, aut fallit homonymia. Sed de hac quaestione in tomum. 3.
units.tr: 4. Ibid. the other after justification, by which man satisfies God in condign manner for punishment. We deny that man can make satisfaction to God in himself, except catachrestically, improperly, as was explained before at chapter 2. But he who affirms that man can satisfy in condign manner either does not know what it is, according to the discipline of the Schoolmen, to merit or satisfy in condign manner, or is deceived by an ambiguity of words. But we shall discuss this question in volume 3.

units.la: 5. Ibid. hic vita aut amittitur, aut tenetur. negamus his verbis iniquam illam & falsam restrictionem probari posse: & ipsa Cypriani hortatio docet verbis argumentationis suae, quae supra expressimus nota I.
units.tr: 5. Ibid. here life is either lost or kept. We deny that this unjust and false restriction can be proved from these words; and Cyprian's own exhortation shows it, by the words of his argument, which we quoted above in note 1.

units.la: 6. Art. 4. Nemo autem Catholicorum docet, culpas lethales remitti in Purgatorio. vbi textus non distinguit, negant Iureconsulti a se distingui oportere: an vero Theologos minus religiosos oportet esse in diuinis rebus? negam ergo distinctione, vbi Chrysostomus vniuersè dixit, rectè adhiberi posse. Tum si ab exemplo Epulonis argumentabatur, nonne Epulo iste & lethalia commiserat, & alia quoque illa quae venialia solent appellari ex Pontificia disciplina? Confirmatur ipsis Chrysostomi verbis: qui vniuersè poenitere, commissa diluere, peccata eluere iubet, non haec aut illa solum. Alioquin ex Bellarmini Logica libebunt peccata venialia, quia interdicun-tur lethalia. quod est ἀ[illegible, ~6 letters], vt supra cap. 4. o-stendimus.
units.tr: 6. Art. 4. Yet none of the Catholics teaches that deadly sins are remitted in Purgatory. Where the text makes no distinction, the jurists deny that a distinction ought to be made by them; but ought theologians to be less scrupulous in divine matters? We therefore deny the distinction here, where Chrysostom spoke in general terms and it can rightly be applied. Again, if he argued from the example of Dives, did not that Dives commit both deadly sins and also those others which are usually called venial by Papist discipline? This is confirmed by Chrysostom's own words, which bid one repent in general, wash away what has been committed, and cleanse sins, not only this or that kind. Otherwise, by Bellarmine's logic, venial sins will be lifted up because the deadly ones are forbidden; which is [illegible], as we showed above in chapter 4.

units.la: 7. Artic. 6. loqui ὡς[?] Ambrosium de remissione mortalium:] idem effugium, cui in proxima nota obstruximus: restrictio falsa. Quid enim? annon & eorum quae dicuntur venialia remissio habenda est, vt perueniatur in beatorum patriam? nec vero aliud demonstrant verba sequentia Ambrosij.
units.tr: 7. Artic. 6. that Ambrose speaks of the remission of mortal sins] The same evasion, against which we have set our face in the next note: a false restriction. For what? Must not the remission of those things which are called venial also be had, so that one may reach the homeland of the blessed? Nor do the following words of Ambrose show anything else.

units.la: 8. Ibid. vitam aeternam vocat gratiam iustificatio-nis, quae est vita quaedam aeterna inchoata.] Quid est torquere auctores & sacras res ipsas, nisi hoc est? Ambrosius dixit de patria beatorum, cui vita aeterna respondet ἀναλόγως. etenim reciprocantur ista & ἰσοδυναμεῖ in patria beatorum esse, & vitam aeternam possidere. Tum quis proprie loquendo censeat aut afferat gratiam iustificationis esse vitam aeternam? est quidem illa vitae aeternae conditio in nobis necessaria: sed non continuo vita aeterna est. Alioquin Angeli in coelo non haberent vitam aeternam: quod est absurdissimum. Caute itaque Bellarminus pronunciat, quaedam vita. Nec refert, quod postea Ambrosius subiicit, vita aeterna remissio peccatorum est: nam figurata est enunciatio, ex qua hic propriam struit argumentationem mutato praedicationis genere.
units.tr: 8. Ibid. he calls the grace of justification eternal life, which is a certain eternal life begun.] What is this but twisting the authors and the sacred things themselves? Ambrose spoke of the homeland of the blessed, to which eternal life corresponds analogously [ἀναλόγως]. For these are interchangeable and equivalent [ἰσοδυναμεῖ]: to be in the homeland of the blessed and to possess eternal life. Moreover, who, speaking properly, would think or assert that the grace of justification is eternal life? It is indeed a necessary condition of eternal life in us, but it is not at once eternal life. Otherwise the angels in heaven would not have eternal life, which is most absurd. Bellarmine therefore prudently pronounces a certain life. Nor does it matter that Ambrose afterwards adds eternal life is the remission of sins: for it is a figurative statement, from which he builds his own argument here by changing the kind of predication.

units.la: 9. Art. 8. appellari satisfactionem eo loco excusationem.] negatur interpretatio, quia genus restringitur ad speciem, & vniuersale ad particulare, vt ante nota 6. & 7. Satisfactio genus est, species excusatio. Hoc confirmat ordo ipse verborum Ambrosij.
units.tr: 9. Art. 8. that there is called satisfaction in that place excuse.] The interpretation is denied, because the genus is restricted to the species, and the universal to the particular, as before in notes 6 and 7. Satisfaction is the genus, excuse the species. The very order of Ambrose's words confirms this.

units.la: Nam primum de verbali excusatione aut etiam cosessione (ut postea loquitur) dicit:non invenio quid dixerit, invenio quod fleuerit.tum de reali: lacrymas eius lego, satisfactionem non lego, postremo autem de communi modo: Sed quod defendi non potest, ablui potest: lavant lacryma delictum quod voce pudor est confiteri. &c. Sequens exemplum rerum humanarum est, ratio in divinis dispar.
units.tr: For first he speaks of verbal excuse, or even confession (as he says later): I do not find what he said; I find that he wept. Then of real satisfaction: I read of his tears; I do not read of satisfaction. Last, of the common manner: But what cannot be defended can be washed away: tears wash away the sin which shame is to confess with the voice, etc. The following example is from human affairs; the reasoning in divine matters is different.

units.la: 10. Ibid. laudat igitur ibi [?]Ambrosius Petrum, quod non excusaverit peccatum suum,] addendum, & quod satisfacere de suo ratione nulla praesumpserit. Disputator falsa restrictione fallit, & insufficiente (ut vocant) enumeratione. nec aliud Ambrosius affirmat sequentibus.
units.tr: 10. Ibid. So Ambrose there praises Peter, because he did not excuse his sin,] It should be added: and because he presumed on no reason to make satisfaction of his own. The disputant deceives by a false restriction and by an insufficient (as they call it) enumeration. Nor does Ambrose affirm anything else in what follows.

units.la: 11. Artic.10. non eodem modo datur istud gaudium, sed diversimodè, pro meritorum diversitate:] falsum, nisi distinxeris: nam eodem modo gaudium beatorum datur secundum statum, sed non eodem modulo vel gradu. in hoc est diversitas.
units.tr: 11. Artic. 10. this joy is not given in the same way, but in different ways, according to the diversity of merits:] False, unless you make a distinction: for the joy of the blessed is given in the same way according to their state, but not in the same measure or degree. In this lies the diversity.

units.la: 12. Ibidem. quibusdam non sine temporalium admixtione poenarum, ut idem B. Augustinus saepissime docet.] negamus temporales admisceri poenas: nisi forte dixeris aequivocè, ut Scholastici loquuntur, de poena damni, vel potius damno morae, ut Ter-tullianus vocat, quia sic gaudent ut tamen haereant quodammodo in gaudij plenioris exspectatione: qua de re in caput 9. & 10. dicebamus. Statuunt enim illi duo poenarum genera, poenam sensus, & poenam damni; quarum illa est afflictiva, haec privatione boni concluditur, sive (ut vocant) carentia. Negamus aliud usquam Augustinum dicere.
units.tr: 12. Ibid. with some not without an admixture of temporal punishments, as the same blessed Augustine teaches very often.] We deny that temporal punishments are mixed in, unless perhaps you speak equivocally, as the Schoolmen do, of the punishment of loss, or rather the loss of delay, as Tertullian calls it, because they rejoice in such a way that nevertheless they cling, in some sense, to the expectation of a fuller joy; on which matter we spoke in chapters 9 and 10. For they establish two kinds of punishment, the punishment of sense and the punishment of loss; of which the former is afflictive, while the latter is comprised in the privation of good, or, as they call it, in want. We deny that Augustine says anything else anywhere.

units.la: 13· Artic. 12. Respondeo, loquitur de locis aeternis:] rectè; recte: sed hanc distinctionem loci perpetui & temporarij Augustinus ignorauit in ratione animarum: tum hoc statuit Augustinus conuenienter primæ philosophiæ & Scripturæ sacræ, in seculo futuro, siue supernaturali, nullum nisi æternum esse & supernaturalem locum. Alium esse disputator si affirmat, probet: nam Augustinus quidem ignorauit.
units.tr: 13. Art. 12. I answer: he is speaking of eternal places: Rightly so, rightly so. But Augustine was unaware of this distinction between a permanent and a temporary place in his account of souls. Augustine rightly held, in agreement with first philosophy and holy Scripture, that in the future age, which is supernatural, there is only one place, and it is eternal and supernatural. If the disputant asserts otherwise, let him prove it, for Augustine certainly did not hold it.

units.la: 14. Ibidem. præter cœlum & infernum fuisse ante Christi passionem sinum Abrahæ, vbi degebant animæ sanctorum Patrum Luc. 16.] petitur τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς, hac interpretatione quam falsò vocat catholicam. Atqui & sinus Abrahæ in cælo est: (nam eò importare dicuntur Angeli electos velut in communem domum)ciuitatisque cœlestis attributum, Luc.16.22. Sed de hac re in libro seq. Non est igitur inepta illa siue Erasmi, siue alterius adnotatio, quam Bellar minus carpit sequentibus.
units.tr: 14. Ibidem. Besides heaven and hell, there was before Christ's passion the bosom of Abraham, where the souls of the holy Fathers dwelt, Luke 16. This begs the question [τὴν ἐξ ἀρχῆς], by the interpretation which he falsely calls catholic. Yet the bosom of Abraham is also in heaven, for the angels are said to carry the elect there as into a common home, and it is an attribute of the heavenly city (Luke 16.22). But I will deal with this in the following book. That annotation, whether it is Erasmus's or someone else's, is therefore not foolish, and Bellarmine criticises it less than he should in what follows.

units.la: 15. Artic. 13. Respondeo, loqui eum de pœna æterna:] negamus: loquitur de pœna communiter; cū ne pœnam quidem temporalem Deus secundum proportionem peccatorum nostrorum exigat, commune indiuisum est, de quo Augustinus dicit. Tum falsum est quod de temporali pœna dicitur, ipsam à Deo in seculo futuro exigi. Seculi futuri non est tempus, sed αἰών siue æternitas omnis, etiam pœnæ, sicut & gloriæ. huius seculi est tempus: & temporales igitur pœnæ huius sunt, non autem illius. De locis Augustini diximus ante in cap.II.nota 20.
units.tr: 15. Article 13. I answer that he speaks of eternal punishment:] We deny it: he speaks of punishment in general, since God does not even exact temporal punishment in proportion to our sins; the common is undivided, as Augustine says concerning it. Moreover, it is false that what is said of temporal punishment is exacted by God in the future age. The future age has no time; it is αἰών, that is, all eternity, including punishment, just as it includes glory. Time belongs to this age, and therefore temporal punishments belong to this age, not to that one. We spoke of Augustine's passages earlier, in chapter 2, note 20.

units.la: 16. Artic. 14. & pro criminibus iam dimissis pœna temporalis lui possit.] Negantur ista omnia: pœ[?]
units.tr: 16. Article 14. & for sins already forgiven temporal punishment may be paid.] All these things are denied.

units.la: K k ij cata levia quædam sic esse coram Deo: nam omnia iustorum levata sunt in Christo, ergo nulla, iniustorum nulla esse levia[?] ipse disputator agnoscit:tum ea purgari in futuro seculo: item pro criminibus jam dimissis poenas lui, nisi commode intelligatur: postremo lui poenas eorum temporales in futuro seculo. Et certè ubi non est locus corrigendorum morum, nec locus esse purgandis peccatis potest, quæ sunt moralia.
units.tr: K k ij [...] that such light sins are so before God: for all the sins of the righteous have been taken away in Christ, so no sins of the unrighteous are light; the disputant himself acknowledges this. Then, that they are cleansed in the future age; likewise, that punishments are paid for sins already forgiven, unless it is understood in a suitable sense; lastly, that their temporal punishments are paid in the future age. And certainly, where there is no place for amending morals, there can be no place for cleansing those sins which are moral.

units.la: 17. Artic. 15. significat Augustinus post hanc vi-tam non crescere merita vel demerita: ] falsum. nam Augustinus de meritis vel demeritis ne [illegible, ~2 letters] quidem: merita, vt Pontificij accipiunt, nulla Augustinus tradit. Tum omnino tollit Purgatorium qui cum Augustino simpliciter dicit, qualis in die isto quisque moritur, talis in die illo iudicabitur. statuit enim, defunctorum statum eumdem permanere, nec vllo modo mutari inde à morte ad diem vsque iudicij, non igitur Purgatorium esse. Alioqui profecto in quo quemque inuenerit suus nouissimus dies, in hoc eum non esset comprehensurus mundi nouissimus dies; & qualis in die isto quisque moritur, talis in die illo non iudicaretur, contra quàm Augustinus pronunciat.
units.tr: 17. Art. 15. Augustine signifies that after this life merits or demerits do not increase: False. For Augustine does not speak of merits or demerits at all; he hands down no merits in the sense the Papists take them. Moreover, whoever says with Augustine simply, as each man dies on that day, so will he be judged on that day, entirely removes Purgatory. For he holds that the state of the dead remains the same, and that it is in no way changed from death until the day of judgment; therefore there is no Purgatory. Otherwise, the last day of the world would not overtake each man in the condition in which his last day found him; and he would not be judged on that day as he died on this one, contrary to what Augustine declares.

units.la: 18. Artic. 16. & quanquam non meminit nisi duorum locorum, tamen non excludit alia. ] negatur solutio: & ipse Theophylactus negat in caput 19. Joannis, dicens euidentius & mentem suam explicans: Tradidit quidem, inquit spiritum Dominus Deo & Patri: ostendens quòd posthac animæ iustorum in monumentis non versantur, currunt autem in sinum[?] patris omnium: sed peccatorum animæ in locum supplicij detractâ, hoc est, in infernum depellentur.
units.tr: 18. Art. 16. And although he mentions only two places, he does not exclude others. The solution is denied. Theophylact himself denies it in his comment on John 19, saying more clearly and explaining his mind: Indeed the Lord, he says, handed over the spirit to God and the Father, showing that the souls of the righteous no longer dwell in tombs, but run into the hands of the Father of all; but the souls of sinners are cast out of the place of punishment, that is, into hell.

units.la: Græce mehùs habentur in ipsa quoque editione Romana: παρέξει τε μὴ τὸ πνεῦμα ὁ κύριος τῇ δεῖ πατρί, ἀποκρινόμενος ὡς ἐκ τῆς τῶν ἐμφιλοσοφῶν [?] ἀξιῶν δι[?] ψυχαί, τρέχουσι δὲ μᾶλλον εἰς χεῖρας τὰ πάντων πατέρας. τῶν δὲ ἁμαρτωλῶν εἰς τὴν τῆς κολάσεως τὸν κατα-[illegible, ~6 letters]
units.tr: The Greek text in the Roman edition itself reads better: the Lord handed over the spirit to God the Father, showing that the souls of the righteous run rather into the hands of the Father of all; but the souls of sinners are cast into the place of punishment [...].

units.la: Peccatoribus non dari Purgatorium ipse Bellarminus asserit: quod si aliorum animæ migrant in manus Patris omnium, quibus animam quoque suam commendauit Christus, quid illis cum Purgatorio? antecedens affirmat Theophylactus, & duo tantum agnoscit loca: ergo nec vllum agnoscit Purgatorium, nec illis tertium patitur assignari locum.
units.tr: The Papists' own Bellarmine asserts that Purgatory is not given to sinners. But if the souls of the others pass into the hands of the Father of all, into whose hands Christ also commended his own soul, what has Purgatory to do with them? Theophylact affirms the antecedent and acknowledges only two places; therefore he acknowledges no Purgatory at all, nor does he allow a third place to be assigned to them.

units.la: 19. Ibidem. dici possunt esse in inferno, quia Purgatorium pars est inferni, vel certè locus vicinus. ] Vtrumque negatur: tum quod de manu Dei dicitur, esse in manu Dei qui non sunt in regno; cùm Christus qui dixit Patri, in manus tuas commendo spiritum meum, idem latroni de eadem re dixerit, hodie mecum eris in paradiso; de eadem autem re Theophylactus agit posteriore loco: tum quod Purgatorium statuitur, eique locus in inferno aut vicinia eius tribuitur.
units.tr: 19. Ibidem. They can be said to be in hell, because Purgatory is part of hell, or at least a neighbouring place. Both are denied: first, because what is said of being in the hand of God is said of those who are not in the kingdom, since Christ who said to the Father, into your hands I commend my spirit, said to the thief about the same matter, today you will be with me in paradise; and Theophylact deals with the same matter in the later passage. Second, because Purgatory is posited, and a place in hell, or its neighbourhood, is assigned to it.

units.la: 20. Artic. 18. vt per cruciatus atque supplicia ad Dominum reuertatur.] locus est totus allegorices, qui in vtrâuis sententiam exponi poterit. Ego pro sententia loci illius manum non verterim.
units.tr: 20. Art. 18. that by torments and punishments he may return to the Lord. The passage is wholly allegorical and could be expounded in either sense. I would not turn my hand to defend the sense of that passage.

units.la: 1. Art.2.cur post remissam culpam adhuc tam multa patimur, & tandem etiam morimur?] respondet Augustinus tractatu 124. in Ioannem (quem locum ante disputator adducebat cap. 11.) tribus de causis ista contingere, quamuis remissa culpa, idque in hac vita solùm. Dicit enim, ad demonstrationem debitæ miseriæ, vel ad emendationem labilis vitæ, vel ad exercitationem necessariæ patientiæ. Si ergo perpessiones, atque adeò mors ipsa tantùm essent homini Christiano pœnæ, ac nihil amplius; valeret consequentia. Sed cùm ad hos quoque fines pertineant, consequentia est mala ex particulari. Nam in hac vita perpetimur, ut discamus recordari cum animis nostris quanta miseria nobis debeatur propter peccatum nostrum, si Deus summo iure experiri nobiscum vellet; ut vitam emende-mus; ut probemur & exerceamur in patientia ad gloriam Dei, ac non solùmmodò ut luamus pœnas peccati nostri. Atque hi quoque fines sunt communes morti nostræ (ut illud taceam quòd transitus illa est à morte ad vitam) si medium illum exceperis quem Augustinus pronunciat, ad emen-dationem labilis vitæ: nam qui euocatur è vita, huic non datur amplius vitæ emendandæ locus.
units.tr: 1. Art. 2. Why do we still suffer so many things after the guilt is forgiven, and at last even die? Augustine answers in tractate 124 on John (the passage the disputant cited earlier in chapter 11) that these things happen for three reasons, although the guilt is forgiven, and that only in this life. For he says: to demonstrate our owed wretchedness, or to amend a fragile life, or to exercise necessary patience. If therefore sufferings, and indeed death itself, were only punishments for the Christian, and nothing more, the inference would hold. But since they also serve these ends, the inference is faulty as an argument from a part. For in this life we suffer so that we may learn to remember, together with our souls, how great a wretchedness is owed to us because of our sin, should God wish to deal with us by his supreme right; so that we may amend our lives; so that we may be proved and exercised in patience to the glory of God; and not merely that we may pay the penalties of our sin. These ends are also common to our death (to say nothing of the fact that it is a passage from death to life), if you except that middle end which Augustine states, to amend a fragile life; for one who is called out of life is no longer given a place to amend his life.

units.la: 2. Ibid.cur infantes baptizati agrotant, qui non sunt capaces peccati actualis?] respondet Augustinus, ad demonstrationem debitæ miseriæ, & gloriæ Dei, Ioan. 9. siue ipsis, siue parentibus & aliis, siue utrisque fiat demonstratio. Frustra igitur disputator arguit.
units.tr: 2. Ibid. Why do baptized infants fall sick, when they are not capable of actual sin? Augustine answers: to demonstrate owed wretchedness, and the glory of God (John 9), whether this demonstration is made to themselves, or to their parents and others, or to both. The disputant therefore argues in vain.

units.la: 3. Art. 3. Applicatio fit per aliis nostros & Sacramenta. ] Hoc verum esse non negamus, sed nec solum, nec principaliter fit modis illis. Fit enim meriti Christi applicatio homini Christiano primo & principaliter virtute & operatione Spiritus Christi: secundo ex parte nostra fit applicatio sive apprehensio fide, cuius fructus sunt opera nostra applicationem non efficientia, sed contestantia: tertio ex utraque parte fit applicationis illius salutaris confirmatio Sacramentis, id est actione sacra & intus & foris veritate & symbolis celebrata. Itaque disputator fallit & insufficiente(ut vocant) enumeratione, & imperitia res plane distinctas & actiones ipsarum confundente.
units.tr: 3. Art. 3. Application is made through our works and the sacraments. We do not deny that this is true, but it is neither the only nor the principal way in which it is made. For the application of Christ's merit to the Christian is made first and principally by the power and working of the Spirit of Christ; second, on our part the application, or apprehension, is made by faith, whose fruits are our works, which do not effect the application but attest it; third, from both sides the confirmation of that saving application is made by the sacraments, that is, by a sacred action celebrated inwardly and outwardly with truth and signs. So the disputant errs both by an insufficient enumeration (as they call it) and by ignorance, confusing things and actions that are plainly distinct.

units.la: 4. Ibid. Per opera autem satisfactoria applicetur ad tollendam poenam temporalem:] prius accipimus, si bene intelligatur: posterius negamus. Sed de eo in tomum 4. videbitur.
units.tr: 4. Ibid. But by satisfactory works it is applied to remove temporal punishment: We accept the former, if it is rightly understood; the latter we deny. But this will be seen in volume 4.

units.la: 5. Ibid. Poena æterna commutatur in temporalem, quando remittitur culpa: ] Negatur. contra enim remissionem culpæ & pœnæ æternæ comitatur pœna aliqua temporalis ad demonstrationem miseriæ debitæ (ut ante ex Augustino dicebamus) nisi misericordiam caperet de nobis misericors Deus. Eadem vero negantur sequentia pleraque.
units.tr: 5. Ibid. Eternal punishment is changed into temporal when guilt is forgiven: Denied. For, against this, remission of guilt and of eternal punishment is accompanied by some temporal punishment, to demonstrate the owed wretchedness (as we said earlier from Augustine), unless the merciful God had shown mercy to us. Most of what follows is likewise denied.

units.la: 6. Ibid. & tamen iustitia exigit, ut peccatum puniatur aliquo modo:] Imo vero exigit ut puniatur peccatum omni modo, & punitum est in Christo, qui factus est peccatum pro nobis ut simus iustitia Dei in ipso, 2.Cor.5.sed acquiescit illius merito misericordia.ex falso nihil sequitur.
units.tr: 6. Ibid. and yet justice demands that sin be punished in some way: Indeed justice demands that sin be punished in every way, and it has been punished in Christ, who was made sin for us so that we might become the righteousness of God in him (2 Cor. 5). But mercy rests on his merit. Nothing follows from a falsehood.

units.la: 7. Ibid. de qua re dictum est aliquid supra, ] locus est capite II. de satisfactione vero in tomum 3.con-
units.tr: 7. Ibid. concerning which something has been said above, The place is chapter II. On satisfaction, however, see volume 3.

units.la: 8. Art. 5. Maximum discrimen est inter Sacramentum ablutionis, & Sacramentum absolutionis, Sacramentum ablutionis baptismum vocat, hoc agnoscimus: quod vero Sacramentum pœnitentiæ & absolutionis vocat, dicit æquiuoce, ut in tomum 3. dictum fumus. Ut sacramentum proprie nunc in Ecclesia dicitur, sacramenta negamus esse: sin pro rebus a-ctionibusve sacris accipit communiter, non impedimus: sed cauēdū[?] monemus ab homonymia. Tum de partibus pœnitentiæ quod dicit, suo loco in tom. 3. expendetur. His obseruatis, dicimus pœnitentiæ nomen in ea argumentatione accipi proprie de plena atque integra pœnitentia hominis Christiani, secundum rationem prioris membri in dilemmate positi. Quamobrem sequentia nihil ad rem, quia ad secundum membrum dilemmatis illius pertinent, quod membrum negamus. Postremo quod ait in absolutione præcipuè consistere Sacramentum pœnitentiæ, de eo in tom. 3. videbitur.
units.tr: 8. Art. 5. There is the greatest difference between the sacrament of washing and the sacrament of absolution. He calls baptism the sacrament of washing, and we acknowledge this. But what he calls the sacrament of penance and absolution he speaks of equivocally, as was said in volume 3. We deny that these are sacraments in the sense in which the word is now properly used in the Church. If, however, he takes it in common usage for sacred things or sacred actions, we do not object, though we warn against confusing the two senses. As for what he says about the parts of penance, it will be examined in its place in volume 3. With these things observed, we say that the name of penance in that argument is properly taken for the full and entire penance of a Christian, according to the first member of the dilemma he has posed. Therefore what follows is irrelevant, since it pertains to the second member of the dilemma, which we deny. Finally, as to his claim that the sacrament of penance consists chiefly in absolution, this will be seen in volume 3.

units.la: 9. Ibid. de clauibus, de indulgentiis, de Purgatorio. Deniq; de omnibus fabulis lucrificabilibus, quæ in Pontificio regno circumueniunt & præfocant veritatem Dei.
units.tr: 9. Ibid. concerning the keys, indulgences, and Purgatory. Finally, concerning all the moneymaking fables that circulate in the Papal kingdom and suppress the truth of God.

units.la: 10. Art. 6. Ad tollendam omnem culpam & pœnam futuri seculi, id est, tam gehennæ quam Purgatorij. Si ergo in baptismo per ablutionem Deus applicat meritum Christi liberalissimè, quid homini baptizato in Christum cum Purgatorio? profectò non magis ad illum pœna Purgatorij, si quod est, quàm gehennæ pertinet: hæc autem nihil ad Christianum ve-rum, nec igitur illa.
units.tr: 10. Art. 6. To remove all guilt and punishment of the future age, that is, both of Gehenna and of Purgatory. If then in baptism God most freely applies the merit of Christ through the washing, what has Purgatory to do with a man baptized into Christ? Surely the punishment of Purgatory, if there is such a thing, pertains to him no more than that of Gehenna. But Gehenna has nothing to do with a true Christian, and so neither does the other.

units.la: 11. Ibid. Ut patet in pueris baptizatis ægrotantibus morientibus.] Hæ nō pœnæ sūt simpliciter, sed documenta, probationes, & purgationes pœnales appellandæ, ut supra cap. ii. nota 13. & sequentibus fuit expositum. de infantibus paulo ante diximus nota 2.
units.tr: 11. Ibid. As is clear in baptized children who are sick, dying. These are not punishments simply, but should be called proofs, trials, and penal purifications, as was set out above in chapter II, note 13 and following. About infants we spoke a little earlier, note 2.

units.la: 12. Ibid. Requirere opera pœnitentiæ, quibus redimamus temporales pœnas,] negatur pœnas opere humano redimi: Christus est nobis factus a Deo Patre omnimoda redeptio & perfectissima, 1. Cor. 1.[?] si quas pœnas temporaleis minime luimus, fit gratiosa Dei condonatione in Christo, non operaria redemptione nostra.
units.tr: 12. Ibid. To require works of penance by which we redeem temporal punishments, We deny that punishments are redeemed by human works. Christ has been made to us by God the Father a complete and most perfect redemption (1 Cor. 1). If we pay off no temporal punishments at all, this comes about by the gracious forgiveness of God in Christ, not by our redemption through works.

units.la: 13. Ibid. Iterum renouari ad pœnitentiam, nimirum baptismalem,] Erratum duplex. Nam 1. non dicit Apostolus ἀνακαινίζει̂ [?] renouari, sed ἀνακαινίζειν reno-uare, ostendens Deum in suis iudiciis aduersus impios iustum & constantem esse, nec seipsum negare posse, ut expositum est Parallelorum sacrorum libro 3. in eundem locum. 2. agit Apostolus de pœnitentia Christiana universe, non de ea solum quam hic disputator baptismalem vocat: restrictio falsa.
units.tr: 13. Ibid. To be renewed again to repentance, namely baptismal, There is a double error here. First, the Apostle does not say [ἀνακαινίζειν] "to be renewed," but [ἀνακαινίζειν] "to renew," showing that God in his judgments against the impious is just and constant, and cannot deny himself, as was explained in the Parallels of Sacred Writings, book 3, on that passage. Second, the Apostle is speaking of Christian repentance in general, not only of that which this disputant calls baptismal. The restriction is false.

units.la: 14. Ibid. Post acceptam notitiam veritatis, id est, post illuminationem baptismi.] angustius: nam significatur omnis communicatio veritatis gratiosè facta a Domino: & agitur de voluntaria ac deliberata omnis divinæ veritatis, non huius aut illius solum, & malitiosa oppugnatione.
units.tr: 14. Ibid. After receiving knowledge of the truth, that is, after the illumination of baptism. This is too narrow. What is meant is every communication of the truth graciously made by the Lord, and the passage concerns the voluntary, deliberate, and malicious opposition to all divine truth, not to this or that truth alone.

units.la: 15. Art. 7. Sequeretur, omnes qui peccant post baptismum necessario damnandos, vel certe Paulū inepte loqui.] negatur sequi ex falsa interpretatione. Id enim tantum sequitur, omnes qui peccant voluntarie in Spiritum Sanctum, totamque notitiam veritatis acceptam, necessario damnandos esse: quod religiose affirmamus. Sequentia itaque nihil ad causam.
units.tr: 15. Art. 7. It would follow that all who sin after baptism must necessarily be damned, or else that Paul speaks foolishly. We deny that this follows from a false interpretation. What follows is only that all who sin voluntarily against the Holy Spirit, after receiving the whole knowledge of the truth, must necessarily be damned, and this we affirm with reverence. Therefore what follows has nothing to do with the case.

units.la: Siue gehenna, siue Purgatorij, ] Negatur diffunctionis posterius membrum ex verbis ipsis Apostoli: nam de igne consumente, non autem purgante se pronunciat agere. Et tota igitur sequens interpretatio falsa.
units.tr: Whether of Gehenna or of Purgatory, We deny the latter part of the disjunction on the Apostle's own words. For he declares that he is speaking of a consuming fire, not a purging one. So the whole following interpretation is false.

units.la: & hæc est quam vocamus satisfactionem.] Negatur, vt supra in caput II. & tomi 3. controuersia de pœnitentia.
units.tr: and this is what we call satisfaction. Denied, as above in chapter II and in the controversy on repentance in volume 3.

units.la: & secundam tabulam post naufragium.] Non sequitur ex figuratis Patrum & demegoricis sermonibus, de quibus in tomum 3. videbitur.
units.tr: and a second plank after shipwreck. It does not follow from the figurative and allegorical sermons of the Fathers, which will be considered in volume 3.

units.la: Quanto est magis ingratus, & maius lumen & auxilium habuit.] Atqui hinc non sequitur illa diffunctio, sed simplex affirmatio, ergo ignem gehennæ experturum esse nec alia Patrum, qui adducuntur postea, sententia.
units.tr: How much more ungrateful is he, who had greater light and help. But from this the disjunction does not follow, only a simple affirmation. Therefore he will experience the fire of Gehenna, and not the other opinion of the Fathers adduced afterwards.

units.la: Vbi homo sui ipsius redemptor & saluator appellatur, ] Negatur. Nam priore loco falsa est interpretatio, vt romi 3. controuersiæ de pœnitentia lib.4. docebimus: posteriore vero figurata, quemadmodum & Ioan. 6. 27. nam propterea opponit Apostolus verbo καταργέω, alterum ἐνεργέω, sequente versu. homo est καταργούμενος vel instrumentum σωτήριον, Deus, ἐνεργῶν. Sed de hac re tomo 4.
units.tr: where man is called his own redeemer and saviour, Denied. In the former passage the interpretation is false, as we will show in volume 3, the controversy on repentance, book 4. In the latter it is figurative, as also in John 6:27. For this reason the Apostle sets over against the verb [καταργέω] the other verb [ἐνεργέω] in the following verse: man is [καταργούμενος], or an instrument of salvation [σωτήριον], while God is [ἐνεργῶν]. But on this matter, see volume 4.

units.la: Nec propterea vlla fit Christo iniuria, ] Falsum, siquidem accipit verbum hoc aut illud ἐνεργητικῶς, cum verbum ἐνεργέω a Paulo diserte verbo καταργέω opponatur, & Deus homini σωτήρ. Sic autem accipiunt Pontificij.
units.tr: Nor on that account is any injury done to Christ, False. They take this or that word actively [ἐνεργητικῶς], whereas the verb [ἐνεργέω] is expressly opposed by Paul to [καταργέω], and God is the Saviour [σωτήρ] of man. The Papists, however, take it in this way.

units.la: Vel potius ipse Christi spiritus in nobis ista operatur. ] Quid ergo parcius nō loquamur de humanis operibus, si Christus aut Spiritus eius semper agit ἐνεργητικῶς, & homo συνεργητικῶς, in omni opere bono?quæ virtus est operis huius in se?quo iure dicatur satisfactio? Sequenti similitudinis ratio dispar est: nam Christus per Spiritum agit in nobis vt principium:primæ verò causæ in secundis non item.Imò ne Deus quidem ipse in secundis causis agit nisi vt principium vniuersale: sed sua permittit, prout dedit, principiis singularibus. Sic enim administrat Deus omnia quæ creauit, ait Augustinus libro septimo de ciuit. Dei capite trigesimo, vt etiam ipsa proprios exercere & agere motus sinat.
units.tr: Or rather Christ's own Spirit works these things in us. Why then should we not speak more sparingly of human works, if Christ or his Spirit always works actively [ἐνεργητικῶς] and man cooperatively [συνεργητικῶς] in every good work? What virtue does this work have in itself, by which right it could be called satisfaction? The following comparison is unlike: Christ acts through the Spirit in us as the principle, but the first cause does not act in the same way in secondary causes. Indeed, God himself does not act in secondary causes except as the universal principle, but he allows them to act by their own particular principles as he has given them. "For God so governs all things that he has created," says Augustine in book 7 of The City of God, chapter 30, "that he allows even these things to exercise and carry out their own motions."

units.la: 23. Art. 12. Scriptura & Patres passim vocant nostra opera satisfactiones & peccatorum redemptiones.] de Scriptura negamus, vt supra nota 20. Patres aliì figuratè dixerunt, alij respectu hominum, ac non Dei, satisfactiones & redemptiones peccatorum à nobis præstari pronunciauerunt: quod est verissimum. Ex falso nihil sequitur, nec ex figurato proprie, neque ex elenchi ignoratione: quibus hic modis Bellarminus peccat.
units.tr: 23. Art. 12. Scripture and the Fathers everywhere call our works satisfactions and redemptions of sins. Concerning Scripture we deny this, as above in note 20. Some Fathers spoke figuratively. Others declared that satisfactions and redemptions of sins are rendered by us with respect to men, and not with respect to God, which is most true. Nothing follows from a falsehood, nor from a figure taken literally, nor from ignorance of the elenchus. In these ways Bellarmine goes wrong.

units.la: 24. Ibidem. Cur non satisfacere pro pœna temporali, quod est minus ?] Vtrumque negamus, antecedens & consequens. Sic supra capite 13. nota quarta.
units.tr: 24. Ibid. Why not make satisfaction for temporal punishment, which is the lesser? We deny both the antecedent and the consequent, as above in chapter 13, note 4.

units.la: 25. Art. 13. Qui modus non videtur mihi improbabilis:] Negamus esse probabilem: nec verò vsque adeo Bellarminus probat, qui modum probabiliorem adfert artic. sequente.
units.tr: 25. Art. 13. This method does not seem improbable to me: We deny that it is probable. Nor does Bellarmine prove it so very well, since he brings forward a more probable method in the following article.

units.la: 26. Ibid. Placuit Christo coniungere nostram satisfactionem.] Negamus hominem facere Deo satis: item satisfactionem hominis ad Dei gloriam pertinere: denique cum satisfactione Christi coniunctam esse.
units.tr: 26. Ibid. It pleased Christ to join our satisfaction to his. We deny that man makes satisfaction to God. We likewise deny that human satisfaction pertains to the glory of God, and finally that it is joined with the satisfaction of Christ.

units.la: 27. Ibid. & tamen voluit totum sanguinem effundere, vt effet copiosissima redemptio.] dispar ratio:nam tota redemptio est in solidum totius personæ Christi, satisfactio vero à personis differentibus præstari dicitur, Christi nimirum & nostra. Sed & suppositio illa sanè intelligenda est, suffecisse vnam guttam sanguinis Christi redimere mundum: nam periculosè dicitur, diuiditurque quod subiecto vnum est, nisi intelligatur commodè.
units.tr: 27. Ibid. and yet he willed to pour out all his blood, so that the redemption might be most abundant. The comparison is unlike, for the whole redemption lies wholly in the whole person of Christ, whereas satisfaction is said to be rendered by different persons, namely Christ and ourselves. But that supposition too must be understood soundly: "that one drop of Christ's blood sufficed to redeem the world." For it is dangerous to say, and to divide what is one in its subject, unless it is understood appropriately.

units.la: 28. Ibid. Altero ex meritis propriis.] Negatur hæc propositio tota, & tomo 3. confutabitur.
units.tr: 28. Ibid. from his own merits. This whole proposition is denied, and will be refuted in volume 3.

units.la: 29. Art.14. ] Quod vna tantùm sit actualis satisfactio, & ea sit nostra: ] Prius concedimus de satisfactione Christi, dicta proprie atque vniuocè, posterius negamus, sed qua mente à Bellarmino dicuntur ista, negamus totum.
units.tr: 29. Art. 14. That there is only one actual satisfaction, and that this is ours: We grant the first, concerning the satisfaction of Christ, taken properly and univocally. The second we deny. But in whatever sense Bellarmine says these things, we deny the whole of it.

units.la: 30. Ibid. per eius satisfactionem habemus gratiam, vnde satisfacimus,] Nusquam ita Scriptura loquitur: Patres quidam verbo satisfaciendi improprie & æ-quivocè abusi sunt. Exegesin itaque sequentem improbamus.
units.tr: Scripture nowhere speaks in this way. Some Fathers abused the word "satisfy" improperly and equivocally. We therefore reject the explanation that follows.

units.la: Art.17. Respondeo, negandam esse consequentiam:] Negatur falsò.
units.tr: "I reply that the consequence must be denied." It is denied falsely.

units.la: 32. Ibid. ad satisfactionem requiritur vt opus quod fit sit pœna'e,[?] ] Addendum fuit, & satisfactorium. nam non omnis pœna satisfactoria est. Quod autem subiicit, opus satisfactorium non requiri ad maritum, id verum futurum esset, si daretur vllum subiectū, quod & satisfactionem non deberet Deo, & apud illum mereri posset. Angeli è cœlo satisfactionem Deo non debent, quia non peccauerunt, sed mereri non possunt, cùm in sæculo futuro, testibus Pontificiis, non exsistat meritum, Iob.4.18. & 25.3.[?] homines & satisfactionem debent, & meritum: neutrum in se possunt, sed Christus in se potest, & in nobis omnia qui factus est nobis à Deo Patre sapientia, iustitia, sanctificatio, & redemptio, 1.Cor.1 30. Sequentia omnia sunt humanæ ratiocinationis, de homine vt subiecto, de actionibus & perpessionibus eius, de statu post mortem, de Purgatorio fingentis tragelaphos. Negamus omnia hæc somnia.
units.tr: The text should have added "and satisfactory", for not every punishment is satisfactory. As for his claim that a satisfactory work is not required for merit, that would be true only if there were some subject that neither owed satisfaction to God nor could merit before him. Angels owe God no satisfaction, since they have not sinned, but they cannot merit either, since by the Papists' own testimony there is no merit in the future age (Job 4:18; 25:3). Men owe both satisfaction and merit, and they can do neither in their own right. Christ, however, can do so in himself, and in us all things, since he was made to us by God the Father wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor. 1:30). Everything that follows is human reasoning: about man as the subject, about his actions and sufferings, about his state after death, and about a Purgatory invented like a goat-stag. We deny all these dreams.

units.la: 33. Art.19. Scriptura & Patres diserte docent, post hanc vitam remitti peccata levia, ] Negamus hoc à Scriptura dici, aut prisci∫cis illis Patribus: post aliquot demum secula error iste est adnatus veritati.
units.tr: We deny that Scripture or those most ancient Fathers say this, that light sins are forgiven after this life. This error grew up alongside the truth only after several centuries.

units.la: 34. Ibid. Gratia finalis non potest remittere peccatum, quod actu placet, immo quod non displicet aliquo modo. ] Hoc verum est de peccato solum in Spiritum sanctum, Hebr.6. non potest autem, quia non vult Deus, nec convenit iustitiæ eius. Alioqui dicit Christus, Matth. 12. 31. quoduis peccatum & blasphemia remittetur hominibus, excepta blasphemia in Spiritum: si remittitur per gratiam, quidni per finalem gratiam? quamobrem sequens hypothesis nihil ad causam.
units.tr: "Final grace cannot remit a sin that pleases in act, or rather one that in no way displeases." This is true only of the sin against the Holy Spirit (Heb. 6), and that is not forgiven because God does not will it and it does not agree with his justice. Otherwise Christ says, "Every sin and blasphemy will be forgiven men, except blasphemy against the Spirit" (Matt. 12:31). If sin is forgiven through grace, why not through final grace? So the following hypothesis has nothing to do with the case.

units.la: 35. Art.21. Ut patet apud Dionysium cap.ult. Eccles. hierarch.] Falsum: prout docuimus ante cap.10. nota 2. & cap.12. nota 22. orationes autem Ecclesiæ supra distinximus cap.9. & 10.
units.tr: "As is evident in Dionysius, the last chapter of the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy." This is false, as we taught before, in chapter 10, note 2, and in chapter 12, note 22. We have distinguished the prayers of the Church above, in chapters 9 and 10.

units.la: 36. Art.22. Tamen est remissoria peccati. ] totam opinionem hanc veram negamus esse.
units.tr: "Nevertheless it is a remedy for sin." We deny that this whole opinion is true.

units.la: 37. Art.23. & prætereà quia est in bono confirmata.] Hæc responsio tota & sequentes duæ negantur simpliciter, quia supponunt rem negatam & falsam, cui superstruant. τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς[?] petitur.
units.tr: "And moreover because it is confirmed in good." This whole reply and the following two are simply denied, because they assume a thing that is denied and false, and build upon it. They beg the question [τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς].

units.la: 38. Art.26. Nam etiam ob culpam præteritam debetur pœna. ] At hoc tamen nihil est impedimento, quominus decrescente deminutaque culpa, etiam decrescat & deminuatur poena: quod exemplis ex iure sumptis probari potest. Sed ista quid ad nos?ad alia itaque transeamus.
units.tr: "For a penalty is owed even for past guilt." Yet this is no hindrance to the fact that, as the guilt lessens and diminishes, the penalty too lessens and diminishes. This can be proved by examples taken from law. But what has this to do with us? Let us pass on to other matters.

units.la: In CAPUT XV.
units.tr: In CHAPTER XV.

units.la: 1. Art. 7. dogma esse fidei Purgatorium, ] nos hoc constanter negamus, & certò.
units.tr: "That Purgatory is an article of faith." We constantly and certainly deny this.

units.la: 2. Art.10. Ex verbo Dei per [?]Apostolos non scripto, sed traduto : quomodo probamus Euangelia & Epistolas Pauli esse diuinas Scripturas. ]Hæc omnia in causa fidei obtendi falsò dicimus, & confutauimus controuersiæ primæ, lib.4. Sequentis probationis eadem plane ratio.
units.tr: "From the word of God handed down through the Apostles, not written but transmitted, just as we prove that the Gospels and the Epistles of Paul are divine Scripture." We say falsely that all these things are put forward as grounds of faith. We have refuted this in the first controversy, book 4. The reasoning of the following proof is plainly the same.

units.la: 3. Art.11. Reuelationes autem diuina partim scripta sunt, partim non scripta. ] Negatur hoc ad res fidei & rationem eius communem pertinere: quod ibidem ostendimus.
units.tr: "Divine revelations, however, are partly written and partly unwritten." This is denied to pertain to the matters of faith and their common basis, as we have shown in the same place.

units.la: 4. Ibid. Tunc enim solum faciunt rem de fide, cum explicant verbum Dei, aut inde aliquid deducunt. ]be-ne est: atqui non est in isto albo Purgatorium, non igitur est de fide. Sic etiam alia quamplurima, qui-bus circumfluit Rom. Ecclesia.
units.tr: "For they make something a matter of faith only when they explain the word of God or deduce something from it." That is well said. But Purgatory is not in that list, so it is not a matter of faith. The same holds for very many other things with which the Roman Church is flooded.

units.la: 5. Art. 12. Patet ex Conciliis & Patribus, quos citauimus. ]& nos confutauimus supra cap.9. & 10.
units.tr: "This is evident from the Councils and Fathers, whom we cited." We too have refuted this above, in chapters 9 and 10.

units.la: 6. Art.13. Patet ex duabus primis rationibus, quas fecimus. ]& hoc confutatum supra cap.11.
units.tr: "This is evident from the first two arguments which we made." This was refuted above in chapter 11.

units.la: 7. Art.14. Constanter docuerunt Purgatorium esse. ] confutatum cap.9. & 10.
units.tr: "They constantly taught that Purgatory exists." Refuted in chapters 9 and 10.

units.la: 8. Ibid. Talia enim ad [?]Apostolicam traditionem referenda esse, ] Si ad traditionem de qua Augusti-nus, nō ergo Scripturis probatur Purgatorium: sin-autem ad Scripturam, ut disputator affirmauit inde à cap.3. quid nobis hic traditiones reponuntur? nam alterum altero euertitur.
units.tr: "For such things are to be referred to apostolic tradition." If they are referred to the tradition of which Augustine speaks, then Purgatory is not proved from Scripture. But if they are referred to Scripture, as the disputant has affirmed from chapter 3 onward, why are traditions offered to us here? For the one overthrows the other.

units.la: 9. Art.15. Orationem pro defunctis esse ἀποστολικὰν[?] traditionem.] Negatur hoc illos dicere, vt cap. 9. & 10. demonstratum: negatur ex eo bonam de Purgatorio consequentiam esse: proinde falsa sequentia.
units.tr: "Prayer for the dead is an apostolic tradition." We deny that they say this, as was shown in chapters 9 and 10. We deny that a sound consequence about Purgatory follows from it. Therefore the inference is false.

units.la: 10. Ibid. & proinde sint in poenis, non sempiternis, sed temporalibus.] Non sequitur. Nam prisci Patres id de poena sensus (vt Scholastici vocant, & intelligunt Pontificij) nunquam crediderunt. defunctos quidem aliquam experiri carentiam (vt loquuntur) boni existimauerunt, quo nomine etiam pro defunctis oratum est: sed poena sensus, id est, afflictiua ista Purgatorij eos affici minime crediderunt. vide in ca.9. & nota secunda & decima, omnino itaque falsa est consequentia a communi, vt vocant, indiuiso.
units.tr: "And so they are in punishments, not everlasting but temporal." This does not follow. The ancient Fathers never believed in the punishment of sense (as the Scholastics call it, and as the Papists understand it). They did think that the departed suffer some privation of good (as they put it), and under that name prayer has also been offered for the dead. But they by no means believed in a punishment of sense, that is, in that afflictive punishment of Purgatory. See chapter 9, notes 2 and 10. So the consequence drawn from the so-called undivided common view is entirely false.

units.la: 11. Articul. 16. Non esse necesse, vt Scriptura vbique omnia dicat.] quis hoc, quaeso, asserit? sed hoc tantum asserimus, necessarium esse, vt Scriptura omnia dicat quae sunt fidei: nec ea vbique dicat, sed alicubi, nempe vbi locus & ratio postulauerit. traditionem in causa fidei reiicimus: nusquam autem Scriptura docet Purgatorium: non ergo est de fide.
units.tr: "It is not necessary for Scripture to say everything everywhere." Who, I ask, asserts this? We assert only that it is necessary for Scripture to say all the things that pertain to faith, though not everywhere: somewhere, namely where place and reason require it. We reject tradition in matters of faith. But Scripture nowhere teaches Purgatory; therefore it is not a matter of faith.

units.la: 12. Artic. 17. in Genesi non fuisse occasionem ponendi doctrinam de Purgatorio.] Falsum: nam si vsquam fuit occasio ponendi eam, fuit in loco illo Geneseos: non ponitur autem: recte igitur ex eo silentio in contrarium concluditur.
units.tr: "In Genesis there was no occasion to set out the doctrine of Purgatory." This is false. If there was ever an occasion to set it out, it was in that passage of Genesis. But it is not set out there, and so it is rightly concluded from that silence to the contrary.

units.la: 13. Ibid. Genesis non est liber dogmatum, sed historia quaedam Patriarcharum. Vtrumque est liber Geneseos. Nā & dogma de creatione, providentia, fide, pro missionibus & minis Dei, & gratuito fœdere in Christo symbolísque eius complectitur: & Patrum exempla historiásque narrans dogmata quoque & sensum fidei cultúmque religionis illorum explicat. Quid? nónne fundamenta omnia gratiæ & fœderis diuini ex libro Genesᵉos maxime à Paulo petuntur passim? vt Rom.4.Galat.3.& 4.&c.
units.tr: "Genesis is not a book of doctrines but a certain history of the Patriarchs." Both are true of the book of Genesis. It contains the doctrine of creation, providence, faith, the promises and threats of God, and the free covenant in Christ with its signs. In narrating the examples and histories of the Fathers, it also sets out their doctrines, their sense of faith and their form of worship. Indeed, do not Paul's chief arguments for the foundations of grace and the divine covenant come again and again from the book of Genesis? See Rom. 4, Gal. 3 and 4, and so on.

units.la: Ibid. Quomodo iustificarentur homines tempore Adæ, Henoch, Noë.] Negatur. hoc enim Deus tradiderat Gen. 3. & ipse Adam aliíque Patres prædicatione fidei, sacrificiis, & toto cultu religiose professi sunt.
units.tr: "How men were justified in the time of Adam, Enoch and Noah." This is denied. For God had handed this down in Genesis 3, and Adam himself and the other Fathers professed it religiously by preaching the faith, by sacrifices and by their whole worship.

units.la: Art.18. Per illud, officiu, intelligere non solum lachrymas, sed etiam orationem & ieiunium?] quis prohibeat intelligere, nisi Hebræa veritas? nihil enim amplius dicit Moses, quàm à conspectu mortui sui, siue à præsentia, quemadmodum & Ixx. Augustino teste, ... Interpretatio illa vulgata abest à verbis Mosis longissimè. quid inde probes?
units.tr: "Does not the word officium signify not only tears but also prayer and fasting?" Who would forbid understanding it so, unless the Hebrew truth does? Moses says nothing more than "from the sight of his dead", or "from his presence", as the Seventy also render it, according to Augustine's testimony. That Vulgate rendering is far removed from the words of Moses. What do you prove by it?

units.la: Ibid. Cupierunt ossa sua deferri in terram promissionis, nisi quia ibi solum sacrificia pro defunctis facienda esse noverant?] Non propterea cupiuerunt: sed tribus de causis cupiuerunt, quarum prima ciuilis est, & duæ religiosæ. Ciuile est, mortuos, viros, præsertim magnos, in patriam suam & sepulchreta familiarica sua exportari: quod vsus communis docet. Causa religiosa est vna, vt sancti illi patres docerent fratres & posteros suos fidem suam hoc symbolo moribundi, & in eadem fide ipsos informarent: altera, vt eadem occasione etiā religiose obstringeret eos exemplo fidei, & præcepto vltimæ voluntatis, & religione iuramenti. vide Genef. 48.7. & 21. & 49. 29. & 50.24. & sequentibus.
units.tr: "Did they not wish their bones to be carried into the land of promise only because they knew that sacrifices for the dead were to be offered there alone?" They did not wish it for that reason. They wished it for three reasons, of which the first is civil and the other two religious. The civil reason is that the dead, men and especially great men, are carried back to their own country and to their family tombs, as common custom teaches. The one religious reason is that those holy fathers, at the point of death, might by this sign teach their brothers and descendants their faith and form them in the same faith. The other is that on the same occasion they might bind them religiously by the example of faith, by the precept of a last will and by the obligation of an oath. See Gen. 48:7, 21; 49:29; 50:24 and following.

units.la: 17. Art. 19. Intelligebantur pro peccatis tam viuorum quam mortuorum, vt patet ex lib. 2. Machab. cap. 12.] Negatur vtrumque, propositio, & auctoritas illius, vt supra cap. 3.
units.tr: 17. Art. 19. They were understood as made for the sins of the living as well as of the dead, as is clear from 2 Maccabees ch. 12.] Both the proposition and the authority of that text are denied, as above in ch. 3.

units.la: 18. Art. 20. Paulus autem consolari volebat eos, vt pater.] Agnosco id quidem. Sed si consolari volebat, & credebant omnes Purgatorium esse, & poenas illius, mutila profecto & imperfecta fuit consolatio, si aduersus horrorem & apprehensionem (vt loquuntur) poenarum illarum non fuisset consolatus eos quos instituerat consolari.
units.tr: 18. Art. 20. But Paul wanted to console them, as is clear.] I admit this indeed. But if he wanted to console them, and everyone believed that Purgatory and its pains exist, the consolation would surely have been maimed and imperfect, had he not also comforted, against the horror and dread (as they call it) of those pains, the very people he had set out to console.

units.la: 19. Ibid. Ponit ignem Purgatorij, & Baptismum laboriosum pro mortuis susceptum.] Negatur, & confuta-tum est supra cap. 5. & 6. & 14.
units.tr: 19. Ibid. He posits the fire of Purgatory and the laborious Baptism undertaken for the dead.] Denied, and refuted above in ch. 5, 6 and 14.

units.la: 20. Art. 21. Theophylacto, Damasceno, & ex ipso Concilio Florentino.] imo Ecclesia Graeca Purgatorium semper negauit constantissime. vide supra cap. 9. & 10.
units.tr: 20. Art. 21. From Theophylact, Damascene, and from the Council of Florence itself.] Indeed the Greek Church has always most steadfastly denied Purgatory. See above ch. 9 and 10.

units.la: 21. Ibid. de Graecis iactatur[?], quod Purgatorium negent, de particularibus hominibus intelligendum est.] Negamus ista omnia, vt supra cap. 2. nota 4. Sed res ita habet, vt nota 2. cap. 9. ostendimus. Graeci in secunda Patrum sententia subsisterunt, animas carere visione perfecta Dei: quam rem si quis Purgatorium diceret, non sunt adeo refragati. Sed Latini pedibus in tertiam sententiam (quam improbamus) abiuerunt. Demonstrant quod dicimus Graecorum verba in proemio, sive (vt Bellarmino placet) sessione prima Concilij eiusdem dicentium ad locum Pauli 1. Corinth. 3. Nam ipsum Purgatorium, non ignem, sed obscurum quendam locum ac laborum plenum esse censemus ([Greek, illegible, ~40 letters]) in quo quidem existentes anima lumine diuino priuantur (non dicit, poenas tor-mentáque perferunt) donec coadiuuante Ecclesia expientur ac liberentur. Sic ergo sentimus de Purgatorio. Postea vero amplius animum suum explicant, dicentes.: Sed in alio quoque differre videmur: ipsi namque tenemus, obnoxias animas ac (vt dicitur) mortalibus peccatis affectas, non satis perfecte in praesentia multari, sed postea quam cum suis corporibus resurrexerint, fore vt perfectissimas poenas pro suis delictis luant: quemadmodum etiam iustorum & sanctorum accidit animabus, quippe qua bono quodam imperfecte fruantur, (hoc videlicet Graecorum Purgatorium, si ita placet appellare) post vero suam resurrectionem felicitatem sibi debitam consequentur: vt Paulus inquit, & hi omnes testimonio fidei probati non acceperunt repromissionem. Vos autem non ita sentire videmini. Haec Graeci de Purgatorio, ac nihil amplius in sessione prima. In eandem sententiam dicunt illi sesione vltima: Nos, pater sanctissime, nullam ad haec respondendi facultatem habemus: tamen ex nobis ipsis proferimus, iustorum animas perfectam laureolam in coelo iam consequutas esse, at impiorum perpetuas poenas luere, medias vero in Purgatorio esse: quod quidem sive ignis, sive obscuritas, sive turbo, sive id genus aliud sit, non referre. Locum videlicet medium intelligentes, in quo non poenam sensus, id est, afflictionis experiantur defuncti, sed poenam damni (vt Scholastici distinxerunt) id est, carentiam boni & difficultatem morae, vt Tertullianus appellauit, perferunt. Atque eo sensu post multas disputationes vltro citroque habitas, in domo Imperatoris Orientis consenserunt Graeci Purgatorium esse: & in literis vnionis conuenerunt item in haec verba: Item, si vere pœnitentes in Dei charitate decesserint, antequam dignis pœnitentiæ fructibus de commissis satisfecerint & omissis, eorum animas pœnis purgatoriis post mortem purgari (pœnas damni & moræ intellexerunt) & vt a pœnis huiusmodi releuentur: prodesse eis fidelium viuorum suffragia, &c. Nihil hoc amplius disputator ex verbis Græcorum etiam in Concilio Florentino habitis probare potest: idque suo priuato nomine, non auctoritate & decreto publico annuentium ad Imperatoris importunitatem.
units.tr: 21. Ibid. What is alleged about the Greeks, that they deny Purgatory, must be understood of particular men.] We deny all of this, as above in ch. 2, note 4. But the matter stands as we showed in note 2 of ch. 9. The Greeks kept to the second opinion of the Fathers, that souls lack the perfect vision of God; if someone called this Purgatory, they would not greatly object. But the Latins, with their feet, moved over to the third opinion (which we reject). The words of the Greeks, spoken in the preface or (as Bellarmine prefers) in the first session of that same Council, on the passage of 1 Corinthians 3, demonstrate what we say: Indeed we judge that Purgatory itself is not fire, but a certain obscure place full of toil ([Greek, illegible]) in which souls, while they are there, are deprived of the divine light (it does not say that they endure punishments and torments) until they are cleansed and freed with the help of the Church. This is how we think about Purgatory. Afterwards they explain their view more fully, saying: But we seem to differ in another point as well: we hold that souls liable to, and (as it is said) affected by, mortal sins are not punished fully in the present, but that after they have risen again with their bodies they will pay the most perfect penalties for their offences, just as it also happens to the souls of the righteous and the saints, who enjoy a certain good imperfectly (this, namely, is the Greeks' Purgatory, if you are pleased to call it so), but after their resurrection they attain the happiness due to them, as Paul says: "and all these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promise." But you do not seem to think this way. These are the Greeks' words on Purgatory, and nothing more in the first session. To the same effect they speak in the last session: We, most holy father, have no power to answer these things; yet we ourselves declare that the souls of the righteous have already obtained the perfect crown in heaven, but that the souls of the wicked suffer eternal punishments, and that the intermediate souls are in Purgatory; whether this is fire, or darkness, or a whirlwind, or any other such thing, makes no difference. They evidently mean an intermediate place, in which the departed do not undergo the punishment of sense, that is, of affliction, but endure the punishment of loss (as the Schoolmen distinguished it), that is, the lack of good and the difficulty of delay, as Tertullian called it. And in that sense, after many disputations held back and forth in the house of the Eastern Emperor, the Greeks agreed that there is a Purgatory; and in the terms of union they likewise agreed in these words: Likewise, if truly penitent persons have died in the love of God before they have made satisfaction with worthy fruits of repentance for what they committed and omitted, their souls are cleansed after death by purgatorial pains (they understood the punishments of loss and of delay) and are relieved from such pains; the suffrages of the living faithful profit them, etc. A disputant can prove nothing more from the words of the Greeks, even those spoken at the Council of Florence; and that was said in their own private name, not by authority and public decree of men consenting under the Emperor's importunity.

units.la: Non potuit Purgatorium ignorare, aut negare, cum tam aperte orationem afferat pro defunctorum peccatis. ] Non sequitur, vt ante docuimus nota secunda, capite decimo. Agit enim Dionysius ex Græcorum sensu, quem proxime expressimus. Quod autem dicit, ideo orari, quia illi per merita huius vitæ dignifacti sunt, quibus preces viuentium prodesse sent, plurimum fallitur, nec bene ad verba eius videtur attendisse. Dionysium Græce dicentem, si placet, audiamus. αὐτὶ δὲ αὐτὰ γνωςάσω, καὶ ἀν- ἀνλίαν ὁ χυς ἀ ἀ δὲ ἀ ἀγαςάσω ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ ἀ [illegible, ~400 letters]. id est ad verbum fere: Petit autem ista fieri, & dare eis, qui sancte vixerunt sanctas illas compensationes: tum ad diuinam imitationem optima specie efformans, aliorumque dona, (id est, quæ in aliis sunt) vt propria gratia beneficia expetens: tum etiam quod illas quoque non mendaces promissiones sciat futuras: vtque iis qui adsunt expresse demonstret, ea qua ab ipso fecun-
units.tr: The author could not have ignored or denied Purgatory, since Dionysius so plainly brings forward prayer for the sins of the dead. It does not follow, as I showed earlier in note two of chapter ten. Dionysius is speaking in the Greek sense that I have just set out. But when he says that they are prayed for because they were made worthy through the merits of this life, and so the prayers of the living could benefit them, he is greatly mistaken and does not seem to have attended closely to his words. Let us hear Dionysius speaking in Greek, if you please. [The Greek text is too garbled in the scan to reproduce.] That is, very nearly word for word: he asks that these things be done and given to those who lived holily, those holy compensations; he shapes them in the best form for the sake of divine imitation, and asks for the gifts of others (that is, what is in others) as benefits of his own grace; and he also knows that these promises are not false, and he clearly shows to those present that the things sought in the sacred law will certainly come to pass for those who have been perfected to the manner of divine life. All things are for the teaching of the living [διδασκαλικά], not aids for the dead [βοηθήματα]: they are instructions and consolations for the living, not help for the dead.

units.la: L1 iij dum legem sacram expetuntur, omnino eventura iis qui ad divinæ vitæ modum fuerint consummati. Omnia viventibus sunt διδασκαλικά, non defunctis βοηθη-ματα[?], institutiones & consolationes viventium, non mortuorum subsidia.
units.tr: (Continuation of the Greek and of the argument as above; the sense is that all these things are instruction and consolation for the living, not support for the dead.)

units.la: 23. Artic. 23. Non dubium est, prodesse oratio-nem defunctis. ] De his omnibus Augustini locis diximus supra capite decimo, nota 22. & 23. & 45. & 49. & 50. quàm male adducantur in hanc sententiam.
units.tr: 23. Article 23. "There is no doubt that prayer benefits the dead." I have already spoken of all these passages of Augustine above, in chapter ten, notes 22, 23, 45, 49 and 50, and shown how wrongly they are brought forward for this opinion.

units.la: 24. Art. 24. Quomodo, quaso, exponemus: constat, & non dubium est, per illa: incredibile non est, & forsan verum est? ] Nullo modo: quia res diversæ sunt quas Augustinus enunciat: inciviliter est autem diversum exponi per diversum. Nam quum Augustinus dicit, constat, non dubium est, dicit de oratione pro mortuis, quos Patres credebant nondum frui visione Dei, sed in sinu Abrahæ versari plenitudinem gloriæ exspectantes, atque ad eam anhelantes sine ullo sensu mali Purgatorii, aut cuiusquam alterius, ut in caput 9. & 16. ostendimus: quum autem dicit, incredibile non est, & forsan verum est, de illa opinione Purgatorii dicit, quam tum invehebant multi humanitatis specie, & Augustinus disputationum rixosarum pro sua modestia fugiens in medio relinquebat, quamvis non dissimulato plane sensu cogitationis suæ. Falsa itaque sunt omnia sequentia, ut quæ superstruuntur falsæ interpretationi illius. vide supra in caput 10. nota 49. & 50.
units.tr: 24. Art. 24. How, I ask, shall we explain: "it is established and not doubtful" by those words: "it is not incredible, and perhaps is true"?] In no way: for the things Augustine states are different, and it is unfair to explain one thing by another different thing. When Augustine says "it is established, it is not doubtful," he speaks of prayer for the dead, whom the Fathers believed did not yet enjoy the vision of God, but dwelt in Abraham's bosom awaiting the fullness of glory and longing for it, without any sense of the evil of Purgatory or of any other suffering, as we showed in chapters 9 and 16. When he says "it is not incredible, and perhaps is true," he speaks of that opinion about Purgatory which many then put forward under the appearance of humanity, and which Augustine, in his moderation avoiding quarrelsome disputes, left undecided, though without wholly concealing the drift of his thought. Therefore everything that follows is false, as it is built on a false interpretation of his words. See above in chapter 10, notes 49 and 50.

units.la: 25. Art. 25. Ideo rectè Augustinus dicit, posse quæri, & nunquam forte inveniri, &c. ] Negamus ista, non solùm Augustino auctore ibidem, sed etiam ipso Bellarmino teste, qui aliam plane solutionem adfert supra cap. 10. vide in eundem locum nota 49. & 50.
units.tr: 25. Art. 25. Therefore Augustine rightly says that it can be asked, and perhaps never found out, etc.] We deny this, not only on Augustine's authority in that place, but also on the testimony of Bellarmine himself, who brings forward an entirely different solution above in chapter 10. See on the same passage note 49 and 50.

units.la: 26. Art. 26. Ad quintum supra responsum est.] & responsio item confutata est supra toto cap.12.
units.tr: 26. Art. 26. The fifth point has been answered above.] And that answer too has been refuted throughout the whole of chapter 12 above.

units.la: DE CIRCUNSTANTIIS PURGATORII, LIBER SECUNDUS.
units.tr: On the Circumstances of Purgatory, Book Two.

units.la: IN CAPUT I.
units.tr: On Chapter I.

units.la: I. ART. I.
units.tr: Article 1.

units.la: DEMONSTRAVIMUS hactenus Purgatorium esse: nunc de circumstantiis Purgatorii,] Vulgatum est in Scholis dictum, non entis non esse accidentia. Purgatorium esse negauimus, & confutauimus: ergo & accidentia vel circumstantias eius ullas negamus esse. Unica a nobis est litura totius libri Bellarminei istius.
units.tr: We have demonstrated hitherto that Purgatory exists; now concerning the circumstances of Purgatory, It is a saying commonly repeated in the schools that accidents do not belong to a non-entity. We have denied and refuted that Purgatory exists, so we also deny that it has any accidents or circumstances. This is the one stroke of the pen we have made against this whole book of Bellarmine's.

units.la: 2. Art.3. Sed videtur esse non eius solum, sed multorū[?] Patrum.]Horum vero omnium sententiam Bellarminus postea interpretatur benignius articul. 7. & nos in eum locum videbimus.
units.tr: 2. Art. 3. But it seems to be the view not only of it but of many Fathers. Bellarmine later interprets the opinion of all these men more kindly, in article 7, and we shall look at that passage then.

units.la: 3. Art.6. Nam in Concilio Florentino seff. ult. definitum est, ] huius Concilij auctoritatem in hac causa iustam negamus esse: rem priore libro confutavimus, cap.2.nota 4. & cap.15.nota 21.
units.tr: 3. Art. 6. For at the Council of Florence, last session, it was defined, We deny that the authority of this Council is just in this matter. We refuted the point in the earlier book, chapter 2, note 4, and chapter 15, note 21.

units.la: 4. Ibid. Constanter Augustinus docet lib. de civit. Dei, cap. 16. vide supra in libro primo, cap. 10. nota 44.
units.tr: 4. Ibid. Augustine teaches constantly in the book On the City of God, chapter 16. See above in book one, chapter 10, note 44.

units.la: 5. Art. 7. Origene excepto, cuius verba in Homil. 14. in Lucam non patiuntur commodam expositionem. ] Nempe si verba accipiuntur ut sonant. Sed mihi videtur Origenes per resurrectionem ex mortuis significare primam resurrectionem: illam videlicet spiritualem nostram, quam regeneratione assequimur: & docere baptismum Christi nobis esse necessarium: non in regeneratione solum, quum ex mortuis resurgimus in Spiritu, verum etiam post regenerationem & resurrectionem hanc ex mortuis, id est, postquam suscitati fuimus, ut ambulemus in novitate vitæ, Rom. 6. demonstrant hunc sensum adiuncta omnia in eo loco Origenis.
units.tr: 5. Art. 7. Origen excepted, whose words in Homily 14 on Luke do not allow a convenient explanation. Namely, if the words are taken as they sound. But it seems to me that Origen by "resurrection from the dead" means the first resurrection, that spiritual one of ours which we attain by regeneration, and that he teaches that Christ's baptism is necessary for us, not only in regeneration, when we rise from the dead in the Spirit, but also after regeneration and this resurrection from the dead, that is, after we have been raised up to walk in newness of life (Rom. 6). All the accompanying material in that passage of Origen shows this sense.

units.la: 6. Ibid. Fatendum est, omnes sanctos, Christo excepto, per ignem transire, ] imo & Christus per ignem transiuit divini judicij perpessione mortis, & pij omnes communiter ignem divinorum judiciorum subeant in hac vita & morte necesse est: quo Patres illi respexerunt.
units.tr: 6. Ibid. It must be admitted that all the saints, Christ excepted, pass through fire, Indeed Christ too passed through fire, by enduring the death of divine judgment. All the godly must undergo the fire of divine judgments in this life and in death; this is what those Fathers had in view.

units.la: 7. Art. 8. Ut transeant per Purgatorium materialiter, non formaliter. ] Negamus istam interpretationem: id sibi noluerunt Patres.
units.tr: 7. Art. 8. That they pass through Purgatory materially, not formally. We deny this interpretation. The Fathers did not intend this.

units.la: 8. Ibid. Habent enim aliquid in se Dei, quod vim flamflamma repellat.] de igne quidem agit Lactantius eo in loco; sed non de Purgatorio Pontificio antecedente resurrectione vltimumq; iudicium Dei. vide supra lib. 1. cap. 10. nota 66. itemque de loco Ambrosij ibidem nota 43. Ruperti authoritatem reiicimus.
units.tr: 8. Ibid. For they have in themselves something of God which repels the flame of fire. Lactantius in that place does speak of fire, but not of the Papist Purgatory which precedes the resurrection and the last judgment of God. See above, book 1, chapter 10, note 66, and likewise the passage of Ambrose in the same place, note 43. We reject the authority of Rupert.

units.la: 9. Art.9. alios vero magis minusve exuri, prout plus minusve materia combustibilis afferebant.] Furfæus ille, si non dormiens, saltem vigilans somniauit μελαγχολῶν[?]. negamus ista, & conclusionem sequentem.
units.tr: 9. Art. 9. others are burned more or less, according as the combustible matter supplied more or less. That Furfaeus dreamed, if not asleep then at least awake, being melancholy [μελαγχολῶν]. We deny these claims and the conclusion that follows.

units.la: 10. Art. 16. damnatos puniendos quidem, sed tamen citra condignum.] de hac exceptione Bellarminus ipse viderit.
units.tr: 10. Art. 16. the damned are indeed to be punished, but not up to what they deserve. Bellarmine himself must see to this exception.

units.la: 11. Art 24. vt indicet se loqui solum de piis Christianis.] vide supra cap.10. nota 52. & 62. in librum primum. Nam hæ solutiones, quas Bellarminus adfert, abludunt à mente Hieronymi.
units.tr: 11. Art. 24. so that he indicates he is speaking only of pious Christians. See above, book 1, chapter 10, notes 52 and 62. For the solutions Bellarmine brings forward here are at odds with the mind of Jerome.

units.la: 12. Artic. 26. multa requirit ad iustificationem impij praeter eleemosynā.] ambigue dictum. Nam ad iustificationem impij coram Deo præstandam nihil requiritur nisi iustitia Christi iustificantis impium, Rom 3. quam Christianus sentit & prehendit fide: sed ad iustificationem testandam coram Deo & hominibus desiderantur multa. Sed de hac re in tomo 4. Quamobrem sequentia nihil ad rem.
units.tr: 12. Art. 26. It requires many things for the justification of the impious, beyond almsgiving. This is an ambiguous statement. For the justification of the impious before God requires nothing but the righteousness of Christ justifying the impious (Rom. 3), which the Christian perceives and grasps by faith. But for justification to be attested before God and men, many things are required. On this matter see volume 4. Therefore what follows has nothing to do with the point.
