units.la: 13. Art.29.(@) aliis locis supra citatis.] nempe lib. 1. cap. 5. & 7. Nos vero sententiam istam veram negamus esse, & distinctiones probationéf-que illius.
units.tr: 13. Art. 29. in the other places cited above. Namely book 1, chapters 5 and 7. We, however, deny that this view is true, along with its distinctions and proofs.

units.la: IN CAP. II.
units.tr: On Chapter II.

units.la: 1. Art.1. vide librum Lutheri de Purgatorio, quem Ioannes Eckius refellit. ] hæc omnia nihil ad Lutherum, cum ea reuocauerit postea quàm melius fuit ex verbo Dei & Scripturis sacris institutus; vt in lib.1.cap.2. ostendimus: quanto minus ad nos, qui ipsos tragelaphos iamdiu Scripturæ spongia deleuimus.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. See Luther's book on Purgatory, which John Eck refutes. All of this has nothing to do with Luther, since he retracted these views afterwards, when he had been better instructed from the Word of God and the holy Scriptures, as we showed in book 1, chapter 2. How much less do they concern us, who long ago wiped those very goat-stags off the page with the sponge of Scripture.

units.la: 2. Art.3. quare loquitur de opere meritorio, vt exponit Hieronymus. ] atqui de opere meritorio Hieronymus nullum verbum. Agit Sapiens de opere personæ, quæ vbi soluta est per mortem, alia in conditione est plane, nec harum est actionum consors quæ in hac vita obtinent.
units.tr: 2. Art. 3. wherefore he speaks of a meritorious work, as Jerome explains. Yet Jerome says nothing at all about a meritorious work. The Wise Man speaks of the work of a person who, once released by death, is plainly in another condition, and does not share in those actions which obtain in this life.

units.la: 3. Ibid. complectitur omnia loca, ad quæ descendebant omnes homines ante Christi resurrectionem. ] id est (vt cum Irenæo dicam) omnia inuisibilia loca animarum. De locis autem illis quæ ante resurrectionem fuerunt, in controuersia seq. videbitur.
units.tr: 3. Ibid. it embraces all the places to which all men descended before Christ's resurrection. That is, as I would put it with Irenaeus, all the invisible places of souls. Concerning those places which existed before the resurrection, we shall see in the following controversy.

units.la: 4. Art.4. quæ non potest de bona fieri mala, nec mala de bona. ] de hoc loco Ecclesiæ videndum supra cap.12. lib.1. nota 3. & 4.
units.tr: 4. Art. 4. what cannot be made evil from good, nor good from evil. On this statement of the Church see above, book 1, chapter 12, notes 3 and 4.

units.la: 5. Art.7. per operari, facere opera meritoria significari. ] hoc nemo illorum ita dixit. verù autem sensum in nota 2. expressimus: opera illa, mi homo, sunt opera viæ, non meriti: vt & sequente articulo exponitur.
units.tr: 5. Art. 7. that by "to work" is meant to perform meritorious works. None of them said this. We have set out the true sense in note 2: those works, my friend, are works of the way, not of merit, as is also explained in the following article.

units.la: 6. Artic. 10. per depositionem à villicatione mortem, per non posse amplius villicare, non posse amplius mereri & lucrari. ] primùm negatur interpretatio. Nam deponi à villicatione non est mori, sed exauctorari & dimitti; & non posse amplius villicare nihil aliud est quàm non posse amplius certa vocationis conscientia servire Domino. Am-brosius autem neque in hanc, neque in alteram par-tem attingit horum verborum interpretationem Theophylactus nouam allegoriam solus induit illi parabolæ. Nam Augustinus & Hieronymus aliter exponunt. Sed placent Bellarmino vana & falsa no-minum crepitacula. Sed hæc, ut diximus, nihil ad nos.
units.tr: 6. Art. 10. by deposition from stewardship is meant death; by no longer being able to act as steward, no longer being able to merit and gain. First, the interpretation is denied. To be deposed from stewardship is not to die, but to be dismissed and discharged. And not being able any longer to act as steward is nothing other than not being able any longer to serve the Lord with a sure conscience of one's calling. Ambrose touches neither side of the interpretation of these words; Theophylact alone devises a new allegory for that parable. For Augustine and Jerome explain it otherwise. But Bellarmine is pleased with vain and false rattles of names. Yet these things, as we have said, have nothing to do with us.

units.la: 7. Art.13. Nota, Lutherum non posse vocari Christianum qualemcunque, ] Contrà verò Christiane lector quisquis es, nota 1. Lutherum illa scripsisse quum adhuc recens esset ex monacho; eaque omnia post biennium aut triennium, ubi melius edoctus fuit, eiusdem prout in præfatione operum suorum Lectorem obsecrat ut iudicium faciat de scriptis suis. 2. Bellarminum hic non facere Christiani officium, qui errores à Luthero abdicatos eiuratósque[?] tamdiu non dubitet reponere contra veritatis & charitatis Christianæ leges. Quod enim Lutherus damnauit, cur in ipso damnes? hæ maleuo-lentiæ & maledicentiæ sunt partes.
units.tr: 7. Art. 13. Note that Luther cannot be called a Christian of any sort. On the contrary, Christian reader, whoever you are, note first that Luther wrote those things while he was still fresh from being a monk, and that he afterwards retracted all of them, after two or three years, when he had been better taught; as he begs the reader in the preface to his works to judge his writings accordingly. Second, Bellarmine here does not perform the office of a Christian, since he does not hesitate so long to revive errors which Luther renounced and abjured, against the laws of truth and Christian charity. For why do you condemn in him what Luther himself condemned? These are the marks of ill will and slander.

units.la: 8. Artic. 16. igitur nunquam liberabuntur. ] Lutherus illa de modo potentiæ animarum in Purgatorio degentium, non de actu ipso enunciauerat, quò iste verba Lutheri rapit elenchi ignoratione. Sed hæc Lutherus ipse confutauit. Valeant ista, quæ neque ad Ecclesias Christi, neque ad ipsum Lutherum (deposuit enim) pertinent. Et quàm bene sequens caput in eadem arena disputator occupat! io triumphe.
units.tr: 8. Art. 16. therefore they will never be freed. Luther had stated those things about the manner of the power of souls dwelling in Purgatory, not about the act itself; Bellarmine snatches Luther's words through the fallacy of ignoring the point at issue. But Luther himself refuted these. Let those things be, since they pertain neither to the Churches of Christ nor to Luther himself, for he has set them aside. And how well the disputant in the following chapter occupies the same arena! Hurrah, what a triumph!

units.la: IN CAP. III.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER III.

units.la: 1. Art.1.Superest argumenta soluere. ] At nobis nihil commune est cum istis argumentis & solutionibus, qui Purgatorium negamus simpliciter, ut postea Lutherus fecit.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. There remains to resolve the arguments. ] We have nothing in common with these arguments and solutions, since we simply deny Purgatory, as Luther later did.

units.la: 2. Art.4. Nulla enim est caritas simpliciter imperfe-cta. ] paradoxum.
units.tr: 2. Art. 4. For there is no charity that is simply imperfect. ] A paradox.

units.la: 3. Ibid. qui seruat verbum eius, vere in hoc caritas Dei perfecta est. ] duplex æquiuocatio. Primùm enim charitas Dei in hoc loco non est ea qua nos prosequimur Deum, sed ea est qua nos prosequitur Deus, ut exponitur principio capitis 3. deinde vero verbum τετελειωμένον[?] aliud est quàm τετελειωμένον[?]. Hoc enim significat perfectum vel consummatum esse: illud vero consecratum esse & sanctificatum. Sensus autem est, charitatem illam qua Deus diligit suos, licet semper in se habeat sanctimoniam perfectissimam, in eo tamen qui obseruat præcepta Dei esse sanctificatam, & illum in ea sanctifi-catum per communicationem Spiritus Christi in ipso habitantis. Ex æquiuocatione nihil sequitur.
units.tr: 3. Ibid. He who keeps his word, in him truly the charity of God is perfected. ] This is a double equivocation. First, the charity of God in this passage is not the love with which we pursue God, but the love with which God pursues us, as is explained at the beginning of chapter 3. Second, the word τετελειωμένον [perfected] is one thing, and the word τετελειωμένον [perfected] is another. For the one means to be perfect or complete, while the other means to be consecrated and sanctified. The sense is that the charity by which God loves his own, although it always has in itself the most perfect holiness, is nonetheless sanctified in the one who keeps God's commandments, and that person is sanctified in it through the communication of the Spirit of Christ dwelling in him. Nothing follows from an equivocation.

units.la: 4. Art.7. animas Purgatorij, quatenus sunt imperfectæ) negamus vllas esse animas Purgatorij: proinde etiam negamus attributa.
units.tr: 4. Art. 7. the souls of Purgatory, insofar as they are imperfect)] We deny that there are any souls of Purgatory, and therefore we also deny the attributes.

units.la: 5. Ibid. in genere gratiæ, ut fiat homo aptior ad magis merendum. ] negamus ista, & tomo 4. confutabimus, volente Domino.
units.tr: 5. Ibid. in the kind of grace, so that the man becomes fitter to merit more. ] We deny these things, and, the Lord willing, we will refute them in volume 4.

units.la: 6. Art.8. reatus poenæ, pro quo satisfaciendum sit. ] has propositiones singulas negamus, nec probari possunt.
units.tr: 6. Art. 8. the debt of punishment, for which satisfaction must be made. ] We deny each of these propositions, and they cannot be proved.

units.la: 7. Ibid. sed per opera satisfactoria, quæ ipsa caritas imperat. ] & hanc distinctionem negamus, cùm Petrus indistincte simpliciterque affirmet; & operum satisfactionem, ut ante.
units.tr: 7. Ibid. but through satisfactory works, which charity itself commands. ] We also deny this distinction, since Peter affirms without distinction and simply; and we deny the satisfaction of works, as before.

units.la: 8. Art.9. Si non ieiuno deo, certe patiendo in Purgatorio.] & haec negamus, & sequentia omnia, quae ex hypothesi dicuntur Purgatorij: nam τὸ ἀρχῆς[?] petitur.
units.tr: 8. Art. 9. If I do not fast for God, certainly I suffer in Purgatory.] We deny this and all that follows, which is said from the hypothesis of Purgatory, for the point at issue [τὸ ἀρχῆς, begging the question] is being assumed.

units.la: 9. Art.10. Christus qui timuit poenas, & ex eo timore sudauit sanguinem] non ex timore sudauit solum, sed ex poenarum sensu, quas hauriebat de calice irae Dei Patris sui: ut controu. 2.lib.4. demonstrauimus.
units.tr: 9. Art. 10. Christ, who feared the punishments, and from that fear sweated blood] He sweated not only from fear, but from the sense of the punishments which he drank from the cup of the wrath of his Father, as we demonstrated in controversy 2, book 4.

units.la: 10. Ibid. non audet peccare ne damnetur, peccatum ut si non timeret damnari. negatur haec tota interpretatio atque distinctio; nam Ioannes agit de metu iudicij Dei: cuius ante meminerat proxime praecedente versu. Hoc ipsum demonstrant verba Apostoli 1. Ioan. 4. Nam postquam dixisset versu 17.pe[?] hoc adimpletur charitas nobiscum, ut fiduciam habeamus in die iudicij, quod qualis ille est, talis & nos sumus in hoc mundo: illico ad hanc ipsam fiduciam respicies subiicit ex contrario, metus non est in charitate, integra charitas sine perfecta foras eiicit metum, &c. quid est autem metus iudicij qui fiduciae aduersatur, si non est & metus poenae?
units.tr: 10. Ibid. he does not dare to sin, lest he be condemned, as if he did not fear to be condemned. This whole interpretation and distinction is denied; for John is speaking of the fear of God's judgment, which he had mentioned in the verse immediately preceding. The words of the Apostle in 1 John 4 show this very thing. For after he had said in verse 17: by this charity is made perfect with us, that we may have confidence in the day of judgment, because as he is, so also are we in this world, he immediately sets over against this very confidence the contrary: there is no fear in charity, but perfect charity casts out fear, etc. But what is the fear of judgment that opposes confidence, if it is not also the fear of punishment?

units.la: 11. Art.11. non posse inueniri aliquid ita perfectum, quod non debeat dici imperfectum respectu perfectionis gloriae.] dicendum fuerat, respectu perfectionis diuinę:nam alioqui coelestes Angeli respectu perfectionis gloriae quo iure dicantur imperfecti, qui gloriam suam perfectam obtinent?
units.tr: 11. Art. 11. that nothing can be found so perfect that it ought not to be called imperfect with respect to the perfection of glory.] It should have been said: with respect to the divine perfection. For otherwise, by what right are the heavenly angels called imperfect with respect to the perfection of glory, since they obtain their glory in its perfection?

units.la: 12. Ibid. tamen illud ipsum erit simpliciter perfectum.] sed aequiuoce, si cum Deo illud comparaue-ris.
units.tr: 12. Ibid. yet that very thing will be simply perfect.] But only equivocally, if you compare it with God.

units.la: 13. Ibid. se perfectum dicit absolute[?] & tamen imperfectum comparatione facta ad beatos. ] nihil se-quitur ex homonymia. Apostolus enim quū dicit, non quod ia[?] perfectus sim, nō loquitur de perfectione beatitudinis, id est beneficij gloriæ siue præmij, sed de perfectione officij siue operis, quo laborabat piè vt apprehenderet Christum & prosequebatur eum:quum vero dicit, quicunque ergo perfecti sumus, non absolute perfectum se dicit, quod Bellarminus somniat, sed comparate de perfectione maiore loquitur secundum gradum quàm aliorum sit, non de perfectione plena secundum statum : quemadmodum adultus secundum gradum est puero perfectior. Quapropter eum locū rectè vertit Beza, quoquot itaque adulti sumus, &c. Alioqui recte veteres eadem mente definiuerunt, quod paucis verbis contraxit Theophylactus; perfecti est, inquit, seipsum non existimare perfectum: hæc enim est perfectio, non confidere[?]: seruata nimirū graduum in ætate nostra comparatione. Nam imperitus puer vel omnia præsumit de se; adultus vero periculo facto infirmitatis suæ, eo perfectus est comparatò, quòd conscius est imperfectionis suæ; & ad iustam perfectionem tendit.
units.tr: 13. Ibid. he calls himself absolutely perfect, and yet imperfect when compared with the blessed. ] Nothing follows from a homonymy. For when the Apostle says: not that I am already perfect, he is not speaking of the perfection of blessedness, that is, of the benefit of glory or reward, but of the perfection of office or work, by which he labored piously to lay hold of Christ and pursued him. But when he says: as many of us therefore as are perfect, he does not call himself absolutely perfect, as Bellarmine dreams; rather he speaks comparatively, of a greater perfection, according to a degree higher than that of others, not of full perfection according to state. Just as an adult is more perfect in degree than a child. Therefore Beza rightly translates that passage: as many of us therefore as are adults, etc. Otherwise the ancients rightly defined the same meaning, which Theophylact summed up in a few words: it is perfection, he says, not to think oneself perfect; for this is perfection, not to be confident, the comparison of degrees in our age being of course preserved. For an inexperienced child presumes everything about himself; but an adult, having tested his own weakness by experience, is in this respect perfect, because he is aware of his imperfection and strives toward true perfection.

units.la: 14. Art. 12. animas Purgatorij non esse in via, sed in termino, quantum ad gratiæ augmentum;] negatur hæc distinctio, & totum simile: nam τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς[?] petitur, quod centies negatum est.
units.tr: 14. Art. 12. the souls of Purgatory are not in the way, but at the goal, as regards the increase of grace;] This distinction is denied, and the whole comparison with it; for [τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς, begging the question] is being assumed, which has been denied a hundred times.

units.la: 15. Ibid. eos qui non dant operam ut proficiant, facile impelli posse a diabolo & mundo in casum, &c.] hæc falsa verborum Bernardi interpretatio. Nam quum dicit Bernardus, in via Dei non progredi esse retrogredi, propositio est (ut Aristoteles vocat) ὑπο-ἀξίωμα[?] affirmans id quod est: Bellarminus vero quū exponit eum qui nō progreditur, impelli posse, &c. ἐξ ὑπάρχοντος ἐνδεχομένως contingenter enuncians id quod esse reipsa dicitur. Non est autem disputator nescius, has duas enunciationes non esse conuertibiles, retrogreditur, & potest retrogredi: item impellitur, & potest impelli: nam prius actionis & passionis est, posterius vero potentiae passiuae, quae duo inter se toto genere differunt.
units.tr: 15. Ibid. those who do not take pains to make progress can easily be driven by the devil and the world into a fall, etc.] This is a false interpretation of the words of Bernard. For when Bernard says: not to advance in the way of God is to go backward, it is a proposition (as Aristotle calls it) of the kind that affirms what is the case. But when Bellarmine explains that one who does not advance can be driven, etc., he is stating contingently [ἐξ ὑπάρχοντος ἐνδεχομένως] what is said to be actual. Yet the author is not unaware that these two statements are not convertible: one who goes backward, and one who can go backward; likewise one who is driven, and one who can be driven. For the former belongs to action and passion, while the latter belongs to passive potency, and these two differ from each other in their whole genus.

units.la: 16. Art.13. habetur enim in Graeco δύναμις μου, id est, virtus mea.] suppositio hoc casu quem negamus, esse Purgatorium; hac tamen responsione non soluitur obiectio: nam Deus non dicit, virtus mea solum, vt quod virtutis est humanae, licet infirmae, excludat. Potest autem secundum Pontificios utraque virtus concurrere, diuina, & humana meritoria in infirmitate ipsius. quod si in hac vita fit, vt illi volunt, quanto magis in illa possunt vt coordinatae concurrere, vbi plus virium, minus impedimentorum habere censentur defunctorum animae? haec omnia ex Pontificiorum hypothesi, vt suo ipsos iumento perire doceatur: nam alioqui, quod ad nos, vel solam meritorum opinionem meditationemque, vt aduersantem beneficio Christi, refugimus.
units.tr: 16. Art. 13. For in the Greek it is δύναμις μου, that is, my power.] The supposition in this case, which we deny, is that there is Purgatory; yet the objection is not resolved by this answer. For God does not say "my power" only, so as to exclude whatever belongs to human power, however weak. Moreover, according to the Papists both powers may concur, the divine and the human meritorious power in his weakness. If this happens in this life, as they wish, how much more can they concur in an orderly way in that life, where the souls of the departed are judged to have more strength and fewer hindrances? All these things are from the hypothesis of the Papists, so that they may be taught to perish by their own yoke. For otherwise, as far as we are concerned, we reject even the mere opinion and meditation of merit as opposed to the benefit of Christ.

units.la: 17. Ibid. sed quia separatur a terra, & plumbo, & similibus.] negatur distinctio tota, simile autem quid iuuat? nam certe aurum remotione scoriae non modo fit lucidius, sed etiam melius, quia probius & purius.
units.tr: 17. Ibid. but because it is separated from earth, and lead, and similar things.] The whole distinction is denied. But what good does a similar thing do? For surely gold becomes not only brighter but also better, by the removal of dross, because it is more upright and purer.

units.la: 18. Art.14. salsissimum esse illud principium Lutheri in rebus permanentibus, solumque habere locum in successiuis,] illudit ex homonymia: nam absorberi dicuntur res duobus modis, consumptione & consumatione [?]. ipsarum. Res pereuntes atque successivae consum-ptione absorbentur; res vero permanentes & metaphysicae consummatione: perficiuntur enim in principio suo, & tum demum consummatae atque perfectae sunt, quum in eo consistunt & unione plena conquiescunt. Disputator autem ad priorem modum restringit absorbendi verbum, cum Lutherus de posteriore dicat, & simili ducto ex priore modo rem illustrare voluerit. Nam communis est utrisque rebus absorptio, quod Lutherus dicit; particularis vero absorptionis in utrisque modus, quod reticet. Quamobrem sequentia absurda vere absurda sunt. De merito & remuneratione videndum controversia seq. & tomo 4.
units.tr: 18. Art. 14. that principle of Luther about permanent things is most salty, and holds a place only in successive things,] He mocks through a homonymy. For things are said to be absorbed in two ways: by consumption and by consummation. Perishing and successive things are absorbed by consumption; but permanent and metaphysical things by consummation. For they are perfected in their beginning, and are then at last consummated and perfected when they remain in it and rest in full union. But the disputant restricts the word "absorb" to the former way, although Luther speaks of the latter, and wished to illustrate the matter by a comparison drawn from the former. For absorption is common to both kinds of things, as Luther says; but the particular mode of absorption in each he passes over in silence. Therefore the absurdities that follow are truly absurd. On merit and reward, see the following controversy and volume 4.

units.la: 19. Art.15. Ad quartum iam est responsum] idemque confutatum supra nota 2.
units.tr: 19. Art. 15. Now it has been answered to the fourth] And the same has been refuted above, in note 2.

units.la: 20. Art.18. tolerare, quatenus considerant ut instrumenta per qua purgantur,] responsionem hanc totam negamus, quia falsa hypothesi & ante confutata nititur, nec probari potest. Sequentia itaque nihil ad illam. & nos agnoscimus quae de tolerandis poenis adferuntur, Purgatorias illas non agnoscimus. Quaecunque autem sic Lutherus argumentatus est, fecit ex Pontificiorum hypothesi, non affirmans, sed supponens.
units.tr: 20. Art. 18. to endure, insofar as they regard them as instruments by which they are purified,] We deny this whole answer, because it rests on a false hypothesis already refuted above, and it cannot be proved. The following points therefore have nothing to do with it. We acknowledge what is said about enduring punishments, but we do not acknowledge those punishments as purgatorial. Whatever Luther argued in this way, he did from the hypothesis of the Papists, not by affirming but by supposing.

units.la: 21. Art. 23. & non in Purgatorio, sed in inferno essent.] has omneis solutiones, quia ex hypothesi sunt, & τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς [?] petunt, & probari nullo modo possunt, negamus plane.
units.tr: 21. Art. 23. and would be not in Purgatory but in hell.] All these solutions, because they rest on the hypothesis and beg the question [τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς], and cannot be proved in any way, we flatly deny.

units.la: 22. Art. 25. solum pro tempore huius vita constituit acceptare bona opera ad meritum, vel demeritum.] Omnia haec quae tu in obiectione, tu in solutionibus demerito nostro adferuntur, negamus: nihil ad nos.
units.tr: 22. Art. 25. only for the time of this life has it determined to accept good works for merit or demerit.] All the things you bring forward in the objection, and in the solutions, we deny as applied to our demerit. They have nothing to do with us.

units.la: 23. Art. 26. quia deest esse viator, nihil amplius meruit.] de hac quaestione diximus controuersiæ 2. lib. vltimo, sub finem.
units.tr: 23. Art. 26. because one who is no longer a wayfarer merits nothing more.] We discussed this question in the last book of the second controversy, near the end.

units.la: 24. Art. 27. non mereri, sed solum impetrare ex meritis praeteritis,] merita negamus, proinde & impetrationem ex meritis.
units.tr: 24. Art. 27. not to merit, but only to obtain by impetration from past merits,] We deny merits, and therefore also impetration from merits.

units.la: 25. Articu. 28. in Purgatorio nullum posse esse meritum nec essentialis, nec accidentalis praemij:] haec omnia nihil ad nos, qui & Purgatorium negamus, & meritum.
units.tr: 25. Art. 28. that in Purgatory there can be no merit, neither essential nor accidental reward:] All these things have nothing to do with us, who deny both Purgatory and merit.

units.la: 26. Ibidem. est remissorius, licet non per modum meriti proprie dicti, sed per modum contrarij tollentis suum contrarium.] negatur remissorium esse: tum vt fingamus remissorium esse, quod falsum, negatur distinctionem esse ex mente Thomae. Nam ipse ibidem proxime ante responsionem ad 1. his verbis vtitur: culpa venialis in eo qui cum gratia decedit, post hanc vitam dimittitur per ignem purgatorium, quia poena illa aliqualiter voluntaria virtute gratia habebit vim expiandi culpam omnem quae simul cum gratia stare poterit. haec profecto ratio non solum est per modum contrarij, sed etiam meriti proprie dicti in Pontificiorum scholis.
units.tr: 26. Ibid. it is remissory, although not by way of merit properly so called, but by way of a contrary removing its contrary.] It is denied that it is remissory. And even if we pretend that it is remissory, which is false, the distinction is denied to be according to the mind of Thomas. For he himself, just before his reply to the first point, uses these words: venial sin in one who departs with grace is forgiven after this life through purgatorial fire, because that punishment, being in some way voluntary, will by virtue of grace have the power to expiate every sin that can stand together with grace. This reasoning is surely not only by way of the contrary, but also of merit properly so called, in the schools of the Papists.

units.la: In Cap. IV.
units.tr: In Chapter IV.

units.la: 1. Artic. 3. animas quae in Purgatorio sunt, habere certitudinem suae salutis.] haec omnia nihil ad nos qui Purgatorium negamus esse, aut probari posse.
units.tr: 1. Art. 3. that the souls which are in Purgatory have certainty of their salvation.] All these things have nothing to do with us, who deny that Purgatory exists or that it can be proved.

units.la: 2. Art. 6. & dici potest coniecturalis certitudinis gradus,] male coniecturalis: nam coniectura opinionum est, in rebus autem fidei quae ad salutem æte[?] nam respiciunt, non vlla opinio nos certiores facit, sed fides promissionibus diuinis acquiescens per Spiritum.
units.tr: 2. Art. 6. and it can be called a degree of conjectural certainty,] Badly called conjectural. For conjecture belongs to opinions; but in matters of faith which concern salvation, no opinion makes us more certain, but faith resting on the divine promises, through the Spirit.

units.la: 3. Articu. 7. sed nihil horum habet locum; ] intellige, in Purgatorio: quod nos negamus, & ista omnia.
units.tr: 3. Art. 7. but none of these has a place;] Understand: in Purgatory. This we deny, and all those things.

units.la: 4. Art. 12. exempla eorū qui se iudicatos testati sunt.] siquidem testati ex veritate sunt.
units.tr: 4. Art. 12. examples of those who testified that they had been judged.] Indeed, if they testified from the truth.

units.la: 5. Ibidem. quum esset mortuus, & iudici oblatus.] & quis, obsecro, fatuus ille viator seu lictor, qui vnum pro altero per errorem obtulit iudici? fabulæ.
units.tr: 5. Ibid. when he was dead, and was presented to the judge.] And who, I ask you, was that foolish traveller or lictor who by mistake presented one man for another to the judge? Fables.

units.la: 6. Ibid. hæc non fieri vero errore,] certè: sed vero errore creduntur tum ab iis qui res sibi visas vuisse narrant, tum ab aliis, qui fidem habent narrantibus ἀνθρώπων.
units.tr: 6. Ibid. that these things did not happen by a true error,] Certainly. But they are believed to be by a true error, both by those who narrate things they say they saw, and by others who trust the narrators of men [ἀνθρώπων].

units.la: 7. Ibid. adhuc viuens vidit sententiam sua damnationis.] & quàm multis istud contigit impiis, postquā scenam huius vitæ improbè transegerunt, & stadium suum impiè decurrerunt!
units.tr: 7. Ibid. while still living he saw the sentence of his damnation.] And how many impious men has this happened to, after they wickedly played out the stage of this life and impiously ran their course!

units.la: 8. Articu. 14. & tertio die, iusto Dei iudicio damnatus sum.] hæc gesta, quo tempore loquebantur mortui, & ij quos præcones esse oportuit Euangelij & veritatis diuinæ erant viuentes mortui, canes muti. Sequentia sunt vero σοφιστικῶς, ὀνειροπόλοι.
units.tr: 8. Art. 14. and on the third day, by the just judgement of God, I was condemned.] These deeds were done at a time when the dead were speaking, and those who ought to have been heralds of the Gospel and of divine truth were living dead, mute dogs. What follows is sophistical [σοφιστικῶς] and the work of dream-interpreters [ὀνειροπόλοι].

units.la: 9. Art. 15. an anima deferantur ad iudicem,] quid in? etenim anima Lazari asportata dicitur ab Angelis in sinum Abrahami, Luc. 16.22. imò, si visis antecedentibus creditur quæ articulo 12. fuerunt posita, iudici afferuntur.
units.tr: 9. Art. 15. whether souls are carried to the judge,] What is the point? For the soul of Lazarus is said to have been carried by angels into the bosom of Abraham, Luke 16.22. Indeed, if, from the preceding visions which were set out in article 12, it is believed that souls are brought to the judge.

units.la: 10. Art. 17. evidenter cognoscet se in inferno nō esse. de Purgatorio. Negamus omnia.
units.tr: 10. Art. 17. he will clearly know that he is not in hell. Concerning Purgatory. We deny all of it.

units.la: II. Art. 19. & tamen non sunt certi an sinus iusti, negatur. Sumus certi quotquot pij sumus, idque vera certitudine a Deo inspirata; licet hi plus, & illi minus.
units.tr: 11. Art. 19. and yet they are not certain whether they are in the bosom of the just. Denied. We are certain, all of us who are godly, and that with a true certainty inspired by God; though some have more and some less.

units.la: 12. Artic. 20. ex coniecturis fallibilibus colligimus eum in nobis esse, falsum, vt proxime praecedente nota dicebamus. Nam si ita est, vbi fides? vide nota 2.
units.tr: 12. Art. 20. from fallible conjectures we conclude that he is in us. False, as we said in the immediately preceding note. For if so, where is faith? See note 2.

units.la: 13. Artic. 23. locum refrigerij, lucis, & pacis, vt indulgeas deprecamur. haec omnia dicuntur de spiritibus visionem Dei & gloriam exspectantibus, ex hypothesi secundae illius sententiae, quam Patres secundo saeculo & sequentibus prisci s habuerunt, vt ante expositum est lib. 1. cap. 9. nota 2. & 10. & alibi saepe: nam ille locus lucis & pacis & refrigerij olim fuit dictus, ob eas causas quas saepe exposuimus.
units.tr: 13. Art. 23. a place of refreshment, light and peace, which we pray that you would grant. All these things are said of spirits awaiting the vision and glory of God, on the hypothesis of that second opinion which the early Fathers of the second century and after held, as was set out before in book 1, chapter 9, note 2, and at 10, and often elsewhere. For that place of light and peace and refreshment was once so called, for the reasons we have often explained.

units.la: 14. Ibidem. cum summis cruciatibus incredibilem consolationem propter certam spem salutis: si cum summis cruciatibus, quomodo in luce & pace & refrigerio? Nam ista quidem minime conuenire possunt.
units.tr: 14. Ibid. with the greatest torments, an incredible consolation because of the certain hope of salvation: If with the greatest torments, how is it in light and peace and refreshment? For these things cannot at all agree.

units.la: 15. Art. 24. & exemplis allatis in prima quaestione, id est, sphyngibus & tragelaphis, quibus Ϸ si forte, nunc habeant fidem.
units.tr: 15. Art. 24. and by the examples brought forward in the first question, that is, the sphinxes and tragelaphs, with which, if perhaps they now have faith.

units.la: IN CAP. V.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER V.

units.la: 1. Art. 2. leguntur integri illi Psalmi. at hoc pro-secto non fuit hominis admodum sapientis & considerati opus, ponere aut Psalmos integros, aut laciniosas Scripturae partes, propter clausulam unam vel alteram quae ad institutum sermonem pertinere videatur: praesertim in officio pro laborantibus; quod βραχύτερον[?], ὑπομονώτερον[?], καὶ ἐμπαθέστερον[?] esse oporteret, ut ipsa natura docet: Viri graves id tantum afferunt quod ad rem facit: spiras verborum trahant ἀπερμόλογοι[?] καὶ βαττολόγοι[?] ἀκκιζόμενοι[?]. & hoc Ecclesia prudens faciat scilicet. de Purgatorio, negamus omnia.
units.tr: 1. Art. 2. Those entire Psalms are read. But this was surely not the work of a man of great wisdom and judgment: to set down whole Psalms or long stretches of Scripture, for the sake of one or two phrases that seem to bear on the matter in hand, especially in an office for the afflicted. Such an office ought to be briefer, more restrained and less emotional [βραχύτερον, ὑπομονώτερον, καὶ ἐμπαθέστερον], as nature itself teaches. Serious men bring forward only what serves the point; they do not drag out long strings of words [ἀπερμόλογοι καὶ βαττολόγοι ἀκκιζόμενοι]. A prudent Church would surely do this. On Purgatory, we deny everything.

units.la: 2. Art. 6. Ecclesia orat pro animabus quae in Purgatorio degunt, ne damnentur ad poenas gehennae sempiternas, hanc solutionem negamus, quia ex falsa hypothesi & confutata centies.
units.tr: 2. Art. 6. The Church prays for souls that dwell in Purgatory, that they may not be condemned to the everlasting punishments of hell. We deny this solution, because it rests on a false hypothesis that has been refuted a hundred times over.

units.la: 3. Art. 10. vel ut refrigerium aliquod doloribus miscentur[?]. ] hae igitur orationes non proprie orationes, sed commemorationes dicendae sunt, ut prisca Ecclesia fecit. Atque haec ratio sequentium.
units.tr: 3. Art. 10. or that some refreshment is mixed with their pains. Those prayers, then, are not properly prayers but should be called commemorations, as the early Church did. This is the reason for what follows.

units.la: IN CAP. VI.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER VI.

units.la: 1. Artic. 1. quaestio tertia, ubi sit Purgatorium.] non est Purgatorium: nec igitur τὸ ποῦ[?] aut locus dari illius potest. negamus ista somnia, & omnia.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. Third question: where Purgatory is. There is no Purgatory, and so no "where" or place can be assigned to it. We deny these dreams, and all of them.

units.la: 2. Art. 3. sed retractavit lib. 2. retract. cap. 24.] falsum: nam de inferis ibi Augustinus agit, de Purgatorio, nullum verbum.
units.tr: 2. Art. 3. But he retracted it in Book 2 of the Retractions, chapter 24. False. Augustine there treats of the underworld, not of Purgatory; there is not a word about Purgatory.

units.la: 3. Artic. 7. ita refert Theophylactus in cap. 16. Lucae.] falsum. non statum Theophylactus, sed translationem & transportationem, μετάστασιν[?], figurate dicit, sive, (ut Sifanus vertit) transitum. Sentit enim Theophylactus ᾅδης accipi pro loco damnatorum simpliciter, quem subterraneum obscurum vocat; aut pro communi loco in quem omnes animae transportantur & bonae & malae, vt centrum. 2. lib. 4. ostendimus. Sed hoc figurate enunciat. Haec Graeca illius verba: τί δέ ἐστιν ᾅδης; οἱ μὲν αὐτὸν φασι χῶρον ὑπόγειον σκοτεινόν, οἱ δὲ τὸν ἐν τῷ ἀέρι [?] τὴν ἀφανῆ καὶ ἀειδῆ μετάστασιν τῆς ψυχῆς ᾅδου ἔφασαν. exponit sequentibus suam sententiam, dicens; ἀχρὶ μὲν γὰρ ἐν σώματι ἐσὶν ἡ ψυχή, φαίνεται διὰ τῶν αἰσθήσεων ἐνεργεῖν. μετὰ δὲ τὸ σῶμα τῷ, ἀειδὴς γίνεται, τότε χρῶ ἐφάσκειν ἐν αὐτῷ τὸν ᾅδην. Sed vale ista.
units.tr: 3. Art. 7. So Theophylact reports in his commentary on Luke, chapter 16. False. Theophylact does not state a place but a transition and transference [μετάστασιν]. He speaks figuratively, or (as Sifanus translates it) a passing over. For Theophylact understands Hades to mean simply the place of the damned, which he calls a dark place under the ground; or the common place into which all souls, both good and bad, are carried, like a centre. We showed this in Book 2 of Book 4. But he states it figuratively. His Greek words are these: "What then is Hades? Some say it is a dark place under the earth; others call it the invisible and unseen transference of the soul to Hades" [τί δέ ἐστιν ᾅδης; οἱ μὲν αὐτὸν φασι χῶρον ὑπόγειον σκοτεινόν, οἱ δὲ τὸν ἐν τῷ ἀέρι τὴν ἀφανῆ καὶ ἀειδῆ μετάστασιν τῆς ψυχῆς ᾅδου ἔφασαν]. He then sets out his own opinion in what follows, saying: "For while the soul is in the body, it appears to act through the senses; but after the body it becomes unseen, and then they say Hades is in it" [ἀχρὶ μὲν γὰρ ἐν σώματι ἐσὶν ἡ ψυχή, φαίνεται διὰ τῶν αἰσθήσεων ἐνεργεῖν. μετὰ δὲ τὸ σῶμα τῷ, ἀειδὴς γίνεται, τότε χρῶ ἐφάσκειν ἐν αὐτῷ τὸν ᾅδην]. But enough of that.

units.la: 4. Artic. 9. Purgatorium esse intra viscera terrae, inferno ipsi vicinum. ] Negamus tum si intra viscera terrae est, non igitur infra. vtrum dicas, elige. Purgatorium inane est: inani autem non est locus, quandoquidem ex Physicorum sententia natura non fert vacuum. Sequentem quoque diuisionem pernegamus. nam locum pro purgandis sustulimus superiore libro; pro infantibus sine baptismo abeuntibus confutabimus tomo 3. pro iustis ante passionem Christi mortuis, quem limbum vocant Patrum, etiam contra 2. lib. 4. cofutauimus, & proxime refellemus.
units.tr: 4. Art. 9. Purgatory is within the bowels of the earth, very near to hell. We deny this. If it is within the bowels of the earth, then it is not beneath them; choose which you mean. Purgatory is empty, and empty space has no place, since by the opinion of the natural philosophers nature does not admit a vacuum. We also flatly deny the division that follows. For we removed the place for those to be purged in the previous book; we will refute it for infants who die without baptism in Volume 3; and for the just who died before Christ's passion, whom they call the Limbo of the Fathers, we have already refuted it against Book 2 of Book 4, and we will refute it again shortly.

units.la: 5. Artic. 10. haec omnia fabulas esse Caluinus dicit ] calumnia: nam certe de inferno hoc nunquam Caluinus dixit: de aliis, quae finguntur, locis diuersa ratio, vt in controuersiam 2. dictum.
units.tr: 5. Art. 10. Calvin says that all these things are fables. This is a slander: Calvin never said this about hell. As for the other places that are invented, the reasoning is different, as was said in Controversy 2.

units.la: 6. Ibidem. quod intra viscera terrae sit locus aliquis animarum, ] locum aliquem esse animarum omnes credimus: sed intra viscera terrae esse min[?] me credimus: quod & certis rationibus ex hac inferiore natura & illa superiore sumptis secundum principia Physicae & Metaphysicae, & documentis Scripturae possumus confirmare. Sed de his in controversiam 2.
units.tr: 6. Ibid. that there is some place of souls within the bowels of the earth. We all believe that there is some place of souls, but we do not believe that it is within the bowels of the earth. We can confirm this by sure arguments drawn from the lower nature and the higher, according to the principles of physics and metaphysics, and from the teaching of Scripture. But of these things in Controversy 2.

units.la: 7. Art. II. esse indicia quædam inferni intra viscera terræ existentis, illos quidem crateras montium igniuomos, vt & Charoneas scrobes & alia quaplu-rimi, esse indicia inferni non negamus; sed communia, non propria; contingentia, non necessaria; separata, non coniuncta vel essentialia; ex quibus concluditur vtcunque, non demonstratur aut confirmatur internum esse. Amplius non dicit Gregorius. Multo minus ex eo igitur doceri potest subterraneum infernum esse, aut intra terræ viscera conditum. non sequitur ex diuerso: negamus igitur circumscriptionem istam. Sequentia itaque nihil ad rhombum.
units.tr: 7. Art. 11. There are certain signs of a hell existing within the bowels of the earth. We do not deny that those fire-spitting craters of mountains, and the Charonean pits and many other such things, are signs of hell. But they are common, not proper; contingent, not necessary; separate, not joined or essential. From these one may conclude in some fashion, but not demonstrate or confirm, that hell is internal. Gregory says nothing more. Much less, then, can it be taught from this that hell is underground or hidden within the bowels of the earth. It does not follow from the opposite; so we deny this limitation. What follows therefore has nothing to do with the matter.

units.la: 8. Ibid. apparere animas, quæ dicant se missi ad illum montem. quidni dæmones humana specie illudentes? nam & illi dæmones sunt animæ, & ad montes, auia, paludes, monumenta, porcos, lacus a Deo mittuntur, vt Matt. 8. aut ipsi mendaces spiritus se vltro offerunt, vt Matth. 12. & alibi.
units.tr: 8. Ibid. Souls appear who say that they have been sent to that mountain. Why not demons deceiving with a human appearance? For those demons are also souls, and they are sent by God to mountains, deserts, marshes, tombs, swine and lakes, as in Matthew 8; or those lying spirits offer themselves of their own accord, as in Matthew 12 and elsewhere.

units.la: 9. Artic. 12. vt videret Lazarum, qui etiam tunc erat in locis subterraneis, sursum versus aspicere debuit. primum hæc parabola est qua Christus in Pharisæos vtitur, vt narrat Lucas: non sequitur autem proprie conclusio ex quibusdam dictis [illegible, ~8 letters] secundo fallit disputator homonymia vocis ᾅδης, qua significatur omnis locus animarum iustarum & iniustarum, pro eo quod est ᾅδης si- gne ᾅδης, vt Græci exponunt, & nos confirmaumus controu.2.lib.4.
units.tr: 9. Art. 12. That he might see Lazarus, who was then also in the subterranean places, he ought to have looked upward. First, this parable is one Christ uses against the Pharisees, as Luke relates; but a conclusion does not follow properly from certain sayings [illegible]. Second, the disputant is misled by the ambiguity of the word Hades, which signifies every place of souls, both just and unjust, and also the Hades which the Greeks explain as the grave; we have confirmed this in Controversy 2, Book 4.

units.la: 10. Ibid.nihil autem remotius centro terræ.] Antecedens, distinguendum est. locus enim cum sit corporalis, aut νοῦς[?] (intellectuale vocant) proprius rei spiritualis & metaphysicæ; omnino remotum & propinquum ex analogia aut corporali modo, aut intellectuali. oportet accipi pro ratione rerum quæ aguntur: hæ autem res sunt spirituales, metaphysicæ, futuri seculi: ergo remotio sive distantia in eadem modum intelligenda est. Consequens autem de remotione seu distantia agit corporalis illius modi. Nihil dicam de motu cœlo eccentrico & statione terræ, quibus propositio ista eludi posset. Certè nec philosophatur, nec Theologum agit Bellarminus commodè.
units.tr: 10. Ibid. Nothing, however, is further removed from the centre of the earth. The antecedent must be distinguished. For place, since it is bodily, is the proper thing of a spiritual and metaphysical reality; or (they call it intellectual) the intellectual place. Remote and near must be understood by analogy, either in a bodily or an intellectual manner, according to the nature of the things being treated. These things are spiritual, metaphysical, of the future age; therefore remoteness or distance must be understood in the same way. The consequent, however, speaks of remoteness or distance of the bodily kind. I say nothing of the eccentric motion of the heavens and the fixed position of the earth, by which this proposition could be evaded. Certainly Bellarmine neither philosophizes nor argues as a theologian with any skill.

units.la: 11. Art. 13. quæ intelliguntur ab Augustino epist. 99. de pœnis Purgatorij,] falsum triplex: nam nec Purgatorium est, nec id Petrus sibi & Scriptura voluit Act. 2. (nam & ipsi Pontificij, prout suis rationibus commodum esse arbitrantur, illa verba de inferno quoque & de limbo Patrum acceperunt) nec id Augustinus usquam pronunciat. Consulatur locus: nam in eo modesta Augustini sententia audacem disputatoris affirmationem tacentibus nobis lifura est.
units.tr: 11. Art. 13. Which are understood by Augustine, Letter 99, concerning the punishments of Purgatory. This is false in three ways. For there is no Purgatory, and Peter did not mean this by it, nor Scripture in Acts 2. (For the Papists themselves, as suits their arguments, have taken those words also of hell and of the Limbo of the Fathers.) Nor does Augustine ever pronounce this anywhere. Let the passage be consulted: in it Augustine's modest opinion will be read, while we keep silent about the bold affirmation of the disputant.

units.la: 12. Ibid. libera animas defunctorum de pœnis inferni, & de profundo lacu.] verba figurata sunt & allegorica, ex quibus qui argumentatur proprie, nugas vendit. Tum quid nos obstringit, ut illius orationis auctoritati cedamus? sed prior responsio certissima.
units.tr: 12. Ibid. Free the souls of the dead from the punishments of hell, and from the deep lake. These words are figurative and allegorical, and whoever argues from them in the proper sense is peddling trifles. Moreover, what obliges us to yield to the authority of that prayer? But the first answer is most certain.

units.la: 13 Ibid. & eodem igne torqueri damnatos, & animas Purgatorij.] vtramque probationem negamus; tum[?] illam Bedæ ex visione ac potius illusione ludicra, tum hanc Theologorum recentium ex communi opinione errantis seculi. In rebus diuinis alia adferri oportet testimonia.
units.tr: 13. Ibid. That the damned and the souls of Purgatory are tormented by the same fire. We deny both proofs: the former, that of Bede, from a vision or rather a playful illusion; the latter, that of recent theologians, from the common opinion of an erring age. In divine matters other testimonies must be brought forward.

units.la: 14. Art. 14. mox in infernum descendere, pœnis tamen disparibus puniendos.] negatur dictum, & Concilij Florentini in quæstione hac auctoritas, quod est recentius.
units.tr: 14. Art. 14. They soon descend into hell, yet are to be punished with unequal penalties. The saying is denied, and so is the authority of the Council of Florence on this question, which is more recent.

units.la: 15. Ibid. fidem catholicam non nosse nisi duo loca vbi homines sint futuri perpetuo; cælum beatorum, & infernum damnatorum.] distinctio ista loci perpetui & temporarij animarum non est ex mente Augustini, vt libri 1. cap. 13. nota 13. diximus. Tum non sequitur ex remotione positio contrarij in hoc argumentorum genere, vt sæpius in librum 1. oftedimus. Nam si quis dicat, hæc duo perpetua solum loca sunt animarum, ergo sunt & temporaria, quis sanus ita argumentantem ferat? Est quidem hæc consequutio in contradicentibus verissima; sed in contrariis negantibusque nulla iusta ratio probauit vnquam. Sequentem opinionem Scholasticorum negamus: supponit enim id quod ante negauimus, & confutauimus; principium petit.
units.tr: 15. Ibid. The Catholic faith knows of only two places where men are to remain forever: heaven of the blessed, and hell of the damned. This distinction between a perpetual and a temporary place of souls is not in the mind of Augustine, as we said in Book 1, chapter 13, note 13. Moreover, the opposite does not follow from the removal of one in this kind of argument, as we have often shown in Book 1. For if someone says, "These two are the only perpetual places of souls, therefore there are also temporary ones," who that is sane would tolerate such an argument? In contradictory propositions this inference is indeed most true; but in contraries and negatives no sound reason has ever proved it. We deny the following opinion of the Schoolmen, for it presupposes what we have already denied and refuted; it begs the question.

units.la: 16. Art. 15. probatum est satis accurate in lib. 4. de Christo, cap. 10.] & nos ibidem confutauimus in 2. controuersia.
units.tr: 16. Art. 15. It has been proved accurately enough in book 4 on Christ, chapter 10.] And we refuted it in the same place, in the second controversy.

units.la: 17. Ibid. vidi, inquit Pythonissa, Deos ascendentes de terra,] negatur sequi: prout etiam ibidem a nobis negatum est.
units.tr: 17. Ibid. "I saw gods ascending out of the earth," says the Pythoness.] We deny that this follows, as we have already denied it in the same place.

units.la: 18. Art. 18. vere Samuelis animam fuisse eam quæ apparuit.] negamus: & negant alij præterea auctores classici, quos ille noluit adducere, vt Theodoretus in eum locum, Hieronymus in Ezechielis.
units.tr: 18. Art. 18. That the soul that appeared was truly that of Samuel.] We deny it, and other classical authors deny it too, whom he did not wish to cite: Theodoret on that passage, and Jerome on Ezekiel.

units.la: 13.& alij.Quapropter Thomas in fumma(cui eft im mortuus) opinionem iftam nuquam aufus eft affir-mare.(Meminit autem tribus, fi bene obferuaui,locis. nimirum p.1.q. 89.art.8. & 2.2.q.95.art.4.& q. 174.art.5.)Sed vtramque fententiam in medium adfert fine praecifa alterutrius affirmatione.
units.tr: 13. And others. Therefore Thomas, in the Summa (to whom it is dead), never dared to affirm this opinion. (He mentions it, if I have observed correctly, in three places: namely, part 1, q. 89, art. 8; 2-2, q. 95, art. 4; and q. 174, art. 5.) But he presents both opinions without a definite affirmation of either.

units.la: 19. Ibid. Auctores citati funt omnes aut incerti, aut obfcuri: ] Falsum:nec illi omnes ita funt,nec ij quos proxima nota adduximus. Sed difputator ἑαυτῷ βλα-λαυδεῖ[?], quod vulgo dici folet.
units.tr: 19. Ibid. All the authors cited are either unknown or obscure.] False. Neither are they all so, nor are those whom we cited in the note just above. But the disputant "speaks against himself," as the common saying goes.

units.la: 20. Ibid. & Augustinus lib. de cura pro mortuis, cap.15. ]Flauij Iofephi Iudaei rerum iftarum infcien-tiffimi in hoc argumento nulla eft auctoritas. Iufti-nus martyr opinionem fuam adfert:fed & erronea, & cum altero infuper errore coniunctam. Non e-nim folum dicit animam Samuelis a Pythoniffa e-uocatam effe : verumetiam axioma fubiicit rationi naturali & oraculis diuinis repugnans, quum ait: Apparet autem , ad eum modum omnes animas viro-rum iuftorum & prophetarum fub poteftatem eiufmodi virtutum cadere,qualem & in ventriloqua illa fuiffe re-bus ipfis declaratur.Hoc quis Theologus,quis Chri-ftianus iam credat? Bafilius in epiftola ad Euftathiu medicum hoc aufquam affirmauit. Haec illius ver-ba , ὡς ἡ ἐγγαστρίμυθος[?] ἐν ταῖς μαγγανείαις αὐτῆς ψυχαγωγοῦσα τὸν Σαοὺλ, τὰς ἐπιθυμούσας ψυχὰς Θεοὺς ἑωρακέναι φησίν[?], quae interpres male tranftulit, nec verius Bel-larminus eft aflequutus. nihil iftorum praedicat Ba-filius quae difputator autumat: & illa, inquit, ventriloquafuis incantationibus Saulem demulcens, animas quae defiderabantur ( videlicet ab ipfa incan-tationibus operante ) Deos vidiffe ait. Hanc pla-ne fuam mentem effe ipfe Bafilius declarat in Esai.8. dicens: Erant enim dæmones, qui stridentes seipsos transformarant in habitum & personam Samuelis, &c. ut amplius postea in artic. 21. perscribetur. Ambrosius loquitur ex fide Siracidæ in libro Ecclesia-stici, de quo postea videbitur. Hieronymo fit in-iuria: nam hoc non affirmat usquam: sed potius contrarium sensum verbis suis ostendit, ut & in Ezechiel. 13. exponitur. Hæc illius verba in Esai. 7.
units.tr: 20. Ibid. and Augustine, in the book on the care of the dead, chapter 15.] Flavius Josephus, a Jew most ignorant of these matters, has no authority in this question. Justin Martyr puts forward his opinion, but it is erroneous, and joined besides to another error. For he not only says that the soul of Samuel was summoned by the Pythoness, but also adds a principle that contradicts both natural reason and the divine oracles, when he says: "Now it appears that in this way all the souls of righteous men and prophets fall under the power of such spirits as those by which that ventriloquist was shown to have been operated upon." What theologian, what Christian, would now believe this? Basil never affirmed this in his letter to Eustathius the physician. His words are: "As the ventriloquist, bewitching Saul with her charms, summons souls, says that the souls that were longed for saw the gods" [ὡς ἡ ἐγγαστρίμυθος ἐν ταῖς μαγγανείαις αὐτῆς ψυχαγωγοῦσα τὸν Σαοὺλ, τὰς ἐπιθυμούσας ψυχὰς Θεοὺς ἑωρακέναι φησίν]. The translator rendered this badly, and Bellarmine has not followed it more accurately. Basil says none of the things the disputant claims. He says: "that woman, soothing Saul with her incantations, says that the souls that were desired (namely, by the incantations themselves working on her) saw gods." Basil himself plainly declares that this is his own meaning in his commentary on Isaiah 8, saying: "For they were demons, who, hissing, had transformed themselves into the appearance and person of Samuel," etc., as will be set out more fully later, in article 21. Ambrose speaks on the authority of the Wisdom of Jesus son of Sirach, in the book of Ecclesiasticus, about which we shall see more later. Jerome is wronged: for he nowhere affirms this, but rather by his words shows the opposite sense, as is also explained on Ezekiel 13. These are his words on Isaiah 7:

units.la: Plerique putant Saulem signum accepisse de terra & de profundo inferni, quando Samuelem per incantationes & artes magicas visus est suscitasse. Dicit visum esse suscitasse, nimirum ἐνδόξως[?], non vere suscitasse. Illu-dit homonymia disputator noster. Augustinus u-tramque sententiam eodem in loco adfert: quid ex eo, bone vir, possis conficere? Hæc Bellarminearum scilicet probationum fides.
units.tr: "Many think that Saul received a sign from the earth and from the depths of hell, when he was seen to have raised Samuel by incantations and magical arts." He says that he was seen to have raised him, that is, in appearance, not that he truly raised him. Our disputant plays on the ambiguity of the word. Augustine sets out both opinions in the same place. What, good sir, can you conclude from that? Such is the trustworthiness of Bellarmine's proofs.

units.la: 21. Ibid. Librum de cura pro mortuis scripsit poste-rius, & re diligentius considerata. ]Prius concedimus: sed quid ex eo sequitur, cum illic Augustinus utramque sententiam ponat, & neutram præferat alteri? posterius probari non potest. Contra vero, ubi sententiæ diversæ afferuntur, si iudicium non interponitur, res aut considerata, aut certe tractata est indiligentius: diligentius facit qui prudenter apponit iudicium suum: atqui in libro de cura pro mortuis iudicium non statuitur in diversitate sententiarum, sed quasi perfunctorie adferuntur. Libro autem se-cundo ad Simplicianum, quæst. 3. iudicium suum Augustinus, licet modeste pro suo more, pronun-ciat in maxima parte suæ dissertationis, inde ab illis verbis: Quamquam in hoc facto[?] potest esse alius far-cilior intellectus & expeditior exitus, ut non vere spi-ritum Samuelis excitatum a requie sua credamus, &c. quem locum postea iisdem omnino verbis Augustinus repetiuit in libro de 8.Dulcitij quaestionibus, in quaest.6.qui liber post illum alterum de cura pro mortuis gerenda perscriptus est, Augustino teste, lib. 2.retractat.cap.64.& 65. Sequentia testimonia e nouitio seculo & Pontificia penu depromta iustam auctoritatem habere negamus posse: sunt enim ex communi errore scripta.
units.tr: 21. Ibid. He wrote the book on the care of the dead later, and with more careful consideration.] We grant that it was earlier; but what follows from that, since there Augustine sets out both opinions and prefers neither to the other? "Later" cannot be proved. On the contrary, where differing opinions are cited and no judgment is interposed, the matter has either been considered, or at least treated carelessly. He who prudently adds his own judgment does the more careful work; yet in the book on the care of the dead no judgment is given on the difference of opinions, but they are cited as if in passing. However, in the second book to Simplicianus, question 3, Augustine, though modestly, as is his way, pronounces his judgment in the greater part of his discussion, from those words onward: "Although in this matter there may be another, easier understanding and a more straightforward outcome, namely that we do not believe the spirit of Samuel was truly roused from his rest," etc. Augustine later repeated this very passage in the same words in the book on the eight questions of Dulcitius, question 6; and that book was written, as Augustine testifies in Retractations 2, chapters 64 and 65, after that other book on the care of the dead. We deny that the following testimonies, drawn from a recent age and from the Papist storehouse, can have any true authority, for they were written in the common error.

units.la: 22. Art. 19. Sunt etiam pro hac sententia fortissimæ rationes:] negamus, & ordine eas infirmabimus.
units.tr: 22. Art. 19. There are also very strong arguments for this opinion.] We deny it, and in order we shall weaken them.

units.la: 23. Ibid. Non diceret, intellexit[?], sed cogitauit, vel pu-tauit, si id non esset verum.] Hanc rationem eneruant Basilius in Esai.8. Theodoretus in 1.Sam.28 & Augustinus lib.2.ad Simplicianum, quaest.3.& lib.de 8. Dulcitij quaestionibus, quaest.6.itemque Thomas,& alij. Sufficiet Theodoretus dicens: Historia eum qui visus est nominat Samuelem; propterea quod sic credidit Saul. Ita etiam Angelos qui Abrahae apparuerunt, & illorum Dominum, nominaut viros, quandoquidem eos ita esse arbitratus Patriarcha mensam apposuit. Ita etiam eos qui non sunt dij, Deos nominat etiam Deus noster qui est supra omnes Deos: ita etiam hic eum qui visus est in figura Samuelis Samuelem vocauit. vide nota 20.
units.tr: 23. Ibid. He would not say "understood" but "thought" or "supposed," if it were not true.] This argument is weakened by Basil in his commentary on Isaiah 8, by Theodoret on 1 Samuel 28, by Augustine in the second book to Simplicianus, question 3, and in the book on the eight questions of Dulcitius, question 6, and likewise by Thomas and others. Theodoret will suffice, saying: "The history names the one who appeared as Samuel, because Saul so believed. So too the angels who appeared to Abraham, and their Lord, it calls men, since the patriarch, supposing them to be such, set out a table for them. So too our God, who is above all gods, calls those who are not gods 'gods'; so here he called the one who appeared in the form of Samuel 'Samuel'." See note 20.

units.la: 24. Art. 20. Cuius testimonij non meminerat, cum scriberet ad Simplicianum.]Sed nec postea meminit, quum ad octo Dulcitij quaestiones responderet. Liber autem de cura pro mortuis raptim exaratus est: duo illi, ad Simplicianum & ad Dulcitium scripti sunt attentius: quod res ipsa loquitur. De Ecclesiastici libro, & auctoritate illius testimonij diximus controu. 1. lib.1. cap.14. & controu.2.libr. 4.cap.10. Hoc inane argumentum esse plurimi Patres offenderunt, quum de divinatione daemonum scriberent. Praeclare vero Basilius in Esai. 8.
units.tr: 24. Art. 20. He did not mention this testimony when he wrote to Simplicianus.] But neither did he mention it afterwards, when he answered the eight questions of Dulcitius. The book on the care of the dead was written hastily; the two others, to Simplicianus and to Dulcitius, were written more carefully, as the matter itself shows. We have spoken of the book of Ecclesiasticus, and of the authority of that testimony, in the first controversy, book 1, chapter 14, and in the second controversy, book 4, chapter 10. Many Fathers, when writing about the divination of demons, perceived that this is an empty argument. Basil, in his commentary on Isaiah 8, puts it admirably:

units.la: Ad eum modum, inquit, & daemones quae sententia ac decreto Dei constituta erant iamque palam euulgata, saepenumero annunciarunt his qui facile in fraudem illiciuntur: sicut fuit Pythonicus ille spiritus quem consuluit Saul per diuinatricem futuram stragem annuncia-uit ministerio daemonum. Erant enim daemones, qui stri-dentes seipsos transformarant in habitum & personam Samuelis: qui quod audissent sententiam condemnationis aduersus Saulem prolatam, quae a Deo prodierat, exponunt & promulgant vt propriam. Haec ille. Deinde vero coniungantur quae Bellarminus dicit ar-tic.26. iam omnia fuisse parata, & acies instructas, &c. an difficilis ei coniectura fuisset rei proximè se-quuntur?
units.tr: "In this way," he says, "demons also, often announcing to those who are easily drawn into deceit things that had been fixed by the decree of God and already openly made known, as with that Pythonic spirit whom Saul consulted through the diviner, announced by the ministry of demons the coming slaughter. For they were demons who, hissing, had transformed themselves into the appearance and person of Samuel; and since they had heard the sentence of condemnation against Saul, which had gone forth from God, they set it forth and proclaimed it as their own." So he. Then consider what Bellarmine says in article 26, "that everything was already prepared, and the battle lines drawn up," etc.: would it have been difficult for him to conjecture what follows from the nearest matter?

units.la: hoc alienum a veritate esse, mox sigillatim docebimus.
units.tr: That this is alien to the truth, we shall show presently, point by point.

units.la: haec omnia probari non possunt: eadem itaque facilitate qua affirmantur negari possunt: & certe negari debent. Sequentia fabulosa sunt ex inepta Iudaeorum incantatorum traditione nata: dignorum testium quibuscum in tenebris mices scilicet. Quis credat daemonas Magis suis Agrippas esse? hem[?] vanitatem. Modestius vero tandem Bellarminus, quod prius affirmauerat, timide enunciat, dicens: Si enim verū est quod Rabbini scribunt, &c. quid his probationibus facias? Hanc vero solutionem vere pariter ac docte in iis locis quos ante adduximus, Augustinus & Theodoretus refellerunt.
units.tr: None of these things can be proved; therefore they can be denied with the same ease with which they are affirmed, and indeed they ought to be denied. The following are fabulous, arising from the absurd tradition of Jewish enchanters: witnesses worthy of trust, forsooth, with whom one gropes in the dark. Who would believe that demons are Agrippas to their own magicians? Oh, what vanity! But at last Bellarmine, more modestly, timidly states what he had earlier affirmed, saying: "For if it is true what the rabbis write, etc." What would you make of these proofs? Augustine and Theodoret, in the passages we cited above, have refuted this solution both truly and learnedly.

units.la: 28.Art.24. Non fuisse latriam, sed reverentiam debi-tam animæ Samuelis.] quid latriam?an ergo vel ἀξιώσεως[?] bona fide vnquam poterit exhiberi dæmo-ni?negat natura, negat Christus Matth. 4. Omnino aut ciuilem ei, aut religiosum honore habuit Saul: non autem ciuilem, nam consulebat pro Deo: religiosum igitur. At non latria, fuit, inquies. Primum distinctionem illam latriæ negamus, & suo loco refellemus in sequente controuersia. Deinde esto, sane, valeat quantum valere potest:at religiosum cig[?] magis Samuel suscepisset, quâ aut Angelus in Apocalypsi, aut Petrus & Paulus in Actis Apostolorū*
units.tr: 28. Art. 24. Samuel's soul was owed not latria but reverence.] What of latria? Can even some kind of honour [ἀξιώσεως] ever in good faith be rendered to a demon? Nature denies it; Christ denies it, Matthew 4. Saul showed him either civil or religious honour; not civil, for he consulted him as on behalf of God; therefore religious. But you will say it was not latria. First, we deny that distinction of latria, and in the next controversy we shall refute it in its place. Then, granting it, let it stand as far as it can stand: yet Samuel would have accepted religious worship no more than an angel in the Apocalypse, or Peter and Paul in the Acts of the Apostles.

units.la: 29. Art. 26. tam non respondendo quando interrogabatur, quàm respondendo quando non interrogabatur:] prius Scriptura affirmat bis expressis verbis: posterius ne innuit quidem. hoc itaque negamus.
units.tr: 29. Art. 26. both by not answering when he was questioned, and by answering when he was not questioned: The first point Scripture affirms twice in express words; the second it does not even hint at. So we deny this.

units.la: 30. Ibid. potuisset Saul declinare bellum, & pœnam sibi à Deo paratam:] negatur consequens: nam Deus Sauli fuisset responsurus pro sapientia, iustitia, & veritate sua: vana igitur argumentatio.
units.tr: 30. Ibid. Saul could have avoided the battle and the punishment prepared for him by God: The consequent is denied. God would have answered Saul in keeping with his own wisdom, justice and truth. The argument is therefore empty.

units.la: 31. Art. 27. Purgatorium, infernum, ac limbos Patrū & puerorum, loca subterranea esse.] Hanc conclusionem inde à nota quarta in superioribus refel-limus.
units.tr: 31. Art. 27. Purgatory, hell, and the limbos of the Fathers and of children are subterranean places. We refuted this conclusion from note 4 onwards in the earlier part.

units.la: IN CAP. VII.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER VII.

units.la: I. Art. I. Quantum ad primum, difficultas est satis magna,] imò nulla plane acquiescentibus in simpli-citate Scripturæ sacræ. Nam distinctio quidem illa quatuor locorum nihil cum ea commune habet.
units.tr: I. Art. 1. As to the first point, the difficulty is quite great. Indeed there is no difficulty at all for those who rest in the plain sense of holy Scripture. For that distinction of four places has nothing in common with it.

units.la: 2.Ib. Cui revelationi multas alias conformes adducit Dionysius Carth.]hæc vigilantium somnia,non probationes iustæ.imò ne digna quidem præsumptio-nis nomine, ut Iurecoss.distinguunt.
units.tr: 2. Ib. To this revelation Dionysius of Carthage adds many other agreeing ones. These are the dreams of the wakeful, not just proofs. They do not even deserve the name of presumption, as the jurists distinguish.

units.la: 3. Art. 5. talem aliquem locum reperiri: caterum e-iusmodi locum ad Purgatorium pertinere.]Utrumque negamus, quia neutrum a Scriptura est. Non enim homines, aut humanas doctrinas: sed Deum & disciplinam ab eo traditam, confessandam[?] nobis esse statuimus, ait dialogo adversus Tryphonem Iustinus martyr. Eadem ratio sequentium.
units.tr: 3. Art. 5. that some such place can be found, and that such a place pertains to Purgatory. We deny both, because neither is from Scripture. "For we hold that it is not men or human doctrines, but God and the discipline handed down by him, that we must confess," says Justin Martyr in his dialogue against Trypho. The same reasoning applies to what follows.

units.la: 4. Art.4. nisi dolorem ex desiderio dilatæ felicitatis.] quàm apte huic toti narrationi adtexueris illud Aristarchi elogium: τὰ ἐν ᾅδου. nam fabulosa sunt & ῥήματα[?] omnia. Nihil ad nos.
units.tr: 4. Art. 4. except from the grief of a happiness deferred. How aptly you have attached to this whole narrative that saying of Aristarchus, [τὰ ἐν ᾅδου], "the things in Hades." For all of it is fable and idle talk. It is nothing to us.

units.la: IN CAPVT VIII.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER VIII.

units.la: 1. Art. 2. Ex inferno damnatorum limbóque puerorum non dari regressum: ex Purgatorio limboque Patrũ, dari.]de inferno quæ dicuntur, agnoscimus: Purgatorium lib.1.limbum utrumque aut plures, si forte, esse negauimus proximè cap.6.& 7.non entis(ut aiunt) non sunt accidentia. Falsa itaque sequentia, quæcunque de his disputator prædicat.
units.tr: 1. Art. 2. From the hell of the damned and the limbo of children there is no return; from Purgatory and the limbo of the Fathers there is. What is said about hell we acknowledge. We denied in book 1, and in chapters 6 and 7 just above, that Purgatory and a limbo (or more than one, if there are any) exist. Non-beings, as they say, have no accidents. The consequences are therefore false, whatever the disputant asserts about these matters.

units.la: 2. Ibid. cœlum clauserat, quod aperiri non potuit, nisi Christi sanguine reipsa effuso:]quasi verò vis & virtus illius satisfactionis & meriti ad sæcula præcedentia tempore non permeauerit: quod aliis in causis omnes fatentur verissimum, cur in hac re negent? sed de hac re controu.2.lib.4.dictum,& controuersia seq. videbitur.
units.tr: 2. Ibid. He had closed heaven, which could not be opened except by the actual shedding of Christ's blood. As if the force and power of that satisfaction and merit did not reach back in time to the preceding ages! Everyone admits this is most true in other cases; why do they deny it in this matter? But this question was discussed in controversy 2 of book 4, and it will be seen again in the following controversy.

units.la: 3. Art.4. Si hæc historia defendi debeat,]quod iniquum: nam historia aliena à pietate & veritate est.
units.tr: 3. Art. 4. If this history must be defended, which is unfair, for the history is alien to piety and truth.

units.la: 4. Art.10. Ubicunque sepeliatur qui moritur cum charitate, damnari non potest] recte: quid ergo tanta su-perstitione & violentia instant[?] de cæmiteriis & re-ligiosis locis Pontificij? quæ de fide informi & for-mata dicuntur, expendentur tomo 4.
units.tr: 4. Art. 10. Wherever a person who dies in charity is buried, he cannot be damned. Rightly so. Why then do the Papists press with such superstition and violence about cemeteries and religious places? What they say about unformed and formed faith will be weighed in volume 4.

units.la: 6. Art.15. Dicit Anathema Origeni, sicut Ario, Nęstorio, & cæteris hæreticis.] Ista omnia Sunt aptina,tricaque[?], & siquid vilius istis. Synodi 5. non fuit ea mens proprie, ut anathema personæ diceret absolutè (nam stat, cadit, aut resurgit quisque Domino) sed doctrinæ illius. Alioquin enim quorsum hominem mortuum feriri anathemate?
units.tr: 6. Art. 15. He pronounces anathema on Origen, as on Arius, Nestorius and the other heretics. All these things are trifles and nonsense, and anything baser than these. It was not the mind of the Fifth Synod to pronounce anathema absolutely on a person (for each one stands or falls or rises to his own Lord), but on that teaching. Otherwise, why would a dead man be struck with anathema?

units.la: 6. Articul. 16. non dicunt, nullo modo posse animas egredi ad nos:] Falsum: considantur[?] loci. Chryfostomus enim & Theophylactus, ut alii, absolutè negant.
units.tr: 6. Art. 16. They do not say that souls can in no way come out to us. False: the passages should be considered. For Chrysostom and Theophylact, like others, deny it absolutely.

units.la: 7. Art. 17. Nimia impudentia esse negare animas interdum ad nos redire Deo iubente vel permittente:] Hæ quæstiones diuersæ sunt, prima, possitne Deus facere ut redeant: secunda, possintne ipsæ redire: tertia, redeantne, aut aliquando rediuerint. Primam omnino credimus: secundam omnino negamus: tertiam distinguimus. Nam animæ nec per se vnquam redeunt redieruntve a statione sua in quam immigrarunt: nec ordinariè, voluntate sua aut nostra: sed tantum potentia diuina extra ordinem, & raro ad testificationem publicam gloriæ suæ. Propterea respondebat Abraham diuiti, Luc. de-cimo & vigesimo nono, Habent Mosem[?] & Prophetas, audiant eos: Et paulo post, Si Mosem[?] & Prophetas non audiunt, ne siquidem quispiam ex mortuis resurgat, persuadebuntur. Quæcunque apparitiones supra hunc modum sunt, a maligno sunt. hæc sententia Augustini in libro de cura pro-mortuis cap.15.& 16.contracta paucis: cui siquid amplius quisquam affinxerit,litet impudentiæ.
units.tr: 7. Art. 17. It is excessive impudence to deny that souls sometimes return to us at God's command or by his permission. These are different questions: first, whether God can cause them to return; second, whether they themselves can return; third, whether they do return, or have ever returned. The first we wholly believe, the second we wholly deny, and the third we distinguish. For souls never return of themselves, nor have they returned from the station into which they were received, nor do they return ordinarily at their own will or ours, but only by divine power, outside the ordinary course, and rarely, to give public testimony to his glory. That is why Abraham answered the rich man in Luke 16.29: They have Moses and the Prophets; let them hear them. And a little later: If they do not hear Moses and the Prophets, neither will they be persuaded though one rise from the dead. Whatever apparitions go beyond this pattern come from the evil one. This is Augustine's opinion in his book On the Care to Be Taken for the Dead, chapters 15 and 16, briefly summarised. If anyone adds anything more to it, it is mere impudence.

units.la: 8. Ibid. De regressu animarum ex omnibus receptaculis, praeterquam ex limbo puerorum.] Negamus ista.
units.tr: 8. Ibid. On the return of souls from all receptacles, except the limbo of children. We deny these things.

units.la: 9. Ibid. & in VII.Synodo,act.4.] Exempla hęc primum distingui necesse est ex iis principiis quæ nota 7.etiam Augustino auctore tradidimus. Tum videndum vtrum apparitione, an vero visione aut somnio per speciem animæ fuerint exhibitæ: vtrum ipsæ, an vero Angeli speciem præ se ferentes ipsarum: vtrum nudæ,an corporatæ: nam personæ ipsæ, ac non animæ solum adfuerunt Christo in transfiguratione. Postremo probandi & hic sunt spiritus, ne quando (vt fit plurimum hoc imperito seculo) pro thesauro carbones accidant: nam istius fabulæ scenici & munerarij diligentissimi sunt dæmones insidiantes saluti nostræ. De singulis vt dicamus,non est huius loci.
units.tr: 9. Ibid., and in the VII Synod, act 4. These examples must first be distinguished by the principles we laid down in note 7, also on Augustine's authority. Then one must see whether they were presented by an apparition, or by a vision or dream in the form of a soul; whether the souls themselves appeared, or Angels bearing their likeness; whether they were naked or embodied. For the persons themselves, not only souls, were present with Christ at the transfiguration. Finally, spirits must be tested here too, lest (as very often happens in this unskilled age) coals be taken for treasure. For the demons who lie in wait for our salvation are most diligent stage-players and jugglers in that fable. It is not the place here to discuss the individual cases.

units.la: 10. Art.18. Vbi Moses apparuit cum Helia in monte Thabor.] de limbo, negatum. de Samuele, Augustinus non affirmat plane, alibi diserte negat, vt in caput 6.docuimus. de Mose & Elia,constat rem extra ordinem dispensatione voluntatis diuinæ ad publicam testificationem gloriæ Dei & Christi confectam esse,vt nota 7.dicebamus. Res tanta,tam extra ordinem, quo iure trahi in exemplum potest,vt confirmetur fratri οὐτιδανῷ[?], siue (vt vulgus nostrate loquitur) Nihil-valet animam patris aut aui Θωσυντος[?] apparuisse?
units.tr: 10. Art. 18. Where Moses appeared with Elijah on Mount Tabor. On limbo, denied. On Samuel, Augustine does not affirm it plainly, and elsewhere expressly denies it, as we showed in chapter 6. On Moses and Elijah, it is established that the event was brought about outside the ordinary course, by the dispensation of the divine will, for public testimony to the glory of God and Christ, as we said in note 7. Such a great matter, so far outside the ordinary course, can by what right be drawn as an example to confirm that the soul of a father or grandfather appeared to a worthless [οὐτιδανῷ] brother, or, as the common people in our country put it, to a "Good-for-nothing"?

units.la: 11. Art.19. qui post triduū a morte se dixit condemnatū.] de Purgatorio,ante purgauimus lib.1. de regressu ex inferno testes certiores velim : nam ipse quoque Bellarminus negabat ante art. 2 & diues ille Luc. 16. fieri non posse nouerat: nam cur alios è sinu Abrahæ submitti voluisset? non ita ex inferno erumpunt animæ, ut ex suis aluearijs apum examina. Brunoniam illam fabulam cap. 4. nota 8. explosimus. Sequentia [illegible, ~5 letters]
units.tr: 11. Art. 19. who said that he had been condemned three days after his death. On Purgatory we purged it earlier, in book 1. On return from hell I would like more reliable witnesses. For Bellarmine himself denied it before art. 2, and that rich man in Luke 16 knew it could not be done. For why would he have wished others to be sent from Abraham's bosom? Souls do not burst out of hell like swarms of bees from their hives. We exploded that fable of Bruno in chapter 4, note 8. The following [illegible].

units.la: 12 Art.20. creduntur fuisse in Purgatorio, aut in limbo.] putantur recepto errore, non creduntur fides: nam fides est ex auditu verbi Dei, Rom. 10. negamus igitur.
units.tr: 12. Art. 20. are believed to have been in Purgatory or in limbo. They are thought to have been so through an accepted error; they are not believed by faith. For faith comes from hearing the word of God, Rom. 10. We therefore deny it.

units.la: 13 Art.21. quia alioqui iniuria illis facta fuisset.] & hæc ἐπιφυλλίδος καὶ συκοφαντίας[?] principio falso superstructa. negamus.
units.tr: 13. Art. 21. since otherwise a wrong would have been done to them. This too is built on a false principle, and is the work of [ἐπιφυλλίδος καὶ συκοφαντίας], carping and calumny. We deny it.

units.la: 14 Art. 22. nisi exstarent exempla quæ negari non possunt.] nos vero negamus pleraque, nimirum ea omnia quæ non facta sunt in eum modum quem circumscripsimus in nota 7.
units.tr: 14. Art. 22. unless examples existed which cannot be denied. We indeed deny most of them, namely all those that were not done in the manner we set out in note 7.

units.la: 15 Art.23. beatos iam exsistentes non posse revocari ad vitam.] quid ergo? Moses & Elias non fuerunt beati? negatio audax. Sed potius ita res habet: qui stationem in cælis habent, non nisi ex officio ab imperatore mandato veniunt ad nos, sive ordinario, ut Angeli & cælo, sive extraordinario per dispensationem singularem[?] ad obsequium voluntatis diuinæ & publicam testificationem gloriæ Dei, ut Moses & Elias. His autem migratione huiusmodi à Deo imperata non amplius decedit gloriæ & beatitudinis, quàm electis Angelis è cœlo descendentibus, quibus honori & gloriæ est Domino obsequi & seruire saluti nostræ. Sequentes igitur distinctiones falsæ, quarum nec auctoritas, nec certa ratio, nec exemplum adduci potest.
units.tr: 15. Art. 23. the blessed, already existing, cannot be recalled to life. What then? Were Moses and Elijah not blessed? That is a bold denial. Rather the case stands thus: those who have their station in heaven come to us only as a duty, sent by their commander, either in the ordinary way, as Angels do from heaven, or in an extraordinary way, by a singular dispensation, for the service of the divine will and for public testimony to the glory of God, as Moses and Elijah did. Yet such a migration commanded by God takes away nothing of their glory and blessedness, any more than it does from the elect Angels who descend from heaven, to whom it is an honour and glory to obey the Lord and serve our salvation. The following distinctions are therefore false, since neither authority, nor sound reason, nor example can be adduced for them.
