units.la: 16 Art. 27. non fuisse damnatos, sed suspensam eorumsententiam,] & illud Soti, & hoc Bellarmini est merum somnium. In hoc igitur Agnes exemplo (quod pono verum esse, Deus nouit) eadem ratio est dicenda plane, quę in exemplo Pauli Eutychum e morte excitantis, Act. 20. Eutychus sublatus est mortuus, ait Lucas, nempe soluta vnione personali inter animam & corpus ipsius: & tamen dicit ibidem Paulus, ne tumultuamini: anima enim eius in ipso est, tamquam si diceret, est quidem secundum vnionis personalis modum anima separata & soluta a corpore, sed non tamen separata loco, quia Deus dispensatione prouidentissima continuit eam in corpore, quamuis soluta vnione personali eius. Corpus in hoc mortuo non est amplius organum animæ, sed locus vel sedes illius, donec restituatur diuinitus & conferuescat vnio. Hic nihil migratione in cælum, limbum, Purgatorium, aut infernum opus, vbi anima ibidem esse dicitur, non agere in corpore tamen, cuius forma essentialis exsiterat. Sic ergo de illo Symphronij filio, quem coram Agne exstinxit dæmon, iudicium fieri potest, autore Apostolo Act. 20. pręsertim cum res eadem hora, non longo interuallo temporis dicatur contigisse. Non suspensa fuit sententia, quod vult Bellarminus, sed migratio e loco vel sede, quod vult Paulus & affirmat euidentissime.
units.tr: 16. Art. 27. They were not damned, but their sentence was suspended. That notion of Soto, and this of Bellarmine's, is sheer dream. In this example, then, of Agnes (which I take to be true, God knows), the same reasoning must plainly be applied as in the example of Paul raising Eutychus from death, Acts 20. "Eutychus was taken up dead," says Luke, namely with the personal union between his soul and body dissolved. Yet Paul says in the same place, "Do not make a tumult, for his soul is in him," as if to say: indeed, according to the mode of personal union the soul was separated and loosed from the body, but it was not separated in place, because God, by a most providential dispensation, kept it in the body, although its personal union was dissolved. In that dead man the body is no longer the organ of the soul, but its place or seat, until the union is divinely restored and warmth returns. Nothing of migration to heaven, limbo, Purgatory or hell is at work here, where the soul is said to be present yet is not acting in the body of which it was the essential form. So, too, concerning that son of Symphronius, whom the demon extinguished in Agnes's presence, judgment can be made on the authority of the Apostle, Acts 20, especially since the thing is said to have happened in the same hour, not after any long interval of time. The sentence was not suspended, as Bellarmine wants; there was a migration from place or seat, as Paul wants and affirms most clearly.

units.la: In Cap. IX.
units.tr: On Chapter IX.

units.la: {1}Art. 1. de tempore, quo Purgatorium permanebit,] Purgatorium non esse docuimus lib. 1. nec ergo datur illius tempus. Hæc itaque omnia nihil ad nos.
units.tr: {1} Art. 1. concerning the time during which Purgatory will last,] We have shown in Book 1 that there is no Purgatory, so there is no time for it either. All of this therefore has nothing to do with us.

units.la: 2 Ibid. nemo enim absque sordibus resurgere potuit.]vide in cap.1. nota 2.& 5.Sequens Augustini locus vitiose adducitur, & ante confutata est Bellarmini ex eo argumentatio lib. 1. cap. 10. nota 44.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. for no one could rise without filth.] See on chapter 1, notes 2 and 5. The following passage of Augustine is wrongly cited, and Bellarmine's argument from it was refuted earlier, in Book 1, chapter 10, note 44.

units.la: 3 Art.5. nullum aliud esse Purgatorium praeter mortem.]Lutheri locum adduci oportuit: nam hoc nunquam dixit Lutherus simpliciter. in dolore quidem mortis purgari reliquias peccati dixit per gratiam, sed dolore mortis purgari minime. Frustra itaque sequens disputatio.
units.tr: 3 Art. 5. that there is no other Purgatory besides death.] Luther's passage ought to have been cited, for Luther never said this simply. He did say that the remnants of sin are purged through grace in the pain of death, but he did not say they are purged by the pain of death. The following disputation is therefore pointless.

units.la: 4 Art.7. omnes istos habitus tolli per primum actum contrarium animae separatae:] negatur. mali habitus non tolluntur actu nostro ullo, anima coniuncta aut separata a corpore, sed tolluntur sola Dei gratia in Christo per Spiritum sanctum transmittentem animas ab impuritate ipsarum ad puritatem filiorum Dei. hic actus in morte nostra plane diui-nus est: quapropter Paulus adoptionem nostram vocat redemptionem corporis nostri, Rom. 8.23.
units.tr: 4 Art. 7. all these habits are removed by the first act contrary to the separated soul.] Denied. Evil habits are not removed by any act of ours, whether the soul is joined to or separated from the body. They are removed solely by the grace of God in Christ, through the Holy Spirit, who transfers souls from their impurity to the purity of the sons of God. This act in our death is plainly divine; therefore Paul calls our adoption the redemption of our body, Rom. 8.23.

units.la: 5 Art. 8. partim purgari, partim non purgari.]hæc negamus omnia, ut libro 1.
units.tr: 5 Art. 8. partly purged, partly not purged.] We deny all of this, as in Book 1.

units.la: 6 Art. 9. martyrium, sine dubio purgat omnes huius-modi reliquias.]non martyrium, sed Christus viuens & agens in martyre per Spiritum sanctum inhabitantem & inambulantem in ipso, 2. Cor. 6.16. Atque haec sententia locorum sequentium.
units.tr: 6 Art. 9. martyrdom undoubtedly purges all remnants of this kind.] It is not martyrdom but Christ, living and acting in the martyr through the Holy Spirit who dwells in him and walks in him, 2 Cor. 6.16. This is the sense of the following passages.

units.la: 7 Art.10. si in morte deberent purgari reliquiae pec-catorum, necessario contrarium fieri deberet.] aliud est in morte purgari, aliud morte, quę iste artifex confundit ut imperitos fallat. non morte purgantur homines, sed gratia Dei in morte per Christum, ut nota 3.dicebamus.
units.tr: 7 Art. 10. if the remnants of sin had to be purged in death, the contrary would necessarily have to happen.] Being purged in death is one thing, and death is another, and this craftsman confuses the two to deceive the unlearned. Men are not purged by death, but by the grace of God in death, through Christ, as I said in note 3.

units.la: 8 Art. 11. quorum patientia sine dubio iuuat ad satisfaciendum, ] at non ad satisfaciendum Deo, ut purgentur peccata satisfactione ipsorum. hoc tomo 3. & 4. confutabimus. Sequens disputatio tota, ut olim de Adonidae fertur dixisse Hercules. οὐδὲν ὑπάρχει[?] fabulae sunt vanissimae: nihil ad nos.
units.tr: 8 Art. 11. whose patience undoubtedly helps toward making satisfaction,] but not toward making satisfaction to God, so that sins are purged by their satisfaction. We will refute this in volumes 3 and 4. The whole following disputation is like what Hercules is said once to have said of Adonis: it is nothing [οὐδὲν ὑπάρχει]. These are the emptiest fables: nothing to do with us.

units.la: 9 Art.15. Res igitur est incertissima, ] imo vanissima salsissimaque. Propterea ad utiliora transeamus.
units.tr: 9 Art. 15. The matter is therefore most uncertain,] Indeed it is most empty and most absurd. Therefore let us pass on to more useful matters.

units.la: IN CAP. X.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER X.

units.la: 1 Art.1. De poena Purgatorij quaedam sunt certa, & quaedam dubia.] imo certissima omnia, nec Purgatorium esse, nec poenam illius. Quamobrem quid hic laterem lauari attinet?
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. Some things about the punishment of Purgatory are certain, and some are doubtful.] Indeed, all of them are most certain: there is no Purgatory and no punishment of it. Why then should I bother to wash a brick here?

units.la: 2 Art. 4. Quod enim aliquis ignis sit in Purgatorio, & inferno, ] de Purgatorio, negamus, & probationes emendicatas refellimus in lib. 1. de inferno, concedimus.
units.tr: 2 Art. 4. For that there is some fire in Purgatory and in hell,] Concerning Purgatory we deny it, and we refute the borrowed proofs in Book 1. Concerning hell we concede it.

units.la: IN CAP. XI.
units.tr: ON CHAPTER XI.

units.la: 1 Art.1. tamen est sententia probabilissima.] negatur: nam qui ignem aeternum materialem & elementarem facit, confundit naturae inferioris cum superiore, & temporis cum aeternitate modum: quę res pugnat cum principiis veritatis.
units.tr: 1 Art. 1. nevertheless it is the most probable opinion.] Denied. For whoever makes the eternal fire material and elemental confuses the nature of the lower with the higher, and the measure of time with eternity; a thing that is at odds with the principles of truth.

units.la: 2 Art.3. dicit enim statim corporaliter urere.] Scholasticorum consensum non moramur, qui sumus discipuli Christi, & audimus veritatem eius. Gregorium vero, Deus bone, quàm male Bellarminus accipit: non typographi error est, vir bone, quum legitur incorporeus apud illum, sed typhi tui error est, quum iubes legi corporeus. Nam illud nisi ser- ues, tota oppositio & gratia sermonis Gregoriani concidit. Hæc verba illius in Iob.2o.[?] Sequitur, deuo- rabit eum ignis qui non succenditur. Miro valde modo paucis verbis expressus est ignis gehennæ. Ignis namque corporeus, ut esse ignis valeat, corporeis indiget fo- mentis: qui, quum necesse est ut seruetur, per congesta ligna proculdubio nutritur, nec valet, nisi succensus, esse, & nisi refotus, subsistere. At contra gehennæ ignis cum sit incorporeus, & in se missos reprobos corporaliter exu- rat, nec studio humano succenditur, nec lignis nutritur, sed creatus semel durat inexstinguibilis: & succensione non indiget, & ardore non caret. Nec secus in anti- quis exemplaribus & idoneis legitur, quæ interpo- lare, Bellarmine, non est tuum. Quid dico, non esse tuum? imo vero vestrum opus est memoria nostra, at non officium vestrum: quod clamant Expurga- torij vestrorum indices quotidie locupletissima fœtura subolescentes. At, inquis, dicit Gregorius ignem illum reprobos corporaliter exurere. Rectè id quidem: sed fallis ambigue. Nam istud corpora- liter: aut ratione subiecti dicitur, quod sit corpora- le, aut ratione obiecti, quod sit corpus, aut ratione denique corporalis modi. De obiecto Gregorius loquitur, non de subiecto, ut vis. Sensus enim est, ignem illum quamuis incorporeum, personas totas exercere, etiam ipsarum corpora, quamuis non corporali modo. Non decet a viro sanctimoniam profitente sanctum Gregorium vestrum ita adte- grari.
units.tr: 2 Art. 3. for he says at once that it burns bodily.] We do not delay over the consensus of the Schoolmen, since we are disciples of Christ and hear his truth. But Gregory, good God, how badly Bellarmine understands him! It is not a printer's error, good sir, when the text reads incorporeal in him; it is the error of your own stupidity when you order it to be read corporeal. For unless you keep the former, the whole contrast and the grace of Gregory's words collapse. These are his words on Job: It follows, the fire that is not kindled will devour him. The fire of gehenna is expressed in a remarkably striking way in few words. For bodily fire, if it is to be fire, needs bodily fuel; since it must be kept alive, it is undoubtedly nourished by the wood heaped upon it, and it cannot exist unless it is kindled, nor subsist unless it is fed. But on the contrary, the fire of gehenna, since it is incorporeal, burns bodily the reprobate who are cast into it, and it is not kindled by human effort nor nourished by wood, but once created it lasts unquenchable; it needs no kindling and lacks no heat. Nor is it read otherwise in the ancient and reliable copies, which it is not your business to alter, Bellarmine. What am I saying, not your business? Indeed, our memory is your work, though not your office; as the indexes of your Purgatory, growing daily into a most abundant brood, cry out. But you say that Gregory says that fire burns the reprobate bodily. Rightly so, but you deceive by ambiguity. For that bodily is said either with respect to the subject, that the fire is corporeal; or with respect to the object, that the thing burned is a body; or finally with respect to the manner of bodily action. Gregory speaks of the object, not of the subject, as you pretend. For the meaning is that that fire, although incorporeal, afflicts whole persons, even their bodies, though not in a bodily manner. It is not becoming for a man professing holiness to mangle holy Gregory in this way.

units.la: 3 Art. 4. in eamdem sententiam propendet lib.xi. cap.io. de civitate Dei.] falsum. Nam Augustinus ex hypothesi capitis proximè præcedentis ibidem loquitur. Statuerat autem ignem eodem modo ac vermem aut corporalem, aut spiritualem dici oportere, aut vtrumque: quod postremum etsi dicit credibilibus, tamen suspendit iudicium suum, & lectori pio permittit. Ex hac igitur hypothesi in quaestione instituta Augustinus pergit capite 10. haesitans, non afferens. Sed esto: at idem tamen distinguit lib. 12. de Genesi ad literam cap. 32. nam vt corporalia esse statuit quibus affliguntur corpora, ita etiam de anima ex contrario dicit: Quamvis non sint corporalia, sed similia corporalibus, quibus anima corporibus exuta afficiuntur, seu bene seu male, cum ipsa corporibus suis similes sibimet appareant, sunt tamen & vera laetitia & vera molestia facta de substantia spiritali, &c.
units.tr: 3 Art. 4. he leans toward the same opinion in book 11, chapter 10, of The City of God.] False. For Augustine there speaks from the hypothesis of the chapter immediately preceding. He had stated that fire, like the worm, ought to be called either corporeal or spiritual, or both; and although he says the last is credible, he suspends his judgment and leaves it to the pious reader. Therefore, from this hypothesis in the question he has raised, Augustine goes on in chapter 10 hesitating, not asserting. But grant it: yet in Book 12 of the literal commentary on Genesis, chapter 32, he makes the same distinction. For just as he holds that the things by which bodies are afflicted are corporeal, so conversely he says of the soul: Although they are not corporeal, but similar to corporeal things, by which souls, stripped of their bodies, are affected, whether well or ill, since they appear to themselves like their own bodies, nevertheless both true joy and true distress are made from a spiritual substance, etc.

units.la: 4 Articul. 5. vt verba Scripturarum accipiantur proprie, quando nihil absurdi sequitur.
units.tr: Article 4, Point 5: The words of Scripture are to be taken literally, when nothing absurd follows.

units.la: ] Atqui nomen ignis proprie si acceperis, aliquid absurdi sequitur, accipiendum ergo figurate. Absurda sequi demonstramus natura, ratione, & analogia. Natura: nam nihil materiatum & physicum absolute potest per se aut in se capere proprietates supernaturales, vt sunt aeternitas, & sedes futuri seculi: ignis corporalis materiatus & physicus est: ergo non est proprietatum supernaturalium capax, in caelo aut inferno esse, in aeternum durare non potest. At corpus nostrum, inquies, capax futurum est. Recte: sed non per se haec capiet, sed per animam, non in se proprie, sed in persona: quemadmodum hic contrario anima nostrae non per se, sed per corpus in persona sunt capaces Physici temporis loci: Quæ res de igne, verme, similibusque non possunt affirmari. Ratione: nam omne agens agit per formam & potentiam actiuam suam in subiecto capace solum, potentiaque passiua praedito: Res autem spirituales & metaphysicæ, vt dæmones, non habent potentiam illam passiuam quæ sit susceptibilis (vt loquuntur) vel capax potentiæ agentis à materiali igne: ergo in eas, & in dæmonas non agit ignis elementaris ille. Est autem idem ignis corporum damnatorum, & spirituum incorporalium, vt ex Augustino lib. 21. de ciuit. Dei, cap. 9. disputator arguit sequente articulo: non igitur infernalis, ignis materiatus & corporalis est. Analogia: nam quæ ratio est ignis in inferno, eadem ratio lucis analogicè est in paradiso, & contrà: lux autem in paradiso gaudiaque cætera non sunt corporalia, licet ad corpus per vnionem & consensum cum anima pertinentia: ergo nec ignis inferni tormentorumque instrumeta in eo sūt corporalia. Sed jā satis est.
units.tr: But if you take the word "fire" literally, something absurd follows, so it must be taken figuratively. We demonstrate that absurdities follow from nature, from reason, and from analogy. From nature: nothing material and physical can, in itself or of itself, receive supernatural properties, such as eternity and the abode of the future age. Corporeal fire is material and physical. Therefore it cannot receive supernatural properties, nor can it exist in heaven or hell or last for eternity. But you will say that our body will be capable of them. Quite so, but it will not receive them of itself, nor literally in itself, but through the soul and in the person. In the same way, our souls are not capable of the things of this present time and place of themselves, but through the body and in the person. This cannot be affirmed of fire, a worm, or similar things. From reason: every agent acts through its form and active power only upon a subject that is capable and endowed with a passive power. Spiritual and metaphysical beings, such as demons, do not have that passive power which is receptive of (as they say) or capable of the power of an agent derived from material fire. Therefore that elemental fire does not act upon them or upon demons. Moreover, the fire of the damned bodies and of incorporeal spirits is the same, as the disputant argues from Augustine, City of God, book 21, chapter 9, in the following article. Therefore the fire of hell is not material and corporeal. From analogy: whatever is the reason for fire in hell, the same reason by analogy holds for light in paradise, and conversely. But the light in paradise and the other joys are not corporeal, although they pertain to the body through union and agreement with the soul. Therefore neither is the fire of hell nor the instruments of torment in it corporeal. But enough of this.

units.la: 5 Art. 6. corpora damnatorum punientur igne post resurrectionem:] sed igne figuratè dicto & analogicè:prout res noui testamenti veteribus umbraculis, & res seculi venturi præsentibus adumbrari solent, & spirituales corporalibus. Nihil sequitur mutato prædicationis genere.
units.tr: Article 5, Point 6: The bodies of the damned will be punished with fire after the resurrection. But the fire is named figuratively and by analogy, just as the things of the new covenant are commonly shadowed forth by the old shadows, and the things of the age to come by things present, and spiritual things by corporeal ones. Nothing follows when the mode of predication is changed.

units.la: 6 Art. 7. per qua peccat quis, per hæc & torquetur,] auctor Sapientiæ accipit voce qua pro eo quod est qualia: vt intelligatur de reb. obiectis & subiectis pro modo ipsarum analogicè. non sequitur ex homonymia. Demonstrat quod dicimus ipsa hypothe-sis, unde hæc thesis eruitur. Proximè enim hæc præcesserant Sapi.ii.16. Pro insipientibus aute ratiocinationibus iniustitiæ ipsorum, quibus errantes colebant repti-lia rationis expertia & viles bestias, misisti contra eos multitudinem animantium rationis expertium ad vin-dictam: ut cognoscerent per quæ peccat quis, &c. non autem peccaverant per animantia, etiam reptilia, sed per eorum similitudines.
units.tr: Article 7, Point 6: By what things a man sins, by these also he is tormented. The author of Wisdom takes the word "by what" (qua) for "of what kind" (qualia), so that it is understood of things objective and subjective, according to their manner, by analogy. It does not follow from the ambiguity of the word. He demonstrates by the hypothesis itself what we say, from which this thesis is drawn out. For immediately before this, Wisdom xi.16 had said: "But for the ungodly reasonings of their injustice, by which, erring, they worshipped reptiles without reason and vile beasts, you sent against them a multitude of irrational animals as vengeance, so that they might know by what things a man sins," and so on. But they had not sinned by animals, even reptiles, but by their likenesses.

units.la: 7 Art.8.de quibus diximus cap. 6.] & nos ibidem confutavimus,
units.tr: Article 8: of which we spoke in chapter 6. We also refuted them in that same place.

units.la: In Cap. XII.
units.tr: In Chapter XII.

units.la: 1 Quomodo ignis corporeus agat in animam incorpoream:] nos negamus in eam per se agere, imo etiam in inferno esse ignem corporeum. Quapropter hæc nos minime feriunt.
units.tr: Point 1: How corporeal fire acts upon an incorporeal soul. We deny that it acts upon it of itself, and indeed that corporeal fire is in hell at all. So these points do not touch us in the least.

units.la: 2 & cum illo simul gaudere & pati,]nempe fit per consensum atque sympathiam ex unione naturali, & συναφεία[?] essentiali ipsorum inter se.
units.tr: Point 2: And to rejoice and suffer together with it. Namely, this happens through agreement and sympathy arising from natural union, and [συναφεία] essential mutual connection of the two.

units.la: 3 Cum inter corpus & spiritum nulla sit proportio?] falsum: nam etsi proportio non est secundum essentiam, est tamen secundum naturam eadem proportio quæ inter materiam formamque essentialem intercedit. proportio est non substantiæ, sed modi.huius autem unionis modus est naturalis, ex naturæ totius,superioris & inferioris harmonia.
units.tr: Point 3: Since there is no proportion between body and spirit? This is false. For although the proportion is not according to essence, it is nevertheless according to nature the same proportion that lies between matter and essential form. It is a proportion not of substance but of mode. The mode of this union, however, is natural, arising from the harmony of the whole nature, superior and inferior.

units.la: 4 ita potest[?] uniri[?] spiritus igni, ut ab illo pœnam tra-hat.] Non sequitur ex dispari: quod modo ostendimus.
units.tr: Point 4: so the spirit can be united with fire, so as to suffer punishment from it. It does not follow from an unlike case, as we have just shown.

units.la: In Cap. XIII.
units.tr: In Chapter XIII.

units.la: 1 Art.2.Maneat igitur & hoc inter secreta, quæ suo tempore nobis aperientur.] imo vero inter falsa deputetur, quæ suo tempore imperitis retegentur à Domino per gratiam.
units.tr: Article 2: Let this therefore remain among the secrets, which will be revealed to us in their time. Indeed rather it should be counted among falsehoods, which will in their time be uncovered by the Lord through grace to the unlearned.

units.la: In Cap. XIV.
units.tr: In Chapter XIV.

units.la: 1 Art. 1. pœnas Purgatorij esse atrocissimas,] negamus Purgatorium, & pœnas illius, velut commentitia ipsius accidentia: & priscos Patres id negamus dicere.
units.tr: Article 1: the punishments of Purgatory are most atrocious. We deny Purgatory, and its punishments, as the made-up accidents of it; and we deny that the earlier Fathers said so.

units.la: 2 Ibid. grauior tamen erit ille ignis, quàm quicquid potest homo pati in hac vita ] vide in lib. 1. cap. io. no-ta 48.
units.tr: Ibid.: Yet that fire will be heavier than whatever a man can suffer in this life. See in book 1, chapter 10, note 48.

units.la: 3 Ibid. & B. Bernardus serm. de obitu Humberti.] hi omnes testes inde à Gregorio sunt recentioris & corruptioris in hoc argumento seculi. horum ergo negatur auctoritas. Reuelationum, quæ proximè adferuntur, eadem est, atque haud scio an ridicula forte sit magis plurimarum auctoritas.
units.tr: Ibid.: and St. Bernard, sermon on the death of Humbert. All these witnesses from Gregory onward belong to a more recent and more corrupt age on this question. Their authority is therefore denied. The authority of the revelations, which are brought forward next, is of the same kind; I do not know whether it is not rather ridiculous, as with very many of them.

units.la: 4 Art. 3. probat ratio, saltem de pœna sensus] negatur: nam ii[?] pœna non est ( non est autem ) certè nec maior, nec minor est, quod non est, id gradus habere non potest. Sequentia ergo nihil ad rem.
units.tr: Article 3: Reason proves, at least concerning the punishment of sense. This is denied. For that punishment is not (and indeed is not) certainly neither greater nor less; what is not, cannot have degrees. What follows therefore has nothing to do with the matter.

units.la: 5 Art. 8. quæ sententia mihi placet:] nobis neutra probatur, quibus nota est fabula Purgatorij.
units.tr: Article 8: which opinion pleases me. Neither opinion is approved by us, to whom the fable of Purgatory is known.

units.la: 6 Art. 12. per quam intelligunt omnes pœnam sen-sus, non damni.] id numquam Augustinus dixit, vt lib. 1 ca. io. docuimus. Aliis humaniter ignoscimus.
units.tr: Article 12: by which all understand the punishment of sense, not of loss. Augustine never said this, as we have taught in book 1, chapter 10. We pardon others with kindness.

units.la: 7 Art 13. apud Bedam lib. 5 hist. cap. 13 ] ista reue-lationum incerta, vana, falsa, fallacia, flocci non facimus. Sequentia omnia Lamiæ (quod aiunt) turres, γραῦς ὑϑλῶν[?].
units.tr: Article 13: in Bede, Ecclesiastical History, book 5, chapter 13. These uncertain, vain, false, deceptive revelations we do not value a whit. All the following are, as they say, the towers of the Lamiae, old wives' fables [γραῦς ὑϑλῶν].

units.la: In Cap. XV.
units.tr: On Chapter 15.

units.la: 1 Art. 2. quæ omnia peti debent ex prima quæstio-ne.] vide libro 1. ca. 3. & sequentibus. Negamus autem suffragia vivorum prodesse defunctis in per-sona eorum apudDeum ad remissionem peccatorum & salutem ipsorum. Alioquin non negamus ea de-functis prodesse in memoria ipsorum apud homi-nes, & in necessariis posterisque ipsorum apud Deum & homines, ad ea omnia quibus homines oratione alij aliis subvenire possunt, aut pia & hu-mana commendatione.
units.tr: 1 Art. 2. all of which ought to be sought from the first question.] See book 1, ch. 3 and following. We deny, however, that the prayers of the living profit the dead in respect of their person before God for the forgiveness of sins and their salvation. Otherwise we do not deny that these things profit the dead in their memory among men, and in their needs and their posterity before God and men, for all those things by which men can help one another by prayer, or by pious and humane commendation.

units.la: 2 Art. 3. ergo debet habere communicationem tam capitis cum membris, quàm membrorum inter se.] con-ceditur: verumtamen non quamlibet, sed analogam tum modulo cuiusque membri, tum modo ordinationis ipsorum inter se. Sine hac distinctione propositio universalis si fiat, falsa est.
units.tr: 2 Art. 3. therefore there ought to be communion both of the head with the members and of the members among themselves.] This is granted, but not with just any communion; it must be proportionate both to the measure of each member and to the manner of their arrangement among themselves. Without this distinction, if the universal proposition is made, it is false.

units.la: 3 Ibid. igitur viventes possunt ac debent iuuare defunctos, vt membra eiusdem corporis.] Conceditur, quia possunt pro suo modulo, & debent ordinatione Dei. Non possunt autem iuuare defunctos in personam ipsorum apud Deum ad remissionem peccatorum, &c. vt nota 1. diximus, nec debent ordinatione Dei, quod isti volunt.
units.tr: 3 Ibid. therefore the living can and ought to help the dead, as members of the same body.] Granted, because they can according to their measure, and ought by God's ordinance. But they cannot help the dead in their person before God for the forgiveness of sins, etc., as we said in note 1, nor ought they by God's ordinance to do what these men want.

units.la: 4 Art. 4. viventes mortuis, & mortui viventibus prosint.] Primum dispar ratio est capitis, unde totum corpus coagmentatur, Eph. 4. & membrorum eius. Secundo conceditur argumentatio bene accepta, puta si intelligatur de vnoquoque membro analogicè, id est, secundum modulum cuiusque, & ordinationem Dei quæ distinxit vocationem vniuscuiusque membri in corpore. Nam, exempli causa, Angeli ipsi possunt ac debent nos hic iuuare ex officio communi, sed neque amplius possunt quàm fert modulus ipsorum, neque amplius debent quàm ordinauit Deus, qui præfigit vocationem ipsorum singulariter. Sequens probatio inutilis: quis enim beneficia Christi in quoslibet vocat in controuersiam? at membrorum ratio omnino dispar.
units.tr: 4 Art. 4. the living benefit the dead, and the dead the living.] First, the case of the head is unlike, from which the whole body is fitted together (Eph. 4), and unlike the case of its members. Second, the argument is granted when rightly understood, that is, if it is understood of each member analogically, according to the measure of each and the ordinance of God who distinguished the calling of each member in the body. For example, the angels themselves can and ought to help us here by their common office, but they can do no more than their measure bears, nor ought they more than God has ordained, who prescribes their calling individually. The following proof is useless: for who calls the benefits of Christ into dispute for anyone at all? But the case of the members is wholly unlike.

units.la: 5 Art.6. defunctorum animae cum Christo regnantes orent pro sanctorum animabus in Purgatorio laborantibus.]hoc recte Dominicus a Soto negauit: nos rectius, qui Purgatorium negamus ipsum.
units.tr: 5 Art. 6. the souls of the dead, reigning with Christ, pray for the souls of the saints who are suffering in Purgatory.] Dominicus a Soto rightly denied this; we more rightly, who deny Purgatory itself.

units.la: 6 Ibid. & eius precibus mortui animam commendet.] haec quidem Augustinus dicit communi errori cedens, & ex hypothesi. Error plus satis inualuerat orationes fundendi pro defunctis: hypothesis erat animas defunctorum non frui visione Dei, sed luce illius in resurrectionis mora. Errorem itaque Augustinus, & ad Episcopum paulo superstitioso-rem scribens, noluit pertinaciter oppugnare: sed ita respondet ambagibus, ut non obscure ostendat se aliter malle, si posset commode obtineri. Nam propterea haec verba praemittit ibidem: Quod si verum est, profecto etiam prouisus sepeliendis corporibus apud memoriam sanctorum locus, bona affectionis humanae est erga funera suorum: quoniam si nonnulla religio est ut sepeliantur, non potest nulla esse, quando ubi sepeliantur attenditur. Sed quum talia vivorum solatia requirantur, quibus eorum pius in suos animus apparet, non video quae sint adiumenta mortuorum. hactenus Augustini simplex sententia. Postea vero ex hypothesi illius sententiae Patrum de statu defunctorum, recepto iam errori cedens, & quem Paulinus literis suis propugnauerat, subiicit illico per concess-ionis modum ista: nisi ad hoc, ut dum recolunt ubi sint positae eorum quos diligunt corpora, eisdem sanctis illos tamquam patronis susceptos apud Dominum adiuuan-dos orando commendent. Prudentior fuit Augustinus quàm ut affirmaret, sed modestior quàm ut publicum Ecclesiæ aut bonos errantes statim commoneret. Priora sunt affirmationis veræ, posteriora, humanæ concessionis ad pacem publicam in Ecclesia Dei continendam.
units.tr: 6 Ibid. and by her prayers let the dead commend his soul.] Augustine indeed says this yielding to the common error, and by way of hypothesis. The error had already gained far too much strength, namely pouring out prayers for the dead; the hypothesis was that the souls of the dead do not enjoy the vision of God, but only its light during the delay before the resurrection. Therefore Augustine, writing to a bishop who was a little too superstitious, did not wish to attack the error stubbornly, but answers with such circumlocution that he does not obscurely show he would prefer otherwise, if it could be conveniently obtained. For he prefaces these words in the same place: But if it is true, surely a place near the memorial of the saints for burying bodies is also a good of human affection toward the funerals of one's own; for if there is some religion in being buried, there cannot be none when attention is paid to where they are buried. But since such comforts of the living are sought, by which their pious feeling toward their own appears, I do not see what aids there are for the dead. Thus far the simple opinion of Augustine. Afterwards, however, from the hypothesis of that opinion of the Fathers about the state of the dead, yielding to the error now received, and which Paulinus had defended in his letters, he immediately adds by way of concession: unless to this end, that while they recall where the bodies of those they love have been laid, they may commend them, taken up by the same saints as patrons, to be helped before the Lord by prayer. Augustine was too prudent to affirm, but too modest to warn the public of the Church or the well-meaning erring at once. The former statements are of a true affirmation; the latter, of a human concession, made to keep public peace in the Church of God.

units.la: 7 Ibid. ut B. Maria intercedente & omnibus Sanctis, animas defunctorum ad perpetuæ beatitudinis consortium peruenire concedat. ] exemplum est erroris communis, qui præiudicare non debet veritati in Ecclesia, columna veritatis.
units.tr: 7 Ibid. that through the intercession of the Blessed Virgin Mary and all the saints, God may grant that the souls of the dead attain the fellowship of everlasting blessedness.] This is an example of common error, which ought not to prejudice the truth in the Church, the pillar of truth.

units.la: 8 Art. 7. visos fuisse orare pro populo Iudæorum viuentium. ] somnium est, non res gesta: quid ex eo concludas certò?tum levis est scripti illius fides atque auctoritas negatur.
units.tr: 8 Art. 7. that they were seen to pray for the living people of the Jews.] It is a dream, not an event that happened. What can you conclude from it with certainty? Moreover, the trustworthiness and authority of that writing is slight, and it is denied.

units.la: 9 Ibid. beneficia exhibita à sanctis defunctis, hominibus hic viuentibus, innumerabilia & certissima sunt.] negamus. Non enim sequitur à sanctis defunctis fuisse exhibita, si in specie ipsorum per visionem aut somnium. A Deo ipso beneficia sunt, etiam per Angelos, quum ita videtur, præstita: ad quæ familiaris species non raro fuit adhibita, propter eos qui beneficia commodius ad signi istius visum erant percepturi. Et quàm multis visa sunt multa, quæ non fuerunt! quàm multa ex opinione, & relatione incerta aut imprudente perscripta! quàm multa superstitiosè ficta!
units.tr: 9 Ibid. the benefits bestowed by the holy dead upon men living here are innumerable and most certain.] We deny it. For it does not follow that they were bestowed by the holy dead if this happened in their form, through a vision or a dream. The benefits come from God himself, even when they are supposedly conferred through angels; to these a familiar appearance was not infrequently applied, for the sake of those who were going to receive the benefits more conveniently at the sight of that sign. And how many things have been seen by many which were not! How many things written down from opinion, and from uncertain or careless report! How many things superstitiously invented!

units.la: 10 Ibid. & Petro Damiano in epist. de miraculis sui temporis.] negatur ita esse: nam ubi locorum Purgatorium est? negatur illorum auctoritate in hac causa confirmari aut probari quicquam posse, qui & communi errore detinebantur, & sine cognitione iudicioque relationes horum & illorum, quos viros bonos putabant, perscripserunt. Iltiusmodi fabulas perscribat Danae filia ἐνεσιόν. Sequentia omnia falsæ hypothesi superstruuntur, quam libro I. confutauimus, Purgatorium esse, &c. negamus.
units.tr: 10 Ibid. and to Peter Damian in his letter on the miracles of his own time.] It is denied that it is so, for where is Purgatory located? It is denied that anything can be confirmed or proved in this cause by the authority of those who were both held by the common error and who wrote down the reports of these and those, whom they thought good men, without knowledge or judgment. Let Danae's daughter write such fables [ἐνεσιόν]. Everything that follows is built on a false hypothesis, which we refuted in book I: that Purgatory exists, etc. We deny it.

units.la: Art.8. cum tamen nec illi viderent Deum.] falsum: & probatio falsa, vt nota 8. dictum.
units.tr: Art. 8. since they did not see God either.] False; and the proof is false, as was said in note 8.

units.la: Art.9. dies in inferno orabat pro fratribus suis, Luc.16.] parabola est causa Pharisæorum appolita, vt diximus supra cap. 6. nota 9. ex cuius singulis partibus argumentationes erui est iniquissimum. Tum esto: nempe dies ille pro iis orabat à quibus recens discesserat perspecta constitutione ipsorum, vt Augustinus quoque obseruauit: an continuo pro quibusuis orent, vt volunt Pontificij? sequentia de pœnis Purgatorij negamus, & doloribus illius.
units.tr: Art. 9. the rich man in hell prayed for his brothers, Luke 16.] The parable is a case addressed to the Pharisees, as we said above in ch. 6, note 9, and it is most unjust to draw arguments from each single part of it. Grant it: namely that that man prayed for those from whom he had recently departed, their disposition being clearly known, as Augustine also observed. Do they pray at once for anyone at all, as the Papists want? The statements that follow about the punishments of Purgatory and its pains we deny.

units.la: Ibid. dolor animabus non perturbat vllo modo iudicium rationis, nec impedit affectum bonum voluntatis:] intellige de iis quæ sunt in Purgatorio (quod negamus) ex disputatoris hypothesi. Alioquin animæ quæ in inferno sunt, & sua vitiositate, & pœnis, & dolore suo perturbantur, Scriptura teste.
units.tr: Ibid. pain does not in any way disturb the judgment of reason in souls, nor does it hinder the good affection of the will:] Understand this of those things which are in Purgatory (which we deny), on the hypothesis of the disputant. Otherwise the souls which are in hell are disturbed both by their wickedness and by their punishments and their sorrow, as Scripture testifies.

units.la: Art. 11. sicut nos de illis solum in genere scimus eas valde torqueri,] negamus: nec in genere, nec in specie, nec in individuo scimus ista, sed contra nullam in Purgatorio esse tam certum est quàm quod certissimum.
units.tr: Art. 11. just as we know of them only in general that they are greatly tormented,] We deny it. We know these things neither in general, nor in particular, nor individually; on the contrary, it is as certain that there is nothing of the kind in Purgatory as anything can be most certain.

units.la: Ibid. cur non etiam prodesse poterunt vivi mortuis?] ex falsis antecedentibus conclusio falsa, nisi modificetur ea distinctione quam nota 1. tradidimus.
units.tr: Ibid. why then can the living not also profit the dead?] A false conclusion from false premises, unless it is qualified by the distinction we set out in note 1.

units.la: Art. 13. nec posse illis uti propria actione, vt comedendo, bibendo, eleemosynas faciendo, &c.] falsa est antecedentis restrictio. Nam sapiens in eo loco non agit de rebus, sed de omnibus hominibus, quicunque tandem illi sint, secundum essentiam, potentiam, & opus ipsorum vniuersè. Demonstrant praecedentia, vbi vnum euentum ipsis omnibus dicit obtingere secundum haec omnia, non autem secundum hoc vel illud solum, quem sermonem prosequutus sapiens copiosius hominem hortatur, ut vitam suam instituat commodè, cùm mortui horum quicquam nec sciant, nec scire possint. Hic disputator rem vniuersè dictam restringit particulariter. Ex hac autem sententia vniuersè dicta omnino sequitur, mortuos à nobis iuuari non posse, cùm nihil nostrum scire possint, quanto minus reipsa percipere ex opere nostro?
units.tr: Art. 13. nor can they use their own actions, such as eating, drinking, giving alms, etc.] The restriction of the antecedent is false. For the wise man in that place is not speaking of things, but of all men, whoever they may be, universally according to their essence, power and work. The preceding words show this, where he says that one event befalls all of them according to all these things, and not according to this or that alone. Pursuing this discourse, the wise man more fully exhorts a man to order his life well, since the dead know none of these things and cannot know them. Here the disputant restricts particularly what was said universally. But from this universal statement it wholly follows that the dead cannot be helped by us, since they can know nothing of what we do, much less actually perceive it from our work?

units.la: 17 Art.15. Ambrosium hic agere de pompa funeris, quam merito vult esse moderatam. ] negatur restrictio: loquitur Ambrosius vniuersè, & ex Abrahami exemplo docet mortuos omnino Deo permittendos post honestam funerationem: eorum esse qui spem non habent, ut defunctorum cineres amplius sollicitent, aut animas inquietent. rectè ergo Caluinus argumentatus est.
units.tr: 17 Art.15. Ambrose here treats of the pomp of funerals, which he rightly wants to be moderate. ] The restriction is denied. Ambrose speaks universally, and from the example of Abraham he teaches that the dead must be wholly left to God after an honourable burial. It belongs to those who have no hope to disturb the ashes of the dead any further or trouble their souls. Calvin therefore argued rightly.

units.la: 18 Ibid. omnibus vos oblationibus frequentabo. ]loquitur nimirum Ambrosius ex hypothesi secundae illius sententiae de statu defunctorum, quae prisco illo seculo in Ecclesia obtinebat, prout distinximus supra lib.i.cap.9.nota 2. & 10. & alibi. Non sequitur simpliciter à dicto [illegible, ~4 letters].
units.tr: 18 Ibid. I will visit you with all offerings. ] Ambrose is clearly speaking on the hypothesis of that second opinion about the state of the dead, which prevailed in the Church in that early age, as we distinguished above at book 1, chapter 9, note 2, and at 10, and elsewhere. It does not follow simply from the saying [illegible, about 4 letters].

units.la: 19 Art.17. Hieronymum loqui de iis qui mortaliter peccant, & sine poenitentia moriuntur, ] negatur cauillatio: & diserte negat Hieronymus, quùm[?] ait, vnumquemque. Quinetiam ex Apostolo negat. Quum enim Apostolus dixisset viuentes succurrere viuentibus oportere, iubens, alij aliorum onera portate, ita complete legem Christi, paulo post rationem illam reddit quam Hieronymus bene obseruauit, post hanc vitam non fore succurrendi locum: nam vnusquisque suum onus portabit, quum in vitam alteram illam transiuerit. Gratianus de impœnitentibus accipiens falsus est: de vnoquoque agitur vniuersè.
units.tr: 19 Art.17. Jerome speaks of those who sin mortally and die without repentance, ] The cavil is denied. Jerome expressly denies it when he says each one. Moreover, he denies it on the authority of the Apostle. For when the Apostle had said that the living ought to help the living, bidding bear one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ, shortly afterwards he gives the reason which Jerome rightly noticed: after this life there will be no place for helping, for each one will bear his own burden, once he has passed over into that other life. Gratian, taking this of the impenitent, is mistaken: it is spoken of each one universally.

units.la: 20 Ibid. Folum iudicis vltima sententia exsequutioni mandabitur. neque hæc solutio verior, sed Apostoli sententiæ aduersatur plane, & confequutioni argumenti.
units.tr: 20 Ibid. Only the final sentence of the judge will be carried out. Nor is this solution the truer; rather it plainly runs counter to the saying of the Apostle and to the consequence of the argument.

units.la: 21 Ibid. post mortem autem nullius pro altero oratio-nem audiendam. Id quidem verum est, Vigilantiũ eo nomine reprehendi, sed diuerso respectu. Nam Vigilantius vniuersè ab omni oratione pro defun-ctis volebat abstineri: Patres vero orari pro luce & refrigerio, & pace defunctorum in resurrectionis mora posse & debere iudicabant, ex illa sententia in Ecclesiam recepta, de qua proximè nota 18.di-cebamus. Non sequitur simpliciter ab eo quod πα π dictum est: nec sequitur ex diuerso, si propter hoc orare fuit legitimum, ergo & propter illud, si propter statum illum, ergo etiam propter statum Purgatorij.
units.tr: 21 Ibid. But after death no one's prayer for another is to be heard. This is indeed true, and Vigilantius was rebuked on that account, but in a different respect. For Vigilantius wanted all prayer for the dead to be altogether abstained from. The Fathers, however, judged that they could and should pray for the light, refreshment and peace of the dead during the delay of the resurrection, from that opinion received into the Church, which we mentioned just above at note 18. It does not follow simply from what was said: nor does it follow conversely that if prayer was lawful on account of that state, then it is also lawful on account of the state of Purgatory.

units.la: 22 Art. 19. non est melius satisfacere per se quàm per alium. nos hîc hominem mereri negamus, aut illic satisfacere: & Purgatorium negamus esse. principium petitur, quia supponitur falsum, & à nobis negatum & confutatum milliès.
units.tr: 22 Art. 19. It is not better to make satisfaction oneself than through another. We here deny that man merits, or makes satisfaction there, and we deny that Purgatory exists. The principle is begged, since what is false is supposed, and what we have denied and refuted a thousand times.

units.la: 23 Art. 21. sicut benefacimus iniustis in hoc mundo, ne prætereantur iusti. Eadem fallacia à dicto secun-dum quid, vt vocant. Nam Augustinus loquitur de oratione quæ pro defunctis olim habebatur, quòd in pœna damni versari crederentur: hic rapit ad defunctos in pœna sensus Purgatoriali, vt putant constitutor. Exemplum verò dissimile est, quia viventium inter se intercedit multiplex communicatio, viventium cum mortuis in effectu nulla est. Communio quidem est in spiritu, sed nulla operum in effectu communicatio, aut communicandi modus.
units.tr: 23 Art. 21. Just as we do good to the unjust in this world, lest the just be passed over. It is the same fallacy, from what is said in a qualified sense (a dicto secundum quid), as they call it. For Augustine speaks of the prayer that was once offered for the dead, who were believed to be in the pain of loss. Here the author of the argument seizes on the sense of punishment for the dead in Purgatory, as they think. The example is not similar, because among the living there is a manifold communication with one another, whereas between the living and the dead there is none in effect. There is indeed communion in spirit, but no communication of works in effect, nor any mode of communicating them.

units.la: 24 Ibid. est meritorium facienti, etiamsi nihil pro-desset ei pro quo fit.] Meritorium vllum opus negamus esse, & tomo 4. σὺν θεῷ[?] confuta-bimus.
units.tr: 24 Ibid. It is meritorious for the one who does it, even if it does not profit the one for whom it is done. We deny that any work is meritorious, and we will refute this in the fourth tome.

units.la: 25 Art.23. nam animæ Purgatorij cupiunt juvari, & nos volumus eas juvare.] at nos animas Purgatorij negamus esse: quid cupiant, obsecro, quæ non sunt? Sed obiectio illa, cuiuscunque sit, friget admodum: auctorem adduci oportuit, si quid forte aliud insuper voluerit.
units.tr: 25 Art.23. For the souls of Purgatory desire to be helped, and we wish to help them. But we deny that there are souls of Purgatory. What do they desire, I ask you, if they do not exist? But that objection, whoever's it is, is quite feeble. The author ought to have been cited, in case he perhaps wished to add something else.

units.la: In Cap. XVI.
units.tr: On Chapter XVI.

units.la: 1 Art.1. sacrificium Missæ, oratio, & opera qualibet pœnalia & satisfactoria,] orationem in suffragiis (ut vocant) numeramus, negamus cætera. Nam nec Missa est sacrificium, nec vllum opus à nobis est satisfactorium, vt sæpe diximus.
units.tr: 1 Art.1. The sacrifice of the Mass, prayer, and any penal and satisfactory works, We count prayer among the so-called suffrages, but we deny the rest. For the Mass is neither a sacrifice, nor is any work of ours satisfactory, as we have often said.

units.la: 2 Ibid. cum tamen etiam ipsa sit satisfactoria,] negatur, vt dictum est proximè.
units.tr: 2 Ibid. although the Mass itself is also satisfactory, Denied, as was said just above.

units.la: 3 Ibid. prosunt nobis & animabus Purgatorij, licet satisfactoriæ non sint.] priorem modum quo orationibus juvari animas defunctorum asserit, negamus plane, posteriorem, vt ordinarium, Ecclesia
units.tr: 3 Ibid. They profit us and the souls of Purgatory, although they are not satisfactory. The first way, by which he asserts that the souls of the dead are helped by prayers, we plainly deny. The second, as ordinary, the

units.la: prisca agnouit, non vt impetratorium liberationis à poena sensus, quàm in Purgatorio animas fingunt luere: sed refrigerij, lucis, pacis, & accelerationis in resurrectionis mora, quam animas defunctorum crediderunt ferre ad secundum vsque aduentum Christi: quemadmodum lib.1.cap.9. & sequentibus ostendimus. Ac beatorum quidem orationes prodesse nobis ordinarie agnoscimus, qua orant communi charitatis motu, non particulari rerum nostrarum sensu, vt controuersia seq. demonstrabimus: orant enim communiter, vt sanctificetur nomen Dei, adueniat regnum eius, & fiat voluntas eius. Animabus vero in Purgatorio negamus prodesse, quì & Purgatorium negamus.
units.tr: ancient Church acknowledged, not as something that secures liberation from the pain of sense, which they feign the souls pay off in Purgatory, but as refreshment, light, peace, and acceleration during the delay of the resurrection, which they believed the souls of the dead endure until the second coming of Christ, as we have shown in book 1, chapter 9 and following. We acknowledge that the prayers of the blessed ordinarily profit us, since they pray from a common motion of charity, not from a particular sense of our own affairs, as we will demonstrate in the following controversy. For they pray in common that the name of God be hallowed, that his kingdom come, and that his will be done. But we deny that they profit the souls in Purgatory, since we also deny Purgatory.

units.la: 4. Art.2. Adhæc iuuantur etiam defuncti indulgentiis, Negamus: & post confutabimus.
units.tr: 4. Art.2. Moreover, the dead are also helped by indulgences, We deny it, and we will refute it afterwards.

units.la: 5. Ibid. Sed de hac re alibi dicendum est. nimirum singulari libro. Nos verò & definitionem indulgentiæ, & quæcunque de indulgentiis humanis hoc loco prædicantur, vera negamus esse, & suo loco etiam confutabimus.
units.tr: 5. Ibid. But this matter must be discussed elsewhere. Namely, in a separate book. We, however, deny that both the definition of indulgence and whatever is preached here about human indulgences is true, and we will refute them in their proper place.

units.la: 6. Art. 3. Sed orationibus animam eius Domino commendandam. Non sequitur ἐν τῷ ἀγῶνι. vide in lib.1. cap.10. nota 17.
units.tr: 6. Art. 3. But her soul is to be commended to the Lord by prayers. It does not follow in the contest. See book 1, chapter 10, note 17.

units.la: 7. Ibid. spiritibus ipsorum per eleemosynas pauperum transmittant. Hæc verba Ambrosij in allegoriis rhetoricè pro suo more exsultantis: Nec tu perdidisti haeredem, inquit matri, qua adiuuas coheredem, sed pro successore corruptibilium mutasti consortem immortalium. Habes qui tibi repræsentet haeredem: solue pauperi quod debetur haeredi, vt non solum materna aut paterna senectutis, sed etiam vitae propriae sit superstes. Plus successori tuo relinquis, si portio eius non ad luxum praefert tium proficiat, sed ad pretium futurorum. Ex his figura-te [illegible, ~10 letters] dictis ad popularem hortationis mo-dum, confici proprias argumentationes iniquū est mutato praedicationis modo. Quid,quòd nō loquitur de rebus praesentibus aut futuris haeredi, sed parentibus ipsius, apud quos portio illa permanet quę futura fuerat hęreditas ei?Falsa igitur interpretatio.
units.tr: 7. Ibid. They send to their spirits through the alms of the poor. These are Ambrose's words in the Allegories, exulting rhetorically in his usual manner: Nor have you lost an heir, he says to the mother, since you help a co-heir, but in place of a successor to perishable things you have exchanged a partner in immortal things. You have one who represents an heir to you. Pay to the poor what is owed to the heir, so that he survives not only your maternal or paternal old age but also your own life. You leave more to your successor if his portion goes not to luxury but to the price of future things. It is unfair to build proper arguments from these figurative words, which are adapted to a popular mode of exhortation, when the mode of preaching has been changed. What is more, he does not speak of present or future things for the heir, but for his parents, with whom that portion remains which would have been his future inheritance. The interpretation is therefore false.

units.la: 8. Art.4. & sacrificio salutari, & eleemosynis non est dubium mortuos adiuvari. ] loquitur Augustinus de poena damni (ut ita loquamur) ex hypothesi illius temporis quam centies exposuimus: non autem de poena sensus, quam statuunt esse Purgatorij. Defunctos enim Patres illi in luce quidem, at non in Dei visione versari statuebant: in huius autem exspectatione illos officiis viuentium credebant adiuvari ad lucem, refrigerium, pacem, & patientiam in resurrectionis mora. Non sequitur à dicto [illegible, ~5 letters].
units.tr: 8. Art.4. And by the saving sacrifice and by alms there is no doubt that the dead are helped. Augustine speaks of the pain of loss (so to speak), on the hypothesis of that time, which we have set out a hundred times, not of the pain of sense, which they posit for Purgatory. For those Fathers held that the dead dwell indeed in light, but not in the vision of God. In expectation of that vision they believed the dead were helped by the services of the living toward light, refreshment, peace, and patience during the delay of the resurrection. It does not follow from what was said [illegible, about 5 letters].

units.la: 9. Art.5. Iuvetur mortuus, non lachrymis: sed precibus, supplicationibus, eleemosynis. ] vide in lib. 1. cap. 10. nota 10. & 11.
units.tr: 9. Art.5. Let the dead be helped, not with tears but with prayers, supplications, and alms. See book 1, chapter 10, notes 10 and 11.

units.la: 10. Art. 6. His adde Angeli testimonium. ] sed utrum atri an albi, boni an mali, veracis an mendacis Angeli? utrum certum testimonium Angeli? certus qui audiuit? certo iudicio qui retulit, his testimoniis, ne si bos quidem vocem edat, credidero. Etsi omnia de poena damni, ut ante, exponi possent.
units.tr: 10. Art. 6. Add to these the testimony of an angel. But which angel: black or white, good or bad, truthful or lying? What is the certain testimony of an angel? Who heard him for certain? Who reported it with certain judgement? I would not believe these testimonies, not even if an ox were to utter a voice. Although all of these could be explained of the pain of loss, as before.

units.la: 11. Art.8. Poenale autem est dare suum, non restituere alienum. ] Totam quaestionem hanc Hiberis naeniis deputamus, qua ad Purgatorium dicitur pertinere. Extra hanc causam verum est Domini à Soto iudicium de defunctis, si duo exceperis: unum, quòd Purgatorij infercit nugas: alterum, quòd satisfactionem humanam ex more Pontificio valere statuit coram Deo, ut bonum opus poenale. negamus ista.
units.tr: 11. Art.8. But it is penal to give what is one's own, not to restore what belongs to another. We assign this whole question to Spanish dirges, which are said to pertain to Purgatory. Apart from this matter, the judgement of Dominic à Soto about the dead is true, with two exceptions: first, that it stuffs in the trifles of Purgatory; second, that it holds human satisfaction, in the Papist manner, to be valid before God as a penal good work. We deny these things.

units.la: 12. Art.9. Ad illas apparitiones respondeo, forte animas non petere restitutionem,] At nos respondemus esse alias μελαγχολώντων [?] somnia, alias superstitiosorum visa, alias daemonum saluti humanae insidiantium ludibria & imperitos sollicitantium. De eleemosyna satisfactoria coram Deo, bellas narrat fabulas.
units.tr: 12. Art.9. To those apparitions I answer: perhaps the souls do not seek restitution, But we answer that some are the dreams of melancholics, others the visions of the superstitious, and others the illusions of demons who lay snares for human salvation and mock the unlearned. As for almsgiving that satisfies before God, he tells pretty fables.

units.la: IN CAPUT XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: 1. Art. 1. Qui potest suffragiis suis iuuare animas, est is qui est iustus:] Negamus posse illos iuuare suffragiis personas ipsas defunctorum apud Deum, vel ad remissionem peccati unici, ut distinximus supra in cap.15. nota 1. & sequentibus.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. He who can help souls by his intercession is one who is righteous:] We deny that they can help the dead themselves before God by their intercessions, or towards the remission of a single sin, as we distinguished above in chapter 15, note 1 and following.

units.la: 2. Art.2. Respondeo, prodesse,] de Missa, negamus, ut tomo 3. de eleemosyna vero distinguimus. Nam prodest percipienti eleemosynam, in bonum, iuvatur enim: praecipienti vero prodest, non ut causa remissionis peccatorum atque salutis meritoria, sed ut opus fidei fructuosum, & fidem charitate operantem testificans. Sed de hac re tomo 4.
units.tr: 2. Art. 2. I answer that it profits,] concerning the Mass, we deny it, as in volume 3; but concerning alms we distinguish. For alms profit the one who receives them, for good, since he is helped. But they profit the one who gives them, not as a meritorious cause of the remission of sins and of salvation, but as a fruitful work of faith, bearing witness to faith working through love. But more on this matter in volume 4.

units.la: 3. Art. 4. Melius esse dari eleemosynam pauperi iniusto quam iniusto:] verum esse facile concedero, si donator sciens prudens fecerit ex certa hominum notitia: sin autem ignarus fecerit ex charitatis communis officio, solutio falsa est, quam recte Seneca lib.1. de beneficiis confutauit. Sed istas utilitates, quae hic finguntur, quaerere non est germanorum filiorū Dei: hi enim faciunt officium reuerentia Pa-tris & debiti sui conscientia, non meriti praesidentia [?] quam à filiis tanto Patri est rependi iniquissimum, Deuter.32.
units.tr: 3. Art. 4. It is better that alms be given to an unrighteous poor man than to an unrighteous one:] I will readily concede that this is true if the giver knowingly and deliberately acts on certain knowledge of the men concerned. But if he acts in ignorance, out of the common duty of charity, the solution is false, and Seneca refuted it rightly in book 1 of On Benefits. But it is not the mark of the true sons of God to seek those advantages that are invented here. For they perform their duty out of reverence for the Father and awareness of what they owe, not out of a sense of merit; and it would be most unjust for a Father so great to be repaid by his sons, Deut. 32.

units.la: In Caput. XVII.
units.tr: CHAPTER XVII.

units.la: 1. Art. 1. Non prodesse beatis, nec damnatis, sed solum iis qui in Purgatorio degunt: ] Prosunt ergo nemini: quia non est Purgatorium, libro 1. non in Purgatorio quisquam.
units.tr: 1. Art. 1. They do not profit the blessed, nor the damned, but only those who dwell in Purgatory:] Therefore they profit no one, since there is no Purgatory; in book 1 no one is in Purgatory.

units.la: 2. Ibid. Pro non valde malis propitiationes, ]Nempe ad lucem, pacem, refrigerium exorandum durante resurrectionis mora, quo tempore animæ illorum abesse adhuc à visione Dei & anhelare ad eam censebantur, ex recepta illius seculi sententia, [illegible, ~6 letters] dictum.
units.tr: 2. Ibid. Propitiations for those who are not very wicked,] namely, to beg for light, peace and refreshment during the delay of the resurrection, a time when their souls were thought to be still absent from the vision of God and longing for it, according to the accepted opinion of that age, [illegible] said.

units.la: 3. Art.2. dicunt sacrificium offerri Deo pro Apostolis[?], martyribus, Prophetis, &c. ] Vide lib.1.cap.9.nota 23. & sequentibus.
units.tr: 3. Art. 2. They say that sacrifice is offered to God for the Apostles, martyrs, prophets, etc.] See book 1, chapter 9, note 23 and following.

units.la: 4. Art.3. Quæ sicut Sanctis tuis prosunt ad gloriam, ] Non ergo ad medelam, remissionem peccatorum pœnarúmve, & liberationem à Purgatorio: quæ res hic agitur. nam dicuntur ista ex hypothesi secundæ illius sententiæ Patrum de statu defunctorum, quam sæpius exposuimus.Et ratio eadem sequentium.
units.tr: 4. Art. 3. Which, just as they profit your Saints for glory,] Therefore not for healing, for the remission of sins or penalties, and for deliverance from Purgatory, which is the matter at issue here. For these things are said on the hypothesis of the second opinion of the Fathers concerning the state of the dead, which we have often explained. And the reason is the same for what follows.

units.la: 5. Art.5. Non ut eis aliquid petamus, sed ut pro gloria illis collata Deo gratias agamus. ] Negatio falsa. Sensit enim Ecclesia prisca secundi seculi, orandum esse pro sanctis defunctis, qui nondum beata visione Dei plane frui censebantur, ut Deus illam pœnā damni (quam vocant) alleuaret luce, pace, refrigerio, &c. quò pertinebat illa ipsa oratio, quam Bellarminus proximè adduxit in artic. 5. Annue quæsumus, Domine, ut animæ B. Leonis hæc prosit oblatio, & quæ quam agnoscit postea mutatam esse adeo sibi Rom-Ecclesia hic constat scilicet.
units.tr: 5. Art. 5. Not that we ask anything of them, but that we give thanks to God for the glory conferred on them.] A false denial. For the early Church of the second century did feel that one must pray for holy departed souls, who were not yet thought to enjoy fully the blessed vision of God, so that God might lighten that so-called pain of loss by light, peace, refreshment, and so on. To this belonged that very prayer which Bellarmine quoted just before in article 5: Grant, we beseech you, O Lord, that the offering of this sacrifice may profit the soul of blessed Leo, and which the Roman Church itself later acknowledges to have been changed, as is clear from this.

units.la: 6. Art. 6. Non petere, ut illi in gloria crescant, ] & haec negatio falsa, ut nota proxima dicebamus. Etenim ab ipso Innocentio solutione sequente evertitur. Nam si cuius gloriae augmentum petitur, profecto petitur quod hac solutione Innocentius negat: id autem est, maior gloriae in ipsis ut membris, & in Ecclesia coelesti ut corpore communi modus: quam rem & nos petimus auctore Christo, dicentes, Adveniat regnum tuum: & Ioannes petiuit Apoc. 22.20. dicens: dicit qui testatur ista, etiam, venio cito. Amen. Veni igitur Domine Iesu.
units.tr: 6. Art. 6. Not to ask that they grow in glory,] This denial is also false, as we said in the note just before. For it is overturned by Innocent himself in the following solution. For if an increase of anyone's glory is sought, then surely what Innocent denies in this solution is sought: that is, a greater degree of glory in them as members, and in the heavenly Church as a common body. This we too ask, under the authority of Christ, saying Thy kingdom come; and John asked in Rev. 22.20, saying: He who testifies these things says, Surely I am coming soon. Amen. Come, Lord Jesus.

units.la: 7. Ibid. & debetur eorum meritis, ] merita nostra apud Deum esse, & meritis nostris a Deo deberi negamus quicquam, nisi supplicium meritum no-strū,qui credimus: miseratio Domini, sic sequentia.
units.tr: 7. Ibid. and is owed to their merits,] We deny that we have merits before God, and that anything is owed to us by God for our merits, except punishment as our merit, we who believe in the mercy of the Lord; so the following.

units.la: 8. Art. 12. Augustinu per tolerabiliorem damnationem intelligere mitigationem poenarū Purgatorij.] Ne-gatur. Nam damnati, vel Bellarmino iudice in hoc ipso libro aliquoties, nihil commune habent cum Purgatorio: quid enim damnatis purgatione opus? Damnationem ergo Augustinus vocat, qua sancti mediocriter boni aut mali subeunt poenam illam damni, quam prisca Ecclesia illo seculo credidit, ne-pe quod plena gloria & visione Dei careret, quamuis in luce illius gloriæ magis aut minus, diutius aut breuius sustentati. Qui ergo ex illa luce euehuntur ad gloriam plenam, ut resurrectione futurum considebant, eis plena fieri dicitur remissio: qui vero plus accipiebant lucis aut citius, eorum damnatio fieri tolerabilior dicebatur. Haec saeculi illius senten-tia, de poena damni, ut vocant, intelligens: no autem de pœna sensus, quam Purgatorio adscribunt Pon-tificij. Nec aliud praecedente diuisione ostendi potest. Alterum Augustini locum siqui adducunt, faciunt imprudentissimè. Nam postquam Augustinus eorum sententiam explosisset qui damnationem non esse æternam putant: συγχωρητικῶς, siue per concessionem ad illum sermonem venit: si ista, inquit, falsa misericordia tantopere arridet ipsis, si hoc eis placet, & quasi misericordia superare Deum ambiunt, ergo existimentur illi & hanc moderationem iudicij sui adhibeant, pœnas damnatorum certis interuallis aliquatenus mitigari, non autem omnino a-liquando terminari: quod sacra Scriptura negat. Quæ tandem affirmatio erui bona fide posset ex concessione eiusmodi? Etsi, ne quid dissimulem, Augustini verba in Bellarmini opere vitiose addu-cuntur. Sed hæc nihil ad nos.
units.tr: 8. Art. 12. Augustine understands by a more tolerable damnation the mitigation of the penalties of Purgatory.] This is denied. For the damned, by the judgment of Bellarmine himself in this same book on several occasions, have nothing in common with Purgatory; for what need do the damned have of purging? Augustine therefore calls damnation that by which saints of middling goodness or badness undergo that penalty of loss which the early Church of that age believed, namely that they lacked the full glory and vision of God, although they were sustained more or less, for longer or shorter, in the light of that glory. Those therefore who were lifted from that light to full glory, as they thought would happen at the resurrection, were said to receive full remission; but those who received more light, or sooner, had their damnation said to become more tolerable. This is the opinion of that age, understood as concerning the penalty of loss, as they call it, and not the penalty of sense, which the Papists ascribe to Purgatory. Nor can anything else be shown from the preceding distinction. If anyone cites the other passage of Augustine, they do so most imprudently. For after Augustine had refuted the opinion of those who think that damnation is not eternal, he came to that discourse by way of concession [συγχωρητικῶς]: if, he says, this false mercy pleases them so much, if it is agreeable to them, and they seek to outdo God, as it were, in mercy, then let them be thought to apply this moderation of their judgment as well, that the penalties of the damned are somewhat mitigated at certain intervals, but are not ended altogether at any time, which Holy Scripture denies. What assertion could be honestly drawn from a concession of this kind? And yet, not to conceal anything, Augustine's words are cited faultily in Bellarmine's work. But these matters do not concern us.

units.la: 9. Art. 13. Esse erroneum concedere, damnatos puniri citra condignum, ]Hoc ne per somnium quidem Augustino in mentem venit: nam aliud plane in eo loco agitur, vt præcedente nota exposuimus. In libro autem 21. de ciuit. Dei, alia omnia, vt libri 1. cap. 10. nota 45. ostendimus.
units.tr: 9. Art. 13. That it is an error to concede that the damned are punished less than they deserve,] Augustine did not so much as dream of this; for something quite different is dealt with in that passage, as we explained in the preceding note. In book 21 of The City of God, however, we have shown all the other matters, as in book 1, chapter 10, note 45.

units.la: 10. Art. 14. Negare orandum esse publicè, vel sacrificandum pro Catechumenis. ] De mortuis intellige: pro eo quod est, nullam istorum[?] in Ecclesia publi-cè faciendam commemorationem.
units.tr: 10. Art. 14. To deny that one must pray publicly, or offer sacrifice, for Catechumens.] Understand this of the dead: that is, that no public commemoration of them is to be made in the Church.

units.la: 11. Art. 15. Nec est verisimile, S. Macarium orasse pro infidelibus. ] hæc omnia (vt verbo vno absolua-mus) ἀντιρρητικῶς[?], nec confutatione digna. Sed & priore fabulam disputator supra cap. 8. confutauit. In posteriore Damascenus ille suum auctorem laudat: ergo falsus est[?] alteruter, aut etiā vterq;, & Damascenus in reipsa,& Palladius in historia Laufiaca.
units.tr: 11. Art. 15. Nor is it likely that St. Macarius prayed for unbelievers.] All these things (to finish with one word) are wholly by way of contradiction [ἀντιρρητικῶς], and not worth refutation. But the disputant also refuted the former story above in chapter 8. In the latter, that Damascene praises his own authority. Therefore one of them is false, or even both, both Damascene in the matter itself and Palladius in the Lausiac History.

units.la: 12. Art.17.qui habent culpam aliquam, sed venialem tantum. Ista negamus omnia. Potius videtur Innocentius auxisse diuisionem Augustini certo consilio quodam;& mediocriter bonos à mediocriter malis eo distinxisse, quòd in mediocriter bonis plus esse boni, quamuis non valde boni essent;in mediocriter malis plus esse mali, quamuis non valde essent mali, videretur. Sed hæc magis non curauerimus, quàm testudo muscas.
units.tr: 12. Art. 17. who have some fault, but only a venial one.] We deny all these things. Innocent seems rather to have enlarged Augustine's division for some deliberate purpose, and to have distinguished the moderately good from the moderately bad by this: that among the moderately good there seemed to be more good, though they were not very good; among the moderately bad there seemed to be more bad, though they were not very bad. But we need not care about these matters any more than a tortoise cares about flies.

units.la: 13. Art.18. difficultas est de animabus Purgatorij.] nobis vero nulla est difficultas, qui Purgatoriū scimus nullum esse, præeunte face veritatis. Quamo-brem ista negamus omnia quę sequuntur apud Bellarminum petentem τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς[?]. vix concha digna sunt.
units.tr: 13. Art. 18. There is a difficulty about the souls of Purgatory.] For us, however, there is no difficulty at all, since we know that there is no Purgatory, with the torch of truth leading the way. Therefore we deny all the things that follow in Bellarmine, who begs the question [τὸ ἐξ ἀρχῆς, the very point at issue]. They are scarcely worth a shell.

units.la: 14. Art.24. habeant saltem auxilium à communi matre, quæ est Ecclesia.] auxilium orationum Augustinus dicebat defunctis præstari ex hypothesi quę tum in Ecclesia obtinuit,pios defunctos subire pœnà damni,id est, nondum possidere plenam perfectionem gloriæ,sed in exspectatione illius alios plº;[?]alios minus laborare. De pœna sensus,id est,Purgatoria illa, quæ tamen hic agitur,nullum verbum. Falsum ergo consequens.
units.tr: 14. Art. 24. Let them at least have help from the common mother, which is the Church.] Augustine said that help by prayers was given to the dead on the hypothesis then prevailing in the Church, that pious departed souls undergo the penalty of loss, that is, do not yet possess the full perfection of glory, but in expectation of it some labour less than others. Of the penalty of sense, that is, that Purgatory which is nevertheless the subject here, there is not a word. Therefore the consequence is false.

units.la: IN CAP. XIX.
units.tr: CHAPTER XIX.

units.la: 1. Art.1.reprehendunt tamen multa circa sepulturâ.] sed in multis superstitionem & tyrannidem superstitiosam maximè.
units.tr: 1. Art.1. they nevertheless find fault with many things concerning burial.] But chiefly with many superstitions and, above all, with superstitious tyranny.

units.la: 2. Art.6.sepulturam re[?] esse bonam & utilem,& ritus omnes Ecclesia infepeliendis mortuis esse antiquos & sanctos.]Prius de sepultura in se agnoscimus: posterius, & omnes ritus & sanctos esse negamus: ut sequentibus demonstrabitur. Etsi vox sancti ante omnia distinguri debet. Nam sanctum dicitur aut natura, aut instituto. Nullus autem ritus natura sanctus est: igitur instituto. Quod instituto sanctum, aut est diuino instituto sanctum, aut humano dicitur ἁγιαστικῶς. Quod autem humano appellatur sanctum (nam de diuino quaestio nulla est) iuris positivi est. Ius autem positivum (ut docent Scholastici) cum tantum habeat de rectitudine inquantum a lege naturae deriuatur & inseruit ei, si vero discordet ab ea, non iam sit lex, sed corruptio legis: plane quicquid sanctum iure positivo est, tantisper sanctum est dum & cum iure naturae conuenit, & effectu afflequitur finem suum. Sin autem aut a iure illo discedit, aut pro sancta aliqua, honesta, & decora significatione in superstitionem vertitur & iugum conscientiae: tum profecto non ius, sed iniuria est: non obligat subditos, sed Praelati absoluere ab eo subditos obligantur. Haec esto praestructio sequentibus.
units.tr: 2. Art.6. that burial is good and useful, and that all the rites of the Church in burying the dead are ancient and holy.] We acknowledge the former, that burial in itself is good and useful. The latter, that all rites are holy, we deny, as will be shown in what follows. But the word holy must first be distinguished. Something is called holy either by nature or by appointment. No rite is holy by nature; therefore it is holy by appointment. What is holy by appointment is either holy by divine appointment or is called holy by human appointment [ἁγιαστικῶς]. As for what is called holy by human appointment (for there is no question about the divine), it belongs to positive law. Positive law, as the Scholastics teach, has its rightness only insofar as it is derived from the law of nature and serves it. If it disagrees with that law, it is no longer law but a corruption of law. Plainly, whatever is holy by positive law is holy only so long as it agrees with the law of nature and in practice attains its end. But if it departs from that law, or, under the appearance of some holy, honourable and seemly purpose, turns into superstition and a yoke on the conscience, then it is no longer law but injustice. It does not bind the subjects; rather, the subjects are bound to be absolved from it by their prelates. Let this be the preface to what follows.

units.la: 3. Ibid. Opus bonum operata est in me, ] Inconsequens, si opus bonum operatus est in me, ergo & meritorium apud Deum. Tum ut quaedam officia bona essent meritoria (quod falsum) non continuo tamen sepulturam accenseri meritoriis oportet.
units.tr: 3. Ibid. It has done a good work in me,] It does not follow: if it has done a good work in me, then it is also meritorious before God. And even if some good duties are meritorious (which is false), burial should not therefore immediately be counted among the meritorious works.

units.la: 4. Art. 7. Semper in vsu Ecclesiae fuerunt. ] semper fuisse negamus omnia, ut nota 2.
units.tr: 4. Art. 7. They have always been in use in the Church.] We deny that all these things have always existed, as noted at point 2.

units.la: 5. Ib. Corpora mortuorum nunc lauatur,] res adiaphora: sed quae tum demum mala fit, si superstitio inuaserit, siue a Iudaicae legis cacozelia, siue a falsò praesumpta
units.tr: 5. Ib. The bodies of the dead are now washed,] This is an indifferent matter; but it becomes an evil only when superstition has crept in, whether it arises from the perverse zeal of the Jewish law or from an opinion of religion and holiness falsely presumed.

units.la: 2. Summa, ex Hist. Ecclesiast. Ecclesi. vols. — præsumpta religionis & sanctimoniæ opinione proficiscens. Eadem sequentium quam plurimorum ratio.
units.tr: 2. Summary, from Ecclesiastical History, Ecclesi. vols. — proceeding from the presumed opinion of religion and sanctity. The same reasoning applies to very many of what follows.

units.la: 9. Artic.9.in terra promissionis sepeliri voluerunt,] nempe quia sacramentum illis erat communis nostræ hæreditatis in cælis:cuius fidem morientes obsignare, & mortui testatam facere posteritati suæ voluerunt, ut legimus in fine Geneseos. vide suprà lib.i.cap.15.nota 16.
units.tr: 9. Art.9. They wished to be buried in the land of promise,] Namely, because for them it was a sign of our common inheritance in heaven. Dying, they wished to seal this faith and to make their testament known to their posterity, as we read at the end of Genesis. See above, book 1, chapter 15, note 16.

units.la: 7. Ibid. corpora fidelium in templis sepulta suis-se] sive in templis, sive ubiuis, modo religiose & honeste: nam omnimoda exempla huius rei extant.
units.tr: 7. Ibid. the bodies of the faithful were buried in temples] Whether in temples or anywhere else, provided it be done religiously and decently; for examples of every kind of this practice exist.

units.la: 8. Art.10. corpora fidelium cum hymnorum & psalmorum cantu sepelienda] sepulta quidem fuisse cum illo cantu dicunt, ut effet comitatui & toti Ecclesiæ ἐκκλησιαστικὸς καὶ ταφικός[?], sed ita sepeliri ex necessi-tate oportere nemo dicit. Nam sui ritus liberi & varii fuerunt Ecclesiis: quæ viuentibus hoc pacto, ac non defunctis consulebant.
units.tr: 8. Art.10. the bodies of the faithful are to be buried with the singing of hymns and psalms] They say that the dead were indeed buried with that singing, so that it would accompany the funeral and the whole Church, in an ecclesiastical and funeral manner. But no one says that they must necessarily be buried in this way. For their rites were free and varied among the churches, which thereby provided for the living rather than the dead.

units.la: 9. Art. II. ad funus fidelium lampades & cerei accensi adhibebantur,] hæc fuit honorifica illorum temporum significatio ab athletis translata, Paufania & Olympiodoro teste, qua significabant pij se honorificè prosequi athletam Christi defunctum suis laboribus & victoria coronatu. Nazianzenus de Constantio συλλιτουργικῷ[?] ἐ.[?] in Iulianum: ὁ μὲν γὰρ πάνυ ἀνταγωνιστὴς[?] τὰ τῶν ἀπιστῶν ἐν τοῖς ἡμετέροις σημείοις, ψαλμοῖς ἐπαίνων τε καὶ ὕμνων[?] καὶ τοὺς τούτοις[?] οὐδὲν ἐν τοῖς ἡμετέροις[?] τιμῶν μετὰ σεμνῶν[?] νομίζουσιν,&c. Ac ille quidem publicis acclamationibus & pompis deducitur; atque his etiam nostris religiosis ritibus, nocturnis cationibus[?] gestationibusque facium, quibus nos Christiani honore prosequi exitum pium solemus legitime. Chrysostomus vero omnium euidentissime homil.4.in Hebr.2.dicens:
units.tr: 9.
