Art. 11. lamps and lit candles were used at the funeral of the faithful,] This was an honourable sign of those times, transferred from athletes, as Pausanias and Olympiodorus bear witness, by which the pious signified that they honourably escorted the departed athlete of Christ, crowned for his labours and victory. Gregory Nazianzen, on Constantius, against Julian: "For the very antagonist [Julian] ... unbelievers consider the things of their own, in our signs, psalms, praises and hymns, and so honour these with solemn ..." And indeed the one is conducted with public acclamations and processions; and by these our religious rites too, with nocturnal songs and processions, which we Christians rightly use to honour a pious departure. But Chrysostom most clearly of all, in Homily 4 on Hebrews 2, saying:

units.la: εἰπέ γάρ μοι, τί βούλονται σου αἱ λαμπάδες, οὐχ ὡς ἀθλητὰς αὐτοὺς προπέμπομεν, τί δὲ οἱ ὕμνοι; οὐχὶ τὸν Θεὸν δοξάζομεν, καὶ εὐχαριστοῦμεν ὅτι λοιπὸν ἐξεφάνωσε τὸν ἀπελθόντα, ὅτι τῆς πονηρίας ἀπήλλαξεν; ὅτι τῆς δειλίας ἐκβαλὼν ἔχει παρ᾽ ἑαυτῷ [?] διὰ τοῦτο ὑμνοι; οὐ διὰ τοῦτο φαλμῳδίας; ταῦτα πάντα χαιρόντων ἐστίν. ἀλλὰ ἐρῶ γάρ, φησί τις, ψαλλέτω. ἀλλ᾽ οὐ τούτοις ἀφοσιοῦνται ἕλληνες. &c. Dic enim mihi, quid sibi volunt lampades illæ claræ? nonne vt athletas eos deducimus? quid autem hymni? annon Deum glorificamus, & gratias agimus quod iam coronauerit defunctum? quod a laboribus liberauerit? quod expedituum ex metu eum apud se habeat? nonne ideo sunt hymni? nonne ideo psalmodiæ? hæc omnia sunt lætantium. Nam inquit ille, bono animo est aliquis? psallito. Verum ad hæc non attendunt Græci. Hæc vera lampadum gestandarum causa aliorumque rituum; quod cum vulgus in publico victores athletas hoc modo prosequeretur ad honorem festiuitatemque victoris, ita Christianos visum est, velut athletas & milites Christi, prosequi hac publica honoris significatione. Sed cum istæ significationes stadij & circi iam olim desiuerint, atque adeo in vulgo sint ignotæ, quid attinet ritus ignotæ significationes obseruari? quid necessitate cogi? quid superstitione imperitos & inscientes implicari? Significatio hæc enim seculo illi, moribus illis nota; nunc huic seculo, his moribus est ignota plane. Ista qui obseruant memoria nostra, aut faciunt vt simia, quod est ridiculum, aut vt in Velabro olearij, quæ res non caret malo. Sed videviderint quibus hæc usqueadeò cordi. plura de hoc usu vide in controv. 7. lib. 2. cap. 4. nota 9. & sequentib.
units.tr: εἰπέ γάρ μοι, τί βούλονται σου αἱ λαμπάδες, οὐχ ὡς ἀθλητὰς αὐτοὺς προπέμπομεν, τί δὲ οἱ ὕμνοι; οὐχὶ τὸν Θεὸν δοξάζομεν, καὶ εὐχαριστοῦμεν ὅτι λοιπὸν ἐξεφάνωσε τὸν ἀπελθόντα, ὅτι τῆς πονηρίας ἀπήλλαξεν; ὅτι τῆς δειλίας ἐκβαλὼν ἔχει παρ᾽ ἑαυτῷ; διὰ τοῦτο ὑμνοι; οὐ διὰ τοῦτο ψαλμῳδίαι; ταῦτα πάντα χαιρόντων ἐστίν. ἀλλὰ ἐρῶ γάρ, φησί τις, ψαλλέτω. ἀλλ᾽ οὐ τούτοις ἀφοσιοῦνται Ἕλληνες. &c. Tell me, what do those bright lamps mean? Is it not that we escort them as athletes? And what do the hymns mean? Do we not glorify God and give thanks that he has at last shown forth the one who has departed, that he has freed him from wickedness, that he has cast out cowardice and now has him with himself? Is it not for this reason that there are hymns? Is it not for this reason that there are psalmodies? All these things belong to rejoicing people. But, someone says, if anyone is in good spirits, let him sing psalms. But the Greeks do not purify themselves with these things. This is the true reason for carrying lamps and the other rites. Since the common people, in public, escorted victorious athletes in this way, to honour and celebrate the victor, it seemed right to the Christians to escort their athletes and soldiers of Christ with this public sign of honour. But since these signs of the stadium and the circus have long since passed away and are therefore unknown to the common people, what is the point of observing rites whose meaning is unknown? Why be compelled by necessity? Why entangle the unskilled and ignorant in superstition? This sign was known to that age and those customs; to this age and these customs it is now plainly unknown. Those who observe these things in our time either do so like apes, which is ridiculous, or like the oil-sellers in the Velabrum, which is not without harm. But let those see to it for whom these things are so dear. More on this practice may be seen in the Controversy 7, book 2, chapter 4, note 9 and following.

units.la: 10. Artic. 12. sacrificium altaris pro eis offertur,] id est, oblatio, quam ultima voluntate sua pro se, id est, loco suo offerri in Ecclesia voluerant, ut ex ea communio fieret in Ecclesiæ cœtu qui ad funus convenerat, vide quæ supra in lib.1. cap.9.nota 2. annotavimus. pia fuit donatio mortis causa, aut fundatio(ut vocant)testamentaria: quemadmodum & sequentia duo.
units.tr: 10. Art. 12. the sacrifice of the altar is offered for them,] That is, the oblation which they wished, by their last will, to be offered in the Church on their behalf, that is, in their place, so that communion might be made from it in the assembly of the Church which had gathered for the funeral. See what we noted above in book 1, chapter 9, note 2. It was a pious gift made in view of death, or, as they call it, a testamentary foundation, just as the two following are.

units.la: 11. Artic. 13. sed etiam die anniversaria pro defun-ctis offertur, & oratur,] offertur pro ipsis nomine ipsorum quod ipsi legaverunt, aut mortis causa donaverunt: oratur tum gratias agendo pro eis (nam & gratiarum actio in Scripturis censetur oratio) tum proiectionem gloriæ liberationemque a poena damni, ut vocant, & refrigerium in ea pacemque illis exoptando; prout tum in Ecclesia obtinuit sententia. hæc autem quid ad opinionem Purgatorij, quæ accreuit postea?
units.tr: 11. Art. 13. but also on the anniversary day prayer and offering are made for the dead,] It is offered for them in their name, which they bequeathed or gave in view of death. Prayer is made for them, both by giving thanks for them (for thanksgiving too is counted as prayer in the Scriptures) and by wishing for them an increase of glory, deliverance from the so-called punishment of loss, and refreshment and peace in it, as the opinion prevailed in the Church at that time. But what does this have to do with the opinion of Purgatory, which grew up later?

units.la: 12. Art. 14. nonfolum die anniversaria, sed etiam die 3. 7. & 3o.) si hoc de Imperatoribus verum, an ergo de omnibus iudicium idem oportet fieri? an imponi iugum? an superstitionem iniicit? Optime Augustinus lib. de cura pro mortuis, cap. 2. Si aliquid prodest impio sepultura pretiosa, obest pio aut vilis aut nulla. ut ex Innocentio dicitur artic. 2. alioqui licere quis negat?
units.tr: 12. Art. 14. not only on the anniversary day, but also on the third, seventh and thirtieth day.] If this is true of the emperors, must the same judgement be made about all? Is a yoke to be imposed? Does it introduce superstition? Augustine rightly says in his book On the Care for the Dead, chapter 2: If costly burial benefits the impious, a cheap or no burial harms the pious. As it is said from Innocent, article 2; otherwise, who denies that it is permitted?

units.la: 13. Artic. 18. multiplicem esse utilitatem sepultura, tam vivis quam defunctis: ] de vivis, concedimus; de defunctis distinguemus postea suo ordine & loco.
units.tr: 13. Art. 18. burial has manifold usefulness, for the living as well as for the dead:] Of the living we concede; concerning the dead we will distinguish later in its proper order and place.

units.la: 14. Art.19. Neque cereos accenderemus, nisi animos viuere post mortem corporum significare vellemus.] hęc olim nō fuit cereorum & facium significatio, vt ex Chryfoftomo nota 9. proximè dicebamus. hoc fe-stiuum Seplafiæ Pontificię ἀντιϛαλλομένου scilicet. vide in controuersiæ feq caput 4.
units.tr: 14. Art. 19. We would not light candles, unless we wished to signify that souls live after the death of bodies.] This was not formerly the meaning of candles and lamps, as we said just now from Chrysostom, note 9. This is a festal custom of the Papist Sephalia, namely the antistallomenou. See in the following controversy, chapter 4.

units.la: 15. Art.23. tamen cupere vt honestè habeantur,] misera coniectura, & dispar ratio similis. Nam animæ cupiunt ad sua corpora reuerti, vel potiùs sua corpora reuerti ad se, quia illa resurrectio corporũ est de perfectione nostra, & perfectione quoque Ecclesiæ siue corporis Christi ad gloriam Dei in causa vero sepulturæ, quid, obsecro, eiusmodi? Ex dispari nihil concluditur.
units.tr: 15. Art. 23. yet to desire that they be honourably treated: a wretched guess, and an unlike comparison that proves nothing like it. For souls desire to return to their own bodies, or rather their bodies return to themselves, since the resurrection of the bodies belongs to our perfection, and to the perfection of the Church, which is the body of Christ, to the glory of God. But in the case of burial, what, I ask you, is of this kind? Nothing follows from an unlike case.

units.la: 16. Art.24. hinc enim per accidens fit, vt à multis pro eis oretur.] si antiqua simplicitate fit, toleramus; si indigna superstitione, quę seculum nostrum in Ecclesia Rom. sæde commaculat, tolerari negamus posse.
units.tr: 16. Art. 24. for thus it happens incidentally that many pray for them. If it is done with ancient simplicity, we tolerate it. But if it is done with the unworthy superstition that defiles our age in the Roman Church, we deny that it can be tolerated.

units.la: 17. Art.25. & frequēter eius patrocinio eos cōmendet.] Vide supra lib.1.cap.10. nota 22. hæc omnia piorum quidem viuentium affectum & studium humanum commonstrant; sed vtilitatem vllam minimè, quæ ex isto affectu ad mortuos redire possit. Qui Gregorij fabulis pascitur, is inter Sofias & Tybios per me referatur licet.
units.tr: 17. Art. 25. and often commends them to her patronage. See above, book 1, chapter 10, note 22. All these things show indeed the affection and human zeal of the living devout, but in no way show any benefit that could come back to the dead from that affection. Whoever feeds on the tales of Gregory may, for all I care, be listed among the Sofias and Tybios.

units.la: 18. Art.26. non sequitur, non esse aliquam eleemosynam, satisfacere desiderio hominis quod habuit dum viveret,] dicatur sane eleemosyna κατ' ἀρχὴν ᾿, per abusionem; at non propterea sequitur officium hoc misericordiæ aut meritorium esse, aut satisfactorium pro mortuo, aut denique personæ illius vtile. Sequęs coniectura somnium.
units.tr: 18. Art. 26. it does not follow that there is no almsgiving, that it satisfies the desire of a man which he had while he lived. Let it certainly be called almsgiving [κατ' ἀρχὴν], by abuse of the word; but it does not therefore follow that this work of mercy is meritorious, or satisfactory for the dead, or finally useful to that person. The consequence is a dream.

units.la: 19. Ibid. per accidens prodesse potest, vt diximus, ratione tione precum amicorum.]negamus prodesse. Quòd si daremus prodesse ad poenam dani leuandam, vt se-cundo illo seculo crediderunt Patres, non tamen ex eo sequeretur prodesse ad poenam leuadam sensus: qualem esse vnanimiter tradunt Pontificij poenam Purgatorij: vt dictum est supra cap.10. Sequentis solutionis eadem plane ratio.
units.tr: 19. Ibid. It can benefit incidentally, as we said, by reason of the prayers of friends. We deny that it benefits. But even if we granted that it benefits by lessening the punishment of the fire, as the Fathers of the second century believed, it would still not follow that it benefits by lessening the sense of punishment, which the Papists unanimously teach is the punishment of Purgatory, as was said above in chapter 10. The reply that follows is plainly the same.

units.la: 20. Art.27. Superstitione Gentilium, qui putabant corpora mortua sentire aliquid.]primum huc Gentilium superstitiosum sensum probari velim: nam falsum puto. de animabus quidem scribunt Poetæ, de corporibus, minime. Secundo vt demus verum esse, negamus tamen ad interdictum istud pertinere posse: quia si ita esset, non de die solum, sed etiam de nocte interdiceretur. Non enim magis noctu quam interdiu licet inquietare spiritus defunctorum. Canon autem interdicit de die solum. vide in controu.7.lib. 2.cap.4.
units.tr: 20. Art. 27. the superstition of the Gentiles, who thought that dead bodies feel something. First, I would have it proved that the superstitious opinion belonged to the Gentiles, for I think it false. The poets write indeed about souls, but hardly at all about bodies. Second, even granting that it is true, we still deny that it can pertain to this prohibition: for if it were so, the prohibition would apply not only by day but also by night. For it is no more lawful to disturb the spirits of the dead by night than by day. But the canon forbids it by day only. See in controversy 7, book 2, chapter 4.

units.la: 21. Ibid. non debere mæstificari lacrymis animam sororis defunctæ.]loquutio est prosopopæetica.turbat, qui ex figurata propriam prædicationem facit.
units.tr: 21. Ibid. the soul of a dead sister ought not to be made sad with tears. The expression is a prosopopoeia. He confuses things who makes his own assertion out of a figurative one.

units.la: 22. Art.28. non esse signum diffidentiæ, sed desiderij & feruoris, repetere easdem preces,)nempe si eadem permanet necessitas,& constat permanere. Defunctos vero premi necessitate Purgatorij; aut si premuntur (quod falsum) permanere in ea, quis vnquam probet? Sequentia exempla constantis fuerunt necessitatis,& certæ;quapropter nihil ad causam.
units.tr: 22. Art. 28. it is not a sign of distrust, but of desire and fervour, to repeat the same prayers (namely if the same need remains, and it is agreed that it remains). But that the dead are oppressed by the need of Purgatory, or if they are oppressed (which is false), that they remain in it, who will ever prove this? The examples that follow were of a constant and certain need, and therefore have nothing to do with the case.

units.la: 23. Art.29. Ad Ambrosium respondimus supra cap. 15.]Vide igitur supra cap.15. nota 17.& 18.vbi eadem adducuntur.
units.tr: 23. Art. 29. We answered Ambrose above, in chapter 15. See therefore above, chapter 15, notes 17 and 18, where the same things are cited.

units.la: 24. Art.30. hanc eleemosynam cum cæteris non nume-ramus.Tota hac responsione disputator Chrysostomo adeo adversatur, ut nescio quid illi venire in mentem potuerit quum Chrysostomum adduceret. Re-spondebit ergo ipse Chrysostomus nobis tacentibus huic solutioni toti, cuius haec verba sunt homil 84. in Ioan. prout Franciscus Aretinus interpretatus est: Ut intelligas nulli curae hoc (Christo esse, inquit enim: Esurientem me vidistis, et dedistis mihi manducare, sitientem, et dedistis mihi bibere; nudum, et induistis me: non autem, mortuum, et sepelistis. Quod ego non ut sepulturam tollam divo, abshit; sed luxuriam et superfluam ambitionem. Affectus, inquis, et dolor, et mortui misericordia hoc suadet. Non est misericordia, sed inanis gloria. Nam si vis mortui misereri, aliam tibi viam ornandi funeris ostendam, et docebo his mortuum vestibus ornare, quae simul cum eo resurgent, et conspicuum reddent. haec vestes nec tineis corroduntur[?], nec tempore consumuntur, neque diripiuntur a furibus. Quaenam haec sunt? Eleemosyna vestis est quae resurget: eleemosyna tanquam signaculum cum eo. his vestibus fulgebunt qui tunc audient, esurientem me vidistis, et dedistis mihi manducare. haec insignes faciunt, haec conspicuos, haec securos: praesentia enim nihil aliud sunt, quam tinearum et vermium esca. Non tamen sepulturam prohibeo: sed modus servetur, ut tegatur corpus, non nudum mandetur terrae. Nam si viventibus praecipitur, nequid habeant praeter vestimentum, longe magis mortuis. &c. His profecto verbis bonus Chrysostomus longe aliter de sumptibus funerum iudicat, quam Pontificiorum nomothetae. Vera igitur est obiectio tenuitatem sumptuum commendans, et excessum prohibens; quem disputator artificiose dissimulat, quamvis in Pontificia Ecclesia frequentissimum. Quae sequuntur, omnia eiusdem sunt argumenti. menti. Pium usum laudamus, abusum atque exces-sum Scriptura & Ecclesia teste improbamus, quo tamen abundant & circumfluunt Pontificij. Qui autem Christianos plane vetuit ὑ[?]λοφεγνεῖν[?], nónne etiam in his externis & aduenti-tiis rebus præcipere τὸ [?]πανυ-[?] νοφεγνεῖν[?] putan-dus est?
units.tr: 24. Art. 30. we do not count this almsgiving with the others. The whole of this reply is utterly opposed to Chrysostom, so that I do not know what could have come into his mind when he cited Chrysostom. Chrysostom himself will therefore answer this whole solution, while we keep silent; these are his words in homily 84 on John, as Francesco Aretino translated them: "So that you may understand that Christ has no care for this. For he says: 'You saw me hungry, and you gave me food to eat; thirsty, and you gave me drink; naked, and you clothed me'; but not 'dead, and you buried me.'" I do not say this to abolish burial for God's sake, far from it, but to abolish luxury and superfluous ambition. "But," you say, "affection and grief and pity for the dead urge this." It is not pity but vainglory. For if you wish to have pity on the dead, I will show you another way of adorning the funeral, and I will teach you to adorn the dead with garments that will rise together with him and make him conspicuous. These garments are not eaten by moths, nor consumed by time, nor snatched away by thieves. What are these? Almsgiving is the garment that will rise again; almsgiving is like a seal placed with him. In these garments will shine those who then hear, "You saw me hungry, and you gave me food to eat." These make people illustrious, these conspicuous, these secure; for present things are nothing but food for moths and worms." Still I do not forbid burial; but let moderation be kept, so that the body is covered, and not committed naked to the earth. "For if the living are commanded to have nothing beyond a garment, much more the dead. And so on." Surely in these words the good Chrysostom judges the expense of funerals very differently from the lawgivers of the Papists. The objection, then, is true, commending slender expense and forbidding excess; and the disputant artfully passes over this, although it is very common in the Papal Church. What follows all concerns the same matter. We praise the proper use; we condemn the abuse and excess, with Scripture and the Church as witnesses, yet the Papists abound and overflow in it. But he who forbade Christians to lament at all [ὀλοφύρεσθαι], must we not think that he also prescribes, even in these external and adventitious matters, not to lament excessively [τὸ πάνυ ὀλοφύρεσθαι]?
